An investment in future updates. Civilization games start out with base mechanics and a small number of Civs over time increasing in content and mechanic fixes. You buy now, you are investing in a later game.
The biggest changes in six are international politics. The developer has changed the AI Civ behavior to like and dislike certain actions and states other Civs will be in. This is how their dispositions are determined. Harold Hardrada of the Danes will like any Civ with a navy comparably large to his, but he will dislike any Civ with a navy much smaller than his. The result is to encourage the AI to specifically declare war on Civs unable to protect their coastal cities from raiding. Ghandi will prefer Civs who don't declare wars with warmonger penalties. King Frederick of Germany will declare war on Civs protecting city states he wants to conquer.
Another change is a random second trait every Civ leader will get. These will encourage things like having a large army and disliking those with small ones, supporting Civs who protect city states, exploring early and disliking Civs rivaling exploration. These add more randomness to the game.
City states in the game are far more fair than in five. Where before any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ could flip a coin and either lose a spy or totally flip a city state to his side, now city state relations are determined by long term relationships between them and other Civs. Constantly sending envoys to your closest neighboring city state should ensure their loyalty, though later on you may need to step up the envoys as they start comming faster and another Civ might focus it to take the city away from your influence.
Finally, no more UN as it was implemented in five. No more bribing the most city states to ram through what you want as inviolable international law masqueraded as the will of the people of the world. No more banned resources nor trading partners. No more of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, easily exploited, game destroying mechanic. If they reimplement it in a later update I will change this review to unrecommended.
So far there are two major flaws I have found in this game. The first is the research pacing. I play this game at its most drawn out speed. Everything is slowed down significantly to increase the number of turns in a playthrough. So far, every playthrough I've started has ended up with either I or another Civ in the industrial era before 1000 AD. This is extremely disheartening and ruins the experience for me. I've since made the effort to clear more techs before advancing eras, but there is always another CIv (usually unmet) who reaches industrial before 1000 AD. The timing on tech research needs to be increased significantly. As you get more science and culture a turn, the research snowballs into a faster and faster pace. The opposite should be true. A game advertised as a mini Earth role play experience should not be this fast paced. I doubt the developers wanted research to go this quickly and probably did not consider how fast research can be made when things are going well. I might start looking for a mod to increase research time, but this should be fixed by the devs.
The second problem was created when the developers fixed a previous problem. The earlier issue was when another Civ would invite you to declare a joint war on another Civ, the warmonger penalty would still apply and the other Civ would condemn you as one. It's already iffy that most Civs dislike warmongers (considering human history), but it's made worse when they hypocriticaly and unfairly condemn you as one. The developers "kind of" fixed this by removing the penalty entirely for joint wars. This started its own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is this. I have two city states under my influence, Ghandi and Frederick are my neighbors and want those cities. They declare joint war on me immediatley after my declaration of friendship with Ghandi timed out and needed to be redeclared. I fight them and first push Ghandi to a peace agreement. Ghandi thinks the terms were fair and immediately returns to praising my peacefulness! ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t! I start pushing Frederick and in the war I take his city neighboring me. This makes me a warmonger! I got out of the mess though, but there is still room for much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with joint wars. Ghandi's AI is set to never declare an unjustified war. The joint war work around means any Civ, even friendly and peaceful Civs, can declare war on you at any time.
My positive review is hopeful that these two major problems are fixed in later updates. This does not mean they will ever fix them though. The choice whether to invest or not is up to you.

I started this game expecting to play it intermittently, slowly playing through the story, I finished it in a week, playing whenever I had spare time.
Pros
-------
Cons
-------
Other thoughts
-------
A few things to know, at the end of the game you are given the ability to start over from any chapter of the game, I beat the game without thinking of backups and I had a moment of panic later when I realized that I may have to replay large portions of the game that I'd just done to test out other endings.
If you have human emotions, this game will make you cry, perhaps even weep. It reduced me to a sobbing mess, to the point where I could barely open my eyes to watch the crying bit. You'll have to make some emotionally devastating decisions that may make you pensive and sad for three days to a week after playing through them. It's worth it, if you've read any sad books before, or watched any sad movies you'll know that weeping at a sad thing is one of the most oddly cathartic things in the world.
Buy this game, even if you don't like story games, even if you don't like games, buy this game. It's an amazing experience that's well worth the $20 and the ~16 hours. It has incredible replay value and incredible value as a story. Wait for it to be on sale if you have to, just find a way to buy this game.
Overall verdict
-------
If I could pay to give this game more than a thumbs up I would, it's incredible. I wish I'd bought it sooner, it's easily one of my favourite games ever and has a story that drew me in more than almost any other story I've experienced. Despite its bugs (bad/buggy facerigging, occasional crashes, some basic graphical glitches) and the ending (some people absolutely hated the endings, I personally found them good.) it's an amazing game.

The Walking Dead: Season Two is an amazing sequel to The Walking Dead (Season One). In this sequel, you star as Clementine as she treks through a new setting with unfamiliar faces. Unfortunately it's nowhere near as good as the first in story. For me anyways, there were way too many instances of "why did she do that?" from the dialogue or actions. It also feels significantly shorter due to a lack of direction. The first game, if I remember correctly, chose a clear long-term goal within the first three episodes; this is different. Season Two is more dynamic and more of a "we have no plans, so make everything up as we go" type of deal. Don't let this fool you though, as it is the choices you make that define the game.
Season One is a must play for this season to make an impact on your emotions because a lot of what you learned and what you experienced makes a difference. There's a minor connection to the 400 Days DLC as well but that is not required.
Overall this is fun. It's compelling to know that every decision makes a change in the future. Lastly, I will say that Episode Five is a conclusion that ends not just Season Two, but Season One and Two.
Also, it would have been nice they had some sort of more keyboard support rather than just use it for movement and quick time events (ex. using the WASD keys to choose answers).
Obligatory score: 8/10

I've been addicted to the Civilization franchise since the first game, but this game very much feels like a backward step since IV and V. The graphics are colourful, and certain new features such as coastal terrains and active progression are great. However, the AI is dreadful, the overall balancing for each difficulty level is botched - AI forward settle within only one or two tiles because of the new soft-border set up, barbarians are rampant and progress through technology faster than actual civilizations, and resources clearly spawn to encourage expansion. There is no benefit of buildng tall as in Civ V, which was a welcome change, and there is no downside to warmongering if all of the AI hate you anyway. Even on low difficulties, there is no time to breathe and enjoy building because diplomacy is broken.
Lastly, I sure that this will change with time - but the current leader roster is devoid of diversity, and the inclusion of countries like Australia and Poland (despite fan popularity) really is a joke when there isn't yet a single South American, South East Asian or Polynesian civilization included so far. European and colonial civilizations also have a massive bias against the rest of the world. Allowing both leaders of Greece to play in a single game feels like a cost-saving excuse to not provide more content, even if you take into account the historic city states.
I'm addicted to the franchise, and hope that further expansions fix issues here. However, I'll only be playing for novelty. I'll be going back to Civ V for my actual Civ fix.

This game is a brilliant reimagining of the series. It retains much of what is loved, but removed some of the oddities of previous entries. It's a little bit more streamlined than Civ V, but still complex. It requires patience and it can be brutally difficult even at the easiest setting, but even a defeat can feel like a victory because you are always learning.
The only gameplay element that bothers me is that the other civilzation leaders are often ♥♥♥♥♥y and petty, but that's not entirely unrealistic. The problem is that the reactions sometimes do not make sense. It does make the game obnoxious at times. Why does the queen of Greece care if I am at war or not?
Also, the game is dragged down by its bugs. It crashes almost every time I play it, usually via some sort of DirectX error. None of my other games crash, so I can only assume it is a problem with just this title. I realize this is a big, complicated game, but I do hope the bugs are ironed out, because a game this great deserves better quality control.

♦ Add variable power levels to barbarians in the setup options, not linked to experience level player selects. I'd play with barbarians enabled if they were super-weak against units (die in 1 hit, 2 hits vs scout) and do only limited damage against military units, but are great territory raiders (maybe destroy 2 tiles per move) as examples of a barbarian settings to fiddle with.
♦ Add a simple function on screen click in order to quickly get rid of foreign civs full screen messages/trades to a player betwixt rounds (only ESC is insufficient).
♦ Declutter message icons, currently the list becomes so long that a player can get clicking to quickly and miss an important one, categorizing in a list might help.
Result: Been playing Civ 5 instead of 6, but as DLCs are added for Civ 6 I will be buying them.  Love the long-game concept of this franchise (especially domination mode) and will continue to support them.  As DLCs are released I'll re-evaluate rating always hoping to make the move from Civ 5 to 6 full-time.

This is actually a pretty fun game. Not quite as polished as a Blizzard title, but few things are. It takes a while to unlock competitive mode as you need to level up each Champion individually, and you also rank with each Champion individually.
The account progression is kind of weird, as I have more gold than I know what to do with even after unlocking all of the Champions. They've reduced the number of talent cards to a small pool, which is good for balance and digestibility, but it makes it pretty trivial to unlock all of the cards you want as well. You can use gold on some simple cosmetics but many of them are ridiculously low-effort recolors of a single element on the hero, such as a bracelet or the color of their eyes. Most of the cosmetics worth getting are only obtainable by purchasing exclusive themed chests. I'm fine with that, as of course they need to make money, but it would be nice if my gold felt like it had some more worth.
The gameplay is solid and the Champions each feel unique and for the most part are fun to play. Lethality is pretty high with the exception of powerful shields on the tank classes. Shields can be easily countered however by earning in-game currency and purchasing single match upgrades which let you shred through them like paper. If you do take that upgrade however, then you can't get the other weapon upgrade which counters healing, or the one that improves your reload speed, etc. So there is some definite decision making to be made from match to match based on how each team drafts their lineup.
Overall the games biggest complaint I have with the game right now is simply the low population on the NA servers. It takes me on average about 10 minutes to find a competitive match (~3-5 for casual), and even then the teams don't always feel like they are the most balanced. You can't really fault the game for that though, and it seems like the population may be rising slowly over time, which is of course a very good sign for the game's future.
I definitely recommend giving the game a try if competitive shooters are up your alley. It is free after all, so you don't have much to lose.

The game is good, let's just start with that. Most of the characters are visually pleasing, though a couple I take slight exception to.
The controls are far easier to learn that SMITE's and the tutorial was a great way to ease a player into playing Paladins. Most of the characters I feel were made so that anyone could learn to use them and have the chance to succeed. I haven't played three or four of the "Champions" available just yet.
The abilities of the Champions sometimes don't seem to make a difference. Particularly the ultimates. The Ultimates don't feel as complete as they could be, Skye's Ultimate could have a slow mechanic applied to its blast radius. Evie's could stand to do a bit more damage, but considering that is slows as well as cripples it's pretty strong anyway, not to mention that it moves. Honestly, take your pick, any of the ultimates would be more useful if it was stronger/lasts longer/heals more or does this as well as that. They aren't gamechangers like I want them to be. Maybe we'll see a card class for the ultimate in the future, who knows?
My major beef with the game, isn't with its characters or its mechanics, no. It's with its players. When I'm playing a competitive game, even casual mode, I WANT TO BLOODY WIN. And when some of the players pick anything other than a tank, they seem to forget that if the objective isn't held or pushed along, the team loses the round. And I get it, the other classes are FAR squishier than the tanks which is kinda the point, but if they would just pile on the objective and hold it until the tank respawns...
TL;DR The game is great, abilities leave little to be desired, some characters easier to grasp than others. FInding players that are teamplayers is difficult.

I really enjoyed the first season of this game, but season 2 so far has been a major disappointment.  It's essentially a dialog simulator interspersed with some quicktime events and a rare non-challenging puzzle or two.
The dialog options don't really seem to make much difference other than so-and-so "remembering" something, which so far appears to have little impact on anything.  As far as the story, it sometimes builds up to something that could play out some tension, or perhaps build some interest, but typically it seems the issue is immediately disposed of somehow, and you're right on to being dragged along with the game.  After this happens a few times, any kind of interest in the game just evaporates, and you're pretty much just following along.
Of the 4-ish hours I've spent "playing" it so far, I'd say I could've walked away from the controller for about 3 of those, with the game happy to go on playing itself without me.  In all honesty, I've put the controller down several times while this game is going, only to grab it to hit one of the seemingly irrelevant dialog options, or frantically mash a button, followed by another random button (is this meant to be enjoyable) in order to move on to the next overly long dialog section.
As far as the characters in the game, they're mostly not given much depth, and seem to disappear before they risk developing some.
I've enjoyed the first season, and I do intend to see where this one goes, but I won't be rushing to pick up the presumably inevitable third season.
Edit - Having finished the season now, I can say for sure that everything I wrote above remains true.
By the end, I've played very little of this game in reality.  It seems like TellTale are moving on from adventure games into mildly interactive fiction.  There's no puzzle solving in this game really; in the rare adventure game style moments, everything you need to do is set out right in front of you.
If you pretend that this isn't supposed to be a game and some sort of movie or animated comic, the game fails as well.  I really didn't engage with any of the characters, there was no feeling of attachment with any of them (perhaps bar one.)
I get that some of you guys love this series or love The Walking Dead as a property which is why I'm getting negged on this review, but this game is really weak.  Season Two is just a massive letdown from Season One.

only friends will read this who are stalkerish enough to check. But for all of you; including them, this game i'm sure you've heard is great with emotional feels. It's true, and I see myself in almost every single way, as the character Chloe Price and no other. Which is """strange""" because it's not the character you play as. You can't pin-point or predict what's going to happen, you really can't. And I would go back and do it all over again. You've seen many reviews before mine, but if you've had some hardships of your own, you may  very well resonate with the games message. My favourite message, although the game makes it very clear it's a fictional story, and to not perceive things this way before you actually play the game. I have 763 hours in Civ V, and I tried so many times to like Civ VI but I honestly cannot. It is intrinsically broken beyond repair.
1. Diplomacy is broken - the warmongering penalty system means that you have to accept being bullied around like crazy and if you defend yourself you basically have to go it without any diplomacy towards anyone
2. The district system hasn't been fully thought through - it limits your optionality and forces you to have many cities from early on to have variety
3. It is prohibitive to invest in early wonders as there is no compensation when you are beaten, which fundamentally means that if you try and fail you might as well start a new game
Unfortunately Civ VI is broken beyond repair. When Civ VII comes out, which I'll make sure to read the reviews before I consider buying, it should attempt to be a progression from Civ V instead.

As of 3/10/2017 I've still been playing Civ 6. I think it's predecessor, Civilizations V, Is the best in the series. Civilizations VI tries to bare the torch of Civ V, but lacks the certain holding technique. What I mean by this is Civ 6 lacks personality and tries to change the series. I love certain aspects of this game and I hate some aswell. Civilizations VI feels like a game YOU want to love but you can't. Think of Dark Souls 2, fans of the series thought it was the weakest link in the series. I'm not saying Civ 6 is weak but it doesn't hold up with fans very well. I started to play civ around civ iv and loved it ever since. My friend got me into the civ games and I can say im fairly decent at the game.
- The Basics -
Civilizations 6 is a solid strategy game, it introduces new aspects such as a new political system(which im fond of) and fixing and refining most of the games bugs and quirks.
- The Good -
I love Civ VI's attention to detail, on how your city actually fits and stonehenge isn't in the water or inside of a mountain. Buildings fit! I love the district type of buildings, Its fun to see your districts producing troops and science, it gives your city personality. I also love the music and multiplayer.
- The Bad -
I'm very mixed with Civ 6, I hate how workers are now, I dont like the instant build system and only having 3+ uses.
I dislike the UI, it feels to sluggish and too off-putting, but this is my opinion, Aswell as the AI. Civ VI has some of the most stupid AI, Kongo is way to overpowered, everyone dislikes you for doing one thing, and finally it has no personality.
- Summary -
My overall feel of Civ VI is mixed, as I stated, it tries to bring fans back but also changes it for them, maybe it could be good for change who knows? But as it is right now its a solid strategy game for new players. Another thing is give it time, The Australia update was very good and if they add more *less bland* civ's then maybe this game will be on everyones radar, This game need to bloom.
TL;DR
Civ VI Is a solid strategy game but steers fans away but also brings new comers to the series. The game needs more time to blossom and AI needs a rework.

I didn't pick up The Walking Dead Season 1 until after the The Walking Dead Season 2 was released. I bought both games based on how much I enjoyed the first episode of Season 1, which is to say 'a lot'. What I loved about the first game was the degree to which it made me feel things I wouldn't expect from an ordinary piece of fiction. Season 1 tells a thoroughly compelling story through an engaging set of strong character arcs that become riddled with intrigue based on the player's choices. These choices are never obvious, nor are they the sort of simple binary moral choices so often found in games. Split second decisions change the game dramatically either way the player chooses. On top of that, the game made me feel a strong sense of nurturing for Clementine, over and above my own character's well-being, which elevated the stakes massively for me. Every choice I made was based on what would be best for her. Overall, I enjoyed the first game immensely, despite feeling like the sort of control I had over my character's relationships with others in earlier chapters was diluted in later chapters. As a work of dramatic fiction it is innovative, thrilling and highly enjoyable. So naturally I expected a lot from Season 2, which may be why I find certain aspects of it so vexing. I want to be clear that I don't hate the game (despite all the problems I had with it, I'd still recommend it) but certain things about it really frustrate me. Some of these frustrations stem from problems I had with the first game, which became amplified by their repetition in the second.
My first annoyance is minor, but it has far-reaching implications. Season 1 allows you the option to turn off notifications of important decisions, which in my opinion allows for a much more immersive experience. The notifications seem to be in place to give the sense that the player’s choices will have consequences, but ironically have the exact opposite effect, because the cast are killed off at such a rate in the first few episodes that renders forming alliances or friendships with other characters somewhat meaningless. At one point, early in the game, the player is notified that a character will remember something, despite never having another opportunity to interact with that character before he is killed. The obligatory notification really took me out of the story at this point.
This brings me to another thing that bothered me about Season two: the way it fumbled the early episodes by effectively recasting each one with a whole new set of characters. In the first game, relationships are everything – your decisions and treatment of others determine their role in the story. Your role as mediator is tested, characters live and die based on how good you are at gauging the right thing to say at a given moment. Season two sees Clementine’s group change so often in the early episodes that this aspect of Season 1’s gameplay is effectively dissolved for the first half of the game. The game redeems itself in the final episode fairly well by maintaining the cast toward the end and effectively divulging the narrative theme that to a certain extent explains the seemingly odd choice to kill off all of the earlier characters. In the end, the game teaches a harsh lesson about the price of duty and loyalty in survival situations. This was something I finally came to understand in the final episode, but in a game in which the most meaningful aspect of player interaction is the formation of interpersonal relationships with the other characters, it seems like a very strange choice. I hate to say it, but it feels as though the scope of the game's story possibilities was intended to be much larger, with options to end up in multiple different groups dependent on the player's actions, but one can speculate that the developers must have realised how much development this actually entailed and backed off because of the cost involved.
The story aside, my biggest gripe with the game is the actual gameplay itself. While there are sections that are captivating (for instance, finding an escape route from a locked room and sneaking into a full house to steal from hostile adults) most of the gameplay is incredibly tedious. Adventure gameplay has one weapon in it’s arsenal when it comes to making a game challenging: choice. A player with three available actions that are potentially useful when combined, needs to be given the opportunity for varying degrees of success: one combination of actions fails, another succeeds but with a drawback and one gets it just right with no downside. This creates a sense of problem solving and challenge. Give players several different actions to perform, but make them solve the right sequence – challenge. Sadly, for the most part, the sections where you search for the right tool or action for a task are painfully linear, obvious and unchallenging and unfortunately, a lack of sufficient challenge is not the worst part of the gameplay.
A significant poblem with the first season of The Walking Dead was that there were more than a couple of sections where the player simply performed mundane button presses where the developers thought they needed to include some interactivity. Sadly this is an even bigger problem in Season Two, where pointless interactivity is even more pronounced by it's placement in one of the most tense moments in the story and in a section where nothing happens to advance the plot. An otherwise high-energy mid-game escape scene is significantly marred by a section where the player literally just holds forward to advance from one cutscene to another. A short while later, the player must perform a QTE to lift a big bottle of water. Succeeding the event does not pick up the bottle however, rather the bottle is then lifted by a companion. These decisions feel like they were shoe-horned in simply to remind the player that they are still playing a video game and feel at best pointless and at worst insulting.
All that being said, the story is still excellent, the characters (despite not being given the time to develop that they deserve) feel real, owing to the beautiful comic-style graphics and the superb voice acting. The sound design as a whole is good too and the selection of songs and music is often so perfect it gives the game an overwhelmingly cinematic feel. Tell Tale's Walking Dead is about complex storytelling and delivery of narrative through the consequences of the player's actions. In this it succeeds in leaps and bounds. However, developers need to take care that the core of what their game is delivering to players is not muddied by development costs or the gameplay itself.

I have been playing Civilization since it's existance. My favorite all time is probably Test of Time. I loved that you could go on to explore the Alien Planet after finishing the Space Race. With that being said.
Civ 6 brought about some pretty cool changes to it.
1) Districts. This is a fantastic addition to civilization because it allows, and in a way, forces you to specalize your cities. Alot of your district placements will depend on the land around you. Some cities are great for religion, others are great for production or science. No two are usually the same.
2) Goverment. Goverments now use a "card system" with each card giving you a specific benfit. Early game they play a big roll in helping you grow and manage your civilization. You can boost the production of different units in your cities, generate great person points, or increase envoy gain speed, and much more. As the game progress though, you will find yourself switching these "cards" less and less as you establish a goverment to your liking.
3) AI Personalities. The problem with some of the past civilization games is that you did not know why a civ acted the way they did to you. Some civs got mad and declared war or another civ suddnely loved you and made peace with you. Civ 6 does a great job of giving the player more information on how specific civilizations react to things. When you meet a civilization in Civ 6 imediaetly open up the diplomacy screen for that civ and take a look at their Agendas. This gives you a good indication on what they like and dislike. Decide who you want to be friends with, then work towards fulfilling the Agenda. (Some prefer things such as strong miilitary, high culture/religion/science, ignoring/working with city states.)
4) City State changes. The City States have been changed to give you bigger rewards for investing in them. Each one gives you a specific benefit depending on their type, and the amount of envoys you place in them. Another benefit to them is you are able to higher their armies by spending gold. (Which you come by easily in most cases).
Cons:
1) Warmonger Penalties are too high. I do like the warmonger penalties as in real life if one country started invading and attacking other countries, it would anger others and drive them into action. With that being said, I think the penalty tends to be way to high, as civilizations tend to denounce you for a good 80% of the game just for taking one city (even if you were not the one to declare the war) I believe they need to balance this by either lowering the penalties recieved, or by decaying it at a faster rate.
2) AI Smarts. The AI don't tend to be very smart even on higher difficulties after you have come to understand tricks of the game. I think in all of my games I have ever played, I have ran into maybe one time when I actually lost a city. They usually attack one unit at a time and then declare peace after a few turns. I do recommend The Walking Dead, but caveat emptor:  In my opinion, this is not a game.
What it is:
Compelling story and great voice-acting in what I would akin to a "Choose Your Own Adventure" animated movie.  I really liked the visual quality, sound effects, music of the 'game' as well.
What it is not:
It's not as interactive as one would expect (unless you played the first season).  It has it's own pace, which you don't have much influence on either.  It has dialog (and some action) choices that have some degree of consequence to the immediate future of the gameplay, but in the end it generally leads to the same place.  It is very linear, but TWD2 is engaging enough to mitigate the typical aggrivation with games that are too linear.
Summary:
Like most reviewers, I recommend TWD2.  Just know going in what it is, and is not.  My only complaint is the darn  credits.  I'm sure the team deserves cudos for such quality work, but they run for several minutes at the end of each 'Episode' and I couldn't figure out how to bounce out of them.  After four episodes of that plus the inline credits at the beginning of each episode, I couldn't help but feel like they were just bragging.  They certainly do deserve credit for an enjoyable, unique experience though <hats off>.

The gameplay is more refined in Season 2, focusing on the game's strengths while reducing the classic point and click sections, which often broke the flow in Season 1, to a very healthy minimum. It is indeed a stellar interactive experience from beginning to end.

That said, despite its flaws, it still has some of the best storytelling in any modern game and should be considered a classic of the genre much like season 1.

As a thirtysomething male first I was a bit sceptical how the teenage girlie girl stuff would fit my taste, but the promise of a well designed decision/action/reaction mechanism begged for a try, and I'm glad I did give it one, and my worries above proved to be absolutley wrong. This is one of the most memorable games I've ever played, although some might not even consider it as a game, more like an interactive movie (a drama, a thriller, a crime movie, a mistery movie) or visual novel, and the episodic release supports this point of view. It's important to emphasize, that it's not meant to be a science fiction, as the time manipulation would seeminlgy suggest, as the reasons behind this power are unknown and not important, we just go on with it. In the end Life is Strange is still an adventure game with classic and innovative elements mixed.
The game consists of a set of intertwined layers. The primary layer is all about making decisions, that's pretty much the core of the concept and works great. Just like in real life, there are no black or white decisions, most of them are somewhere in between, and what seems to be a logical or rational choice at a time, might prove to be problematic from another point of view later. Consequences can be immediate, rewind can help here exploring the other possibilities, but usually consequences appear later in the same episode or even in a later episode. A great example is the "RV on the beach" scene in Episode 4, where a literally wall sized flowchart would be required to visualize the complex network of different factors affecting our options. The final and ultimate decision however doesn't seem to be connected to the about 4 major and 10-12 minor decisions per episode, which would otherwise mean a large number of variations and combinations in the story, we always have the same two options to choose from, no matter what we did from the very beginning of the game. That's not neccessarily an issue, but it might have been interesting to explore more and different options here as the climax of the story. The replay value this way is not defined by the conclusion of the game, but rather by the road the player gets there, as different choices mean additional scenes or certain scenes removed compared to other playthroughs.
Another layer is the athmosphere, where the visual and audio parts create persons and locations so full of life. The game itself utilizes the still awesome Unreal Engine 3 with handdrawn or handpainted loooking visuals, which is still realistic and unique. The way the developers play with light and shadow, warm and cold colors always supports that is currently happening on the screen or the main characters actual state of mind. The voice actors do breathe life with quite entertaining slang and celver wordplay into their characters, which have a precisely developed backstory and connections, and all of them walk or fight their way towards a massive character development. The original and licensed soundtrack of the indie rock genre, combined with the weakening warmth of the october sun create a really nostalgic athmosphere, which is obviously not a coincidence.
The game features a really rich subtextual content, which means a "hella" lot of references, smybols and easter eggs. Every episode title, name, item, poster, t-shirt, license plate, animal, literally everything means something that might not seem to be important or relevant first, but enlarges the big picture (and reveals the tremendous background research and popcultural influences the developers brought in). So do the additional sources of information, the diary, which Max keeps always up to date after something happens to her, the SMS exchanges on the phone, and the so called collectibles like optional photos, and people and locations of the journey.
Not many games dare to present social issues and deviancies of the modern day, this one does and wisely lets the player decide how to approach them: online and real life aggression and bullying, suicide, teenage pregnancy, drugs, post-war integration, homelessness, conflicts in blended family structures, euthanasia, suffering from bad judgement calls of the past are just a few to name. The value of mental and physical health, life, friends and beloved ones is up to the player to deal with responsibly. The game also features a female protagonist, however not under the "sex sells" flag, but rather because the kind of friendship and chemistry Max and Chloe share demands young women, so this is also absolutley functional, yet still not an issue for the mainly male player base to relate to the main characters, but surely opens towards the female audience.
Playing for the first time instinctly or for another time self-aware and somewhat manupulative, and the way you hesitate over certain seemingly low-weight decisions let you learn about even yourself a lot, meanwhile enjoying the story the game offers. Life is all about decisions, and you always do decide, even if not in a formal or conscious way, usually between bad and worse choices, and have to live on with the consequences whatever they might turn out. And if you opt to rewind time after reading this review, well, you've already read it, so nothing's changed. Yep.
Still one of the better games to sit back, relax and play along!

Honestly, I'm a bit of an Overwatch fanboy as I imagine a lot of us are on this reddit, but I just feel like Paladins is awful compared to OW. I really tried to give it an honest shot, but it just didn't do it for me at all. So just as a point of reference, I have about 100-150 hours playing OW probably, and about 5-10 playing Paladins, so my comparisons will be based on that.
Matches in Overwatch feel much more dynamic, even though the basic premise of each match is about the same.
In Paladins, I honestly felt like every game is basically this: a) zerg the control point, b) team fight/skirmish near control point, c) one side wipes on said control point, d) the winning team walks with the siege tank to the door, e) team tries to do a little damage to door, but falls back when enemy team arrives as it's not worth it to team fight near the enemy team spawn, f) heal/set-up at next control point g) rinse/repeat until the base falls down.
The card system is a let-down. I don't know the game well enough to know what cards are best for each hero. But even after just playing a little bit, you kind of feel nerfed if you don't randomly pull the cards you want.
The heroes in Paladins have lots of various movement abilities--some of these abilities are fun, but it leads to games that feel like extremely fast bunnies bounding around all over the place. The movement abilities in Overwatch feel a lot better and more..."grounded"...for lack of a better word.
Heroes felt very generic to me compared to OW. I didn't feel an affinity with any of them in my brief time, whereas in OW I would be excited to try a new character I hadn't played before. All the weapons in Paladins feel pretty much the same--this could be due to my relatively short time playing it, but meh, first impressions are important too. In OW, I really can't think of two heroes where even the act of shooting their primary feels the same as another hero. For instance, Tracer/Mcree/Soldier are all hit-scan, but the way each of them play feels really very different.
There are two maps (I think) in Paladins. I don't even know why they included two. They feel pretty much identical both in gameplay and style. Overwatch's maps are extremely unique in terms of style, and I'd argue in terms of gameplay as well.
All in all, I wasn't a fan of Paladins and I haven't had the urge to fire it up even once since the OW beta went down. I have really high hopes for it too. I'm a fan of Smite and Tribes, so I was pretty excited to see what Hi-Rez would bring, but so far, it hasn't been much.
In fairness though, I think Paladins is WAY earlier in development than OW, so time will tell.

Ill make this brief and helpful.  Compared to Civ 5, this is a mobile game.  It has smaller maps, less troops, less techs, less options.  The tech tree is linear and bound by what resources are near your starting point, but it always plays out the same way.  Splitting the tech tree into Purple and Blue paths does nothing but make each one more linear.
AI is just ridiculous.  They do not engage in anything after the Iron Age, and just stagnate.  Civs will STILL randomly declare war on you or hate you for no reason.  Diplomacy is completely monodimensional.  There is no negotiation or communication.  You can give them gold or not.
Other Civs are monomaniacal and will base their entire interaction with you on whether or not you do one certain thing or not do that thing.  If you have a big army,  one Civ (the same one every time) will like you and another will not.  It's always the same, it's always one dimensional, and after putting over 500 hours into Civ 5, it's nothing new.
The Fog of War and map are hard to discern.  The colors don't work.  The graphics are cartoony and silly, without adding anything to the game.  I can play it at 4k, which is nice, but still adds nothing.
In fact, Civ 6 is nothing new.  Every system here is just a watered down version of a previous Civ title.  The beginning of the game is so similar that you could easily forget which game you were playing, 5 or 6.  I can't even bring myself to start another game given how many times I've played Civ 5, which I loved, and Civ 4, which I really liked.  This whole endeavour reeks of money grubbing salesmanship.  They take a venerated title like Civ, cut the budget as low as possible, make screenshots look cool and make a big deal out of simple features, and rely on the brand's past to sell the initial copies of a broken, incomplete game.  After the initial influx of cash, the developers patch things that should have been done before release, and start the arduous process of squeezing out DLCs to further weaken your wallet, preying on your hope that the DLC will fix the game and make it what you know it should be.
In summation, all fluff no substance, yet.  DLCs seem to be pathetic.  Its not easy to make a game like this, I get it.  But with a name like Civilization and Sid Meyer, it has to be good.  This one is not.  Maybe subsequent DLCs and patches will liven it up a bit, but right now, stick with Civ 5.

This game is inferior to Civilization 5 in almost every respect, with the exception of a few new game mechanics.
The art style is terrible. Looks similar to a mobile game/children's game. They decided to go completely cartoony (Victoria from Civ 5 looks like a leader, Elizabeth in this looks like a poorly designed doll) which is, imo, a very strange design choice that really takes me out of the experience.
The AI is absolutely terrible as well. I won my first game (on Emperor difficulty) and had no issues throughout the whole match. Same with the second match. The AI was not great in Civ 5, but on higher difficulties they did at least build strong armies and kept them modernized, to an extent. All matches I;ve played of this resulted in knights and bowmen being used well into modern era (1900s +).
The new Civics tree is completely redundant (no difference from the Tech Tree) and seems broken, in terms of me completing it well before the end of the game and stuck just continunally researching the two last techs. The new government system allows for a dynamic enhancement system (each government type allows for limited "cards" to be used by researching specifics Civic technologies to provide bonuses to either your military, cities, diplomacy, etc.) and is an alright addition, but I do not find it any more interesting than the old Social Policies from Civ 5. Due to it being a carbon copy of the tech tree, it's fairly boring and is not interesting enough to warrant any praise.
The District system of specializing cities into different production paths (military, Wonders, Faith, etc.) is the best new addition. It makes the map feel more lively and adds more strategy by making cities not the only important target (pillaging was important in Civ 5, but burning down a Campus or theatre District is far more devastating). Combining similar units into Corps is also a good addition as it allows for less clutter on the map.
All-in-all, this game has potential. But the horrendous art design, unbalanced gameplay and brain-dead ai make this game rather unplayable, especially with Civ 5 and 4 having graphics and mechanics that match this dud. Please, save your money and do not buy this game.

Honestly, I'm a bit of an Overwatch fanboy as I imagine a lot of us are on this reddit, but I just feel like Paladins is awful compared to OW. I really tried to give it an honest shot, but it just didn't do it for me at all. So just as a point of reference, I have about 100-150 hours playing OW probably, and about 5-10 playing Paladins, so my comparisons will be based on that.
Matches in Overwatch feel much more dynamic, even though the basic premise of each match is about the same.
In Paladins, I honestly felt like every game is basically this: a) zerg the control point, b) team fight/skirmish near control point, c) one side wipes on said control point, d) the winning team walks with the siege tank to the door, e) team tries to do a little damage to door, but falls back when enemy team arrives as it's not worth it to team fight near the enemy team spawn, f) heal/set-up at next control point g) rinse/repeat until the base falls down.
The card system is a let-down. I don't know the game well enough to know what cards are best for each hero. But even after just playing a little bit, you kind of feel nerfed if you don't randomly pull the cards you want.
The heroes in Paladins have lots of various movement abilities--some of these abilities are fun, but it leads to games that feel like extremely fast bunnies bounding around all over the place. The movement abilities in Overwatch feel a lot better and more..."grounded"...for lack of a better word.
Heroes felt very generic to me compared to OW. I didn't feel an affinity with any of them in my brief time, whereas in OW I would be excited to try a new character I hadn't played before. All the weapons in Paladins feel pretty much the same--this could be due to my relatively short time playing it, but meh, first impressions are important too. In OW, I really can't think of two heroes where even the act of shooting their primary feels the same as another hero. For instance, Tracer/Mcree/Soldier are all hit-scan, but the way each of them play feels really very different.
There are two maps (I think) in Paladins. I don't even know why they included two. They feel pretty much identical both in gameplay and style. Overwatch's maps are extremely unique in terms of style, and I'd argue in terms of gameplay as well.
All in all, I wasn't a fan of Paladins and I haven't had the urge to fire it up even once since the OW beta went down. I have really high hopes for it too. I'm a fan of Smite and Tribes, so I was pretty excited to see what Hi-Rez would bring, but so far, it hasn't been much.
In fairness though, I think Paladins is WAY earlier in development than OW, so time will tell.

The Walking Dead remains an example of fine storytelling. I had hopes that this breakout series from Telltale would iterate, evovle, and build upon the formula. I imagine a story that we could each steer to our slightly unique destination. And why wouldn't they have the funds to do this given the success the first season. But it has not come to pass.
The first season gave us a hard road with small detours that ultimately led to the same conclusion. It never lived up to the promise of 'Mass Effect with zombies', but it compensated with some intense situations and choices which mattered - at least in the short term, over an episode or three. Sure, if you tugged at the strings hard enough, the illusion came crashing down, but you had the feeling that an honest effort was made, one perhaps tempered by realistic budgets. By contrast, the path laid out by season two is largely a straight line, with "choices" often being resolved within the very same dialoge tree. Choosing the "Silence option" in conversation often results in the other character responding with a suitably vague response that would have adequately covered the other three conversational choices. The dramatic "end of episode" choice you make in episode 3 is revealed to have had almost no input into episode 4, being resolved in the first 30 seconds. And I have no reason to expect that the almost identical choice you make at the end of episode 4 will play out any differently. I am ameniable to granting the game a suspension of disbelief, but that doesn't mean you should take advantage of that. This violates the contract between player and game and you find yourself increasingly unwilling to give them the benefit of the doubt. You need to put forth a little more effort to make this more than a two hour cutscene. The end of episode "Important decisions" screens are telling - "Who did you sit with at dinner" is not an meaningful gameplay choice.
So I get what they're saying. There is no stable family group for Clementine. She is adrift in an unforgiving world, and making bonds with other characters is hardly worth the effort because everyone leaves in the end. And you fall into that rhythm along with her. It's easy to throw in the towel. "Jimbo will remember that" means little when he's out of the picture 20 minutes later. And when you have half an episode to make a connection to a character, there's no real sense of tragedy when they're gone. Contrast this to the first season when a beloved character was mauled or shot. Has the magic been dispelled, or have we just become numb to tragedy, or was it an intentional design? Being helpess to save anyone but yourself may be an important lesson, but it is an unsatisfying pill for a player to swallow when we are expected to play out that role in someone else's shoes. We don't have enough time in each episode to have this lesson be the bittersweet one they want us to see. It's presented too fast out of necessity, and becomes trivialized.
So if we can't explore deep relationships with other characters, that narrows the domain of notable choices down to ones related to our character's environmental situation. However Clementine is not old enough to make any fundamental decisions about her adventure. I agree with this. She shouldn't be making any of the major calls for the group. Clementine is a young girl, but as players we bring the benefit of wisdom to her choices. Thankfully the game doesn't force us to make silly childish decisions, but neither does making her a battle hardened survivor who abitrates all group decisions feel quite right. Not yet. But that leads us to the question. If the themes that are being explored do not particularly lend themselves to an interactive format, then is this the story that should have been told? We're stuck in limbo here, with no easy solution in sight.
What's more, fewer of the situations are as captivating. Think back on the first four episodes of season 2 and try to remember anything that really stood out. The dog. The, um. Christmas ornament.  Can you remember what happened in episode two? I think an ingredient is missing.
I think this form of storytelling has legs and Telltale is onto a fantastic idea with their recent games including Wolf among us. I enjoy the time I sit down with each episode. I'm being critical and a little hard on Season 2 because I see such a bright future here and I look forward to new installments of these series a great deal. They are fantastic games you can play alone, or play with a friend, or play separately and then talk about the next day. They are powerful stories and you are at the heart of them. Yet, a little reflection shows that we still have a long ways to go with this format, and I am already impatient waiting for progress. But if it isn't Telltale which brings us to that next plateau -- then who?

This game is awesome. After playing for over 100 hours, I feel I can write an informative review directed at newcomers to the series.
If this were the only Civilization game ever released, it would be a very solid game. It looks great, it's intuitive, and like every other Sid Meier game (except maybe Beyond Earth) it is an incredible time-suck. However, it suffers from one huge problem: When compared to its older brother, Civilization V, it seems to be lacking in a big way.
I have almost 400 hours played in Civilization V, and I can honestly say that I like it better than Civ VI. Not by much, but I do like Civ V better because it's about as close to perfect as a video game can get. Every expansion to Civ V added tons of new features and made the game better in every way possible. It has had years to perfect itself, and if I had to recommend one Civilization title to anyone new to the series, I would recommend Civ V.
Civ VI is still a great game. Like many reviews before mine, I just have to say it feels incomplete. I purchased the Digital Deluxe Edition thinking, "Firaxis will add at least three giant expansions in the coming months/years after release, just like they did with Civ V" but so far, I've only seen a handful of new Civilizations and some new scenarios. Personally, I can't stand stand the scenarios. Even in Civ V, I barely played them. So that's not really a draw for me. I essentially paid $20 for a few measly civilizations.
I don't know if that was Firaxis' plan all along (to just release a few civilizations and call it good) but they need to add some meat to Civ VI. I like the districts concept, I like having to work for amenities, I like the more aggressive barbarians and civilizations, I like the graphics improvements. I don't like having to click through two screens when talking to people, I don't like their passive-aggressive faces during every conversation we have, and if you thought Civ V was too cartoony, Civ VI will do nothing to change your mind.
One great expansion is all Firaxis needs to add at this point to change peoples' minds about Civ VI. It is a great game, and on its own it would definitely be worth the money. However, when you release a game as good as Civ V, people expect the next game to be even better, which this game is not. It's kind of like Neymar: He left Barcelona because he could not thrive playing in Messi and Suarez' shadows. In its current state, anyone who says Civ VI is better than Civ V is crazy, just as anyone who says Neymar is better than Messi is crazy. Yeah they're good, but they're not that good.
I really like Firaxis games, partilculary the Civilization and XCOM series, and I'm usually pretty impressed with the decisions they make as a company. There is time to save this game and change peoples' minds so they stop saying "Yeah it's good, but Civ V is better", but they need to release an awesome expansion soon. As it sits right now, I've reinstalled Civ V and uninstalled Civ VI. I'll check back in a few months to see if the game has improved.
Long story short: if you've never played a Civ title, buy the Civ V complete edition on sale for around 12 bucks. If you are a diehard Civ fan, you probably already own this game.

Pros:
- Half decent graphics.
This game includes good graphics but usually allocates a lot from your GPU.
- Addictive.
This game is hard to get bored of. This is because the combination of the graphics, gameplay and music creates an immersive atmosphere. As your civ develops, tactics become more complicated, but if your victory chances seem too decisive, it could lead to your game becoming boring.
Cons:
- Random disconnections at times of a large percentage of players.
This ruins the multiplayer game and usually causes everyone involved in the game to quit.
- Barbarians are unfair.
Barbarians add a more challenging game start if you encounter them. If you happen to spawn around them (e.g. when their camps surround your starting city), this can stop players from getting a fair and equal start. When this occurs in multiplayer games with highest difficulty for example, it can make the game completely unfair for one and ruin their tactics. This is because they usually will not stop spawning in and will require a lot of troops to remove them.
- Needs a better discount.
From what I have seen, this game has not had any good discounts. It's mostly been stuck at the same approximate value for a long time. It's not worth the full 60$+ in my opinion. I would personally value this game at around 40$.
- Diplomacy is broken.
Lots in this game is broken about diplomacy. For example, promises or discussions between mainly AI is mostly ignored. Also, the warmonger penatly is too harsh. This is because, if I decided to take some random city state for example, mid-way in the game where the penalty was high, you'd likely lose AI ally relations, friends and you could possibly provoke an AI into declaring a war against your civ. However, this issue mainly persists in single-player but can occur in multiplayer with AI civs.

One of the best, most thoughtful and thought provoking games I've played. There was some frustration in slow moments or wanting control before a cut-scene finished, but nothing that prevents a perfect rating. The graphics are nice, the background sounds and music are good, the voice acting is good, and the characters are interesting and fairly realistic. The issues tackled are ones real people face. Things real teens face in schools everywhere today. Frankly, even though this is a game, it could be one hell of a good teaching tool. No matter how you play it, like life, there is no such thing as perfection. I'm glad the developers went this route instead of allowing a perfect end to each and every situation. If you aren't needing constant action, enjoy a good story, and don't mind some emotional moments, then you will likely love this game. The game does carry warnings for people with siezure disorders and counseling information for people disturbed by the content. So, be forwarned. The game does deal with life and death, drugs, depression, suicide, school violence and other sensitive issues. Yet, it is a game to be cherished.

The game itself is great fun, and will keep you thinking about new missions to perform long after you've shut down the computer for the day.
What really makes it an incredible buy is the extremely prolific modding community! You can add anything from robotics, to cartography, to realistic cockpits, to blimps and life support. This gives the game unprecedented replayability.
Suggestion: maybe use CKAN to manage your mods, otherwise it will take a long time... We all started with "oh, I'll just add this little mod here" and wound up with 80.

Life is...
Every once in a great while a game comes out that captivates it's audience. Life Is Strange is an episodic decision based game which means it is broken up into distinct parts much like a TV show, and player choice plays a main role. It starts off slow and lighthearted, and as the storyline progresses quickly takes a turn down a dark path that grips the player.
The immersion only continues when the player makes decisions that alter events in the future, much like Heavy Rain did. These decisions are what keep us playing the game, and curious as to what will happen next. The story is well thought out in each of it's 5 distinct episodes, however the final episode left much to be desired.
Life Is Strange uses a unique artstyle which is hand drawn much unlike mosts games today. The artstyle helps capture the photographic nature of the game and really allows the characters to have unique styles.
The cast is very well voice acted, and is complimented by an amazing soundtrack that really matched the story.
Spoilers would absolutely ruin this game so avoid them at all costs until you have completed the game. Overall, Life Is Strange is a solid game that kept me thinking about it even when not playing, and is an impressive coming of age story that shouldn't be missed.

Roosevelt in a suit, in 4000 B.C. or Montezuma basking in the glow of a firepit in the modern age), the fact that unit stacking was no longer a reality also hurt the strategy aspect as it created a cumbersome and difficult logistics issue when moving units around, and those things carried over into Civilization VI.
However, in addition to issues with immersion in Civilization VI (such as brick and masonry buildings in cities in 200 A.D., Skyscrapers in 1360 A.D., and infantry in 1500 A.D.) The Artificial Intelligence of the other opponents is the beginning of a great idea that feels incomplete, rushed, and unpolished. Not to mention the acceleration of science in the game. I can't recommend this title, the immersion is gone and I feel Firaxis is starting to mimic Electronic Arts in that they only want the money.
Edit: In short, this isn't a labor of love.

Here are I my thoughts on on Civ 6: I've over 1000 hours on civ 5 (and probably 2000hrs combined on all previous civs) and approaching 100 on Civ 6 (I've never played Civ BE) and I think they missed the mark on this one  . Let me explain:
When I first played Civ 6, I didn't like the cartoonish art, was not a fan of the new builder mechanic and didn't like the monotonously colored map aka fog of war. I played several hours and then, to my delight, I started to understand the builder simplicity, appreciated the new art style. The new map style I still hated however. I finally started to get it.
But, after dozens of hours of play, I couldn't ignore the painfully broken AI with completely random wars, behaviors and the strangest “friend” requests. They'll ask you to be your friend and suddenly DOW your butt. There are so many weird issues that I simply can't list them all here but to name a few more: the AI rarely attacks you after a DOW, does not defend it's positions at all and sometimes will nag you every turn for things like alliances which just slows the game down. AI has always been the worst part of the Civ series but it seems to be at its worst in the newest Civ game. There are also some graphical bugs but the game is still fairly new so I can ignore these.
What really made me dislike Civ 6 however, was not particularly its flaws, but it was when I returned to Civ 5 and realized just how much of step back Civ 6 is. Everything from the map detail to color pallete (there seems to be a really nice contrast in Civ 5) to the game interface seemed “better”.
I can't recommend this latest Civ game at its current stage but I hope that future add ons for it will help it “evolve” such as G&K and BNW did for Civ 5. In the meantime, I do highly recommend that you pick up Civ 5 and see for yourself the points I have outlined above.

Civ 6's big problem is that the game is less than the sum of its parts. On paper, it has all kinds of cool mechanics. The religion system looks cool, the new individualized Great Person system looks cool, everywhere you look there are cool, inventive mechanics that seem like progressions of Civ 5. In addition, the game is probably more feature rich than any other civ game on release.
The problem is that the game doesn't implement these features in a polished or good way. For example: the AI, as of right now, cannot take a walled city. It's simply too stupid, too incompetent at using it's military. This is a KEY feature, the ability of the AI to make war is important, and the AI just can't do it.
Here's another example: the way the game is balanced, you produce way, way too much research and way too little production. It's very easy to be running around with modern technologies when the game's faux-date says you should be in the renaissance. The 'date' has always been a goofy, fun approximation mainly for flavor, but I can't remember seeing it fall apart like this in another civ game. To be clear, I'm not good at Civ 6. This was literally the 3rd or 4th game I played, playing very blind and just picking what looked good, it's just way too easy to surge through the tech tree at blinding speed.
The game just isn't tuned, it's like they picked placeholder values for all the numbers and didn't really change them.
The AI is really awful and fails at basic tasks. As mentioned before, it can't take walled cities and can't make war or use units well. But there are tons of small ways it fails too. The Diplomacy system is simply broken - it's hard to design a fun diplomacy system, but this isn't even about 'fun', the system feels like it wasn't tuned in a way that functions, the AI acts psychotic and completely unpredictable. It forgets to claim goodie huts right outside its borders. It gets confused and suicides it's non-combatant units. It's so bad.
I absolutely regret buying this for full price at release, and this is the only Civ game I can say that of. It's the least fun civ game I've played, a huge disappointment. The last game I played I just forced myself to finish, while just feeling really bored and frustrated, and decided I wasn't going to play this game until it gets a big update. Such a bummer.

"Even numbered Civs are the best." But that's not much of a review, so let me try again...
My guess is that these people are not professional programmers! It's possible to improve the AI by using techniques similar to chess programs. But for 8 civs, the game would have to simulate the equivalent of 28 chess programs simultanously, except that Civ is far more complex than chess. And with the new complexities of districts giving far more choices each turn, those simulations would take a very long time. Few Civ players would want to wait that long between turns. So, as with all incarnations of Civ, the AI is a compromise mostly based on heuristics. It'll take time to get it right.
Districts. This new mechanic gives a richness to the planning of every city. Great innovation.
City states: Simplified interaction means no more tedious influence tracking.
Cultural victory and tourism: Confusing? No. It's really enjoyable and great for learning every part of the game.
Look and feel: I thought I'd hate the graphics and the colors. I was wrong. It really works.
I don't really like the new movement calculations, but I can live with them.
Is Civ6 perfect? No. Is it better than Civ5 at the same point in its release cycle? Yes, and by a long way. Civ5 wasn't interesting or enjoyable until around 18 months after release. Civ6 is far more addictive straightaway.

Difficult to review this one.   As a long time fan of the series, and having sunk a frankly embarrassing amount of hours in to Civ 5 I am aware that some of my dislikes may just be a result of "change" and as such a bit unfair.  However I cannot escape the fact that I played this for a month or two after release, but then stopped.  And this perhaps speaks loudest about my feelings for this game.
Firstly the positives.  I enjoyed the graphics and music.  It felt smoother and quicker than Civ 5.  In-game advice was good when getting used to the changes.  I liked the splitting of the typical Civ tech tree into science and culture, that can be researched simultaneously.  I was also impressed with the research / wonder quotations and video things.
I found the new movement mechanics extremely frustrating, and I can't help feeling it is a step backward from Civ 5.  Though I am very willing to admit this is due to being a change, rather than a negative point.  I guess only a newcomer to Civ could answer this.  There are perhaps too many barbarians to float through the early eras, but I actually kind of enjoyed this aspect and found the experience gain for units (and the need to build so many military units early on) satisfying.
The biggest negative for me is sadly something that is integral to the gameplay and that is the district system.  While the concept of districts is not necessarily a bad thing, and the added complication in city planning is actually welcome, I cannot get over the simple concept of buildings that would in real life be at the centre of any city, end up getting built many tiles away.  There is something so unrealistic about this and it bothers me more and more with each play through.  I would much rather have had an in-city micro-management system involving building location planning than this weird thing.  Though, this same system is effective with certain wonders.
Also, the AI seems to be extremely bad at conducting economic strategies, or warfare in general.  The UI is really clunky and things that should be on the same place, are split over several tabs of menus.  And without any mod support to fix this easily (I know, mods coming in the summer 2017 and there is a mod out there that fixes this, but its complicated to install now I am so used to Steam Mods).  I miss workers building roads, the new trade route system was so longwinded I ended up always playing the Civ with the free road bonus.   Also, dripfeeding civilizations to play with, and then charging for them is quite a bit insulting (Modders to the rescue in the summer again I suspect).
So overall, there are many fun things about this game.  But for me, unlike any previous Civ game, the negatives outweigh the positives.  I stopped playing before Christmas.  I also noticed that Youtubers who regularly do Civ videos also seem to have downgraded the game in their playlists.   Last week I uninstalled it from Steam.  Very sad to do so.  Will reinstall Civ 5 instead I think, as my gaming life is emptier without Civ in it.  But I hope that newcomers to Civ will have a better time of it.
I am going to recomend it (as I have to pick one to review).  But I am more recomending the Civ series rather than this game specifically.

This is my first game review so I hope this helps people. This has to be one of the best, if not the best games that I have ever played. I'm not a big gamer but I decided to pick this game up based on reviews and the price. I am extremely happy that I did. For me playing a game is about the experience. I'm not into much action games and storytelling is always, always important. Life Is Strange does not disappoint.
The game is filled with beautiful scenery and design just as you would expect from Square Enix. The story is very rich and although it has a "butterfly effect" plot that other games and movies have used Life Is Strange has it's own take on things and separates itself from the rest of those types of media. A lot of parts had me on edge and squirming in my seat while others gave me a relaxing eperience. The game always keeps you on your toes because you don't know what is next. You have the option to rewind time and the situation you are in so if a certain part of the "scene" doesn't work out you can easily go back and change how things go. This is fun to do because you get a chance to look back at different choices you will make and how they affect the characters and the game itself. Your morals and intelligence are equally tested and many parts of the game you have to pick between one of the two.
Please just buy this game. You won't be disappointed.

Hello reader, you are reading a review of a long-time Civ fan (I even played the 'Call to Power' version! Windows 95 anyone? I know, I know, not that old to have played Civ I, but still). So with that in mind, and all the nice previews and screenshots and videos, I decided to pre-order. Needless to say, I was massively disappointed.
TLDR: The game is not finished. I'd say about 65-70% state. If there was a demo, or you could play it at a friend - perfect. Get a hang of the new mechanics, get used to the new visual style. But it's a mistake to pay for the game now.
The bad:
Lacks polish in general. While the visuals are mentioned below as being one of the 'good' things about this one, there are still some small things like seeing half your city's name in the lower right corner when you open the build interface. Going on about the interface, there is no organized list of all your units whatsoever - the only way to do it now is to click a unit's name and then scroll through your entire roster - imagine that on a big map at the end of the game. No sorting, no anything, just look them up on the map. Oh, and if you miss-clicked and left a Catapult fortified somewhere in antiquity, there's no way of finding it unless you accidentally stumble upon it when plotting a course for your now regular Modern Armor. Also, the interface buttons (all of them) can be bigger, it's a pain to click them on a bigger screen, they're just tiny circles. I understand it may be for the purpose of playing with the map instead of the interface, but they took it too far. Also, the diplomacy interface is a mess. It's hot garbage, really. Diplomacy screen in Civ VI makes me wanna throw my mouse at the wall more than the non-existent AI issue.
The AI goes without saying. It's just there and it does nothing except declaring you a warmonger and swarming you with religion units. That's it. All it's able to do. It's been said about a thousand times up to this point in all the reviews, people cried for the AI to be at least semi-good before the release, they begged for it. Right now, the game is only playable if all the players are Human. City-states perennially remain in antiquity or progress really slowly. Diplomacy is non-existent: you are the devil and everyone hates you, might as well steamroll every game with your armies while the AI tries to convert all your cities to their religion. The AI also can't defend or attack at all. When you learn their pre-programmed action, you easily coax them into doing a stupid thing all the while doing what you need to do. For example, a coastal city will automatically attack a level-1 submarine if it's in range, disregarding all the fat level-4 tank armies and rocket artilleries that pose a much bigger threat obviously. This is just ridiculous. It's like a calculator app done in Visual Basic. And the airplanes...well i've seen them stationed, but not one ever left the field to bomb or assault me. This is just not done, AI in this game is like 25% ready. It can do all the basics, but it's like beating a dead rat with a hammer.
The good:
This version's new visual style is a clutter-fest at first, but it slowly grows on you, becoming more and more of a love-fest the more you play. Most of the stuff is well designed and positioned, aside from the few polishing touches that need to be done like the button size mentioned above. The interface really leaves you a lot of space to play with the map itself, and it's good, because critical information is there and it's very informative. The un-stacking of the cities and semi-stacking of the units is very visible and you can easily understand what's what with just one look at the map. It goes hand-in-hand with the mechanics part, which is also a very pleasant surprise. This is Civ Hex mechanics done completely right. Gone are the days when you are swarmed by stacks of 20 similar units, or conversely you can't fit your army around a city because it just has 3-5 free hexes around it. Unit-stacking and promotions are very intuitive and rewarding, I've never felt so much comfort operating an army in a Civ game before, this is a huge, remarkable success for the franchise. The districts system is also a big win. In general, you know consider each and every decision you take with your surrounding land VERY carefully, compared to previously just leaving it to automated workers. And making the workers un-automatable is a huge plus as well, even if it adds a big chunk of micro-management with it. In general, game mechanics are awesome. It makes sense to play the great artists in the theaters and buy Inquisitors for Faith points, it makes sense that great people do really different random things even within the same type. Wonders are good eye-candy too, this is well done.
To summarize, in my personal opinion, the game is plain unplayable circa March 2017. Much remains to be done by the developers and I really really hope that they fix this game because it has very good potential, the mechanics, the game design, the sensible visuals - it's all there! Too bad it's all ruined by the game being forced onto the market in a half-finished state. Make a rule for yourself: never pre-order a Civ game. I know I will make one for myself. I still recommend it out of pure potential and as fanboy, just find a way not to spend money on it yet.

Take Two is definitely doing some scummy stuff with GTA V and owners of KSP are now giving this game poor ratings in protest of Take Two- who is yet to harm KSP. Don't get me wrong, Take Two's C&D order was definitely scummy. However, claims that KSP is getting microtransactions or micro-DLC with outrageous prices is ridiculous. Just because Take Two has made questionable decisions with one game doesn't mean every single game/developer they own is equally scummy. For instance, when was the last time you saw Civ V or XCOM or Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion or any other game Take Two owns (outside of GTA V) flooded with poorly made DLC and microtransactions?
Don't damage the well-deserved prestige KSP has recieved just because their owner has made bad decisions on an entirely different game with a completely different dev team in a completely different market.
