Since Episode 1 is all that I have played so far (I own the whole game, but I haven't gotten to playing the rest yet), here is my review of Ep. 1 of Life is Strange.
The story, for what it has shown, is basically a play off of various other teen dramas many people are familiar with. Girl moves to a new high school for arts and photography, is nervous about fitting in and succeeding, etc. But wait! You suddenly get the power to rewind time and therefore have power to influence various events that both yourself and others deal with within this place, and with dreams of a monsterous storm ripping through your town and potentially ruining everything, you're left trying to figure out what to make of the whole thing while trying to go about your teenage college life.
Here are my impressions about it:
The writing sucks for the concepts its dealing with. I'm not talking about any specific characters here, or even relations between characters, I'm talking about how they write with the rewind ability or time manipulation playing into the story. Its not that good, and this episode alone shows it when its supposed to be the best foot forward especially since this episode costs nothing now. What do I mean? Well, the writing is inconsistent as to whether or not your time manipulation wants to behave consistently or not, regardless of the experiences you just used it previously. The second major "choice" of this episode showed this glaringly to me, because if your powers actually acted as we had previously been shown when we first used them, this second "choice" would not have been a choice, it would have been a puzzle with an optimal single result as a result of your ability to hold onto items you rewind with being unchanged as a result of physically holding onto said objects (as we had been previously shown to be possible, apparently the game's story chose to forget this was option in order to arbitrarily make a non-choice into a choice section).
Why am I so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it? Because this is episode 1 and that wasn't even that complicated of a situation to write the concept into, and they screwed it up! What the hell am I supposed to expect from later in the game, where I assume even more complicated situations show up when the writers have shown they will just completely forget what they wanted their powers to do at the drop of a hat for the sake of making some ludicrous choice that shouldn't be a choice with these powers! The "oh but the powers are completely random when they want to be and are beyond your understanding or wish" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to me, because the game spent so much effort at the beginning explaining exactly how they worked that it makes it very easy to notice when the game bends the rules for no other reason than the plot says so.
I'm also really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it because I heard from all kinds of people that this game had an AMAZING story, and then I find this crap in the first episode where its mediocre mistakes that feel like it was made by amateur writers playing with concepts they don't understand and cannot write consistently.
But what else besides the writing? Music is good for what it is, the graphics and art direction are nice, and the voice acting is pretty good (even though I find some the characters to be cringeworthy, I cannot really hold the fact that most of them are blatantly unabashed archetypes against them), and the rewind mechanic does lend itself to make you really think hard about decisions when its applied effectively.
I will say that one problem that contributes to you thinking hard is that you're not really given any clear character goal in this episode. Unlike similar games in this genre like Telltale Games The Wolf Among Us, The Walking Dead, and Tales From the Borderlands where you have a fairly well defined overall goal and purpose throughout the game (Enforcing the law/tracking down criminal cases, surviving and helping others survive a zombie apocalypse, or trying to screw over your enemies and stay alive while also getting rich quick in a brutal world), this one IMO lacks one. Are you supposed to be worried about averting your visions of a monster storm destroying everything? Succeeding in school? Making new friends? Mending fences with old friends? Looking for the missing girl who's picture is plastered over every wall in the school? Abide by your parents' wishes? All of these things? Call me uncultured, but only a couple of those sound even remotely interesting to me to play when I have almost no reason to care about the main character, her life, or her fictitious world that does its best to try to emulate real life while also taking great liberties to make it fantastically unrealistic at times. How can I make decisions for a character who is obviously not me since she is her own character, but doesn't even have any firm set of priorities to help guide my basis for decisions? I kept being taken out of character in this game when I should have been in-character when making decisions. I should feel individually like Max like I felt like Bigby Wolf or Lee Everret, Rhys or Fiona. But every time I begin to, I get drawn out.
The other problem being that, at least in this episode, most of the decisions don't seem to amount to much when you actually see some kind of pay off, even "major" ones appear to have reached a resolution without feeling like it changed much. So its not THAT good of an RPG so far in that sense. I really don't see 90% of the decisions made in this episode having ANY bearing for longer than 10 minutes within its own episode, and probably having hardly any effect on later episodes.
All in all, not a very good first impression IMO. By the end of the episode I was left thinking "Okay, so some interesting stuff may happen later, but do I really enjoy this enough to care to push through to it?" All in the knowledge that almost everything I've heard about the ending is that the ending sucks. IDK. Eventually I'll play the rest since I own them all, but ep. 1 didn't impress or hook me enough to immediately keep going. And I think its mostly because of the writing. It sucks compared to what I was led to believe.
But, its a free game for the first episode, so I recommend you at least try it based on that.
Personally, The Walking Dead Season 1, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands all have infinitely better first episodes.

Disclaimer: Since there is no "Maybe" option for "Do you recommend this game?" I am putting "Yes". I really mean, "Yes, for people who LOVE a challenge and who want to play the latest Civ game."
I've been playing Civ since number 2, which I spent an absurd amount of time playing during my formative years and I love this series to death, but I have no idea how I feel about this game. It feels like an abusive relationship that I can't escape because I just keep believing that the game will treat me right if I just do it better next time...and then it slaps me in the face again and tells me to shut my mouth.
I love some of the changes and additions they made to the game such as making you think about placement of cities, districts and improvements because it has a huge impact on your future, the change to governments and the civics tree, technology and civics boosts, and the improvement of trade routes and trading posts. I especially love the changes to city states and the awesome bonuses they give you for becoming suzerain/sovereign of them.
On the other hand, I don't understand how they think the AI is coded correctly in any way. They will declare war on you for no reason, constantly refuse requests for friendship even if they are "friendly" toward you; and once they are at war with you, they will barely assault a single city (usually just my capital so far). I've just sat there and picked off troops one by one with my city defenses as they just stand outside my city not attacking it. Meanwhile, the civs I'm not at war with denounce me because they think I'm a warmonger, when all I've done is DEFEND my cities and never once declared war on anyone!
It's nearly impossible to appease any of the other civs. First impressions of you? Negative; almost always. Have more positive numbers going for you than negative in the relationship window? They're still unfriendly toward you even though the math they show you on screen should put you at neutral or above. Pumping all of your resources into culture? Brasil, who likes civs with more science and culture than they have (and hates those with less), still won't like you because you're dumb and have less science than they do. After Montezuma finally grew tired enough of waging war on me and not winning (because he barely sent any troops and they just stood outside my gates), he offered me peace and a TON of his luxuries. Which would be great, except that his main personality trait is that he hates anyone who has more luxuries than him/luxuries he doesn't have yet. So...he made peace and completely set himself up to get mad at me again later.
Also, barbarians are insane. I spent ALL of my time until the medieval era trying to get rid of them and they still were everywhere; I could barely get anything built in my cities! Now if they spawn near horses, they have horsemen. And they have scouts that report back once they see your city and get the barbarians to come attack it. I only got to play long enough to get to the modern era after turning them off.
All of my above experience has been on the standard difficulty. Maybe I'll try one of the wimpy difficulties and see if I can just crush the civs that will become a pain before they grow powerful enough to matter.
Firaxis, PLEASE fix the AI in this game. I love this series and hate to see "features" that are just clearly bugs. I can't possibly fathom how you coded it so that the pacifistic defending civilization can be seen as a warmonger. If my feelings on the game change I will update my review, but for now my relationship with Civ VI remains...strained.

The Walking dead has been a great game from seaon 1 up until now. With finishing the game i loved how it just kept hitting hard as you play. In episode 1 losing Christa and then having to see what happened to the people that got her (or didnt it wasnt said what happened). then in episode 2 seeing kenny again. that was just an amazing moment. Well you get the point every episode hits hard in multiple ways.
Here im going to post my thoughts on each episode.
Episode 1 :  I felt that it was a great spin of things to play as clementine instead of lee. I think it may have been nice to see how clementine grew up so fast but in essence i loved this episode. from losing Omid to being alone was just heartbreaking. Meeting Luke seemed a little iffy at first but it seems that it was a goo thing after all.
Episode 2 :  In episode 2 i loved how the game really went through telling everyones story. It was fun getting to know everyones personal stories. from Sarah being sheltered and up to Rebeca not knowing whos baby it was. It was amazing. I felt they had a well balance of the personal stories and the groups overall story. meeting Carver for the first time was a wierd experience. I liked the way that you didnt know him but could still make an impression on if your with him or the group.
Episode 3 :  Episode 3 was like a roller coaster for me. I liked the insight on how the group used to live but at the same time i didnt really like the feeling of bing trapped. Although i have to give it to telltale it was fun being put back in my place as clementine. Another thing i didnt like was that the story seemed pretty liner in this episode. most choices led to the exact same outcome. Like i said though it had a great impact on the overall story and i loved that part of it.
Episode 4 :  When episode 4 came along i really like going back to the feeling of "whats gonna happen next?". It was cool seeing the group have its ups and downs. My favorite part of the episode and im sure it was alot of other peoples favorite as well, was Jane. I loved the bond that clementine and Jane had. hearing Janes story was very touching and i really felt bad for her. Another great part of the episode was the baby. Seeing the baby gave me hope that maybe the group could make it. of course it being the walking dead that thought was ripped away from me. The gun shots at the end made me wonder many things. It made we conemplate all week about what had happened. at first i thought that everyone would have died exept for clem and the baby. then I had this crazy idea that maybe just maybe they were shooting at the heard and not the group. It left me wondering and that makes for a good story.
Episode 5 :  Well what can i say. episode 5 was amazing. fist off having to choose between myself and a baby made me think...oh man this is gonna be rough. I had never liked Arvo and when he got Luke and Bonnie killed i wanted to see him and punch his head in as much as Kenny did. Seeing kenny break even worse was crazy. I knew kenny was insane ever since i saw him hiding his past from Serita, but its Kenny. I thought that no matter what i would never leave Kenny. and sure enough when i got the opertunity to kill him i took it. When it happened i burst into tears as i realized it was just me and Jane. but let me back up. When Arvo shot me i felt terrable i thought well its over. and then when i saw the dream with Lee i cryed the whole time. Im not usually the one that crys at a video game but damn that was a touching moment. Back to the present when i was with jane i felt ok. but what i didnt like is that i didnt have a choice were to go. I may have overall agreed with Jane but i still wanted to look for Wellington which the game gave me no chance to find. At the warehouse i felt this relief seeing Carver's dead body. It made me feel safe. When i saw the 3 coming up i thought well this could be a problem. and as soon as the guy got angry i knew it would be another Kenny. And that pushed me to send them away. Thes last episode gave some really tough choices and still didnt answer some questions. but i loved it anyways... thanks telltale

Since Episode 1 is all that I have played so far (I own the whole game, but I haven't gotten to playing the rest yet), here is my review of Ep. 1 of Life is Strange.
The story, for what it has shown, is basically a play off of various other teen dramas many people are familiar with. Girl moves to a new high school for arts and photography, is nervous about fitting in and succeeding, etc. But wait! You suddenly get the power to rewind time and therefore have power to influence various events that both yourself and others deal with within this place, and with dreams of a monsterous storm ripping through your town and potentially ruining everything, you're left trying to figure out what to make of the whole thing while trying to go about your teenage college life.
Here are my impressions about it:
The writing sucks for the concepts its dealing with. I'm not talking about any specific characters here, or even relations between characters, I'm talking about how they write with the rewind ability or time manipulation playing into the story. Its not that good, and this episode alone shows it when its supposed to be the best foot forward especially since this episode costs nothing now. What do I mean? Well, the writing is inconsistent as to whether or not your time manipulation wants to behave consistently or not, regardless of the experiences you just used it previously. The second major "choice" of this episode showed this glaringly to me, because if your powers actually acted as we had previously been shown when we first used them, this second "choice" would not have been a choice, it would have been a puzzle with an optimal single result as a result of your ability to hold onto items you rewind with being unchanged as a result of physically holding onto said objects (as we had been previously shown to be possible, apparently the game's story chose to forget this was option in order to arbitrarily make a non-choice into a choice section).
Why am I so♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it? Because this is episode 1 and that wasn't even that complicated of a situation to write the concept into, and they screwed it up! What the hell am I supposed to expect from later in the game, where I assume even more complicated situations show up when the writers have shown they will just completely forget what they wanted their powers to do at the drop of a hat for the sake of making some ludicrous choice that shouldn't be a choice with these powers! The "oh but the powers are completely random when they want to be and are beyond your understanding or wish" is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to me, because the game spent so much effort at the beginning explaining exactly how they worked that it makes it very easy to notice when the game bends the rules for no other reason than the plot says so.
I'm also really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥about it because I heard from all kinds of people that this game had an AMAZING story, and then I find this crap in the first episode where its mediocre mistakes that feel like it was made by amateur writers playing with concepts they don't understand and cannot write consistently.
But what else besides the writing? Music is good for what it is, the graphics and art direction are nice, and the voice acting is pretty good (even though I find some the characters to be cringeworthy, I cannot really hold the fact that most of them are blatantly unabashed archetypes against them), and the rewind mechanic does lend itself to make you really think hard about decisions when its applied effectively.
I will say that one problem that contributes to you thinking hard is that you're not really given any clear character goal in this episode. Unlike similar games in this genre like Telltale Games The Wolf Among Us, The Walking Dead, and Tales From the Borderlands where you have a fairly well defined overall goal and purpose throughout the game (Enforcing the law/tracking down criminal cases, surviving and helping others survive a zombie apocalypse, or trying to screw over your enemies and stay alive while also getting rich quick in a brutal world), this one IMO lacks one. Are you supposed to be worried about averting your visions of a monster storm destroying everything? Succeeding in school? Making new friends? Mending fences with old friends? Looking for the missing girl who's picture is plastered over every wall in the school? Abide by your parents' wishes? All of these things? Call me uncultured, but only a couple of those sound even remotely interesting to me to play when I have almost no reason to care about the main character, her life, or her fictitious world that does its best to try to emulate real life while also taking great liberties to make it fantastically unrealistic at times. How can I make decisions for a character who is obviously not me since she is her own character, but doesn't even have any firm set of priorities to help guide my basis for decisions? I kept being taken out of character in this game when I should have been in-character when making decisions. I should feel individually like Max like I felt like Bigby Wolf or Lee Everret, Rhys or Fiona. But every time I begin to, I get drawn out.
The other problem being that, at least in this episode, most of the decisions don't seem to amount to much when you actually see some kind of pay off, even "major" ones appear to have reached a resolution without feeling like it changed much. So its not THAT good of an RPG so far in that sense. I really don't see 90% of the decisions made in this episode having ANY bearing for longer than 10 minutes within its own episode, and probably having hardly any effect on later episodes.
All in all, not a very good first impression IMO. By the end of the episode I was left thinking "Okay, so some interesting stuff may happen later, but do I really enjoy this enough to care to push through to it?" All in the knowledge that almost everything I've heard about the ending is that the ending sucks. IDK. Eventually I'll play the rest since I own them all, but ep. 1 didn't impress or hook me enough to immediately keep going. And I think its mostly because of the writing. It sucks compared to what I was led to believe.
But, its a free game for the first episode, so I recommend you at least try it based on that.
Personally, The Walking Dead Season 1, The Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands all have infinitely better first episodes.

This is my first game review so I hope this helps people. This has to be one of the best, if not the best games that I have ever played. I'm not a big gamer but I decided to pick this game up based on reviews and the price. I am extremely happy that I did. For me playing a game is about the experience. A lot of parts had me on edge and squirming in my seat while others gave me a relaxing eperience. The game always keeps you on your toes because you don't know what is next. I'm writing this as a review for season 1 and 2. Yes, they're zombie games and those have been done to hell and back, but never one that has been done this well. These games manage to rip and tear at every conceivable emotion available to the player.
Much like many of Telltale's games these are separated into episodes and once you start an episode, it's hard to quit playing. These aren't your typical games however. They're more or less a choose your own adventure TV series. The game has a very simplistic UI and control scheme. Moving the mouse around will highlight areas of interest and you simply click once to interact with it. Action sequences are essentially quick time events and the only way to die is to fail these segments.
The beauty of the game is in the storytelling and how your decisions have an impact in later episodes. Many times throughout the series I found myself making some very heated decisions based on the feelings that the game evoked and I had to live with those choices. The game does a trememdous job of making you question if you made the right decision. I've actually lied awake at night on a couple occasions really regretting what I had done.
If you're not the type to care about storytelling, this isn't going to be the game for you. There's not enough substance in the core gameplay that would be appealing to someone that doesn't play games to follow a story. If that hasn't turned you away yet, the game does suffer some minor narrative issues. There are decisions you can make that really don't carry any weight, encountered more often in season 2, and ultimately the game moves along as scheduled.
TL;DR
If you enjoy good narrative based games, these would be hard games to pass up. The storytelling and your ability to react to the story are outstanding.

Turn-Based games are often difficult to get into due to the complexity of their mechanics: planning your moves ahead of your opponent, be it an AI or a human, forces you to think ahead much like chess would do.
Getting better at a turn-based game demands from the player the understanding of the metagame in place. This means knowing in advance from your previous knowledge of playing the game, what moves could yield in the desired effect.
A basic early game strategy for Civilization VI (one of many) would be to rush Astrology and a Holy Site if you encounter a Natural Wonder in the first turns, so you can get ahead in the religious path with an associated Great Prophet permitting you to create an early religion.
This is an example of a meta: you find a Natural Wonder in the early turns (a), you research Astrology (b), you build a Holy Site (c), you get your Great Prophet in time (d), you found your religion (e).
There are plenty of those and the secret is to know in advance which one you will use to get to your goals. It's the motto of Civ VI and Sean Bean tells it to you during the trailer when launching the game "you must adapt and press forward if you are to reach your journey's end".
Now here comes the problem: the AI will actively cockblock your strategy and ruin whatever meta you are trying to go for,

In other words the AI will constantly try to counter what you are doing in a way that is unproductive for itself and thus, will focus on destroying whatever sparks of creativity you are trying to put into the damn game.
In higher difficulties, this behaviour
. It simply gets percentage related boni on everything.
It has some good points despite the AI mess however, the art direction is good accross the board and many animations are top-notch despite having a mobile game feel going on (it's only a feel though).
Also, It is probably a nice experience when played in multiplayer, with an AI limited to controlling barbarians...
Avoid this at all costs if you plan on mostly playing the singleplayer. Go for the previous iteration (Civilization V) or Endless Legend.

Turn-Based games are often difficult to get into due to the complexity of their mechanics: planning your moves ahead of your opponent, be it an AI or a human, forces you to think ahead much like chess would do.
Getting better at a turn-based game demands from the player the understanding of the metagame in place. This means knowing in advance from your previous knowledge of playing the game, what moves could yield in the desired effect.
A basic early game strategy for Civilization VI (one of many) would be to rush Astrology and a Holy Site if you encounter a Natural Wonder in the first turns, so you can get ahead in the religious path with an associated Great Prophet permitting you to create an early religion.
This is an example of a meta: you find a Natural Wonder in the early turns (a), you research Astrology (b), you build a Holy Site (c), you get your Great Prophet in time (d), you found your religion (e).
There are plenty of those and the secret is to know in advance which one you will use to get to your goals. It's the motto of Civ VI and Sean Bean tells it to you during the trailer when launching the game "you must adapt and press forward if you are to reach your journey's end".
Now here comes the problem: the AI will actively cockblock your strategy and ruin whatever meta you are trying to go for,

In other words the AI will constantly try to counter what you are doing in a way that is unproductive for itself and thus, will focus on destroying whatever sparks of creativity you are trying to put into the damn game.
In higher difficulties, this behaviour
. It simply gets percentage related boni on everything.
It has some good points despite the AI mess however, the art direction is good accross the board and many animations are top-notch despite having a mobile game feel going on (it's only a feel though).
Also, It is probably a nice experience when played in multiplayer, with an AI limited to controlling barbarians...
Avoid this at all costs if you plan on mostly playing the singleplayer. Go for the previous iteration (Civilization V) or Endless Legend.

I'm going to have to say, "No" on this one. Here's why:
I didn't expect my choices to matter much. They didn't matter much in the first game. Even less so here, and that's fine.
Why I bought the game was for a quality story with well-written, fleshed out characters and an interesting plot. That's where the game falls short, for me.
Without divulging spoilers I'll simply point out a few things.
- The adults in this game are shallow, vapid and near-idiotic humans who seem unable to make even the most minor decision without consulting an 8 year old girl. That this was done as a means of getting you, the character, involved seems obvious.  But the writers forego any attempt at logic or reason in the method they chose to get you involved.  The group doesn't know whether to trust person X.  "Clem, what do you think?"  The group isn't sure where to go to avoid the next traumatic event or to deal with a current situation. "What should we do, Clem?"  In this sense the adults nearly all only exist as a means to an end, the end being making you feel as if the things you say and do matter.  They don't. Most people familiar with the first game know they don't matter. Keeping up the pretense at this point comes at the expense of actually having to make these characters think and act like... people.
- Likewise there's inconsistency in their behavior. For the most part you, Clem, will be the voice of reason, the arbiter of justice, the pacifier of aggression, etc.  Until the game feels it's time to remind you that you're just a little girl, again. At that point the rest of it goes out the window and the adults are suddenly knowledgeable and efficient and wise and you're just a wee little lass who's lost and alone and probably needs a hug, yeah?   Okay. Humans are inconsistent, self-contradictory, forgetful, all of those things. The trouble is the writers didn't bother to put any sort of justification in to explain this idea or expound on it, with one or two exceptions.  There are a couple of decent characters here whose inconsistency and reluctance to make hard decisions is directly tied to their past experience. The rest not so much, if at all.
- The dialogue choices I was given often left me wondering whether the people writing them in one scene were at all aware of the things written in other scenes.  You're presented with a choice at one point, say, and then later that situation is referenced, but you're given no option at all to remind anyone of the previous conversation or interaction or meeting or whatever it was.  It completely pulls you out of any immersion in the story, and leaves you feeling as if you could just as easly have clicked things at random as they popped up.  Again, this isn't about making a difference in the overall plot or the fate of any particular person. It's about consistency, and it misses the mark in a big way for me.
In short, at full price the game doesn't even stack up to the first Season, much less improve.  If you can get it on sale at half price... yeah, sure, as long as you don't expect too much from it in the way of a compelling cast of characters that you'll get invested in, or consistency in their behavior and atittudes.   Otherwise, save your money for something else.

The Walking Dead will try to sell you on the premise that you will influence the story and the world around you. You will not. Telltale Games claims that "As Clementine, you will be tested by situations and dilemmas that will test your morals and your instinct for survival. Your decisions and actions will change the story around you, in this sequel to 2012’s Game of the Year." In truth, players experience the illusion of choice. Without writing spoilers into the review, all I can say is that the choices players are faced with actually hold no real consequence. People will tell you "No but you effect the story in small ways, changing the dialogue and characters reacting to you." This does happen, but only in independant scenes, with no real long term relationships forming. If a character reacting negatively/positively to Clementine is written into the plot, it happens regardless of player input. If a characters life is at stake, you can bet that character isn't sticking around much longer than the current/next episode.
However, this isn't my only gripe with the game. Mechanically, it's shoddy at best; with action scenes playing out as boring quick time events, poor lip syncing and animations, flat bland textures, and no real challenge in the form of puzzles or brain teasers. As a story driven point and click adventure game, it's weak. As a "Make your own story" visual novel it's weak. On these merits I cannot recommend this game.

That bug is by far the biggest frustration with the game, but S2 is lacking in other ways.

Season 1 had a character (or two, depending on your tolerance for teenagers) so unlikable I imagine most players, like myself, wanted them dead. The writers exploited this, killing off some likable characters long before they finally offed the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This totally worked for me, maximizing the tension caused by the creep and creating a mood of the unfairness and futility of it all (without making the game feel unfair or futile).

That the writing and direction of S2 are lacking isn't surprisingly; the director and lead writer for S1 left Telltale to start their own company, leaving TTG to complete TWAU and S2 without them. With the majority of the game released I think I can make a review for the game. I’ll probably come back and edit this review once the last episode is released.
Season 2 is overall weaker than the first game in many ways. One big thing is that it falls hard into the pitfalls that the show and comic do, they just have characters just to kill them off to make everything seem grimdark instead of developing them as real characters. Season 1 didn’t do this and that's one of the reasons it’s such a fantastic game and why it’s better than everything else in the franchise. When characters died in Season 1 it was genuinely shocking and it helped that you got to know the characters beforehand. In Season 2 it just feels they need to fill a quota to kill characters off and leaves you feeling unattached and uncaring to what's going on. The severe railroading that Telltale's games have been doing post Wolf Among Us Episode 1 makes it worse because while you couldn't change the plot in Season 1 the game at least accommodated your choices so your relationship with the characters and overall mood and tone of the story could differ entirely from other people. Season 2 doesn't do this nearly as well and it feels like if you don't make the choice Telltale wants you to they pretty much strong-arm you into what they want, characters be damned. It just feels really lazy.
On the other hand, Clem is still a great character and really carries the game, it would be much weaker without her. She has some great lines and while the characters are weaker she can have some quality interactions with them. The quality of Season 1 seems to shine here and there throughout the game but with the departure of Sean Vanaman and Jake Rodkin, two of the major designers of Season 1, it really feels like the rest of the Telltale staff really can’t capture the same magic and instead just fumble around and fall into the clichés that ruin the rest of the franchise.
Despite the complaints it’s still a good game, but it’s a big disappointment compared to Season 1. Just temper your expectations accordingly and you'll have a good time. I definitely don't have as much faith in Telltale when I was coming off of the end of Season 1 so I don’t think I’ll be buying their games day one like I did with this and Wolf Among Us but I still feel that it was worth it unless the ending is utterly awful or something.
*Edit* Last episode came out. It had its fair share of super contrived conflict and the like but it actually has multiple endings and the one I got brings a really satisfying ending to Clem's story. It would be fair to argue that Season 2 wasn't overall good enough to earn such a quality ending, but I'm not really complaining. Overall Season 2 is a lot weaker but still a good game and worth playing.

In Kerbal Space Program (KSP for short) you can explore a fictional star system and its planets. You have total freedom of what you want to do, be it to build a giant rocket to haul a big fuel tank to orbit, or build a plane and explore Kerbin (your homeworld).
Pros:
*Very detailed physics with functioning aerodynamic drag.
*A LOT of replay-ability (there is a reason why most people in the review section have 200+ hours played).
*The freedom to build or do almost anything you want.
*A great tool for learning physics and orbital mechanics.
Con(s):
*Very steep learning curve. You'll be lucky if you manage to get to orbit on your first 15 hours, let alone land on Mun or Minmus (the two moons of Kerbin, your homeplanet)
*A lot of trial and error. (Which might be a good thing, depending on who you ask)

The time-travel mechanic is a delight, as it mirrors what I would tend to do in this kind of game if time travel weren't available -- go back to a previous save and see what would happen if I made the alternative choice. I have this game in 2 accounts because of buying physical and digital copy . I have over 160 hours in the game in total . I am playing this series since Civilization 3 back in 2001 . But while reviewing this game I WILL have to compare it with Civilization 5 and 4 .
Pros :-
1) Sid meier's civilization 6 is the most "feature complete" civilization game to ever launch .
:- International trade routes , religion system , finally a religious victory and tones of other stuffs . But World congress/ UN and AP is missing because according to the developers need more data on how players are playing this game to implement it and thanks beerus because of the AI (Coming back to AI later , in short it is HORRENDOUS )

2) District mechanics is awesome . And one of my favorite feature added in Civilization 6.
:-Because it gives us a lot of building strategy by adjacency bonus , deciding which tile to be used for improvement or wonder or district , it makes each city look distinct and beautiful . There are 13 district including city centre in total in this game .
3) Government / Policy :- Now the tech tree we know in previous Civilization titles is divided into technology and civics tree . Civics tree unlock policies , government types , 3 districts and buildings. This tree is culture focus tree. Now you can have government and this government system is a lot different than Civilization 4's government system and I like this one better because of the HUGE depth but I also miss having state religion in Civilization 6 .Now each
government type give some permanent bonus and a temporary bonus . Permanent bonus increase over the time as long as you have the perticular government and it get stack over permanent bonus of other government type . You can shift to the new Government type you unlock without any consequence but to get back to a Government type again you will face temperory anarchies . Each giverment type also has limited Civic slot for different type of policies . You can change polcies for free in the turn you unlock a new civics but other than that it will cost you gold .This system is very well thought out and works great and I freaking love it because of the different combinations and tactices . At first I was really suspicious about this change because  sometime you need certain technology to get certain civis and separating those doesn't made sense but not after trying it my opinion changed .
Because of districts and Governments/policies alone When Civilization 5 came out after few weeks I went back to
Civilization 4 but after Civilization 6 it is impossible for me to go back to Civilization 5 even with some great mods .
This review is getting big and tidious I guess so I will try to shorten it from now on .
4)City state Suzerein Unique bonuses
:- It is really unique and this make each city states different .
5)GPP mechanics :-
I love the GPP mechanic of this game more than previous title and so I really sometime want to Nuke brazil (Because of
his agenda , ill come back to it) .
6) Limited Unit stacking maintaining 1 UPT
:- Well you can for corps and army by unlocking certain civics and yeah it works and feel great . But this feature is limited and you won't be able to exploit it .
7) Music :- Mr Tin and other composers did a fantastic job .
Neutral feature ( You might ot might not like )
Builders get a limited amount of charge after that they dissapear . I like this feature it make the game more of an active experience.
builders have limited charge so then again I don't think this is the proper way of doing it or historically accurate as fireaxis think .
Traders are the only source of making road in the early stage of the game . I don't really get this but I do understand
Primary Agenda  and random agenda :- This feature in theory sound awesome and I was excited for it but it is TOTALLY BROKEN BECAUSE OF THE INCOMPOTENT AI . And one of the most annoying feature in any video game .
Visual and Art style :- Before you guys tell that I am a mobile gamer , I am actually an indie game programmer / and embeeded system programmer , I game on PS4 base model , X1 base model , N3DSXL and GTX 1080 AMP extreme , 6700Oced to 4.4 Ghz , 32 GB DDR4 3200 Mhz Gskill Ram  and I also have 2 txp build in my office for image processing stuff .
But I actually wanted to put it in pros but because of different taste of art style I didn't . I was excited by the art style in the very first screenshot ever posted of this game by fireaxis . I know how good a AAA game can look from first hand experience but I was totally in for stylish art style of this game . Being active in game development I have now even more respect for Civilization 6's art designer . I got inital hype because of the art style only but I do get if someone hate the hurt style . Graphical detailing is also great and that Day night cycle is beautiful according to me .
There are other pros as well I am not listing .
Cons :-
AI :- AI is a deal breaker for this game . And well agenda system make it extremely difficult to make friendship with AI and everything is so random even with primary agenda . Most of the time it doesn't even make any sense . AI civs are really annoying and that is the reason I play this game so less . Developers are continuously trying to improve the AI little by little but still no significant change after Australian update . I do have hope in them . Combat AI is also really bad but it did improve in the winter update . Like now settler do get escorted by another support unit and some other fixes . AI is still really bad in combat , they can't even take a walled city unless they have a HUGE force.
Everything about the AI is broken . For a game like Civilization , if played in Single player it is a major issue and I do think you should not buy it until it is fixed unless you are a sadist .
Bugs - There are a few small bugs and one of those are intoduced in winter update and not fixed in Australian summer update but nothing major . Also they fixed most of the other major bugs .
Balance issue :- Fireaxis is fixing balance issue really fast and most of the common balance issue is fixed . They are also causing a lot of balance issue in the recent patch like nerfing the harbour district is making an already weak civilization like UK weaker . They did fix the biggest balance issue with stacking regional building in the very first update .
Mod tools - Missing DLL and world builder other than the unfinished world builder in firetuner .
Verdict :- I reccomend this game if you want to play MP and some very casual SP while waiting for the AI to get fixed  ONLY. AI is too bad to recommend it for some serious single player challege or game . Other than that I am impressed with the game . And could be the best Civilization game ever from the worst Civilization game ever if it is fixed .

Civ VI isn't an upgrade to V; it's in the vein of Civ IV: a different game.

I've played Civ series since the first one and it used to be my favourite game. Now I can tell that it doesn't get any better, actually even worse. New great graphics or 1 good new mechanic does't make the experience any better, when the AI is probably at the same level of development as it was in 90's. To put it simple, the game is very unchallenging, boring and I think it is the first one I actually felt that I am wasting my time playing it when I could be doing more interesting things. Everything comes down to terrible AI.
Thanks to the awful AI, Civ 6 gives you only an impression that you have many different tools and that there are many layers in the game but in reality you could be playing against a one arm bandit machine with the same results. AI is basically taking out all the fun from the game. Civ 6 is like a very old laptop put into a new case - new look, with some extra bells and whistles but it is the same old engine. Therefore I feel cheated after paying for this expensive game that doesn't bring much new to the table.
Pros
- Great new graphics
- Newly introduced districts mechanic is very refreshing and I liked it a lot (however it does require some fine-tuning)
- City-states mechanic feels better than the previous one (not sure if people will agree though)
- New division between social policies and science discoveries is also refreshing and interesting
- Regular trade system feels ok (through traders)
Cons
- All of the above is ruined by terrible AI. The
and is the same as it has always been (read: pointless, not working as intended, i.e. not increasing difficulty). It doesn't matter how many guns you will give to a blind person, he/she is still blind!
-
- AI during
and doesn't mater how big army it has. It will send at you any random units, in any random order, disregarding everything that happens around. You have a huge navy parked near his city? It will embark land infantry to sail to/near your battleships. Sometimes I got an impression that AI actually tries to fight my navy with embarked land units (like cavalry).
AI will almost never build planes or use them.
The usual problem with AI developing in such a way that it is very hard to have a proper war using units from the same era. AI seems to never upgrade units, so expect the usual nonsense battles between pikemen and tanks. Changing speed of the game didn't really help with that (maybe unit queues are still too long? or it just comes down to stupid AI).
The whole concept of diverse military units is broken, when AI doesn't know how to use artillery, air strikes, close combat units etc. It just doesn't care what it uses, in which order and how.
AI will come into my territory, get hit, pull back, come back unhealed, die without reaching a target. Honestly, it is very hard to imagine what the target could be, because AI moves seem so random. It will randomly embark and disembark units continuously when trying to defend its city (?). It disregards everything: position of my units, their type, number, strength, the target they are hitting etc.
-
is as bad as it used to be. Absolutely pointless part of the game, filled with ridiculous mechanics. Doesn't matter how hard you try, you will almost always end up being hated by almost everyone around. Deals? If an AI player doesn't like you (soon or later it will happen), it forgets about any economy logic and offers so ridiculously expensive deals that they are not worth it. I understand "good" vs "bad" deals, but AI seems to be going off the scale like a lunatic. It will have 0 economic power, 0 army and ask (demand) many valuable resources for free. Why? Because it doesn't like. Why? Because you haven't built any plane yet, or something stupid like that, or because you got involved in a war, for which it will hate you for 1000 years.
Luxury resources seem to be an important part of the game (keeping society happy) and I see how diplomatic deals could be important here but in the current state diplomacy is almost useless. Alliances bring no benefits, except for some minor trade routes bonuses.
-
is as bad as it was. Again, AI ignores geopolitical situation. It will build a city, which wont develop much as it is taking those few hexes in the middle of my cities. It just doesn't care that it is settling its people in the center of my lands, i.e. the area surrounded by my cites from each side and while doing so it cuts me off my road. Later I cant transport my units, because AI decided to build a city blocking any road to it.
Maybe create 2 different levels of settlements?, so that razing (removing) one doesn't cost you ruined diplomatic relations for the eternity. However, fixing logic when creating new settlements should take the priority.
- Spy... so you can have only few spies in the game and when they get caught you have to pay (make a deal) to get them back. Otherwise your "spy slot" will be occupied for the rest of the game and you will never be able to replace it with a new spy. So all you need to do is to catch all enemy spies and never let them leave your prison. Catching a spy is not such a hard thing to do and even if it was, still this mechanic is plain stupid. Catching a few spies = no espionage ever... oh my, so real. There should be a price for losing a spy but keeping him in a prison for eternity is a stupid idea.

- Culture victory usually happens much before you can profit from modern wonders and buildings era bonuses.. well unless you set the starting era to be much later.
- AI seems to be spending fortune in gold buying Great People. It seems to be obsessed with them and rarely waits for the points to accumulate.
There is too much of this stuff, so I finish here...

tl;dr: generally okay season, but don't go into it expecting it to be as good as season 1.
The season isn't even done yet, we still have one unreleased episode at the moment, but I still feel like I know enough to say that it probably will not be worth it. Season 2 does not live up to the impression Season 1 left on me, and, as a whole, I think I liked the season 2 cast more. But it doesn't matter, in the end.
We complain about our choices not mattering in Season 1, because no matter what you do, everything converges onto one point by Episode 5 - Omid and Christa make it out of Savannah, and Lee sacrifices himself for Clementine. But never have I had so many of my choices invalidated in one episode than in Season 2. Having just played Episode 4 - nothing I did mattered that episode. None of my choices. Major characters dying without speaking lines, major characters dying in the most bogus ways possible, yet Telltale still tries to pass it off as shock factor.
And at this point? It's not. I played Season 1, and I know it's the zombie apocalypse and that people are going to die. Maybe that's meta gaming, but it's going into the game knowing exactly what I bought. I bought the game for the cast I knew I'd eventually come to love. The cast I knew I was going to die, but I knew I'd do my best to keep them alive. The cast I wanted to get to know, the stories of the survivors I wanted to hear. We get... almost none of that, here. In Episode 4, we get more about one character's backstory (whom we met in the previous episode) shoehorned into 90 minutes of gameplay than we have any of the other characters we've spent the rest of the season with. Only for that character to bow out, because she 'doesn't want to see Clem fall.' Ridiculous.
The writing is good, when it wants to be. When it needs to be, it falls flat. But yeah, the story is still as emotional, but now I don't know if I'm crying at a character's death because I'm genuinely sad they're dead - or because I'm disappointed at the loss of potential.

Life Is Strange
I can honestly say that I wasn't expecting to experience such an emotional response from this game, but I did, I really did. Those feelings were invoked, manipulated and tested to thresholds that I didn't believe a game could reach.
I managed to pick up this game recently, with almost no knowledge about the game, the characters, or the story line. I was even lucky enough to miss any spoilers for the game, which really added to my first play through of this.
You quickly realise that your choices throughout the game have an incredible impact on the world around you, and the people you encounter.
I found myself feeling solely responsible for the well being and safety of almost all the characters I encounter. That some of the choices made, were upsetting to make and stick with. You find yourself doubting your choices, going back to make improvements, making things better, then worse, then fixing everything, only to realise that a choice you made hours ago, has come back to knock you off of your feet with an outstanding impact.
The soundtrack for this game is perfect, for lack of a better word. It represents the choices you make, the emotions that Max and the others feel, the guilt for choices made, and even hits you hard during the moments of solidarity.
This isn't a game for people with personal problems, at home, at school, or work. I think some people might just find parts of this game a little too close to their own lives, and the emotional burden you put yourself through can be overwhelming stressful.
That being said, if you have a strong disposition, and can deal with the tears blurring your vision, your heartstrings being pulled, and your moral compass being poked, then go play this.
It's a unique and immersive story, completely worthy of your time, and your money.

Sid Meier's Civilization VI is the newest entry in the 4X Turn-based strategy franchise that has been running for over a quarter-century (Civ 1 was released in '91). I've been playing Civ games since I was a wee lad - started with Civ II Gold on my Dad's old Windows ME Laptop (I know, sounds horrible, but at least it could play Civ, Mechwarrior 2, and Half Life!) and while I never got around to playing Civ III or IV, when V eventually came out I played the ever loving crud out of that game. So obviously when I heard VI was on it's way, I paid serious attention.
Unfortunately, this game disappointed me on so many levels.
I'm just going to go ahead and skip to what I like about this game, because that's much shorter than the alternative.
Unfortunately, that's where the positives end for me. Now, on to the negatives:
The AI is, by far, the worst part of this game. Overly-aggressive, unforgiving of simple acts, antagonistic, and dumber than a sack of rocks. The AI will go from being your closest ally to your eternal enemy and you will have absolutely no idea how or why it happened.
I once had a situation where Gandhi, my ally, was at war with Gorgo of Sparta (more on her later) who, unsurprisingly, had instigated the war for apparently no reason. I, as the Sumerians, thought it would be a nice thing to do for my buddy and went ahead and declared war on Gorgo. The game had told me that I would receive absolutely zero warmonger penalties for this.  However, as soon as I declared war as an act of
, my
immediately turns around and denounces me as a warmonger and, as soon as our alliance ends, declares war on me. Oh, and Gorgo also denounced me as a warmonger, which by itself is funny, but it just made everything else all the more infuriating. So I guess the game lied to me about me receiving no warmonger penalties?
Speaking of which,
She has this policy where she dislikes any civilization that hasn't been to war. You know what that means, right? If you start the game with her being the first Civ you discover, her attitude will immediately begin to deteriorate because you haven't been to war with people you didn't even know existed yet. This negative impact seems to never go away even if you eventually start going to war, and will eventually progress to a point where Gorgo will just straight-up declare war on you for no reason. Oh, and as I mentioned before, I've had Gorgo denounce me for warmongering despite the fact she is supposed to like people who go to war.

Dealing with the AI is always frustrating. The diplomacy options are bare-bones, and they are always getting on your nerves. They have no respect for your territory (they will constanly land-grab near your cities) but will get extremely upset if you settle within seemingly 10 tiles of their borders, and you havve no way of telling them to screw off and stay away from your land until they've already settled and stolen your resources. Even then, they sometimes just don't listen and will even
promises they made to you.
They're also extremely incompetent. I don't know why anyone would ever try to achieve any victory other than military domination, as even on the hardest of difficulties the AI will only muster laughably-sized armies that can easily be crushed by most players. Warmongering penalties don't even matter - you could easily fight off every other civilization at once in this game if you only focused on building strong military units.
Speaking of which, this game is extremely tedious. It takes forever to do anything. Since builders can only be used three times instead of just automated like in every other Civ game since II, you constantly have to intterupt your build order to build more builders. The district system is a total miss. Districts take forever to build, and even once you have them built they give you no advantage whatsoever until you start making the buidlings dedicated to those districts. These are all turns that could instead be used on military units, builders, or settlers. These are buildings that in previous Civ games didn't require a district to be built first, so honestly it's just a total waste of time. Also, the districts take up a tile and remove all improvements on that tile, which means you can't put down a farm / mine / quarry on that tile. Which means districts can end up being a detriment to your economy in the long run.
I honestly cannot recommend this game in it's current state. Unless it gets a huge overhaul in some future update or DLC, I think this game is just not worth it at all. I regret buying it. As it stands, Civ V is still the best Civ game (in my opinion, anyways), and if you're looking for a good Civ game I recommend getting that one and it's expansions.
I really hope Firaxis comes to their senses, but I don't see it happening.

This game is fun, and sometimes hilarious because how bad it can be at simulating real-life events and physics.
This game is really simple and complicated at the same time,  If you don't aproach it in the right way you may struggle to make functional ships and conduct successful missions around the solar system.
As fun as it is making death traps for your fellow kerbin inhabitants such as  mounting nothing more than a flimsy cockpit onto the biggest rocket motor you can find as a make-shift inter-stellar missile or seeing how fast you can make the lunar lander spin before it tears it self apart, I'd highly reccomend you watch a few tutorials and complete the in-game ones so that you have an idea of what you're doing.
Sandbox mode - easily the most fun as it has no limitations onto what you can do, other than how good your pc spec is.
I don't know whether I'd recommend playing this first, but having access to all the parts currently availible in-game could definitley help in getting to know all the different parts and getting your ideas going.
Career mode - the hardest mode to play, but easily the most rewarding : you start off with little resources, limited support and funds, and inhibited ambitions- in order to move forward you must complete company contracts and science experiments in exchange for funds, public support and scientific developments - this game mode is far more punishing than all the others and you must approach each mission as if you were conducting it in real life.
whatever you do, I'd like to think you'll have as much fun as me CX

While the overall story is still very gripping, I feel that there is very little actual choice when it comes down to it. While decisions in the first game would not always result in drastically different outcomes, it felt like there were sufficient real choices to make the game fun to play 5 times through and still leave avenues of choice unexplored. The second game was dull the second playthrough with far too many linear instances where once you know what is going to happen it becomes a very tedious trek from point A to point B with atmospheric effects that only worked the first time because you had no idea what would happen, but subsequent times felt like you were walking through a cheap haunted house yawning at the ghostly moans and twitching curtains.
Aside from the lack of replayability, I found myself often wondering why tough guys who had apparently survived the hostile new zombie world thus far were suddenly putting their lives in the hands of a small girl they barely knew. While Lee in the first game was a capable, quick thinking young adult that I found was very easy to trust, it felt very wrong that the same trust was put in a small girl, who was often quite frightened herself.
Yet if you enjoyed the first game, you don't care to play the game to death and you can see past the few thinly veiled plot tweaks designed to make our character the hero, then I would recommend this second season as good fun, intense and well drawn.

This is an addicting game that's easy to have fun with but gets extremely hard to master.
It's also not a 100% realistic space sim (although there's mods for that) but do the few starting tutorials that help you explain how to go in the right direction and you will learn some basic rockets science in the process.
Definitely do the tutorials, or watch some youtube videos about it though (Scott Manley has some good ones); this game has a very very sharp learning curve without those.
The graphics are basic enough to where even your macbook air can run this thing. Honestly, I'm surprised there isn't a smartphone version 'cos it doesn't take much more than that. If you want some more spiffy graphics, though there's mods for that, too.
There isn't proper official multiplayer yet though but Squad's been having notes about those in their patch notes for a while, so soon. But until then, there's (a rather legit) mod for that.
Mastering your first orbital flight will take less than an hour if you watch the tutorials. Setting up a space station, maybe a day. Traveling out to Jool (the solar system's Jupiter-like gas giant) will take probably a week of planning. It's intense. But fun. And when you finally get there holy cow do you feel like you've accomplished somthing.
Capturing asteroids is another thing, too. And then when you start scanning for resources and building advanced outposts. Man, this will suck your time away as if you've warped through your free time.
But it's extremely fun. Especially when you add in some of the mods - like B9 Aerospace, KW Rocketry, Infernal Robotics, Kerbal Attachment System, and others. You actually do learn a non-trivial number of rocket science concepts. And you also gain at least some appreciation for the people who do this for a living.
11/10, a difinitive recommendation. Even if you suck at building space ships, download the Dark Multiplayer Mod and have a race to the Mun (Moon) or a drinking game or download a weapons mod and have some jet fighter battles.
P.S. In case you didn't get the hints, the stock game is awesome, but the mod community really brings this game up to 11. There's mods for everything - to autopilot, to help you figure out how many boosters you need, to make sure you don't skip over maneuver nodes, and to make the game look downright beautiful. The mods alone are worth this game's asking price.

People are complaining that builders are not infinite now, and run out after 3 uses. It's in 90% of the negative reviews on this page at time of writing. At the bare minimum, using a builder I trained in 300 BC to help build my first tank factory makes little to no sense. This being a strategy management game, making a resource that is a massive part of the world's collective cost (labor) makes sense both in the context of the game and the entire spirit of how to succeed at Civ.
People are also talking about the AI. I have every Civ game on Steam, and I can tell you, you only have to read the first half of 70% of the comments to realize most of these people have no idea how ANY of the rules you don't learn in the tutorial work. This is an addicting game that's easy to have fun with but gets extremely hard to master.
It's also not a 100% realistic space sim (although there's mods for that) but do the few starting tutorials that help you explain how to go in the right direction and you will learn some basic rockets science in the process.
Definitely do the tutorials, or watch some youtube videos about it though (Scott Manley has some good ones); this game has a very very sharp learning curve without those.
The graphics are basic enough to where even your macbook air can run this thing. Honestly, I'm surprised there isn't a smartphone version 'cos it doesn't take much more than that. If you want some more spiffy graphics, though there's mods for that, too.
There isn't proper official multiplayer yet though but Squad's been having notes about those in their patch notes for a while, so soon. But until then, there's (a rather legit) mod for that.
Mastering your first orbital flight will take less than an hour if you watch the tutorials. Setting up a space station, maybe a day. Traveling out to Jool (the solar system's Jupiter-like gas giant) will take probably a week of planning. It's intense. But fun. And when you finally get there holy cow do you feel like you've accomplished somthing.
Capturing asteroids is another thing, too. And then when you start scanning for resources and building advanced outposts. Man, this will suck your time away as if you've warped through your free time.
But it's extremely fun. Especially when you add in some of the mods - like B9 Aerospace, KW Rocketry, Infernal Robotics, Kerbal Attachment System, and others. You actually do learn a non-trivial number of rocket science concepts. And you also gain at least some appreciation for the people who do this for a living.
11/10, a difinitive recommendation. Even if you suck at building space ships, download the Dark Multiplayer Mod and have a race to the Mun (Moon) or a drinking game or download a weapons mod and have some jet fighter battles.
P.S. In case you didn't get the hints, the stock game is awesome, but the mod community really brings this game up to 11. There's mods for everything - to autopilot, to help you figure out how many boosters you need, to make sure you don't skip over maneuver nodes, and to make the game look downright beautiful. The mods alone are worth this game's asking price.

Picked the game up for 24 or so dollars early access, before it was added to steam. Needless to say, not all of my hours are presented here.
While I don't necessarily agree with what is currently a $39.99 price tag, the game is good. I might wait for a sale, but it is definitely a worthy game at the 24 dollars I paid for it. Poured in tons of hours, and learned a little about space and space travel in the process of trying to get better. This is an educational game if I ever saw one!
The joy that comes out of building a space station on a far off planet, or even on the home planet itself is amazing, and the game always inspired a sense of childlike wonder for me, personally.
I'm currently out of a phase where I enjoy games that require learning like this one, and if I wanted to get back into this, I'd have to relearn some stuff cause it has been a while! However the learning you'll have to do will get you invested, and when you finally conquer each of the planets on your own without any overpowered mods or cheats, it'll feel amazing.
Only problem I can remember is that the tutorials were...not the most descriptive, however I think that may be a strongsuit as well because it encourages going out there and learning it yourself. Getting your hands dirty and perhaps learning along the way.

This is an emotionally intense game. I admit it, I cried a few times. But then, I not only felt pain and sadness, I experienced revolt, anger, horror, disgust.. and also joy and happiness. The story took me through different spells of emotions as I played as the fragile but courageous teenage girl hero, Maxine Caulfield, who discovers she can rewind time.
This is a beautiful, touching game. There are contemplative moments, there are exhilarating moments, all served by a wonderfully perfect soundtrack that helps paint the mood. The art with its impressionist atmosphere, the writing, the music, the dialogues, the superb voice acting come perfectly together in this coming of age drama. The game made me think about the movie "Stand by me"... It is not because it is also taking place in Oregon, or that there is a junkyard or a train scene... but the portrayal of the many teenage characters reminded me of the movie protagonists, their complex backgrounds and their relationships, the bittersweet tone and because the story is ultimately about friendship.
This is an intelligent game. The storytelling puts time manipulation to great use, sometimes forcing on the player a clunky gameplay but nevertheless serving an inventive writing. Rewinding time opens new routes as the main character gains knowledge and put it to use, and it is not a simple "quick game reload" gimmick. The choices made throughout have small and big impacts on how the different characters develop and interact, and the attention to details is the testament of the hard work and passion the developpers poured into their creation. The mature story, the depth of the characters' psychology, the serious themes being brought up by the plot speak to a young adult/ adult audience. It is not because it is a "game" that it is for kids, as it definitely is not. This is not a game that one plays "for fun", as sometimes the different pieces take some time to click together, playing "Life is strange" is more like experiencing the slice of life of a teenager trying to make the "right" choices, eventhough like in real life, there won't be any true "right" choice but the one the player chooses to make at the end. Because it is a game, it is interactive, as opposed to other media where you are only a passive spectator, and since the player is involved in the storytelling process, it drives the point of living with the consequences of his or her choices all the more forcefully home.
Completing "Life is strange" is like finishing a good book. There is a little melancholy but also a sense of finally reaching the destination of this beautiful journey prepared by the game makers.
"Life is strange" is definitely the game that touched me the most in recent years.

This is an addicting game that's easy to have fun with but gets extremely hard to master.
It's also not a 100% realistic space sim (although there's mods for that) but do the few starting tutorials that help you explain how to go in the right direction and you will learn some basic rockets science in the process.
Definitely do the tutorials, or watch some youtube videos about it though (Scott Manley has some good ones); this game has a very very sharp learning curve without those.
The graphics are basic enough to where even your macbook air can run this thing. Honestly, I'm surprised there isn't a smartphone version 'cos it doesn't take much more than that. If you want some more spiffy graphics, though there's mods for that, too.
There isn't proper official multiplayer yet though but Squad's been having notes about those in their patch notes for a while, so soon. But until then, there's (a rather legit) mod for that.
Mastering your first orbital flight will take less than an hour if you watch the tutorials. Setting up a space station, maybe a day. Traveling out to Jool (the solar system's Jupiter-like gas giant) will take probably a week of planning. It's intense. But fun. And when you finally get there holy cow do you feel like you've accomplished somthing.
Capturing asteroids is another thing, too. And then when you start scanning for resources and building advanced outposts. Man, this will suck your time away as if you've warped through your free time.
But it's extremely fun. Especially when you add in some of the mods - like B9 Aerospace, KW Rocketry, Infernal Robotics, Kerbal Attachment System, and others. You actually do learn a non-trivial number of rocket science concepts. And you also gain at least some appreciation for the people who do this for a living.
11/10, a difinitive recommendation. Even if you suck at building space ships, download the Dark Multiplayer Mod and have a race to the Mun (Moon) or a drinking game or download a weapons mod and have some jet fighter battles.
P.S. In case you didn't get the hints, the stock game is awesome, but the mod community really brings this game up to 11. There's mods for everything - to autopilot, to help you figure out how many boosters you need, to make sure you don't skip over maneuver nodes, and to make the game look downright beautiful. The mods alone are worth this game's asking price.

People are complaining that builders are not infinite now, and run out after 3 uses. It's in 90% of the negative reviews on this page at time of writing. At the bare minimum, using a builder I trained in 300 BC to help build my first tank factory makes little to no sense. This being a strategy management game, making a resource that is a massive part of the world's collective cost (labor) makes sense both in the context of the game and the entire spirit of how to succeed at Civ.
People are also talking about the AI. I have every Civ game on Steam, and I can tell you, you only have to read the first half of 70% of the comments to realize most of these people have no idea how ANY of the rules you don't learn in the tutorial work. This game is complex. There are lots of reasons leaders can dislike you, and sometimes it's just their warlike personality or you making trades with their enimies. There are SO many nuances to this game that you have to play or read about it for hours knowing everything to really see the entirety of the situation at hand. Sorta like, you know, ruling a nation. Some of the reviews say "get 5" and those are the people who have only played Civ 5, lemme tell you. Each one of these games is a different version of itself, and everything has a purpose. The game is fun, but underwhelming. The scope and magnitude feels greatly diminished from Civ 5. The cartoony aesthetic may appeal to or repulse, depending on your tastes. I was strongly in the second camp, but found it easy to get used to. Sean Bean's performance as the narrator has received a lot of praise, but doesn't carry the gravity of previous incarnations. Sadly, when put together, these elements make the game feel like you're playing "Sid Meier's: Civilization Jr."
For now, the DLC situation is frustrating bordering on insulting. Individual civilizations should NOT cost $5.00 USD or any localized equivalent. I felt a sense of sick irony, when rewatching the opening cinematic. A moving video, illustrating the pinnacles of human achievement, which once, literally brought me to tears and convinced me to buy the game. Now when I watch it, I can't help but reflect on Firaxis/2K's greed, and how they are trying to nickel and dime their player base. The lofty ambitions of that intro video feel a bit insincere now.
If and when some major DLC is released and bundled in an affordable package, I may change this review. Until then, Civilization 5 is a much, much, better and more complete experience.

A straight downgrade from Civ 5. Maybe it will follow the civ tradition and have every expansion back be a great overhaul of the system, but as it currently stands this game simply isn't worth full price.
Visuals: the most subjective category, but I find this game wholly unappealing artistically. The Civ leaders look like pixar rejects and the landscapes are bland and uninspired.
UI: The UI is a mess, with often incredibly important information hidden or poorly represented. It also takes an egregious amount of clicks to accomplish simple tasks, like re-assigning spies to a location they are already at. Individually this wouldn't matter as much but the number and rapidity of it across a 300+ turn game is very aggravating.
Music: Seems like it's mostly variations of the same track modified over the years. After my first game I was already muting in favor of a playlist in the background. Also the quotes are garbage.
AI: Arguably the most incompetent released in the franchise, at least this decade. If you played civ 5 at X difficulty you can basically bump it up by 1-2 in Civ 6 because outside of early game rushes the AI is completely worthless at waging a war. Also, AI are pretty much insane, and establishing reliable relationships with one is all but impossible. Bonus points; even if you do succeed in this, they will still arbitrarily declare war on you just because. There is no late-game diplomacy akin to the U.N., so by industrial period most everyone dislikes you but it doesn't actually affect anything, turning the end of the game into a monotonous slog.
Game mechanics: Aside from the fact that the game is still significantly unbalanced, there are many problems plaguing this title. The change to workers being charged base means you have to waste time spamming them into your build queues, but doesn't really add anything to the game in terms of enjoyment or skill, it's just micro-management for its own sake. Wonders take a ridiculous time to build (50-80 turns) and take up a tile, so they're often not worth it at all. Districts, what should have been the great new addition to the title, have mostly been relegated to a few essentials that are spammed forever due to the aforementioned imbalance. Lastly, the removal of any kind of happiness or corruption mechanic means that every empire will go wide every single game because there are no reasons not to. While going tall was a bit too reliable in Civ 5, swinging hard the other way isn't actually better.
At the end of the day, I kick myself for buying this game so soon after launch. Take my advice and just tide yourself over with something else until they bother to fix this mess, because until then it's really not worth your time or money.
