This is an emotionally intense game. I admit it, I cried a few times. But then, I not only felt pain and sadness, I experienced revolt, anger, horror, disgust.. and also joy and happiness. The story took me through different spells of emotions as I played as the fragile but courageous teenage girl hero, Maxine Caulfield, who discovers she can rewind time.
This is a beautiful, touching game. There are contemplative moments, there are exhilarating moments, all served by a wonderfully perfect soundtrack that helps paint the mood. The art with its impressionist atmosphere, the writing, the music, the dialogues, the superb voice acting come perfectly together in this coming of age drama. The game made me think about the movie "Stand by me"... It is not because it is also taking place in Oregon, or that there is a junkyard or a train scene... but the portrayal of the many teenage characters reminded me of the movie protagonists, their complex backgrounds and their relationships, the bittersweet tone and because the story is ultimately about friendship.
This is an intelligent game. The storytelling puts time manipulation to great use, sometimes forcing on the player a clunky gameplay but nevertheless serving an inventive writing. Rewinding time opens new routes as the main character gains knowledge and put it to use, and it is not a simple "quick game reload" gimmick. The choices made throughout have small and big impacts on how the different characters develop and interact, and the attention to details is the testament of the hard work and passion the developpers poured into their creation. The mature story, the depth of the characters' psychology, the serious themes being brought up by the plot speak to a young adult/ adult audience. It is not because it is a "game" that it is for kids, as it definitely is not. This is not a game that one plays "for fun", as sometimes the different pieces take some time to click together, playing "Life is strange" is more like experiencing the slice of life of a teenager trying to make the "right" choices, eventhough like in real life, there won't be any true "right" choice but the one the player chooses to make at the end. Because it is a game, it is interactive, as opposed to other media where you are only a passive spectator, and since the player is involved in the storytelling process, it drives the point of living with the consequences of his or her choices all the more forcefully home.
Completing "Life is strange" is like finishing a good book. There is a little melancholy but also a sense of finally reaching the destination of this beautiful journey prepared by the game makers.
"Life is strange" is definitely the game that touched me the most in recent years.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 game, like its predecessor, is story driven game that is able to create the same sense of mystery, suspense, and action.  Improving on a lot of the systems, you have chances to mend broken relationships and create all new connections with new and old characters as you continue your story through the eyes of Clementine.
The Walking Dead: Season 2 continues a few months after the events in season 1 bringing together a whole new cast of characters with characters from its predecessor where new connections, relationships, and decisions will be formed.  Along with the new characters is a new perspective, where you once playing as an adult who had the strength to deal with the walkers head-on, you now play as Clementine, a young girl who has to use her wits in order to survive.  As with the predecessor, you are in control of your life, making various decisions for good or for bad to help mold Clementine into the character that you want her to be seen as; I feel as though the decisions have been changed for the better as they still impact you, but will not create as drastic of changes as to how each character views Clementine.  Although your decisions can change certain outcomes to an extent, you are generally tied to the story and will be limited in what can actually be changed.  Although the changes may be limited, the story is still full of mystery, suspense, and action to lead the player to want to know what comes next.
+ Unique story
+ Improved decisions system
+Connect with characters
+ Point and click style
- Decisions cause limited impact towards the world
- Episodic, can take a month or two for the next episode

Many people compare civ6 with civ5 complete and are not convinced in the worth of the new edition. Before i continue, i'd like to say i'm a hardcore civ fan and pre-ordered the deluxe edition of civ6, so you may accuse me of trying to justify that purchase.
In short: after playing civ6 for a while, i just can't go back to civ5.
- interface of civ6 is MUCH better, information is easier to access and assess. of course, it takes a while to get used to it, just like in any other new game.
- new movement rules (units need to fulfill the full movement points requirement to enter a tile) and support units add massive depth to the tactical side of the game.
- religion had a significant rework and you know what's the best thing about it? you can totally skip it. you can literally don't care about religion, and you're just fine. i take this as a plus, i never liked waging religious wars. just don't forget - religious victory is a thing, so keep yourself informed about this.
- espionage had a significant rework, too, and it's much easier to use. in civ5 i've always turned this feature off, as it was so annoying. civ6 improves on this.
- agendas and leaders' personalities are very distinct. in civ5, different civs just have different bonuses, however, in civ6 leaders add a great deal of personality. they may be predictable, but the "roleplay" element is totally fun!
- multiple leaders of the same civ - a major step forward! i'd like to see more leaders of existing civs!
- laws and governments. another innovation for the series which is, imho, a success.
- resource management - having "levels" of resource abundance feels more natural, you either have the iron to build your swords, or you don't.
- great people generation and usage is yet another new approach and they do matter!
- unstacking cities has direct impact on your tactical performance, as well as for espionage. it matters where you place your districts, it matters a lot! and more importantly - it's impossible have one mega-city with all the world wonders.
how civ6 can be improved:
- world congress - it's a major missing feature, i bet they'd add it with the next major expansion, but until then - it leaves a real gap.
- more leader options for the same civs
- mid-to-late game still requires micromanagement, which (for me) makes the game tedious. i feel this can be improved, i think this one has been plaguing the series for a long time now.
- culture victory. this has been nearly copied from civ5. i didn't like it much there, i don't like it much now. but it's just me, i guess.

It is a really tough call whether to recommend this game or not. I gave it overall a thumbs up because I do not think it's deserving of all the negative reviews it's getting and that people are putting too much emphasis on the bad. I'm not going to cover the good and bad in depth here as so many people have already done that. Basically, districts are an amazing concept, the roster of civs is very diverse, the art and music is very spot on, and almost everything good about the previous civ games is present in this one. So why is it getting so much hate? Because the AI, which has always been shaky in the past, but is still acceptable, is pretty bad in this game. They are dreadful at waging war and always seem to be mad at you unless you really go out of your way to make friends by specifically conforming to their sometimes outrageous agendas. The only thing that isn’t really worse is trading, which I feel the AI now offers you better deals from Civ V, even if they’re mad at you. Now essentially what it boils down to is that this game is one good AI patch/expansion from being an amazing game. But until then, I can only recommend this to the truest of fans (like myself) that want a little change up from Civ V. There are a few other problems, such as the one dimensional nature of religious victories, but the AI is the major thing that stands out. To be clear, *this is not a bad game* (that's why I gave it a thumbs up) but it is not nearly as good as the complete version of Civ V. Just think about how bad Civ V was on its launch though. Like Civ VI, it had many AI and balancing problems which needed addressing. Civ V Vanilla was pretty rough, and in my opinion, worse than Civ VI Vanilla. People said the same things about how much better Civ IV complete was than V when it was released. However, now look at it. Civ V is one of the best games of all time after patches and two major expansions. This game has a lot more potential and could even surpass Civ V in the future, but until then, Civ V complete is probably the better way to go. Just do not count this game out until the final version is released.

Compared to the first series, as of episode 3 it's a pale cousin. But if you're invested in the story of clementine and loved the first series, you won't be disappointed. I think the main issue is that unlike the first series where you played as lee, you had far more control over the direction the story would take and could be far more pro-active. This series is different. Clementine is different, she's a child swept up into situation and I think that while it's great to have that sense of helplessness, and a different perspective about the end fo the world it's also perhaps different to what we've been accustomed to.
Still very much worth the price tag, but go play the first series first and then make the call.
**EP 4 REVIEW UPDATE**
Episode 4 has turned the table of the series. While it does feel very much like the stakes are rising, and with characters dying left and right and that there's a lot to lose - it left me dispassionate.
The only problem I've been having with this series is the way they treat their characters. Now with offscreen deaths, little to no character development with well set up arcs and with taking on a more decidedly interactive film quality I feel that while the series is still something to hang out for, its quality is slowly degrading, just like the world the characters inhabit.
The real heart of this series is and has always been the story. But unlike characters like Ben from series one, who are given careful consideration into how their ♥♥♥♥ups affect plot and their journey - possibly to some form of redemption, the same archetype is discarded without much care in episode 4. The gameplay needs to be there too. Where there were puzzles and choices that needed to be carefully considered, we now have quicktime events and "wander around this set and look for clues".
In closing, pacing is becoming sloppy. The story now feels more and more geared towards being "edgy" with a complete sidetrack to interact with a character, who while being a pragmatic and genuinely interesting person to be around detracts from established characters. The gameplay is now less about the puzzle element and feels more like a fetch quest and poorly planned jump scares.
The series is good, but I hope it care return to its roots and focus more about the integral things that made the first series so good.

Honestly, this game is pretty great.  It's so far out of my wheelhouse that I still find it hard to believe that I bought it.  But, I'm glad that I did; it was worth the money (although I did get it on sale).
This game is heavily based on storyline.  Not that most games aren't, though; I just meant that this game involves player choices, which directly affect the storyline.  You're forced to carefully think over every conversation, every action that you take (or don't take), etc.  I honestly enjoyed that about it; a lot.
The graphics aren't overly "modern," meaning that it's got a very artistic and almost "cartoon-like" style to it.  That doesn't mean that they're anything to shake a stick at though; they're very well done, and I enjoyed the overall atmosphere that they created.  The audio is just as well done, and suits the game well.
In terms of controls, I don't have any complaints.  Everything was very simple and easy to grasp.
As for the storyline itself and what I thought of it, all I can say is that I loved it.  It's so far outside of my wheelhouse, which I really enjoyed.  It wasn't something that I felt like I'd played through in a dozen games before.  The choices you're given in the game and the outcomes of each add to the experience greatly.
There were multiple parts of the storyline that left me feeling a little crushed; in complete shock and awe.  I feel like the fact that some of my choices actually caused these moments of shock and awe is what made them hit as hard as they did.  At some points I actually had to take a minute to collect myself after certain things happened, and actually had to pause the game to think through some of the choices I could make.
What a really great experience!
All in all, this game was worth the money, and worth the time it took to complete.  It's got a lot of replay value, since you can play through it multiple times and do things differently each time to see how your choices will affect the outcome of the storyline.  For me, it was a pretty emotional experience, and I'm not an overly-emotional person.
10/10; would play again.

Life is Strange is an episodic graphic adventure game, about Max, a shy mysterious girl who likes taking pictures. A normal girl at first, that is until she discovers she has an incredible power.The first episode is set in an American High School. The girl you play as, Max is only really interested in one thing: keeping her head down, and pursuing the success of her photography course. However as soon as she finds she has the ability to affect change in the time and events around her, she decides to take action.
The game plays in a similar way to Telltale's graphic adventure games. You'll be put into conversations and make certain choices that effect how characters react, as well as an impact on the greater narrative. Of course, Max's ability to change time makes quite a big difference in what we would expect from these type of games. In your standard narrative game you make a choice, depending on what you believe to be the leser of two evils, but in this no matter what you choose, there's always a negative outcome for someone, regardless. Allowing you to see one of these options play out, then rewind and choose another doesn't always mean you can choose the better option, just one that will have a different chain of effect.
Snooping and searching plays a big part of this game, you're able to search other's rooms, and go through a lot of their stuff, most of the time this snooping is purely optional and not part of the puzzle solving - but you get a much richer narrative picture when you take the time to hunt down all those little details.
Finding out about all of the characters is very interesting, and deciding which of those characters to help - then considering how the choices you make will effect them, and whether or not to put yourself first. That said, the rewind mechanical as a way to solve puzzles is interesting, however sometimes you'll hit a point where you need to choose a different dialogue option by anticipating what you know the character wants to hear, because you just heard them say that, which isn't particularly challenging, however the rewind system can also remove the stress that would play a good role in some of the scenes. When trying to find a hiding spot in Max's friends bedroom, it creates a tense moment as you struggle to find someone to hide before her stepfather comes in. However due to the rewind feature it means you can constantly rewind, until you find a spot to hide in. The feature in this scene removed the stress, and took from what could have been a really intense scene.
Once you've finished they show the percentages of other player's decisions against yours, this is a nice feature, and can make you contemplate the choices you've made - long after you've chosen them.
The game has a great story, deep and well-fleshed characters and some of the most beautiful cutscenes. Detail has been lovingly put into the environment, and creates a mysterious, and wonderful games. It'll be interesting to see what the other episodes have to offer. This is definitely one of the best games I've ever played.

A good Civilization game, evolved from Civilization V, with great mechanics on a bad implementation.
I liked a lot the addition of districts, cards and differentiation of social and science advancement trees. I also welcomed the new religious victory condition (even if it's kinda flawed, will write about it later).
On the other hand the new graphic style and the lack of “penalties” for large empires (the game actually forces you to rush creating new cities in your empire, will write about it later) dragged things a bit down for me.
So, in detail, the overall mechanics of this new Civilization game are very good, overall positively evolved from Civilization V, but since the game forces you to rush on city building you get a few very bad side effects:
Capturing cities feels like a joke, for example you may end up capturing 10 to 15 cities in just a few turns with no real side effect on your empire.
For the same reason (too many cities) religious victory condition is a mess, you will see 3~4 priests per city battling (yeah… that is lame) for religious supremacy which is beyond annoying.
Again for the same reason it's just easier to colonize to get certain resources rather than initiate trading with other empires or trying to acquire influence over state-cities.
To get you the idea,
forget about Civilization V Enrico Dandolo play style, it's just impossible with the current state of the game.
Something I was worried about, because so many people pointed that out, was bad AI, but I have to say that in my 2 games AI was quite good, just a bit too aggressive, in everything (e.g. Teddy building a city in a tile between two of my cities, ending up with a oblong, space crippled city or Hojo declaring war just to move through my territory).
Finally I have to say that at the moment leaders offer you a little bit of variance only at the very start of the game, middle and ending phases of the game are more or less the same whichever leader you get to play: huge empires, fought at least two or more wars, fairly high in all compartments (science, culture, etc).
Would I recommend this game, yes, no doubt about it, but don't get it right now, wait till a few DLC are out (or even better a GOTY edition “final” pack) because there are both “flaws” and lack of diversity at the moment.

Positives (in comparison to Civ V)
- Simplified menus, such as the city screen, so it's easier to know what the heck you're doing.
- Great People are more intersting, having a large variety of effects rather than just one while still being effective.
- Religious victory adds a nice twist, better than diplomatic victory where you either had to convince the other players to vote for you or buy out every city state.
- Don't have to use builders to make roads, trade routes do that by default. Also builders only take a turn to build/clear something instead of a bunch of wasted turns.
- Leaders + Civilizations each have their own benefit, so you're not restricted to only one benefit that may not work out for you in the long run.
- Tile management, adding another layer of strategy.
- More combat unit types to keep things more interesting, such as seige units to make melee attackers stronger against cities.

EDIT 3: The Fall 2017 patch fixed some of the issues from the previous patch (AIs trading away great works for 1 gold, etc), but introduced some far more severe bugs. Unit Alerts no longer function as intended, which means you are often surprised by an enemy unit / barbarian you should have been notifed of. But more importantly, the starting positions script is totally broken. You can start enclosed by mountains, or in the arctic. People can start literally right next to each other. City states can spawn too close to be able to settle, and then stop existing. I don't like 5-15% of the players being eliminated turn zero, because when I pick an 8 player game I expect it to be an 8 player game. And a whole MONTH after this bug was reported, they released a hotfix... that doesn't even fix the issue completely. This is unacceptable, and, quite simply, unplayable. It's incredibly frustrating because I have really been wanting to enjoy a game of civ lately, but it is simply not possible with the outstanding gamebreaking issues.
EDIT 2: The Summer 2017 patch broke far too many things to recommend this game anymore. My last 3 games have irrecoverably crashed in the modern to info eras. AI trade deals are completely broken. Countless bugs from release still aren't fixed, yet they introduce more bugs instead of fixing them. I want to play this game, but feel I can't, since I have to manually restrict myself from abusing the AI's poor trade logic, and I know the game will just break later on and become unfinishable.
EDIT: With the latest patch they have finally added team multiplayer. And, while the game is still far from perfect, I finally feel satisfied with my purchase now that I can actually play with my gf and friends. Changing my review from thumbs down to thumbs up.

Life is Strange is really well made piece of art. It's hard to tell much about game content itself without spoiling it. So I will focus on simple pros and cons.
Pros:
- It's beautiful. Both characters and environment in game are really well made.
- Sounds are great and there's plenty of well made voiceacting.
- Everything works smoothly and I never had lag, bug or single crash.

Cons:

Start of last episode was great but soon everything felt kinda pointless and I was just waiting for game to come to an end.
That's it. From my point of view this game has way more pros than cons. I really love to see that nowdays there are masterpieces like this game with deep well thought story and characters. I thought those days are gone.
10/10! If you know "story rich games" as well made as this, feel free to recommend them to me.

Honestly, this game is pretty great.  It's so far out of my wheelhouse that I still find it hard to believe that I bought it.  But, I'm glad that I did; it was worth the money (although I did get it on sale).
This game is heavily based on storyline.  Not that most games aren't, though; I just meant that this game involves player choices, which directly affect the storyline.  You're forced to carefully think over every conversation, every action that you take (or don't take), etc.  I honestly enjoyed that about it; a lot.
The graphics aren't overly "modern," meaning that it's got a very artistic and almost "cartoon-like" style to it.  That doesn't mean that they're anything to shake a stick at though; they're very well done, and I enjoyed the overall atmosphere that they created.  The audio is just as well done, and suits the game well.
In terms of controls, I don't have any complaints.  Everything was very simple and easy to grasp.
As for the storyline itself and what I thought of it, all I can say is that I loved it.  It's so far outside of my wheelhouse, which I really enjoyed.  It wasn't something that I felt like I'd played through in a dozen games before.  The choices you're given in the game and the outcomes of each add to the experience greatly.
There were multiple parts of the storyline that left me feeling a little crushed; in complete shock and awe.  I feel like the fact that some of my choices actually caused these moments of shock and awe is what made them hit as hard as they did.  At some points I actually had to take a minute to collect myself after certain things happened, and actually had to pause the game to think through some of the choices I could make.
What a really great experience!
All in all, this game was worth the money, and worth the time it took to complete.  It's got a lot of replay value, since you can play through it multiple times and do things differently each time to see how your choices will affect the outcome of the storyline.  For me, it was a pretty emotional experience, and I'm not an overly-emotional person.
10/10; would play again.

Here's the bullet point review:
- If you liked The Walking Dead Season 1, you'll probably enjoy this. However...
- The writing comes across as much lazier than last season. For instance,there's still very little consequence to most of your choices, and a replay of the episodes so far confirm that there's really no point to replaying this - it all turned out the same anyhow. There's also a few points where actions which should have consequences just don't, so expect some head-scratching.
- Overall though, gameplay is still very immersive, and it's enough for you to become emotionally invested in the outcome of the story, though, as I said above, sometimes your actions/choices don't seem to come to anything.
- The UI upgrades are nice. They're minor, but just enough to improve on the previous season's gameplay and don't require any additional learning curve really.
- The episodes seem - and from all I can tell are - shorter than Season 1's, at least if my gameplay time reported in Steam is to be trusted. For dollars per hour played, the value is pretty low.
- I actually really enjoy playing as Clem, a character who as a child gets underestimated and yet still has a lot of strengths because of her experiences in Season 1. Still, she's not given much chance to show off her toughness and is still talked down to a lot.
It's maybe worth getting if you loved Season 1. Expect shorter episodes and a decrease in the quality of the story and writing. Get it on sale if you can, full price seems way too much for my tastes unless you're a die-hard fan.

I have played Civ since the great Civ4 brought me wholly into the franchise, permanently scarring my experience of any other history sim because it wasn't up to Civ standard, and I can tell you this is a gem. The tried-and-tested play as a historical leader and control everything in your chosen country formula is back with more additions. While Civ 5 felt like a glorified graphics pack for Civ 4, the introduction of non-confusing victory goals, a clever and streamlined card-based government system, Great Works and Great Work storage (though I
run out of space for them early game) and the superb, if disjointed-looking, District and City Expansion features. They also finally turned down the general OPness of military strats and now democratic and cultural societies are as valuable as bashing Montezuma and his Aztec Swordsmen to bits.
There are still ways to improve the mechanics and functionality of the game, as Civ 6 consumes RAM like a wolf (geddit?!) and makes my computer hyperventilate regularly, you still have to choose between 1 or 2 leaders per country, city states are just kinda there, and gold is so, so easy to acquire in large stacks. Other than that, perfect!

Updated for Episodes 4 & 5
First off, compared to Season 1:
- The wierd/dodgy textures are fixed, it looks pretty good
- The movement (relative to POV) makes more sense
- More interesting quicktime sequences
And now to business:
I found S1 to be a thrilling game, I tried to protect Clemetine from bandits, cannibals and just plain wierdos - but I was unable to do so much of that, and it left me feeling guilty, sad and feeling quite a bit of empathy for both Lee and Clementine. After Lee's end at the conclusion of S1, S2 takes the view of Clemetine as the active protagonist; but here, I found, was the biggest problem that I had with the new season.
There were plenty of moments of surprise, intruige and danger as with the previous game, but to me it felt less like a true experience, and more like the generic cut-and-paste of other similar games. Lee tried to protect Clementine, only letting her do the dangerous bits when there was no choice - and I felt terrible letting her risk being eaten by fanatic cannibals; but here, its just the expected - Clementine's the lightest, send her off to steal something from a group of homicidal maniacs...
I'm not saying this is a bad game, not at all. What I am trying to say is that, although still great, it doesn't have the same depth as the first game. Sure, you try to protect a girl with a mental disability, and don't want friends to suffer even more loss, but it's not as a leader, making hard decisions, it's as a child, instead adding some sympathy to a situation out of your hands. This is the fatal flaw: you have no control (or illusion of it at least), it doesn't matter what you say or do, people will live or die on their own, and you can't save any of them.
Ep 4, 5:
Part of The Walking Dead is people dying, and having to deal with the consequences of bad choices. S1 really made you feel that, whereas the first part of S2 didn't. Episodes 4 and 5 however added a lot more depth to the emotion, it wasn't just watching people die anymore, here you had the option; do I save A or B? Do I risk my life and/or everyone else's to save one person? This was the major improvement that I noticed, I really felt involved in the game again, and right at the end it was a heart wrenching choice between friendship and survival - it honestly had me tearing up.

Civ IV was the last title worth paying for.  Once you learn a decent build order in V/VI there is no point playing beyond the Ancient Era. The game will be snowballing in your favor and the AI will *never* comeback.
Unstackable troops and ranged defenders allow you to easily advance through the game with a single ranged unit defending each base. The AI will randomly declare war, throw away 2-4 units and sue for peace.
When two AI factions are warring with eachother, wait until a city defense is low. Declare war and annex/raze the city on a single turn. The victim will sue for peace and the attacker just moves on. Rinse and repeat.
There is no punishment for these tactics. They will lead to a quick and easy domination win on the highest difficulties while producing only a handful of units.
Without stackable units the only way to make the game challenging is to DISABLE WAR COMPLETELY. What a joke. Don't buy.

I must start this by saying: I'm usually playing survival/strategy/shooter/horror games. Positive reviews made me try this "boring relationship simulator" and well... how wrong I could be! This game really surprised me in positive way!
Life is Strange is really well made piece of art. It's hard to tell much about game content itself without spoiling it. So I will focus on simple pros and cons.
Pros:
- It's beautiful. Both characters and environment in game are really well made.
- Sounds are great and there's plenty of well made voiceacting.
- Everything works smoothly and I never had lag, bug or single crash.
- Story. Even as "oldbie" who plays totally different kind of games normally, I was totally hooked in story of Life is Strange. As episodes move on, story goes deeper with many nice surprises. It kept me interested from episode 1 to maybe 4.5. More about this on cons.
- Your choises actually matter and some of them have severe consequenses in others.
- There's lots of "optional" things to do in this game and between episodes game lets you know how you have done things when compared to other players.
Cons:
- Some of game statistics were wrong between episodes. Special game mechanic must have been confusing things up.
- This same mechanic (which was cool and nice at first) was slowly starting to annoy me. In last episode things were starting to be way too shattered and I was kinda losing my focus. Start of last episode was great but soon everything felt kinda pointless and I was just waiting for game to come to an end.
That's it. From my point of view this game has way more pros than cons. I really love to see that nowdays there are masterpieces like this game with deep well thought story and characters. I thought those days are gone.
10/10! If you know "story rich games" as well made as this, feel free to recommend them to me.

This game is beautiful. The choices you can make are intense and the story is so deep. Some parts of the game are so intense that you will be bring to tears. The plot twists and the ending are gorgeous. You can even relate to the history.
Why, then, am I not recommending this game?
Because the premise of the game is basically a fraud.
First, the choices you make doesn't really matter. The main story is always the same and only a few elements are different. Elements that are, at best, simple spices. In the free episode, for instance, you can choose to tell about a guy with a gun or hide the truth. If you tell about him, he's summoned to the principal's office and then he confronts you, making the possibility to meet a new NPC. Makes sense. If you choose to hide the truth, without a reason, he still confronts you and yet, you again meet that NPC. Why would he fight you? It doesn't make sense! The story could have been different, you didn't meet this NPC, the story goes to a whole new one... but no. It sticks to the same every time.
Second, the game, considering the vast choices you can make, only have two endings. How can a game that defines itself as "everything has a major consequence" have only two simple and generic endings? True, the endings can change a little bit from time to time, but only for one or two extra NPCS. Lame.
Third, this game has no replay value at all. The consequences are, unlike everything is presented, lame and simple. It will always happens the same way, nothing major changes. The story at first is amazing, but discovering that it cannot be altered despiste of what choices you make gives you a boring game.
This game had the pottential to be an epic gem with an ever changing story deppending on your actions, but it barks more than it bites. It's nothing but a little upgrade to go to the movies. If you love the story you may stick to it for a few times, but don't expect hours and hours of fun, because they aren't.

The long awaited sequel to the acclaimed Telltale adventure, The Walking Dead: Season 2 offers just as much excitement and emotion as its predecessor. The game now allows players to take the role of the beloved Clementine, whom we saw abandoned at the close of Season 1. Clem is now older and more hardened to her cruel apocalypse life. Players quickly meet new characters (friends and foes) that have many mysteries behind them. Though at first it is hard to accept those that feel like replacements for our lost allies of the first game, after Episode 1, I found I had warmed up to this interesting bunch. The new threat of a captivating villain known as Carver paralells events which have occured throughout the universe before. Although it seems like a repeat of the "evil group" trope we've come to know, this plot line (without giving away too much) has some twists. Many moments throughout bring heartache, tension, and moral conflicts the likes of which are not often given in video games. The final scene of the newest episode, In Harm's Way, is one of the most thrilling and hard-hitting gaming experiences I have ever had, causing my heart rate to rise and sticking with me for hours after (but again, no spoilers). Aside from some minor graphics errors (ie. objects phasing through each other) here and there, Season 2 has shown a great improvement. The controls are much easier to handle, allowing for better sensitity and a more user-friendly "choices" interface. The game also implements new actions, mostly involving the use of the arrow keys for dodging and loosening items. Overall, this game is a must have. I am very excited for the next installment, and hope that the story of Season 2 rounds of as amazingly as I expect it will.

Without a doubt my favourite game from my childhood. Being able to relive my old memories from the game and to be able to change between old and remastered graphics as well as sound was amazing. For its current price it may seem a little pricey for such an old game, but considering the remastered graphics sound and music, it is worth paying the full price to relive the old memories of it (if you have played the original game) or if you would just like to play a classic that is well remastered, go ahead and buy it.
Pros:
-Able to switch between original pixelated and newly remastered graphics as well as sound with the click of a button
-Great story
-Easy to use controls
-Newly added main menu, allows you to save, load saves, has a bonus menu and more
-Selective dialogues
-Skippable cutscenes
-Skippable Dialogue
-You are able to interact with certain objects in the game and as you progress further, you will need to find certain objects along the way.
-Able to interact with other characters, this being talking to or fighting other bikers on the road with your fists, feet, or weapons that you find along the way
Cons:
-During cutscenes, the audio is out of sync, sometimes by 5 or more seconds (This was an issue that I and some others encountered, apparently there is a fix which did not work for me), this only happened to me during cutscenes, during normal conversations in the game there was no delay in the audio
-Short game, can be finished in under 3 hours (The original game was released in 1995 which is understandable)
-Can seem 'too easy', requiring simple thinking to continue further through the story
TL:DR
Overall I would rate this game 9/10, with my only real issue in the game being the out of sync audio during conversation cutscenes. The game may be short but it is worth replaying to get 100% completion. The game allows for overall great interaction with the other characters, being fighting other bikers, using objects scattered around the world to progress further into the game and the dialogue with other characters. Easy at times, certain parts will leave you thinking or send you off to Google to find out how to pass it. Other than that, I cannot find more fault in the game, it remains my favourite game from my childhood.

This is a really solid graphic adventure with an intruiging story and interesting time travel game mechanics. When Max Caufield witnesses a girl get murdered in the rest room, strange things happen and she discovers she can rewind events and change the outcome of the future. The girl she saved turns out to be an estranged friend, Chloe, and over the course of the 5 episode story arc, the two will slowly rebuild their friendship while trying to uncover the mystery of a missing girl.
The gameplay mostly takes place in the school and around town, it's basically like a high school drama, only with time travel and dark secrets. Some of the dialogue can be a bit hokey, but over all I really liked Max and Chloe as characters, and I built up a strong relationship with them as the series went on, which really helped the emotional moments of the game carry weight. I cared about what happened to them, despite some clunky lines, so kudos to DontNod for that.
There are lots of twists and turns in the story, and if you have ever seen anything that involves time travel, you probably already guessed that messing with the timeline is never a good idea and its just as true here. The way its incorporated into the game is clever though and it's always fun to mess around with it, even while you are asking yourself "What am I screwing up this time around?.
As far as general gameplay goes, it reminds me a little of Telltales work in that it's a very cinematic, narrative experience. Though I'll be honest, I felt that Life is Strange is a bit less linear and more interactive than the typical Telltale title.
If you are on the fence, watch some of the trailers or download the first episode. It's free. If you like what you play through, get the series, as it just gets better as they go along. There are two endings, though unless you are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, there is really only one. Just saying.

This "game" is seriously challenging, but it is also so much fun that I have clocked more hours in this game than any other I own.  You build a rocket or plane and try to make it do whatever the missions require you to do.  Sometimes the physics engine will ruin your day.  Sometimes things blow up and you just don't understand why.  That said, I still love it.  It makes you think.
The flight simulator aspect of this (think airplanes) is not as accurate as some flight simulators on the market.  However, the space simulator aspect of it is better than anything I've played.  There are limitations to the game engine, yet that doesn't stop me from trying 'just one more time' to make the perfect rocket or to build another colony on another planet.
That said, this is not a 'casual' game and requires some good math skills and comprehension of physics to do well.  Yet, the amount of math and physics that I've learned just from playing Kerbal Space Program more than justifies all of the headaches and frustration that my little Kerbals have suffered with me.
The online forums are full of very intelligent people who discuss the various apsects of the game.  I currently run almost 100 mods in my game because the modding community is very serious and they add so much more to the game than the original developers did.  For example, there are mods to add the challenges of Life Support (food, water, waste), replace the Kerbin solar system with one that mimacs our own Sol system, Interstellar planets and warp drives, and graphics mods to add more 'Wow' to everything you see.
If you are on the fence about purchasing, there are LOTS of YouTube videos and websites dedicated to KSP and you should check them out to help you decide and to help you do well in the game.
Whether you are Elon Musk or a 14 year old who thinks math and science is boring, you'll definitely find something to challenge you in Kerbal Space Program.

I recommend this game to pretty much anyone but I have a few problems with season two as a whole.
First off the decision making isn't satasfying compared to season one. Lee helping Kenny or Lee telling Kenny to go F himself felt way more meaningful than compared to Clementine telling Sarah to grow up and quit crying. Making decisions in season one were that impactful it almost made or did make you want to reset the game just so you could make the opposite decision, I don't get that feeling with season two. Season two so far feels rushed, each episode takes around 1 hour to an hour and a half tops to complete and the stroy feels like it hasn't even progressed since the end of the last episode to the beginning of this one. The narrative feels weak in season two as apposed to season one. Season two feels like an animation which is some what interactive and I use "some what" loosely. The narritive feels dominant so expect to be sitting with your chin inthe palm of your hand waiting for a dialogue option. The cast of characters in my opinion are very weak as compared to the cast of characters in season one.  Why is an eleven year old character the main potagonist? It takes all believability away from the story and setting that TTG are trying so hard to create. The build up for Kenny's return was sloppy and it fell flat on it's face. The player left Kenny in a "he's not getting out of that alive situation" and in season two we're just meant to live with the fact that he survived it, there's no explination, flashback or anything to give the player a realistic idea. The character writting in my opinion is appalling, Kenny being the way he was in season one was okay. That was because we had such a strong lead character - Lee that could keep him grounded, their personalities in that aspect gelled perfectly. No character in season two has a personality that can combat Kenny, now it feels like a grown man who is having his time of the month. For the player, it will get annoying FAST. There is nothing to really complain about in terms of voice acting, except that TTG really should start bringing in more actors instead of giving the parts to the same few people. Adam Harrington being the best voice actor in my opinion to voice act. The transition from Lee - a thirty seven year old to Clementine - an eleven year old was a very bad idea in my opinion. The way characters like Luke and Kenny trust only Clementine to watch their back is innocent in itself, but when they trust her over other adults with guns is completely unrealistic. Sarah is my favourite character for one reason. She is the only believable character, she treats the zombies or "walkers" like real threats instead of Luke taking Clementine to clear a bridge full of walkers like it's no deal what so ever. The fact that only one character in The Walking Dead season two treats the enemy as a dangerous threat really annoys me. Sarah is older than Clementine and is treated like an infant when compared.
In all, The Walking Dead is a masterpiece. I tried to give an honest overview rather than being a straight up "fanboy" If you haven't played it, I'm sorry to say but you're missing out.

Somehow the game manages to transcend ordinary storytelling where events are happening ‘in-front-of’ the viewer/player and rather makes them feel like they are happening ‘to’ the player. Caution: this game can hit you hard enough to wake you. Or even break you.

is a turn-based strategy game (TBS) in which players attempt to steer a historical civilization (such as the Romans, Arabs, Chinese, etc.) to world domination by any and all means. The sixth game in the
franchise, it does a very good job of maintaining the series' reputation for addictive gameplay that will keep you up all night.
- The game doesn't hog resources, and should run well on most systems, even older PCs and laptops/netbooks. You might not be able to max out all of the graphics settings, but you should still be able to get reasonable quality without sacrificing performance. However, those playing on older, slower machines will likely suffer from fairly long load times.
- Initially, many people were concerned about the game's art style, which was criticized as being "cartoony" and resembling a mobile phone game. The final version of the game, however, looks quite attractive, with the new art style making it somewhat easier to differentiate between different units, tile improvements, etc. It looks good, even on lower settings, although in these cases textures may get a bit blurry if you zoom in too far. The game's audio design is also excellent, with the soundtrack providing a good deal of ambiance without becoming intrusive or distracting.
- All of the game's playable civilization each have a distinct playstyle, with each being stronger in different portions of the game and more attuned towards certain victory types. For example, Scythia gets free cavalry in the early game, encouraging military expansion, while Brazil gets bonuses toward Great Person generation, encouraging culture and tourism.
- The old "culture" system from previous games has been completely revamped. Culture still drives order expansion, but, rather than being "banked" and used to unlock bonuses from specific trees, cultured is now used much in the same way as research, gradually unlocking "civics" which allow new buildings, units, and policies. "Policies" canbe slotted in and out within the basic framework of a certain type of government (Oligarchy, Democracy, etc.), making it easier to customize your civilization's government on the fly.
- Most buidlings are now constructed within specialized "districts" outside of the city center. These districts are divided into certai specializations (culture, production, etc.) and are limited in number, forcing players to plan strategically rather than simply constructing every building in every city. The spread-out nature of districts also serves to make raiding far more attractive as a military option.
- The enemy AI tends to be somewaht disorganized and passive. Rival civilizations will often simply expand aimlessly for much of the game, rarely focsuing on a specific strategy or trying to actively interfere with the player's attempts to win.
- With the overhaul of the culture system, research has been reduced in importance somewhat. There are now only a handful of techs for each era of the game, mostly focused on unlocking new military units. The effect is that developing new technologies now feels less important than it probably should, seeming to function more as a glorified upgrade tree for military unites than a major gameplay mechanic.
- During certain stretches of the game, it can feel like there are not enough different types of military units. For example, "knights" upgrade straight to "tanks", with nothing in between.
- While the diplomacy system does introduce some interesting new concepts, such as hidden AI "agendas", much of it is locked until fairly late in the game, making diplomacy a bit of a useless exercise for much of the game.
- The UI is somewaht poorly layed out, with essential information often spread out across multiple menus, making managing a large late-game empire needlessly frustrating.
- The current crop of DLC for the game is of good quality, but feels somewhat overpriced ($5 for a single scenario, for example).
This should be a good game for parents of young children. It doesn't have child-unfriendly things like gore and nudity, and encourages planning and critical thinking. Plus, it can help to teach them about history, and about other cultures.
Despite the somewhat-ineffective AI and other issues, this is still both a great strategy game, and a great
game. Addictive, and highly recommended.

So if you like the Civ genre and you have some familiarity with Civ V, I think you will find just about the same game waiting for you here. However, the game is less cluttered and less automated.
The game does not feature:
-production queues
-automated workers
-trade spreadsheets or memory
-golden ages
-ideologies and separated social policy trees
Also, workers also expire after a number of uses.
The game has new features like:
-religious war
-districts, which are like mini-cities on an improved tile
-a new great person scheme: you compete with other civs for great people
-a policy tree exactly like the tech tree
Also, the game lends itself to war, instead of peace due to the AI being basically the same, but with a second goal as an additional variable to their decision making. Personally, I feel that the game is like a more mature version of Civ V, but unrelated to Civ IV. One last thing: strategic view is pretty amazing. Check it out.

Life Is Strange is an overall stunning game that has left its players stumped back in reality with emotions not often felt in such amounts. The story that this game tells is an extremely compelling one that gets harder and harder to put down the more progress you make into it. The characters will capture your heart and the world they live in will capture your mind. The artstyle of the game is unique and it does well for it, combined with the skillfully chosen soundtrack, this game really seems more like a fine piece of art than a 'game'. While the experience does not carry billion poly characters in super dazzling 4K resolution, you'll find the game as visually spectacular as its story is gripping. The gameplay is similar to other story-telling games like many of the TellTale series and other related titles, and at times can be tedious and immersion breaking. Despite this, Life Is Strange has left a special place in my heart and likely a reminder to others that video games can be so much more than just the yearly COD rehash. I would highly recommend that even if you're only considering, put the game on your wishlist and nab it when it goes on sale. You won't regret it.

A poor, almost amateur, rendition of a AAA game. This game continues the trend of the popular Civilization series to coast on popularity and good looks, pouring a large budget into game assets while ignoring the AI. Despite its importance in a single player strategy game, the AI continues to get stupider with Civilization VI. Not only is the AI essentially broken, the game design is fundamentally flawed as it turns the playing experience into an exercise in micromanagement that is difficult to balance and is a nightmare to write AI for. This micromanagement serves to distract the player from the game's shortcomings: it is a single player strategy game with a hopelessly incompetent AI and poor game balance. After playing every game in the series, it is sad to see it develop like this.

If you haven't played season 1, leave right now. Other than that, no spoilers from season 2, I promise.
Mechanically, the game plays out the same as season one, with slight changes here and there- the action select bar has been improved, making it less easy to try to pick up a gun and have your character say "Wow, a gun." They also added in a faster walk mechanic- I won't say sprint becauser sometimes it is just a fast walk. These seem like minor changes, but they make a great game even better.
The game has you playing as clem, following Lee's little "accident", and initially, I have to admit, I didn't really like playing as her that much. Without Lee always at her side, she felt somewhat dry as a character. However, after playing a bit, i started to see that Clem has much more personality than I thought. She just kind of hides it in an attempt to stay strong.
Overall, the game gets  a 9.5/10 from me so far. My one honest complaint is that the episodes feel a bit shorter, but maybe thats because when i start one I end up tanking through the whole episode. It's a great game, and if you liked season 1, you'll love this one.

Is this game similar to Overwatch? Yes. Is it Overwatch? No.
The biggest thing I enjoy about this game is the customization of a characters abilities with cards. You have 12 points to spend on customizing, each card costs 1, and you have to select 5. From there, you can upgrade each card for 1 point per upgrade. I have fully enjoyed it and making a character more my own instead of the same thing each and every time. And being able to save multiple decks allows you to play a game how you want to play.
You also earn credits during matches in which you can spend on upgrades. Lowering cool down timers, increasing your speed, increasing damage, decreasing reload times, etc.. They are only saved per match and everything resets when you go to another game.
The game is free to play. And it means it. Every item that affects how the game plays can be earned by playing. No pay to win tactics, and they are not severly over priced. I already unlocked 2 more characters with 4 hours of playtime. Could have been 3 but I also purchased some cards.
The game feels like Overwatch, and it is great that it does for me, but this is not Overwatch.

Life Is Strange is an overall stunning game that has left its players stumped back in reality with emotions not often felt in such amounts. The story that this game tells is an extremely compelling one that gets harder and harder to put down the more progress you make into it. The characters will capture your heart and the world they live in will capture your mind. The artstyle of the game is unique and it does well for it, combined with the skillfully chosen soundtrack, this game really seems more like a fine piece of art than a 'game'. While the experience does not carry billion poly characters in super dazzling 4K resolution, you'll find the game as visually spectacular as its story is gripping. The gameplay is similar to other story-telling games like many of the TellTale series and other related titles, and at times can be tedious and immersion breaking. Despite this, Life Is Strange has left a special place in my heart and likely a reminder to others that video games can be so much more than just the yearly COD rehash. I would highly recommend that even if you're only considering, put the game on your wishlist and nab it when it goes on sale. You won't regret it.

There comes a time when you play a game and you just think to yourself.."This is why I play games.." The Walking Dead is just one of those games.
I know that for a lot of people what makes a game good or bad is a subjective experience but for me just seeing the consequence of my actions and how I interact with the universe that's been created for me is so much more gratifying then watching it unfold passively or just mindlessly shooting monsters.  Being able to connect with the characters as well as feel the pangs of regret when you made the wrong choice affecting their survival makes a game that much more memorable.
This game may not have state of the art graphics or challenging gameplay, but if you love a meaningful, artistic and emotional storytelling experience then this game is definitely for you. The only negative I can find about this game for me is the agonizing wait for the new episodes to drop.

I made a joke review about this game a while back,so i decided to make a new one which is more serious. At the moment Civ 6 is very unbalanced. Problem 1: Civilizations declaring war and not sending troops (or sending only a small amount). This has happened 2 or 3 times to me, but that doesn't mean it's always going to be like that. Most of the time i see nations doing this, when i'm moving troops next to my borders.

Norway hates me, because i have no navy, i build 1, i repeat, 1 ship  and they compliment me. Aren't they supposed to have a big navy? I've encountered this '' issue" alot.
Problem 4 : Call for aid. So in my playtrough my delcared friend asked to join his war against Spain. I utterly destroy him and Capture his cities, everybody including my declared friend denounces me because i'm warmongering. It's just so dumb.
And those are the major ( or at least what i think are major) problems.
But it is still a fun game to play. If you don't want to spend 60 euro on this that's fine. And trust me when civ 7 comes out than its going to be the same.

I am a big fan of Overwatch and Battleborn. All I knew about this game is that it was very similar to these two games, but free to play. And a couple of my friends had said that it was blatantly copying Overwatch.
So, I was pleasantly surprised, when I downloaded it on a whim, to find that there is, in fact, more to this game than that. It is a fairly enjoyable game, and it is surprisingly unique...
Unfortunately, there are a few problems that I have. I know that this is a video game, and that most people would tell me to suck it up, but the presentation of the women characters in this game is goddawful. It is disgusting. They are designed for sex appeal, and no other reason beside that. This was something that turned me off from the game, initially.
The game also lacks things to do. I found that the two gamemodes and the handful of maps don't get old as easily as you would think, but they are definitely starting to wear a little thin for me. I understand that this is a beta release, and that this will probably get changed, but until then I feel like I might be getting bored with this game somewhat soon.
Now, all that being said, this game is a very good game. Surprisingly so. It is fun, and it is different. Despite several characters being almost the exact same as an Overwatch character. I would definitely recommend it, especially if you lack the specs or the money to play Overwatch.

A unique gem that, in my honest opinion, has to be played at least once in one's life. An experience that can't be really put in words because it has so much to offer, from the intriguing story, the well-developed, easy to relate characters and incredible and emotional voice acting all the way to the incredible amount to details, the nice little gameplay idea and also the soundtrack, which, in my opinion, is simply the best a game has to offer because it adds such a high amount of emotion. It is so easy to get immersed and lose yourself into the experience not only because of the characters but also because of the story itself which presents real life problems like suicide, friendship, drugs, violence, abuse and many more – thank God that Square Enix offered the developers the creative freedom that they needed!
Of course, there are a few little bugs here and there, most notably some missing lip syncing in the last episode. However, I didn’t experience anything else that could break the immersion. Performance-wise, the game ran great on my laptop and it can be easily run even on lower-spec computers.
For such a low price, I can’t recommend this game enough as it will remain in my heart for a very long time. So prepare yourself for a rewarding emotional experience, one that could even change your life!

1) The AI is out of control. It's one of the worst Civ AI's yet. They will literally declare war for nothing, even if you ignore every trade request or if you give them gifts. It makes very little sense.

3) The Game is too easy. It can be beaten on the hardest difficulty much, MUCH easier than Civilization V.
4) There's still no punishment for quitters in multiplayer. I've tried to get into multiple matches, and every single one has resulted in people quitting after early wonders are built.
5) The game is way more combat based than the other civs. It seems like every time I *try* to go for some other sort of win, the AI forces me into combat and I find it easier to simply march over the enemies after their poor attempts at city-capturing.
It's disappointing, hopefully the game will get better with expansions. It's too bad that most people depend on expansions to make games great nowadays instead of the core game being good.

This game, like Season 1, is a brilliant adaptation of the comic books. Gameplay is very dialogue-based as opposed to action-based, which I see as a big plus. I tend to be very invested in the characters and the decisions they make, so I enjoy those parts more than the fighting and killing zombie parts. Nevertheless, combat is easy enough to master that even someone not very used to fighting games can get the hang of it. Season 2 seems to have a lot less action sequences overall, making some of the most recent episodes feel more like you're watching a movie and occasionally picking dialogue. The plot is solid and enticing, and definitely leaves you waiting for the next episode's release. Although both Season 1 and 2 involve making a lot of choices for the group, after you make choices and do some research you find that your choices have very little effect on the plot and major characters living and dying. I completely get that it would be difficult and probably pointless for the developers to make entirely different "segments" of the game that different players get to experience based on their choices, but I often feel that my choices don't count for all that much, aside from how the characters view me.

It has same lacks as Civ V, stupid AI in warfare and diplomacy, unbalanced difficulty where AIs get unfair bonus and just build more armies and try to erase you earlier.
It has some improvements which entertain me enough to spend a couple of hours to discover them.
67 hours and I'm now done. It's nearly 1€ per hour. It's up to you to agree with that. I don't and I'm pretty disappointed to have bought it.

I am a big fan of Overwatch and Battleborn. All I knew about this game is that it was very similar to these two games, but free to play. And a couple of my friends had said that it was blatantly copying Overwatch.
So, I was pleasantly surprised, when I downloaded it on a whim, to find that there is, in fact, more to this game than that. It is a fairly enjoyable game, and it is surprisingly unique...
Unfortunately, there are a few problems that I have. I know that this is a video game, and that most people would tell me to suck it up, but the presentation of the women characters in this game is goddawful. It is disgusting. They are designed for sex appeal, and no other reason beside that. This was something that turned me off from the game, initially.
The game also lacks things to do. I found that the two gamemodes and the handful of maps don't get old as easily as you would think, but they are definitely starting to wear a little thin for me. I understand that this is a beta release, and that this will probably get changed, but until then I feel like I might be getting bored with this game somewhat soon.
Now, all that being said, this game is a very good game. Surprisingly so. It is fun, and it is different. Despite several characters being almost the exact same as an Overwatch character. I would definitely recommend it, especially if you lack the specs or the money to play Overwatch.

Instead of being a guardian and leader, the role has switched to being a lesser member of the group that is not as strong or as capable as others. However, therein lies the beauty of the game. There is so much more importance in dealing with other characters and managing group cohesion. Season 2 highlights how important relationships are and knowing what to say to certain people at the right time- something most games seem to ignore.

Unfortunatley it's a far cry from the previous games in the series and not one I'm a huge fan of. I was really looking forward to Civ VI's after having played all the previous sequels and still having played Civ V quite regularly, although it's starting to feel dated.

Not only are there too many restirictions that even the original Civilization game didn't have (which barely ran on my 386SX-16 back in the days), but it has a lot of idiosyncrasies that just makes it frustrating to play.
The new districts are a cool idea, but they don't allow you to extend the reach of your city, instead they limit what you can build. The forced placement of wonders can also be annoying, especially as 90% of the time, the only place you can place them is on top of a resource.
The lack of world map options are also disappointing compared to Civ V, even the base game. The fact that you can't remove districts if you build the wrong thing by mistake is just plain silly and a lot of the wonders feel like they lack usefulness compared to the past games.
Somehow Civ VI feels like it has lost the heart and sould of the Civ series of games and I actually regret buying in hindsight as I haven't enjoyed playing it. In fact, it's been so frustratingly annoying at times, that I've only finished a single game.

A unique gem that, in my honest opinion, has to be played at least once in one's life. An experience that can't be really put in words because it has so much to offer, from the intriguing story, the well-developed, easy to relate characters and incredible and emotional voice acting all the way to the incredible amount to details, the nice little gameplay idea and also the soundtrack, which, in my opinion, is simply the best a game has to offer because it adds such a high amount of emotion. It is so easy to get immersed and lose yourself into the experience not only because of the characters but also because of the story itself which presents real life problems like suicide, friendship, drugs, violence, abuse and many more – thank God that Square Enix offered the developers the creative freedom that they needed!
Of course, there are a few little bugs here and there, most notably some missing lip syncing in the last episode. However, I didn’t experience anything else that could break the immersion. Performance-wise, the game ran great on my laptop and it can be easily run even on lower-spec computers.
For such a low price, I can’t recommend this game enough as it will remain in my heart for a very long time. So prepare yourself for a rewarding emotional experience, one that could even change your life!

The game is great and "bla bla bla" like most reviews say. If you like simulation games and/or space stuff, get it, you'll like it.
Now, if you're new to it, or if you're coming back after playing older versions, you may find this helpful (regarding the new aerodynamics and heat systems):
1 - If your rocket is flipping right/soon after launch, add some wings to its bottom. If it's happening on the 2nd or later stages, still within the atmosphere, add wings to the appropriate stage's central area.
2 - If you're failling to get back into the atmosphere after leaving it, put a heat shield at the bottom of your bottom-most part (out of those left when you're coming back), hit the atmosphere in an angle as close to the horizontal as possible (from orbit, pull the periapsis in, stop as soon as it sinks into the planet and let your vessel fall by itself from there) and head in butt-first (heat shield up front, your pod facing retrograde).
The game still has some annoying bugs. Again, it's great, like everyone says, but:
Sometimes when leaving Kerbin (already above 100km high, beyond the atmosphere, not accelerating nor anything, just chilling...) your rocket will start circling around-- not spinning nor flipping, but it's core/axis actually moving around in space-- and half of it will explode. You'll have to build a new rocket... and if you rebuild exactly the same one, that will, most likely, NOT happen again.
Sometimes, after re-entering the atmosphere and close to landing, what's left of your rocket will simply explode when opening your parachutes (the last time it happened to me, at 100m/s, 2km high).
So, some unexplainable, illogical stuff happens once in a while-- and way more frequently than you'd like: a part that allows you to lay a "sheet" over other parts above it, to protect them from heat, (although I'm very fond of it...) might decide it doesn't want to close, so you will have to start a new rocket from scratch; your Space Center's launch pad may decide to explode all of a sudden for no reason whatsoever when you're about to launch something into space; while doing something important way out there, half-way through your mission, your ship may stop responding (but when this happens, you can mess with the game speed or go to the map and back and it'll start working again).
The save feature also annoys me-- because it should have been perfected about 7 years ago (or so) when they first release Kerbal Space Station in early access. Every time you want to manually save your game, the game opens a small box written "quicksave" in it, so you have to re-type your save's name every single time. To know what save-games you have, you either must go to the "Load" screen or take a guess (when saving and trying to overwrite one). The "Load" screen also doesn't give you enough information about "when" each game was saved so you have to either remember yourself or go by trial and error. This is something minor, of course, but given how basic this is and how long the game has been under development, it's really crappy.
Even with these issues, the game is still very fun. There's a strong sense of reward when you manage to pull off something hard and it also teaches you some interesting stuff about space navigation.

If you wanna experience pain and torture without leaving the house, then this is the game for you.

Kerbal Space Program is THE prototype of a successful indie game, and argueably one of the best space exploration games. "But why?", you may ask. And this why I'm writing this review here.
The short answer is, "Because space is awesome!" but I'm not here to give short answers. The real thing is, this game takes the math-filled boring science stuff that lies behind the concept of space travel and hides it behind an easy-accessible and fun environment: A rocket that leaves the ground is built in a matter of minutes. Only a short click on the 'launch' button and a bunch of death-defying kerbonauts makes their way towards space... only to find that they are coming back sooner than expected. The wonderful thing is, that the nature of the game encourages the player to use trial and error. If you don't get far enough into space, add moar boosters, if the whole rocket wobbles like a flying worm, add moar struts. What would cost billions of dollars (and probably many people's lives) in real life is every day work in KSP: if your flight didn't work quite as intended, just hit 'revert' and that whole thing never happened, except you can now try to fix what was wrong before and take another shot.
But the best part is, although your green companions' comic reactions will make every fatal disfunction of your vessel hilarous as hell, there is a lot of serious business behind the game - Although trial and error will eventually get you to your goal, your missions are going to be a lot more successful if you understand the physics of this game, which closes the cycle: the game makes you WANT to know all that math-filled boring science stuff that lies behind the concept of space travel I mentioned earlier. And surprisingly, it is a lot more satisfying to return from a successful mission if your calculations told you beforehand that it should work.
Plus, its career mode will always provide you with fun challenges that go beyond "Land on object XY".  Building space stations, deploying satellites, taking surveys, redirecting or landing asteroids, etc. are possibly objectives of the contracts that fund your space program. So if you always wanted to manage your very own space program, this is the perfect game for you.
And if you still not have enough, that game has one of the liviest communities I've seen so far. Hundreds of mods already exist and if you'll ever feel like anything should be added, there's a 99% chance a mod that implements that already exists.
TL;DR:
It's a wonderful, easy-accessible, fun and actually educating game that really outstands in a time where soulless shooters are the majority.

Real review:
The first Sid Meirer game I got into was Civ 5, loved the game, got all the DLC, it was fantastic. So I felt th at possibly this next installment would be even better! You take your accomplishments with you and you learn from your mistakes, right?
Well, not so much with Civ 6.
Civ 6 is very fun to learn, all of the planning needed to make an addition to your kingdom is actually very enjoyable, I love that part, planning your districts and great wonders is very fun! But one thing that just RUINS the game for is the AI, you have to understand that normally I'm a pacifist and just try to get a bunch of science and gold/turn. Let me tell you about one of my saves that I documented.
Turn 42: Spanish + Empire of Kongo declare war, for no known reason, not even near my borders!
Turn 61: Brazil and India declare war, they're even FARTHER from my borders.
Turn 76: Germany thinks my units are near his borders, nearest Archer is 5 tiles away, ON MY CITY. He has 4 warriors and 1 slinger near my border, he's a declared friend.
Turn 88: Norway declares war, I just met him 2 turns prior via units, we don't know where each other's cities are.
Turn 106: India wants 66 gold/turn in exchange for peace, none of our units have died, the Spanish are moving units towards my cities again.
Turn 121: Germany, my previous friend, declared war on my for no known reason, though they were near my borders, maybe they wanted to expand?
Turn 127: The Spanish declare war, possibly to try to expand, I'm now at war with 5 out of 7 (excluding myself) nations.
Turn 147: Sumerian Emp. delcared war, we've had great trade relations.
This is just SOME of the crap you encounter with the AI, this of course was one of my worst saves, but there have been many too close to this. I understand Civs declare war on eachother more frequently and for less of a reason in the early game, but this, this is too much. Then if I take one of their cities, they will never stop denouncing me for it!
Although, I still recommend this game, 7 out of 10 I'd say. I'd really like to see some adjustments to the AI, and some of the units, Infantry and Mechanized Infantry take WAY TOO MUCH to kill. The 3 star Infantry with no upgrades took 2 strikes from Jet Fighters, 1 strike from Artillary, 1 Strike from Modern Armor, and an attack from my city. That's way too much.

This is a great simulator-game. I really like the realistic physics; if you's expect it in the real world, you can probably expect it here in terms of the physics department. Center of mass, center of lift, and center of weight are all rather important issues for planes and large rockets. Piloting the ships and collecting data is pretty fun. Ship building is a rather complex process, but that's a good thing. It really makes you think about the design of your ship. Sure, you can add a lab for research, but you better figure out how to provide enough thrust to lift it, and enough fuel for the thrust. And you always tell yourself, "one more launch," or, "one more tweak," but... Well, it just sucks you in.
I'd recommend this to any space or physics nerd (both of which I am).
PS: If you do get this game, try science mode to start out with. You don't have the nagging constraints of monetary restriction and public relations in it, but you are required to collect data to research new parts. This will help pace you by starting you off with basic parts and adding more complex stuff later as opposed to being overwhelmed by all of the parts in creative that you don't know what they do.
