I have to say, as a longtime fan of Civ 4 (and having never played 5), that this game is a great example of that system redesigned to work better, and to be more fun. I do like this game. The animations are fantastic, the unit system has be reworked nicely (no death stacks!), the science is more rewarding, and the new religion and culture systems are very well designed. The district system works very well, and has you planning what you're going to do with your cities LONG before you have the ability to do what you want with them. You must actually plan what type of victory you're trying to achive and go all in for it from the very beggining, and you are NOT able to switch gears halfway though.
That all being said, this game looses quite a few points for it's AI. The AI loves to hate you. Just you. They'll have plenty of friends to bring into a war, they'll have many things to throw against you, and if you aren't holding a strong military, they will attack you, they will capture and raze your cities, and the other AI don't seem to care. When you do the same, it puts you in a VERY bad postition with other leaders, so having one enemy is nearly impossible. It's also VERY VERY hard to go through the game without igniting a war. I haven't managed a peaceful playthough yet, though I have played quite a few hours.
A religious victory is completely out of the question, unless you happen to get stonehenge, boost your religion, and throw it everywhere before they have a chance.  They will often accuse you of doing things you aren't doing, and even if you're following what they want you do be doing, they will still denounce you if you slip up once. They also have a system where you can get open borders, perhaps because you need to get through thier terf to get to a hated enemy, but then, moving your troops though, they'll denounce you, and force all your troops out of thier borders, because you moved troops too close to thier cities. The AI feels unfair, but if you're trying for a warmonger playthough, or you aren't trying to make friends, they still don't like to upgrade units, or make smart war decisions. I've had the AI declare war on me, I destroy a couple of thier outdated galleys with submarines, than they sue for peace, attempting to hand me half of thier avaliable funds and receources.
And for the love of god, turn down the barbarians. You expect them to plauge you for awhile, but when I'm in the modern era, or the Information era, and I still have barbarian outposts popping up litterally EVERY SINGLE TURN WITHOUT STOPPING, you may need to tune it own just a bit. I can't count the number of times I've been right outside my territory, moving my army, or builders or something, and they pop an outpost right outside sight range, so if I'm moving a builder, I have to stop, move them back, move  military unit to clear it, than procede, and it happens again. If it's an army, I have to hold the rest of the army up for a turn while one of them deals with the outpost, than hold to heal, start going, and it happens again. This is annoying, and not at all good design.
THOSE bits aren't fun, but if you can overlook that, or play on an easier difficulty, I do recomend picking it up.
POST UPDATE EDIT: I have had a bit more time, and have been able now to pull off a religious victory with a peceful playthough. Still had to keep a decently sized military (they don't like it when they found a religion and you convert thier citizens) and it was a very low scoring run, but it is now possible. They also seemed to have tweaked the AI to be friendlier to you, as the AI is now sending me delegations when we first meet, and sem to accept mine more often. Mind that this is on King, anything higher than that, and they may start attacking you just because difficulty.

I have to say, as a longtime fan of Civ 4 (and having never played 5), that this game is a great example of that system redesigned to work better, and to be more fun. I do like this game. The animations are fantastic, the unit system has be reworked nicely (no death stacks!), the science is more rewarding, and the new religion and culture systems are very well designed. The district system works very well, and has you planning what you're going to do with your cities LONG before you have the ability to do what you want with them. You must actually plan what type of victory you're trying to achive and go all in for it from the very beggining, and you are NOT able to switch gears halfway though.
That all being said, this game looses quite a few points for it's AI. The AI loves to hate you. Just you. They'll have plenty of friends to bring into a war, they'll have many things to throw against you, and if you aren't holding a strong military, they will attack you, they will capture and raze your cities, and the other AI don't seem to care. When you do the same, it puts you in a VERY bad postition with other leaders, so having one enemy is nearly impossible. It's also VERY VERY hard to go through the game without igniting a war. I haven't managed a peaceful playthough yet, though I have played quite a few hours.
A religious victory is completely out of the question, unless you happen to get stonehenge, boost your religion, and throw it everywhere before they have a chance.  They will often accuse you of doing things you aren't doing, and even if you're following what they want you do be doing, they will still denounce you if you slip up once. They also have a system where you can get open borders, perhaps because you need to get through thier terf to get to a hated enemy, but then, moving your troops though, they'll denounce you, and force all your troops out of thier borders, because you moved troops too close to thier cities. The AI feels unfair, but if you're trying for a warmonger playthough, or you aren't trying to make friends, they still don't like to upgrade units, or make smart war decisions. I've had the AI declare war on me, I destroy a couple of thier outdated galleys with submarines, than they sue for peace, attempting to hand me half of thier avaliable funds and receources.
And for the love of god, turn down the barbarians. You expect them to plauge you for awhile, but when I'm in the modern era, or the Information era, and I still have barbarian outposts popping up litterally EVERY SINGLE TURN WITHOUT STOPPING, you may need to tune it own just a bit. I can't count the number of times I've been right outside my territory, moving my army, or builders or something, and they pop an outpost right outside sight range, so if I'm moving a builder, I have to stop, move them back, move  military unit to clear it, than procede, and it happens again. If it's an army, I have to hold the rest of the army up for a turn while one of them deals with the outpost, than hold to heal, start going, and it happens again. This is annoying, and not at all good design.
THOSE bits aren't fun, but if you can overlook that, or play on an easier difficulty, I do recomend picking it up.
POST UPDATE EDIT: I have had a bit more time, and have been able now to pull off a religious victory with a peceful playthough. Still had to keep a decently sized military (they don't like it when they found a religion and you convert thier citizens) and it was a very low scoring run, but it is now possible. They also seemed to have tweaked the AI to be friendlier to you, as the AI is now sending me delegations when we first meet, and sem to accept mine more often. Mind that this is on King, anything higher than that, and they may start attacking you just because difficulty.

Sono un fan della serie dai tempi di civ 2. Prima di recensirla ho voluto giocare per un po’ perché,di primo acchito, sono rimasto un po’ perplesso. Innanzitutto dirò che ho trovato questa versione particolarmente innovativa e, per quanto mi riguarda, credo di aver bisogno di più tempo di gioco per capirla bene. Tutta la strategia generale è diversa, lo sviluppo tecnologico è svincolato da quello delle politiche sociali,e le città si sviluppano in maniera abbastanza autarchica. In sintesi, mentre nella precedente versione bisognava pianificare la nascita delle nuove città (ad evitare deficit di moneta sul bilancio generale ed altri problemi), qui ho l’impressione che sia meglio costruire città subito ed in fretta. La gestione della città richiede una studiata pianificazione, il nuovo sistema dei distretti impone di organizzare bene dove e cosa costruire, una grande rivoluzione rispetto alle serie precedenti dove si procedeva in modo piuttosto meccanico. La diplomazia resta,purtroppo, un disastro e,se proprio devo dirla tutta, mi sembra la peggiore di tutta la serie. Pare quasi del tutto impossibile sviluppare un sensato percorso diplomatico, dato che gli avversari agiscono secondo schemi piuttosto irrazionali (ed anche ripetitivi). Di conseguenza i rapporti con le altre civiltà sono quasi sempre fortemente conflittuali, non si riesce in alcun modo a stabilire una logica interazione diplomatica. La religione ha una fortissima componente conflittuale che ,devo dire, potrebbe anche essere un po’ noiosa per la sua eccessiva invasività. Si viene infatti assaliti da orde di missionari sin dalle prime fasi, sono talmente tanti che in alcune partite ho lasciato che si scontrassero fra loro (ogni esponente attacca in “battaglia teologica” chiunque sia di fede diversa) per poi attaccare i superstiti….Le unità sono molte di meno,anche se ne compaiono alcune davvero utili e divertenti(tipo il medico ed il pallone da osservazione). Del tutto nuovo l’uso dei Lavoratori : ora la costruzione della miglioria è immediata ma si ha un numero limitato di interventi ,fatti i quali l’unità scompare. Inoltre ,stranamente, non possono costruire strade : queste le realizzano solo gli ingegneri militari (ma hanno pochissimi interventi disponibili) o le carovane commerciali. Questo sistema è piuttosto limitativo nelle possibilità di creare una buona rete stradale. Le varie schermate riepilogative(diplomazia, commercio, etc.) andrebbero migliorate, specie quella del commercio è piuttosto sommaria e poco intuitiva. L’AI è pessima, sinceramente mi aspettavo (visto che è il sesto capitolo) qualcosa di meglio. In realtà il problema è che,secondo me, il gioco è uscito in anticipo, ed è poco più di una beta. Sicuramente seguirà la solita messe di aggiornamenti e DLC (a pagamento e non) che porteranno il gioco a più alti livelli. In conclusione dirò che con tutti i suoi difetti, è un gioco che mi sembra abbia grandissime potenzialità e perciò il mio voto è positivo, nella convinzione che i prossimi aggiornamenti risolveranno i numerosi problemi presenti.

I'm a little shocked that I cannot recommend Civilization VI, given that I have played every game in the series (almost religiously) since Civilization II.
While I feel there are numerous positives to this game, there are also far to many drawbacks for me to recommend this product. The most glaring issues, from my perspective, are two things:
Want to build tall? Do you dream of establishing a small, powerful empire that can stand the test of time? Well, you best keep dreaming. In Civilization VI, since there are no penalties for founding cities, more cities = more bonuses. The game requires you to focus on expansion until there is simply no land left to colonize. If you do not make claiming everything around you your number one priority, rival civilzations will become too large to effectively deal with. While I have no issue with playing wide, it is frustrating to be forced into playing a particular style during the early portions of the game.
Why does Cleopatra hate me? Am I not tall, handsome, or Italian enough for her? She's on the other side of the world, yet she randomly sends letters telling me how much she despises me.
The AI in this game is exhausting to play against. Not exhausting in a 'difficult' way, it is exhausting in a
type of way. In Civilization VI, you would be wise to assume that everyone hates you. Yes,
. Did you just meet Queen Victoria? She hates you. What does that telegram from Teddy Roosevelt say? He's just reminding you of how much he hates you. Did you just see Gandhi waving at you from across the border? He's waving goodbye to you, because he completed the Manhattan Project 20 turns ago and the guy loves thermonuclear induced winter.
At the end of the day, Civilization VI has potential, however it lacks the magic of previous entries in the series. When I play this game, I do not feel like I'm going on adventure into the unknown with my empire. Too many gameplay elements make my decisions feel predetermined, which makes me no longer wonder of what lies ahead for my own civilization.
Stick with Civilization II, III, IV, V, or even Alpha Centari.

The follow up to the first season of Tell Tale's excellent "The Walking Dead" game follows Clementine, the little girl from the first season, and her misadventures with a group of generally unlikable people when compared to the first group of survivors. Gone are the days of lanky college kids who royally ♥♥♥♥ up even the smallest things, but in the end, strive for redemption in the eyes of the man he has wronged the most, only to gain the forgiveness of him when he least expects it.
Gone are the fantastic voice jobs by Dave Fennoy in the role of "Lee Everett", who makes a much better Pro-tah-gonist than Clementine does.
Speaking of Clementine, this game gets some flak for allowing you to go against her sweet and caring nature in the first game, and play her more as if Ted Bundy and Jeffrey Dahmer have claimed joint ownership of her body, which isn't exactly a bad thing. So what if you can threaten a pregnant woman, and tell a little girl to suck it up after her dad belts her acrossed the face? This is a post apocalyptic word, people. Even the kindest people are going to get hardened by seeing their closest friends and family taken from them in the blink of an eye.
While Season 2 isn't anywhere near the excellent narrative piece of the first season, it's still quite the experience. You even get to meet an old friend, who I was especially excited to see, even if his reason for being there is an excellent example of the writers just hand waving his mere existence at this point and time as mere fan service.
Also of note is, that as of this review, The Year of our Lord 2014, June 26th, there are still about two episodes left to be released, so when you complete the game, you can wait for the next episodes in real time! Talk about padding!

The walking Dead Season 2 is yet another game from Telltale games and I am getting increasingly wanting to play their other point and click adventure games. Back in 2012 when season 1 was brand new, I didn't get it for ages because despite the hype it was a point and click adventure game, how boring does that sound?! I eventually bought it on Sale and was not disappointed, worth every cent and more! Season 2 takes off of course after Season 1 and the "400 Days" DLC in-between the two seasons with every choice you make from Season 1 and the DLC 400 Days carried on into Season 2. Just like Season one the graphics were phenomenal and were very appropriate considering the game (and the TV show by the same name by the way) are based off a series of comic books so it fits to have the art style the way it is, but the HUD or well, dialog boxes certainly changed and it was a bit weird and hard for me to get used to but after a few minutes I was fine with it plus it also made more sense.
For me the first scene was intense then it got boring then it really picked up after a very unexpected thing happened from being nice, oh I guess I should mention that in Season 2 you play as Clementine rather than Lee who is the protagonist in Season 1 which is very weird but at the same time it was good to get the perspective from an 11 year old girl in the middle of a zombie apocalypse. For those of you who know anything about the game/story you know Clementine is a very smart girl, she can think and act quickly, she can shoot and she can take down zombies or "walkers" as they are referred to in this game quicker than a few of the adults, she really is a kick♥♥♥♥♥chick.

The story is as good as season 1, spectacular, funny, nerve-racking, scary, action-packed and some of the lines and the way some characters spoke, you can tell the developers didn't half♥♥♥♥♥it and they certainly went all out. There were ups and downs, it was like an emotional rollercoaster! This has got to be one of the only video games (besides season 1 of this series) that I have sat in front of my computer and legitimately cried over something happening in the game, other times I sat there frozen with my hands over my mouth having to take a minute to process what went on. The thing that really gets me is at the end of an episode it will show you a screen letting you know how popular one of the main decisions were and if I am over 50% I am happy but in episode 3 I got one saying "You and 31% of players did this.." and I started thinking "Opps, I did the wrong thing" but the truth is there is no "wrong thing" I played the game the way I wanted to play it and the way I think I would have gone about things in that situation and you don't get to redo that stuff if it was for real so why should you redo it just to get the best possible ending. This is all based on Episodes 1-3 of Season 2 (the second game in The Walking Dead series) with Episodes 4-5 to be released in Summer 2014 but keeping in mind that's probably the American summer. This is another job well done to the guys over at Telltale studios and I applaud them for their outstanding work on such an amazing game and to this day I am yet to know of a game with a better story, or a show/movie I care about the characters more than the characters in The Walking Dead video game.

Towards the mid to late game you are likely to have a spy come and steal some gold from your treasury (which is fine it seems like something they would do) but the problem lies in the fact that for some reason, a spy stealing from you will result in you unable to earn gold... ever. No really, even if you are running a + budget you will still continue to lose money and become bankrupt. As of today (12/02/17) there is no fix for this bug yet it remains a game-breaking issue which has sadly left me unable to finish a single game. The controls are easy to use, but hard to master, and you will almost always explode on your first try of making a successful rocket. But who cares? Just sit back and watch the fireworks. KSP has plenty of planets and moons to visit, all of which provided their own challenge and hidden easter eggs (all of which tend to be very amusing). One thing to beware of is the Kraken. He will destroy your ships and send Bill Kerman flying off on an unintended trajectory if provoked. They say the Kraken was killed/patched and is gone forever. All in all, amazing game full of explosions and fun. Ten outta ten.

Remember when Civ was a strategy series? Where you were informed of what was going on and there were ways to combat certain things? That's not in this.
Civs are incredibly imbalanced. Scythia can potentially quadruple all other Civs in cavalry output the entire game, while Sumer is essentially worthless beyond the classical era as barb camps dry up and other Civs progress beyond their unique unit.
The game is totally arbitrary at some points, from the 'Eureka' system that relies on finding things that may not even be in reach, to the random AI agendas (I have been denounced god knows how many times by Norway for not having a navy for my landlocked Civ, and Victoria just does it because I had the misfortune of spawning on a different continent).
Firaxis has also made it a lot more punishing to play this game in arbitrary ways. Wonders not only take up space that could be used in other ways, if you fail to complete them you get nothing back. Wars cripple both players involved to an extreme degree, destroying amenities (Civ 6's equivalent to happiness) for both sides, meaning that the defender also has their production destroyed while trying to defend.
This game is not fun, and I regret the amount of money I spent on this greatly.

Hello. It’s worth starting out by saying that this is a fantastic game. It's "set the bar" for the Tell-Tale style storytelling genre. As such, the main draw is the story, which is always hard to review without spoiling or sounding pretentions and vague. But, I shall do my best to inform the buyer with minimal spoilers by hopefully capturing the most important aspect of any story: the tone.
Firstly, I just want to say the game runs great. The shadows were a bit finicky for me, but nothing immersion breaking. There are a few known bugs that can pull you out of the experience, but they’re so few, far between, and unlikely that I won’t go into them in detail.
The art style is quite charming and playful, but doesn’t detract from the seriousness of the story. It’s in that golden-zone of stylized and realistic, and will likely look just as good 50 years from now as it currently does. The game relies quite heavily on visuals, so I regard this as a massive boon.
Gameplay is as you might expect from a story based game. There’s dialogue choices, branching paths, difficult decisions, and lots of walking and just looking at stuff. The main mechanic that separates this title from others in the genre is the rewind ability, which you get at the very start of the game. You get to rewind discussions and big decisions, and it encourages you to explore all the dialogue options without resorting to save scumming. Overall, it’s a fitting mechanic for the genre and only adds to the experience. However, the success of a game like this entirely depends on its story, so it’s time to stop skirting it.
I will be blunt: I was not entirely sold on the idea of playing as a young female adult in a late high school setting. I find it overdone and boring. Additionally, I wasn’t originally thrilled with the notion of time travel. Time travel plots are horrendously difficult to do well without using clichéd tropes. However, the game exhibits a healthy amount of self-awareness, and largely steers clear of overdone time travel shenanigans that cheapen both your decisions and the established story. In fact, the shenanigans that are present really add to the narrative, which largely revolves around your helplessness. The player does have the ability to affect reality for better or worse, but you learn quite quickly that – even with superpowers – you can only do so much.
If you’re concerned that you’ll just be playing an angsty teen drama with time travel, then fret not. The first episode or two sort of falls into this, but this is not a traditional coming of age story. In fact, the whole coming of age story – a crossing between innocence to maturity – is treated largely as a sham and even used antagonistically. The characters aren’t trying to “find themselves” or something of that ilk either. Everyone is written with a strong personality and as a real person, and I’d say the characters are overall quite compelling. The cast is kept fairly small to prevent the use of throwaway characters, and they all have plenty of dialogue to flesh them out. This small and consistent cast helps keep the story and tone focused.
Speaking of the tone, I’d like to start by saying that it’s rather difficult to pin down without spoilers. However, I’d say it attempts to take the ups and downs in life and really crank them up using supernatural plot devices. This gives the game a really great and pervasive bitter-sweet feeling, and forces the player to accept the fact that they can’t fix everything. They can only do their best with what’s given to them. I won’t spoil the ending, but it’s a great punctuation to the story and doesn’t feel like an♥♥♥♥♥pull.
Overall, the game is aesthetically pleasing, well written, tonally focused, and interesting. The gameplay complements these strengths, and the mishmash of buddy-cop, time travel, horror mystery, and high school drama somehow works without ever conflicting. It’s a true testament to what can be accomplished when a story is written to themes and tone; not to check off plot points on a list.
This got longer than I anticipated, but hopefully it’s still useful for informing a purchase.

TL;DR - A unique story-driven game that will leave you thinking about it long after you put it down.
In an era when we have a “new” FIFA, Battlefield, CoD, AC, etc. come out every 6-12 months Life is Strange is a real treasure. Don’t get me wrong. I can enjoy those games as much as the next guy. But there’s something to be said for originality, and Life is Strange is definitely an original. You won’t find another game like it.
Life is Strange is an episodic game similar in structure to those from Telltale Games. You play as Maxine “Max” Caulfield, an eighteen-year-old photography student at an elite art academy in Oregon. At the beginning of the game Max discovers that she has the ability to reverse time, which becomes the game’s main mechanic and story driver.
There is a little more exploration and puzzle-solving than most episodic games I’ve played, but the emphasis here is definitely on the story. There’s no real “challenge” or “difficulty” here. I found some of the exploration/puzzle sections a little tedious, and the time reversal mechanic could have been a little more precise, but those are relatively minor complaints.
The story starts out a little slow, and I’m a bit embarrassed to say that I almost gave up on the game. I’m glad I didn’t though, because it picks up quite quickly. I found myself growing attached to the characters and genuinely moved by what they went through. Life is Strange also serves up plenty of mystery with twists and turns that keep you guessing without feeling cheap or forced. Any fan of episodic games owes it to themselves to pick this game up, especially if it’s on sale.

Hello. It’s worth starting out by saying that this is a fantastic game. It's "set the bar" for the Tell-Tale style storytelling genre. As such, the main draw is the story, which is always hard to review without spoiling or sounding pretentions and vague. But, I shall do my best to inform the buyer with minimal spoilers by hopefully capturing the most important aspect of any story: the tone.
Firstly, I just want to say the game runs great. The shadows were a bit finicky for me, but nothing immersion breaking. There are a few known bugs that can pull you out of the experience, but they’re so few, far between, and unlikely that I won’t go into them in detail.
The art style is quite charming and playful, but doesn’t detract from the seriousness of the story. It’s in that golden-zone of stylized and realistic, and will likely look just as good 50 years from now as it currently does. The game relies quite heavily on visuals, so I regard this as a massive boon.
Gameplay is as you might expect from a story based game. There’s dialogue choices, branching paths, difficult decisions, and lots of walking and just looking at stuff. The main mechanic that separates this title from others in the genre is the rewind ability, which you get at the very start of the game. You get to rewind discussions and big decisions, and it encourages you to explore all the dialogue options without resorting to save scumming. Overall, it’s a fitting mechanic for the genre and only adds to the experience. However, the success of a game like this entirely depends on its story, so it’s time to stop skirting it.
I will be blunt: I was not entirely sold on the idea of playing as a young female adult in a late high school setting. I find it overdone and boring. Additionally, I wasn’t originally thrilled with the notion of time travel. Time travel plots are horrendously difficult to do well without using clichéd tropes. However, the game exhibits a healthy amount of self-awareness, and largely steers clear of overdone time travel shenanigans that cheapen both your decisions and the established story. In fact, the shenanigans that are present really add to the narrative, which largely revolves around your helplessness. The player does have the ability to affect reality for better or worse, but you learn quite quickly that – even with superpowers – you can only do so much.
If you’re concerned that you’ll just be playing an angsty teen drama with time travel, then fret not. The first episode or two sort of falls into this, but this is not a traditional coming of age story. In fact, the whole coming of age story – a crossing between innocence to maturity – is treated largely as a sham and even used antagonistically. The characters aren’t trying to “find themselves” or something of that ilk either. Everyone is written with a strong personality and as a real person, and I’d say the characters are overall quite compelling. The cast is kept fairly small to prevent the use of throwaway characters, and they all have plenty of dialogue to flesh them out. This small and consistent cast helps keep the story and tone focused.
Speaking of the tone, I’d like to start by saying that it’s rather difficult to pin down without spoilers. However, I’d say it attempts to take the ups and downs in life and really crank them up using supernatural plot devices. This gives the game a really great and pervasive bitter-sweet feeling, and forces the player to accept the fact that they can’t fix everything. They can only do their best with what’s given to them. I won’t spoil the ending, but it’s a great punctuation to the story and doesn’t feel like an♥♥♥♥♥pull.
Overall, the game is aesthetically pleasing, well written, tonally focused, and interesting. The gameplay complements these strengths, and the mishmash of buddy-cop, time travel, horror mystery, and high school drama somehow works without ever conflicting. It’s a true testament to what can be accomplished when a story is written to themes and tone; not to check off plot points on a list.
This got longer than I anticipated, but hopefully it’s still useful for informing a purchase.

THE SUMMARY:
"The game's bones are good, but it needs a little more meat on them." 7/10 - Buy on sale, or wait for expansion.
To cut to the chase, this game is pretty good. Buy it on sale, or wait for some expansions. I'd say it's worth a good $50 or so. The artistic direction and gameplay choices are generally clever and efficient, and I'm glad to see some real innovation on the classic Civ mechanics. There are legitimate gripes concerning the AI, and I can agree with those - diplomacy is muddy and ineffective. Overall, though, it feels, looks and sounds solid - and the adventurous nature of the mechanical changes makes me feel like future updates and expansions will contribute to a pretty classic experience for a few years to come.
MAJOR CONS
- AI feels very simple and ineffiectual.
This is by far the biggest problem. AI have no sense of character or player influence. They all behave roughly the same,    and do what they want - typically involving attacking you and slowly being destroyed whilst refusing any deals you propose.
- Some mechanics are pretty opaque.
The game doesn't always give you a good view of what's doing what. Choosing the correct places to put your buildings, wonders and districts is not especially well explained and takes a good number of playthroughs to get a feel for. It's sometimes hard to tell what things you did well or poorly.
- A lot happening under the hood.
For a game with so much going on, you may sometimes feel that you're just waiting things out. Depending on how you play, it's easy for the game to slip into being monotonous. The game's bones are good, but it needs a little more meat on them.
MAJOR PROS
+ Solid gameplay.
It works, it makes sense, and it feels like Civ.
+ Game mechanic improvements.
Makes some fantastic choices compared to Civ V. In particular, trade routes and road-building are genius, both thematically and in terms of gameplay. Similarly, districts are a beautiful handling of mechanics in a somewhat diegetic way. These are both examples of designers clearly putting serious thought into the game.
+ Clean audio/visuals
The look and sound is pretty polished up. It may or may not be to your taste, depending on what stylistic choices you enjoy - but it's a game that'll still feel right in a couple of decades.

TL;DR - A unique story-driven game that will leave you thinking about it long after you put it down.
In an era when we have a “new” FIFA, Battlefield, CoD, AC, etc. come out every 6-12 months Life is Strange is a real treasure. Don’t get me wrong. I can enjoy those games as much as the next guy. But there’s something to be said for originality, and Life is Strange is definitely an original. You won’t find another game like it.
Life is Strange is an episodic game similar in structure to those from Telltale Games. You play as Maxine “Max” Caulfield, an eighteen-year-old photography student at an elite art academy in Oregon. I might come back and edit this review in a few months.
So I just bought Civilization VI on sale for 79.96NZD and was majorly disappointed. Luckily, you can get refunds. My main problem with the game is that it isn't fun. Not nearly as fun as Civilization V. I enjoyed the art style, a few of the mechanics, but honestly, it wasn't great - as a game.
Every other negative review talks about AI problems. This one is no exception. The other leaders are... stupid, to say the least. I was playing as Arabia, with Rome and Brazil in my world. I was taking a while to expand my nation as I was focusing on building up my capital first. I had a few warriors and builders. Overall, I was smaller than the other two nations I had met, but not tiny. Suddenly, on the 50th turn (roughly) both Rome and Brazil decide to declare war on me after... no issues, land disputes or anything of the kind. Both of them tried to kill me. The two nation's units start flooding into my capital and there's really not much I can do. It was a disaster. That was after absolutely no previous troubles with either of them. In fact, I had been gifting gold to both leaders occasionally. I don't expect that to stop a war, but come on.
The new additions of city districts and what not are okay, but you don't get much help with it. You're advisor will say "My leige, we've just discovered some new information about [something to do with your city]." and expect you to get on with it. It's not like I need a 50 page manual, but I need a bit of assistance with new features. I've watched Youtube videos and gameplay of the game and yet I found it unorganized and difficult to get a hang of.
The gameplay is stale, too. It felt very slow and tedious, it took a life time to produce stuff with my cities because the turns were taking so long. This was on a small map, as well. There were only a few leaders and city states to have turns for. My computer is also very capable. I couldn't understand why, but I was genuinely bored playing this game. I didn't want to be. I had spent a good chunk of money on this game, I wanted it to be enjoyable. But it wasn't.
I would recommend sticking with Civ V for the time being. At least until they fix the moronic AI. Maybe watch a few series online. I'm not here to tell you how to spend your money, but in my opinion, right now, the game isn't worth how much they're charging. Thanks for reading.
Edit: After spending a bit more time on the game, and installing some very necessary mods, my overall experience has improved. However, it still fails to interest me like Civ V did. The most I can spend on this game at a time is an hour max, whereas on Civ V I once sat for 6 hours and didn't even realise it.
Basically, if you REALLY want to play this game but don't enjoy the AI, look for mods, they may help you out a bit. I also have one that adds a production queue which is really helpful.
Still would not recommend, unfortunately.

*Edit in September 2017*
There have been many more developments since my review from awhile ago. First off, I'd like to mention that there have been some definite AI improvements and diplomacy is easier to get a grasp of, though the leaders will still act erratic and annoying from time to time. The workshop is FANTASTIC now and has many great game improving mods and overhauls, which make the game immensely more entertaining and playable. DLC's are a bit pricey, but they always are when they first come out for civ games, and eventually there will probably be a game of the year bundle package that has them all together if you're patient enough for that, and some of them are absolutely worth it. Overall, while things like the art style and the gameplay take some getting used to, you'll find it very addictive and time consuming, I believe. The new city building details, and the addition of the Social/Government tree are major differences that add depth and make the world feel much more alive than Civilization 5, regardless of the fact that, yes, it is a bit buggier than Civ 5.
TL;DR There's a large learning curve for most when you first pick up a copy of Civilization 6, don't let that discourage you. Gameplay elements that may seem daunting at first actually make the game a much more meaningful experience. The workshop mods, which help fix quite a few issues, are an absolute must-have, and several of the DLC's are fantastic.

TL;DR - A unique story-driven game that will leave you thinking about it long after you put it down.
In an era when we have a “new” FIFA, Battlefield, CoD, AC, etc. come out every 6-12 months Life is Strange is a real treasure. Don’t get me wrong. I can enjoy those games as much as the next guy. But there’s something to be said for originality, and Life is Strange is definitely an original. You won’t find another game like it.
Life is Strange is an episodic game similar in structure to those from Telltale Games. You play as Maxine “Max” Caulfield, an eighteen-year-old photography student at an elite art academy in Oregon. At the beginning of the game Max discovers that she has the ability to reverse time, which becomes the game’s main mechanic and story driver.
There is a little more exploration and puzzle-solving than most episodic games I’ve played, but the emphasis here is definitely on the story. There’s no real “challenge” or “difficulty” here. I found some of the exploration/puzzle sections a little tedious, and the time reversal mechanic could have been a little more precise, but those are relatively minor complaints.
The story starts out a little slow, and I’m a bit embarrassed to say that I almost gave up on the game. I’m glad I didn’t though, because it picks up quite quickly. I found myself growing attached to the characters and genuinely moved by what they went through. Life is Strange also serves up plenty of mystery with twists and turns that keep you guessing without feeling cheap or forced. Any fan of episodic games owes it to themselves to pick this game up, especially if it’s on sale.

An excellent continuation of the First Season, I once again find myself totally immersed in the story of the apocalypse. Again, it's a movie-like expericence where the feels are real, the story flows beautifully, and I feel every joy and cringe at every loss. The characters are even more realistic and the situations even more delicate, making every choice potetially life-changing.
There's only one complaint I have, and sadly it is again to do with the control interface. Trying to chose how to interact with an object (look, pick up, etc.) is even harder than in the first season, and the new click-and-drag mechanic is a pain in the @$$ and doesn't work half the time, even when I'm running my mouse across the entire mousepad. The click-and-drag is also so poorly explained even with the help option turned on that I had to look up a tutorial after monkeying around for a good 10 minutes just trying to figure out *SPOILER ALERT* how to stitch Clementine's arm *END SPOILIER*. Thankfully, you don't have to do too much dragging around.
Overall, I'd highly recommend getting this game. Some minorly gimmicky controls aside, this adventure is a piece of art, and I honestly cannot wait for Chapters 4 and 5 to come out. Just don't forget your Kleenex, you'll be needing them again for this roller-coaster ride.
**CHAPTERS 4 AND 5 UPDATE/EDIT**
Wow. Just... wow. This game. There's no denying it, it's downright intense. Somehow this finale stepped it up a notch from last season's, and things just got tougher. Poor Clem, she's gone through a lot.
Also, props to the developers, it seems they tweaked the click-and-drag mechanic to be a little more responsive. Thank you for that.
If there is a third season release, I'm definitely getting it. This series produces such a feeling of raw realism, and never shies away from the gritty reality that life s*cks. The quality behind the storytelling far surpasses many interactive games I've seen, and definitely wouldn't mind taking another crazy ride on this franchise. Well done, Tell Tale Games. Well done.

Summary: 3 of 5 stars, don't buy it if you don't like poor UI or poorly designed game systems.
If you liked Civilization V, then there are many things about VI that you will find welcome improvements. Graphically, Civ VI has improved for the better, and although the style can sometimes seem too 'cartoony', there are many things to love including the fantastic character models and animations for the leaders. There are some things that bother me, like the tiny missile ship that is the upgrade for the massive battleship unit, but these are minor. The UI is clean and reminiscent of the Civ 5 UI, but is a step down in many ways. Interactions with AI leaders, for example, has slowed down to a crawl forcing you to wait 1-2 seconds for a 'goodbye' button to appear after a leader taunts you. And, many times, you will be taunted once per leader per turn making the experience past the first play miserable and tedious. It is things like this that make me wonder how often the people who made the game played the game. I think if the UI designers had played several long games of Civ 6 with this UI they would have fixed it. Similarly, the information dials on the right side of the screen are strangely unresponsive taking a great system from Civ V and making it feel worse.
The same feeling that the devs didn't play their game often enough while making it goes for the new 'warmongering' penalty system. This is one of the poorest designed systems I have seen in a game. It is downright broken. In fact, I think this system single-handedly ruins the core experience of the game and, if you have issues with poorly designed game systems, you should pass on Civ VI just for this feature alone. An example of how your first and all of the rest of your games will go, from the very early game through the end of the game, is this: An AI invites you to a war. You join it. That same AI denounces you for being a warmonger on the next turn and for the rest of the game - even thousands of years later. Additionally, all AI will denounce you as a warmonger. Being denounced as a warmonger will happen if you get attacked as well. You don't even have to start a war -- all you have to do is be in a war and the AI will denounce you. Poor game design and a flawed system that should have been caught by the designers or QA before the game shipped.
Lastly, the AI is dead stupid. The way the game launches attacks and uses the terrain is really very poor. I felt like battles against the AI were more desperate somehow in Civ 5 - like the AI better handled combat and attacks. The Walking Dead Season 2 doesn't support normal folder redirection for the save game files (which worked fine on Season 1).  You can run the game and play it, but it will not import the Season 1 save files, nor will it save your progress if your Document folder is redirected to a network server using UNC paths.  You can fix this by changing folder redirection to use a mapped drive instead of UNC paths.
Steps to fix this (on my Windows 2012 server):
1). Install (or move) the game to C: drive default Steam folder (I originally had it installed to my data drive but it won't work).
2). Use group policies (or logon script) to add a drive mapping to the User folder (e.g. U: to \\server\users).
3). Change Documents and Save Games redirection to U: (it will fill in the username and Document folder automatically).
This fixed the problem for me, and I can now play and save the game correctly.

I might come back and edit this review in a few months.
So I just bought Civilization VI on sale for 79.96NZD and was majorly disappointed. Luckily, you can get refunds. My main problem with the game is that it isn't fun. Not nearly as fun as Civilization V. I enjoyed the art style, a few of the mechanics, but honestly, it wasn't great - as a game.
Every other negative review talks about AI problems. This one is no exception. The other leaders are... stupid, to say the least. I was playing as Arabia, with Rome and Brazil in my world. I was taking a while to expand my nation as I was focusing on building up my capital first. I had a few warriors and builders. Overall, I was smaller than the other two nations I had met, but not tiny. Suddenly, on the 50th turn (roughly) both Rome and Brazil decide to declare war on me after... no issues, land disputes or anything of the kind. Both of them tried to kill me. The two nation's units start flooding into my capital and there's really not much I can do. It was a disaster. That was after absolutely no previous troubles with either of them. In fact, I had been gifting gold to both leaders occasionally. I don't expect that to stop a war, but come on.
The new additions of city districts and what not are okay, but you don't get much help with it. You're advisor will say "My leige, we've just discovered some new information about [something to do with your city]." and expect you to get on with it. It's not like I need a 50 page manual, but I need a bit of assistance with new features. I've watched Youtube videos and gameplay of the game and yet I found it unorganized and difficult to get a hang of.
The gameplay is stale, too. It felt very slow and tedious, it took a life time to produce stuff with my cities because the turns were taking so long. This was on a small map, as well. There were only a few leaders and city states to have turns for. My computer is also very capable. I couldn't understand why, but I was genuinely bored playing this game. I didn't want to be. I had spent a good chunk of money on this game, I wanted it to be enjoyable. But it wasn't.
I would recommend sticking with Civ V for the time being. At least until they fix the moronic AI. Maybe watch a few series online. I'm not here to tell you how to spend your money, but in my opinion, right now, the game isn't worth how much they're charging. Thanks for reading.
Edit: After spending a bit more time on the game, and installing some very necessary mods, my overall experience has improved. However, it still fails to interest me like Civ V did. The most I can spend on this game at a time is an hour max, whereas on Civ V I once sat for 6 hours and didn't even realise it.
Basically, if you REALLY want to play this game but don't enjoy the AI, look for mods, they may help you out a bit. I also have one that adds a production queue which is really helpful.
Still would not recommend, unfortunately.

Ignore the time played here; I've played a lot more on my Mac, and I got that edition of the game off the Apple app store on sale.
Is it not quite as good as Civ V? In some respects yes. However there is a lot more level of detail as far as city building goes in, and it's a more difficult challenge in some ways which can be refreshing. I think the only thing sorely missing was a better diplomacy system. The new diplomacy system is vague and hard to understand, although the addition of hidden randomized agendas was definitely a nice touch. Overall it's still a good game, maybe just wait for a good deal to come along. It'll test other aspects of your strategic skills that other Civs perhaps didn't, and it has potential if they release some good DLC at a decent price.
*Edit in September 2017*
There have been many more developments since my review from awhile ago. First off, I'd like to mention that there have been some definite AI improvements and diplomacy is easier to get a grasp of, though the leaders will still act erratic and annoying from time to time. The workshop is FANTASTIC now and has many great game improving mods and overhauls, which make the game immensely more entertaining and playable. DLC's are a bit pricey, but they always are when they first come out for civ games, and eventually there will probably be a game of the year bundle package that has them all together if you're patient enough for that, and some of them are absolutely worth it. Overall, while things like the art style and the gameplay take some getting used to, you'll find it very addictive and time consuming, I believe. The new city building details, and the addition of the Social/Government tree are major differences that add depth and make the world feel much more alive than Civilization 5, regardless of the fact that, yes, it is a bit buggier than Civ 5.
TL;DR There's a large learning curve for most when you first pick up a copy of Civilization 6, don't let that discourage you. Gameplay elements that may seem daunting at first actually make the game a much more meaningful experience. The workshop mods, which help fix quite a few issues, are an absolute must-have, and several of the DLC's are fantastic.

This game is one of the biggest "interactive storytelling" games to come out of a western studio, but it plays like a 3rd-person over-the-shoulder exploration experience. A key theme is the ability to rewind time and "do over" key decisions in life, so those who liked speculative timeline plots like Donnie Darko or Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind will find a kindred story here.
It plays very forgivingly - you never get any sort of "game over" screen, as the timeline ability lets you rewind and avoid inescapable situations. But the main enjoyment of the game is in social interactions and moral/ethical choices when dealing with people. The setting is in a sleepy Oregon town with a preppy high school and hints of dark secrets, but the main tension in the game comes from conversation choices: what information you share with other characters, and what emotional tone you give them. There is an element of exploration and clue-hunting as well.
All in all, a fascinating look at a strong entry into the interactive storytelling genre, with high production values and a slick graphical presentation (the indie soundtrack also highlights themes of friendship, teenage uncertainty, and aimlessness very well). Hopefully this will do for the interactive storytelling genre what Baldur's Gate did for the CRPG genre and help it flourish in the marketplace.
Those with a non-gamer significant other, or a family member who's more comfortable with a TV drama series than a mainstream computer game, may find Life Is Strange to be a gentle and engaging gateway title to bring them into computer games.

Best game ever made for anyone who loves space. Build your own rocket designs and fly them around a very nice solar system. Fantastic, non-violent game for children to learn about rockets and orbital mechanics. This game should be a class in schools in my opinion.
At first you will be overwhealmed with all of the things to learn. However, after a while of really trying to figure things out, you will get it. It really seems much harder than it is. There are nice tools/mods you can download for this game to help you get to where you want to go. Mech Jeb is a must have for beginners. It would be really nice to see steam workshop support for this game. Mods are not that difficult to implement though. Just read instructions.
Try to use some of the pre existing ships to learn what a multi-stage rocket does and how the game has managed to capture this uniqe and thrilling aspect. You are not limited to just space ships though. You can make an SSTO (single stage to orbit/space plane), rovers, hover craft, recently just released boat planes thanks to new water physics, planes for flying around the atmosphere of Kerbin, and pretty much anything else you can think of. Space stations in orbit around planets as well.
This game really captures the feel of a space faring nation and what they can achieve. Be creative and take your time. Think it all through. Learn what stages are and how to use them. Learn about action groups as they are a very nice feature.
A couple of critisizms for the devs are the building snap to is broken in many cases. I have trouble getting parts to snap to eachother quite often. This is extremley annoying and must be fixed ASAP. My next thing is multiplayer. I want this built into the game. If a mod can do it, then you certainly can build it into the game. There is a way. I understand due to the time scale it is difficult to implement when using warp. However, there is always a way. Please make this game MP as it needs to be. Also as I mentioned before, steam workshop NAO!
In summation, this is by far the best space race builder and sim ever created. I cannot believe it is an indie game. Please give it a really good chance before dismissing it. You will not regret it!!

The short - if you ever wanted to peek behind the curtain of spaceflight, build insane things that go boom or stick you flag in soil untouched by man or kerbal this is the game for you. KSP leaves the “what and how” of rockets to you, it will suggest things to accomplish but ultimately it is up to you to pick the challenge that you want to overcome.
I have spent far too much time playing KSP, and I’ve realized it’s an odd game. It combines several different games into one sandbox: rocket and plane builder, flight simulator, and space sim. Basically it all boils down to being a NASA simulator as you have to take on all the roles of NASA from astronaut, to engineer, to mission planner and deal with most of the challenges that come with those jobs. Therfore it has a steep learning curve, weight to trust ratios, orbital maneuvers, rendezvous and docking, aero-breaking, and dreaded geo-breaking aka crash landings. But don’t get too intimidated the community loves to help new players learn the basics of space travel and they will walk you through the 101 of, rockets, planes, and whatever else you might need help with.
How ambitious you are drives  the difficulty of the game, whether you’re happy just flying by the Mun or do want to land on it or are you sights set on more distant worlds, do plan to bring your crew back or find one way trips to be best budget friendly solution. In KSP don’t be afraid to fail it’s part of the fun, watching a rocket spin out of control and explode, I’ve dragged the broken remains of many a crashed rocket back to Kerbal on their last engines. If something does go wrong and your kerbonauts are stranded, will there be  rescue mission? It’s all up to you, the where, how. And will they ever see Kerbal again or will home just be a twinkle in an alien sky.

The thing I probably like the most about this game is that these different roles actually have completely different types of gameplay and strategy. Unlike many F2P FPSs (I'm looking at you Warface), you can't play support or flank as damage (well, at least not usually). To win the game, front line has to be on objective, support has to support, especially the front line, damage is used to give out as much damage as possible, and flank is used to sneak up behind front line and anyone on objective. All that to say you have to play your role correctly to win almost every single time, and to me that shows a very well balanced game. The only con to that is that your teammates won't always realise that they need to play their character's role and get destroyed by the enemy. But often enough you'll get a game where people realise how to play and do so, giving one of the most enjoyable F2P experiences I've ever had. And yes, this is from a completely F2P perspective.
EDIT:
A lot of people have been complaining about the essence patch. Honestly, the only way it can be a problem is if you want to fully customize every single character. It never became P2W, just pay to have complete customizability. For the people that  have already created for themselves a strategy for every character, that can be a problem. However, I am generally satisfied with the cards already given me, with a few exceptions. And for the characters that I really like playing, I have PLENTY of essence to customize them however I want.

This game is pretty much amazing entirely.
The way the game works is stunning, and the game does a good job of making flying a spaceship both fun, and challenging. Build a small rocket, it's easy to control. Build a big one, and be ready to lose control! The game does a great job with orbits, and giving the kerbals a good feel.
There's not a campaign or a story, and that's one of the best things about it! You get to pretty much make your own story! Perhaps you're saving Jebdiah and Bill who are lost on the Mun, or maybe you're are invistigating the massive planet Jool!
You won't find another game where you can launch rockets off into space like this one! I've always wanted there to be a game dedicated to space exploration, and this is it! With the addition of spaceplanes, things just get better!
The kerbals themselves are pretty funny! Watching them scream and yell as they veer off into space is comical! The generic names is also an added bonus!
Sadly, there is no multiplayer. Hopefully this will be added in the future to some extent!
Playing alone and by yourself is fine though! You can always find something to change so that you can go further into space, and eventually spread the kerbal race everywhere!
Though there are not any Steam achievements, in career mode you can climb milestones as you go along. Perhaps eventually there will be achievements for getting into orbit, landing on the Mun, reaching Jool, etc.
The graphics aren't fantastic, but they aren't bad either! It would be kind of cool to see clouds, and other weather instances without mods.
There's definitely a lot of replay value in this game. Simply because there isn't another game like it, you'll come back to it a lot with some new crazy project.
Overall, this game is really good! Though it may be a bit expensive for my taste, the enjoyment, the mods, and the fact that the game will recieve updates adding in new things as time progresses really makes it worth every penny!

A lot of people say the AI is broken. I disagree. I'd argue that there IS NO AI in the game right now. Six months after release, the game feels like it's still a work-in-progress. Kind of like one of those early-access games that promise to get better, but with barely any/no updates and solely existing to sucker people. But hey, I guess it looks pretty, right?
Let me be clear: The AI in this game is a farce. It is not designed to play intelligently. It is designed to be a minor obstacle to be overcome and to delay your progress, rather than be a true opponent. For example, the first AI you encounter will, 100% of the time, rush settlers. And instead of land-grabbing all the good tiles, and developing themselves at the most crucial point in the game, their number one priority will be throw them next to your cities to provoke you. They will then all rush a holy site and/or Stonehenge to try to delay you founding a religion, leaving them with pretty much no military to speak of to defend their city spam. You don't actually have to build settlers in the early game, because the AI does it for you. For every start, you just rush slingers and you win, or on higher difficulties, declare war and mop up all the free unprotected settlers. Unpredictable AI my left testicle. You can't even force it to stop. I blocked off access to all my territory one game, and the AI had only two cities bordering my territory as close as possible, with an entire continent worth of resources on the other side left untouched. For 100 turns!
And that's my main issue with the AI: It's not designed to actually WIN, it's designed to provoke you and delay your victory condition. They will build a ton of units to delay your domination, but cannot wage war or move around the map effectively at all. They will spam apostles and missionaries to delay your religion, but are incapable of generating the massive faith needed to convert enough cities to win. They will rush production based wonders, such as the ever popular Petra and Ruhr valley, to delay your science victory, but will only go as far as building a few measly spaceports. They will rush and buy out every artist and writer they can to delay your Culture victory, but won't actually USE them, instead preferring to park them in their cities for eternity to both prevent you from being able to trade for them, which renders the entire Great Work swapping system pointless, and preventing them from generating enough Tourism to win. They. Don't. Pursue. Victory. EVER. They either wipe you out in the early game, or it's a slog to end the game sometime before turn 500.
In fact, there was actually an experiment someone did in an AI only game where it was left to its own devices for 600 turns (100 over the normal turn limit), and none of them even got close to winning. And yet, they won't even us nukes, which would delay your progress by hundreds of turns.
All this just SCREAMS to me dumbing down for the sake of not scaring casual players.

Here're lots of critics about this game. I must say I agree with them in some conditions. But from my experience, something are not that bad, and maybe some problems come from playing patterns one may follow.
The impact of this game's parameters is complicated. For example, game speed is not just adding some more turns to your gameplay. It will also significantly make difference on your game strategy and especially the diplomacy. Many reviews say that warmongering denouncement is rediculous, such as declaring war once, the penalty would last forever. But my finding is that warmongering penalty will drop as time goes by, maybe some 50 turns would flat up -18 penalty. This observation somes from the slowest speed，Marathon. And for faster game, the decreasing time is almost the same, which means you can feel free to declare a war in slower game. Another thing about the warmongering decreasing time is that it may be related to your relation with other AIs, the 50 turns decreasing time happens when I allied almost every AIs. It seems that the closer you with an AI, the shorter the decreasing time from the perspective of that AI.
I don't want to counter those critics one by one. They really exist in this game, but I think some of them are not the major problem, especially about the gaming strategy and how to win a game.
The major problem is that the gaming guide is not enough. For example, what I mentioned above about the warmongering penalty, there's nothing about how this value influenced by other facts. You must play a lot to observe what would happen. Sometimes you need to build a series of games to test a single parameter. It takes too much time to learn this game. And surely this game is not balanced well. Maybe by chance, you find a way to beat the most difficult AI every single game, then you may think that's it, and don't want to learn this game anymore and conclude that other aspects of it are total garbage.
For sure, Civ VI is supposed to be a game with diversity of ways winning. However, since its AI is really don't know how to win a war, win a game relying largely on military force is the most powerful strategy, as long as your science doesn't fall far behind the AIs. But still you can try other things in Civ VI. I don't want to blame on the AI design, because it's really hard to build a clever enemy me for you for this kind of game. By observation, you can figure out its logic when undertaking a war. I must say even such a crippy mind they build, it still takes some half a minute to compute on an I7 CPU in the late game. And actually, they can build a strategy easily beat players by simply letting the AI's army attack you regardless unit lost. Because of the advantage the deity AI have, AI must win by this way. Right now, I think AI's strategy is attacking when they would not lost unit and can kill one unit in a turn. Barbarian is more likely to attack than AI civilization, and more likely to prillige player's district and improvement. If AI civilization follows the Barbarian strategy, player would also be defeated easily in deity difficulty.
However, the developer didn't try to bully player by this way. I think this is a good choice, since it gives a way to other gaming strategy, though leave military force too strong, so that people would not like to use others. But still you can try them.
Civ VI has its own logic, so some change is not that bad as long as you jump out of the box, like the limited charges of the builder. Civ VI is not friendly to the game style that build one or two big city from the beginning of the game and seek a culture or religion victory. It encourage expanding via some war in early game, and if some conditions hold you can do that in late game. Though AI is not good at war, the warmongering penalty is serious, so player can not do whatever you want if a domination victory is not the choice. It's very interesting to find a way to go war against other civilizations and they still love you. So if you find yourself nothing to do in some time period or have to stop building a wonder and build a builder first, maybe you're not quite get the logic of the game. You can blame on that they excluded some possibility here, but I don't like either the idea of a builder who can work forever.
To summarize, the main drawback of Civ VI as a game, is the lack of guidence to show some important details of its system, and players really need to learn to find the way more enjoyable, e.g. the warmongering system is really annoying at the first place. Other stuff depends on your way of gameplay. I think most people can find some enjoyable parts and also be frustrated by some others. Since Civ is not a PVP game, I would not blame on its balance. Many ways can win a game, although by war is much easier. To me, this is a simulation game, not a strategic one.

Kerbal Space Program is an amazing game that introduces those of minimal knowledge in aerospace and rocket engineering into those respective fields, exposing gamers to real-world concepts of just how complicated running a space program can truly be.
The interface is very user friendly, and the the learning curve is not steep; just don't go expecting to being able to build something big and complicated that works on your first try.  There is an assortment of parts to choose from in order to satisfy anyone's wildest engineering imaginations with regards to building vehicles such as a space shuttle, an atmospheric lander, or perhaps something that can go from one end of the Kerbal system to the other.
In short, I really recommend this piece of art to all gamers, especially those having a deep interest in space technology, or have the urge to build something with as many rockets as it can muster and see it sail off into the cosmos.

I don't want to counter those critics one by one. They really exist in this game, but I think some of them are not the major problem, especially about the gaming strategy and how to win a game.
The major problem is that the gaming guide is not enough. For example, what I mentioned above about the warmongering penalty, there's nothing about how this value influenced by other facts. You must play a lot to observe what would happen. Sometimes you need to build a series of games to test a single parameter. It takes too much time to learn this game. And surely this game is not balanced well. Maybe by chance, you find a way to beat the most difficult AI every single game, then you may think that's it, and don't want to learn this game anymore and conclude that other aspects of it are total garbage.
For sure, Civ VI is supposed to be a game with diversity of ways winning. However, since its AI is really don't know how to win a war, win a game relying largely on military force is the most powerful strategy, as long as your science doesn't fall far behind the AIs. But still you can try other things in Civ VI. I don't want to blame on the AI design, because it's really hard to build a clever enemy me for you for this kind of game. By observation, you can figure out its logic when undertaking a war. I must say even such a crippy mind they build, it still takes some half a minute to compute on an I7 CPU in the late game. And actually, they can build a strategy easily beat players by simply letting the AI's army attack you regardless unit lost. Because of the advantage the deity AI have, AI must win by this way. Right now, I think AI's strategy is attacking when they would not lost unit and can kill one unit in a turn. Barbarian is more likely to attack than AI civilization, and more likely to prillige player's district and improvement. If AI civilization follows the Barbarian strategy, player would also be defeated easily in deity difficulty.
However, the developer didn't try to bully player by this way. I think this is a good choice, since it gives a way to other gaming strategy, though leave military force too strong, so that people would not like to use others. But still you can try them.
Civ VI has its own logic, so some change is not that bad as long as you jump out of the box, like the limited charges of the builder. Civ VI is not friendly to the game style that build one or two big city from the beginning of the game and seek a culture or religion victory. It encourage expanding via some war in early game, and if some conditions hold you can do that in late game. Though AI is not good at war, the warmongering penalty is serious, so player can not do whatever you want if a domination victory is not the choice. It's very interesting to find a way to go war against other civilizations and they still love you. So if you find yourself nothing to do in some time period or have to stop building a wonder and build a builder first, maybe you're not quite get the logic of the game. You can blame on that they excluded some possibility here, but I don't like either the idea of a builder who can work forever.
To summarize, the main drawback of Civ VI as a game, is the lack of guidence to show some important details of its system, and players really need to learn to find the way more enjoyable, e.g. the warmongering system is really annoying at the first place. Other stuff depends on your way of gameplay. I think most people can find some enjoyable parts and also be frustrated by some others. Since Civ is not a PVP game, I would not blame on its balance. Many ways can win a game, although by war is much easier. To me, this is a simulation game, not a strategic one.

This is a fast paced First Person Shooter. There are 4 different types of champions, front line, damage, support, and flank. The thing I probably like the most about this game is that these different roles actually have completely different types of gameplay and strategy. Unlike many F2P FPSs (I'm looking at you Warface), you can't play support or flank as damage (well, at least not usually). To win the game, front line has to be on objective, support has to support, especially the front line, damage is used to give out as much damage as possible, and flank is used to sneak up behind front line and anyone on objective. All that to say you have to play your role correctly to win almost every single time, and to me that shows a very well balanced game. The only con to that is that your teammates won't always realise that they need to play their character's role and get destroyed by the enemy. But often enough you'll get a game where people realise how to play and do so, giving one of the most enjoyable F2P experiences I've ever had. And yes, this is from a completely F2P perspective.
EDIT:
A lot of people have been complaining about the essence patch. Honestly, the only way it can be a problem is if you want to fully customize every single character. It never became P2W, just pay to have complete customizability. For the people that  have already created for themselves a strategy for every character, that can be a problem. However, I am generally satisfied with the cards already given me, with a few exceptions. And for the characters that I really like playing, I have PLENTY of essence to customize them however I want.

EDIT: Yes I realize i only have 20 hours in this game but my review will explain why.
Having played 600+ hours on Civ V and hopping over to VI a few weeks after it came out, I am underwhelmed. The AI is poorly made, There is no build queue, You weren't even able to rename your cities when it first came out. They ALREADY HAVE DLC. What a horrible way to kick off a game.
I can only honestly recommend this game if you play with friends and ONLY with friends. Unless of course you're sadistic and you play against the easy-as-pie Deity AI then go right ahead and do that.
But in all seriousness I simply cannot recommend this game in its current state... at least not until it's fixed up and has an actual workshop. I know I have basically been repeating the same stuff as all the other reviews so let me add something of my own.
A major problem (in my opinion) with this game is the fact that multiplayer is STILL broken. It was broken in Civ V and now it is broken again. Whenever there is a turn timer and someone disconnects, the game freezes up and does not let the turns progress. HUGE oversight with both games that I feel needs to be addressed.
PROS:
The district system is very well-done. It adds an extra depth to the game that the others didn't. Good job on that regard, Firaxis.
The trade route system. The fact that roads are built as a result of having a trade caravan is a good addition in my opinion.
Loading times. YES PLEASE. The loading times have been SIGNIFICANTLY reduced in this installment of the Civ franchise. Instead of waiting 20 minutes for the game to load and another 10 to load up a map like in Civ V, it now takes a minute or two to load the game AND the map combined. Well done.
All in all, go buy Civ V with all the DLC if you want to have a good time. Don't play Civ VI unless you're a masochist or something. AI is garbage, multiplayer is broken, there is no build queue, there is already DLC. This is a sad excuse for a Civ game, to say the very least.

but its no longer a civ game because you have to manually place districts, the game forces you to make all the decisions that in civ 5 are below your level - you are the RULER not the city council or governer of every town you found. YOU have no business (imo) doing city planning - you as ruler need to be thinking strategically and let your subordinates - in this case whoever you have in charge of the city - build what you need and decide where to place it for you. civ vi is more like sim city x number of cities you found/conquer.
im still hoping some of the patches to come will do more to address this; i dont want them to totally roll back to civ 5: i have no problems with cities organically growing out of a single hex, but the hexes need to be smaller on the map and the maps a lot lot bigger than they are. and then you have the issue with the unit graphics etc being designed for larger hexes...
i will still recommend the game, but if you want to experience the real civilisation series i would say start with 5. its worth trying civ vi if you have to only pick one but it doesnt have the mods civ 5 does yet (there is time though) and i really am waiting for an IGE mod for this like i have with civ 5 before i give it another go.

First of all: I actually have hundreds of hours on KSP; as before i played on a "BORROWED" copy. But the game is so damn good, i gave the developers their due and bought the game.
KSP is a sandbox space exploration game with basically limitless possibilities; the light-hearted and comedic story of a race of little green men who begin their exploration of space much like we did. You design and fly your own rockets, spaceships, aircraft and probes using hundreds of different parts; you could recreate any historical rocket or airplane, replay the Apollo moon landings, recreate projects that never took off; ect. There is no "set in stone" way to design a rocket or aircraft, you are free to design the most simplistic or outrageous and nonsensical) you want to.
The physics follow the actual laws of physics so there is no "handwavium super magic space drives" involved, this is a realistic simulation (even if the solar system and planets are scaled-down versions of our own, the laws of physics remain the same) involving a lot of planning and a lot of learning about how orbital mechanics and rockets work.
Of course you don't need to be a rocket scientist to play (many of them actually love this game); you will learn as you go and develop an innate understanding of how the physics work and will be able to achieve whatever you set your aims to.
The game has an extremely large, active and passionate following that puts out a huge number of quality mods for it; the available mod content is just staggering. You can download more parts, realistic life support or radio systems, telemetry plug-ins (Telemachus), programmable autopilots (kOS and Mechjeb), a full-scale realistic solar system, realistic weapons and sensor systems (BDArmory, my favorite) the list goes on.
Get this game. It's fun for everyone who has ever dreamed to go to space or likes rockets, fast things and big explosions.  Wether you are 7, 30 or 50 years old; this game won't dissapoint you.
Addendum: The mod compatibility issue is quite annoying. The big modding community suffers from the pace of update for the game, and some of the best mods for playing the game to the fullest don't work on the latest version. If Squad could select the best mods once in a while and incorporate their features into the game, that would be great.

When I first started this game, judging by my characters voice and appearance, I literally thought I was in middleschool, only to later find out she's in college.
