Paladins is a team based, objective oriented, first person shooter. The shooting and pace of the game is arcadey and hectic, easy to play, but hard to master. This plays more like an arcade shooter as you're frequently in hectic gun battles. However, this game is also tactical as it's difficult or near impossible for a single person to hold off 3 or more attackers on their own, especially if contesting the objective. Also, tactics and strategy come into play when choosing which champion you'll play in your team. Champions are divided into 4 categories: Frontline (tanks), damage, flank, and support. Too many of 1 type or the lack of a frontline/support champion can often spell defeat for a team. More importantly, each champion within its category plays differently. Such as some support characters heal better than others and others do more damage.
The game only offers two objective game modes at the moment, Siege and Payload:
Siege is a 5v5 struggle for control of a central objective. Once the objective is captured, a cart (payload) spawns in that the capturing team must escort to the opposing team's spawn point within a time limit. You get 1 point for capturing the objective and the capturing team can score a 2nd point by successfully escorting the payload to the opponent's spawn. If the capturing team doesn't successfully escort the payload, the opposing team is given 1 point for defending. The first team to reach 4 points wins.
Payload plays as a attackers vs defenders situation. The defenders are given time before the match begins to choose strategic locations to slow the attacker's approach as the attackers attempt to escort a payload from their spawn all the way across the map to the opponent's spawn. If the attackers fail to escort the payload to the defender's spawn then the defenders win. Regardless of the outcome of the round, the teams switch roles for the next round. The first team to get 2 round victories gets the win.
Overall, despite the lack of different game modes and only I think 4 different maps for each mode, the game is very solid and you should definitely give it a try :D

Disclaimer: This is my first time playing any Civilization game.
I played RTS before (Warcraft 3, Age of Empires 3) and I played city builder games (Cities: Skylines), but I had no idea what this would be like.
If you are new to Civilization, please ignore the complaints about the AI. You would have to play 100s of hours to understand the nitpicks people are pointing out. The AI is an output of hidden agendas, which you access through diplomacy. It's exciting to interact with these AI personalities and you should treat them as resources (or obstacles) like any other aspect of the game. If you are still concerned, simply search "Winter Update Civ 6" online to see the AI changes being added. We can probably expect a Spring update too!
PROS:
- Excellent civilization theming. The music is different for each civ and it changes throughout the ages. The buildings and character models change too. If you are new to Civilization, the most exciting aspect of trying out new civilizations is the perks of each one.
- Recommendations from the computer. I started with the tutorial, but dropped it for a real game because I was eager to get going. Don't worry! The computer gives you recommendations for next technologies to research, for settlement locations, and for improvements to make.
- Rewarding exploration. The early and mid game are exciting phases where you choose settlement locations to gain access to luxury resources (whales, mercury, etc.). You can also discover tribal villages and natural wonders, both of which provide exciting advantages. In the late game, you can even have an archeologist search for ruins and shipwrecks (also providing unique advantages).
CONS:
- Late game micromanagment. The late game is my main complaint. Lets say you have 20 units and 6 cities to manage. That's 26 actions you would be taking per turn, not to mention deciding on what technologies and civics to research. So whereas during the early game the turns took under a minute, the late game turns can take 5 minutes. Given that the game cuts off at 500 turns, you can see why my first game took 20 hours to finish. I really like getting to the late game, but the micromanagement needs to be simplified. You do have the option of putting units to "sleep" though. So it's manageable.
- Lacking UI. Some people say there is too much clutter, but I say there isn't enough. After placing districts, it's hard to tell what benefits you were promised as you were placing it. Science campuses, for instance, give more science points per turn if placed by mountains. But it's hard to find that number after it's been constructed. You really have to dive down in the reports to make sense of many game elements. But that's fun too! :)
OVERALL: 9/10 BUY THIS GAME IF YOU HAVE NO IDEA WHAT TO EXPECT. IT DELIVERS!

Paladins is a team based, objective oriented, first person shooter. The shooting and pace of the game is arcadey and hectic, easy to play, but hard to master. This plays more like an arcade shooter as you're frequently in hectic gun battles. However, this game is also tactical as it's difficult or near impossible for a single person to hold off 3 or more attackers on their own, especially if contesting the objective. Also, tactics and strategy come into play when choosing which champion you'll play in your team. Champions are divided into 4 categories: Frontline (tanks), damage, flank, and support. Too many of 1 type or the lack of a frontline/support champion can often spell defeat for a team. More importantly, each champion within its category plays differently. Such as some support characters heal better than others and others do more damage.
The game only offers two objective game modes at the moment, Siege and Payload:
Siege is a 5v5 struggle for control of a central objective. Once the objective is captured, a cart (payload) spawns in that the capturing team must escort to the opposing team's spawn point within a time limit. You get 1 point for capturing the objective and the capturing team can score a 2nd point by successfully escorting the payload to the opponent's spawn. If the capturing team doesn't successfully escort the payload, the opposing team is given 1 point for defending. The first team to reach 4 points wins.
Payload plays as a attackers vs defenders situation. The defenders are given time before the match begins to choose strategic locations to slow the attacker's approach as the attackers attempt to escort a payload from their spawn all the way across the map to the opponent's spawn. If the attackers fail to escort the payload to the defender's spawn then the defenders win. Regardless of the outcome of the round, the teams switch roles for the next round. The first team to get 2 round victories gets the win.
Overall, despite the lack of different game modes and only I think 4 different maps for each mode, the game is very solid and you should definitely give it a try :D

Where to begin with Garry's Mod. It's almost less of a game and more of a community platform. The sandbox in of itself is worth the price of admission, but there are so many user-created gamemodes to play that it's almost mindboggling. TTT, Prop Hunt, Murder, RP, etc. etc. etc. The game is so freeing, and while the community can be somewhat toxic at times, when you find the right server with the right rules and the right people, it's like being a part of a whole community.
The only real downside is that, as it's based on textures from CS: Source, you have to buy that game as well (unless you like endless "ERROR"s and pink/black textures). But even for the price of two games, Garry's Mod is more than worth it. Buy the bundle and give it a shot, you won't regret it.

Incredibly overrated, but a bad game? No. There's a lot of great things about this game. There's a huge amount of things to do, a ton of choices you can make that greatly affect the outcome and in general is an immersive universe. The big downside to me is it seems that it was created to cater to a very niche crowd. The melodramatic hipster "alternative" acoustic guitar music gets very obnoxious as it's this game's primary soundtrack choice and painfully attempts to project some sort of sad sensitivity.
When I first started this game, judging by my characters voice and appearance, I literally thought I was in middleschool, only to later find out she's in college. It's kind of ironic that in so many shows and movies the main cast looks so much older than they actually are, but in this, everyone looks so much younger than they really are. Another unfortunate issue is that everyone besides the main character is portrayed as so shallow, narrow minded and simple, allowing things so miniscule as missing their phonecall to drive them to bring it up a dozen times in the future and simply not let it go. The teachers are the classic people who are ridiclously skeptical of anything you tell them and none of it really feels like college, it feels more like the media portrayl of a really shallow highschool with dumb cheerleaders, jocks and geeks.
I have trouble relating to the character, not because she's female, as I loved Clementine in the Telltale Walking Dead, but because she's a bland, hipster, white knight. Although your choices certainly affect the outcome, you have a very concrete personality that you have very little control over it. This is the classic game that for some reason hundreds of people will cry out and rave about how it's the greatest game ever made, how it made them cry and anyone who doesn't think the devs of this game hung the moon and stars is a bigot who can't invest themselves into a female character. This just has one of -those- playerbases. Which is why I'm sure I'll get plenty of downvotes for this review, but oh well. I certainly reccomend this game as it's a fun, will written storyline, but it's far from flawless and if you go into it thinking it's as great as most of these reviews say it is, you'll be disappointed.

Paladins is a free to play hero first person shooter developed by HiRez Studios, the creators of SMITE, currently in open beta.
Starting with the presentation, the character design is colorful, though a bit plain at times, but the overall voice acting more than makes up for it, each of them having their own personality. Can't say the same about maps unfortunately, while their general design is good, they feel a little bit empty at times, at least some of them. They're huge and it feels like they could add more things in to make it look more interesting.
Gameplay-wise, it's your typical hero first person shooter. The game is often compared to
, and while there are some similarities (and controversies in comparing the two in the first place), I think that
feels different enough to hold my interest - while indeed some characters feel heavily similar to one another between games (Viktor to Soldier: 76, Drogoz to Pharah, Fernando to Reinhardt etc.) there are also some that are unique and don't feel even moderately similar to something else. (Like Ying, a support who uses mirror illusions of herself to shift her position, heal and damage enemies)
There are two main modes available: Siege and Payload. The former is a fusion of KotH and your standard payload-pushing game. Each round, the teams compete to capture the central control point which grants them a point to their score. Afterwards, they have to push the payload on a short track to the enemy base to score another before the timer runs out. Should the enemy succeed in defending however, they gain a point instead. The teams fight until one of them scores 4 points. The latter, Payload, is basically just what it says - push the payload to the end of the track. After the first round, the teams switch sides and the second team has to either push it further than the other team (if they didn't make it all the way through) or do it faster (if they did).
There are four main classes: Frontliner (basically tank), Damage, Flanker, and Support. There is a few different characters available in each category, possessing different abilities and a game-changing ultimate ability that has to charge up. You start out with a couple heroes and have to grind a bit to unlock the rest (or buy them), but it doesn't take very long. The TTK in general is pretty high, and hitboxes are quite infamously lenient. (If you thought Hanzo was shooting logs, take a look at Sha Lin.)
Then there's the card system which I have a mixed opinion about. Basically every character can create a deck of five cards, each going from level one to four, with a total combined level of them being 12. They modify certain abilities and sometimes give them new properties as well. Some might say this increases customization and depth, but it also makes the game less predictable in general. You don't know what your enemies are gonna bring to the table, and there are also of course optimal decks and in case of some characters even single cards that are must-haves for that character to actually be worth a damn. (Healing Rain for Grohk comes to mind.)
There are also those items you can purchase during a game for credits you gain for performing well, and I would be fine with that if it wasn't so horribly balanced...
Which brings me to my next point. What ultimately pushed me away from the game is that HiRez seems to have no idea how to balance the game properly. Said item upgrades are a perfect example of this - some are so painfully useless that you only hurt yourself by taking them (Aggression is infamous for that, being only a +5%/level increase in damage, and it's also obviously a noob's favorite), but there are two that are so blatantly overpowered I can't even begin to comprehend what they were thinking. Namely Cauterize and Wrecker. Cauterize reduces healing on targets you shoot - seems simple enough... except the increase is +30%/level. Yes, at max level you reduce healing to only
of what is normally is. Needless to say healing-focused supports are considered useless because of it. The other one is Wrecker, which is a +75%/level increase in damage to shields, basically forcing frontliners to build agressive, self-sustaining builds and basically ignoring their shield abilities because they're completely useless. The kicker? HiRez, after looking at frontliners wrecking stuff with their non-shield-focused builds in high-level play, decided that this is happening because frontliner shields are too strong and to
. They missed the point by such a huge margin that they only made the problem worse. It's hilarious.
While I don't disagree with them on everything, some of their balance changes no one is able to comprehend. Like nerfing Grover, who's considered to be the weakest support character, simply because when looking at statistics his casual winrate was very high. If this is the stuff they base their balance changes on, then I don't predict a good future for the general balance in this game.
What ultimately made me quit playing it is the announcement of a new third-party anti-cheat - Easy Anti-Cheat. While it isn't what MMOs commonly use from the research I did, it still is prone to having loopholes and also working in a questionable manner, as a few snippets in the EULA of it will show. The points about monitoring the user's PC and even taking screenshots without asking is where I draw the line.
My verdict as of now is negative. The game is fun, but the balancing is questionable at best and the new anti-cheat has a lot of personal security concerns. It's not bad, but needs a lot more polish, and for devs to actually think a lot more deeply about all of this.

Incredibly overrated, but a bad game? No. There's a lot of great things about this game. There's a huge amount of things to do, a ton of choices you can make that greatly affect the outcome and in general is an immersive universe. The big downside to me is it seems that it was created to cater to a very niche crowd. The melodramatic hipster "alternative" acoustic guitar music gets very obnoxious as it's this game's primary soundtrack choice and painfully attempts to project some sort of sad sensitivity.
When I first started this game, judging by my characters voice and appearance, I literally thought I was in middleschool, only to later find out she's in college. It's kind of ironic that in so many shows and movies the main cast looks so much older than they actually are, but in this, everyone looks so much younger than they really are. Another unfortunate issue is that everyone besides the main character is portrayed as so shallow, narrow minded and simple, allowing things so miniscule as missing their phonecall to drive them to bring it up a dozen times in the future and simply not let it go. The teachers are the classic people who are ridiclously skeptical of anything you tell them and none of it really feels like college, it feels more like the media portrayl of a really shallow highschool with dumb cheerleaders, jocks and geeks.
I have trouble relating to the character, not because she's female, as I loved Clementine in the Telltale Walking Dead, but because she's a bland, hipster, white knight. Although your choices certainly affect the outcome, you have a very concrete personality that you have very little control over it. This is the classic game that for some reason hundreds of people will cry out and rave about how it's the greatest game ever made, how it made them cry and anyone who doesn't think the devs of this game hung the moon and stars is a bigot who can't invest themselves into a female character. This just has one of -those- playerbases. Which is why I'm sure I'll get plenty of downvotes for this review, but oh well. I certainly reccomend this game as it's a fun, will written storyline, but it's far from flawless and if you go into it thinking it's as great as most of these reviews say it is, you'll be disappointed.

It's everything we've come to expect from a Civ game - including a broken AI. The game is good, a little dumbed down in some areas, a bit more complex in others - the perfect degree of change from V, but the AI is, once again, broken. Not only is it functionally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but it also once again suffers no consequences for failing to meet the game's maintenance expectations - unhappiness or negative balance do not affect AI as usual. In addition to that, the Spy system is broken almost completely - you can get spied for money (basically a high powered money theft directly from a city) but the enemy can steal more money than you have. This will immediately plunge your empire into chaos, with no indication of how much longer you still need to survive with 0 gold until this imaginary debt has been repaid. Add to that the fact that it is impossible to defend every district of a city from spies, and that this game encourages you to have more than 4 cities, and you end up in a money draining fight against yourself. Your empire crumbles, revolutions happen, units disband, and you lose. All because of a single spy.
Until this is fixed, I cannot recommend the game as it is simply not enjoyable. It would be another thing entirely if spying could be disabled like in V, but that option does not exist this time around.

If you enjoy the sound of Sean Bean telling you what a wonderful ruler you are, then this is the only game that can deliver that for you.  (And if you don't enjoy the sound of Sean Bean telling you how wonderful you are, what kind of soulless creature are you?)
Compared with previous Civ entries, culture has been toned down a little and makes more sense, religion has been completely overhauled, and the separation of the 'technology treee' from the 'culture tree' adds a layer of interesting choices.  The military game moves away from an 'all or nothing' situation because barbarians are a much more meaningful threat, and the most pacifist strategy will still require a meaningful defensive force.

Civilization 6 is a much more intricate game than it's predecessor, which is sort of mixed blessing. There's more to do, and more ways to do it but it's also much easier to get bogged down in fiddly details.
Eureka moments
One of the major ways game has changed is that almost every tech or civic (a culture tech) can be half researched for free if specific conditions are met. For example, founding a city on the coast will give you a bonus to "Sailing". These moments are laid out in smart ways to flow into different play styles and chasing them helps your research a lot more than just building universities and turtling up. The down side is that since all the technologies have different conditions, it takes a while before you can effectively plan strategies around these Eureka moments.
Districts and Wonder placement
Another huge change is that Wonders and Districts (a specialized city building zone) are now placed on the map, as opposed to existing on a city's tile. There's a variety of placement rules and benefits, ranging from +2 gold for building a commercial district near a river to requiring the Colosseum be built on flat land next to an Entertainment Complex. Expect to devote significant thought to planning out your cities (and to screw it up on your first few playthroughs).
Leader Diversity
My favorite thing about Civilization 6 is how all of the new mechanics open the door to a plethora of interesting leaders. This isn't just a slightly stronger unit or minor building improvement, there's a bunch of special district variants or unique terrain improvements or flat out OP sounding abilities (use workers to rush wonders?) that really give each faction a clear identity. Additionally, City-States and Great People now give unique bonuses, further diversifying each playthrough.
It comes down to what you're looking for. If you liked Civ5 but found it getting a little stale on repeated playthroughs, Civ6 will probably be great for you. However, if you felt Civ5 had just the right level of tactical engagement, then you'll probably find the new additions unwelcome and frustrating.

A worthy successor to Civ V. Reasonable people can disagree about which is the superior Civ game.

The dominant strategy of "sprint science, then pivot to tech, political, or culture victory as desired" doesn't work as well in this edition; you are encouraged to pick your focus early. With most PC games pre-publication development is divided into an Alpha and a Beta stage. When it comes to the Civilization series, there is a third gestation period; the Gamma stage if you will. This covers the period between the official game launch and the inevitable release of the two expansions that will properly flesh out and re-balance a good game and make it great and add enough new content to come within a couple of miles of justifying the added cost.
If you are a big fan of turned-based strategy games and money is no object or you like being in on this third larval stage, then Civilization VI is a smart purchase right now. Otherwise, exercise some restraint and wait for the total package. If you have and still enjoy any of the older Civilization titles, keep playing them.  If you don't have them, buy now and discover the many pleasures of this wonderful series.
In a year or so, Civ VI will be genuinely complete and available at a reasonable price and the Gamma version of Civ VII will be on the horizon.

I played the game these past days and played through all five episodes back-to-back. Here are my thoughts.
You play as Maxine “Max” Caulfield, a teenage girl at the prestigious Blackwell Academy a private boarding school in small-town Arcadia.
The game takes heavy inspiration from Telltale’s style of adventure game, half of the game is walking around and listening to Max comment on her surroundings. The other half is made up of long choice-ridden dialogue sequences, Complete with its own “That Was An Important Decision” indicator.
And for the most part, you’re a teenage girl with teenage problems. Bullies. Suicide. Overbearing parents. Absent parents. Trying to figure out how to stand up for what you believe in. Trying to figure out what you believe in. Navigating cliques and drama. Hanging out with your best friend, Chloe.
There’s a level of artifice to it a feeling, sometimes, of “Do kids talk like this?” (And the subsequent “No, no they don’t.”) It’s not so much an accurate appraisal of teenage-dom as it is someone’s earnest recollection of what it felt like to be a teenager.
But the ideas are real. If Life is Strange doesn’t completely capture its subject matter, it at least hits on truth enough of the time. Feelings of insecurity, of “playing at adulthood,” are powerful and not-often-explored in video games, given our tendency towards trying to escape those same feelings through supercharged power fantasies.
Life is Strange has its flaws. The game’s usage of slang is particularly questionable, sometimes cringe-inducing. And the cast is maybe six or seven characters too large, with a few who just...do nothing. They exist apparently to exist or are short-shrift after a strong set-up in the first two episodes.
I was surprised, though. Life is Strange makes the mundane compelling, episode after episode. Looking through old photographs. Listening to Max talk about her childhood or comment on how she’s outgrown bits of pop culture. Eating pancakes at the diner. Swimming in the pool after curfew with Chloe. Standing on a beach watching the sunset. Or trying to keep this spoiler-free seeing how the smallest of actions can have big consequences. These are the game’s strengths.
Back to the future
The irony is that these menial glimpses of “real life” are the most compelling part of Life is Strange, and it’s the gamest pieces that fall apart.
Moving through Life is Strange’s five episodes, we simultaneously move further and further away from Max-as-Teenager. The low-key character study of earlier episodes is steadily supplanted by two larger stories: 1) Max’s ability to rewind time and 2) The disappearance of another Blackwell girl, Rachel Amber.
Max discovers the time travel ability early in the game and, to its credit, the game makes good use of it. Since this is a choice-driven game, you’re given the ability to make a decision on how events play out, then rewind and see how the other option plays out, then decide. It’s the type of have-your-cake-and-eat-it-too plot branching players usually get by save-scumming, but codified into the actual game mechanics. And I like that.
The time travel in Life is Strange makes more sense as a game mechanic than as a plot device. It doesn’t hold up to scrutiny—at all. Any rules about Max’s ability are largely arbitrary, held to only until the moment the story calls for them to be broken. Plot holes abound. And the mystery of how or why Max was granted this ability? Never properly addressed.
It’s fortuitous she got it when she did, though. Rachel Amber’s disappearance is a near-constant presence in Arcadia Bay, her face staring out from dozens of Missing Person posters. There’s something wrong with Blackwell Academy, and Max dons her deerstalker cap to try and uncover the school’s darkest secret.
Life is Strange doesn’t pull punches. There are some truly depraved moments in the story, the likes of which I’d expect more from Condemned than some twee game about high school kids. And what’s worse: Some of those moments are avoidable, if you make the right choices. Knowing you caused something horrible is far worse than knowing it was destined to happen.
The denouement fizzles, though. Despite some incredible sequences, Episode Five is largely on-rails and nullifies many of the choices you’ve made throughout the earlier chapters. Numerous characters are relegated to supporting roles and are never given a proper ending. And the villain? Life is Strange abandons its trademark subtlety and knack for writing morally-gray characters, turning the villain from a “real” person into a caricature.
It’s not that Life is Strange ends on a particularly bad note. It merely doesn’t measure up to what came earlier—in part because it stops focusing so much on Max, The Troubled Teenager and starts focusing on Max, The Video Game Character Who Needs To Save The World. And the latter’s not as interesting.
Bottom line.
After wrapping each episode of Life is Strange, a bar of text would crawl across the screen saying “The next episode is out now!” which seemed a bit redundant since I’d already obtained the whole game. But after finishing Episode Five, the line changed to something like (paraphrasing from my potentially off-base memory) “If any of these themes resonated, let us know.”
The themes. Not the time travel. Not the Rachel Amber plot. It’s clear that developer Dontnod understands that what makes Life is Strange special is Max and her experience as a teenager. And the experiences of the other kids in her life—their insecurities, their private confessions, their feelings of love and betrayal and loneliness and murderous rage. It’s a cacophony of emotion, a time where the days pass slowly, and each is either the best day of your life or the end of the world.
At least, that’s Dontnod’s idealized fiction of being a teenager.
The rest—what we’d I guess call the “main story”—is forgettable. What I’m left with now, what I’ll return to when I think of Life is Strange, is the small(er) moments: Fond memories of Blackwell, of watering my plant or watching Blade Runner with a friend or laying in bed listening to Bright Eyes.
Normality can be poignant. Low stakes can feel high, given the correct context. Escapism is optional. This is Life is Strange’s legacy, regardless of whether it always followed through.

What is a game? It is a creation of goals, rules, challenges, interactions and the not always necessary but almost always needed soundtrack. The Walking Dead: Season 2, in the first three episodes that I have played so far, have given me a sense of belonging in the world created by Telltale. The goals were somehow clear- survive. But that is always easier said than done in The Walking Dead, as the choices you make are tailored to your story so that your first decision could impact your last. There are no rules in the Walking Dead, as I have witnessed things which broke every day moral boundaries and confused the compass of my natural instincts. But aren't rules meant to be broken anyway... The interactions between characters are as strong as they ever were and given the fact that you play as Clementine you get a feelings of awe when faced with the dangers of the real world. You must have a thick skin to survive because people are not as merciful as they once were. Let's just say that you need more than sad puppy eyes to make it. Lastly the soundtrack is gorgeous, from the most subtle scenes when gazing into the reality of the situation to the fast paced chases by zombies and other humans and lastly to the beautiful songs of the credits after every episode, you are sure to have your heart filled with feelings. The Walking Dead S2 was the greatest game I have played since the S1 and it is sure to leave the same impact on people who enjoyed the harsh realities that must be endured in this game. I do not recommend rushing the game, but rather soaking in every detail and paying close attention to the characters. My whole journey so far has been somehow influenced by what Lee told me in S1: JUST KEEP MOVING! And that is what I did. I kept moving always trying to find a way to stray away from what it is to come, because believe me when I say it, darkness will come and there is no way you can stop it, so to survive, you must WALK AWAY!
I hope this review will help you get a feel for my experience with the game, without giving away any spoilers. I recommend this to anyone who values all the above in a game.

All time best turn based strategy game. Removing the reducdant parts(like diplomatic victory, which depends solely on your money to buy the citystates) and adding brand new systems (spy, intelligence, more complicated trade route, etc) makes Civ VI absolutely better than Civ V.
It seems the only large drawback of Civ VI is the stupid A.I. LOL.

Now to business.
If you thought Civ V with all DLC was at about the right level of complexity, you'll probably find Civ VI too complicated and unfocused.  If you thought Civ V with DLC was too simple, Civ VI might be a good choice for you.
I really wanted to like Civ VI.  The graphics are gorgeous, and I think the interface is much cleaner and more beautiful than that of Civ V.  Hex visability is a lot more obvious, and the cartographic style of the map (i.e. it looks like a literal paper map) is a really nice touch.
That said, I have started, briefly played, and then abandoned at least three separate games, and I don't feel like I got a lot out of the hours I spent on those games.  Civ VI introduces a raft of new mechanics, most blatantly a second tech tree (a "culture" tree), but also city districts, a number of new resources (including housing and city-state influence), per-city happiness (needlessly renamed to "amenity"), a much more elaborate social policy system, and so on.  Individually, none of these changes are "bad" as such.  But there are many of them, and they all seem to pull the game in different directions.
Expansionism has been curtailed in a somewhat indirect way.  Tiles surrounding a city are more cumbersome to upgrade, especially in the early game, because of the need to continually replace your builders as they are expended.  Thus, they either occupy slots in your build queue, or they consume an unreasonable amount of gold.  Worse, settlers now reduce population by one when finished instead of halting city growth while under production.  The combination of these things makes it a lot harder to spam settlers and build lots of cities early.  I imagine this was an intentional balance change.  But unfortunately, it makes the early game boring and tedious because I don't feel like I'm accomplishing enough.
Cities are also more complicated to administer.  Happiness ("amenity") is now per-city instead of global, and each city has a housing limit (raised by various buildings and improvements).  Districts and wonders occupy tiles outside the city, so you need to expend a bit of cognitive effort deciding where they should land... for every single district or wonder you build in every single city you control.  Combined with the reduced expansionism, this makes it feel like I'm expected to manage fewer cities more intensively.
The increased load on the build queue from builders affects city development, too.  So you have to choose between developing your cities, developing your tiles, pumping out army units, and not going broke buying things outside the queue.  And, of course, if you have fewer cities, then you can build fewer things at once.  In short, you have to manage your build queue a lot more carefully than in Civ V, which is annoying and not much fun.  No more "Ooh, I want that thing.
."  In practice, this means wonders are a lot less practical to build because you can't fit them into your build queue.
At the other end of the abstraction spectrum, the social policy trees from Civ V have been coalesced into a single culture tree, which was probably the right move.  Unfortunately, they combined this good change with a substantially more complicated social policy system.  Now, you unlock policies and systems of government (via the culture tree).  You get to have one system of government active at any time.  Each system gives you some fixed bonuses, and a few slots for policies.  The difficulty with this is that it requires you to decide which policies you want to use (unlike Civ V, where the answer was "all of them"), which again imposes a moderate amount of cognitive load on the player.
Naturally, once policies are unlocked, they remain available in the "pick your active policies" screen forever.  So the screen rapidly fills up with useless clutter that you never wanted and don't care about.  The game does at least highlight the new ones with an icon, but the interface gets quite full even in the Classical era.  I can't imagine how ugly it must be in the Modern era.
City-states got more complicated, too.  You now build up "influence" with them, which translates into "envoys", which (finally!) translate into fixed bonuses.  No more "give me X gold for Y influence" silliness.  Again, the old system sucked.  But that doesn't mean the new system is necessarily better.  You have to decide which city-states should get your envoys, which determines the bonuses you receive.  You only have a limited number of envoys and have to pick your favorite bonuses.  Sound familiar?
You also get free envoys for completing "quests," which are a combination of reasonable things like "build a trade route with {city state}" and various random activities which also give half-off discounts on specific items in the tech and culture trees.  Individually, many of these make sense (e.g. founding a city on the coast halves the cost of sailing research).  But collectively, they end up feeling more like a per-game tutorial, which is odd because the game already has a tutorial.

What is a game? It is a creation of goals, rules, challenges, interactions and the not always necessary but almost always needed soundtrack. The Walking Dead: Season 2, in the first three episodes that I have played so far, have given me a sense of belonging in the world created by Telltale. The goals were somehow clear- survive. But that is always easier said than done in The Walking Dead, as the choices you make are tailored to your story so that your first decision could impact your last. There are no rules in the Walking Dead, as I have witnessed things which broke every day moral boundaries and confused the compass of my natural instincts. But aren't rules meant to be broken anyway... The interactions between characters are as strong as they ever were and given the fact that you play as Clementine you get a feelings of awe when faced with the dangers of the real world. You must have a thick skin to survive because people are not as merciful as they once were. Let's just say that you need more than sad puppy eyes to make it. Lastly the soundtrack is gorgeous, from the most subtle scenes when gazing into the reality of the situation to the fast paced chases by zombies and other humans and lastly to the beautiful songs of the credits after every episode, you are sure to have your heart filled with feelings. The Walking Dead S2 was the greatest game I have played since the S1 and it is sure to leave the same impact on people who enjoyed the harsh realities that must be endured in this game. I do not recommend rushing the game, but rather soaking in every detail and paying close attention to the characters. My whole journey so far has been somehow influenced by what Lee told me in S1: JUST KEEP MOVING! And that is what I did. I kept moving always trying to find a way to stray away from what it is to come, because believe me when I say it, darkness will come and there is no way you can stop it, so to survive, you must WALK AWAY!
I hope this review will help you get a feel for my experience with the game, without giving away any spoilers. I recommend this to anyone who values all the above in a game.

Now to business.
If you thought Civ V with all DLC was at about the right level of complexity, you'll probably find Civ VI too complicated and unfocused.  If you thought Civ V with DLC was too simple, Civ VI might be a good choice for you.
I really wanted to like Civ VI.  The graphics are gorgeous, and I think the interface is much cleaner and more beautiful than that of Civ V.  Hex visability is a lot more obvious, and the cartographic style of the map (i.e. it looks like a literal paper map) is a really nice touch.
That said, I have started, briefly played, and then abandoned at least three separate games, and I don't feel like I got a lot out of the hours I spent on those games.  Civ VI introduces a raft of new mechanics, most blatantly a second tech tree (a "culture" tree), but also city districts, a number of new resources (including housing and city-state influence), per-city happiness (needlessly renamed to "amenity"), a much more elaborate social policy system, and so on.  Individually, none of these changes are "bad" as such.  But there are many of them, and they all seem to pull the game in different directions.
Expansionism has been curtailed in a somewhat indirect way.  Tiles surrounding a city are more cumbersome to upgrade, especially in the early game, because of the need to continually replace your builders as they are expended.  Thus, they either occupy slots in your build queue, or they consume an unreasonable amount of gold.  Worse, settlers now reduce population by one when finished instead of halting city growth while under production.  The combination of these things makes it a lot harder to spam settlers and build lots of cities early.  I imagine this was an intentional balance change.  But unfortunately, it makes the early game boring and tedious because I don't feel like I'm accomplishing enough.
Cities are also more complicated to administer.  Happiness ("amenity") is now per-city instead of global, and each city has a housing limit (raised by various buildings and improvements).  Districts and wonders occupy tiles outside the city, so you need to expend a bit of cognitive effort deciding where they should land... for every single district or wonder you build in every single city you control.  Combined with the reduced expansionism, this makes it feel like I'm expected to manage fewer cities more intensively.
The increased load on the build queue from builders affects city development, too.  So you have to choose between developing your cities, developing your tiles, pumping out army units, and not going broke buying things outside the queue.  And, of course, if you have fewer cities, then you can build fewer things at once.  In short, you have to manage your build queue a lot more carefully than in Civ V, which is annoying and not much fun.  No more "Ooh, I want that thing.
."  In practice, this means wonders are a lot less practical to build because you can't fit them into your build queue.
At the other end of the abstraction spectrum, the social policy trees from Civ V have been coalesced into a single culture tree, which was probably the right move.  Unfortunately, they combined this good change with a substantially more complicated social policy system.  Now, you unlock policies and systems of government (via the culture tree).  You get to have one system of government active at any time.  Each system gives you some fixed bonuses, and a few slots for policies.  The difficulty with this is that it requires you to decide which policies you want to use (unlike Civ V, where the answer was "all of them"), which again imposes a moderate amount of cognitive load on the player.
Naturally, once policies are unlocked, they remain available in the "pick your active policies" screen forever.  So the screen rapidly fills up with useless clutter that you never wanted and don't care about.  The game does at least highlight the new ones with an icon, but the interface gets quite full even in the Classical era.  I can't imagine how ugly it must be in the Modern era.
City-states got more complicated, too.  You now build up "influence" with them, which translates into "envoys", which (finally!) translate into fixed bonuses.  No more "give me X gold for Y influence" silliness.  Again, the old system sucked.  But that doesn't mean the new system is necessarily better.  You have to decide which city-states should get your envoys, which determines the bonuses you receive.  You only have a limited number of envoys and have to pick your favorite bonuses.  Sound familiar?
You also get free envoys for completing "quests," which are a combination of reasonable things like "build a trade route with {city state}" and various random activities which also give half-off discounts on specific items in the tech and culture trees.  Individually, many of these make sense (e.g. founding a city on the coast halves the cost of sailing research).  But collectively, they end up feeling more like a per-game tutorial, which is odd because the game already has a tutorial.
All this micromanagement is probably fun for some people, but it isn't my cup of tea.  I reluctantly have to give Civ VI a thumbs down for being too complicated in too many different areas of gameplay at once.

Valentina set off on her Munshot a young pilot, full of vim and vigor. Achieving a stable orbit was a breeze. Her grasp of orbital mechanics, while rather crude, was more than sufficient to the job. She set her pod on an elliptical orbit that, Kerb willing, would intersect that of the Mun. Success!
Burning retrograde at Mun encounter she entered stable orbit around the Mun. She recorded her observations, and as per an agreement with Mission Control, sent those readings back. It was then everything in her pod went dark. She couldn't turn, the reaction wheels dead. All she had was a tank full of rocket fuel and her seemingly limitless supply of oxygen and heat in her suit. After one orbit of the Mun she realized that her rocket was in an orientation that, if timed correctly, could be used to drop back into orbit around Kerbin. Performing seat-of-the-pants estimations she burned and found herself dropping to a safe but rather eccintric orbit of Kerbin, where again she timed her burn based on where luck had her pointing her thrust.
Six orbits of aerobraking, re-entry plasma, and one parachute later she was telling the story to Mission Control and Tracking. Now the KSA launches craft with battery backups and Tracking has had a facilities upgrade to assist Kerbals in orbit with navigational calculations.
TL;DR: Don't fly to the Mun in career mode without batteries or the ability to drop Manuevering nodes. I got lucky, have a story to tell, and a deep love of this game as a result.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played to date! There's a very rich story, lots of interactivity, lots of choice, and you have free reign to decide how the life of the protagonist progresses based on the decisions you make.
Now, I won't pretend this is a game for everyone; there's a lot of repetitiveness in some parts of the game where you have to redo portions or rewind time to explore different possibilities and you have to sit through some of the same events happening again. There's also not a lot of action in the traditional sense (of real-time need, since you can manipulate time).
Instead, what you'll get out of this game is a very well connected and well polished, story-rich game where you can make choices that really do have an effect that gets tied back later. In some other games, you'll make choices which are generally inconsequential, but Life is Strange does a fanstastic job of really making your choices drive the story. It's a very well-written game more than anything--the characters feel very real and you can sense the tension between different characters and the pivotal role each of them has.
Overall, you'll love this game for the story more than anything else. As you progress, the game gets more intense and emotional, and at times it definitely gave me goose bumps. If you enjoy well-developed story lines and well-made decision driven games, then this one is for you

While some people will no doubt dislike the ending(s) upon reflection I think you'll find that the most obvious ending was inevitable and suited the tone of the story perfectly.
I played this on a Steam Link with a PS4 controller with no issues and got it on sale.
Get it If you like: time travel stories, the Butterfly Effect movie, story over gameplay, Telltale style games, female protagonists, murder mysteries, photography, great soundtracks (indie music style), soft science fiction.
Avoid it if you: don't like time travel, want a real branching storyline with multiple endings, need the ending to live up to the rest of the game in terms of story quality and satisfaction (it doesn't) or need a explanation of how or why the time travel mechanic is happening to the main character.

All time best turn based strategy game. Removing the reducdant parts(like diplomatic victory, which depends solely on your money to buy the citystates) and adding brand new systems (spy, intelligence, more complicated trade route, etc) makes Civ VI absolutely better than Civ V.
It seems the only large drawback of Civ VI is the stupid A.I. LOL.
In one word; Amazing.

Now to business.
If you thought Civ V with all DLC was at about the right level of complexity, you'll probably find Civ VI too complicated and unfocused.  If you thought Civ V with DLC was too simple, Civ VI might be a good choice for you.
I really wanted to like Civ VI.  The graphics are gorgeous, and I think the interface is much cleaner and more beautiful than that of Civ V.  Hex visability is a lot more obvious, and the cartographic style of the map (i.e. it looks like a literal paper map) is a really nice touch.
That said, I have started, briefly played, and then abandoned at least three separate games, and I don't feel like I got a lot out of the hours I spent on those games.  Civ VI introduces a raft of new mechanics, most blatantly a second tech tree (a "culture" tree), but also city districts, a number of new resources (including housing and city-state influence), per-city happiness (needlessly renamed to "amenity"), a much more elaborate social policy system, and so on.  Individually, none of these changes are "bad" as such.  But there are many of them, and they all seem to pull the game in different directions.
Expansionism has been curtailed in a somewhat indirect way.  Tiles surrounding a city are more cumbersome to upgrade, especially in the early game, because of the need to continually replace your builders as they are expended.  Thus, they either occupy slots in your build queue, or they consume an unreasonable amount of gold.  Worse, settlers now reduce population by one when finished instead of halting city growth while under production.  The combination of these things makes it a lot harder to spam settlers and build lots of cities early.  I imagine this was an intentional balance change.  But unfortunately, it makes the early game boring and tedious because I don't feel like I'm accomplishing enough.
Cities are also more complicated to administer.  Happiness ("amenity") is now per-city instead of global, and each city has a housing limit (raised by various buildings and improvements).  Districts and wonders occupy tiles outside the city, so you need to expend a bit of cognitive effort deciding where they should land... for every single district or wonder you build in every single city you control.  Combined with the reduced expansionism, this makes it feel like I'm expected to manage fewer cities more intensively.
The increased load on the build queue from builders affects city development, too.  So you have to choose between developing your cities, developing your tiles, pumping out army units, and not going broke buying things outside the queue.  And, of course, if you have fewer cities, then you can build fewer things at once.  In short, you have to manage your build queue a lot more carefully than in Civ V, which is annoying and not much fun.  No more "Ooh, I want that thing.
."  In practice, this means wonders are a lot less practical to build because you can't fit them into your build queue.
At the other end of the abstraction spectrum, the social policy trees from Civ V have been coalesced into a single culture tree, which was probably the right move.  Unfortunately, they combined this good change with a substantially more complicated social policy system.  Now, you unlock policies and systems of government (via the culture tree).  You get to have one system of government active at any time.  Each system gives you some fixed bonuses, and a few slots for policies.  The difficulty with this is that it requires you to decide which policies you want to use (unlike Civ V, where the answer was "all of them"), which again imposes a moderate amount of cognitive load on the player.
Naturally, once policies are unlocked, they remain available in the "pick your active policies" screen forever.  So the screen rapidly fills up with useless clutter that you never wanted and don't care about.  The game does at least highlight the new ones with an icon, but the interface gets quite full even in the Classical era.  I can't imagine how ugly it must be in the Modern era.
City-states got more complicated, too.  You now build up "influence" with them, which translates into "envoys", which (finally!) translate into fixed bonuses.  No more "give me X gold for Y influence" silliness.  Again, the old system sucked.  But that doesn't mean the new system is necessarily better.  You have to decide which city-states should get your envoys, which determines the bonuses you receive.  You only have a limited number of envoys and have to pick your favorite bonuses.  Sound familiar?
You also get free envoys for completing "quests," which are a combination of reasonable things like "build a trade route with {city state}" and various random activities which also give half-off discounts on specific items in the tech and culture trees.  Individually, many of these make sense (e.g. founding a city on the coast halves the cost of sailing research).  But collectively, they end up feeling more like a per-game tutorial, which is odd because the game already has a tutorial.
All this micromanagement is probably fun for some people, but it isn't my cup of tea.  I reluctantly have to give Civ VI a thumbs down for being too complicated in too many different areas of gameplay at once.

I have always wanted to write a review about this game, but nothing I’ve ever written could express how amazing it was.
I started playing it by myself, and soon my sister and father joined me, so I played on a bigger screen and they didn’t left the couch until I had finished the game. I must say that my sister has the same soft heart that I have, but I had never seen my dad cry with a movie or a game until then.
And the whole experience never leaves your mind. I’ve caught myself talking about it to friends on a bar; I have met people – both on and offline –, who related deeply to my feelings; and even the ones who only knew the game via gameplays (which I strongly do not recommend, by the way, the fun lies in making your own choices and regretting them later) came to me to talk about how amazed they were by the story.
makes you become so attached to its characters and relate so much to their actions that I ended up barely dehydrated and begging for more. I was truly happy when they announced the prequel, even though I haven’t found the time and mood to play it yet.
I felt the need to make a title out of this because when I say everything, I really mean
. And maybe that’s what makes this game a piece of art: you play as a girl who has the power to rewind time and yet it feels so much like our lives.
Max Caulfield one day finds out she can turn back time and change the course of the events. But you get caught in situations where there is no easy choice, where you have to measure which one will not put you or anyone you care about in trouble; and you’ll also see yourself in situations where you could’ve helped someone in many ways if you had payed a little more attention to them.
Well, this is life, isn’t it? A series of choices that makes you who you are and has an impact on everyone around you. That’s probably why the game hits so close to home.
The storyline is amazing and it doesn’t have failures when it comes to details. Even though you’re Max, the other characters have their own backstory, their own dramas, and this is not one of those games where the player gets a omnipresence feeling, since everything you’ll know will be something you saw or heard about.
Its achievements are a side quest where you have to take photos of some hidden things in the scenario. It felt rewarding to get them because I had the feeling I was exploring something that could’ve been easily missed.
Arcadia Bay, where the game takes place, is a delight to our eyes. The game will even offer you moments where you can just sit or lay down and do nothing but enjoy the scene and hear the music.
By the way, this game has one of the better soundtracks ever. I’m always listening to it and never seem to get tired. Every song fits the scene so perfectly that, even if when you hear them months after playing, you’ll feel the same melancholy or happiness or comfort that you felt while playing the game.
Although I may have made it sound like it’s a beautiful fairytale, don’t be fooled by the pretty scenario or the beautiful characters: the game brings up a lot of dark themes. I won’t get into much detail on them because I don’t want to spoil anything, but they surely contribute to the emotional impact of the game. Rest assured that they aren’t triggering, though.
I have experienced only bug while playing it: sometimes their speech would not be synchronized with their facial expressions but that might be my laptop’s fault, since I have not seen anyone complaining about it.
is a must play, definitely. Even if this isn’t your type of game, it is a worthy experience.

Season 1 was absolutely fantastic. I'll admit I cried like a little girl at the end of it.
Season 2 is no exception. Has you on the edge of your seat throuought.
Decisions from Season 1 and the 400 Days DLC are imported if you choose and the events of Season 2 will be altered based on those prior choices. While Season 2 can be started without playing the prior season, I highly recommend doing Season 1 first so that you have a better understanding of what is happening and to have your choices imported rather than being randomly selected for you
On the emotional side:
Sometimes I want  to play through the entire season 2 in one sitting because it's such a great game. But, I can't. It's too hard. Too emotional. So I have to take breaks. Playing more than two sittings of The Walking Dead a day or every other day is very rare because of the strong heavy emotions it causes. And that is just one of the many reasons that The Walking Dead 2 is such a good game; it causes people to feel real emotions: emotions of hate, love, sadness, scardness. Emotions I can not say I've experienced in quite a while, especially in a game?!. If you can not handle that ^ then don't bother playing this game. because that's what it revolvs around.
On a technical side:
Graphics are great, (no surprise there). The camera movements are real, as if you're watching a movie with real people in it. The camera pans in and out and over. Great.
The soundtrack is absolutely fantastic throuought, and if you are into music I definitely reccomend listening to the song at the end of every episode while the credits run; most of the time if not aways, it is related to the episide you just completed.
Voice acting is smooth and powerful with real emotion just like the first season, and unlike any game I have ever seen.
One tiny negative bit I noticed with this Season is that you cannot use your mouse wheel to scroll down the list of responses to the conversations that you are having, like you were able to do in the first Season. You were also able to scroll through your actions of what you do in the game as well so in this season I find myself misclicking something on the screen because I'm used to scrolling, or I find myself nearly missing a timed answer in a conversation because I remember that I can't scroll and have to click.
This minor detail can easily be dealt with, however, because mouse sensitivity on this game (as opposed to Season 1) is much more smooth despite no option to change it, and thus makes choosing one of the choices simple and effortless.
To recap: Fantastically emotional, personal, and powerful. Music is the best. Unbelievably top notch graphics and mouse movement, with a small change in controlls that can be more than easily dealt with and learned.
If you can not already tell, The Walking Dead: Season 2 is just as fantastic as the first Season, and is definitely (besides The Walking Dead: Season 1) the best game I have had the happy pleasure of playing in the longest time.

So 100 hours in, I think I've mastered some basics of this game.... unfortunately that is not a joke.
Negatives:
If you like easy games, then this is probably not for you. You can play sandbox mode and mess around with putting rockets on your rockets so that they can rocket more, but ultimately you'll probably struggle to get the rocket (or plane!) to fly correctly.
I highly recommend watching some youtube tutorial vids of this game (scott manley for example), they are needed.
Positives:
So you managed to get a rocket into orbit. Now what? Now you try to aim for the Mun, or Duna, or Eve. You get halfway to realise you're not going to be able to slow down enough to get into an orbit around them. At this point you're ultimately doomed. But then you notice you have enough fuel to fly *into* the assigned mission. CLOSE ENOUGH.
This game is frustration but so rewarding. When you finally manage to accomplish your mission, you can fist punch the air. This weekend as part of my career into space exploration I managed to: Dock with a space station that I put up there; fly a probe *into* Eve (oops); Fly a probe into orbit around Eve (fist pump); Then a different one around Duna (smaller fist pump cause I already did it for Eve).
I've barely scratched the surface of this game. 100 hours in.....! Still plenty to do (mooore planets, their moons, manned missions to said planets, planet bases, planet rovers, asteroids, I'm sure there is others too).
This game is a tough nut to crack but when you do its glorious. Nothing quite like it. I normally hate SIM-style games, but this has found the missing ingredient for it. Not sure what it is, but it works!
6/10 Accessibility for noobs (terminology is huuuuu?)
9/10 Gameplay
1/10 Kerbal survival rate
This game has a huge community, Check reddit.
Finally: modding. So just when you start to get bored of the game, add some mods and then stuff can be significantly different (planets, more ship parts, graphical effects, physics)
100 hours in, and I'm not bored ;-)

I have always wanted to write a review about this game, but nothing I’ve ever written could express how amazing it was.
I started playing it by myself, and soon my sister and father joined me, so I played on a bigger screen and they didn’t left the couch until I had finished the game. I must say that my sister has the same soft heart that I have, but I had never seen my dad cry with a movie or a game until then.
And the whole experience never leaves your mind. I’ve caught myself talking about it to friends on a bar; I have met people – both on and offline –, who related deeply to my feelings; and even the ones who only knew the game via gameplays (which I strongly do not recommend, by the way, the fun lies in making your own choices and regretting them later) came to me to talk about how amazed they were by the story.
makes you become so attached to its characters and relate so much to their actions that I ended up barely dehydrated and begging for more. I was truly happy when they announced the prequel, even though I haven’t found the time and mood to play it yet.
I felt the need to make a title out of this because when I say everything, I really mean
. And maybe that’s what makes this game a piece of art: you play as a girl who has the power to rewind time and yet it feels so much like our lives.
Max Caulfield one day finds out she can turn back time and change the course of the events. But you get caught in situations where there is no easy choice, where you have to measure which one will not put you or anyone you care about in trouble; and you’ll also see yourself in situations where you could’ve helped someone in many ways if you had payed a little more attention to them.
Well, this is life, isn’t it? A series of choices that makes you who you are and has an impact on everyone around you. That’s probably why the game hits so close to home.
The storyline is amazing and it doesn’t have failures when it comes to details. Even though you’re Max, the other characters have their own backstory, their own dramas, and this is not one of those games where the player gets a omnipresence feeling, since everything you’ll know will be something you saw or heard about.
Its achievements are a side quest where you have to take photos of some hidden things in the scenario. It felt rewarding to get them because I had the feeling I was exploring something that could’ve been easily missed.
Arcadia Bay, where the game takes place, is a delight to our eyes. The game will even offer you moments where you can just sit or lay down and do nothing but enjoy the scene and hear the music.
By the way, this game has one of the better soundtracks ever. I’m always listening to it and never seem to get tired. Every song fits the scene so perfectly that, even if when you hear them months after playing, you’ll feel the same melancholy or happiness or comfort that you felt while playing the game.
Although I may have made it sound like it’s a beautiful fairytale, don’t be fooled by the pretty scenario or the beautiful characters: the game brings up a lot of dark themes. I won’t get into much detail on them because I don’t want to spoil anything, but they surely contribute to the emotional impact of the game. Rest assured that they aren’t triggering, though.
I have experienced only bug while playing it: sometimes their speech would not be synchronized with their facial expressions but that might be my laptop’s fault, since I have not seen anyone complaining about it.
is a must play, definitely. Even if this isn’t your type of game, it is a worthy experience.

At 35 hours of game time, I should say that during those 35 hours, NOT A DIME WAS SPENT. Paladins is one of very few F2P games that DOESN'T keep half the gameplay behind a paywall. However, you do not start out with all of the champions, but you can buy them with gold, which is the currency you get from... playing the game! I got my first hero within about five or six games if my memory is right, and I had a selection of about a third of the champions from the start to play up to that point. But that was a long time ago. Now with how you get gold, if you win your first three matches (which you probablly will, because the first few matches you play are against bots regardless of whether you selected to be against bots.) So, now we get to good part. The gameplay. Paladins has two gamemodes, seige and payload. In payload, you push a cart or stop the othere team from doing so, and whoever pushes it farther, wins! In seige, you play king of the hill for a capture point, and when when team captures it they get a point and they must push a payload into the enemy base and if they, fail, then the other team gets a point. You need four points to win, and you can't win with a defense. Now, the champions themselves. Most people complain that they are really similar to Overwatch, but with the card system, no one character is alike. The card system is where you select five cards and they buff your abilities or self. There are at the time of this review, 19 champions, and none of them share abilities, so have fun finding the ones you like to play! Now, I feel like I should mention a few negatives. I STILL have not unlocked the competitve mode because you need to play about five to six games on twelve different champions before you can. I just don't know how many games of three supports and two flanks I can handle. But, overal, I give paladins a solid 9/10 for being fun, but something just not quite capping of to a perfect 10/10.

Robert Kirkman is a man of entertainment and many talents. And he's a kinda a guy you would give Oscar to or slap so hard.
Well, judging by franchise decisions for "The Walking Dead", Kirkman's should be greatly awarded AND punched in the face even harder. The guy, alongside his collagues gave us AWESOME COMICS, pretty solid novels, some great games and probably the ♥♥♥♥♥iest zombie show that ever stumbled on our screens. Yes, I am talking about AMC's The Walking Dead and I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ HATE IT. In case you need to ask why, you either don't know what "The Walking Dead" is all about, or you're ignorant and you should be slapped, too.
Now, let's get back to episodic adventure game "The Walking Dead" that's published by Telltale Games. In 2012 we got Season One, consisting of five episodes, and now we're stuck in the middle of Season 2, with Episode 4 on the way, biting our nails and hailing a great villain Bill Carver voiced by one and only Michael Madsen.
In case you haven't tried The Walking Dead before, it's an episodic not-really-adventure-but-more-of-a-interactive-novel game that puts you in position of choosing dialogues and actions which will directly influence the story - yes, it's a game that requires less reflexes than any other zombie game. Without need to dissect the Season 1 here, I'll skip to Season 2 right away.
Season 2 leans even more toward storytelling mode. It's a story driven season that will require even less actions, movements, but the decisions shall be huge and will leave you wanting more. As for the characters, Clem is back and she's back in black, you're gonna love her 'new' character. You'll meet some ol' friends and enemies, and if you have your Season 1 and 400 Days saves - the game will continue directly based upon your choices in previous Telltale TWD games.
Characters are portrayed pretty nicely, most of 'em are not flat and you'll have your own satisfaction or disappointment with their destinies and what you choose for them, and that thing is pretty important when it comes to games that are story and emotions driven.
The Walking Dead Season 2 needs some more action, but it gets you pretty pumped up with a story and therefore, I can't really complain. It's violent and hectic and if you love the world of TWD comics - this, in a pretty good way, comes pretty close.
Either way, you have to be ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy not to acknowledge the following - AMC's should seek game producers to work for their show, because this is WAY BETTER than that lame a$$ stuff served for fourth year now. If you've played Season 1 - get it. If you did not - get Season 1 first.

This is probably one of the best games I've ever played to date! There's a very rich story, lots of interactivity, lots of choice, and you have free reign to decide how the life of the protagonist progresses based on the decisions you make.
Now, I won't pretend this is a game for everyone; there's a lot of repetitiveness in some parts of the game where you have to redo portions or rewind time to explore different possibilities and you have to sit through some of the same events happening again. There's also not a lot of action in the traditional sense (of real-time need, since you can manipulate time).
Instead, what you'll get out of this game is a very well connected and well polished, story-rich game where you can make choices that really do have an effect that gets tied back later. In some other games, you'll make choices which are generally inconsequential, but Life is Strange does a fanstastic job of really making your choices drive the story. It's a very well-written game more than anything--the characters feel very real and you can sense the tension between different characters and the pivotal role each of them has.
Overall, you'll love this game for the story more than anything else. As you progress, the game gets more intense and emotional, and at times it definitely gave me goose bumps. If you enjoy well-developed story lines and well-made decision driven games, then this one is for you

I loved the first game.  Unfortunately, this one comes nowhere close to it.  It is no longer an adventure game meant to cause the player to reflect on how their values hold up when pushed to the limits (a stressful post-apocalyptic setting where ideals are never realized).  Instead, it is a 3D virtual novel with very little agency at all.  It was very rare that Lee ever did anything that directly conflicted with my agency.  However, Clementine's options never seem to fit how I want to react, and many situations are not only uninteresting, but simply convenient writing.
Also, although this is not an inherently negative aspect, each episode takes substantially less time to complete than the previous game, so on top of being unsatisfied with the content, I'm also getting less of it to judge it on.  Unfortunately, I regret my purchase quite a bit.  I don't feel down that I'm out $20; I'll gladly add that to them as extra payment for how great the first game was.  Instead, I feel cheated on the time I invested into the game.  No, you should not carbony copy a game when making a sequel, but this really isn't even in the same realm as the first game.

After numerous shorter games, and romperstomping my way through a huge map with 11 AI players, conquest only victory and epic timescale, I really feel that I've played enough to say that the AI in this game is an absolute joke. Really, this game isn't worth your time... Get Civ V instead - it's a far superior game...
My key issues are as follows:
1) The AI repeatedly declares war, sends nothing to attack you, then begs for peace some turns later prostrating themselves before you with offerings of gold and luxuries.
2) When at war with the AI, they never attack. I remember playing Civ IV, and seeing armies building up on my border before the AI declares war. No behaviour of that sort is to be seen here.
3) The AI is schizophrenic and utterly moronic. They will condemn you for warmongering, while frequently attempting to encourage you to join in their wars. Involving yourself in even a single war during an otherwise peaceful playthrough can lead to unanimous loathing from the AI, with constant denouncements being shouted at you.
4) The AI never uses aircraft...
5) The AI settles cities in any location they can, and leaves them completely undefended. The AI does not choose efficient locations for city building, and thus irritates that player into having to declare war in order to raze the cities and more efficiently use the land.
6) The victory screen statistics are total garbage. There is no map replay.
7) The UI feels a bit awkward, with various essential tools seemingly overlooked. There is, for example, no list of all units. If you want to find your builders, you must do this manually by scrolling over your empire. A further oversight is the lack of a global politics overview. If you want to know who is at war with whom, you must "speak" to each leader in turn, and look at their current relationships.
Complaints aside, however, I have to say that this game is looks stunning - it is rich in detail and vivid in colour, and the wonder animations are an absolute delight. The sound design is fantastic, and music is memorable and quite beautiful. The new district system is absolute genius - making the process of building and laying out a city a substantially more interesting and nuanced process compared to Civ V. It's a terrible shame that the AI is just such garbage - it ruins the game. I used to play "comp stomps" with my friends on a fairly regular basis, but doing so in Civ VI would be a waste of time.
Edit:
Some people have suggested that I play the game on harder difficulties, but my understanding is that higher difficulty levels simply add a multiplier to the AI's output (e.g. they get a 2x production multiplier so that they can always outproduce you), and does not affect their behaviour. Since my biggest problem with the game is its broken AI, playing on harder difficulties simply gives them an advantage, but does not make them "smarter".
Additionally, I think it's valid to compare the game to Civ V. I played Civ V from its initial 'vanilla' release, and (I realise that I'm referencing personal memories from ~6 years ago) do not recall being as disappointed with the AI after making the jump from the mature game of Civ IV to the then new game of Civ V. Therefore, I stand by my statement that Civ V is a better game. It is not more content that I desire, but a challenging, inteligent AI.

Lesson learned? Nope! forgot batteries again... While adding more boosters, you begin to think about efficiency and revise your older solutions. Even to reach the nearest body next to your home, you need to juggle lots of variables. But beware: this game has a steep learning curve, so if you can't handle that, better go play some Call of Duty: BlackOps on your console or your favourite Pay2Win title. Well, you need alot of dedication to get anywhere within KSP.
The devs still care for their game and improve it beyond what was expected. This is a ongoing story of success and sets a example for others developers. (I personally judge indie-devs in scales of Squad now) Well, if you ever get bored with this game... just install some mods and increase the depth of simulation, change from Kerbol to the Real Solar System, make altimetry maps with SCANSat, build a communication network with RemoteTech or start to develop mods yourself. Which is easy compared to other games, because everything is plaintext and C#. The huge modding community never fails to amaze. Collaborating modder-thinktanks dish out alot of delta-V, which propels KSP far out from the sphere of influence of crappy games.
This game uses the multiplatform unity4 engine which (gave rise to the Kraken and) allowed a native 64bit linux binary. All the more reason to buy this piece of art.  (if the game would not have a native linux binary, I wouldn't have recommended it at all :)
Community is awesome, devs are awesome, mods awesome.... which equals to awesome game in my world.
