I honestly enjoy playing the game, but in order for the major fixes to be fixed, it needs to be given a down grade.
Pros/Things Civ fixed from last game:
Happiness: Now luxuries can go to multiple cities and each city has its own happiness
Districts/Wonders: Gave a brand-new aspect to the game, gives each city its own specialty from a science/culture city to a military/gold city and everything inbetween. Wonders now are placed on titles of their own which leads to a more space management system which is interesting.
(I will say that if the districts are pillaged, then it takes forever to rebuild them, needs a fix)
Army/Navies: Now you can combine military units into corps (2 in 1) and armies (3 in 1) starting in later years. Something I personally have been waiting for a long time since Revolution. Great adition and helps with waging wars
Workers: debuffed workers so they have a specific number of builds while also making them cost less. Great idea and still very easy to industrialize nation.
Governments/Policies: Made 9 types of governments that have specific sections of military/economic/diplomacy/wildcare sections to personalize the governments. So now you can have a merchant republic with a conscription card. Great addition but needs to be given greater variety in terms of number of governments
Cons/Need to change:
Diplomacy: Again, Civ seems to have made diplomacy even worse now. Wars that you start immediately makes everyone hate you, even if you are asked to declare war by someone else. Being attacked and then taking a city in retalition makes everyone hate you. Doing something that is against the other civ's personality (ie: Not have a strong army with Egypt in the game, Egypt hates you). This makes the game more interesting but still annoying
Barbarians: Completely buffed barabarians to make them as strong as your units without a special card, and even with it, still a pain to fight off. Most of the time i play without them because its just so annoying. Spawn rate for them is also buffed, you basically have to get as strong of an army as to take on another civ, just to take out a village or 2.
Trading: Civ made the Ai hate you even more during trades, makes it so you have to give up twice what you are getting in return so only if you are really desperate will you trade with them. The only way you get a fair 1:1 trade is when you have declared friendship, and with the picky nature of Ai, its much more difficult to declare friendship with them. Its almost like you have to specifically play a certain way to get 1 Ai to be your friend.
Maps/your placement on them: I dont know quite what Civ did but somehow, getting placed on maps got worse. About 1 in every 5 map placements are decent, and the other 4 are either being placed directly in tundra, within 2 titles of tundra, in deserts, or in jungles which aren't so bad. Doesn't matter what type of map you use. I also noticed you dont get many resources near you unless you click the abundant resources in the map settings. This part isn't really bad, just weird to me.
No mod tool yet: Absolutely no way for modders to come in and help the game's bugs and just plain not readiness. Currently they say its under production and will be out soon so don't quote me on this one.
Overall: Great game base, foundation really solid and new and ready for the fixes to come. Honestly game still seems to be in a late beta mood and just needs the diplomacy fix and a few tweaks here or there.
Recommendation: Buy the game and enjoy the aspects that are good, and wait for them to be fixed. Or if you want a finished game, wait for the mod tool to come out, thats when the game can be fixed properly.

Life is Strange is a game about a girl called Max, who moves back into her hometown, Arcadia Bay, after a long time to attend college. Max soon discovers that she has the ability to control time and she gets a vision of a storm destroying Arcadia Bay. She later meets her old friend Chloe in a crazy way and the two try to unravel what is going on in Arcadia Bay. The devs rely heavily on plot, narration and dialogue to try to create a memorable game and succeed in doing so. The choices you make, mostly during dialogue, will affect the game world in a lot of ways.
However, there is not much gameplay to it. Most of the time you would be walking, conversing with someone or solving a puzzle using your time-manipulation abilities.
The overall plot is great even though the writing is questionable at times (words like 'awesomesauce' are annoyingly common). Also, a lot of things in the plot that I was eager to find out were left unaddressed.
The soundtrack and the visuals in this game are really nice. There are some lip-sync issues that ruin the immersion sometimes.
Despite its flaws, Life is Strange is a beautiful game.

I can't begin to understand how I was able to finish this game.
Frankly it took me months before I even got to the fifth and final chapter, and it's not because the game is bad or lacked a key factor to properly engage its audience. Truth is, I had to take long breaks in between playing each episode because I didn't think I can handle the emotional baggage that this game has to offer in one fell swoop.
There is something innocent yet incredibly complex in the choices this game gives its players. You choose a path, believing it to be the best, only to find out that choice leads to devastating consequences. Despite having the ability to manipulate time, I constantly felt trapped and incapable of making a choice.
This game will make you doubt your own self and morals. But at the heart of it, Life is Strange teaches us that it is our choices that make us the sort of person we are and sometimes we're just going to have to be okay with what Life will eventually bring us.

When Steam, my gaming service, offered me some free stuff in exchange for playing a game called Paladins, I knew I was getting myself into a world of pain.
This game was created on August 3, 2016 and is for the PC. It’s currently rated T (Teen) for violence, even though there’s no blood or gore. While Steam invites players to “enter a fantasy world of ancient technology in Paladins, a team-based shooter with strategy elements and deep character customization,” I see it as the free-to-play, rip-off of Overwatch. Overwatch is also a first person shooter in which you can play in a variety of classes, each with unique abilities. In my opinion, there’s no discernable difference between the two games.
However, there are plenty of problems with Paladins. All the mechanics in the game are broken, especially the special power. Worse, there’s no balance between the characters.
And how many characters do you start with? Three. Out of 18. And how much does each character cost? Around $2.00. Clearly, the game favors wealthy players instead of skilled ones. I can’t forget to mention all the skins/costumes that you can “unlock” – really, buy – for your character are also $2.00. I actually calculated how much it would cost to buy every skin and character: $180.00. Why don’t you donate that money to charity, or save it for college instead of supporting a company that will probably either raise the price or make more stuff for you to buy.
Overall, Paladins is an abomination that doesn’t live up to the sound of its name. Paladins are fierce warriors who fight to the death. These characters in the game, however, just throw turtle shells and chickens at each other.
I rate this game 7.5/10, boring game-play and uninspired design.
Basically, they just want to take your money under the guise of free-to-play.

The AI is so weak.
AI stupidity is conveniently hidden by the fog of war.  So most of the time you just won't see how poorly it performs. Sometimes you'll get a hint when you declare war on them and find they don't have any army. But why not remove FoW and see what's happening globally?
Start a game on deity (yes!!), run a cheat code "reveal all" in console to remove fog of war. It requires enabling console first, google how to do that it's very easy. Then build a ton of units and defend against first few AI attacks (which are guaranteed to happen without any apparent reason). Build city walls, miitary districts more units, fortify so nobody can threaten your position. Then you can comfortably enjoy the show.
What you'll see will make you laugh.
1) You'll see AI declare wars on enemies so far that it can't even reach (including you, in the early stage of the game if you reveal your capital).
2) Apart from rushing few city states in the first 30-50 turns the AI will almost always fail to take another civ's city.  It just can't do that, you'll see many times that it can't place a catapult on a proper hex to fire at a city. In late game it will sometimes bring catapult to a mech infantry fight :). Yup. Hard to understand some of the negative reviews. No, at the present time, this is not as complete of a game as Civ 5, nor as balanced. It certainly has some issues. BUT this is the biggest single overhaul of the Civ franchise so far. They've introduced a lot of really interesting and innovative concepts that admittedly do need some tweaking, but are not inherently flawed, and in fact really make it a unique and fun product.
There are some big cons that need to be addressed, but as I will get to, all of the negatives are fixable problems. The core gameplay is as good as any version of Civ, and will only be built upon.
Now let's get to the breakdown.
PROS
+ The district system is excellent and makes you think a lot more about how you want every city to play out
+ The concept of builders really removes the tedium of worker management that has plagued every other version of Civ
+ NO GLOBAL HAPPINESS. The worst concept of Civ 5 has been thrown out the window in place of a localized amenity (happiness) system, and for the better.
+ The return of large empires. A lot of people seem to see the fact that you're encouraged to expand more as a negative, but to me it's definitely a positive. You now feel like you're building large, sprawling EMPIRES, but it's not just settler spam everywhere. That said, victory paths for building tall are still available for those who wish to play that way.
+ The graphics are absolutely gorgeous. Yeah, I know people miss the realistic graphics of Civ 5, but I find the graphical style of 6 to be far more aesthetically pleasing. I love the colors and the way the maps look.
+ Better-designed maps. Movement across maps feels more natural and the maps just feel less crowded.
+ City-states are better. In 5, you could get by without significant city-state diplomacy unless you were going for a diplomatic victory, but they feel like a much more important and impactful part of the game now. Suzerain bonuses were an excellent addition.
+ Early game pacing also feels better than in 5
+ The religious victory is a great addition, and religion in general just builds off of what 5 gave us and turns it into a more dynamic, impactful feature. The most fun games I've had have usually focused on religion.
+ Tech tree specialization encourages different play-styles and advancement paths. Splitting of tech tree into science and civics is a cool idea.
+ "Card-style" civics system to replace social policies is great for adjusting play style to current conditions.
+ Love the idea of leader agendas, although there will be more about this in the "cons" section.
+ Spies are so much more useful and flexible than in 5.
+ Can combine units into corps and armies in mid/late game, which is excellent for unit management.
+ Combination of civics cards, tech tree branching, and district usage encourages alternative play-styles and long-term strategic thinking to a greater extent than in any previous version.
+ Most importantly, it still has that great "just 1 more turn" Civ feel.
CONS
- Diplomacy has been nerfed. Aside from luxury trading and war, there's not much reason to contact the AI. Deals often feel imbalanced as well (although the 2 patches so far have helped somewhat). There's no World Congress or diplomatic victory in general, which makes the late game feel a bit empty.
- Diplomacy is especially bad when it comes to the "leader agendas". It's impossible for every civ to like you because I think the diplomatic bonuses/penalties are too weighted towards agendas. The AI denounces you far too often. In 5, when you were denounced, it was a big deal. In 6, being denounced just happens all the time. This is made worse by the overly long diplomatic animations (the animations themselves are great, but they're too intrusive).
- AI is mostly incompetent when it comes to warfare, especially when it comes to taking cities. They're too passive, cannot use siege/ranged units effectively, and don't upgrade their units often enough.
- The pacing of the late game doesn't feel right. You blow through the tech tree too quickly, and production times just get too long in the late game. It's possible to advance far along on either the civics or science tree while leaving the other behind, and there's far greater tech disparities between civs than ever existed in previous versions. I often finish the tech tree before properly utilizing late game units.
- Tech tree is TOO branchy. There's too many dead end techs, and some missing prerequisites that allow advancement along certain tech paths to be too OP/simply not make sense.
- Missing a few key notifications (such as a notification for city bombardment) and some of the UI feels incomplete or cluttered (city screens need an overhaul, for example, and trade routes really need to be sortable).
- NO TEAM GAMES. Come on Firaxis, what are you doing here? This is one of those things that feels generally inexcusable.
- No Workshop support yet (not a huge deal for me personally at the moment, but something that is definitely vital for the community).
That may seem like a long list of cons, but the thing about the cons is that they're ALL FIXABLE PROBLEMS. Firaxis has created an excellent base game, and a wonderful set of features that gives 6 the potential to be a very deep, consistently compelling game. I have faith that they can fix the AI to at least reach an enjoyably competent level, and that further patches and eventual expansions will add additional diplomatic options. Some big-time balancing is needed in the late game especially, but again, that's a fixable problem. People want to compare it to Civ 5 with all of its patches and expansions. Honestly, 6 is a more complete game than 5 was on initial launch, and I remember people complaining about a lot of the same things.
I have no problem with any of the base features of the game. The cons all have to do with the AI, diplomacy, and balance that I have faith will be sorted out with time!
Currently would give an 8.5/10, but there's the potential for a 10/10 game here. Still would recommend, ESPECIALLY if you aren't going to compare every feature to the complete edition of Civ 5.

Life is Strange is a game about a girl called Max, who moves back into her hometown, Arcadia Bay, after a long time to attend college. Max soon discovers that she has the ability to control time and she gets a vision of a storm destroying Arcadia Bay. She later meets her old friend Chloe in a crazy way and the two try to unravel what is going on in Arcadia Bay. The devs rely heavily on plot, narration and dialogue to try to create a memorable game and succeed in doing so. The choices you make, mostly during dialogue, will affect the game world in a lot of ways.
However, there is not much gameplay to it. Most of the time you would be walking, conversing with someone or solving a puzzle using your time-manipulation abilities.
The overall plot is great even though the writing is questionable at times (words like 'awesomesauce' are annoyingly common). Also, a lot of things in the plot that I was eager to find out were left unaddressed.
The soundtrack and the visuals in this game are really nice. There are some lip-sync issues that ruin the immersion sometimes.
Despite its flaws, Life is Strange is a beautiful game.

When Steam, my gaming service, offered me some free stuff in exchange for playing a game called Paladins, I knew I was getting myself into a world of pain.
This game was created on August 3, 2016 and is for the PC. It’s currently rated T (Teen) for violence, even though there’s no blood or gore. While Steam invites players to “enter a fantasy world of ancient technology in Paladins, a team-based shooter with strategy elements and deep character customization,” I see it as the free-to-play, rip-off of Overwatch. Overwatch is also a first person shooter in which you can play in a variety of classes, each with unique abilities. In my opinion, there’s no discernable difference between the two games.
However, there are plenty of problems with Paladins. All the mechanics in the game are broken, especially the special power. Worse, there’s no balance between the characters.
And how many characters do you start with? Three. Out of 18. And how much does each character cost? Around $2.00. Clearly, the game favors wealthy players instead of skilled ones. I can’t forget to mention all the skins/costumes that you can “unlock” – really, buy – for your character are also $2.00. I actually calculated how much it would cost to buy every skin and character: $180.00. Why don’t you donate that money to charity, or save it for college instead of supporting a company that will probably either raise the price or make more stuff for you to buy.
Overall, Paladins is an abomination that doesn’t live up to the sound of its name. Paladins are fierce warriors who fight to the death. These characters in the game, however, just throw turtle shells and chickens at each other.
I rate this game 7.5/10, boring game-play and uninspired design.
Basically, they just want to take your money under the guise of free-to-play.

That said, there's a ton of depth to this game, and almost limitless possibilities for challenge and innovation. It's a challenge to get to other continents, moons, and planets (and moons of other planets), and once you've done one thing, there's always a bigger challenge.
When you put it all together, it gives this game a lot of replay value, all while teaching the basics of rocket science. The realistic physics models make it impossible
to gain an intuitive understanding of orbital physics, space exploration, and rocket design that ... while it's not going to bring skills you can take straight into a real-world job, is still valuable knowledge for interacting with the real world. Great game to play as a grown-up, or for kids.

This game is fantastic. Honestly. It may just be the nerd in me, but I have so much fun playing this game! For those who are unaware, Kerbal Space Program is basically a game that uses realistic physics in an ingame solar system. There really is no goal for the player, save maybe to get to other planets. The player has at their disposal, many different rocket parts, as well as plane parts (for those aero enthusiasts such as I) to do, well whatever they want. There are three different game modes, Career, Science (!), and Sandbox. Career mode places the player in control of the Kerbal Space Center (or KSC) and your goal is to complete contracts and get to other planets. You have to balance your budget, while at the same time getting enough science to unlock new parts. Your buildings also have limitations, such as the launch pad only being able to launch rockets that are say 15 tons. As you progress, it is necessary to upgrade these building to bigger and way more awesome vehicles. In Science (!) mode, you begin with every building at the highest level, and without the worries of balanceing your budget (fancy way for saying there is no money), and your only goal is to launch missions and get science to unlock more parts. Finally there is sandbox mode. For those gamers out there unfamiliar with the term, sandbox is generally used to refer to a gamemode in which everything is unlocked, and you may run wild. That said, in this gamemode, you may run wild. There is no goal whatsoever and you have everything in the game. I play the game while running mac OS X El Capitan (for those who don't know their OS, on apple computers, click the apple on the top left of your screen and click "about this mac" and it will tell you) the game is very well polished and I haven't run into any atrocious glitches yet. I highly recommend this game and I hope that if you get it you have great fun.
Happy gaming,
Mackels.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a point and click adventure game based on Robert Kirkman's The Walking Dead graphic novels. Season 1 gave us a hell of a ride on the feels train. Season Two now has Clementine taking the main role as the protagonist. She refers to what Lee taught her when she talks about her past experiences, which is a really important part of the story. It's what really links Season one and two together. Over the past few episodes of season two, the character development progresses one chapter at a time. The choices you make CAN effect the main story line, but some of these are small and won't set back the story at all. However, dire decisions where you have to choose between certain characters, whether they live or die, really adds the tension. When these dire choices happen, it will have you in a moment of slow-motion, then you have to act quickly as the decision bar runs out. The dialog is getting better and better each episode. However, I wish Telltale would make longer episodes once in a while. Sometimes they can seem short, but as they say; 'Time flies while you're having fun'. And Season Two so far, is proving that games don't need to be AAA, have groundbreaking graphics to be a good gaming experience. It's the story that draws us in, we want to find out what happens the next episode. We want to know how these choices affect our story and the characters themselves. Some characters will return from Season One and 400 Days. There will be twists and turns on this train track of feels, but Telltale does a damn good job!

This game is fantastic. Honestly. It may just be the nerd in me, but I have so much fun playing this game! For those who are unaware, Kerbal Space Program is basically a game that uses realistic physics in an ingame solar system. There really is no goal for the player, save maybe to get to other planets. The player has at their disposal, many different rocket parts, as well as plane parts (for those aero enthusiasts such as I) to do, well whatever they want. There are three different game modes, Career, Science (!), and Sandbox. Career mode places the player in control of the Kerbal Space Center (or KSC) and your goal is to complete contracts and get to other planets. You have to balance your budget, while at the same time getting enough science to unlock new parts. Your buildings also have limitations, such as the launch pad only being able to launch rockets that are say 15 tons. As you progress, it is necessary to upgrade these building to bigger and way more awesome vehicles. In Science (!) mode, you begin with every building at the highest level, and without the worries of balanceing your budget (fancy way for saying there is no money), and your only goal is to launch missions and get science to unlock more parts. Finally there is sandbox mode. For those gamers out there unfamiliar with the term, sandbox is generally used to refer to a gamemode in which everything is unlocked, and you may run wild. That said, in this gamemode, you may run wild. There is no goal whatsoever and you have everything in the game. I play the game while running mac OS X El Capitan (for those who don't know their OS, on apple computers, click the apple on the top left of your screen and click "about this mac" and it will tell you) the game is very well polished and I haven't run into any atrocious glitches yet. I highly recommend this game and I hope that if you get it you have great fun.
Happy gaming,

By the Nine Divines, what has happened to one of my favorite time sink series? The game looks shiny and neat, and I like the idea of districts and being forced to specialize cities and expand instead of turtling up in two or three key cities. But that's about where my praise stops.
There is no such thing as peace, no matter what you do. At the lower difficulties you'll be spammed by denouncements and eventually Joint (and not the fun kind) War declarations solely because you're doing better than everyone else. And while your enemies are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥marks at the lower difficulties, the tedium of endless war and the constant dedication of resources to the war machine result in the map ending up like Aleppo. Normally carving a huge swathe of destruction Sherman-style would be a good thing, right? But somehow Firaxis winds up sucking the fun out of mass genocide.
Then there's the City-States, which are a neat idea implemented worse than the Bay of Pigs. If one isn't planted square on your doorstep then it'll be on the nearest resource you absolutely have to get. If you want to take it for yourself then you'll either have to befriend them and send envoys to get their resources and aid, which pisses off about half of the Leaders, or taking it by force. Good luck there, because I have yet to see a City-State with a military that could fit into it's borders. You can mod them out, but I'll get on that in a moment.
So let's say that, like me, after about 20 hours of endless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that sees you endure the pain to the Industrial Era once before you quit for something more fun like Overwatch or smoking, you identify the above problems and search for mods to help. Firstly, good luck finding a mod to fix your problems, it took me clicking TWO links in my google search to find one to remove City-States. but then when you kick off your next game you notice something: Without the massed forces of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥-States fighting back the Barbarians, you're going to be responsible for curbing all of them. So now resources must be dedicated to the war machine to fight off an almost literally endless horde of enemies. that's fine and all, except the game also has this odd tendency to plop a Barbarian Camp spawning horsemen every five turns right outside your borders.
"♥♥♥♥," you say to yourself, "I've got an option to remove Barbarians, why don't I do that?"
Because by know you should know how this is going to go.
So now you start your new game, a good old classic Civilization game on a big ol' Continental map. Should be good! But then you take a good look at the map, proud of setting your third city, only to notice that every single other smeglord has twice your cities, equal to yours in pop, with districts and buildings galore. And that's at all difficulty levels.
I want to have fun with the game so bad. You can see how much time I've put into it. But there is, as of yet, no way to find any kind of balance to the game that makes any strategy other than spamming military viable. I'm sure that even on a huge world consisting solely of myself and one other civ would end in a massive fireball a decade after we made contact.
It's a shame I can't return this for a reduced amount now that I've played it for so long trying to find the fun and joy that the series has brought me up until now. I can honestly say that after the first couple games I have had almost no enjoyment from the game. I'm still playing (in fact it's open in another window right now), and probably will keep doing so, but only because I'm an idiot who hopes that maybe, just once, I'll have a good run that doesn't feel like a chore.

A definite recommendation for KSP!
First of all, I can see no cons. I really can't. The game launched out of early access recently, after it was maintained and developed like few others, building a huge fan community along the way.
the game itself:
For some it's a game, for others it's training, seriously! You build rockets and planes (and whatever you can think of, really) with a realistic physics model. You can, but you don't have to, calculate all variables that are relevant for the type of space flight you're aiming for. there is a lot to learn, and in the beginning it is very hard to get even close to what others in the community have achieved. But then, some people have hundrets of hours on their KSP clock! You can get lost in the game with all lits stock metarial. And then there are mods! some add new parts, alter some aspects of physics, or replace the entire universe to make it even more realistic. The stock game has a scaled down version of a solar system so it doesn't take too much skill and new players can get into the game more easily. All equations still worh though, and it's a matter of replacing some values to get everything right. There is even a classroom version of KSP to teach about physics and engineering methods!
The story mode - a progressive unlocking of parts really - relies on achievements and missions you fulfil as you go. The mission system has been worked on for a long time, and it gets better. Right now it reacts to your current status in your space flight agenda and generates missions that complement your previous achievements. The resources are money, prestige (gos down when you blow up astronauts or fail contracts) and science from doing experiments in certain environments. Alternatively, you can just hop into sandbox mode and slap everything together as you please and go straight for the complex missions: other planets. Also, there are lots of eater eggs to be found, and a special KSP-humor along with side references to space programs and astronauts/cosmonauts of the past.
Typically the progression is this:
- launch to a certain altitude
- get to orbit and back to Kerbin (Earth)
- dock two spacecraft in orbit
- orbit the Mun (Moon) and/or Minmus (smaller moon)
- land on and return from the Mun and/or Minmus
- catch an asteroid
- mine resources from other bodies of the system
- send probes to other planets such as Duna (Mars) or Eve (Venus)
- send astronauts to Duna and return them, the latter being the really hard part
- send spacecraft to the Jool system (Jupiter) which has several moons, even with atmosphere (check here for me - haven't gotten further with my 300-odd hours)
- land and return from the moons of Jool
- land on the extreme planets close to Kerbol (the Sun) or in the far reaches of the system, all without an atmosphere
My last mission was an attempt at a grand tour fo the solar system with a mothership that can be disassambled into landers which take on astronauts, prospecting and resource mining respectively. Pros:
There's a lot of cool changes to the tech and civic trees, and the way support units and corps are handled is an excellent change. Same with Great People, where things now feel like more of a direct competition, and wars for territory feel much more natural. Tall cities are mostly a thing of the past as you must expand to maintain supremacy with regards to any of the victory conditions, and the districts system is a wonderful addition. Barbarians are now much more interesting without being arbitrarily more difficult, and AI opponents now have clearer explanations for their behaviors.
Graphics are nice as well.
Cons:
They removed a bunch of the hyperlinks in the Civilopedia, so it's harder to navigate, and they also have several gameplay mechanics that are not explained properly in the tutorial and aren't explained in the Civilopedia either. This is forgiveable, what is not forgivable is:
The crippling stupidity of the AI. Don't get me wrong, the AI might kill you by throwing a bunch of units at you in one of the first three or so era. They're certainly not going to kill you by being clever, but you're playing catchup to their bonuses and initial lead they have a good chance of eating you at higher difficulties.
However, if you can get, say to the industrial or modern era, they are no longer a meaningful threat. The AI does not appear to be actively seeking out victory conditions, the AI opponents won't gang up on you if they see you approaching final victory, they're terrible at upgrading their units (which matters more in Civ 6 than it did in Civ 5), and they will attempt to attack your naval ships with embarked units. They also declare war before moving their units into position, seemingly immediately upon you reaching some internal negative influence with them, so they lose any element of surprise.
In Summary:
The game is much better as far as gameplay mechanics, and against a group of human opponents it would be excellent. The AI is unfortunately dumb as bricks, and if you can survive their initial wave from their difficulty bonuses, they become less and less of a threat.

As someone who is familiar with the Civ series - I played with each one of the series, except Beyond Earth - this game is a worthy pretender of the throne. The game kept the hexagonal, one combat unit / tile system of the 5th game, which was probably the best thing among all the things Civ 5 introduced. The game is not perfect tho', as someone who is struggling with Deity level AIs in Civ 5 (I mostly played on Immortal difficulty, and I have ~1000 hours+ of gameplay), in Civ 6, i am confident of beating a random game in Civ 6 on Deity (after ~200hours of gameplay). It kinda feels like playing on Immortal on Civ5, with the last difficulty setting is missing somehow.
The communication with the AI feels deeper, and the Cassus Belli system is interesting to play with, however with the absence of diplomatic victory you probably never care to liberate city states or keep them out of harms way. They are just there for the taking in most cases. Hopefully an upcoming expansion pack of some sort will bring back that victory type, because without that the existence of CS-s are not really relevant.
Overall the game is OK, I would recommend to fans of the series - but I alos have to highlight that it does not feel like a complete game at this point.

This game has done a wonderful job setting itself apart from previous entries thanks to some significant revamps. The most obvious changes came from diplomacy. It's much more intricate and realistic, though a number of AI actions still don't make much sense. But, it's far more dependent on how the player reacts as opposed to the AI programming, and that's a huge step forward for the franchise. The next big change is the districts mechanic. The series standard has been to cram all your buildings and wonders in the city proper. Now you can build different districts (such as science, culture, commerce, etc) and wonders onto their own hexes. This makes managing your space far more important and also makes even the most passive players have to consider putting in some work on their military as AIs in particular like to use hit and run tactics on those spaces when you're at war. I don't think the franchise has ever looked better, and it's a good thing because the soundtrack, while good, doesn't quite live up to the glorious standards of Civ V. Thanks to this game's numerous tweaks and balances and bold revamping of major mechanics, this should be a must buy for any strategy fans and an inivitation to return to those who felt jilted by Beyond Earth.

In December of 2014, my brother introduced me to what quickly became (and has remained) my absolute favorite video game, and one of my preferred modes of entertainment- Civilization V. As someone who has always enjoyed studying history and playing turn-based strategy games (i.e. Risk), Civilzation V was a dream come true. Because of my experience with Civ V, I was very excited for the release of this game, and (after initially restraining myself from pre-ordering) actually decided to shell out $60 to buy the game shortly after its release instead of waiting for a sale. You can see from the gigantic red thumbs-down next to this post that I was disappointed. Since I bought the game, I've tried over and over again to enjoy it or, at the very least, find some way to justify spending as much as I did on this, but I can never stick with it for very long.
Other than how bare-bones this game feels when compared to Civ V (which, admittedly, has had 6.5 years not to be expanded upon), my largest issue with this game would have to be the change in the way players can interact with other civilizations. The diplomacy feels much more superficial and the interactions are much more limited- for example. you can no longer pay a civilization to declare war on another. Also, diplomacy in Civ 6 doesn't seem to be very useful- asking civilization to stop sending missionaries and apostles to your cities doesn't seem to have any effect, other than to give you casus belli when they invariably break their promise by sending wave after wave of missionaries and apostles (which are prohibitively expensive for players, but surprisingly common for AI) to convert your cities back.
I understand that comparing a game that had (at the time I purchased it) 4.5 years of enhancements and bug-fixes to a (now) 4 month old game is not going to be a fair comparison. That being said, I don't believe that this game is currently worth the ~$60 that I paid for it. If you are a fan of the Civilization franchise, stick with the other installments for awhile- if you haven't yet played any of the Civ games, I would suggest paying the $45 to buy Civilization 5 Complete, which is currently a much better and more complete game, instead of spending $60 on Civ 6.
Since it's 2 in the morning and I'm exhausted, I have to throw this onto the end: I do like the introduction of districts in this game and the emphasis that places on city planning, as well as the separate research trees for technology and civics. I also like the way you have to unlock governments, each of which provide unique bonuses and provide different policy card slots.

A definite recommendation for KSP!
First of all, I can see no cons. I really can't. The game launched out of early access recently, after it was maintained and developed like few others, building a huge fan community along the way.
the game itself:
For some it's a game, for others it's training, seriously! You build rockets and planes (and whatever you can think of, really) with a realistic physics model. You can, but you don't have to, calculate all variables that are relevant for the type of space flight you're aiming for. there is a lot to learn, and in the beginning it is very hard to get even close to what others in the community have achieved. But then, some people have hundrets of hours on their KSP clock! You can get lost in the game with all lits stock metarial. And then there are mods! some add new parts, alter some aspects of physics, or replace the entire universe to make it even more realistic. The stock game has a scaled down version of a solar system so it doesn't take too much skill and new players can get into the game more easily. All equations still worh though, and it's a matter of replacing some values to get everything right. There is even a classroom version of KSP to teach about physics and engineering methods!
The story mode - a progressive unlocking of parts really - relies on achievements and missions you fulfil as you go. The mission system has been worked on for a long time, and it gets better. Right now it reacts to your current status in your space flight agenda and generates missions that complement your previous achievements. The resources are money, prestige (gos down when you blow up astronauts or fail contracts) and science from doing experiments in certain environments. Alternatively, you can just hop into sandbox mode and slap everything together as you please and go straight for the complex missions: other planets. Also, there are lots of eater eggs to be found, and a special KSP-humor along with side references to space programs and astronauts/cosmonauts of the past.
Typically the progression is this:
- launch to a certain altitude
- get to orbit and back to Kerbin (Earth)
- dock two spacecraft in orbit
- orbit the Mun (Moon) and/or Minmus (smaller moon)
- land on and return from the Mun and/or Minmus
- catch an asteroid
- mine resources from other bodies of the system
- send probes to other planets such as Duna (Mars) or Eve (Venus)
- send astronauts to Duna and return them, the latter being the really hard part
- send spacecraft to the Jool system (Jupiter) which has several moons, even with atmosphere (check here for me - haven't gotten further with my 300-odd hours)
- land and return from the moons of Jool
- land on the extreme planets close to Kerbol (the Sun) or in the far reaches of the system, all without an atmosphere
My last mission was an attempt at a grand tour fo the solar system with a mothership that can be disassambled into landers which take on astronauts, prospecting and resource mining respectively. The last update brought new, smaller sized resource gathering parts, which would make the whole operation more manageable (as in: smaller mother ship, fewer complications, faster travel). so maybe I'll start over - or I'll just send a replacement module.
game development:
- the game is in development even after launch, with performance and content updated to be expected
- the devs can be talked to, which is awesome!
- many many mods are being released by the community, although they need to be updated for newer versions of KSP, which does not always happen
- devs even hire out of the mod community occasionaly
- it runs on my 2007 mid-range laptop computer. amazing!
Get this game! It is worth it's price tag. I got it when it was 12.50 Euros on a discount while it was two years from release. It is worth even 50 Euros in my opinion, because the replay value is enormous!

In December of 2014, my brother introduced me to what quickly became (and has remained) my absolute favorite video game, and one of my preferred modes of entertainment- Civilization V. As someone who has always enjoyed studying history and playing turn-based strategy games (i.e. Risk), Civilzation V was a dream come true. Because of my experience with Civ V, I was very excited for the release of this game, and (after initially restraining myself from pre-ordering) actually decided to shell out $60 to buy the game shortly after its release instead of waiting for a sale. You can see from the gigantic red thumbs-down next to this post that I was disappointed. Since I bought the game, I've tried over and over again to enjoy it or, at the very least, find some way to justify spending as much as I did on this, but I can never stick with it for very long.
Other than how bare-bones this game feels when compared to Civ V (which, admittedly, has had 6.5 years not to be expanded upon), my largest issue with this game would have to be the change in the way players can interact with other civilizations. The diplomacy feels much more superficial and the interactions are much more limited- for example. you can no longer pay a civilization to declare war on another. Also, diplomacy in Civ 6 doesn't seem to be very useful- asking civilization to stop sending missionaries and apostles to your cities doesn't seem to have any effect, other than to give you casus belli when they invariably break their promise by sending wave after wave of missionaries and apostles (which are prohibitively expensive for players, but surprisingly common for AI) to convert your cities back.
I understand that comparing a game that had (at the time I purchased it) 4.5 years of enhancements and bug-fixes to a (now) 4 month old game is not going to be a fair comparison. That being said, I don't believe that this game is currently worth the ~$60 that I paid for it. If you are a fan of the Civilization franchise, stick with the other installments for awhile- if you haven't yet played any of the Civ games, I would suggest paying the $45 to buy Civilization 5 Complete, which is currently a much better and more complete game, instead of spending $60 on Civ 6.
Since it's 2 in the morning and I'm exhausted, I have to throw this onto the end: I do like the introduction of districts in this game and the emphasis that places on city planning, as well as the separate research trees for technology and civics. I also like the way you have to unlock governments, each of which provide unique bonuses and provide different policy card slots.

The Bottom line:
As of right now, you don't really need both Civ V AND Civ VI.
The TL;DR:
This is definitely the most expensive Civ V expansion on the market.  On the other hand, Civ V + Gods and Kings + Brave New World is $100, but you can get what's almost the equivalent of a Chinese bootlegged version of it right here for $60.  On the other other hand, Civ V + G&K + BNW on sale is about $40, and Civ VI on sale is about $55.
The "Long Story":
The game does provide some good changes and nice reworks to some mechanics in Civ V (government, city-states, city-planning, and culture are most noticable).  However, in its current state as an expansion to the Civ V expansions, I have hard time justifying the $60 price tag.  And if Civ VI ends up like Civ V, this price tage will only increase  - quite substantially - over the next few years in order to get the complete experience. Personally, I do not support the "famous company offers you a new computer game for just $50 or $60 (DLC not included)" business model.
Another thing I am ambivalent about is in the graphics department.  The graphics in Civ VI features its own angular animation style as well as an Age of Discovery theme and a clockwork-looking UI.  Although I believe that graphical style trumps resolution, but I found the new graphics to be a bit ... distracting.  It's a bit harder for me read.  The very graphics feel more laidback and doesn't resonate the same sort of intensity that Civ V  does (in my mind).  Maybe it doesn't bother you.  It bothered me.
Despite the fact that all I've done here is compare Civ VI to Civ V and found it a bit wanting, I do recommend it.   I still think you should try to play Civ V or CIv VI if you havent played Civ at all.  I played Civ V.  But not everyone plays Civ V.  I get it.  Someone who played a lot of Civ V is probably going to be more disappointed in Civ VI, but that doesn't mean Civ VI isn't a good game.  The only problem is that Civ VI didn't give $60-worth of cool, new things for the Civ V fans to enjoy. You might feel like you wasted your money if you buy both, and you might be right.  But you'll be okay to only play one or the other, and you can certainly choose to play Civ VI or Civ V.
EDIT: I'm still optimistic that, a few years down the road, the Civ VI expansions and DLC will be worth it in the end.  On sale.

The improvements of this game are vast and the unstacking of cities will likely be viewed as at least as monumental of a change as the unstacking of units in V's system. The units (although need aesthtic development) are overall alright although the new movement feature that leaves you with 0.25 of a movement credit left that you can't use is somewhat irritating when playing on faster game modes. However for every step forward, Firaxis has seemingly learned nothing from even the fully developed civilization V game. The AI is without any better word to describe it is "f*cking atrocious and idiotic". The fact that you can use the diplomacy system to gain trust only to be declared war upon and denounced is unbelievable. At the start I anticipated the "era penalty reductions" to solve this but the slightest transgression will result in an all out war. Science victory's and the collective rest of the possible conditions are only fully possible if you can face off the brunt of the attack and eventually beat them into submission in order to ensure they dont raid your land again. This has happened every game I have played up to emperor (and I imagine the trend will continue and only make the game more difficult to play, and not in a good way). This game is well rounded in style and intial ideas but it needs major work in order to become a fully fledged game worth of the Civilization heritage it claims.
In conclusion, wait for the DLC, wait for AI improvements, if they never come (to my potential chagrin) then save your money and time and stick with V unitil VI goes on sale.

I was a bit hesitant to get into this season as I hoped it would be a completely new/seperate story.  This is not the case, as you play as one of the characters from the first season (taking place after the events of the first season).  However, after playing through the first three episodes I can say without a doubt this game is fantastic.  It's shaping up to be better than the first season - and that is no small feat.

I really, really wanted to love this game.  Early signs were encouraging, Civ IV represents the high water mark of the entire series, even a decade after release, so I was very pleased to read that Firaxis had recruited some of the original Civ IV team.
Civ VI brings some new concepts on board, namely the ability to divide your sprawling city into districts, with a limited number of spaces available for cultural wonders.  Also, you now have not one, but two research streams to manage - one for technology and the other for social policy.  New policy discoveries unlock new forms of government in the same way that new technologies will unlock military units.  Also, the AI has been tweaked, with each rival civilization pursuing their own public and hidden agendas.  Moreover, the barbarian factions of old have been rehashed and are now more agressive and will continue to be a destabilising influence in the latter stages of the game when they will inexplicably turn up with heavy weaponry and battleships.  To cap it all, Sean Bean has been recruited to lend his vocal talents to the game.
Early reviews looked very promising and if I'm honest, a little too good to be true.  Criticism seemed muted, there were murmurs of gripes at the game's AI but nothing that set alarm bells off, but being a Civ fan, I went ahead and bought it as soon as I could, anyway.
First impressions weren't good.  The game was galacially slow on my four year old 3750K / 8GB RAM system, with the game being practically unplayable as the AI took an age to complete turns.  None of the reviews mentioned this.  A subsequent upgrade to a 16GB 6700K helped matters, as the game now chugs along reasonably well but you'll need to pay careful attention to the recommended system spec.
Then there's the AI.  Your rivals are always placed very close to you so it's extremely difficult to expand your civilization early in the game.  The Policy tech tree proves to be a missed opportunity as the various forms of government aren't unlocked until much later in the game compared with Civ IV and V.  The AI will also do some inexplicable things, such as forcing a neighbour with no diplomatic disputes and a healthy trade relationship to suddenly declare war on you.  War itself is hugely costly in terms of gain vs investment, so you tend to become bogged down in WW1-esque stalemates very quickly.  Your opponent will sue for peace, but will inexplicably declare war on you again a few turns later.
Hopefully, modders will be able to address some of the criticisms I have levelled at the game.  I have no doubt that Firaxis will release the usual spin offs and add ons to Civ VI, but it remains to be seen whether they will fix some of the more frustrating aspects of Civ VI.
In summary, the very poor AI, the plodding pace of the game and the sudden outbreaks of unwinnable wars results in a game that simply isn't much fun to play.  It pains me to say this, but the game is a huge disappointment and simply isn't worth buying at full RRP.  While the issue of game speed will be addressed in time as hardware continues to improve, there's no getting away from the fact that right now you won't be able to enjoy this game or play the larger maps unless you've a high end system sporting a video card with a lot of on-board memory.  Even a whizzy PC won't address the terrible AI, however.  Perhaps Firaxis will address some of these concerns in a subsequent patch?

Civ 6 is a good game, but there's a lot that bugs me about it.  They could have made a good game in to a masterpiece had they kept some of the Civ V features.
I don't find Civ 6's civilizations as interesting as those in Civ V.  The only real Native American civ is Aztec.  Some new civs similar to Iroquois and Shoshone would have been fun.  Polynesia could have been really fun, and I can think of several others.  Not enough civs to choose from in Civ 6 either.
Maps generated in Civ V also interested me more than those in Civ 6.  There aren't as many map options to choose from.  I like to play in strategic view, and I'm really glad they kept it (the game would have lost me without it, I remember Beyond Earth, I hated it for this reason).
Where's the United Nations?
Why can't I turn city states on or off, or at least adjust the number?  Seems like a lot of advanced game customization options that used to be available are just chosen for you now.
When I want to restart a game, I can't just hit restart from Turn 0 - I have to go all the way back and customize the whole game again.
Not a fan of having to start next to a 2-point move til with 2 movement points in order to land on it.  Not a fan of promoting a unit ending that unit's turn.
Pros:  With those gripes said, the new gameplay system is pretty cool.  The districts are my favorite new feature!  Some of the new resources are fun, and I like the builder system.  Mixed feelings about the trader/road system...I still miss the Civ V way.  Some really cool new wonders and natural wonders.  While I miss the old Civ V culture tree, the new Civ 6 way is cool in it's own different way.  I love choosing governments.  I wish we could choose from two leaders for each Civ rather than just one, with the exception of Greece - why do they get two leaders?  Are more going to be released for each civ? others have complained about the career modes lacking a win state. What do they want? A big flashing screen with trophies when they reach the edge of the Kerbol System saying “You're Winner!”? I really, really wanted to love this game.  Early signs were encouraging, Civ IV represents the high water mark of the entire series, even a decade after release, so I was very pleased to read that Firaxis had recruited some of the original Civ IV team.
Civ VI brings some new concepts on board, namely the ability to divide your sprawling city into districts, with a limited number of spaces available for cultural wonders.  Also, you now have not one, but two research streams to manage - one for technology and the other for social policy.  New policy discoveries unlock new forms of government in the same way that new technologies will unlock military units.  Also, the AI has been tweaked, with each rival civilization pursuing their own public and hidden agendas.  Moreover, the barbarian factions of old have been rehashed and are now more agressive and will continue to be a destabilising influence in the latter stages of the game when they will inexplicably turn up with heavy weaponry and battleships.  To cap it all, Sean Bean has been recruited to lend his vocal talents to the game.
Early reviews looked very promising and if I'm honest, a little too good to be true.  Criticism seemed muted, there were murmurs of gripes at the game's AI but nothing that set alarm bells off, but being a Civ fan, I went ahead and bought it as soon as I could, anyway.
First impressions weren't good.  The game was galacially slow on my four year old 3750K / 8GB RAM system, with the game being practically unplayable as the AI took an age to complete turns.  None of the reviews mentioned this.  A subsequent upgrade to a 16GB 6700K helped matters, as the game now chugs along reasonably well but you'll need to pay careful attention to the recommended system spec.
Then there's the AI.  Your rivals are always placed very close to you so it's extremely difficult to expand your civilization early in the game.  The Policy tech tree proves to be a missed opportunity as the various forms of government aren't unlocked until much later in the game compared with Civ IV and V.  The AI will also do some inexplicable things, such as forcing a neighbour with no diplomatic disputes and a healthy trade relationship to suddenly declare war on you.  War itself is hugely costly in terms of gain vs investment, so you tend to become bogged down in WW1-esque stalemates very quickly.  Your opponent will sue for peace, but will inexplicably declare war on you again a few turns later.
Hopefully, modders will be able to address some of the criticisms I have levelled at the game.  I have no doubt that Firaxis will release the usual spin offs and add ons to Civ VI, but it remains to be seen whether they will fix some of the more frustrating aspects of Civ VI.
In summary, the very poor AI, the plodding pace of the game and the sudden outbreaks of unwinnable wars results in a game that simply isn't much fun to play.  It pains me to say this, but the game is a huge disappointment and simply isn't worth buying at full RRP.  While the issue of game speed will be addressed in time as hardware continues to improve, there's no getting away from the fact that right now you won't be able to enjoy this game or play the larger maps unless you've a high end system sporting a video card with a lot of on-board memory.  Even a whizzy PC won't address the terrible AI, however.  Perhaps Firaxis will address some of these concerns in a subsequent patch?

Civ 6 is a good game, but there's a lot that bugs me about it.  They could have made a good game in to a masterpiece had they kept some of the Civ V features.
I don't find Civ 6's civilizations as interesting as those in Civ V.  The only real Native American civ is Aztec.  Some new civs similar to Iroquois and Shoshone would have been fun.  Polynesia could have been really fun, and I can think of several others.  Not enough civs to choose from in Civ 6 either.
Maps generated in Civ V also interested me more than those in Civ 6.  There aren't as many map options to choose from.  I like to play in strategic view, and I'm really glad they kept it (the game would have lost me without it, I remember Beyond Earth, I hated it for this reason).
Where's the United Nations?
Why can't I turn city states on or off, or at least adjust the number?  Seems like a lot of advanced game customization options that used to be available are just chosen for you now.
When I want to restart a game, I can't just hit restart from Turn 0 - I have to go all the way back and customize the whole game again.
Not a fan of having to start next to a 2-point move til with 2 movement points in order to land on it.  Not a fan of promoting a unit ending that unit's turn.
Pros:  With those gripes said, the new gameplay system is pretty cool.  The districts are my favorite new feature!  Some of the new resources are fun, and I like the builder system.  Mixed feelings about the trader/road system...I still miss the Civ V way.  Some really cool new wonders and natural wonders.  While I miss the old Civ V culture tree, the new Civ 6 way is cool in it's own different way.  I love choosing governments.  I wish we could choose from two leaders for each Civ rather than just one, with the exception of Greece - why do they get two leaders?  Are more going to be released for each civ? There's a magic element to games with quality stories that causes us to lose sense of our realities, to be drawn into an entirely different world. This game accomplishes that task like nothing else I've witnessed, and I've been gaming since before I could read.
The imperfections and flaws of Life is Strange simply don't matter in my mind, because they either contribute to the charm of the stylistic choices or fail to distract from the adventures of Max and Chloe. This game is certainly not for everyone, but if you're into exploration and in-depth interaction look no further.
The amazing soundtrack, the beautiful lighting, the voice acting, the characters - it all combines to form an experience that just can't be replicated. I've become connected to the two main characters as if they were part of this world, as if they were people I knew.
Life is Strange has the potential to change your life and shape the way you view not only the world around you but the people you hold most dear.
As for me, I'm heartbroken that I can't go back in time and discover this gem for the first time again and again.

After playing this game for a considerable amount of time (many offline hours not counted) here is my opinion.
Pros~
~The District System is Very Neat and I think it is a Wonderful Addition to civ. It allows much more diversity when planning how to plan your cities.
~New Policy system is quite unique and fresh. That being said I would love to see the indrodution of having to choose negative policies. (your Government can be all positive ya know)
~less reliance on building wonders (Civ 5 you pretty much win the game if you could build the wonders before your opponents)
~City states have been greatly updated since civ 5 (all kinds of unique and cool bonuses)
~improved multiplayer. (Way better then Civ 5)
~Great people now have new system which is really cool

Cons~
~ AI is terrible. Prob the worst AI I have ever seen. Not only are the AI absolutely terrible at combat but they often impossible to please. ie. most every game i have played result in every nation being Angry at me even when i have never declared war.
+note on AI in all the games i played it was clear that some of the AI Leaders have clear Advantages over the other AI leaders. For example Germany was almost Always at the top, and Egypt at the bottom of the score board.
+ note AI has been receving updates and may improve in the future.
~ Religion Has not changed at all since Civ 5 . (the Ai also spams missionaries and apostles and blankets your map with them, this can be really irritating)
~ Personally I did not like the art direction, after Civ 5 i was hoping that the developers would pursue a more realistic aproach to the the next game. The leaders look extreamly goofy in my opinion.
~ No Dlipomatic victory yet ( There is now a Religion victory)
~ Diplomacy with AI is Pretty Bad
~ Alliances with AI are pointless ( if you get attacked you ally will never come to help you)
I could go on but, these are the main points I feel should be brought up. I want to say i was really torn on to give a positive or a negative review. there are lots of things that i liked but there are also things that i wish that could be undone. If you are a Civ fan I can't really say if you will like it or not, it has it's weaknesses and strengths. I would say if its on sale buy it but, at its current price its not worth it. Hopefully the DLC will spice things up in the future.

Plainly stated this is a terrible base game. When compared with vanilla Civilization V, this game is unplayable. Civilization IV, which I wasn’t fond of, and Civilization V by far, are more coherent and fun to invest my time playing. Civilization VI on the other hand, suffers massively due to the A.I, terrible/useless Civ bonuses, lack of a decent user interface and overall terrible design. The game does benefit from certain aspects, consisting primarily of the superb soundtrack, leader animation, leader personalities, and voice acting; however, the good doesn’t out way the bad, far from it actually. Even though the leaders are nicely animated and voiced, in my opinion, the selections for many are questionable, especially for the Civs they’re representing. I don’t understand, and maybe this is because I love history, why Firaxis couldn’t get certain historical aspects correct. I understand it’s just a history game but Europa Universals, the Total War series, and Hearts of Iron, all try their best to accurately name countries and leaders. Civ V had this issue but it’s profound in Civ VI. The creators should have stuck with Civ V and adapted fan made mods into the base game. The A.I at least made some sense in Civ V as well, but in Civ VI, I had a game where I met a civilization and next turn they declared war on me without a reason. This gets frustrating constantly when compared with how the human player must declare war. I don’t understand why they didn’t mix Civ IV and Civ V’s diplomacy together for Civ VI, an example from Civ V is when the A.I is able to ask about troops on their boarder, but why couldn’t the human player get that in Civ VI? Mods adopted that ability in Civ V and it worked perfectly, so why leave it out again for the human player? The art, besides the leaders, is so lazy in this game compared to its predecessor as well. The religion icon selection is terrible and uninspired, just like Civ V. Honestly, it’s best to wait until this game is granted steam workshop support or until game changing DLC is announced.
Lastly, I preordered the game and received the soundtracks as a bonus. The Civilization VI soundtrack, like I mentioned was terrific, but the 25th-anniversary soundtrack was a joke. It seemed like it was just thrown together last second and added in to convince people that they hadn’t forgotten about the 25th anniversary. A digital art book would have been nice and a more thought out anniversary soundtrack would have been appreciated.

There's a magic element to games with quality stories that causes us to lose sense of our realities, to be drawn into an entirely different world. This game accomplishes that task like nothing else I've witnessed, and I've been gaming since before I could read.
The imperfections and flaws of Life is Strange simply don't matter in my mind, because they either contribute to the charm of the stylistic choices or fail to distract from the adventures of Max and Chloe. This game is certainly not for everyone, but if you're into exploration and in-depth interaction look no further.
The amazing soundtrack, the beautiful lighting, the voice acting, the characters - it all combines to form an experience that just can't be replicated. I've become connected to the two main characters as if they were part of this world, as if they were people I knew.
Life is Strange has the potential to change your life and shape the way you view not only the world around you but the people you hold most dear.
As for me, I'm heartbroken that I can't go back in time and discover this gem for the first time again and again.

Been waiting to review this to see what the updates would be like. Because let's be honest, it's a Civ game - this version will last about 3-5 years and not be GREAT till about year 4 lol.
My own personal gripes:
1) Diplomacy is pointless. No matter what you do, the AI will like and dislike you randomly. The devlopers tried making it more complex, and in doing so just broke it lol. They should really know their game and their players by now. We don't want a Diplomacy simulator. Though if we did, we'd want it to actually work lol. No, what we want is to create our own CIVILIZATION. Oddly enough that is implied in the title of the game lol. So stop trying to turn the series into a hodge podge of everything. Other Civs should be obstacles or tools.
I miss being able to gift technology to another Civ. I miss being able to bribe them into attacking each other. Felt like a game of chess. Not ...whatever this mixed up crap is now. Oh I built the pyramids, now everyone hates me. Well, shoot. Oh I did nothing for 10 turns except build buildings and the like. BUT BECAUSE I DIDN'T EXPAND, everyone hates me. Alright, I've expanded....denounced lol
Come on.
2) Barbarians. Used to be just minorly annoying. An obstacle or resource during the early game, and forgotten about mid to late game. AS IT SHOULD BE!
Now, seems raging barbarians is just the default setting. With districts and the fact builders have limited charges - they capture a builder or damage an improvement, and you're set back way more than you should be. Fair enough though - a challenge. However, it doesn't FEEL like a challenge. Feels like a fly buzzing in your ear. Challenge in killing the fly, but you'd rather it just leave you the h3ll alone.
Either make the Barbarians what they WERE, or make them more relevant - with named barbarian generals, greater perks for beating them, and maybe barbian held cities. Instead of, oh here are 5 camps around you that spit a unit out every few turns. Have fun rebuilding workers and traders.
3) Builders. Do not like limited uses. At all. I mean, I get it - they build stuff instantly now, so have to nerf it down to make for balanced gameplay. That said....it takes the same amount of time only in a less realistic way. Building things SHOULD take turns to complete. When have you ever seen a building or mine erected instantly out of thin air? lol Having builders not burn out too is MORE realistic.
Revert it back please. It's annoying and really throws off the flow of the game.
My gripes aside, the game itself is not worth buying RIGHT NOW. Wait till they add more Civs. Because it's pretty sparse at the moment. They touted the whole, "ohh now the same Civ can have different leaders with different agendas and different perks" only....by that they meant Greece. Greece and only Greece lol. Also, seems you can have both Greek Civs on the same map. Really odd. And btw, the perks aren't that much different from each other lol.
Wait till they add more stuff. Get the game. Have fun. Till then, play Civ 5

This game has potential to be great, but it's not there yet.  They are clearly borrowing concepts from competitors like Europa Universalis and Endless Legend, but the marriage of these concepts isn't yet executed well and it leads to rage-quits.
There are lots of smaller things, like how the "most recently built" item in the city description window actually shows the item you built 2 items ago, instead of what was just completed, as well as the clunky and unorganized menus and spread of information.  You can open up details about the city, but good luck finding what you're looking for.  Three months after release, for such obvious concerns as these to still be unaddressed is really disapointing.
Then there are some big things.  The wacky AI that forces you into a militaristic play style no matter what approach you take (you'll always end up♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone, you're constantly at war).  All of the civs feel too specialized to operate with only one strategy, to the point that it's like a shonen lineup (I'm the one who likes espionage!  And I'm the one who likes great people!), which in combination with the previous point means that the militaristic civs are most likely to succeed.  Don't even think of trying to take a city from an opponent in a defensive war.  Even if you're trying to remove their ability to continuously, again, and again, and AGAIN declare war on you, the AI will consider YOU to be the warmonger and denounce you, then declare war on you.  And, if you have my luck, Ghandi will have the Nuke Happy hidden trait.
My most recent rage-quit came as a result of the espionage system.  After the neighboring Greek ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s kept conducting missions to siphon money from my capital, I trained a spy and stationed them on my commercial district for counterespionage - which is EXACTLY what you're supposed to do, and is the only thing you can do to try and fend off other spies.  Well, after my money continued to get siphoned, my spy finally caught the Greek spy, but in the same turn my economy became "bankrupt", even though my treasury balance displayed as an even zero with a positive income (+84, the highest it had been that whole game).  Well, it turns out something somewhere said I was still in the red, because the game said I was bankrupt and my units had to be disbanded.  I didn't get to choose who got disbanded, and you know who the game decided for me to disband?  MY.  FREAKING.  SPY.  The only line of defence I had against the crap that put me into this hidden bankruptcy, the game took the spy away from me.  Just for laughs, I kept playing a few turns after that.  My income amount increased to +90, but my treasury amount stayed at zero, and my army continued to slowly get disbanded.  I had no idea how "bankrupt" I was, what I could do to stop it, or how long it was going to last.
I'm a longtime fan of the Civilization series (since Civ2) and it pains me to have to give a recommendation against this game, but in its current state it just isn't an enjoyable experience.  I will probably give it another try once a major expansion comes out, and hope that within the next year or two they address these serious issues.

Life is Strange is a very story rich game centered around the protagonist Max Caulfield. The first episode immerses you into this beautiful universe and allows you to explore, learn the characters and their stories and introduces the rewind ability which is the main focus of the game and ultimately leads to a dramatic conclusion. This game is fantastic in my opinion, I have never been so invested in characters in a video game in a long time and there were many up and downs, but ultimately, I have never had a game bring a tear to my eye.  This game is a must have if you like story driven games. It is not a shooter, it is not a simulator, but it puts you in the feet of a young woman trying to save her friend and help everyone she possibly can.
Each episode ends in a cliff hanger of sorts just making you want more. Every character somehow has their personality shown in great detail in the short time you interact with them. Beautiful graphics in this game show the true potential for non-photo realistic graphics and does it very well with an almost oil painting-esque style.
The soundtrack is by far the best matching music for a game that I have ever heard, every song perfectly fits the scene and emotional moments that transpire.
Game performed very well with no drops in framerate, my only complaint was the terrible lip syncing. It's seriously terrible, it looks like someone munching on sand, it doesn't sync well at all, but if you can get past this, then the game is that much better.

Civilization VI is the latest installment where one is tasked with building an empire that, as the game's famous motto goes "Will stand the test of time."
Getting to choose one of about a dozen civilizations you guide your empire from a single town to, possibly, a sprawling empire spanning continents while you engage in trade, espionage, diplomacy, building a distinct culture, the spreading of religion and conquest. This, in a nutshell, is Civilization VI and herein it faithfully follows its predecessors. So let's look at the game as it stands on itself, as well as how it compares to its most immediate predecessor, Civ V.
The good...
One of the great things about Civ VI as opposed to V is that it comes as a much more complete package. Where V needed two expansions to introduce things like religion, tourism, more expansive trade and a more varied amount of luxury resources, Civ VI already comes with all of those.
For those familiar to the game already, the civics and policy aspect has also been greatly expanded, now running seperate to the familiar tech tree, allowing for greater specialization and diversification in how one wants to run their empire. So, mentioning these two things alone, Civ VI looks and feels like a much more complete product upon launch.
The bad...
How complete and finished can we really consider it though, when it also suffers from some almost unforgivable flaws? The biggest flaw most players will cite, and this reviewer is one of them, is the ridiculously bad AI. It is next to impossible to build good relationships with other AI civs when playing single player, and their behaviour is eratic, illogical and hostile in all fields; whether it is diplomacy, trade or warfare. Where originally it would be a point to laud Firaxis for delivering a comparatively more complete product compared to Civ V, it also feels rushed, unbalanced and poorly thought through.
The difficulty scaling system also remains unimproved, though it has been much maligned in previous installments as well. Rather than facing progressively clever AI, players rather have to deal with AI opponents getting 'cheating' bonuses to make the game more difficult. In the eyes of this reviewer however that quickly leads to gameplay that is more frustrating than challenging.
The silly...
And this is what ultimately makes the game rather silly. The great ideas of engaging in diplomacy, trade, religious 'warfare' are all undone by a hamfisted AI that is agressive, stubborn and illogical, forcing the myriad of possible playstyles down a bottleneck where warfare and militarism is the only real viable option to play and win the game, especially on the higher difficulty setting. By still continuing to ignore or at least not being able to address what so many players have complained in previous installments, many aspects of the game quickly become silly and better to try and ignore in pursuit of victory.
My final judgement is that it is still a game with great potential if the AI and some glaring bugs are adressed. As it stands it feels the game has been released too soon and the developers got tangled up in their own ambitions.
