Civilization VI, hereafter referred to as "Civ 6" for simplicity's sake, is definitely a serious improvement over the previous Civ games. That being said, it ain't perfect. Allow me to explain.
Civ 6 takes many steps forward over Civ 5: it allows you to group the same type of unit together for added combat strength, thus saving much more tile space during full sieges, where ordinarily you'd have 9 groups of Modern Armor clustered all over the place, but now you have three groups of three; it has different specialty "districts", that provide different bonuses to cities; the previous game's culture system has been replaced with a Civics tree that in many respects is like a second research tree; and many other improvements that you'd just have to notice on your own.
What it DOESN'T do, however, is get its AI and certain game settings right.
At the current time of this review, I can confirm that every single AI civ is a Gandhi in that they immediately declare war on you the turn after you first make contact. They also denounce you left and right for no justifiable reason, but of course that means nothing when they muster every last unit they own into a compulsive siege of your empire.
With the districts that I spoke of before, they add a number of new gameplay mechanics into the mix, one of which being a system called "Amenities", which is both very helpful and very harmful if not managed properly. Basically what Amenities do is fill the role that Happiness had in Civ 5, though it does dictate how fast cities grow, perhaps more so than having food for them. The problem with Amenities is that there are times ingame when you can't do anything to appease the negative Amenity amount, and if that stays on long enough, large amounts of Barbarians (representing rebellious citizens) scaled with your most advanced unit per research level will spawn, effectively enabling Civ 5's "Raging Barbarians" option, but with no way to deactivate it. When you're in the Information Era and three Modern Armor and one Rocket Artillery units pop up out of nowhere, that's a serious issue.
One minor, minor gripe is that Builders (which is what they're called ingame, I think) are both a step ahead and a step behind over previous installments' Workers. They build tile improvements (minus Wonders) instantly; that's awesome. They have limited uses, forcing you to train more; that's not so awesome. One might argue that it's balanced, but the Builders only get three uses total, which is kind of low in my opinion. Again, my opinion, but one shared with my friends and many other Civ veterans who aren't entirely in agreement with this change.
Again, as of this writing, Civ 6 does NOT have a Workshop, which was a bit of a "Say whaaaaaaaaaaaaaat??!" moment for me, though it does have plenty of mods, and most of the mods are things that patch up the problems I listed before; there's a Builder mod that gives the Builders 10 charges instead of three; another mod is an "AI+", which simmers down the AI civs; an enhanced diplomacy menu that tells you exactly what you've been doing to either win the approval or the antipathy of the AI, and what you can do to raise their opinion of you; a mod that adds a build que (I have no clue why they took it OUT of the game; yeah, I forgot to mention that there isn't a build que like there was in the previous games); and many, many others that make life much less stressful.
I do strongly recommend Civ 6, since it offers many new improvements over Civ 5; it does, however, have many, many areas of fault, but mods have done the selfless favor of patching up those loose areas.

Life is Strange is a very story rich game centered around the protagonist Max Caulfield. The first episode immerses you into this beautiful universe and allows you to explore, learn the characters and their stories and introduces the rewind ability which is the main focus of the game and ultimately leads to a dramatic conclusion. This game is fantastic in my opinion, I have never been so invested in characters in a video game in a long time and there were many up and downs, but ultimately, I have never had a game bring a tear to my eye.  This game is a must have if you like story driven games. It is not a shooter, it is not a simulator, but it puts you in the feet of a young woman trying to save her friend and help everyone she possibly can.
Each episode ends in a cliff hanger of sorts just making you want more. Every character somehow has their personality shown in great detail in the short time you interact with them. Beautiful graphics in this game show the true potential for non-photo realistic graphics and does it very well with an almost oil painting-esque style.
The soundtrack is by far the best matching music for a game that I have ever heard, every song perfectly fits the scene and emotional moments that transpire.
Game performed very well with no drops in framerate, my only complaint was the terrible lip syncing. It's seriously terrible, it looks like someone munching on sand, it doesn't sync well at all, but if you can get past this, then the game is that much better.
It's definitely a good game, not to mention it's free to play, but it just makes me wanna play overwatch instead everytime i play it.

I am a long time fan of Civilization series, starting since the first installment.
I remember playing I, II, III days and days, but this version just does not have that anymore.
I also played IV and V as much as I could.
I don't know whether it is the slow passing of turns, superficial novelties like
placing buildings in neighbourhoods that do not affect gameplay, or some minor quirks
like the map visibility only being updated at the end of the unit move. Unit movement is
sluggish, turns take ages to finish and somehow the game just feels sleepy. There is no "one more turn effect" anymore, with all previous Civs I at least wanted to win the game once or twice, here I quit while I was winning and uninstalled.
The unit graphics look similar to the lightweight Civs on iOS made in China, and while those were pretty good games for the platform, this one does not capture the "epic" proportions of the previous PC installments of the series. I suspect outsourcing to save costs, but somehow the spirit is lost.
Unfortunately I can not give a recommendation to buy. If you are a owner of Civ V and expansions, you will not find much here worth your money. The game is slow even on a new PC and there is not much really new. My advice would be to buy Civ V and Expansions when it is on offer, and skip this version entirely.

This is an interim version, I hope that the next Civ will bring the series back on the epic track.

Unfortunately in this games current state, this game would not be something that I would be willing to recommend.
Firstly, the games performance is fantastic, coming from early Civ V's consistent crashing and disconnecting in multiplayer, you will find Civ VI's loading screens and multiplayer performance a pleasant surprise after coming from Civ V. I have experienced absolutely no issues while playing this game.
I feel that this game visually appears a bit crowded and difficult to decipher, the colours aren't very distinct from each other in some environments and when zoomed out the map kind of appears just like a big blob of very dull colours, when in environments like the desert however the game feels bright and visually appealing.
There is something about it that I can't quite place my finger on, but with the current look of the game I struggle to get the same immersive feel that I can get in Civ V, possibly as a result of the new cartoonish art style that takes the game away from feeling like you're controlling an expansive empire and closer to the experience of a casual mobile game.
Similar to a casual mobile game, the DLC are uninspiring, boring and honestly a complete waste of money. A single civilization and 'scenario' are hardly worth the $5 USD, especially if you intend on just having the DLC civilizations as an AI nation in your single player games.
The AI are awful. There is simply no other way to put it. Diplomacy feels completely void of any real effect to the game, upon meeting an AI it is not whether they will be a vital ally or mortal enemy, but rather how long until you inevitably anger them to the point where they will hate you for the rest of the game? I have failed to have at least one successful alliance with any AIs in the game. Inviting their delegations appears to have no effect, and if it does, I would not know what it is, a feeling you will commonly have in this game where tool tips are either unhelpful or non-existant. Casus Belli system while welcome seems useless because worrying about your warmonger status is pointless due to the fact that everyone already hates you.
In addition to the terrible diplomacy regarding other AI nations, the city-state system, while I actually appreciate the envoys that have been added to the game, losing the ability to pledge protection to a city state, be called into their wars and gift units to a city state makes it utterly useless to have any real alliance with them as you would be able to acheive in Civ V. You will now find yourself making the decision of declaring a war upon the AI invading the city-state itself and having a full scale war, or allowing them to destroy your faithful city-state ally, losing the ability to fight a form of proxy-war where you are providing units but not formally at war again allows Firaxis to continue to completely destroy any immersive feeling that may have existed in Civ VI.
The UI is minimalist, and disappointing, things such as your GPT and science per turn are now presented as tiny little numbers in the top left corner. While this in itself is a bit annoying, as it really doesn't draw your attention like the previous Civ V top bar did, the real thing that disappoints me is the fact that when you are in negative GPT, it doesn't even change colour or warn you. You now have to keep up with the job of pulling out your magnifying glass every turn to see whether or not you are even making money. A similar experience with the new minimalist notifications, which again are completely unable to grab your attention with the crowded visuals of the game and you will frequently miss events.
I thoroughly enjoy the new districts, religion and wonder changes, seeing your wonders stand tall next to your cities is fantastic and a great addition to the game, religion is similar to Civ V and works like a treat, the only fault that I would give it is the waves of missionaries that infect your land as you get further in the game as well as the poor AI 'agendas' which will leave you as an enemy forever despite any other diplomatic events that had occured if you do not match another nations religion.
Overall, the words that I would use to describe this game is; disappointing and boring.

As I started the second season of TellTale's popular interactive storybook tale based on the popular AMC television series, I felt very deeply immersed in the story that was revolving around the protagonist. I was given tough choices and had a strong emotional response to every consequence.
The continuation from Season One feels seemless now that I recall the events of the past, especially when I see the consequences of the choices in that game affecting the story in this sequel in meaningful ways. At first, the choices I made in Season Two didn't seem so meaningful, but it is slowly creeping up on me as I make progress and the plot begins to unfold. Even the smallest choices have the potential to twist the plot.
However, I highly recommend not reading the names of the achievements in this game before returning to the zombie apocalypse. And I personally wouldn't find it enjoyable unless I completed Season One. I can't imagine not experiencing Season One and then even pretending that I understand the protagonist to Season Two.
All of what matters to me personally aside, expect a lot of button context actions, dialogue options, and forshadowing that inevitably kicks you in the gut. I honestly don't know why TellTale bothered with so many achievements in an interactive storytelling game, but I can't help but look the other way because this story is told so well that I can't quite put it down. If this series were a physical "Choose Your Own Adventure" book, then I'd read it until I had to start taping pages back together.

Unfortunately in this games current state, this game would not be something that I would be willing to recommend.
Firstly, the games performance is fantastic, coming from early Civ V's consistent crashing and disconnecting in multiplayer, you will find Civ VI's loading screens and multiplayer performance a pleasant surprise after coming from Civ V. I have experienced absolutely no issues while playing this game.
I feel that this game visually appears a bit crowded and difficult to decipher, the colours aren't very distinct from each other in some environments and when zoomed out the map kind of appears just like a big blob of very dull colours, when in environments like the desert however the game feels bright and visually appealing.
There is something about it that I can't quite place my finger on, but with the current look of the game I struggle to get the same immersive feel that I can get in Civ V, possibly as a result of the new cartoonish art style that takes the game away from feeling like you're controlling an expansive empire and closer to the experience of a casual mobile game.
Similar to a casual mobile game, the DLC are uninspiring, boring and honestly a complete waste of money. A single civilization and 'scenario' are hardly worth the $5 USD, especially if you intend on just having the DLC civilizations as an AI nation in your single player games.
The AI are awful. There is simply no other way to put it. Diplomacy feels completely void of any real effect to the game, upon meeting an AI it is not whether they will be a vital ally or mortal enemy, but rather how long until you inevitably anger them to the point where they will hate you for the rest of the game? I have failed to have at least one successful alliance with any AIs in the game. Inviting their delegations appears to have no effect, and if it does, I would not know what it is, a feeling you will commonly have in this game where tool tips are either unhelpful or non-existant. Casus Belli system while welcome seems useless because worrying about your warmonger status is pointless due to the fact that everyone already hates you.
In addition to the terrible diplomacy regarding other AI nations, the city-state system, while I actually appreciate the envoys that have been added to the game, losing the ability to pledge protection to a city state, be called into their wars and gift units to a city state makes it utterly useless to have any real alliance with them as you would be able to acheive in Civ V. You will now find yourself making the decision of declaring a war upon the AI invading the city-state itself and having a full scale war, or allowing them to destroy your faithful city-state ally, losing the ability to fight a form of proxy-war where you are providing units but not formally at war again allows Firaxis to continue to completely destroy any immersive feeling that may have existed in Civ VI.
The UI is minimalist, and disappointing, things such as your GPT and science per turn are now presented as tiny little numbers in the top left corner. While this in itself is a bit annoying, as it really doesn't draw your attention like the previous Civ V top bar did, the real thing that disappoints me is the fact that when you are in negative GPT, it doesn't even change colour or warn you. You now have to keep up with the job of pulling out your magnifying glass every turn to see whether or not you are even making money. A similar experience with the new minimalist notifications, which again are completely unable to grab your attention with the crowded visuals of the game and you will frequently miss events.
I thoroughly enjoy the new districts, religion and wonder changes, seeing your wonders stand tall next to your cities is fantastic and a great addition to the game, religion is similar to Civ V and works like a treat, the only fault that I would give it is the waves of missionaries that infect your land as you get further in the game as well as the poor AI 'agendas' which will leave you as an enemy forever despite any other diplomatic events that had occured if you do not match another nations religion.
Overall, the words that I would use to describe this game is; disappointing and boring.

A little Overwatch, a pinch of Unreal tournament and a tablespoon of Team fortress, and you have Paladins! I've been playing all morning and I'm heavily enjoying myself, I have my nitpicks about the overall game but otherwise, it's a lotta fun. But like I said, there are nitpicks
Locked abilities and champions-
This is the one really bad thing that I can say about the game it has a lot of locked things like cards, champions and items which at first glance sounds like P2W, but it actually doesn't unbalance the game at all. Yes it's a little frustrating that there is a champion you want to try and play but can't unless you save gold or buy crystals but the ones that ARE availible are still unique and loads of fun, viktor, drogoz, and skye are in my top 3.
Immediate tutorial. While this isn't really my nitpick, I can see how this might come across as a bad thing for new players. Once you've finished the setup process, and made an account on hi-rez if you didn't have one the game will launch and you will IMMEDIATELY be loaded into the tutorial. So when you launch up don't panic lol.
No level specific matchmaking for new players- I have read 1000s of reviews ♥♥♥♥♥ing about matchmaking and I'm here to say STOP. it's early access and does need tweeks, but I personally understand and comply with this. in about the 3 hours I've been playing NONSTOP (so all-together that's about 32 matches) I had ONE bad game, and it didn't even end horrible. But the main issue I will add to this list is that Paladins' matchmaking system isn't level or time specific meaning if you JUST launched the game and have no prior knowledge or experience with first person shooters or even games in general, quote of south park, You're gonna have a bad time. And even if you are experienced, there will be times you'll be matched into a clueless team vs high level players, it happens unfortunately. Perhaps if I could ask the developer for one change, it would be to take that into account if he ever decides to update the game.
I suppose when I said I had "some nitpicks" I could only write 2. SO, I'm just gonna put stereotypical complaints about the game and add my own rebuttle.
"DIS GAME IZ PAY TO WIN!" Absolutely not! the model design for the champions, card abilities and sets is actually perfect in it's own right, and by far the only game I've seen that utilizes it fairly. On my very first match today, I was fresh from the tutorial and ready to play, selecting viktor as he was used for the tutorial. I was up agains't a level 3 Drogoz with a full set of abilites from point shop, a level 2 Androxus with an expensive and a few other classes whose names I haven't actually learned yet, bit scatterbrain right now. I wasn't even level 1, I didn't use the point shop and I was using the basic viktor set. With that all being said, how did you imagine my gameplay? Horrible right? I would have thought so too. But by merely being careful, utilizing all my special abilities IE grenades, sprint, iron sights. I made 1st on the leader board not play of the game but I had a 6 killstreak my very first life, regardless of anything else considered "pay to win"
"LAWL IS OVERWATCH RIPOFF!" Similar, of course, a ripoff? Not in the slightest. They do have similarities in the mechanics, the cartoonish graphics and unique story line, and even the musical quality but overwatch is not a game I would consider fun or even playable, it currently has a lot of balance issues, cheaters, and is so overpriced and not worth it, the saving grace is it's storyline and enjoyable characters. In all honesty, I doubt the dev even had overwatch in mind when putting this together, as a tribute or a poor mans OW? maybe but I refuse to believe that he intentionally used it as a base, considering he has melded FPS with common MOBA mechanics and feels to it.
Anyhow, if you read through even a bit of that, I thank you. Download the game, and you'll see everything I mean, this game is worth the time it takes. GLHF

Alright, so after finishing Walking Dead Season 1, I was entirely impressed with the story, and how attached I was to characters such as Clementine, Lee, Kenny, ext.. The main part of Season 2 falls into place 16 months after the events of season 1, and let me just say WOW. I got this game while both ep 1 and 2 of the Season have been released, and I am once again hooked on this series. I will now go through, what I feel, are the negatives and positives of this game. Please advise I will try reviewing without giving away too many spoliers and info about the story itself, that is up to you guys to discover and play for yourselves. :)
-------POSITIVES---------
-Price - I definatly have gotten my money's worth out of this game. For just 25 bucks currently you get episodes 1 and 2, and the rest for free as they are released. If you are NOT SURE ON GETTING THIS GAME, then I would advise you waiting for one of the Steam sales before purchasing.
-Story - The lore of the story is so good, it is almost unbelievable. The game continues off of choices that you had made in Season 1 AND in the DLC for Season 1, 400 Days. You do have the option to choose to continue from different Season 1 saves, or just to not continue from Season 1 at all. If its the case you want to do that, the game will randomly generate choices from Season 1 from episodes you didn't complete. Now back tot he story, the voice acting is, in my opinion, pretty good, and whoever voice acts Clementine has hit it spot on. There are many surprises throughout what I have played, in fact,    the game kind of slaps ya in the face, not even 10 minutes into the game. Also, Im not going to spoil anything, but there is a major suprise in episode 2, and for anyone who has played Season 1 like me, your going to be jumping for joy, or kicking yourself in the shin depending on how you played the game. To summarize, this game has a great story with many twists and turns that any true Walking Dead fan is going to love.
-Voice Acting - I know I talked about it a bit up there, but I think that it was so good, it deserved its own place. I have no clue where Telltale gets their voice actors, but they definatly hit a home run with it. At times the voice acting may be a little dull, especially with 1 or maybe 2 characters in perticular, but overall, an amazing job by the voice actors.
-Decision Making - This is yet another area of the game where I think the developers did another amazing job. There are many spots in the game where it requires you to make a tough decision. While not all of them may really matter in the long run, the game really makes you think "Wow this is an ACTUAL decision someone might have to make in everyday life, and if I pick this one, then I'll feel bad for that character. However if I pick this one, then I'll feel bad for that character." Now don't go thinking that this is a game of life or whatever, because it's not. It's a zombie game, and there are alot of decisions that put one or the other's characters lifes' on the line. So you really do have to make every choice with the thought in the back of your head that, "Hey! Maybe if I do this then that character won't like me and he won't help me when we're in trouble later. Of course you won't be thinking THAT far ahead because of the intense storyline that is taking place right in front of you, but the thought is always there.
-Lag/Framerate - For me, the game did a decent job of keeping everything running smooth. I had a little to no framerate problems, while in Season 1, during the first few episodes I had some trouble with lag. I was glad to see the lag didn't carry over to this game aswell.
--------NEGATIVES---------
-Episode Shortness - There aren't too many negative thing about this games, but if I could pin point one big one, it would be that the episodes, SO FAR (episodes 1 and 2) are REALLY short. I'm not too experienced at these types of games, and I was able to finish both episodes in about 3 hours worth of time. Hopefully the future episodes are longer, but since I'm making this review before episodes 3, 4 , and 5 have came out, I can't say anything about them. But that, so far averages at about 1.5 hours per episode, altough episode 2 was longer then episode 1, so either way the episodes were considerably shorter then Season 1. I put 15 hours into Season 1, not including the extra hour that the DLC gave me. Im really hoping the next episodes will be longer.
-[WARNING BEFORE PLAYING] Gruesome Scenes - Although I personaly dont mind, nor do I care if a game has gruesome scenes, I thought I'd warn the younger players aswell as those with a faint heart that there are gruesome scenes in the game.
And that was my review. I hope I helped some of you decide whether or not you want to buy this game. :)

"Adventures of Enkidu" bonus: May declare war on anyone at war with their allies without warmonger penalties. When at war with a common foe, they and their allies share pillage rewards and share combat experience gains if within 5 tiles. Means that basically, the way you farm early XP is by sitting 3-5 tiles away from other civs fighting barbs, and you end up racking ~5-7xp per turn for doing nothing, and on top of that you're scott-free to stab them in the back one by one during ancient at any time, AND YOU'LL NEVER GET PENALIZED FOR IT, EVER. Let me start by saying I think this is a great game overall.  I only got into the Civ series starting with Civ 5, but I played at least 200 hours in that one.  There are already tons of reviews for this game, so I'm going to try not to restate a lot of what people are already commonly saying about it.  More, I just wanted to talk about how the AI in the game is getting blasted currently.  Some of the criticism is correct, but I'm also seeing many reviews lamenting poor AI, in places where I think the AI is actually working as it should.  One review I read claimed this:
"You have to declare war just to stop settler spam from wiping out your civ. If you want to be a peaceful civ, then expect to lose the game - unless going for a tech victory."
- This is completely untrue.  While it is more important to build a defensive army in Civ6 than Civ5, you can definitely win games peacefully if you're careful diplomatically.  I just finished a game where I was allied with 3 civs, never went to war, and claimed a cultural victory.  I have also gotten a science victory in a game, where there was only one minor skirmish early in the game, and that was only because the China AI had gotten boxed in early and had no choice but to fight to expand.
I have heard critisicm of barbarians being to tough as well.  In my experience, while they are definitely tougher than in civ 5, if you make a couple military units early, you can definitely deal with them fairly well.  There are also civics you can access early which give you bonuses to fighting them, making them even more manageable.  I see claims that they are even a major threat into industrial/modern era.  I think understanding how they spawn is important to this.  They can only create new bases where no civs can currently see.  If I have undevelopped areas close to my empire later on, I simply station a few military units to keep an eye on that section of land, this keeps them away from me.
The last complaint I've heard I want to address is the seemingly frustrating nature of how the AI views the player diplomatically.  Seemingly flip flopping back and forth.  Or declaring friendship, only to declare war as soon as it expires.  Some seem to think it's a flaw in the game.  I think the system is working well.  If you spend some time in the diplomacy screen you can see the different motivations all the leaders have for who they will like.  One of them is public knowledge, the other requires a higher level of diplomatic visibility to see.  You can also see a breakdown of all the things currently affecting their attitude towards you, and suggestions on how to improve relations.  I spend a lot of time trying to keep good relations in my games because I don't like getting bogged down by war.  I form my strategies based on what I know other nations will like.  If a neighbor likes large empires, I expand.  If they like a large navy, I build boats.  If I can't get a foothold because they won't let me build an embassy, I give gifts and send them a trade route.  And perhaps most importantly, I don't settle immediately on anyone else's border, unless I really have no choice. (They really hate that, understandably.  I hate it when they do it to me too!)  While the AI is a bit weak sometimes, I think most of the time the diplomacy aspect of it is done quite well.  It's just easy to miss why a change in attitude has occured if you're not actively focused on that.
Anyway, hope this helps at least one person out there.  I really like this game and wanted to post a defense to some criticism I thought was a bit unfair.

But that's not even half the problem, since districts could be looked at differently just based on your playstyle preferrences (like if you're a big science player, and want to max out your science yields).
The combat, on the other hand? Bro - compared from civ5? Completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥; the balance is completely out of whack and makes it entirely too easy to attack. Case and point, Summeria. "Adventures of Enkidu" bonus: May declare war on anyone at war with their allies without warmonger penalties. When at war with a common foe, they and their allies share pillage rewards and share combat experience gains if within 5 tiles. Means that basically, the way you farm early XP is by sitting 3-5 tiles away from other civs fighting barbs, and you end up racking ~5-7xp per turn for doing nothing, and on top of that you're scott-free to stab them in the back one by one during ancient at any time, AND YOU'LL NEVER GET PENALIZED FOR IT, EVER. Epic Quests: When you capture a Barbarian Outpost, receive a Tribal Village reward in addition to the usual Gold. This is HUGE; it means you're getting tribal bonuses for farming barb camps, which you should be doing anyway, and this just carries over once you're dominant in your continent and just pushes you that much farther ahead than any other competition left.
Unique unit: War-Cart. Not only the strongest ancient unit in the game, not only available to build IMMEDIATELY, but also has 4 movement on flat terrain, 3 on rough, but gets ZERO combat penalties against spears. Bro - holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is
R E T A R D E D
Who in the unholy hell though in the office that this unit would be remotely balanced?? It basically translates to this: you spam early War-carts, farm barbs by first sitting back and letting other civs hit a camp, then steal the camp kill for gold PLUS tribal bonuses, declare war, murder their wounded warriors, get ZERO warmonger penalties for it, and just level the whole map with early god-tier units that the other civs can't do a god-damn thing to stop. (Also for those unfamiliar with Civ6's combat mechanics vs. Civ5's mechanics - basically ancient cities without walls cannot defend themselves, cannot return fire on enemies...so, basically you only need two units at most, and that's their starting capital gone. It's like beating up a helpless baby!)
So, tl;dr - Sumerians went from mediocre in 5, to now they're literally god-tier in ancient, districts are just annoying, and walls/defending cities in ancient is not actually a thing. So, spam early War-Carts, farm xp off other civs/steal barb camps because LOL Epic Quests, stab them in the back with no warmonger penalty, and flatten the whole map with War-Carts because B A L A N C E D. Let me start by saying I think this is a great game overall.  I only got into the Civ series starting with Civ 5, but I played at least 200 hours in that one.  There are already tons of reviews for this game, so I'm going to try not to restate a lot of what people are already commonly saying about it.  More, I just wanted to talk about how the AI in the game is getting blasted currently.  Some of the criticism is correct, but I'm also seeing many reviews lamenting poor AI, in places where I think the AI is actually working as it should.  One review I read claimed this:
"You have to declare war just to stop settler spam from wiping out your civ. If you want to be a peaceful civ, then expect to lose the game - unless going for a tech victory."
- This is completely untrue.  While it is more important to build a defensive army in Civ6 than Civ5, you can definitely win games peacefully if you're careful diplomatically.  I just finished a game where I was allied with 3 civs, never went to war, and claimed a cultural victory.  I have also gotten a science victory in a game, where there was only one minor skirmish early in the game, and that was only because the China AI had gotten boxed in early and had no choice but to fight to expand.
I have heard critisicm of barbarians being to tough as well.  In my experience, while they are definitely tougher than in civ 5, if you make a couple military units early, you can definitely deal with them fairly well.  There are also civics you can access early which give you bonuses to fighting them, making them even more manageable.  I see claims that they are even a major threat into industrial/modern era.  I think understanding how they spawn is important to this.  They can only create new bases where no civs can currently see.  If I have undevelopped areas close to my empire later on, I simply station a few military units to keep an eye on that section of land, this keeps them away from me.
The last complaint I've heard I want to address is the seemingly frustrating nature of how the AI views the player diplomatically.  Seemingly flip flopping back and forth.  Or declaring friendship, only to declare war as soon as it expires.  Some seem to think it's a flaw in the game.  I think the system is working well.  If you spend some time in the diplomacy screen you can see the different motivations all the leaders have for who they will like.  One of them is public knowledge, the other requires a higher level of diplomatic visibility to see.  You can also see a breakdown of all the things currently affecting their attitude towards you, and suggestions on how to improve relations.  I spend a lot of time trying to keep good relations in my games because I don't like getting bogged down by war.  I form my strategies based on what I know other nations will like.  If a neighbor likes large empires, I expand.  If they like a large navy, I build boats.  If I can't get a foothold because they won't let me build an embassy, I give gifts and send them a trade route.  And perhaps most importantly, I don't settle immediately on anyone else's border, unless I really have no choice. (They really hate that, understandably.  I hate it when they do it to me too!)  While the AI is a bit weak sometimes, I think most of the time the diplomacy aspect of it is done quite well.  It's just easy to miss why a change in attitude has occured if you're not actively focused on that.
Anyway, hope this helps at least one person out there.  I really like this game and wanted to post a defense to some criticism I thought was a bit unfair.

I have loved Civ since Civ III. I have bought and played evry game, every expansion, and evry DLC. So for me it seemed like a no-brainer to buy the digital deluxe when Civ VI released. Well, I wish I hadn't and here's why.
1) the digital deluxe was supposed to save me money over buying the DLC seperately. $20 extra for 4 DLC. Seems fair. Except the 2 DLC that have released so far have each been less than $5, so if the next 2 aren't more substantive then I've actually paid MORE by purchasing the bundle.
2) I expected ACTUAL content. So for the two DLCs have given me 1 new civilization and 1 scenario. You want me to accept that THIS is worth $10? A miniscule addition to the game and a scenario I'll probably never play? No. It isn't.
3) Firaxis PROMISED a complete game at launch for Civ VI. Unlike Civ V, this was supposed to be a fully functioning game from day one. It is not. It is buggy as all hell. The diplomacy system is TERRIBLE. The religion and great person system feel like they were just tacked on as a last minute addition with little to no incorporation into the rest of the game. The amenities and housing resources are almost impossible to track or manage, especially since they are now entirely localized, unlike happiness was in previous games. Lastly, all of the information is presented in such tiny text and with completely new icons that honestly don't clearly match what they're meant to represent that it is nearly impossible to manage anything without missing some crucial element.
Long story short, Civ VI has a lot of great ideas and could become something great, but right now it feels like an indie game with good graphics and too many pieces, not a flagship product from an established company.

A figurative dice roll is made at the beginning of every matches.
Then you win or you lose depending on the dice roll, which is what the other team will be composed of.
You get crushed or you're the ones crushing.
You can forget any middle ground what so ever. Because there's no strategy involved. At all.

Unfortunately, its free-to-play nature, as well as its core design, have led to the game turning into a cluster♥♥♥♥.
For one thing, while skills are far more crucial than the main weapon, heroes with rapid-fire weapons instantly get a boost, because of the giant hitboxes. The number of times I've ended up dead behind walls is too funny. If I didn't know better, I'd say Hi-Rez can't do hit-detection for♥♥♥♥♥♥

June 10th (Update): Alright, so we've had a few DLC now and I still have to say it's pretty eh. The game is easy and the A.I is arguably the most terrible of any Civ game I've played. The game has no strategic uncertainty to balance out the terrible A.I, so it's even worse when you steamroll and there's no way for the A.I to catch up. The game still sorely lacks the World Congress, and it's pretty apparent how much that actually detracts from the main game.
Here's some general complaints
- Growing a city seems a lot harder this time around, and almost impossible to get a city above 10 population.
- People who want to play tall (a few really good cities) will always be beaten out because there's no penalties to playing wide (which is fine, but at least give tall players some bonuses).
- Religious victory is incredibly overpowered and easy to accomplish, and inredibly boring as well because there's only 3 religious units.
- The Science progression is out of wack and Civs will often be 4 Eras ahead or behind one another, including the player.
- Unit sizes are still incredibly small
The game has a lot of potential, and it's arguably better than any other Civ game at launch, but the main thing it needs to improve on is the difficulty.
------------------------------------------------------------------
January 22nd:
Pre-ordered the game, and frankly I played right at launch and I've had no reason to really go back to it. There are still no mods, the "DLCs" they have are still extremely lackluster (especially as someone who pre-ordered I'm disappointed that the only real thing we've got was a Poland DLC). Sound track is phenomenal, and brilliantly designed, but I just can't get behind the rest of the game. Gameplay could have been so much more, and while I definitely appreciate all the things being there at launch, the A.I is still terrible, and the game speed just feels... wrong.
The A.I will spam out outdated units like warriors well into the reinassance, especially if it's a city-state it which case they just drape the damn things until the entire continent is filled with them.
Multiplayer is better, and easier this time around.
Whatever game speed you played on in Civ 5, play on one higher in this, because production and tech takes like 30% longer.
The addition of another special ability has helped add even more variety, which makes the game a lot more fun.
I still don't really like the graphics as well. Initially I hated them, then I warmed up, and now the game just feels odd when you see any battle animation. The inflated unit sizes just make the game a walking cartoon. I wouldn't even mind the graphics style so much if it weren't for the fact units are so big.
I'll change my review to a positive when we pre-orderers (I know, I know) get any good DLC (either a few Civ ones or an expansion), and when the A.I feels the need to act more intelligently than a 2nd grader mismatching pages in a history book.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summer Update: Still terrible, all the DLC is still terrible, only thing they added really was slightly tweaked AI, and being able to (thankfully) manage trade routes a bit better.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Winter Update: Still no bueno, unfortunately. Wouldn't recommend getting it above $10, $15 if you really like it. They also have  the gall to release an expansion for $30 without making the AI fuctional still.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I feel like after 30 hours I can gauge this game pretty well.
I enjoyed this game, and I'm glad I bought it. It's definitely an improvement over Civ 5.
Here are my personal pros and cons...
(-) The AI can feel spuratic at some times, but other times its very reasonable.
(+) The UI is vastly superior to Civ 5, easier to access and use
(-) Doesn't have the promised workshop support yet
(+) The new civics tree adds an interesting twist to the game, very nice
(-) Instead of important fixes the devs are releasing overpriced DLC
(+) Districs add another cool twist onto the Civ series. Instead of mindlessly building wonders/buildings, you have to consider where you build things. It adds another form of strategy. It's fun and interesting.
(-) The graphics are cartoony.
(+) The graphics look infinitely better than Civ 5 lets be real. The textures/shadows/lighting are much better.
(-) There isn't co-op multiplayer, only FFA.
(+) Amenities and housing are infinitely better than universal happiness included in previous Civ games.
Overall I like this game more than civ 5, but maybe I'd hold back until march.
Most of these cons will be fixed in a few short months, I gurantee it. Fireaxis is hard at work figuring out these issues.
We'll see workshop support/co-op multiplayer/improved AI within months.
If you're feeling skeptical, maybe you should wait a few months, but if you feel comfortable with those pros and cons, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome.

Kerbal Space Program is exactly the kind of game that I love.  You get to build stuff.  You get to use your imagination.  It's space themed.  It requires attention to detail.
So why the bad recommendation?
Because I'm not playing it.  I'm trying to figure out why the resolution resets itself, and forces me into windowed mode.  Or why after how many years in development they haven't implemented joysticks like every other game that I have ever owned.  So I am scouring the internet trying to find out why trying to set up my joystick freezes the game.  And how to reset everything to stop it.  And how it loses my settings after every game.  And how to calibrate my joystick once I do get the game to recognize it.  And how the game doesn't have joystick calibration.  And how other people are getting around the problem.  And how it only sometimes works and then sometimes doesn't.  I just want to play the game, not screw around on the net trying to troubleshoot problems.
I went back and tried this again.  I am having fewer problems and it really is a great game.  The joystick issues are just stupid though.  I can map the axes and buttons manually, however my old, worn out saitek cyborg evo is all that is calibrated correctly in the game.  There is no ingame calibration.  Your joystick can be calibrated perfectly outside the game, but ingame, for example my thrustmaster top gun fox 2 pro usb, it won't be calibrated.
I got over my joystick related negativity and recommended KSP.

This follow-up to Telltale Games' critically acclaimed 'The Walking Dead' is tonally different from its predecessor. Whereas the first put you in the shoes of a steadfast adult, this time the player assumes the role of Clementine, the girl the player had to protect in the first season. This allows the writers to inject much vulnerability and fear into the story, but also allows the player to grow with Clementine, making some difficult decisions along the way that would determine her moral path. It's kind of like raising a child -- you're not quite sure what will happen and how she'll turn out, but it's also an exciting journey. This season culminates in an exciting final episode full of difficult decisions that will leave you craving for the third season.

This is a terrific game format in my opinion. It will be especially pleasing to fans of the comics/graphic novels. The stylized graphics are not just static comic frames either, they are animated and it is a wonderfull way to see this game unfold visually in the same way The Walking Dead was originally created and intended to look. The storyline is very well written, captivating and it pulls you in. It really makes you care about what is happening to the characters around you, and I will go out on a limb here and say that when you reach the end of each episode you will be eagerly baited and waiting for that next episode. They can never come fast enough. For those of you who are fans of the television series, you will also enjoy this game because it is in NO WAY a simple point and click adventure. This game is so intriguing and engrossing that you will feel very invested in the plot as it is unveiled before you, and your choices affect the way the game progresses. People can live and die by your actions and what you choose to do can have far reaching implications to the story. I play a lot of games, and they sometimes almost seem to blur into one another with common themes and genres. This game was a fresh, original and highly entertaining change from the norm for me, and I give Telltale **** stars for this game. Have you ever wanted to be an astronaut? Have you ever wondered what it would be like to design and direct the Apollo Moon missions? Do you have an idea of how to colonize mars? Do you want to learn about orbital mechanics and greatly enjoy physics?
If you answered yes to any of these questions, Kerbal Space Program is for you!
KSP is a game that accurately models a scaled-down solar system, and you take control of a race of sentient green bipeds that have a unwavering desire to see it all firsthand. You will be building rockets, launching probes, landing on moons, designing shuttles, and maybe even messing with some near-future technology.
However, KSP is not easy. You will need to have steady hands, good planning skills, and a passing knowledge of rocket science to excel at this game.
Rarely does a game immerse me so deeply that I just keep coming back to it, week after week. Kerbal is definitely one of those games. Please read the entire review, there is an edit at the bottem, talking about my chang of heart.
ORIGONAL: When it comes to this game, there are two things people often complain about; the graphics and the AI. But there is also a lot this game does right. First, the good stuff. This game, purely from a mechanics standpoint, is awesome. Everything that worked in Civ 5:BNW is back, and refined to be better than the origonal expansion pack. From the districts to the concept of packing multiple units into corps, this game makes a lot of great changes. However, the games graphics are somewhat of a mixed bag. The models of the other leaders, buildings, and units on the map, are increadablely detailed. The Terrain itself, is okay, but can look oversaturated to some people/on some moniters. I am also a bit torn on the UI design as well. In some ways, the simplicity and look it has makes it feel much improved; in other ways it feels like a cheep tablet or mobile game.
Really though, those are just nitpicks. What really breaks this game is the AI. It is not that it is not challenging. It just isn't very fun to play against. Dipomacy with them is the weakest it has ever been in the franchise. In CK2, where there can be 500+ characters on the map, I still get several times as many diplomacy options for each and every one than this game. Well, okay, if diplomacy is dull, how about warfare? Well, actually, tactics may be one of the best abilities of the computer oponents. But they never upgrade their F*****g units, and rarely produce any beyond the origonal set they make in the anchient or classical era. This leads to late or even mid-game wars turning into sessions of mowing down warriors, archers, and catapults with field cannons. Hence, every war during the renisance and after is a complete joke. Hell, even this game uses districts to make a fantastic espianege system, the AI only really uses it to shut down production centers in your civ's cities.
TD:LR: HOWEVER, this game is probably preatty damn awesome if you bring some friends along to play. Bringing a few extra humans to fill the seats of your games, even if they don't fill ALL the places, can greatly decresse the issues with the horrible AI. If you are going to buy this game, get it either:
1) On Sale of at least 50%
2)Have some friends who also want the game and will play with you.
3)Wait until Firaxis may or may not fix the AI. If they do, they will get a thumbs up from me.
EDIT: As promised, the AI has been improved signifacantly. It is not perfect, though it still warrents a recomendation, as long as this improvement continues. I have more playing this than any other civ game. Still, would only recomend if on sale, unless you are a huge Civ fan. And deffenetly get some friends to play with you, if you can.

This review is coming from a new player with a new perspective and this is directed towards new players or people thinking about jumping in.
Positive:
+Fun factor. It's fun.
+There's a good amount of diverse characters to play.
+The unlocked characters can be unlocked for FREE.
+It doesn't really take too long to unlock a player.
+Customization in skins has potential for the future (for example, there's a few Halloween skins available now for certain characters-Cassie and Bomb King).
Negative:
-Matchmaking. Other players have complained about this a lot and I agree. A lot of the games you play feels like you're playing against more experienced players. And there's no ELO score that indicates the people you're playing against are of the same level as you. Also, my level 3 Drogoz has been owned by characters of level 0 and 1. I get it, this isn't like in RPG games where the higher level means you're stronger, but if I spent time with my character, and a person just started learning theirs, I should have the upper hand/advantage. Yet, this isn't the case in this game. You're not playing with people who, just like you, are learning the ropes. You play with people who (it often feels like) they've been playing this game for longer than you. So the matchmaking system is a problem.
-Feels unbalanced. Certain characters like Skye and Viktor feel like they have the advantage. You don't have to take my word for it, just read the reviews of those who've played more than I have, pointing this out. But if I, at a little over 6 hours of gameplay noticed this, then imagine what the players who've put in many more hours must be thinking/feeling about these characters.
If the length of the negative elements of this game didn't showcase the importance of addressing those two issues, I want to emphasize that they are critical and need to be addressed, especially going forward if people are going to be turned off from how unfair and unbalanced it may feel playing the game.

While this game does share many features and mechanics with Overwatch, I find the common perception that this is poor man's Overwatch to be a misconception, so I'd like to point to some of the major differences here.
First, characters are - by default - much less specialized than in Overwatch. Most characters are a bit more resilient, shields tend to last somewhat longer, and the in-match upgrade system allows for players to be less reliant on a healer to survive or a tank to soak damage. Instead, there is a card system whereby a player can spend in-game or real money currency to purchase upgrades for a character's individual skills or for the character directly. These allow for a great deal of customization of a character's playstyle and role within the team. This has both advantages and marked disadvantages when compared with Overwatch's strictly static role-based character selection. On the one hand, it allows for some extra player freedo, but on the other, it also makes for a much less defined role for each hero, and teams don't tend to give as much thought to composition.
Second, the cast of characters, while certainly sharing (and occasionally outright plagiarizing) many ideas with Overwatch, feels more colorful and diverse to me. While the cast of Overwatch is certainly diverse, it does consist of about 20 humans, a robot, an ape and a dwarf. Paladins, however, really lays the fantasy theme down thickly, giving us a bipedal turtle, a goblin piloting a sentient mech, a tiny mad scientist fox... thing, and whatever Bomb King and Mal'Damba are.
The third and perhaps most significant difference to me is the gameplay and pacing. While Overwatch gives players large, semi-linear maps and progressive spawn points, with many characters able to traverse distances rapidly, Paladins does quite the opposite. Maps are generally  shorter and more confined, and player movement abilities tend to be focused on moving around a skirmish rather than traversing the battlefield. Additionally, each player rides a mount from spawn to wherever they choose to dismount or where they first are hit by an enemy shot or ability - whichever comes first. The result is that good Paladins matches tend to be more consistently focused around the objectives - as any team losing sight and engaging on the fringes will begin to lose quite wuickly - and often feel much more intense, as more of each player's time is spent directly engaged with the enemy. This is the key difference for me as a player, as I find that the often long, boring hikes back into the fight in Overwatch break the pacing of otherwise excellent gameplay.
Before I close, I'd like to speak to the free-to-play elements. Many visual customizations are exclusive to the bought currency, rather than the earned, however there are a number which can be bought with the earned currency as well. Gameplay customizations, however, are all (as far as I can tell) available with both earned and bought currency, and while they alter character and ability stats, they do not inherently alter balance (meaning that Pay to Win is not present here, in this reviewer's opinion) and earned currency is readily acquired in sufficient amounts to customize characters regularly. I will say, however, that the visual customizations are poor, generally being simple palette swaps. If Hi-Rez hopes to support this game on the free-to-play model they currently are using, I feel that much more time and effort needs to go into making these skins much more interesting and diverse.
All in all I wouldn't say that this game is either better or worse than Overwatch overall. It's simply different. Despite the all-too-obvious similarities, the gameplay manages to be distinctive from its AAA, premium cousin's and the MOBA elements and customization give it a twist of something different. I would encourage anyone to give this a fair shot, even if they own Overwatch. It's a great deal of fun and has a lot of potential as its own game, rather than as poor man's Overwatch.

First of all, i'd rather write my opinion without recommending the game or not. I clicked yes only because it's a great game with great potential but there are many core flaws.
Basically, the plane research and the rover research are quite far and requires a lot of investment and research points. Everytime I give this game a shot, I end up grinding hard after getting most of the research available on Kerbin. It's stupid that rovers and planes, which are perfect for starting a new game, cost so much to get. By the time you get to use rovers and planes, they're nowhere near as useful.

You get 50k per contract if you're lucky and everything you upgrade cost 1M$+ which is required if you want to unlock the research to get more than the basic stuff.
I'm also not fond of practical systems being locked until you upgrade a building. The devs obviously had no idea what kind of progress upgrading a building would get, so they made practical systems part of it, such as the Action groups. Seriously, action groups are there because the main "stage" system is flawed, it wouldn't even be needed in the game if they would fix the damn stage system instead of doing a similar duplicate system. But now they lock it, so there's a multitude of things you simply cannot do during "stages" unless you commit to grinding and paying that 1M$.
It seems to me that it would be more logical to use planes and drones/rovers on Kerbin, then getting basic rocketry to send drones out there. After a few missions of that, you could then send Kerbins out there and all the rest.
But as of right now, the research tree is all wrong. If you want to make drones/rovers or a plane with something more than the single basic jet engine, you have to, not only get more than 700 research points but also to pay 1M$+ in upgrades.
Also, i'm not sure if this one is a byproduct of other problems i've encountered but I find that research, in general (if you're not using R&D outsourcing) is harder and harder to get as time pass by but the researches cost more and more as you climb the ladder, giving you a dreadful feeling when you just spent an hour doing a mission for 40 science when you need 300 to get the research that you need to research the research that you actually want.
Btw, wrote this review because my game crashed while I was on the runway and it killed Jebediah, wasted my money and saved the game. So now I have to start that 20 hour grind all over again... and fiddling with the career settings to get more funds and more research makes me feel empty inside, makes me feel like a dirty no-good cheater. And since i'm OCDing hard on having a dead kerbin, Jebediah of all kerbins, I just HAVE to start a new game. This game is such a love-hate thing for me, it's starting to feel like XCOM all over again.

An amazing game at first.  Having logged over 3,000 hours on 5, and played all of the others since Civ 1 I consider myself a fan of the series.  This game has so much potential but falls flat on it's face as of right now.  If you thought the AI was bad in Civ 5 (improved somewhat over time), well welcome to the Civ 6 horror show.   The AI is clueless on how to play its own game.  The barbarians will actually give you more trouble.  The AI can't wage war, and can't capture your cities even on the hardest difficulty levels.  In a YouTube video directly from the Dev's they said in every single (out of many) AI vs AI matches no one ever wins by domination.  No kidding.  Diplomacy is horrendous.  Nearly impossible to get the AI to like you, and if it happens your lucky and it's most likely short lived.  They almost always hate you regardless of the victory type you go for.  So they created this wonderful complex game that's so much fun initially, but then you find out there's zero challenge because AI can't make any sense of the new features.  It could barely figure out 1upt (1 unit per tile) in Civ5 although got a little better, but in Civ6 forget about it, DOA.  I think I knew the minute I upgraded my Battleships into the Missle Cruisers that look like tugboats that they screwed up.  They should focus all their efforts on improving the AI and reworking diplomacy so it makes sense.  The Devs have fixed a huge amount of bugs etc, but nothing doing so far on the AI.  Same team from Civ5 so I think any AI improvements will be marginal but I really really hope I'm wrong.  And ditch the tugboat, we want an actual Missle Cruiser.  Thanks.
Update:  Yeah, well after playing as many hours as I've played I can't very well not recommend the game as I originally did.  Anyways it is a lot of fun but it's still not without it's problems.  The modding community has done a tremendous job helping with some of the issues and keeping me interested.  The AI is still dumb....

Kerbal Space Program, giving you the power to be your own NASA
Graphics - 8/10 - the graphics engine/ physics engine in Kerbal Space Program is not the best, to be brutally honest (EDITED- The game has received several updates and patches, improving the aesthetic quality of KSP). The textures of terrain is pretty bad - NOW BETTER :D (at least on Kerbin, all the other planets and moons are slightly better on surface textures). The quality that has been put into the spaceplane and rocket parts really makes you feel as though you are working your way through history, working your way up from nothing to enrmous and actually quite beautiful rocket and spaceplane designs. The physics themselves, are quite realistic it can be scary, one wrong move on a perfect launch/ takeoff can tear your vehicle to shreds or plant it into the ground with an almighty explosion and some dead Kerbals.
The physics engine does struggle though (EDIT- since posting this review KSP has moved the game over to Unity engine, providing much better FPS along with graphical improvements), once you start building bigger rockets (in order to go further[obviously]), as soon as you start sending rockets with 300+ (NOW 500-600+) parts you will really see some lag in the performance of the game until you eventually hit the stage button and drop your excess weight.
Gameplay/ Replayability - 9.5/10 - The gameplay... where do I start? Well you have just started a new career. You have accepted your first contracts and built your first launch vehicle. You launch, run out of fuel, and return to Kerbin by parachute. You get your 20 or so science points and unlock the next tiers in the R&D building. You find out you can now build something that can almost make an orbital insertion, taking you higher and further, giving you more science points and $$ for completing contracts. The first few science levels (up until you start spending 90 Science per tech) make the game slightly more difficult than you would expect, mainly due to lack of better parts. However. Once you get to the point where you have started unlocking 90 point techs you have likely set foot or rocket on the Mun by now, or at least Minmus. Once you have done that, and you have gotten your science points/ data back to kerbin, you start to realise the full potential of your space program. you could explore every planet and moon, or you could simply focus on just the Kerbin planet and its 2 Moons, you could flyby extremely close to the sun, there are so many possibilities and opportunities for you to take advantage of that it's often difficult to choose what to do. Find a planet you like and want to visit, and make it happen, because you cant beat the feeling when you finally make contact on the surface of the 'unreachable' after all that you have worked for you are there. Kerbal Space Program is a game, but the sense of achievement and victory just my meeting one of your in game goals, it is unbeatable.
PRICE - 7.5/10 - KSP is unfortunately a very good game but with a very high price tag, I have my 160+ hours on record playing only about 5 hours a week. KSP does offer alot of game, but it feels like you really have to struggle sometimes to make it feel like its worth the full price of US$40.... If and when this is on special, if you are somewhat interested don't hesitate, buying KSP is a fantastic learning experience, and it really is a lot of fun when you have put the time into it.
(EDITED- Since writing this review I withdraw my statement regarding the price tag. Now with 260+ hours, and with the latest update brought in, I can easily see myself hitting the 300 hour mark with no difficulty)
Total Score - 8.5/10 - I recommend this game to anybody who is interested in space exploration, engineering, aircraft engineering, simulation games and tycoon/ business management games. Kerbal Space Program may have its few downsides, but all in all they are just part of what really makes KSP so much fun to play, and also one of the reasons it feels so good to finally do what you want to do with the available technology. Fantastic game, decent graphics, good physics and hundreds of hours of gameplay with thousands of different rockets and planes that you can build, test and crash to your hearts content.

The first Season of The Walking Dead was one of the best gaming experiences i ever had, and if you did not shed at least a tear during some of the many heartfelt moments, you have no soul. I was eagerly awaiting Season 2.
After the first episode, i was taken a little aback. There was a lot of new information to take in, and after playing Lee for so long, only watching out for Clem, the transition to actually playing Clem was not easy. But by the end of episode 1 i was firmly entrenched into her mind, determined to put the lessons Lee had taught me to good use.
Heartbreak, tough decisions, close calls. Those are the trademark of The Walking Dead and they are in full force here throughout both episodes. Kicks to the gut are plenty, and this Season may be even more bleak than the first one. But they are not without a happy surprise or two. One reunion in episode two in particular had me very surprised and happy at the same time.
Episode 1 was a little weak compared to most others, but episode two kicked the story into high gear and may be the second best yet in the franchise. Hopefully they can get this going, and i simply can not wait to play the rest...
Apart from the story (and that is what we really are here for anyway), i have to say that the interface has been sleeked down a little (easier? not sure, i have not been able to hot key the responses yet, since they are not 1-4 anymore but just four boxes side by side). There is a little less interaction and exploration than in the first Season, which MAY make you feel railroaded. But that should not be a problem really, since the story is very good. Ultimately it is more an interactive novel than an adventure game anyway. The quicktime events are a little more variable (you get to duck and weave as you evade Walkers) You can die, but then just try again... All in all it seems that the UI was just optimized, but it is not really better or worse than before.
(will update after each no episode, probably).
So far, this is 4 and a half out of 5. Fans should get it, and everybody else NEEDS to play Season 1 first and if they like that, they should get this too!

For me, this game is just a straight up steaming pile from beginning to end. I pre-ordered it (big mistake) and played it right as I got it. I am very old in gamer terms and have played each Civ as they came out, starting with 1 on my Amiga 500 in the early 90s. The thing all these game gave me was a sense of wonder and immersion into (fake) history. I still remember my mind being blown when Civ 2 came out with those gorgeous wonder movies (at the time).
This one left me cold right from the get-go. So much to hate:
* Fugly, uninspired and rushed/cheap looking opening credits with beyond horrible font
* Intro movie and music is fine - I'll give them that
* Menu is just a huge step back in terms of appearance
* Whose idea was it to hire Sean Bean as narrator? I love GoT, but I don't feel him reading these quotes
* Graphics - while technically nice, the art direction just blows for me. Maybe it appeals to mobile addicted Millenials. IDK, but I feel like I'm tuned into Nickelodeon
* What's up with this new unit movement system? What was the actual point of this?
* Why did you have to change all the key bindings AND remove some of the most crucial ones altogether? Now I have to click everything. Absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and just tells me the developers were clueless about Civ gameplay or just have a perverted sense of humor. "OK, unit needs my attention" (hits "C", random menu pops up) "Oh, I need to click for the next unit now? Great. WHY DON'T YOU JUST CYCLE TO THE NEXT UNIT FOR ME, THEN?"
* Why is it that the mouse cursor seems broken half the time when moving a unit or aiming for a ranged attack
* What's up with the spam of fricken missionaries? Can't go anywhere for all the holy men everywhere
* Leader animations, technically great but not my cup of tea to have these cartoon figures
* Let's talk about the AI. What a joke. This is sort of the lifeblood of the game for someone like me who doesn't play the game online and likes to putter around with a game in peace and quiet. This is just ridiculous. Nothing, nothing, nothing then all of a sudden war. Whoa, they're really rolling in with their forces here. Crap! Well, then we take 40 turns of them standing around my city while I bombard each of them to death in orderly fashion. No attempt to scale the walls, no pillaging no nothing. When their army is sufficiently weakened, they sue for peace and give me stuff. Then everyone else in the game seems to thing I'm the worst thing since Yersina Pestis and that remains so until the end credits.
* Speaking of end credits, I've lost games where I had no idea what happened (I think dominant religion). I've won games with such underwhelming pay off that just turns you off playing.
Firaxis, you have delivered what can only be described as a POS and from reading the reviews of the other gamers, it seems your only actual 'game' now is to milk them for DLC money. You clearly have no professional pride or artistic merit anymore and as such, I can guarantee you 26 years will be all I was prepared to give you. It's ok - the kids are all grown and have left the house, but just know it's not me. It's you.

Rubbish game that doesn't meet expectations. It takes forever to get anything done and quickly becomes repetitive. AI factions behave like headless chickens and it is nearly impossible to please any of them, resulting in all your allies turning on you towards the midgame. To rub additional salt in the wounds, the game features some useless cinematic diplomacy screen, where these factions regularly interrupt your gameplay to yell some insults at you. You have to click this screen away not once, but twice, every time this happens. Usually within a few turns of proclaiming how much they hate you, they'll demand that you give them free goodies, again through this highly annoying diplomacy interface. No matter how much stuff you give them, they'll continue to hate you, make war with you and insult you.
If this was the only bad thing it'd be somewhat acceptable, but the rest isn't much better. Buildings can take dozens of turns to construct, making it highly annoying to build up additional cities from scratch. Construction times are mainly determined by the production in the city, which is modified by the terrain of the tiles around the city. You'll need builders to transform this terrain into something more useful, but once again it takes forever to recruit a builder and to add insult to injury, the builders expire after several uses, so a lot of clunky micromangement is needed and the game pace slows to a crawl.
In undiscovered tiles Barbarians may spawn, but these either do nothing useful or are a complete bane to your existence in the early game. As mentioned before, everything takes a zillion turns to do, so if you're in the middle of constructing a building and a Barbarian spawns, it can take a dozen turns before you finally get a military unit to deal with the threat, because military recruitment and building construction both use the same production points. Highly annoying and stupid.
AI isn't just annoying in diplomacy, but also a complete pushover as they do not play the terrain modification game well, so they quickly fall behind in the technology race. It is also terrible managing its armies and having some long-ranged units typically defeats most AI armies without taking any losses as they're too stupid to close the gap or position their own long-ranged stuff in a place where it can actually hit anything.
I almost forgot the graphics. They are atrocious and look like some mobile freemium garbage game. Ah, maybe that's there they got their ideas for their DLC policy from.
