Kerbal Space Program, giving you the power to be your own NASA
Graphics - 8/10 - the graphics engine/ physics engine in Kerbal Space Program is not the best, to be brutally honest (EDITED- The game has received several updates and patches, improving the aesthetic quality of KSP). The textures of terrain is pretty bad - NOW BETTER :D (at least on Kerbin, all the other planets and moons are slightly better on surface textures). The quality that has been put into the spaceplane and rocket parts really makes you feel as though you are working your way through history, working your way up from nothing to enrmous and actually quite beautiful rocket and spaceplane designs. The physics themselves, are quite realistic it can be scary, one wrong move on a perfect launch/ takeoff can tear your vehicle to shreds or plant it into the ground with an almighty explosion and some dead Kerbals.
The physics engine does struggle though (EDIT- since posting this review KSP has moved the game over to Unity engine, providing much better FPS along with graphical improvements), once you start building bigger rockets (in order to go further[obviously]), as soon as you start sending rockets with 300+ (NOW 500-600+) parts you will really see some lag in the performance of the game until you eventually hit the stage button and drop your excess weight.
Gameplay/ Replayability - 9.5/10 - The gameplay... where do I start? Well you have just started a new career. You have accepted your first contracts and built your first launch vehicle. You launch, run out of fuel, and return to Kerbin by parachute. You get your 20 or so science points and unlock the next tiers in the R&D building. You find out you can now build something that can almost make an orbital insertion, taking you higher and further, giving you more science points and $$ for completing contracts. The first few science levels (up until you start spending 90 Science per tech) make the game slightly more difficult than you would expect, mainly due to lack of better parts. However. Once you get to the point where you have started unlocking 90 point techs you have likely set foot or rocket on the Mun by now, or at least Minmus. Once you have done that, and you have gotten your science points/ data back to kerbin, you start to realise the full potential of your space program. you could explore every planet and moon, or you could simply focus on just the Kerbin planet and its 2 Moons, you could flyby extremely close to the sun, there are so many possibilities and opportunities for you to take advantage of that it's often difficult to choose what to do. Find a planet you like and want to visit, and make it happen, because you cant beat the feeling when you finally make contact on the surface of the 'unreachable' after all that you have worked for you are there. Kerbal Space Program is a game, but the sense of achievement and victory just my meeting one of your in game goals, it is unbeatable.
PRICE - 7.5/10 - KSP is unfortunately a very good game but with a very high price tag, I have my 160+ hours on record playing only about 5 hours a week. This is Civilization game. 25 years old concept that still works. "One more turn" is still here. This is, basically, improved CIV 5. But it is far from perfect.
Overall , there is a lot to learn and to play with. Districts, civics, governments, new leaders, units. It is all refined. At the same time, there are a lot of weird design decisions. Terrain movement cost ( in\out rough terrain cost) is strange.Where is railroads? Units upgrade paths are confusing. Horsemen upgrading to cavalry ( classic era to renaisans)? Chariot to knight ? Knight to Tank ? Promotion for units is weird too. Main melee units 2nd tier promotions are all about amphibious warfare. What if i play on pangea ? I don't even talk about how , still, useless AI at naval warfare.
Diplomacy is better than civ5's, but it has a lot of weird concepts. Why AI is always trying to offer unfair deals? Warmongering is strange too. Now you have casus beli mechanic. It's great. But why warmonger penalty is so high in all ages ? Warmongering in dark ages , really ? If you will want to steal worker from city state , think twice. Because this will cause everyone hate you.
AI is somewhere at the same level as in CIV5, maybe a little bit worse. AI declaring joint war against you and you don't see a single enemy unit at your borders ? Naah, it's ok. Strange target prioritizing during warfare. AI doesn't like to upgrade units. Who will like it,if your archer to crossbowman upgrade costs 300 ?
Visuals. I was really concerned about visuals from the start. Mainly , about units and leaders. In the end i have completely different opinion. Visuals are cartoonish , but you can used to it. Units are very dynamic and they serve their purpose. No complains. Leaders are awesome. They have very nice animations that makes them alive. It's the best leaders representation in civ series. Terrain is terrible. It looks blurry , low detailed. Add to it all of terrain props and building and you will have rainbow screen. This makes dense areas unreadable.
I hope Firaxis will follow the path of CIV 5 and will release big add-ons that will fix all the weird stuff that is in the game. Still, it is most feature packed and complete vanilla CIV to date.

Is Episode 1 worth downloading? Absolutely. Are episodes 2-5 worth downloading? If you enjoyed Episode 1, then the following episodes are a must have.
Life is Strange hones down on the different personalities and motives of its characters to drive the story. The game has honed down on creating drama between classmates, friends, family, and 'adults'. We see our protagonist juggle between responsibility and personal safety, and at the same time supporting characters and antagonists react greatly to the decisions made by the player.
Max's time traveling ability acts to lead to interesting character development and challenge players' thinking. Us players end up second guessing ourselves in our decisions not because of a flaw in the game's story, rather an urge for players to consider alternative story lines to be 'right'.
Life is Strange's graphics are very good, but not perfect. Don't get me wrong; it is clear that the game designers were meticulous with their cutscenes, providing stunning scenes for players to really absorb the atmosphere and wonder that the characters are feeling. With photogoraphy being a prominent aspect of all five episodes, the game really "captures the moment" in their cutscenes. Unlike many other games, the cutscenes in Life is Strange are worth paying attention to.
I don't have much to say about the sound besides "it's good". The music pairs very well with the visuals to immerse players into the story.

Life is Strange is, by far, the most engaging story I have ever encountered in any game. The actual storytelling is something I don't think we will see surpassed for a long time and your choices actually do seem to matter. I've played a lot of interactive story games and often you wonder whether your choices actually had any impact. Here - they do. Really!
Furthermore, the choices you're presented with are often genuine moral tests. It's often not a case of black and white as much as it is two (or more) murky shades of grey. Even the ability to rewind time, and experience different options, often won't make you feel any better about your decisions. I think this game actually reveals to you a lot about yourself and it'll make you happy, confused, scared, anxious, and definitely oh so sad.
I'm glad nobody watched me play it because I teared up more than I'd like to admit.
I don't think I can link to someone else's review, but I thought that RedviperUK put it well:
"This game is a moral self-torture simulator... Steps for successfully experiencing LiS:
1. Buy it.
2. Begin to play it.
3. Make poor choices.
4. Alter poor choices.
5. Realise new choices are worse.
6. Eventually stumble to the end feeling like you've almost held it together.
7. Make monumentally poor choice.
8. Open the bottle of Jack Daniels you keep by your desk.
9. Begin drunken reflection on reality.
10. Remember why you failed Philosophy.
11. Drink some more.
12. Ponder if this game has set an impossible bar for videogame storytelling.
13. Conclude it has.
14. Decide to write negative review of game because it made you feel sad.
15. Change it to positive BECAUSE it managed to make you feel sad.
16. Begin the slightly hollow search for something that can offer a similar experience."
For the record I don't think that anything else on the market right now actually can offer you a similar experience and I would recommend this to virtually anyone.

Rubbish game that doesn't meet expectations. It takes forever to get anything done and quickly becomes repetitive. AI factions behave like headless chickens and it is nearly impossible to please any of them, resulting in all your allies turning on you towards the midgame. To rub additional salt in the wounds, the game features some useless cinematic diplomacy screen, where these factions regularly interrupt your gameplay to yell some insults at you. You have to click this screen away not once, but twice, every time this happens. Usually within a few turns of proclaiming how much they hate you, they'll demand that you give them free goodies, again through this highly annoying diplomacy interface. No matter how much stuff you give them, they'll continue to hate you, make war with you and insult you.
If this was the only bad thing it'd be somewhat acceptable, but the rest isn't much better. Buildings can take dozens of turns to construct, making it highly annoying to build up additional cities from scratch. Construction times are mainly determined by the production in the city, which is modified by the terrain of the tiles around the city. You'll need builders to transform this terrain into something more useful, but once again it takes forever to recruit a builder and to add insult to injury, the builders expire after several uses, so a lot of clunky micromangement is needed and the game pace slows to a crawl.
In undiscovered tiles Barbarians may spawn, but these either do nothing useful or are a complete bane to your existence in the early game. As mentioned before, everything takes a zillion turns to do, so if you're in the middle of constructing a building and a Barbarian spawns, it can take a dozen turns before you finally get a military unit to deal with the threat, because military recruitment and building construction both use the same production points. Highly annoying and stupid.
AI isn't just annoying in diplomacy, but also a complete pushover as they do not play the terrain modification game well, so they quickly fall behind in the technology race. It is also terrible managing its armies and having some long-ranged units typically defeats most AI armies without taking any losses as they're too stupid to close the gap or position their own long-ranged stuff in a place where it can actually hit anything.
I almost forgot the graphics. They are atrocious and look like some mobile freemium garbage game. Ah, maybe that's there they got their ideas for their DLC policy from.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This is Civilization game. 25 years old concept that still works. "One more turn" is still here. This is, basically, improved CIV 5. But it is far from perfect.
Overall , there is a lot to learn and to play with. Districts, civics, governments, new leaders, units. It is all refined. At the same time, there are a lot of weird design decisions. Terrain movement cost ( in\out rough terrain cost) is strange.Where is railroads? Units upgrade paths are confusing. Horsemen upgrading to cavalry ( classic era to renaisans)? Chariot to knight ? Knight to Tank ? Promotion for units is weird too. Main melee units 2nd tier promotions are all about amphibious warfare. What if i play on pangea ? I don't even talk about how , still, useless AI at naval warfare.
Diplomacy is better than civ5's, but it has a lot of weird concepts. Why AI is always trying to offer unfair deals? Warmongering is strange too. Now you have casus beli mechanic. It's great. But why warmonger penalty is so high in all ages ? Warmongering in dark ages , really ? If you will want to steal worker from city state , think twice. Because this will cause everyone hate you.
AI is somewhere at the same level as in CIV5, maybe a little bit worse. AI declaring joint war against you and you don't see a single enemy unit at your borders ? Naah, it's ok. Strange target prioritizing during warfare. AI doesn't like to upgrade units. Who will like it,if your archer to crossbowman upgrade costs 300 ?
Visuals. I was really concerned about visuals from the start. Mainly , about units and leaders. In the end i have completely different opinion. Visuals are cartoonish , but you can used to it. Units are very dynamic and they serve their purpose. No complains. Leaders are awesome. They have very nice animations that makes them alive. It's the best leaders representation in civ series. Terrain is terrible. It looks blurry , low detailed. Add to it all of terrain props and building and you will have rainbow screen. This makes dense areas unreadable.
I hope Firaxis will follow the path of CIV 5 and will release big add-ons that will fix all the weird stuff that is in the game. Still, it is most feature packed and complete vanilla CIV to date.

One of the things that I was most excited about was the fact that the decisions I made during Season 1 would carry over and have an impact in Season 2. And indeed, the game found my save files and imported them properly, but I didn't notice anything during the first episode that had anything to do with what I had done during Season 1.
Being that Clementine is a lot smaller than Lee, the combat played out much differently. Instead of struggling with the zombies and trying to bash their heads in, Clementine usually runs and dodges away from whatever is chasing her. There were also far fewer puzzles, and those that were present were fairly straightforward. Honestly most of the episode was a continuous push forward, with few hub areas to simply explore and talk to people.
Overall I would call this episode a setup episode. Telling you what it is setting up would be a spoiler, but it might be in your best interest to wait and find out how good the next episode is before deciding whether or not to buy the whole season.
I wasn't really sure what to expect from the second episode because the first episode didn't have much going on in it. I didn't know enough about the group of people I met to make predictions about what was going to happen. Luckily the second episode picks things up; well, it's not lucky for the characters in the game, but you know what I mean.
The most important thing that happens in this episode is the people in your new group get fleshed out more in a big way.
would fail completely if it didn't have strong characters that you care about. I found myself drawn to the people in the group to varying degrees, much as I would in real life.
The biggest challenge Telltale faces in this game is finding ways to give the player agency in ways that make sense for an 11 year old girl. For the most part I think they succeeded, though there were a few exceptions; for example, who would leave Clementine alone to figure out how to turn off a wind turbine?
Unfortunately I cannot go into the best things about this episode without spoiling everything, but trust me:
is officially now worth getting. There were a lot of surprises, which I was not expecting. I thought I was prepared for anything that Telltale could throw at me, but I was very wrong.
Much like the first episode, they end with a huge cliffhanger. If you hate dealing with those, you might want to wait until the third episode comes out, but that will probably end on a cliffhanger as well. I'm enjoying playing it one episode at a time, but I wish I had somebody I could discuss things with.
This episode was structured very differently from the other episodes we've seen so far from
. It almost felt like the story it told could stand on its own, with some fleshing out of course. In particular the ending had so much closure I'm not sure where they are going to take the series next, other than the obvious problem of continuing to survive in a zombie apocalypse.
My favorite thing about this episode was how Clementine really came into her own. In previous episodes the writers came up with ways for her to influence events without being the main actor. Here she does almost everything that is needed for the group's plans to work. Of course one of the characters brings up how crazy this is, so the writers were not unaware of the stretch they were taking here. I hope this opens up the door for Clementine to do even more cool stuff.
I believe that I have now seen all of the characters from the 400 Days DLC, though most of them showed up briefly and had very few lines. I am looking forward to seeing them more in future episodes. If Telltale doesn't use them more I am going to be pretty disappointed.
This episode didn't let up on The Walking Dead's tendency to be emotionally taxing. I kept alternating between cheering characters on and cursing at the screen when things went wrong. And that's just the way I like it.
brings us back to the more familiar Telltale formula, with action sequences interspersed with characters talking while walking and even a hub area where you can take a break and look around a Civil War memorial.
I mentioned in the last episode that Clementine carried the group in a way that is not normal for an 11 year old girl. This episode did feature Clementine contributing heavily, but not in ways that felt forced by the writers. The flow and pace of the episode felt much more natural, with almost no moments that pulled me out of the game.
There were even a few genuinely humorous moments, mostly provided by my new favorite character, Mike. I wish he had gotten a chance to shine earlier, and I certainly hope that they do not kill him off. Small chance of that.
I was hoping that I would be able to make it through a season finale of
without making any decisions I immediately regretted or crying. I failed. It was a fool's hope anyway.
Much like the finale of season one, there were very few times where they give the player the opportunity to take a break and look around. It was mostly a constant push towards the end of the episode. They did give the characters a break at one point, which also let me become more attached to them. This was no doubt part of their grand plan to break my heart, but those are not things that you realize while playing.
There was one situation that I saw coming from a mile away because the writers focused on it so much for the last couple of episodes. On the other hand there was another closely related situation that I did not see coming at all.
As a whole I enjoyed the second season of Telltale's The Walking Dead, though not as much as the first season. I would say that the main factor was the faster turnover of characters. I did not get enough time to get attached to most of the characters before they died or were otherwise removed from the group. I cannot remember many of their names, or how they died. In contrast I remember almost all of the characters from season one.
I am not sure if Telltale will make a third season, and frankly I am not sure how wise it would be for them to try. It is easy for the player to become jaded to the loss they are constantly subjected to in this series. The second season also had much less of a cultural impact; out of my Steam friends, the number of people who have played the second season is less than half that of the first. I would certainly play a third if they made it though.

Is Episode 1 worth downloading? Absolutely. Are episodes 2-5 worth downloading? If you enjoyed Episode 1, then the following episodes are a must have.
Life is Strange hones down on the different personalities and motives of its characters to drive the story. The game has honed down on creating drama between classmates, friends, family, and 'adults'. We see our protagonist juggle between responsibility and personal safety, and at the same time supporting characters and antagonists react greatly to the decisions made by the player.
Max's time traveling ability acts to lead to interesting character development and challenge players' thinking. Us players end up second guessing ourselves in our decisions not because of a flaw in the game's story, rather an urge for players to consider alternative story lines to be 'right'.
Life is Strange's graphics are very good, but not perfect. Don't get me wrong; it is clear that the game designers were meticulous with their cutscenes, providing stunning scenes for players to really absorb the atmosphere and wonder that the characters are feeling. With photogoraphy being a prominent aspect of all five episodes, the game really "captures the moment" in their cutscenes. Unlike many other games, the cutscenes in Life is Strange are worth paying attention to.
I don't have much to say about the sound besides "it's good". The music pairs very well with the visuals to immerse players into the story.

Life is Strange is, by far, the most engaging story I have ever encountered in any game. The actual storytelling is something I don't think we will see surpassed for a long time and your choices actually do seem to matter. I've played a lot of interactive story games and often you wonder whether your choices actually had any impact. Here - they do. Really!
Furthermore, the choices you're presented with are often genuine moral tests. It's often not a case of black and white as much as it is two (or more) murky shades of grey. Even the ability to rewind time, and experience different options, often won't make you feel any better about your decisions. I think this game actually reveals to you a lot about yourself and it'll make you happy, confused, scared, anxious, and definitely oh so sad.
I'm glad nobody watched me play it because I teared up more than I'd like to admit.
I don't think I can link to someone else's review, but I thought that RedviperUK put it well:
"This game is a moral self-torture simulator... Steps for successfully experiencing LiS:
1. Buy it.
2. Begin to play it.
3. Make poor choices.
4. Alter poor choices.
5. Realise new choices are worse.
6. Eventually stumble to the end feeling like you've almost held it together.
7. Make monumentally poor choice.
8. Open the bottle of Jack Daniels you keep by your desk.
9. Begin drunken reflection on reality.
10. Remember why you failed Philosophy.
11. Drink some more.
12. Ponder if this game has set an impossible bar for videogame storytelling.
13. Conclude it has.
14. Decide to write negative review of game because it made you feel sad.
15. Change it to positive BECAUSE it managed to make you feel sad.
16. Begin the slightly hollow search for something that can offer a similar experience."
For the record I don't think that anything else on the market right now actually can offer you a similar experience and I would recommend this to virtually anyone.

I can't recommend this game over Civilization V.
In 6, we see some improvements to gameplay, like city districts.  City districts are amazing.  We see some really great ideas like with highly customizeable government policies.
But inevitably I compare this game with Civ V, and I feel that VI is needlessly complicated.  Civ VI seems to give you more choices to make, more mechanics to micromanage... but the reward for your effort feels very low.  In V, you pay attention to the little details, and it helps you out immensely, but in VI you pay attention to the little details, and it might help you out some.
A lot of this bland-ening of difference in choices seems to be to make the game more evenly matched across all of the civilizations.  Unfortunately it removes that rewarding feeling you get as a player that you used to get in V, when you settled near the right resources as
, or got that great unit trade with an almost-dead Japanese unit.
Being strategic in V takes some skill feels rewarding.  Being strategic in VI takes more skill and feels less rewarding.
And don't even get me started on the cartoony direction it's going...

Civilization is always a facinating journey. Playing the single player is what most people enjoy. Being able to dominate a once thought allie or throwing some religion on them. The game is highly replayable, if turn based if your kind of thing, but eventually it'll get old and you'll long for something new to come (within 6 months).
Civilization games have always intrigued me when it comes to turn based games but Civ 6 is special in it's own way. In most ways it feels like an upgrade from Civ5 but in some, I still feel as if I'm playing that old Civ5 game. Most games now-a-days feel as if they just repackage the same idea but changed the skins, I.E. Call of Duty, Battlefield, Gears of War, ETC. Which is exactly what I feel when playing this game. Firing it up, I felt amazed at the opening video, yet the start felt just so similiar. I get you obviously must start your city and all but maybe just updating Civ5 would have sufficed.
I'll keep playing Civ6 cause obviously I spent almost 70 hours on it but maybe next time I'll rethink before dishing out $60 on a brand new game like I've told myself in the past after being let down by the developers of some highly anticipated games (No Mans Sky).
I recommend Civ6 if you're new to Civilization but if you're still playing Civ5 just stick with it and save that cash for possibly another let down or something so amazing you'll thank me.

The Walking Dead Season 2 is ofcourse a must-play after the emotional finale of season 1.
However, I must admit I was a bit worried when hearing you would play "as" Clementine in season 2. How interesting could a game be in which you would play a child, would you still be able to influence situations like in season 1 or would you just be given some crayons and be told to "play over there"?
After playing the first 2 episodes all my worries were gone regarding this: Clementine is a great protagonist, mature beyond her years and easisy as relatable as Lee. And Telltale once again holds no punches and the stuff Clem has to deal with is in many ways even worse than what Lee got on his plate in season 1. It's actually pretty sad and depressing how much this girl has to suffer.
About the game itself: the episodes are even shorter than those of season 1 and there is even less "gameplay" than in the first season (The Walking Dead is now basically has become an interactive movie). This would not be a problem if the story itself would've been as thight as that of season 1: however, while there are amazing scenes, there are also quite some illogical plot twists that seem to have no other function than to shock. It's 1,5 years after the apocalypse: you would've expected that after all that time some people had stepped over their ego's to actually work together once in a while, but no, it's one childish conflict after another...
Also, the rate with which new characters are introduced and killed off is so high that, in combination with very short episodes, the player barely has time to get acquainted to some, thus lessening the emotional impact of the hard choices you have to make.
Still, even with these story issues, season 2 still was pretty good and like I stated earlier, a must play for fans of the first season. For me all that remains is waiting for the inevitable season 3, all the while hoping Telltale will clean up their act, focus their story some more and once again reach the greatness of season 1.

TLDR: This game has the potential to be absolutely amazing, but its terribly broken diplomacy and AI leaves me, and many other fans of the series, dissapointed.
Civ 5 was one of my favorite games of all time. I will admit, when it first came out, it was not a very good game, and had many problems. Through the various DLCs, however, Civ 5 evolved to be a legendary game. One can only hope that the DLCs will make Civ 6 what Civ 5 was, but this review is focusing on what Civ 6 is in its current state.
Let's talk about the pros of the game first. The developers definitely deserve a lot of credit, and this game has alot of amazing aspects that make it amazing:
1: Graphics: This topic is completely up to personal preference. Alot of people complain that this game looks like a free to play mobile game for 10 year olds, but I dissagree. I really like the graphic style, and it is a really bold move by the developers. Nonetheless, it looks great and it really adds to the aesthetic of the game.
2: Districts/City Building: The mechanics of building your own civ, and everything to do with your own civ in this game is great. I'd say its better than Civ 5 even. The district concept is a great addition to the game, forcing you to use a lot more strategy in where you place farms and buildings, along with dictating where you settle. The housing and new amenity system (a replacement for civ 5's happiness) is absolutely great, limiting your population growth in a way that doesn't just♥♥♥♥♥♥you off (like happiness did to me in civ 5).
3: Military/combat: The new combat system is interesting, and while I think it was equal to civ 5's, some people think it is vastly superior. Instead of focusing your military on pure size and strength, there is a lot more strategy and thought that goes into building your military. Units take longer to build and cost more to buy (for the most part), so you have to be thoughful of what you are builidng/spending your money on. The corp and army system is interesting, even though I find it useless, but it still adds to the game. But the most interesting aspect to military are the new support units. These units can stack with your other units, and provide massive boosts to your battalions in battle. They include battering rams, which make your units do more damage to city walls, siege towers, which work similarly to batting rams (allowing you to ignore a city's walls), Medics, which heal adjacent units, etc. Civ 6 sacrifices the aspect of having a large military, and replaces that with a more specalized military. I do think that there arent enough units in the game (Knights upgrade directly into Tanks, with no heavy cavalry in between), but I definitely think future DLC's will add more Units into the game.
Okay. Now that I said everything good at the game, its time to talk about diplomacy.
Diplomacy is completely broken. When I say diplomacy, i just mean AI and their interactions with you (and how they play).
First off, let's start off with how the AI plays. The AI doesn't know how to play. That's pretty much it. On prince difficulty, where neither the player or the AI gains bonuses, the AI falls behind almost immediately, and by the end of the game, you feel like you are playing on Chieftan. The first game I played of Civ 6 I won a science victory on turn 295 (I had 3 capitals by turn 40 because the AI didnt know how to protect their cities early on, so I had monsterous science and production), Anyways, the second place AI was still in the Renaissance era. When I was on mars. I was making 500+ science per turn, they were making 40. But this can be fixed quite easily, just play on a higher difficulty. What can't be fixed, is diplomacy:
Leader Agendas:
This is one of my least favorite things about Civ 6 in general. Leader Agendas are how the AI thinks of other players. I'll give an example: Gorgo, of the Greeks, has a leader agenda where she dislikes Civilizations that have never been to war. However, if you declare war on someone, she calls you a warmongerer. She either denounces you for not decaring war on people, or denounces you and calls you a warmongerer. k. Another example is Brazil. They dislike civilizations who recruit great people. They will literally denounce you (tell the entire world that you can't be trusted) if you recruit too many great people. Leader Agendas makes it so that you can't be friendly with the AI, no matter how hard you try, there are always conflicting Leader Agendas, or ones that are impossible (Norway will hate you if you don't have a navy, even if you are completely land-locked). Not only that, but Leader Agendas should dissipate upon entering later eras. Imagine if today, Japan hated America because our people aren't faithful enough. They wouldn't trade with us, and would tell the entire world that we can't be trusted, because we don't have enough faith in religion.
Warmongering:
In Civ 5, I thought the AI's reaction to war was extreme. I was wrong. In Civ 6, one war and the AI hates you for the rest of the game. Literally. Even if another player declares war on you, and you take over ONE city, You lose 35 relationship points with the ENTIRE WORLD. In comparison, being an ALLY with a civ increases your relationship points by 16. Taking 1 city from a civ that DECLARED WAR ON YOU makes you lose all diplomatic relations with the entire world. After the AI denounces you constantly, calling you a warmongerer, they will declare war on you themselves. (hypocritical, much?) Not only that, but there are some civs that will NEVER make peace with you, no matter what happens. Even if they lose cities, they will not make peace. It doesn't make sense. Finally, the AI does not realize when it has a disadvantage in war. I have been declared war on by civs that are 4 eras behind me. They attack me with Archers when I have Cavalry and musket men, and their entire military is destroyed in 1 turn.
Glitches:
If the diplomacy isn't bad enough as it is, there are some glitches that make it even worse. Sometimes, the turn you meet a civ, they will declare a formal war on you (to declare a formal war, you must have denounced a civ 5 turns ago...meaning you must have met them for 5 turns). In the first game I played, the turn I met Ghandi he declared war on me, and didnt make peace for 215 turns (the game ended, and he was still at war with me). Also, I have had it happen to me twice where MY LEADER DECLARES WAR ON ME? I was playing as Gorgo, and I see a cutscene where Gorgo declares war on me. (That was when Ghandi declared war on me as well).
Overall:
I dont think this is a bad game, but it gets boring REALLY quick when there is no positive interactions with other AI. If you don't care about diplomacy at all and you only want to conquer the entire world, then pick this game up when it's on sale. Otherwise, if you care about how the other AI interacts with you, I'd wait until this game goes very cheap on sale, or just don't buy it at all.

This game boasts as being a beautifully crafted, convoluted story full of emotion and if you shut your brain off the entire time and stopped having any minor rational thought, then yes this would be emotionally impactful on some level. However, it's one of the most asinine, "trying to be edgy" games I have ever experienced. Truly, it is appaulingly shallow, easy to call right from the start, and its intrinsic moral lesson is lost int he shuffle of "wtf why does this game hate me so much? why does it disrespect my intelligence so much?". The "best friend" character is as endearing as a pike to the eye and I admit I did enjoy the game at more than one time just on the fact I could watch her die several times.. in my mind, my Max was getting petty revenge on Chloe for her constant nagging, berating, and blaming of dear Max. And speaking of Max, I have never been so angry at a main character for being ignorant and obnoxious. Her voice sounds very much like a stereotypical community actor, overplaying it in all the wrong places and trying to do some kind of voice? But it never comes out as anything other than emotionless and awkward. The pacing and writing is laughable and confusing while the dialogue is cringe-worthy. Cinematography is pretty good and if the direction for most of the scenes was "be as hipster as physically possible.. not in a "this is the setting cause it's near Portland" kind of way.. just try and be edgy and hip for real.. but FAIL at it" then they did really well.
And I'm not just hating on it because I "didn't get it" or I'm "not en emotional gamer" or "you've never felt loss". I'm a very emotional gamer. I often feel moved on a deep, soulful level and feel compelled to tell everyone to experience what I did. Dear Esther, A Machine For Pigs, Nier, Undertale, Bastion, etc etc etc it can go on and on. This is not one of those games. When someone can call the entire plot of a game, including the villain and their motivations AND the overarching meaning, within the first half of episode 1? That's really REALLY disappointing.. and for the record.. I called the villain and the motivations within literal minutes of playing (once you hit the real world). That... is... just awful. By the end of Episode 2, it was so glaringly obvious what the entire game was about I almost stopped playing entirely, because it wasn't going to get any smarter if I did... but I continued.. and it degraded as quickly as assumed.
I'm honestly depressed I spent money on this. Like a David Cage game, it relies on visuals, music, the illusion of choice, and the assumption that its audience isn't smart enough to pick up on the scam. Unfortunately, I picked up on it. And if I can save someone else from buying this hack of a game and wasting money, then I've done my job. If you don't like my opinion and you think this was vastly deep... then the makers of this game have been proven right; the audience isn't smart enough to recognize the scam.

In short I really love this game but this style of game isn't for everyone.  If the game sounds interesting I recommend picking up episode 1 for free and then immerse yourself fully into the environment.
This game is effectively a STORY with a game wrapped around it.  While you have choice I believe the choice is a "very good illusion of choice" as opposed to a fully dynamic experience where your choices will  cause the game to diverge radically.  However on a first playthrough things feel pretty good so I'm satisfied based on that standard.
You'll like this game if:
-- You like many of the "Telltale Games" like Walking Dead
-- You like point & click games
-- You're more interested in immersing yourself into the environment / talking as opposed to non=stop action
-- You like dialog heavy / reading heavy games
-- You don't mind the "illusion of choise"
-- You only intend to play the game through one time
People that won't like this game:
-- People that need replay value
-- People that prefer SANDBOX games where they do what they want as opposed to playing "on rails"
-- People that don't want to be in an interactive [point and click] story driven game.
Final recommendation:  If you're still interested in the game then pick it up on sale [I did!!] ... You won't regret it.
You will wanna to play it over and over again.

I have put many many hours into the Civ franchise, over 100 on Civ VI alone, and while the game isn't terrible I cannot recommend it.
There's a lot of small changes to get used to, not a big issue, however a lot of important functionality has been lost in the process. One of the biggest peeves I have is the chaining of road building to merchants. No reason to send a merchant to any one of your many cities? Well most likely there will never be a road leading to that city. It's a terrible way to manage roads and serves no purpose except to make the incredibly stupid idea of disposable builders hurt a little bit less.
Two, disposable builders: this is the worst change in the game. You get a few "charges" to construct improvements and then they're gone. Whomever thought this was a good idea needs to skip the planning meetings going forward. It's an awful idea that leaves a player spending loads of turns wasting away making builders. There's no longer any strategy to protecting them, simply churn out a new unit and build your improvements. There's no improvement upgrades as far as I have noticed, so once their wad is blown that's that. It's insipid at best. Also no roads get built by builders, as mentioned previously, it's impossible to connect your cities if you don't waste 20 turns of your trader's time. Considering 20 turns can be in-game equivalent to 200 years you can see how mental of a system this is (seriously 20 turns to establish a road to a city 6 hexes away in the early game is just stupid).
Three, it's boring. The game very quickly becomes dull and lifeless with no real point. You pretty much have to play aggressively which means you pretty much only ever get conquest wins unless you purposefully retard your army and hold back. Not fun. There's no real sense of accomplishment, just this repetitive cycle of tech, war, and building that doesn't really matter. Just build a big army of archers in the first 50 turns and kill everyone, game over. Dull.
I wanted to like this game, maybe they're saving a nice update that will make the game fun for a future $60 expansion pack, either way I'm done with it. This is a sad and unenjoyable chapter in the civ franchise, lacking basic common sense functions like road building and generally taking way too long to get anywhere in the game if you want to play other than Ghengis Khan style. Mid-game is a dull slog up the tech tree to the atomic era where you're still bored, but now have nukes. I appreciate all of the work that went into the game, but can't recommend this game at all. I have no idea why the Civ team seems to think they need to reinvent the wheel with every iteration of the game but this reinvented wheel is mostly square and doesn't roll along very well.

There's a fair amount of criticism of this game regarding its graphics, pacing, and how the UI obfuscates the game's new features like districts and city-planning.
Most of these can be fixed by subsequent patches and expansions, much like Civ V was. However, what concerns me most is the AI.
Or rather, the lack of it. AI is sluggish, incapable of waging war or planning, and too easy to conquer. Yes, it will take time, but only in my early plays did I encounter any difficulty at all. I play on Emperor now and I'm not *that* good at Civ, so something's amiss. Invading civs still send piecemeal armies - basically harrassing you and achieving nothing other than annoyance.
The diplomacy is taking a lot of fire, but there's a lot of potential here. The personalities of the leaders are welcome, and the game does a decent job of showing those priorities. The wonders, districts, and general gameplay is different and innovative enough to make it a good game, just not one I'll play for hundreds of hours until the resolve the AI. Yes, the UI needs work. Yes, some of the nitty-gritty about districts is too hard to find or non-existent.
The bare bones of a great Civ game are here. I love the potential, and I can tolerate the foggy UI, but...
Just fix the AI, Firaxis. I don't care about any of your DLC, and if you want me to buy Civ VII, show me you can give me AI that can put up a fight and not roll over like shamed mongrel.
So I do NOT recommend it, not until they patch the AI and perhaps flesh out the UI and a few other systems. Wait and see how Firaxis fixes their game, or what the modders eventually do with it.

Civilization 6 is a good game, but not if you compare it to Civilization 5, which is just a much better game. Some things that I liked in Civ 5 are worse in civ 6, like statistics, map, A.I, resources and religion.
One thing that might be insignificant to you is the map showing owned water tiles as if they were land tiles. To me that is just a fun killer since I love looking at the map to see the empire I have created. In this system it just looks like a blob instead of an empire.
The A.I in Civilization 6 is pure garbage. In one game I played I had declared war ONCE in the entire game. One time in 354 turns (1932 A.D) and every single A.I denounced me for being a warmonger when I did it on like turn 100, and renewed their warmonger denouncements continualy through the rest of the game, despite me not starting a single war since then. I think this is why the A.I for some reason counts wars declared against you as you being a warmonger, which is just beyond stupid.

Oh man, was I excited for this game. Now, for a new player to Civilization in general, I wasn't too informed on how in-depth this game goes with everything. From the long branches of both the technology and culture trees to the expanding empires you can create or destroy in your world. This game has it all. While, yes it has some issues here and there, I think its pretty good when compared to the older games.
The graphics. I rather like the design they put, while yes very cartoonish, very simplistic and not too much detail. Yes, the more realistic looks of characters would be appropriate for the game, I just think the simplicity in the design makes it better. It also gives it a, for all ages appeal to the game rather than the teen and up rating we had with the very medivial look of Civ 5 and the previous games. While that's my opinion, the design will probably be liked by most and some may hate it based on personality.
The design of the game. Strategy has always been a big plus of mine in games and this fits the bill to the mark. From the begginning to the end, the game depends on what you do, what you did in the past, and what you will do in the future. That being said, you're not alone in this game and certainly does the other civilizations affect your strategy as well. Civilizations that focus on a certain victory goal affect your decisions that will have to decrease that particular civilization from winning the game. The aspect of your actions influenced by the simple actions of others is the best aspect of this strategy game.
The variety. The game gives you plenty of civilizations to try out and see the different ways to play the game. Some civlizations require you to focus on naval researches, units, exploring, and even battling to success. While, other civilizations require you to focus on more land aspects to the game such as spying on nations, expanding borders, and even trading with neighbors. The possibilities are ultimately endless in the amount of ways you could play the game and the more civilizations or updates they do, the more possibilities there will be.
All in all the game is wonderful and I would recommend anyone with a good amount of patience and a good computer to try this out for themselves.

I'm sad that I cannot recommend this game in its current state. It feels like the dev team rushed to include many items into the game but did not take the time to ensure they all mesh together and (very importantly) that the AI is ready to handle them. Virtually everything feels shallow and in many ways a silly representation of what we came to expect from the Civ series. From religious units that block movement of military ones (and the silly religious combat that represents nothing from real life), to the poor implementation of Eurekas that rather than making you form a unique civilization instead it allows you to be in atomic era by 200 AD. The game overall becomes a silly clickfest that ultimately ends with a victory condition you probably wasn't planning on.

Oh man. This game. This is the game that you wish existed when you were in grade school, and you wish you had a computer lab teacher cool enough to buy licenses for it. It is both fun, and wether you want to or not, you will learn a thing or two about flight, space travel, rocket science, physics, and management if you have aspirations of sending eager green astronauts to the black void.
The kerbals are only permitted to show disloyalty in thier facial expressions, and they will do so every time you strap them onto a large solid-fuel booster with no parachutes just to see how far it'll go. Their memories will live on at the space center, or at least until you remove them from the roster because who needs that kind of bummer?
The ever-expanding parts list is fun to peruse, and takes an amount of effort to unlock properly. You will be expected to go to far-off planets and moons in the name of science, wielding thermometers and canisters of goo, and eventually bringing mining equipment and fuel processing devices. There's a good sense of progression as you go along and unlock cooler, and more expensive parts, which let you pull off more and more insane builds; I'm talking like DaVinci's helicopter insane.
There's a lot of trial and error, or more accurately error error error, watch some Scott Manley videos, error error error, visit the wiki, error success! So if you are easily disuaded or get frustrated easily maybe skip this one. But it's a wonderful game to learn on, and you come away with a better understanding of the world than when you started, even if this world is run by small, suicidal green men(and women now too!).

Is Civilization VI a good game? Somewhat. There is a lot to it why I dislike this game.
Things I enjoy that were added in:
Districts, however they are a pain when you have little space to use them. It's also quite annoying that there are very few buildings that can be built in the city center, regardless of the district. Good idea, poorly executed.
(Some) of the Visuals: The day/night cycle is awesome, as well as the new fog of war, which looks like a map. These are what I think were pretty nice about the visuals. However, I do dislike the cartoony feel of the game and leaders.
New civilizations: These are mainly Kongo and Scythia. They are quite interesting how they were added in.
What I dislike
Diplomacy: As said by everyone. It is a complete and utter mess. Civilizations will hate you for everything you do to win. There is no point in even working with them because they'll end up hating you in the end.
War: Warmongering penalties are annoying. I've had scenarios where war was declared upon me, yet when I fight back in retalliation, I gain a major war penalty and all the civs have another reason to denounce me.
Units/Combat: Look! Culurally diverse units! Finally! Wait....... All the units look the same but with minor color differences (such as tanks will be gray or green, however it is not like in Civ 5 where the color of civs was on the unit) and skin color. yay. All the European civilizations look the same (except Rome and Greece, in which also look exactly the same), the Asian civs look the same, the American (Except for US, they have European civ skins) civs look exactly the same. I find this completely stupid. I like having differentations between what is mine and what is my enemies. Having every unit from each civ look the exact same makes it seem very bland. At the same time, there is no point of corps or armies. You basically expend a perfectly good unit and it's experience just to get a "stronger" one which you probably will never use do to the fact that war sucks.
Religious victory: An interesting idea, however it just leads to the massive spam of religious units all over the place. It gets annoying.
The lack of modding tools: I'd love to see a good mod that actually adds in unit diversity by nation, but it'll take a while because FireAxis didn't even both to allow players to mod the game that easily. Now it is much harder for modders to mod.
The DLC: I pre ordered the game just to get the Aztecs earlier instead of waiting 90 days. Didn't really do much for me. However, for those who bought the deluxe edition it wasted the "free" DLCs they were supposed to get with expansions that should've already been in the game. Seriously? I have to purchase the Poland DLC just to get 1 civ? It's over priced (to some) as well. Fireaxis is just trying to leech money off of their customers like most game companies are doing now.
If you're going to get a civ game, get Civ 5. The base game and DLCs are amazing compared to this.

Oh man. This game. This is the game that you wish existed when you were in grade school, and you wish you had a computer lab teacher cool enough to buy licenses for it. It is both fun, and wether you want to or not, you will learn a thing or two about flight, space travel, rocket science, physics, and management if you have aspirations of sending eager green astronauts to the black void.
The kerbals are only permitted to show disloyalty in thier facial expressions, and they will do so every time you strap them onto a large solid-fuel booster with no parachutes just to see how far it'll go. Their memories will live on at the space center, or at least until you remove them from the roster because who needs that kind of bummer?
The ever-expanding parts list is fun to peruse, and takes an amount of effort to unlock properly. You will be expected to go to far-off planets and moons in the name of science, wielding thermometers and canisters of goo, and eventually bringing mining equipment and fuel processing devices. There's a good sense of progression as you go along and unlock cooler, and more expensive parts, which let you pull off more and more insane builds; I'm talking like DaVinci's helicopter insane.
There's a lot of trial and error, or more accurately error error error, watch some Scott Manley videos, error error error, visit the wiki, error success! So if you are easily disuaded or get frustrated easily maybe skip this one. But it's a wonderful game to learn on, and you come away with a better understanding of the world than when you started, even if this world is run by small, suicidal green men(and women now too!).

AI is terrible. It tries to use land-based melee units (warriors in my case) to attack naval units, despite this being impossible. My ship got surrounded by embarked enemy warriors, and slowly killed each one while the warriors just stayed in place, waiting to drown.

It is not reasonable on any level.
Basic functions from civ V such as build queue and unit alert are lacking.
The new workers, called "builders", are nice in the early game, but later in the game it becomes just more micromanagement hell.
They made navies useless too, for 2 reasons. First, naval trade routes are no longer giving double yields, so they are not worth the added risk of being pillaged. Second, water tiles have really bad yields and cities do not need to be on the water to have harbors (due to harbor districts), so navies can't conquer/defend cities either, only escort land units across water. You don't need to make more than one ship the whole game, and that one is just for a little exploration.
The combat system is micromanagement hell like in civ V, except this time there's a bunch of religious units spammed over the map that will interfere with your troops movement, too. Horsemen is all you need to make to win.
Game has it's good points: nice visuals, districts, and some other things. But overall, too much microing and too bad AI. It quickly gets boring to play.

Military is also a great example, despite the amazing feature of adding squadrons/combining units there seems to be a weird spurt in units, the gap between technologies in which you unlock any military is huge along with the fact that it feels like there aren't many units in the first place. This doubled with the fact that the AI seems to be very questionable, playing on King difficulty the enemy despite having more units decided to retreat and spend the entire time running circles in the ocean watching their capital burn. I heavily suggest going to Civ V until this game is optimized more.

The game is immersive and it is an almost perfect realization of "just one more turn". The new rules make it more engaging, as with each city you build you have to solve many small problems. There are always new small goals on the way to achieving victory. The special rule sets for religious debate, improved hex combat with corps/fleets and support units, museum theming etc. fit into the main game nicely and make the sketchier parts of CivV really interesting.
The look and sound are great. I love the music, and this is one of the very few games in which I don't turn the music off after my first 30 mins. The interface is easily legible, and there are just a few glitches which don't prevent actions or hide meaningful info.
Some drawbacks are AI issues, inadequate diplomacy, the opaque mechanism of culture victory (you never know until you win it) and lack of a diplomatic victory condition. They don't ruin the game, I believe, and overall these issues are probably important only for very skilled players, which I am not. At my level these things don't matter that much.
Now we are used to constant patches and improvements in our games. This one lags behind and still has some troubles, but it's still a masterpiece despite its flaws.

A poor man's overwatch.
Like a very poor man.
Like a man so desperate to play Overwatch that he deals with what can only be described as the hands-down worst matchmaking system in the history of matchmaking systems.
While the game itself offers a small selection of decent champions to choose from, and the balancing of those heroes relies almost exclusively on how well-stacked your card loadout of buffs to each champions abilities is, it lacks in fun when it comes to being matched with teams that far out-rank your skill level, especially when the other team is queued together as a party and have Diamond or higher ranks through the entire party, while your own has Bronze-Gold and are still fairly new to the game.
Fun for those who enjoy Overwatch but want to also enjoy a hyperdeath simulator while in online matches.

This is one of the best games I have ever played. It transcends the category of "games." Simulation and sandbox. Frustrating and immensely satisfying. I feel like rolling out the "game" parts (i.e. the actual "space program" in Kerbal Space Program) has been a bit rocky, but it is getting better all the time. I can't say enough good things about Kerbal Space Program. It is one of my favorite things in the world. I love playing it. I love thinking about it. I love watching other people play it. I love talking about it. It's just too good.

The f'ck'n AI is still messed up! So...prepare to get attacked every now and then...even by your best friend neighbour. You simply can't trust any computer controlled empire. As soon you reach atomic age, all will be permanent angry on you, no matter what you do to avoid missunderstandings. Just forget about working diplomacy and sign treaties only on a ad-hoc base for actual benefits.
Usually I'd give bad review, but all in all I encountered lot's of smaller and bigger upgrades toward former Civ games.
At least upgrading/melting similar units into Corps (2x) or Armys (3x) enhances gameplay in the later eras. Remembering the awfull moving problems if your army wanted to attack a city surrounded by hills in Civ5. Now you just melt your 3 infantry into a powerfull single infantry army and go for the fight. This really changes gameplay into much better tactical experience.
Also the city buildup with specialized 'gated communities' leaves you a lot of interesting choices. You pick one land/sea tile for your special site, like harbour or religious area. After this, you encounter lot's of enhancements to that site, like maybe lighthouse for the harbour, which doesn't need you to pick another tile for the build. This offers every city the possibility for unique shape. Ok, the basic system is copy from Endless Legend, but it fits quite nice into Civ6.
What really get's me mad is the permanent threat of war, so you can't play game like scientist or peacefull builder as in former versions. On the other side, you are permanently questioned to do important judgments to deal with the threats. I do hope they'll patch this in the future, otherwise the game has turned into a war-beast.
Anther spitting in customers face is the price level they ask for Civ6. If you could grab the game for half of current requested fee, you may get what you pay for. Any higher charge...well, how about sending me your email, so I could give you my PayPal contacts and you could just send your spare money over instead of wasting it? *subtle irony off*
One may be disappointed by more and more comic graphics, but hey, it is a strategy game and I also had fun with games which only showed letters on a map instead units. So, for me it isn't too much of a problem...and the landscapes, trees, surroundings, day-and-night circle and other aspects do compensate in my eyes.
There are allready mods out there (civfanatics and else), so you may also grab the common version and wait for later season pass offers.
So...my short impression at the moment is, they managed to keep the 'only one more turn' feeling, but have to upgrade their way to early released beta. But except Paradox, all distributors throw out games too early at the moment. ^^

As of writing this review I've put about 60 hours into this game and beaten the game on Prince difficulty.   I am not a hardcore 4X player so if you're looking for that kind of perspective I'm afraid I can't help you there.  I am writing this review for people like me who don't play Civ on punishing difficulty and just enjoy building empires with an opponent difficult enough to be an obstacle.
It is my opinion that despite diplomacy being unpredictable that this game plays much better than Civ 5.   If you have enjoyed previous Civilization games, I'd recommend that you at least consider this game.  And if you're new to the franchise I think that this is an excellent choice for your first taste of these games.   I'll speak in more detail below.
Long Version:
The two things that make Civ 6 a vast improvement over Civ 5 are the progression system and the city district system.
I'll start with progression
In Civ 5 you build your city and then you improve tiles to gain resources.   You then use these resources to build buildings and wonders in your cities.   These buildings  are the driving engine that progresses your Science, Culture, and Faith, as well as your productivity to build units.   That's a lot of things to progress, but the problem is that you just produce x amount of science, faith, and culture passively.  Your decision making is all about generating resources and then you hit the turn button until the research bar fills and you get the technology, or cultural policy or whatever.
In Civ 6 culture and technology are both researched in a tree, but you can accelerate each advancement by doing something on the map.  For example you research sailing and currently it will take 10 turns.  You can trigger what the game calls a "eureka moment" for sailing by creating a city on the coast.   This cuts the research time in half.  So now you can actually plan to build units or improvements and take certain actions to blitz your way to certain technologies quicker.  All of the sudden you're actively progressing your civilization with the choices you make.    I cannot describe the huge difference that this change alone brings to the table.
Then we have the district system:
In Civ 5, all your buildings and wonders are contained inside your city and around your city are only improvements to gain additional resources, give defense bonuses, or roads to speed your units across the map.
In Civ 6 you stil use builders to create tile improvements however you can only build a small number of buildings within your city.  The rest can only be built in seperate city districts that take up seperate tiles on the map.   For example you want to boost science.  First you have to build a campus district.  This district benefits from being located next to mountains, so you want to place it next to as many mountain tiles as possible.  Then once you build this district, you can build science buildings for your city.   You can only build a limited number of districts per city so you will have to specialize your cities.  And furthermore wonders occupy seperate tiles from the city as well and come with restrictions on what kind of land they can be built on.  So now the tiles around your city have to be juggled between traditional improvements, districts, and wonders.   This adds so much strategy beyond the simple planning of Civ 5, where you just make your decision based on having an abundance of hills, plains, or water and spam mines and farms.
It's these two changes that prevent the progression through the science and culture trees from becoming a soul crushing grind like you could get in Civ 5.  You have so many decisions to make just from these changes, and I haven't even covered the new government system, where you can thoroughly customize your goverment policies to fit your civilizations shifting needs at any given time.  The religion system is probably the progression system they changed the least from Civ 5 but it gets the job done, and it works well in tandem with the government sytem to give you a lot of choosable benefits that can aid your particular playstyle.
So my final thoughs are that Civ 6 just has more customizability and more active progression than Civ 5.  So even with some wonky AI or some weird diplomacy the game is still so much more engaging.   I honestly love it, and even though I just won a science victory, I plan to continue playing.  Maybe I'll go for a cultural victory or a Domination victory the second time.  But I know regardless that I'll keep coming back to this game.

Soundtrack - Amazing. As an amateur Drummer since I was 7 years old I love music and all/most genres. Graphics are great - frame rate good, no cpu hog, etc. Of course check out the reccomended to see if your system can handle it, but its free, so at least give it a shot if your specs are borderline.
Like I said before, the Storyline is great, as well as the controls - very intuitive and simple.
I also love the fact that you can interact with so many things in your environment - which will give your character an opportunity to voice her opinion or worldview on said items.
Bottom line: As of this writing, for the price of one fast-food meal (a very chep one at that) will give you hours of gametime.
The only con is replayability - I'm not big on replay, but this is a game of choices and there seems to be some replayablility by going a different route the second time around. Not really a negative since, in my humble opinion you more than get your money's worth.
Hope that helps you decide to at least try Episode 1. You won't be sorry!

I want so badly to give this game a 100% rating. Generally, when getting used to new Civ games, I go with a domination style victory. Simple, to the point, and helps learn the mechanics. Unfortunately the game got a little more frustrating at that point.
Diplomacy: Nearly Impossible. There is little to no way to maneuver around other civilizations to achieve a true diplomatic victory. The other civ's are extremely aggressive and seem to be willing to go to war over the smallest disgressions. This also makes beneficial trade difficult. Now, this doesn't mean its impossible, it's simply difficult to predict or maneuver around the personalities of the different leaders.
Overall, this game is the best Civ yet. Despite that, there's room for improvement. Most of the shortcomings are in the AI realm, things that will take time for Firaxis to perfect. I think that when they get it right (and I have faith that they will), this game will be truly excellent.

In Civ 5 you build your city and then you improve tiles to gain resources.   You then use these resources to build buildings and wonders in your cities.   These buildings  are the driving engine that progresses your Science, Culture, and Faith, as well as your productivity to build units.   That's a lot of things to progress, but the problem is that you just produce x amount of science, faith, and culture passively.  Your decision making is all about generating resources and then you hit the turn button until the research bar fills and you get the technology, or cultural policy or whatever.
In Civ 6 culture and technology are both researched in a tree, but you can accelerate each advancement by doing something on the map.  For example you research sailing and currently it will take 10 turns.  You can trigger what the game calls a "eureka moment" for sailing by creating a city on the coast.   This cuts the research time in half.  So now you can actually plan to build units or improvements and take certain actions to blitz your way to certain technologies quicker.  All of the sudden you're actively progressing your civilization with the choices you make.    I cannot describe the huge difference that this change alone brings to the table.
Then we have the district system:
In Civ 5, all your buildings and wonders are contained inside your city and around your city are only improvements to gain additional resources, give defense bonuses, or roads to speed your units across the map.
In Civ 6 you stil use builders to create tile improvements however you can only build a small number of buildings within your city.  The rest can only be built in seperate city districts that take up seperate tiles on the map.   For example you want to boost science.  First you have to build a campus district.  This district benefits from being located next to mountains, so you want to place it next to as many mountain tiles as possible.  Then once you build this district, you can build science buildings for your city.   You can only build a limited number of districts per city so you will have to specialize your cities.  And furthermore wonders occupy seperate tiles from the city as well and come with restrictions on what kind of land they can be built on.  So now the tiles around your city have to be juggled between traditional improvements, districts, and wonders.   This adds so much strategy beyond the simple planning of Civ 5, where you just make your decision based on having an abundance of hills, plains, or water and spam mines and farms.
It's these two changes that prevent the progression through the science and culture trees from becoming a soul crushing grind like you could get in Civ 5.  You have so many decisions to make just from these changes, and I haven't even covered the new government system, where you can thoroughly customize your goverment policies to fit your civilizations shifting needs at any given time.  The religion system is probably the progression system they changed the least from Civ 5 but it gets the job done, and it works well in tandem with the government sytem to give you a lot of choosable benefits that can aid your particular playstyle.
So my final thoughs are that Civ 6 just has more customizability and more active progression than Civ 5.  So even with some wonky AI or some weird diplomacy the game is still so much more engaging.   I honestly love it, and even though I just won a science victory, I plan to continue playing.  Maybe I'll go for a cultural victory or a Domination victory the second time.  But I know regardless that I'll keep coming back to this game.

" The walking dead " is the same, from the fall-off comic book graphic to the point & click - mechanics, you walk with WASD and click on the subject of the investigation or to pick them up.
It is the main character who is the big difference. Clementine is more exposed and vulnerable than Lee was - she is after all still a child. But she's not just physical plant since the first game. Here she is more capable : able to handle weapons, use the environment to their advantage and have basic survival skills . This requires the need that she must use their accumulated knowledge to cope.
How and what I choose Clementine to say or do will have consequences later on. These choices - that must be done on time, is the essence of the game. The moral choices are of course the most exhausting. Should I help a character or not? Who should I save the life of? There is no right answer. But as the game quickly and well manage to establish the characters, there is an emotional effort on my part, that makes these choices grab. It gets heavy, ruthless and crippling to see terrible events pass and know that I could have chosen differently.
Clementine is superbly written, feels incredibly human in their desperation and loneliness, and proves at the same time smart, stubborn and have good instincts. Clementine was in the last game chiselled sympathetic and courageous. Here she gets an expanded emotional spectra, through the choices you make - she may, for example, behave suspiciously , sad or friendly. She becomes a much more interesting person and in the coming episodes will hopefully evolve even more.

Life Is Strange tells loosely the story of Max, a socially awkward teenager in her first year of college who has ambitions of becoming a photographer. To this end, she moves back to the town she left some four years ago, to attend a university with a famous photographer teacher on staff. Here, she experiences typical teenage girl in college drama; she’s a little too introverted to be part of the cool crowd, so she carves a quiet corner for herself among the hipsters and the nerds. She’s more or less unnoticed, save for the odd bout of casual bullying, but tells herself that she’s mostly okay with wandering the tightly packed corridors of her school without her peers paying her much heed. Her biggest concerns are what she plans to do about her coursework and what music she should play next on her MP3 player. That’s until she wanders into the bathroom, watches a girl get shot and discovers that she has the ability to rewind time.
This unexpected discovery completely shapes Life Is Strange on every level. Max now has the power to spin back time and stop the girl from copping a bullet to the gut. But she can also use it for more mundane things. If she’s embarrassed that she can’t answer a question in her art lecture, she can just wait for a more well-informed student to give the correct response, jump back in time and give that answer herself. The game’s quick to let you get used to this feeling of invulnerability; you can test out all the available replies to any conversation and, if you don’t like where it’s going, rewind and try again. Or even learn a little more about the topic, then spin back and pick an entirely new response. With the really hard questions that you know are going to eventually start creeping into the plot, being able to explore all the verbal pathways to see how they turn out is empowering. It constantly feels like you’re hedging your bets; going into each choice significantly more informed than perhaps you should be.
So, when the game suddenly takes that ability away from you at key points, the simple act of making a choice suddenly feels like a mammoth pitfall. Perhaps representing the apex of Life Is Strange, the end of the second episode does just that, robbing you of your ability to feel out conversations and forcing you to slowly plot out your own course. It’s significant, because for the first time since the fated trip to the bathroom, there’s more at stake than just your social or academic standing. And there’s a very clear difference between success and failure. Not getting this right will prove to have far reaching consequences until the end of the game.
