My experience with Civ6 has compelled me to write my first ever steam review. I really would like to recommend this game, but in its current state the game has enough problems that you should wait some time for them to all get hammered out. Fortunately most of the issues seem very fixable. A bit of background, I've played every civ game since 2, logged almost 300 hours on Civ5 and have logged almost 75 hours on civ6, having beat my last playthrough on Emperor difficulty.
I really like the new district system. It's added a level of complexity and 'urban planning' to the game that previous iterations lacked. It encourages you to develop many cities rather than stacking 10 wonders in your power capital like you would do in previous civs. The new cultural, policy, and government system is also a welcomed new addition. The added flexibility is nice versus in Civ5 where once you had made policy decisions you were stuck with them for the rest of the game.
The eureka/inspiration system is also a cool way to add side quests to your decisions to help boost a certain policy or technology. Finally, having great people actually do different things is another interesting way to vary up gameplay, although it would be nice if some of the writing/artist/music great people could do something other than create great works.
I don't think the new city-state 'envoy' system is an improvement. I do like the unique bonuses that each city state can give you, but I think civ5's system of actively courting (well, bribing) city-states to be your friend was a stronger system.
I do like how happiness (now called amenities) is now per city, but it's so easy to maintain happiness level that building as many cities as possible is the best possible strategy. In civ5, there were repercussions to building/conquering too many cities, and I think civ6 went too far in the opposite direction.
I don’t mind the new art style and there are some changes to the map and UI that are helpful, such as lenses that give more pertinent information about the map based on context (such as seeing religion levels when moving a religious unit), but for some odd reason a lot of useful features have been taken out of the UI. For example, in most information screens, you can’t sort information. Scrolling through a list of 20 cities to see which one is producing the most science becomes more difficult than it should.
As has been said in many other reviews, the A.I. has problems. Contrary to what I've seen others say, I actually find the A.I. in the early game to be somewhat respectable. Despite the fact that they sometimes are hyper-aggressive, it is challenging to fight them, along with the ever roaming barbarians. However, part of this early challenge is due to how bad the A.I. cheats on harder difficulties. On my emperor playthrough, every other civilization I encountered had 2-3 cities with multiple workers and military units within the first 30 turns. I had barely built my first worker. When the A.I. declared war on me, units appeared to just spawn from nowhere. I don't mind a challenge, but spawning units for free in a game like this is very frustrating. Because of these bonuses, the AI will also completely dominate in culture/science. I think in the year 200 A.D., I saw Kongo change its government to a Democracy and enter the modern era. 200 A.D.!

Yet despite all this cheating, the A.I. has major flaws in the mid to late game that makes them nearly harmless towards the end game. For one, once they've built around 5 cities, they stop.  They will try to conquer each other (and you), but their tactical management of units isn't very good. But this biggest issue, is that for some reason, the A.I. will not upgrade their units. An A.I. in the atomic era will still have spearmen and slingers. One tank army can almost single handedly destroy an entire A.I.’s military. I'd almost wish they'd cheat and spawn throngs of tanks and infantry to just provide a challenge, but after the medieval era, they just stop caring about their military.
And to pile on to the diplomacy-side of things, once you decide to conquer a city, you can forget about diplomacy for the rest of the game. Warmonger penalties, even for wars you didn't start, cannot be surmounted with any amount of diplomatic good will. For a frame of reference, an Alliance is worth +18 in relationship with the A.I. Conquering one city is -15. Conquer two cities, and you are at -30, and your ally will denounce you. Never mind you conquered the cities of a civilization your ally is also at war with. It's nonsensical.
Beyond the A.I., there are a few other issues. The pace of the game doesn't feel right. I think it's because you can now 'research' two trees at once, so you get through the tech and policy trees faster. Eureka and inspiration bonuses also cause this. In Civ5, I would reach a certain era at least within a century of when that era actually happened in history (e.g., industrial era around 1800 A.D.). In civ6, I discovered flight in 1100 A.D. This is on standard speed. It feels like there are gaps in both trees that might get filled in with new techs in later expansions, so hopefully this issue improves over time.
If you were new to the civilization franchise, there really would be no reason to play Civ6 over Civ5. Every civilization game has been fairly different than the previous. Whether you liked Civ5 over Civ4 or not, no one can deny that Civ5 was a completely different experience than Civ4. Civ6 feels like Civ5 with a few things refactored. And with the current A.I. and pacing issues, Civ6 isn't as enjoyable as Civ5.
Nearly everything that bothers me about Civ6 seems easily fixable. I remember when Civ5 first came out, it had a lot of problems, but with two expansions and many patches, it is a really good game. Civ6 feels like it is a few balancing patches and one expansion away from being a good game. The glaring omission of a United Nations in Civ6 leads me to believe the nearly absent diplomacy of this game will be fixed in the future.
So, should you buy this game now? No, don't waste your time. Buy Civ5 if you haven't already or if you already have Civ5 then start another Civ5 game. Or try another 4x game. But just like Civ5, give this game a year or two to hammer out it's issues and it will probably be great.

I had a hard time deciding how to rate Civilization 6, on one hand I really like it. It introduces a nice level of complexity that I felt Civilization 5 was missing, and there are many conceptual improvements. The empire-wide happiness mechanic is gone, which means that settling more than 4 cities is once again a staple.
At the same time, this game was released unfinished. It's clear that it will need many more months of development, maybe even years, to reach the level of polish that Civilization 5 currently has. That's a shame too, they should not have sold the game as a finished product knowing its problems, but here we are. The short of it is, if you aren't a dedicated Civilization player or a fan of the series, go pick up Civilization 5 instead. It's cheaper, has more content, and is decently balanced. This game is not.
The DLC for this game is also pretty underwhelming. Adding additional Civs to play as is nice, charging $5 each is not.

This is actually a great game and probably one of the best in the series yet. I was a little bit intrepid at first reading some of the negative reviews, which do have some validity in them. Unfortunately I think the negativity was simply due to not enough game time to understand the new systems.
At first I didn't like the game as I didn't really have a clue what was going on. But with a little perseverance I am beginning to love it and can't wait to try out different strategies and approaches, which appear to far exceed previous generations of the series.
Unit management is so much better, especially air units where fighters can be deployed to cover air sectors. Engineers can be used to build forward bases. I would prefer less of the cartooney feel on some of the units.
Now the AI is absurd. One turn you are friends, and then all of a sudden a couple of civs decide to gang up on you. Teddy Roosevelt decided he didn't like my peaceful activity on the contentenant with a very small army. I suppose he objected to me building a barracks. This guy seems to think people should be defenceless.
The city destacking makes for more interesting city planning and building, although I feel things start to get a bit crowded. I think they should have expanded the city radius a bit so we can have more fields and countryside.
If trying to play a peaceful game, never take an opponents city every time you are attacked otherwise you stupidly get labelled as a warmonger. Might as well go for total war once tagged as a warmonger. Nobody likes us and we don't care!

I honestly don't know what more I can say that has not already been said about Life is Strange.

EDIT: I posted the original review early in January 2017. Now (October 2017) I have amended the review to "Recommend". They have released some good content for the game as well as making some tweaks to improve the AI and gameplay. I still think it's best to wait for a sale but it is no longer a game I would dissuade people from purchasing.
For returning Civ players, the game is quite good, except for a couple big mistakes that unfortunately make it not recommended.
1) The AI in this game is horrible. Absolutely atrocious. That, combined with a subpar diplomacy system, means you should not expect to have any sort of decent AI interaction at all. Also, the AI is terrible in war, meaning your conquests will feel unfulfilling.
2) Religion is underwhelming. There is nothing unique about religion, and you feel no obligation to actually gain a religion at all. This is disappointing because I loved playing for religion in Civ V.
3) The developers have unfortunately become too greedy. They are releasing half-baked DLCs in an attempt to get as much money out of their player base as possible.
I would wait till the game falls into the $30 range, or if it goes on sale bundled with DLC. Until then, stick with Civ V.

Amazing game if you are into physics, astronomy, problem solving, exploration, or sandbox games.  Amazing game if you want to build and, most likely, destroy reiculous aircraft.  Amazing game if you want to look at fake stars through a lcd display.  9/10, benifits greatly from mods.

There is a decent learning curve whether in sandbox or career mode, but not the game is not unforgivingly difficult, however, KSP is not kind to those who give up under frustration.  It isn't uncommon to build a spaceplane only to have it fail, so expect lots of trial and error followed by troubleshooting.  You may need tutorials, or an autopiolet mod, for skillful manuvers like, say, transfering to Duna (Mars anologue) or landing on the moon.  This is a good thing; I got downright giddy after landing on the Mun after several few tries, and the Mun (Moon) is supposed to be easy!
The modding community for KSP is incredible.  You can find hundreds of parts, all largely without bugs, ranging from adapters or propellers to autopiolet modules and warp drives, or even entire, pre-built crafts.  AI, multiplayer, and weapons are available as well for the current (1.0.4) version.  While these all should be, and hopefully will be, included in future updates, they're still easy to find online.
The graphics are the most noticable fault, but I can't complain.  The game runs great when over 4 gigs of ram, even with a 4 year old GPU.  Be weary when using 32bit, it isn't terrible by any means, but worth mentioning.
9/10.  Could use more stock parts and options, but thats easily fixed with community add-ons.

I own Overwatch, I pre-ordered the Origins Edition, and I have to say; this game feels a lot more fun than Overwatch. The thing is, there is polish, but there is also too much polish. Paladins is relatively polished--which is a good thing. It's not perfect by any means, but perfection is boring. While there are some glaring similarities between the two games, the differences in playstyle are immense, and the card loadouts and in-game progression make the game feel a lot more alive. Ultimates aren't game changing, there are no press Q/E and win abilties, the ultimates are more of an extension of the character's kit rather than a mandatory goal like they are in Overwatch. Each hero is unique, but Hi-Rez is not afraid to release heroes that may be deceptively similar, but overall completely different from each other, and always fun.
The customization options are aplenty here, with 6-7 slots for customization, 3 of which are mix-and-match apparel, so it is not often you find another player rocking the same style as you. With new costumes, weapons, and hats being added every patch, the options will eventually be overwhelmingly glorious. There are voice packs available for every hero, and they can be bought with the money you earn in-game.
The game is not pay-to-win at all, the only thing that paying real money will get you is aesthetic or a minor shortcut to things you can get in-game anyways. You can buy the founder's packs which are definitely worth it, unlocking every hero in the game forever for $20, which is essentially buying the game if you think about it. The epic and legendary founders packs are really just there for the diehard fans who want every cosmetic ever immediately; and I admit that I am one of those people, haha.
Pros
+Fun gameplay
+Good customization
+Good F2P model
+Familiar/easy to get in to
+Lots of different ranks to flaunt your experience
Cons
-6 Maps for the main gamemode
-Stigma for being an "Overwatch clone"
-There are "noob-traps"
-Less than ideal matchmaking

In my opinion, it's not correct to compare this game to Overwatch. Indie vs AAA, Free to Play vs $40-60, Beta vs Released. This should pretty much sum up what this game is, indie beta F2P, but I'll elaborate anyway.
So, here we have unfinished, unpolished, not quite balanced game (there are some problems in characters, there are too easy ones, there are piano ones). Which is free to play, as in - there are plenty of pointless unlockable (for gold) skins, there is paywalled content, and most irritating - the game will constantly remind you that you didn't pay for it. You get cut xp and gold, but you could get bonuses. You get 3 items from radiant chest, but you could get 4 (fourth being rare). And it's on every corner and quite every step. Yes, I understand that game has to live on donations, but I wouldn't want to be constantly smacked in the face with ads and sales. Team Fortress and Dota live without this somehow.
Now to the actual content. World, characters, maps - a mixture of fairytail and hi-tech. Some characters would have some explaining to do, what are they and why they use particular weapons. For example - a treeant with an axe. Yeah, I can see the irony, but not the sense.
However, all the nonsense aside, this is quite good. Enjoyable voice acting, decent video quality (Unreal Engine 3), rather low system requirements (runs great on mid-low end laptop).
What I actually dislike about this game is that it requires external launcher and a new account. It's a minor problem, but it's there.
Now about constant comparisons with Overwatch... There are tons of other games with similarities and same ideas, same game modes, same weapons or weapon systems, yet somewhy it's a rare thing that somebody calls it out. Think about it: Much loved Serious Sam series almost straight cloned and expanded Quake 1 weapon system. Team Fortress is a Quake multiplayer mod. Fallout is actually a failed Wasteland sequel. Assassins Creed and Saints Row IV are inspired by The Matrix movie. What I'm saying is - copying and expanding ideas is a normal thing, it's everywhere, so just stop comparing and play the game for fun, pleasure, enjoyment or whatever do you play it for.

Kerbal Space Program is probably the most fun you can have in any game whilst failing wretchedly over and over and over again. And there is no other game I can think of that really gives you quite such an amazing sense of achievement and satisfaction if you get anything to work exactly like you wanted it to.
The fails make me screech with laughter, and the Kerbals' expressions are priceless, it has awesome moments of pretty (especially with a couple of mods), and whilst it's easy as Lego to build stuff, it's very hard to master -- probably because it literally is rocket science.
The Kerbals themselves are a stroke of genius -- they transform the game from serious sim into a slapstick comedy but also makes the experience quite personal: when Jeb gets stuck on the Mun because you messed up the fuel needed, he's got such a trusting face, you feel obliged to rescue the poor lad. Each kerbal somehow matters, which makes the game much more tense and high stakes -- killing a kerbal through bad design is at once comic but also has a guilt level up there with kicking a puppy.
It is also one of the few games that has a large community of modders dedicated to making your game even more terrifyingly complicated and difficult to succeed at.
I'm at 1700 hours, and I've got absolutely nowhere (Kerbin's Moons, Duna & Eve - in my defence, there have been multiple resets as career mode evolved and mods were added). Even so, with very little progress to show, I'm having a blast. I have created rockets, shuttles, SSTOs, landers, probes,  rovers, jets, gliders, tugs, refuellers, space stations, satellites and almost countless craters full of scrap metal. It hasn't got old, and it's still fun. The only other game that comes close to this sort of replayability is the ArmA series which I've been playing - in it's various iterations - for 14 years.
It's even good to watch -- youtube has some splendid lunatics doing hilarious and epic things. Kurtjmac's channel is hilarious, Scott Manley shows you how it should be done, and some of the others are just jaw dropping -- Thor LP showcases some of the foolishness you can accomplish if you put your mind to it.

The number one spot is just dripping with personal bias but I don’t care because it’s my list. Life is Strange is a game that is willing to deal with so many subjects most games won’t touch with a ten-foot pole. From victim mentality, to date♥♥♥♥♥♥ to cyber bullying, to suicide, to post-war PTSD, to psychopathy, to abuse of power and status. There are few issues this generation faces that aren’t covered to some degree over the course of its story. Though a few of these are a bit heavy-handed, when you cast a net as wide as this a few fish are bound to slip through. Most however are executed so superbly that I didn’t even realize how many social problems that this game tries to address until I started ruminating on this list. We view these issues through the lens of our main character, Max Caudwell, who is attending a private school in her old hometown of Arcadia Bay for photography during her senior year of high school. She uncovers that she can rewind time and begins using this power to solve exponentially important tasks. Everything about the setting is familiar but at the same time distinct. The world is wonderfully crafted and weaves a story that really resonated with me and emotionally impacted me more than just about anything else I’ve ever experienced. There is a decent learning curve whether in sandbox or career mode, but not the game is not unforgivingly difficult, however, KSP is not kind to those who give up under frustration.  It isn't uncommon to build a spaceplane only to have it fail, so expect lots of trial and error followed by troubleshooting.  You may need tutorials, or an autopiolet mod, for skillful manuvers like, say, transfering to Duna (Mars anologue) or landing on the moon.  This is a good thing; I got downright giddy after landing on the Mun after several few tries, and the Mun (Moon) is supposed to be easy!
The modding community for KSP is incredible.  You can find hundreds of parts, all largely without bugs, ranging from adapters or propellers to autopiolet modules and warp drives, or even entire, pre-built crafts.  AI, multiplayer, and weapons are available as well for the current (1.0.4) version.  While these all should be, and hopefully will be, included in future updates, they're still easy to find online.
The graphics are the most noticable fault, but I can't complain.  The game runs great when over 4 gigs of ram, even with a 4 year old GPU.  Be weary when using 32bit, it isn't terrible by any means, but worth mentioning.
9/10.  Could use more stock parts and options, but thats easily fixed with community add-ons.

**edit, original below**
After playing the game for another 20+ hours I would like to revise my review a bit.  My original complaints such as poor AI, victory progression speed and empire size are still an issue, but they aren't nearly as bad as my first impressions lead me to believe.
The AI is bad and sometimes stupid, but also more complex and realistic than I initially gave it credit for.  To form alliances and diplomatic bonds you need to do more than avoid war, and to make trade deals every now and then.  Things like active trade routes, establishment of embassies, gifts of gold or resources and pointless trade deals (deals for small amounts of gold or luxury resources you already have) are all factored into another empire's relationship.  In short good diplomacy takes a lot more work in this game.
My main complaint about victory progression speed being too fast for science based empires was a bit premature, the indicators for victory progression are 3 bars that fill up as a task is completed (build a spaceport, launch moon landing, launch habitat parts, etc...).  These bars are a bit misleading as the first two fill up quite quickly as the tasks are fairly easy, the third and final bar however will take a LONG time to fill up as the final tasks are more difficult.  This makes it seem as if you are well behind your competition until it takes them 20 end game turns (looong turns) to complete only one of the five required final tasks.
My last complaint was being forced to build wide, you cant really get by on 3 cities like you could in civ 5, but you can still be competative with 5 or 6 cities as opposed to the 9 in my original review.
All in all, the more I play the game the more i like it, maybe having 1200+ hours in the last one skewed my feelings too much.
Now the pros:
- Higher tier scouts (capable of surviving mid game)
- The art
- Great people (Most have different abilities and perks and you get to pass on recruiting them if they don't interest you)
- Government policies (Whole new research tree)
- Strategic resources (only need 1 of a resource to build multiple units that require it)
- More stuff but I'm lazy and this review is already too long
All in all the game still has a number of flaws that need to be addressed in future expansions, but I think that its still a fun game and probably worth the money if you are a fan of the 4x genre.

All in all, I would recommend waiting for the first expansion, or atleast waiting till it goes on sale.  That being said, I think civ 5 with all the xpacs is a far better game than civ 6 is currently.

In it's current phase, I would NOT recommend this game to Civilization newbies or veterans alike.  This agonizes me to give it a 'Not Recommended,' and I really am optimistic I'll change the recommendation, but, this stuff has got to be fixed as it's ruining a potentially classic game.
Here are my reasons, and they are petty and nitpicky but there's so many of them that they add up to major, deal-breaking problems to a game that could have a TON of potential.
The Bads:
-No mods or Steam Workshop (yet).  Hopefully some modders will come up with tweaks for some of  the nuisances I'm describing below.
-"I just moved this unit, let me select this next one and move it".....NO!  WRONG!  I'M THE GAME AND I JUST AUTO-SELECTED ANOTHER UNIT RIGHT OUT FROM UNDER YOU AND MOVED THAT ONE!  **** YOU, THAT'S WHY!  Seriously, out of all the problems, this one infuriates me!  Get in the habit of saving at the beginning *and* end of each turn.
-I finally warmed up to the idea of districts, but....why not have the option to share the tile for Wonders that relate to the districts?
-Speaking of Wonders, how is it the AI civs have already completed The Oracle, Stonehenge, The Great Library, etc, by turn 3?  I exaggerate, of course, but, even on the simpler difficulty levels, they will beat you to all of your favorite Wonders.
-Warmonger penalty lasts for all eternity.  "Hi, I'm that Civ you just met after turn 273.  We've had no prior contact with you, or any of your neighbors but we will hate your guts in a few turns because you had to raze a poorly placed city an enemy civ, which declared a surprise war on *you*, btw, placed in a **** poor location just out of reach of rivers, or the coastline.  Here's your Denouncement!  Forget about trading or improving relations with us now, ****head!"
-Why can't you raze enemy capitals?  There's some debate about whether or not it's possible...it isn't.  So, the ****-***-stupid location the AI picked for their capital...you're stuck with it.
-You could remove City States in Civ. 5, you can't do it on Civ 6.  Why is this important?  They do give really good bonuses after all!  Well, anyone playing civilization for any amount of time will tell you how finicky Civ Fans are in terms of city placement....like, it's obsessive-compulsive/OCD levels of pickiness.  And, of course, the City States are invariably in less than ideal placements, and, right in the way of where you wanted to place your next city.
-Speaking of placement, even if you select the Balanced Option from Player Start when firing up  a new game, the AI and city states have a strong Bias to be placed near you.  It should be random, civs should be spread out evenly and fairly.  I get that this gives the player an experience that puts them in the action quicklly, but I like playing against a lot of different civs. As many as I can, but what happens, even on huge maps with islands, is I'm already fighting tooth-and-nail in a mad grab for land just a few turns in.
-Barbarians.  I love fighting against them, but, if you have them turned on, they will ignore the AI in favor of attacking you.  This one doesn't bother me too much, but, it happens every time.  They'll skip over an AI unit right next to you just to play the role of spoiler.
-@Firaxis - you guys are really taking it on the chin for your DLC and the pricing.  Might want to rethink that model of nickel-and-diming for more civs and mostly 'meh' maps and scenarios.  Bundle it, or maybe lower the price or throw in a freebie?  I can't tell you what to do, but people are voting with their feet.
-Builders have a limited amount of builds, and no longer build roads.  This isn't too much of a deal breaker, but it's annoying that they changed it after so many games in the series.  I actually don't like the insta-build for tile improvements....why add that and take away the option to build roads?  Insta-build kills any sense of accomplishment for building a farm or mine, and it takes away the intensity if you are trying to sneak in an improvement before getting raided.  I get that most major roads in reality were based off of trade routes but why isn't that an option we can control through the game setup?
The Goods:
-At first, I wasn't warm to the idea of districts, but, after playing a few times through, I like the idea now!  It makes sense, you have Holy or Economical districts, and it seems to reason that those are the tiles that have your Temples and Banks, for example.
-Boosts for research and civics: If you've been practicing at mining, or building a large standing army or a certain type of district or improvement, it makes sense your Civ would already have a little experience with whatever you're researching.
-Sean Bean.  Leonard Nimoy was my absolute favorite, but, I'm also a fan of Sean Bean...and he doesn't die in this (I think?)!
What I'd like to see:
-There's only a finite amount of tiles in each city zone.  With districts and Wonders now occupying a tile, the cities growth is really stymied compared to the other games in the series.  Why not have the districts act as a container for builder/tile improvements or Wonders?  Can't the icons size be reduced for this?
-Gotta refine diplomacy.  I can't make friends with any AI civ.  They either want to pull a surpise war on you, which will cause them to refuse any deal up to that point, or they will hold a grudge against you for wars you had to fight against Civs they never met for centuries.  And you can always tell they are leading up to a Surprise War, as they will pile troops around your borders, or ask for open borders a few turns before the War declaration.
-Allow us to choose our experience and play the game as we've been used to.  How about a checkbox for City-States On/Off, or Builder options to build roads, or allow 'X' amount of builds?  Maybe a diplomacy option that tones down the Jerk-Level of the AI Civs?
Well, I've said my piece.  It's your dough, I'd recommend you hang onto it for now.  Even if Firaxis (or a Steam sale) lowers the price, they need to hear us.  Let them address the concerns of the people buying and playing the game.
P.S. For Steam - I'm glad I copy/pasted the content of this to notepad before hitting 'Post Review.'  Thanks for nuking the review and losing the content.  I had a nagging hunch that was going to happen.
P.P.S. Third time is a charm.  I guess they took exception to the harsh language?   ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

I have played most of the CIV series games. The changes from CIV V to CIV VI are clever and add to the playability. Each victory option needs to be planned thoughfully else the AI will get ahead and while you are seeking a science victory, they can slip in a religious victory.
The battles appear more balanced. A horseman attacking a tank will see the tank win every time, even against a herd of horsemen. Seiges against cities also seem more effective with the right mix of troops and more difficult when facing walls and better defenses. Objectively this makes all the preparation for the attack seem worth the effort.
The game flow feels more balanced and if you get a head of the AI, you'll more likely stay ahead, but while having a sense that the AI might do something to ruin the moment. The overall game pace is good but when you get to the end of the science tree there is nothing more to research – and now all you have is a bunch of science buildings doing “nothing” and costing maintenance until a victory condition is met. This makes me think the tech tree is short. You cannot sell buildings so it just feels like waste of effort. Here is an opprtunity to use science to gain further advances and improvements to other districts.
The districts are an interesting way to build and plan a city. It has me thinking more strategically about their placement, but the game does give a handy hint. (Place the commerce district on any tile that will give it more gold per turn.) Though it is a pain to suddenly find your hard built district plundered by the AI or another player. One thing to look out for is a fully populated district can be plundered in a single turn, but will take several turns to repair significantly hurting the industral districs.
I enjoy playing this game. I will likely retire from CIV V and CIVBE to focus on this title.

VI is the best of this long long series so far. It seemed like a natural continuation of Civilization after Brave New World. I enjoyed the first season being a big fan of the original comic and Telltale did it justice, it had the right balance of gameplay and characterization and I felt content with what they had given us, I didn't feel the need for a second season but due to the success of the first game... It's here!
Unfortunately it's not very good, the gameplay is focused around the plot instead of the other way around, there's no real puzzle elements or hub areas in which you can talk to characters to get a better feel for them instead the game is consistently scripted at a brisk pace to keep you "entertained" with the story element over everything else. The game is full of QTEs and there's very little in the aspect of "point and click" beside what dialogue choices you're given that won't matter much because the actual choices you go with really do not alter the story in any real way, shape or form.
The choices you're given don't really branch off into anything that truly mixes up or re-directs the narrative of the game, I find the choices just throw out an alternate of two potential scenes then goes right back into the main flow of the actual plot without any change beside a character dying or a character commenting on something you've done. You're never really given a breather with the game either, it's a constant push for the next thing to happen in the story rather than to settle in a calm before the storm and it's a rather inane way of creating immersion for the player.
Ultimately I find myself enjoying it to an extent but it's not the same as the previous season and the quality shows. Aside from the original key writer and director of the first season leaving Telltale to form their own company and Telltale biting off more than they can chew when it comes to franchises to convert into video game form the quality has dropped and with the wait of three months inbetween each episode I think it's fair to say that the ball has been dropped and Telltale have really messed up.
I'd give this season so far a weak 6/10.
I'm not invested in the emotional aspect of the game, it's just an illusion to hide behind the lack of quality this season brings to cater to a very dumb audience of emotionally starved gamers.

In my English class I had an assignment to create a review of anything I wanted but it had to be in the format of a magazine. So I chose something I genuinely cared about, my favourite game: "Life is Strange." I put in so much time and effort into this assignment that I was pleased when the teacher gave me a 94% and claimed she's interested in playing Life is Strange even with her general dislike of video games.
If you'd like to see what the review looks like with the format of a magazine, here is the
though the format still got messed up while posting it as a pdf, the white spaces are the top and bottom of pages that got merged together :/

Life is Strange is an episodic, choice-driven story game developed by Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix. It has 5 episodes that were released throughout 2015 following the game’s initial release.
In Life is Strange, you play from the perspective of a 18 year old girl named Maxine Caulfield (Hannah Telle), the game begins with Max waking up from a nightmare about a storm with a tornado that rips through Arcadia Bay, the town she lives in. She wakes up in her usual photography class.
One of the first actions you can perform is taking a “selfie” with Max’s Polaroid camera, this is quite a humorous
contrast compared to what is soon to unravel.
After the class, Max rushes to the restroom to compose herself because of the nightmare. There, she witnesses Nathan Prescott (Nik Shriner) murder a girl. In one single effort, she throws her arm up and accidentally rewinds time only to end up back in her photography class. Knowing what is about to happen, she rushes to the restroom after class and sets off the fire alarm before Nathan can kill the girl. Max finds out that the girl she saved was actually her childhood friend, Chloe Price (Ashly Burch). And from there, the game unfolds.
Life is Strange is more than it might seem at first, to some it’s just your usual graphic adventure game that continues through choice. But that’s not exactly true, Life is Strange adds the aspect of time travel, meaning you can rewind time to change the choices you have made, you can see every outcome and sometimes there isn’t a “right choice” or “correct way” to do it. This can lead to some regrettable and heartbreaking choices.
The developers behind Life is Strange have made a very out-of-place game in today’s society.  Life is Strange tackles subjects that are usually taboo in videogames. Some aspects of the game are about social division, parental conflict, online bullying and even teen suicide. This is a very bold move to put all this into a game, but it genuinely works really well and adds a very “real” value to all the characters even if some are based off stereotypes.
In my opinion, this is possibly the greatest game I have ever played, which will probably surprise people I know. I bought the first episode within the month of its release and I loved it so much I bought the entire game before it was even fully released. I played every episode the day it came out and each episode left me laughing or in tears. Many choices in the game seemed to me, impossible to make. The character development and my personal love or hatred of characters made things even more difficult. But I think that was Dontnod Entertainment’s goal. There shouldn’t be an obvious “right” or “wrong” choice.
In some cases there were lip-syncing problems and to some people, Dontnod Entertainment was using “cheap” ways to progress the plot. But people are just too used to high budget games. Life is Strange started with a development team of only 15 people, that’s unbelievable to me considering every texture and piece of art in the game is hand drawn to have a really unique and distinct look.
Because of the sorts of themes in Life is Strange, suicide, online bullying, etc. The people behind Life is Strange have opened up a page on the game’s website dedicated to suicide/crisis hotlines in 14 different countries. This proves that the Life is Strange team recognises that these problems and issues seen in the game are actually real and happening everyday.  This dedication makes the game even more amazing to me.
When it was announced that a limited edition version of the game would be released as a physical copy, I took that opportunity and bought one the day it was released. It included the soundtrack, a disc for the game and a book of concept art drawn before the game’s release. The concept art was actually really amazing to look at, some of it had been loosely drawn and coloured with what looked like water colour pencils. Some was more neat and tidy, but in general the artwork was really stunning.
Overall I’d have to say Life is Strange is a 9.5/10. Everything about it was purely amazing, even though there were very sad moments throughout;  it was an absolute pleasure to play. I’d say I’m happy with the choices I made and the way it ended for me.

Hmm i'm still in episode 2, but I thought i'd write a review as the game progresses.
It uses the much-loved interactive story format which was done so well in The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, etc. The gameplay is very good and generally there's nothing to complain about. Except for the FOV. There is a FOV hack that can make the game look much better (and less headache-inducing) on widescreen monitors.
Voice acting is good, except for the main character. She seems to whisper a lot and without any energy. The setting is good too, capturing a small town feel.
First thoughts about the story: it's ok, but it doesn't deserve the rave reviews. The thing that stands out the most for me is how "feminist" the story is the SJW-ness of the story. If you're conservative or have conservative values, you're not going to like this game that much. For starters, there's a rather large number of women in the game with short hair all colours of the rainbow. All the men in the story (thus far) are feminist stereotypes: there's the beta male Warren. There's the rich goon Nathan. There's the authoritarian step dad. There's the shifty school principal. The creepy maintenance man. There's even the obligatory anonymous person sending threatening phone messages calling her a "feminazi", etc etc. There's a bit of climate change stuff in there as well (which isn't bad in itself, but it's one of the favourite talking points of SJWs). And there's a girl who has had an abortion. References to casual hookups, etc. There's also drug use. Thus far there has not been even one positive male role model in this story.
The religious girl Kate is portrayed well and sympathetically though.
I will continue to update this review as the game progresses, but for now those are my thoughts.
Overall, feminist women will enjoy this game a lot, but others probably won't think this game deserves the rave reviews. This game is nowhere near TWD or TWAU in storytelling.

As a long-time a fan of the series, I’m greatly disappointed by this installment, at least in its current shape. Apart from the new city district system, nice graphics and great Sean Bean as the narrator, almost everything seems to be done in real hurry, what is rather surprising. The biggest issue is the AI, which is utterly ridiculous. Regardless of the difficulty level, diplomacy and trade with other civilizations is pointless. Even if there is an alliance forged and the relations between nations are constantly friendly, the situation will always end in betrayal. The civilizations wage wars all the time, even if they use their outdated units, which they never modernize, and the player has WMDs and missile cruisers. I’m always being attacked by limitless waves of missionaries and apostles and the AI always ignores my pleas for not spreading their religions. My efforts in the same area end up in denouncements and, yes, wars. Also, their personalities are seriously messed up with their two agendas – one fixed, one random. Gandhi is one of the most bloodthirsty leaders despite denouncing everyone for warmongering. I’ve even encountered moments when civilizations that supposedly  respect military might, constantly called my armies weak, even though I had the biggest forces on the globe. Overall, given the price of the game, the expectations I had for this title and the following disappointment I can’t recommend Civilization VI at this time. Maybe after some patches/overpriced expansions the experience will change.

Imagine a universe where alternate realities exist. Now associate that with your life events. How far would you go to travel between parallel timelines so that you can save and savour that one moment you can never let go. The life event that defines who you are. Maybe family and friends. Maybe secrets that you wanna hold back. As Maxine Caulfield, a tender teenage girl who aspires to follow in the footsteps of the renowned Mr. Jefferson of photography art, you will face tough decisions as you uncover mistery of the serial killer that has haunted and amused everyone at the Blackwell Academy school.
Would you take the matter of life and death into your own hands? Would you play God? What's the price? For Caulfield, little does she know that destiny has a far more retched plan as she meddles with time. She confides her super power in her best childhood friend, Chloe. At first, it seems fun proving it to her and amusing her by predicting future events. Maybe even going rogue around Arcadia Bay (the story is set around this place) to such lengths as breaking into the principal's office and tracking down the drug ring (and the serial killer).
The story follows Maxine's and Chloe's adventures of fun and frolic. The two are inseparable detective freaks. Oblivious to Maxine, the impending disaster to Arcadia Bay will test her 'time' and bring her back to that one most precious moment, the most important of all, the final destination, the butterfly moment, the 'Butterfly Effect'. Torn between emotions and rage, Maxine must 'fix' everything she has sacrificed her power for and save Arcadia Bay from the disaster that is. But what would it mean for her best friend Chloe? What would it mean for her photography fame and career under Mr. Jefferson? What would it mean to live and die?
This was one hell of a rollercoaster ride! Be prepared to cry. Be prepared to feel desperate. Be prepared to be the incredible Maxine Caulfield!

In my English class I had an assignment to create a review of anything I wanted but it had to be in the format of a magazine. So I chose something I genuinely cared about, my favourite game: "Life is Strange." I put in so much time and effort into this assignment that I was pleased when the teacher gave me a 94% and claimed she's interested in playing Life is Strange even with her general dislike of video games.
If you'd like to see what the review looks like with the format of a magazine, here is the
though the format still got messed up while posting it as a pdf, the white spaces are the top and bottom of pages that got merged together :/

Life is Strange is an episodic, choice-driven story game developed by Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix. It has 5 episodes that were released throughout 2015 following the game’s initial release.
In Life is Strange, you play from the perspective of a 18 year old girl named Maxine Caulfield (Hannah Telle), the game begins with Max waking up from a nightmare about a storm with a tornado that rips through Arcadia Bay, the town she lives in. She wakes up in her usual photography class.
One of the first actions you can perform is taking a “selfie” with Max’s Polaroid camera, this is quite a humorous
contrast compared to what is soon to unravel.
After the class, Max rushes to the restroom to compose herself because of the nightmare. There, she witnesses Nathan Prescott (Nik Shriner) murder a girl. In one single effort, she throws her arm up and accidentally rewinds time only to end up back in her photography class. Knowing what is about to happen, she rushes to the restroom after class and sets off the fire alarm before Nathan can kill the girl. Max finds out that the girl she saved was actually her childhood friend, Chloe Price (Ashly Burch). And from there, the game unfolds.
Life is Strange is more than it might seem at first, to some it’s just your usual graphic adventure game that continues through choice. But that’s not exactly true, Life is Strange adds the aspect of time travel, meaning you can rewind time to change the choices you have made, you can see every outcome and sometimes there isn’t a “right choice” or “correct way” to do it. This can lead to some regrettable and heartbreaking choices.
The developers behind Life is Strange have made a very out-of-place game in today’s society.  Life is Strange tackles subjects that are usually taboo in videogames. Some aspects of the game are about social division, parental conflict, online bullying and even teen suicide. This is a very bold move to put all this into a game, but it genuinely works really well and adds a very “real” value to all the characters even if some are based off stereotypes.
In my opinion, this is possibly the greatest game I have ever played, which will probably surprise people I know. I bought the first episode within the month of its release and I loved it so much I bought the entire game before it was even fully released. I played every episode the day it came out and each episode left me laughing or in tears. Many choices in the game seemed to me, impossible to make. The character development and my personal love or hatred of characters made things even more difficult. But I think that was Dontnod Entertainment’s goal. There shouldn’t be an obvious “right” or “wrong” choice.
In some cases there were lip-syncing problems and to some people, Dontnod Entertainment was using “cheap” ways to progress the plot. But people are just too used to high budget games. Life is Strange started with a development team of only 15 people, that’s unbelievable to me considering every texture and piece of art in the game is hand drawn to have a really unique and distinct look.
Because of the sorts of themes in Life is Strange, suicide, online bullying, etc. The people behind Life is Strange have opened up a page on the game’s website dedicated to suicide/crisis hotlines in 14 different countries. This proves that the Life is Strange team recognises that these problems and issues seen in the game are actually real and happening everyday.  This dedication makes the game even more amazing to me.
When it was announced that a limited edition version of the game would be released as a physical copy, I took that opportunity and bought one the day it was released. It included the soundtrack, a disc for the game and a book of concept art drawn before the game’s release. The concept art was actually really amazing to look at, some of it had been loosely drawn and coloured with what looked like water colour pencils. Some was more neat and tidy, but in general the artwork was really stunning.
Overall I’d have to say Life is Strange is a 9.5/10. Everything about it was purely amazing, even though there were very sad moments throughout;  it was an absolute pleasure to play. I’d say I’m happy with the choices I made and the way it ended for me.

Best vanilla Civ I've played. Just one disclaimer, to those complaining about the diplomacy: If you play it like a typical 4x, chances are you'll make everyone hate you pretty quick. Think about how a real world kingdom would be viewed during the colonial era, if they were to build early, often and everywhere, right up to the borders of another empire. Do that, and other civilizations will see you as greedy expansionists who will surely come for their land in a matter of time, and of COURSE they'll hate you.
Further, you have to take into account what each individual civilization's agendas are, as they go a long way towards dictating relations. I've been good friends with Greece for over 250 turns because I've stayed out of their back yard and haven't competed with them for city state attention. Meanwhile, Harald hates me because my navy is weak, and he respects a strong navy.
I've had the AI actually come to ME with reasonable trade deals that are utterly reasonable, and accept reasonable offers from me... so long as they didn't hate or distrust me. So while I've seen some of the complaints on the diplomacy in Civ VI, I'm here to say that I personally haven't come across some issues, but it may be due to my unorthodox playstyle. (I play to enjoy the journey and "roleplay" more than I play to win.)
I'll just address a couple points from a review that ALMOST made me avoid buying the game, as these are points where my actual experience showed something very different:
CLAIM: AI CIVS WILL HATE YOU WHEN YOU'VE DONE NOTHING WRONG
MY EXPERIENCE: This is generally due to the leader's Agendas, one of which is clearly visible on the diplomacy screen. Victoria is a colonizer and literally hates other civs just because she doesn't have a city on their contient. Essentially she distrusts (or is perhaps jealous...?) of nations who possess land she has no claim to.
Likewise, Harald looks down on those with a weak navy, and Cleopatra those with a weak army. I've also heard complaints about being denounced simply because your government systems aren't the same, but look at how friendly nations in the real world will officially trash an element of the other's political process despite being on good terms. Denouncing another civ doesn't ALWAYS mean you loathe them, no matter how sour the expression of the leader.
CLAIM: TRADE IS POINTLESS, THE AI EXTORTS
MY EXPERIENCE: Recently, I was offered Open Borders for Open Borders by Cleopatra, and Victoria asked me for one of my two Mercury units in exchange for 5 gold per turn in the early game, 5 gold up front, and opening her borders to me. We weren't even on particularly friendly terms.
CLAIM: YOU ARE DENOUNCED BY EVERY NATION FOR REFUSING TO ACCEPT PEACE WHEN ATTACKED. YOU CAN BE A WARMONGER WITHOUT EVER DECLARING WAR.
MY EXPERIENCE: Tested it out and it does seem to be the case, but it's logical. I mean let's stop and think about it for a moment. You literally are.
Think about how it would look in real life if one nation attacked another, got beaten up, then sued for peace, complete with offers to pay for damages incurred by the defender. Now imagine the defender said "Nope, we're gonna use our defense as a casus belli to take everything from you." It would be the definition of warmongering.
No one in Civ VI holds being attacked against you. But once the attacker asks for peace, you're no longer under threat. There is no defense. Continuing to fight after that point means you become the aggressor, for no other reason than petty revenge. Throwing more lives - theirs as WELL as your own - into the line of fire because you were slighted by a rival would logically be seen as despicable by other world powers. Particularly if you use it for conquest.
Hell, this is essentially Rome by definiton, and there's not a scholar in history who doesn't think Rome were warmongers.

It will be good.  Eventually.  For now, it is death of a thousand needles. No one thing is wrong, but the game is full of so many minor flaws (with 2K/Firaxis giving no indication that they are rushing to fix things) that I cannot recommend it right now.
Some of the issues:
-Unbalanced civs
-Stupid AI (If you thought Civ V AI cheated but was stupid, wait til you see this)
-AI personality is overshadowed by stupid AI/diplomacy balancing/bugs (they declared war on you 5 centuries ago and now consider you to be a warmonger because of it)
-Terrible UI, both in-game and in the menus
-No support for Steam Cloud game saves (which Civ V had)
-Very limited custom game options or maps (no teams, and less than 10 map options with most of those being bad to play on. 6-pointed start with 10 players? Sounds legit)
-Maps are limited to smaller and less players than Civ V
-City-states are more random chance and luck than previous. (All players essentially get equal points to assign to city-states, so you can't really focus/ignore them)
-Bugs.  Bugs.  Bugs.
For now, it is fun but frustrating. Once these get fixed, then I will consider it good, but until then, stick with Civ V.

Warning: Some things may be spoiled for those who have not played the second episode.
So far, two episodes of season two have become public. When episode one was finished, I began having high hopes for season 2. Now, after finishing episode 2, I really don't know how to feel. (Spoilers begin here)
When the first episode ended, I just had to take a few moments to go "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; after all that went down. It was better than expected, due to the constant fear of the switch in character view points (from Lee to Clementine) wouldn't be done well. Though, I was happily surprised. The change in respect you're given (since now you're a young girl instead of an adult male) was shown in a way that makes sense; i.e. people didn't know whether to trust you or to pity you or to even help you when you clearly need it. I don't want to give too much of the story away but, when it ended, you get this sense of "I did alright as Lee and teaching this little girl how to survive".
Now, for episode two...In Episode two, you're thrown right into the cliff hanger of the last episode. (I went with Pete instead of Nick so it may be different, depending on who you go with.) The beginning of the episode is filled with drama as you are forced to leave Pete and meet the (current) main antagonist which causes your new group to be on the run again. Now at this point, I felt like "Crap, will we able to get our group to safety?" due mostly to the fact that the group started trusting Clem (even though it seems too soon for them to really trust her) and the fact that now Nick is getting close to mentally breaking.
Though it starts going all downhill after the bridge scene. Now, this is where the whole episode really just becomes meh to me. When your group gets to the ski lodge, you run into more survivors who seem really nice and kind but then this just huge bombshell just drops on you. Kenny is still alive and has been living with these new survivors. (GG to all those who thought Kenny was still alive. It makes me question if Elvis is actually still alive.) Don't get me wrong, I smiled like an idiot and was happy to see him but it still just feels weird. How the hell did he get all the way up here? How the hell did he even survive? He doesn't really tell you. He just kind of "Gets lucky and lives". (Kind of lazy writing there, Telltale but whatever.) You also run into someone else that you might remember if you played 400 days. Though the reveal will make you wish you had killed them when you had the chance.
(end Spoilers) I've written a lot so far but, I suppose I'll wrap it up with just saying. I'm really curious as to what happens next. Considering the trailer for the next episode and the picture telltale has made for it, it's looking really good.
Anyway, TL;DR version: Season two seems to be a melting pot of emotion and drama. Play it for yourself. Then come talk to me about it, I seriously need to discuss this game with someone.

I'm genuinely not seeing a huge number of negatives to this game. I've put quite a lot of play time into now so I reckon I can give a pretty fair review.
The thing I think I like most about Hi-Rez and their games is their attitude to Pay2Win. Gems (the real money currancy) really don't do much other than help you get things quicker but that really is about it. You start with enough paladins to make life interesting without spending a dime and then gain gold for logging in/levelling your character/levelling yourself. Each paladin costs roughly 5000gp or 200 Gems. Getting that 5k really doesn't feel like a grind at all, rather part of a natural progression. I've been playing for a little over two weeks and only have four characters left to unlock, and that isn't by playing solidly for hours on end. If you get into the swing of things now while there aren't too many characters and you play smart you'll have all of them in no time and just need to save for the newest one they add every so often.
So what then? Well each character has customisable loadouts in the form of cards. These come in chests which cost gems, though you get a free chest each time you level your account. You can buy cards with gold though and there's plenty to collect. Okay so you've got all those? No problem go and spend your gold on skins, yes you can customise your characters for free! So really genuinely literally everything in the game can be attained through patience. Certain things can only be found in chests or bought with gems but if you log in daily you'll get gems instead of gold at the end of the week. A collosal chest costs 75 gems, again, with a bit of patience you'll get everything.
The gameplay is really solid and it's not hard to find a few favourite characters that you'll want to play over and over. For the most part the community, (from what I've seen,) are also generally friendly and helpful. There's nothing worse than going into a game as a genuinely new player and being made to feel useless by the rest of your team. I haven't experienced this in Paladins, not saying it doesn't happen, just not to me.
There are obviously a few cons. There aren't a ton of maps, but then this isn't necessarily a bad thing, there are also only two game modes so far. These are things that may well be remedied in time, the game has a lot of room to evolve and after all this is still the open beta.  The only really iritating thing is their banning system. Basically if the game thinks you are playing unfairly it will ban you for a given period of time and this is fine in principle, the problem is that this often happens for the wrong reasons. If you don't pick a character you'll get a 15 minute deserter ban, fine if you're not getting the character you want so you just sit there but really annoying if your connection drops and you physically can't pick. The same applies for extended afk, leaving the game early etc etc but not being able to play because your are having technical issues isn't great. This needs tweaking to something like a three strike rule, if someone is playing deliberately unfairly they aren't just going to do it once.
This being said, absolutely brilliant game. In the time you've been reading this you could have been downloading it. Go on then, get playing.

Secondly, there is a good possibility that most of the items in this review have already been posted.  The problems with this game that I have are:
1) Poor interface.  It is very difficult to navigate in the new interface:
a) The tooltip balloons do not delay no matter how they are set in the options
b) Trying to review the now stacked information items on the right of the screen is almost impossible because no only is the info selected, so is whatever is below it (terrain, unit, city, etc.) so it all sits on top of each other hiding the text below it

In my English class I had an assignment to create a review of anything I wanted but it had to be in the format of a magazine. So I chose something I genuinely cared about, my favourite game: "Life is Strange." I put in so much time and effort into this assignment that I was pleased when the teacher gave me a 94% and claimed she's interested in playing Life is Strange even with her general dislike of video games.
If you'd like to see what the review looks like with the format of a magazine, here is the
though the format still got messed up while posting it as a pdf, the white spaces are the top and bottom of pages that got merged together :/

Life is Strange is an episodic, choice-driven story game developed by Dontnod Entertainment and published by Square Enix. It has 5 episodes that were released throughout 2015 following the game’s initial release.
In Life is Strange, you play from the perspective of a 18 year old girl named Maxine Caulfield (Hannah Telle), the game begins with Max waking up from a nightmare about a storm with a tornado that rips through Arcadia Bay, the town she lives in. She wakes up in her usual photography class.
One of the first actions you can perform is taking a “selfie” with Max’s Polaroid camera, this is quite a humorous
contrast compared to what is soon to unravel.
After the class, Max rushes to the restroom to compose herself because of the nightmare. There, she witnesses Nathan Prescott (Nik Shriner) murder a girl. In one single effort, she throws her arm up and accidentally rewinds time only to end up back in her photography class. Knowing what is about to happen, she rushes to the restroom after class and sets off the fire alarm before Nathan can kill the girl. Max finds out that the girl she saved was actually her childhood friend, Chloe Price (Ashly Burch). And from there, the game unfolds.
Life is Strange is more than it might seem at first, to some it’s just your usual graphic adventure game that continues through choice. But that’s not exactly true, Life is Strange adds the aspect of time travel, meaning you can rewind time to change the choices you have made, you can see every outcome and sometimes there isn’t a “right choice” or “correct way” to do it. This can lead to some regrettable and heartbreaking choices.
The developers behind Life is Strange have made a very out-of-place game in today’s society.  Life is Strange tackles subjects that are usually taboo in videogames. Some aspects of the game are about social division, parental conflict, online bullying and even teen suicide. This is a very bold move to put all this into a game, but it genuinely works really well and adds a very “real” value to all the characters even if some are based off stereotypes.
In my opinion, this is possibly the greatest game I have ever played, which will probably surprise people I know. I bought the first episode within the month of its release and I loved it so much I bought the entire game before it was even fully released. I played every episode the day it came out and each episode left me laughing or in tears. Many choices in the game seemed to me, impossible to make. The character development and my personal love or hatred of characters made things even more difficult. But I think that was Dontnod Entertainment’s goal. There shouldn’t be an obvious “right” or “wrong” choice.
In some cases there were lip-syncing problems and to some people, Dontnod Entertainment was using “cheap” ways to progress the plot. But people are just too used to high budget games. Life is Strange started with a development team of only 15 people, that’s unbelievable to me considering every texture and piece of art in the game is hand drawn to have a really unique and distinct look.
Because of the sorts of themes in Life is Strange, suicide, online bullying, etc. The people behind Life is Strange have opened up a page on the game’s website dedicated to suicide/crisis hotlines in 14 different countries. This proves that the Life is Strange team recognises that these problems and issues seen in the game are actually real and happening everyday.  This dedication makes the game even more amazing to me.
When it was announced that a limited edition version of the game would be released as a physical copy, I took that opportunity and bought one the day it was released. It included the soundtrack, a disc for the game and a book of concept art drawn before the game’s release. The concept art was actually really amazing to look at, some of it had been loosely drawn and coloured with what looked like water colour pencils. Some was more neat and tidy, but in general the artwork was really stunning.
Overall I’d have to say Life is Strange is a 9.5/10. Everything about it was purely amazing, even though there were very sad moments throughout;  it was an absolute pleasure to play. I’d say I’m happy with the choices I made and the way it ended for me.

If you're conservative or have conservative values, you're not going to like this game that much. For starters, there's a rather large number of women in the game with short hair all colours of the rainbow. All the men in the story (thus far) are feminist stereotypes: there's the beta male Warren. There's the rich goon Nathan. There's the authoritarian step dad. There's the shifty school principal. As Lee you were given the chance to explore the area and solve puzzles, but also speak with your fellow survivors Mass Effect style. The game generally lacked such interactions, so there wasn't any real attachment to the characters like the first game. Most deaths didn't really matter, they just felt cliche. I found myself saying "oh well" rather than "oh no", and only one or two deaths really affected me. Then there's a problem with Tell Tale's story telling, where it become obvious what is going to happen. If given the choice to save someone, that person is going to die later, making your actions pointless.
Don't get me wrong though, this is still a good game. Their where some moments that really hit home, and where well worth playing through. The game tests your morals and reminds us that there might not always be a right or wrong choices. You just need to make them, and keep moving forwards. The game is worth playing if you've played and loved the original.

Overall I'd rate Cvi-6 high and look forward to any patches and future expansion packs.

Update (11/17): There has been a lot of complaining about the DLC for this game. I've bought and downloaded 4/6 DLC so far, and they have all been good. I have no complaints about any DLC that I bought. My only regret is not buying the duluxe edition! It also seems like the AI is better with the last Fall 2017 patch. The games I have played have been more competitive even on Prince. I also like the changes made to religion in the last patch. Religion seems a bit more fleshed out. It could still use some expansion though.
Overall, Civ VI is a very good game that has already provided me with over 100 hours of game play fun. Is it perfect? No, but it is very fun and worth the price. With that said, it is the most complete initial release of a Civ game that I can remember. I have played every Civ game that has ever been released, and Civ VI is a major step forward for the franchise. The new systems re-work the way I think about Civ, but don’t sacrifice the feel of a Civ game. It’s still Civ, and that’s important. This review is my take on Civ VI. There are a lot of reviews out there that go over all of the new things in Civ VI. If you need background information on things like city districts, victory types, inspiration or eureka moments please see other reviews that introduce and explain those concepts. I do not have the time to explain those here.
Some things I really like about Civ VI:
Cities
The way cities are placed and constructed in Civ VI is completely different. When placing a city in previous Civ games all you had to do was to look for good resources around the city and you were off. With the change to city districts in Civ VI the planning process of the initial city placement is completely different. You have to think far ahead (into the atomic/information era) to plan out a good city. Common questions that I ask before I place a city in Civ VI are: Does it have good food sources? How about production? Does it have fresh water or easy access to a mountain to get fresh water (this is a BIG one and they need to be within one hex of or preferably next to the city center)? Are there areas that have good adjacency bonuses for production, commercial hub, harbor, campus, and holy sites? In Civ VI regional building effects go from the district to the adjacent city center (usually within 6 hexes). So, what about regional building effects such as factories? Are they close enough to another city’s industrial zone to reap those benefits? What about wonders? Is there space for those? Lots of questions to ask before you place those cities! However, to me, this is the best aspect of Civ VI. I love planning out my cities in the ancient era, and watching them develop and grow into what I envisioned for them in the information era! This is Civilization at its best!
The Map
The map in Civilization has always been important. In Civ VI it takes center stage. A lot of the Eureka and Inspiration bonuses come from your interactions with the map and the world. Build an iron mine and get a Eureka bonus! Meet another Civ and get another Eureka bonus! Find another continent and get an Inspiration bonus! More than ever in Civ VI it’s important to explore the world. In fact, scouts now gain experience from exploration alone. Another aspect of exploring your world is to discover, early on, where oh where those darn barbarian camps are! If you do not find out where they are and deal with them early on they will find you and deal with you en mass! Don’t ignore the barbarians! However, I like this aspect of the game. It keeps you on your toes in the early parts of the game, and forces you to build your military right away. I also love how the art and artistic style revolve around the map. It is just breathtaking. You can see waves crashing on cliffs and lapping at the shoreline. The new lighting system is also nice in that the time of day constantly changes, and things look very different at night. In Civ VI you can really “play the map”. What I mean by that is you can form your Civ, and determine the victory type that you seek, by how the Map is drawn. This is true more so in Civ VI than in past Civ games. For example, if you have a lot of mountains surrounding your civ then you might want to think about a science or religious victory. Without those mountains those two victories might be a lot harder (not impossible, just harder).
Music
I love the music in Civ VI. The opening song by Christopher Tin is wonderful, and I enjoy listening to it every time the game loads. The in game music is also good in that it changes depending on the civs that you meet, and what era those civs are in. The dynamics of the music also change depending on what is happening in the game.
Some things in Civ VI that need more work:
AI
While the AI is not terrible, it’s not great either. Right now the AI is good enough to push you to keep going in whatever victory that you are seeking, but it can still make some really dumb moves. To me, really good AI is important, but it’s not a deal breaker. Since I love the complex way that you can explore and interact with the Map, and the challenging city development system the lack of a strong and smart AI is not that big of a deal to me.
Religious Combat, Diplomacy, and Spies
These are three things that really could use some work. I can totally see an expansion that includes a diplomatic victory, expanded diplomacy, expanded religious combat, and better capabilities for spies. I do like the addition of religious combat, but I feel that it needs to be expanded. I like the promotion system of military units, but that system was not brought into the religious combat system or the spy system. It just feels like it needs to be expanded and polished. I feel the same way about diplomacy. I like the new levels of access, and that the more you interact with a civ the more information that you get about that civ, and I also like that you can see why a civ likes or dislikes you. However, diplomacy also needs some expansion and polish. It’s not bad, but it could be better.
Conclusion
In conclusion, I would not hesitate to recommend Civ VI to anyone who likes strategy games or who has liked Civilization games in the past. Civ VI is truly a wonderful game. Overall, Civ VI is a high quality game despite its minor deficiencies. It is a good addition to the franchise, and I look forward to expansion packs and future DLC! Just one more turn….

I recommend any game that make me play 20+ hours, and so I ofc recommend Civ 6. One major improvement is how it handle mods - they are easily imported and activated by default and it seems to be easier to make stable mods in Civ 6 than Civ 5.
However there are flaws, there are several ways to victory, one that defeated me in my first game on the easiest difficult lvl on the smallest map vs one opponent - Egypt - was religious victory. Before I had even made a swordsman I was suddenly swarmed by missionaries and lost becuse the Egypt religion became dominating. So be careful with open borders...
But the BIG flaw I really saw when it comes to war I did see when I had AI-only game with all starter Civs (no Aztecs) on the biggest World map out there. Starting Age Renassaince, true starting locations, domination victory only. I followed it from 1500 to year 1750 before I got to bed. Greece was a dominating force in Europe, Egypt and Kongo split Africa with Spain in one corner. Brasil was better at expanding than USA, China and India - all nations with plenty of room to expand and barbarians to fight.
So when I checked the game again it was 1932 and to my... annoyance? there seemed to have been very little progress. More citys had been added, but no borders had been moved because of war and it was not because of lack of war, the AI is simply incompetent of doing sustained war at the moment it seems, even the smallest nations were still around. And first I thought the science had been screwed up because there were a lot of units around but the land units were mostly crossbowman and muskeeters and the sea units were frigattes. But looking around I found units like infantery and ironclads - but they were few indeed.
A Civ 5 game would never have turned out like this and I think it comes down to how ranged attack has been nerfed and that stacking is back, because what I saw was these old units stacked in armies with 3 musketeers forming a unit that could go to toe with far progressed single units. And upgrading armies are costly because you need money to upgrade three units at once, so the AI doesn´t bother. In Civ 1-4 games you had artillery and bombers to deal with stack of units because such attack could weaken several units in the stack at once - that isn´t the case here; because it count as one big unit.
Put this togheter and you have a pretty stale war game there science progress isn´t nearly as important as it was in Civ 5. Production is the King and religion is much more important now.

Civ 5 had left me with an extremely high standard for the next installment in the series that has yet to be met. Watching previews and seeing early gameplay, I was very pleased with what I was seeing. I loved the way the game looked and was excited to see how new city mechanics would change the game. What those first looks could never of prepared me for was how my expeince in the actual game would play out.
I find myself getting bored with my games a lot quicker than before. Because of issues with the AI, which I am not even going to adress because it is so frustrating, the only way I can stomach a game is by playing agressive against other nations. You can not play a diplomat role and stay out of conflic like other games, but the second you find youself in a war (for any reason) taking a city will label you as a warmongerer for the rest of the game. So, buckle up for hours of defensive gameplay and watching waves of missionaries roam your country. I also want to add that during this time every other AI is spending every minute denouncing one another for god knows what reason. I hate that I can no longer build roads, and even though I can, I can only build two at a time unless a send caravans to my cities. There are just so many small details about Civ 6 I can't stand but none surpass my issues with the AI.
I hope that patches come soon or that mods relased will bring back the same joy I had with Civ 5, because I  am trying to force myself to love this game.
