I will be comparing this to past Civilization games.
Lets Start off with how the game runs. The graphics are tuned down and given a more artistic style rather than the realistic style that Civilization V had. I get a Civlization Revolution feel when playing this game. With the dumbed down graphics, the game runs smoother. The turns and movements run really seemlessly and its hard to even tell when it's your turn. That being said, the game suffers from random crashes. Everytime I start a game an online game, my friend crashes at least once due to a different problem each time. I even felt the wrath of crashing before I wrote this review. All this being said, the game starts up quicker than past civ games but still rapes your ears with extremely loud music. If you can deal with the occasional crashes, and the simpler art style, then Civilization VI is your game.
Next lets talk about the Content in the game. Civilization VI has 18 civilizations in total with the Aztecs being a preorder civ, but available after the 90 day launch for free to play. Now, to compare this to Civilization V after all its dlc was released, there was 43 civs. Now obviously we can't compare an at launch game to a game that has gone through many dlcs, and game updates. I expect Civilization VI to have th same amount of Civs after all its dlc has been released, or maybe even more. 18 Civs is a good number and offers a wide variety of replayability since every civ plays differently. Whether you want to go to the conquest route that Germany offers you or the Cultural route France offers you, every single one of your play styles is there.
What did they add? So a lot of things have changed from past civ games. Civilization VI now has 2 trees to go down, a Science and a Culture tree. With the addition of the Culture tree, you know can specifically select which play style you want, rather than rushing Science in order to get a cultural victory like in past Civ games. Tech such as Civil Service is now in the cultural tree. It now makes more sense. Another thing that was added was Amnenities and Housing. Amnenities has now replaced Happiness and works the same way. If your Amnitity is too low, your production will slow down and your  population can revolt. It seems though, it's not as big of a concern as happiness was in Civilization V. Many a times did I have revolutions on my hand because my happiness was too low. There is also housing. Housing can affect how your population grows. If you don't have enough housing, your population will slow to a halt and will not expand. Near mid game, housing tends not be an issue due to the new Housing District which I will now talk about. One of the coolest things that has been added that was not in previous civ games is Districts. Districts can be built in a city and take the place of one tile and allow you to build specific buildlings. A Campus (Science) allows you to build universities and libraries. It also allows you to use a Great Scientist on it. Almost each resourse has a district. There is one for Housing, Amenities, Science, Culture, Gold, Military, and even production. The districts allow your city to look more diverse and be beautiful rather than the lands just be farms.
Lastly I just want to talk about the AI. This is the thing that really drove me to make this review. The AI suck... They almost always hate you and will turn on you in a second. Civilizations have 2 traits that a player can try to appeal to and it determines whether or not they like you. I will use Rome as an example. Rome has 2 traits, one is a set trait that he will alwyas have and one is a random trait. The set trait is, Rome likes civlizations that expand. The unkown can be anything. It is the most difficult thing to appeal to more than one Civ because their traits all vary largely. There was a time that I become friends with a civ and then they denounced me the next turn. The AI are very unstable and Ghandi is stil a warmongering♥♥♥♥♥ If you want a guarenteed win in Civilization VI, go down the Militaristic path beacuse you will go to war with atleast 6 nations whether you are friendly or not.
After reading all of this, you're probably wondering if I recommend you buy it. Yes. I do recommend you pick this game up...when it's a cheaper price. The game isn't the $60 price tag for the issues it has. Maybe if the price goes down or they fix the issues that are present, will I then recommend you go out and buy it now. But if you have Civilization V, just stick with playing it.

A game that, if it fixed the one major flaw, would be an easy recommend.
Main issue: A.I. is beyond braindead. Each civilization you meet has an agenda you can see. It tells you that a certain civilization likes it if your science is superior to theirs or if they hate warmongers. The problem is, these agendas don't seem to matter. I've gotten declarations of friendship from civilizations I am directly going against their agenda while civilizations that SHOULD like me more for meeting their "likes it when..." agenda denounce and declare war on me. Now, this would be acceptable IF the AI understood what "war" is.
My last game, I had both the Kongo and China declare war on me on the same turn with no actual provocation. Ok, however, 30+ turns later, I finally see China has sent its' army to attack me, still no sign of Kongo's armies. The problem goes even deeper here as China's "army" consists of two warriors. I easily repel China's pitiful display of force and they negotiate peace with me by giving me lots of money. During the same game, Russia declared friendship with me and one turn later declared war on me.
The A.I. doesn't seem to have the ability to properly pursue goals so it blindly and almost randomly makes decisions. What little the AI actually pursues, it seems to pursue counter to what it pursues. Washington hates warmongers, so it declares war on me and not the guys with a warmonger penalty.
IF Civ6 fixed the AI's issues, I would easily recommend the game, but as is it just isn't fun playing against an AI that is easily the worst AI I've seen in years.
The less bad issues: UI
The UI is alright, it's nothing stellar. I've still not found a good screen that shows detailed info about my Cities and I seem to run into problems as such. Diplomacy is needlessly slow (Leader says something, then slowly another menu appears in the lower left of the screen, then slowly another menu appears). Shortcuts for toggling the different map filters (showing best places to settle, etc) are placed in submenues (was a better system in Civ5 imo). The UI is hardly a deal breaker, it's functional, but it does have room for improvement.
The good:
Relatively few bugs. I've yet to really run into a noticable bug.
Civilization 6: Complete edition! Civ6, unlike Civ5 or Beyond Earth, doesn't feel like a game that needs two expansions to make it a complete game, it's its' own game that will be improved by expansions rather than rely on them.
Sound! I love the music in the game. It's just good music. The voiceacting is good (miss Nemoy though...).
The indifferent:
The art style. I'm not entirely sure how to feel about it. It's nice in some ways, but sometimes the art style makes it hard to differentiate certain terrains imo. I don't think it's bad, I don't think it's good.
TL;DR: Don't recommend solely due to the braindead AI that doesn't know what it wants or how to obtain what it seems to want. Overall, a great game ruined by a single issue.

Street Cred: I come from the position of having played a complete Civ 5, 1600 hrs, with 90% of those hours devoted to modded gameplay.
for newcomers to civ: The vanilla game (which is what the current version of this release is, Jan 2017,) is a good game that you will most likely sink several days into if you're into 4X/strategy/empire-building-type games. I give it an 8.5/10. However, if you are a newcomer to civ and want as close as you can get to a 10/10 experience: get the complete Civ 5 bundle and download the Vox Populi modpack from civfanatics, instead of Civ 6. This is what I've played for the longest time,
you can't go wrong with it. Then, when you consider yourself a veteran, read the paragraph below on considering purchasing Civ 6.
for civ veterans & those considering cost/worth ratio: Wait until this game comes out with a steam workshop, official sdk/mod tools, and a first expansion, and preferably on sale/bundled overall costing you no more than $60. These are the requirements, I think, that make it the most attractive purchase in contrast to Civ 5. You might see these requirments met sometime in Q4 of 2017. If you're that eager/that much of a civfanatic however, (then why don't you have the game already?) as I say in the above paragraph, you can't go wrong with buying the game now. I repeat, YOU CANNOT GO WRONG WITH ACQUIRING THIS GAME. It's the same civ you know but with slight changes that I'll explain below, including select changes that I like above Civ 5's game mechanics.
But first,
Explanation of some of the negative reviews: I assume a good number of the negative reviews that you'll read are from civ veterans that wanted a newly-polished COMPLETE Civ 5 or Civ 4 variant with everything from all the previous versions+ a new twist- even though it took them several days of gameplay to come to this verdict, they still give it a negative review, and here's why: What they're doing is just comparing the complete Civ 5 to 6 AS THEIR REVIEW instead of objectively critiquing Civ 6 for what it is individually. But guess what? I agree that Civ 6 doesn't compare to Civ 5... And so in the BLUF's above I mentioned what to do in regards to this.
I also suspect that the recent $5 DLC for 1 new civilization is also what's generating a bit of hate at the moment too, BUT THEN DON'T DOWNVOTE THE GAME, DOWNVOTE THAT PARTICULAR DLC INSTEAD.
But alas, my critique of the game,
This game is classic Civ: Don't expect an IBM's Watson-level AI. If you do want that experience, play multiplayer. Hopefully you won't be versing a toddler.  But, what makes the AI competitive is the advantages it gets on higher difficulties above Prince (which equals normal diffiiculty, or rather a setting that give no AI advantages nor any advantages to the player.) Personally, I find that on Emperor (3rd hardest difficulty,) that the AI gets considerable advantages akin to "cheating," and thus you'll have to GUARANTEED pump some military muscle in order to achieve victory. Sorry, but that's the way all Civ's are, newcomers, (and what 4X isn't like that?)
And thus because the AI isn't too logical, Diplomacy is kind of subpar... IF you do virtually nothing in regards to interacting with the AI. The only real diplomacy that I felt that I've been able to achieve is through "military detente," or rather aggressing a neighbor to have them not want to get crushed by my military. There exists a warscore/cassus belli system which I find stupid because the AI barely ever tries to sensibly use these game mechanics and in my experience, will only end a war if YOU or them, have a significantly higher warscore than the other. I imagine in future patches that this can be fixed to include an, "Oh crap, their navy/army is too powerful for me to successfully defend against, I should plead peace," option. Only when they're on the edge of seriously being cut down do they feel like negotiating, favorably in your manner. Note: a neutral "Let's just end this war" option does happen every now and then and isn't impossible.

And yes, there's still that outrageous trade deal negotiating that AI will attempt IF you're not friendly with them, i.e., thinking that their 1 spare luxury resource is worth 5 of your spare/not spare resources + a high Gold per turn.
There also (still) exists an automatic 15/30/45 turn [gold per turn] deal trade option which I think should be modified to include a negotiating of an exact number of turns you can pay the AI a certain gold per turn.
Next, unit upgrades: I feel that the unit upgrades lack a little depth, as in there should be more in-between units or a more fluid promotion system, or an earlier option to form a corp/army, fleet/armada to curb that advantage.
Resource allocation: Why can you only get the aluminium resource from desert tiles only?!?! It wasn't like that in Civ 5, which could be found on desert, plains, hills,  and tundra. I've had a game where I had to settle on another continent across an ocean just to get my own local aluminium.
Espionage I haven't used too much except to use my spies as counterspies to thwart the AI from sabotaging my districts. Note: the AI WILL use the espionage system to disable your district buildings, steal gold, and steal great works, so I guess it has a purpose. I've experienced the AI attempting to mess me up most often whenever I was the one in a culture/science/economic lead.
Districts are a nice addition to the game considering how in Civ 5 you could puppet an enemy city during a war but then during the capturing process, lose a bunch of buildings in the city to include factories, museums, banks, and universities thus crippling a civ from ever being able to resurge later on because of how poorly their economic, cultural, and scientific prowess had been diminished. With districts however, and in comparison to real-life Germany post WWII, razing a city entirely is the only thing you can really do to make sure another civ doesn't resurge, if for some reason you don't give the city back.
I just wish there was a way to rush/expedite the production of new districts except by just using the Aztec's special ability.
OMG, the new Civics/government system is amazing and a well thought out change to the game that makes sense. In Civ 5 you a had social policy trees that you couldn't choose to rearrange at your behest, but now you can reestablish you government easily to suit your current objectives which is NICE.
The changing of using amenities instead of happiness and localizing it to cities instead of having global happiness makes the game a whole lot simpler in regards to keeping your population from revolting/ruining your city output. It seems too easy in trying to resolve a lack of amenities and it seems more of annoyance when that requirement comes up, e.g., "Oh, well I guess I have to get that done then."
The new city-states have cool bonuses if you ally with them which is good, but the AI that controls them can be really stupid in not being able to develop their own city which sucks if you plan on using their military, so you better hope that city-state has good land.
They did a good job in being able to have different leaders for a civilization exist, this way you can vary playstyles but with the same civ which is good.
Lastly, don't let the graphics turn you away. I run Civ on DX12 with a Radeon R9 380 which works for me. It may look cartoon-like but trust me when I say this in contrast to all Civ games: it's gonna get better with patches, mods, and expansions in the future. This is a deep game that has an insane amount of replayability which definitely makes it worth the money.
------------------------------------------------------------
All in all, it's a good game with some of the same shortfalls Civ 5 had, but the (vanilla game) is different enough and a little better from Civ 5 vanilla to warrant buying it. Otherwise, follow my BLUF advice.

Im not really understanding the recent negative reviews of this game, here are a few points that people are complaining about that I dont think is justified, or at least are only partly justified.
- The artificial intelligence decision making: I think people may be under-estimating the difficulty of programming an AI for a very complex game. The true value of this game lies in multiplayer if you can find some friends that are commited to seeing a game through to the end. I too wish the AI was better, it will get better up to a point with new patches. Was Civ 5 AI amazing? People hated Civ 5 AI but it is considering one of the best in the civ franchise....
- Lack of clear artifical intelligence decision making to the player: The AI has a clear definable agenda system which is a positive development considering none of the previous Civ games had clearly definable agendas. - The recent DLC: Everyone is complaing about a $5 DLC, I mean come on its $5, it adds a few scenarios to the game, is it really what people are calling a "rip off"? A game that, if it fixed the one major flaw, would be an easy recommend.
Main issue: A.I. is beyond braindead. Each civilization you meet has an agenda you can see. It tells you that a certain civilization likes it if your science is superior to theirs or if they hate warmongers. The problem is, these agendas don't seem to matter. I've gotten declarations of friendship from civilizations I am directly going against their agenda while civilizations that SHOULD like me more for meeting their "likes it when..." agenda denounce and declare war on me. Now, this would be acceptable IF the AI understood what "war" is.
My last game, I had both the Kongo and China declare war on me on the same turn with no actual provocation. Ok, however, 30+ turns later, I finally see China has sent its' army to attack me, still no sign of Kongo's armies. The problem goes even deeper here as China's "army" consists of two warriors. I easily repel China's pitiful display of force and they negotiate peace with me by giving me lots of money. During the same game, Russia declared friendship with me and one turn later declared war on me.
The A.I. doesn't seem to have the ability to properly pursue goals so it blindly and almost randomly makes decisions. What little the AI actually pursues, it seems to pursue counter to what it pursues. Washington hates warmongers, so it declares war on me and not the guys with a warmonger penalty.
IF Civ6 fixed the AI's issues, I would easily recommend the game, but as is it just isn't fun playing against an AI that is easily the worst AI I've seen in years.
The less bad issues: UI
The UI is alright, it's nothing stellar. I've still not found a good screen that shows detailed info about my Cities and I seem to run into problems as such. Diplomacy is needlessly slow (Leader says something, then slowly another menu appears in the lower left of the screen, then slowly another menu appears). Shortcuts for toggling the different map filters (showing best places to settle, etc) are placed in submenues (was a better system in Civ5 imo). The UI is hardly a deal breaker, it's functional, but it does have room for improvement.
The good:
Relatively few bugs. I've yet to really run into a noticable bug.
Civilization 6: Complete edition! Civ6, unlike Civ5 or Beyond Earth, doesn't feel like a game that needs two expansions to make it a complete game, it's its' own game that will be improved by expansions rather than rely on them.
Sound! I love the music in the game. It's just good music. The voiceacting is good (miss Nemoy though...).
The indifferent:
The art style. I'm not entirely sure how to feel about it. It's nice in some ways, but sometimes the art style makes it hard to differentiate certain terrains imo. I don't think it's bad, I don't think it's good.
TL;DR: Don't recommend solely due to the braindead AI that doesn't know what it wants or how to obtain what it seems to want. Overall, a great game ruined by a single issue.

Im not really understanding the recent negative reviews of this game, here are a few points that people are complaining about that I dont think is justified, or at least are only partly justified.
- The artificial intelligence decision making: I think people may be under-estimating the difficulty of programming an AI for a very complex game. People who are expecting to go up against an AI with human level intelligence have expectations that far exceed what is reasonable. The true value of this game lies in multiplayer if you can find some friends that are commited to seeing a game through to the end. I too wish the AI was better, it will get better up to a point with new patches. Was Civ 5 AI amazing? People hated Civ 5 AI but it is considering one of the best in the civ franchise....
- Lack of clear artifical intelligence decision making to the player: The AI has a clear definable agenda system which is a positive development considering none of the previous Civ games had clearly definable agendas. If you want the AI to like you then dont warmonger, or perhaps use the "cassis beli" system for once
- The recent DLC: Everyone is complaing about a $5 DLC, I mean come on its $5, it adds a few scenarios to the game, is it really what people are calling a "rip off"? If you dont like scenarios dont buy it. People are complaining that the game is coming out piecemeal, which it is, but do we want the developers to incrementally add onto the game for years to come? I do! For that to happen they need an income stream.
- Crashes: I have had none, the game works smoothly and responsively.
- Uninspiring after hours of gameplay: Some people are complaining they are bored of it after clocking over 200 hours in it, need I say more? If you play a game for 200 hours it must be somewhat addictive. I have logged close to 200 hours. I might not play again for a while, but when they add new content (which they will) I will surely pick it up again. Over 200 hours in a game makes it well worth the money...
I love this game and I support the developers as they continue to develop it. Keep it up Firaxis! I appreciate you!

Don't let anybody fool you. This is not a game you play. This is a story you live. And a very touching one.
It will reach deep down into your soul and reveal your true self.
"Life is what happens while you are busy making other plans." Remember?
This experience might even make you think about your real life, about you, your friends and the choices you make every day. It will make you smile, laugh, angry, sad, you might even cry.

And after so much **** you will have to go through, when you feel it's going to get better, then ... BOOM ... there is the ending that will just blow into your face and leave you with maybe the hardest decision you ever had to make in a "game" (that feels way too much real).
It breaks my heart that it even has the end. If even could it last forever ... Well ... Everything good has to end eventually. Right?
"Welcome to the real world..."
So if you are looking for a game, well ... this is not the place. On the other hand if you are looking for an incredible and unforgettable journey that might leave a mark on you - this is a great choice.

I would very much recommend the game to casual gamers interested in a visual novel. Though the game doesn't take every choice to heart (your choices don't effect the overall plot but they do effect your relationship with people as well as future decisions), your choices do have to be careful as making the wrong choice can block certain decisions and effect how characters respond to you. The story line of the game is rich and very engaging with dark twists as well as some happy moments, and the music to the game was soothing and perfect (I personally listen to the album now when doing homework). The only cons the game has is that the mini games can sometimes be annoying and tedious, and sometimes the rewind ability bugs out (not often but it occurs) so you have to save frequently. But these small problems don't effect how well the game is made and how much I love it.
Pros:
Amazing plot
Real characters
Realistic choices (I hate interactive novels that give you three stupid choices and one decent choice)
Great music
Beautiful art and cut scenes
Story progresses very well
Choices effect relationships with characters
Cons:
Save frequently in the event of glitches (which happen if you rewind too much)
Minigames can be tedious and annoying

To me right now it's 8/10 :)  But all the negative reviews here make me worried I'll hit a wall in a few dozen hours ...
Anyway, to sum-up: unless you're die-hard hardcore strategy fan (and probably Civ 5 would not have suited you either as well because of ... unbalance etc.), Civ 6 has the same feeling of grandeur of civilization, conquest, history, etc.  And very good production value, amazing sound-track etc. I certainly recommend it!

What if you took the best interactive stories from the good FPS games, but then you weren't constrained by having to justify an FPS theme with lots of weapons and lots of baddies to shoot, and you could just make a good interactive branching story with any theme you wanted?
It might be as good as this Interactive Adventure Story.
It's not a 'game,' though. It just isn't. It has a mechanic that I would call a Story Mechanic, not a "game mechanic." I say this because the only thing affected by mechanic is the path you take to the singular conclusion. There are no other game elements, unless you count some minor Steam acheivements for finding every little interactive object in the game. There is no moment like: "You reached the least impressive ending of five different endings, are you sure you don't want to play again and do better?"
You get Life Is Strange because you want to watch a movie with a good story that you have a fair measure of control at key moments, which makes it a very interactive movie, but still a movie, not a game.
That said, I could see playing through a second time to make different decisions and see how that plays out. Because of the length, quality, and possibility of wanting to play it through a second time, I think it is worth the asking price for the full episode list.

TL:DR: If you are looking for something new in the Adventure game genre. Then, this is the game.
I grew up with point and click adventures... played all the classics. Simon the Sorcerer, Full Throttle, Grim Fandango. Saw the rise through the 2D years and the decline that followed as the market was taken over by FPS. I think the genre is finally coming to itself with these new games (like Life is Strange and Tell Tale games). It is finding a new spirit in the 3D world. One that connects much deeper emotionally than any of the predecessors, and Life is Strange is the best of the new breed so far.
For anyone following the genre, this was a long time coming. Thinking of Grim Fandango, Fahrenheit, or Dreamfall as steps in the way to "Adventure Game" maturity and the Life is Strange as the pinnacle. Each earlier step was a brilliant, yet flawed step to "Adventure Game" as a form of art. Life is Strange brings together a great scenario (Donnie Darko anyone?), relatable characters, and great visual style into a captivating whole.
And on top of it all, it works in Linux flawlessly!

I thoroughly enjoy Civ VI. It's far superior to Civ V at launch, including many features Civ V added in expansions and doing them well. There are few to no bugs from what i've seen and the art style, animation, music and leader scenes are wonderful. They added some interesting additions to diplomacy, however it feels rather useless. Right now there is no point in denouncing or trying to gain favour with other civs as the way the ai reacts via the agenda system pretty much guarantees everyone will dislike you. Denouncing is pointless as it doesnt do anything from what i can tell. They added cool intrigue features however which made knowing what your enemies and friends were up to much more interersting and important. The diplomacy still just feels too bare bones; civ IV had far better diplomacy to this day, the leaders need to feel alive, there needs to be a reason and system to do diplomacy.
The main negative for me is the AI when it comes to war. The new casus belli system adds a whole new level of potential with politics, however that is squandered by the fact going to war will ruin your entire playthrough. Every civ will deem you a warmonger, no matter the circumstance, if you capture one city, that's all it takes. I find myself avoiding war to the point im gimped the entire game, because i so badly want to do trade and diplomacy.

What if you took the best interactive stories from the good FPS games, but then you weren't constrained by having to justify an FPS theme with lots of weapons and lots of baddies to shoot, and you could just make a good interactive branching story with any theme you wanted?
It might be as good as this Interactive Adventure Story.
It's not a 'game,' though. It just isn't. It has a mechanic that I would call a Story Mechanic, not a "game mechanic." I say this because the only thing affected by mechanic is the path you take to the singular conclusion. There are no other game elements, unless you count some minor Steam acheivements for finding every little interactive object in the game. There is no moment like: "You reached the least impressive ending of five different endings, are you sure you don't want to play again and do better?"
You get Life Is Strange because you want to watch a movie with a good story that you have a fair measure of control at key moments, which makes it a very interactive movie, but still a movie, not a game.
That said, I could see playing through a second time to make different decisions and see how that plays out. Because of the length, quality, and possibility of wanting to play it through a second time, I think it is worth the asking price for the full episode list.

TL:DR: If you are looking for something new in the Adventure game genre. Then, this is the game.
I grew up with point and click adventures... played all the classics. Simon the Sorcerer, Full Throttle, Grim Fandango. I think the genre is finally coming to itself with these new games (like Life is Strange and Tell Tale games). It is finding a new spirit in the 3D world. One that connects much deeper emotionally than any of the predecessors, and Life is Strange is the best of the new breed so far.
For anyone following the genre, this was a long time coming. Thinking of Grim Fandango, Fahrenheit, or Dreamfall as steps in the way to "Adventure Game" maturity and the Life is Strange as the pinnacle. Each earlier step was a brilliant, yet flawed step to "Adventure Game" as a form of art. Life is Strange brings together a great scenario (Donnie Darko anyone?), relatable characters, and great visual style into a captivating whole.

I bought this game 3 times, kind of by accident. But gosh, I do recommend this game.
One of the reasons I admire this game is that, in spite of it's name, there's more to it than drifting in Orbit, or poring over statistics screens.
You're responsible for everything, and it's not just Rockets, but stations, probes, rovers, aircraft, bases and the like. But Squad have made it very easy to approach, with not only tutorials but (relatively) forgiving flight controls, modular vehicle construction, and also fine tweaking options which include part orientation, direction and resource level balancing.
The Engineer's report is your Friend.
Of course, this doesn't stop you from getting serious, though, and this is a good thing. If you're like Scott Manley, then you're probably one to step back and crunch a few numbers, and the game supports this to a more than acceptable extent. Maneuvers such as Gravity Turns, Orbital Slingshots and Atmospheric Braking are wholly possible, but your craft can only be in one celestial body's sphere of influence at a time, which means lagrangian points can't be reached.
The game offers a sandbox, where your actions are inconsequential if you want them to be, but each save is a persistent world (or Solar System) which can be revisited and added to.
I could list off the features, learn to write better reviews, or I could end this by saying that it's easy to see what you're buying.
I mentioned Scott Manley earlier; he is amongst a wealth of people who pushes this game to and beyond it's limits, but if you don't want to watch videos, then download the Demo build.

Been a fan of all the Civ games (except probably the Revolution version, more on that later), but I just can't recommend this one.
Here's a shortlist of the things that really brought me to a negative recommendation:
1.  Price based on other shortcomings.
2.  No user mods (one of things that kept bringing me back to other versions)
3.  Purchasable DLC as the only form of 'mods'
4.  Religion mechianic is so irritating.
There are also plenty of other things I don't particularly like about this version, but which I could overlook.  Most of those issues have been discussed at length, so I won't bother going into detail, but they are Diplomacy issues, Districts vs Improvements vs Wonders decisions, Spies guarding only disctrics, Culture and Religion victories unbalanced (far too easy to get these, so if you want to win other ways you pretty much have to disable them or get so far ahead in them and then choose not to win them), etc.
As for my original list of problems, here's my experience.  I played through a few times at release, and it was ok.  There was some issues, so I put it away for a while and just now came back to the game to see if it improved.  It hasn't.  Religion is probably the biggest problem for me.  I find myself spending half of my time managing religious units and trying to spread religion.  Seen those negative reviews for UI?  Well, that includes religion.  I didn't bother to dive into it further, but it seems like the only way for you to see how much of your religion vs an opponent's religion is in a city is to activate a religious unit.  If you don't have any, you can't see.  On top of that, the religious color overlay when you select a unit makes it really hard to see other units on the battlefield.  But the main problem is the amount of time you have to spend on religion, especially if you leave it as a victory condition and have to defend against other religions.  I turn off this victory condition now, and the game is slightly more enjoyable.  Similarly, cultural victories are pretty easy too, so I had to disable that to have a chance at the Space Race, which is arguably the most difficult to victory to achieve (although domination feels nearly impossible with game mechanics on a large map).
So after playing through it again recently, I went to see if there were any mods that might improve gameplay like in past Civ releases.  Some of the alternate scenarios and setups (Faerun, Westeros, etc) really kept bringing me back to the game.  After looking through the menus and not seeing any option for mods, I got worried, and sure enough, Firaxis hasn't released any mod tools, so NO MODS?!?!?  I could rant on an on about how this is a bad business decision and doesn't provide the experience many of us expect from playing past Civ games and all the other things wrong with it, but I'll pass and just say that it significantly drops the value of the game for me.  When I'm looking to play some more Civ, I'm going to go back to Civ 5.  I pre-ordered this and the last few Civs, but I won't be doing that again, and I won't be paying for any of the DLC included while it's full priced, if ever.
I gave the game a shot, then another shot, and I don't expect I'll be giving it another.

When I purchase an $80 game I have slightly higher expectations than when I purchase a game for $20.
Most notably, for $80 I anticipate a game with few, if any, bugs.  This game has game crashing bugs and it's been out for three months now.  For example you can't exit from the game to the Desktop without it freezing and requiring a work around to close, and from my researches this problem has existed since the game came out and clearly hasn't been addressed with some form of hotfix.  Simply unacceptable.  UPDATE: Some other silly bugs that would seem can be easily fixable: when you trade artifacts, you should be able to assign the artifact to the slot you want to put it in, otherwise you get weird effects where an artifact that would complete the theme in one museum gets put in an empty museum where it becomes locked until that museum is filled up, blocking you from having a themed museum for several turns.  Also the Persian Immortal being a "melee" unit with a range attack but because it has a ranged attack they can't capture cities.  These are the kinds of things that suggest sufficient bug testing has not been done, and considering the game has been out for awhile now and has DLCs that seems really bothersome.  Maybe focus on fixing problems before adding new stuff.
That said, about the game in particular I have mixed feelings.
I love what they did with Wonders.  It always bothered me the wonder stacking one would do in past Civs, that they have fixed this I highly commend.
The Districts thing I'm not entirely sold on yet.  It's a novel idea and I like the theory, in practice though novelty quickly wears thin and it just makes your gameplay even that much more dependent on map placement.  To truly maximize efficiencies what role your city plays is entirely determined by the landscape.  Are there hills nearby?  Industrial city.  Are there mountains and/or jungle nearby?  Science city.  Are there rivers and coastlines nearby? Trade city.  This was still somewhat true in past Civs, but with the new district system it's become even more pronounced, and the problem with this is your gameplay is railroaded.  Did you want to play for a Science victory?  Well, there are no mountains or jungle nearby so too bad, pick another path.
I was disappointed by the Civics and Great Person systems.  Although I had massive expectations on those.  I predict they'll likely be dealt with in future DLC.  For Civis my problem is the lack of interesting options.  Usually there are one or two such obviously best picks then the rest just clutter up and do nothing.  For Great People there's also a lack of options.  You can either take the current one or pass, not knowing what the next person might be.  Personally I think it would have been better if you were given the choice of two or three Great People and deciding which you wanted, that would've been more interesting.  The bios for Great People also need to be massively edited.  They are way too long, and are desperately in need of a quick tl;dr at the start of the bio to just give a quick summary of why said person is Great and important.  If I want to read the essay about their life I'll go to the Civilopedia.
Religion is a much more engaging mini game now, so that's cool.  That you only get two random perks to select on leveling up is a touch too random, as some abilities (Proselytizer and Martyr) are *so* much more useful than others (whatever one converts Barbarians and the medic one).
From early play throughs my general impression is that Buildings seem to take *way* too long to build.  Especially compared to unit production.  This Civ is feeling more like a strategic war game and less like a 4X.
Espionage has been improved IMO but the odds of success seem way off.  I consistently lose Spies to 3% death chances.
Despite all these issues I still like the game, I'll still spend hours on it, but I had greater expectations for $80, and I'm not satisfied this product in its current state lives up to my expectations.

Been a fan of all the Civ games (except probably the Revolution version, more on that later), but I just can't recommend this one.

Most of those issues have been discussed at length, so I won't bother going into detail, but they are Diplomacy issues, Districts vs Improvements vs Wonders decisions, Spies guarding only disctrics, Culture and Religion victories unbalanced (far too easy to get these, so if you want to win other ways you pretty much have to disable them or get so far ahead in them and then choose not to win them), etc.
As for my original list of problems, here's my experience.  I played through a few times at release, and it was ok.  There was some issues, so I put it away for a while and just now came back to the game to see if it improved.  It hasn't.  Religion is probably the biggest problem for me.  I find myself spending half of my time managing religious units and trying to spread religion.  Seen those negative reviews for UI?  Well, that includes religion.  I didn't bother to dive into it further, but it seems like the only way for you to see how much of your religion vs an opponent's religion is in a city is to activate a religious unit.  If you don't have any, you can't see.  On top of that, the religious color overlay when you select a unit makes it really hard to see other units on the battlefield.  But the main problem is the amount of time you have to spend on religion, especially if you leave it as a victory condition and have to defend against other religions.  I turn off this victory condition now, and the game is slightly more enjoyable.  Similarly, cultural victories are pretty easy too, so I had to disable that to have a chance at the Space Race, which is arguably the most difficult to victory to achieve (although domination feels nearly impossible with game mechanics on a large map).
So after playing through it again recently, I went to see if there were any mods that might improve gameplay like in past Civ releases.  Some of the alternate scenarios and setups (Faerun, Westeros, etc) really kept bringing me back to the game.  After looking through the menus and not seeing any option for mods, I got worried, and sure enough, Firaxis hasn't released any mod tools, so NO MODS?!?!?  I could rant on an on about how this is a bad business decision and doesn't provide the experience many of us expect from playing past Civ games and all the other things wrong with it, but I'll pass and just say that it significantly drops the value of the game for me.  When I'm looking to play some more Civ, I'm going to go back to Civ 5.  I pre-ordered this and the last few Civs, but I won't be doing that again, and I won't be paying for any of the DLC included while it's full priced, if ever.
I gave the game a shot, then another shot, and I don't expect I'll be giving it another.

I bought this game 3 times, kind of by accident. But gosh, I do recommend this game.
One of the reasons I admire this game is that, in spite of it's name, there's more to it than drifting in Orbit, or poring over statistics screens.
You're responsible for everything, and it's not just Rockets, but stations, probes, rovers, aircraft, bases and the like. But Squad have made it very easy to approach, with not only tutorials but (relatively) forgiving flight controls, modular vehicle construction, and also fine tweaking options which include part orientation, direction and resource level balancing.
The Engineer's report is your Friend.
Of course, this doesn't stop you from getting serious, though, and this is a good thing. If you're like Scott Manley, then you're probably one to step back and crunch a few numbers, and the game supports this to a more than acceptable extent. Maneuvers such as Gravity Turns, Orbital Slingshots and Atmospheric Braking are wholly possible, but your craft can only be in one celestial body's sphere of influence at a time, which means lagrangian points can't be reached.
The game offers a sandbox, where your actions are inconsequential if you want them to be, but each save is a persistent world (or Solar System) which can be revisited and added to.
I could list off the features, learn to write better reviews, or I could end this by saying that it's easy to see what you're buying.
I mentioned Scott Manley earlier; he is amongst a wealth of people who pushes this game to and beyond it's limits, but if you don't want to watch videos, then download the Demo build.

I'm still fairly new to this game but I felt I should leave a review anyway, based on my experience so far:
Positive:
Great music, nice graphics (this is subjective, some people don't like the cartoonish look).
The game runs a lot smoother than Civ 5 in terms of taking turns, it's quicker to cycle through players and doesn't bog you down
Menu is simple and sleek, I love it. Easy to navigate around.
A lot of the gameplay feels simplified and more automated like "set and forget" compared to civ 5. I think this is a good thing though. There's a lot to manage in a game like Civ 5 and the last thing you want is your teammate spending all night taking his turn. I think the City-State improvements are excellent.
I'm going to say the builder system is a positive. Originally I hated what they did with builders, and how they behave, but now I can see that it makes sense and it's a welcome addition to the new game.
Negatives:
The multiplayer is fun, but my friend and I felt ourselves left wanting. The game, on the surface, feels very much like Civ 5, with only deeper aspects of the gameplay having been tweaked by the devs - not a bad thing, just an observation. The Civic tree and Government system are all different, and the technology tree is similar but you can look ahead to what you want, and set and forget it. Top stuff.
The game still makes me feel like I need to gear myself towards a particular victory type from the get go...and it always feels like military. Teams walking in on my territory and building bases right next to me and generally just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off...I feel the only way to get the spots I want on the map are to kill others for it...great if you like a militaristic style of gameplay but that isn't for everyone.
Still the same old barbarian behaviour, invading my base from a very early game and setting me back dramatically, it doesn't feel any different from civ 5 in that aspect.
My biggest gripe is with the UI. There are a lot of issues with this. Moving the mouse to the edge of the screen moves the map, and I was thrilled to see this was an option - until I moved my mouse to what I thought was the top of my screen - but no - Civ 6 game deems the "top" of my screen to be the section immediately below the bar at the top of the screen - the most annoying thing I've ever experienced and I don't know why the game does this. It drives me mad having to click and drag, or use the arrow keys to scout across the map. Please fix this.
The other issues with UI are minor, like when you hover over a notification at the side of the screen, all it does is tell you info about the tile in the background.
Overall I'm loving Civilization VI and I think for anyone who has played the previous games, this is a must have. Civ V still has plenty of life left in it but most certainly I will be playing this game for a long time.

I have been playing Civilization since the very first installment. Unlike the 3rd, which was a horrible mess, the 6th one has a lot of potential.
A lot of the gameplay changes make sense and actually improved a game series that already  was pretty great. I like the idea of wonders taking up tiles, merchants building roads behind themselves and the concept of districts.
The game has some issues, though. The AI is a mess. Other civs will declare war on you for no apparent reason other than you merely existing. After the war has ended, you will be the only one stricken by warmonger penalties (no matter, if you actually started it) and other Civs WILL declare war on you pretty early. It is not a matter of "if"... you can basically set your clock according to it. Barbarians will go horribly out of their way, just to chase down player units, ignoring all others, even if it kills them one turn later. The graphics were a bit too cartoonish for my taste in the beginning, but I actually got used to it. The only thing about the art stye that stil bothers me a lot, is the fact that the game map is a horrbile cluster f*ck. You can barely recognize anything, because the icons for ressources (you can turn them off, but that really destroys the last bit of overview) and the general art style don't go together very well. Icons and numbers will be obstructed by units and the colors of different tile types are hideous at times.
It seems that they focused the AI too much on hindering the player than actually simulate a breathing world. I don't always want to be the epicenter of everything going on in a game world. I want to relax and enjoy watching two tribes going to war, or barbarians take down the opposing scout, just before he reaches that tribal village. Sadly this doesn't happen, because all the AI actions seem focused on the player.
Still, I would recommend it anytime, if you are a Civilization fan. They already did some minor improvements ("Alert" option was missing for units .... really? It still doesn't work, though. Your units won't "wake up" properly.) and I bet more will follow. It is still an enjoyable Civ game, even with its current flaws, although the AI issues can be game ruiners at times.
P.S.: Sean Bean is awesome as narrator :)
P.P.S.: A lot of you guys need to remember that Civ 5 was actually close to unplayable until the first expansion came out.

I have been playing Civilization since the very first installment. Unlike the 3rd, which was a horrible mess, the 6th one has a lot of potential.
A lot of the gameplay changes make sense and actually improved a game series that already  was pretty great. I like the idea of wonders taking up tiles, merchants building roads behind themselves and the concept of districts.
The game has some issues, though. The AI is a mess. Other civs will declare war on you for no apparent reason other than you merely existing. After the war has ended, you will be the only one stricken by warmonger penalties (no matter, if you actually started it) and other Civs WILL declare war on you pretty early. It is not a matter of "if"... you can basically set your clock according to it. Barbarians will go horribly out of their way, just to chase down player units, ignoring all others, even if it kills them one turn later. The graphics were a bit too cartoonish for my taste in the beginning, but I actually got used to it. The only thing about the art stye that stil bothers me a lot, is the fact that the game map is a horrbile cluster f*ck. You can barely recognize anything, because the icons for ressources (you can turn them off, but that really destroys the last bit of overview) and the general art style don't go together very well. Icons and numbers will be obstructed by units and the colors of different tile types are hideous at times.
It seems that they focused the AI too much on hindering the player than actually simulate a breathing world. I don't always want to be the epicenter of everything going on in a game world. I want to relax and enjoy watching two tribes going to war, or barbarians take down the opposing scout, just before he reaches that tribal village. Sadly this doesn't happen, because all the AI actions seem focused on the player.
Still, I would recommend it anytime, if you are a Civilization fan. They already did some minor improvements ("Alert" option was missing for units .... really? It still doesn't work, though. Your units won't "wake up" properly.) and I bet more will follow. It is still an enjoyable Civ game, even with its current flaws, although the AI issues can be game ruiners at times.
P.S.: Sean Bean is awesome as narrator :)
P.P.S.: A lot of you guys need to remember that Civ 5 was actually close to unplayable until the first expansion came out.

I wouldn't recommend this game in its current form. It needs some pretty hard tweaking on the numbers for it to be a viable game. Certainly the gameplay of every iteration of the civilization franchise has changed from the previous one, but in this version there are many things that are lacking.
1. The AI. The ai is often incredibly dumb. They couldn't fight their way out of a paper bag. The number of suprise wars is staggering, yet making peace is just as easy. You are constantly inundated with the AI's "advice" about your country, but soon these screens are annoying as they take up too much time.
2. The production costs. In the game units/buildings/districts take way too long to produce. I'm playing on the "online" speed (double the speed of the normal game) and it still takes forever. The cost of districts is simply too high, it feels like players need to be focus on hammers/production much more than ever before.
3. The interface is just bad. The mouse over to expand elements is finicky at best and downright frustrating at worst. The game will NOT let you do things out of order easily. When I'm in the middle of waging a war I want to go focus on managing units, not being FORCED to pick science and production for my cities first (and sometimes you are FORCED to deal with certains things at certain times regardless of what you want.) Additionally, the diplomacy screens drone on and on, and even getting to the menu to click through them takes a long time. I LOVED them at first, the animation quality and emotive content was great, but now it's tiring to have to wait so long.
Overall civ 6 feels like a bad move, it seems like they took the idea that a game of civilization should last a long time and turned it up to 11, in a BAD way. Things take way too long, the interface is confusing, there is a conspicuous lack of options to alleviate these minor problems, and the game just feels unpolished. I play games to relax, and I only have a limited amount of free time to play them. It's frustrating when it seems like someone designed a game to take a long time on purpose, not designed an awesome well paced game I want to spend a lot of time playing.

Life is Strange is an episodic mystery game. It’s all about the story, and the gameplay mostly serves as a bridge between new bits of the story. The gameplay is normally solving simple puzzles or finding items, along with a couple minor stealth bits. The puzzles in the earlier episodes can be a bit annoying to figure out, but as time went on the developers learned to make the puzzles less time consuming and let the gameplay take an even bigger backseat to the story. In short, you definitely do not buy this game for the gameplay.
The visuals in Life is Strange are absolutely amazing. The graphics themselves are fairly low quality even on max settings, but they serve their purpose just fine. The game makes good use of color and shadows throughout to fit the tone of scenes. The most impressive part of the visuals, however, is how each shot in a cutscene is done. The game mimics the focus of a camera in every shot. More than that though, you can tell that every shot in every cutscene was set up with meticulous care. The level of attention that is given to how the camera is positioned in every cutscene is on the level of a movie; honestly it’s a lot better than most movies. The result is cutscenes that have so much more emotional impact than if time hadn’t been put into the framing of shots, as well as appearing truly visually stunning at many points.
The story is an extremely engrossing mystery tale that has some unexpected twists and turns. All of the major twists in the game are hinted at in subtle manners, making me have a lot of “oh my god, I can’t believe I didn’t see that coming” moments while playing. You’re also expected to make a lot of dialogue choices that do actually have impacts on the story at large, which makes what happens in the story all the more meaningful to the player. I personally found myself crying at multiple points in the story.
Lastly, the characters come off as fairly real and believe. There’s a few voice actors whose performances seemed somewhat weak in my uneducated opinion, but the voice actors for the two main characters (Max and Chloe) both did an excellent job. The game really does an amazing job at making you feel for the characters that are part of its story, even making you feel bad for most of the game's “villains” at one point or another (except for a certain shitbag who will not be named for spoiler reasons).
All in all, Love is Strange is a remarkable story with great visual direction. I would strongly recommend this to anyone who has the slightest interest in story-driven games. It is one of the few games that I have played that is truly deserving of a 10/10 score.

Telltale's The Walking Dead Season 2 is a fantastic game that continues off of the first Season, which was possibly the greatest story ever written, and definetly the best story in a video game that oyu will ever find. +Characters: The characters, both new and old, are all fantastic. There are some who you will like and trust, and others that you will hate(not due to bad writting) right off the bat. It's just as good as the first Season in this regard, and does a great job introducing the new cast for this Season. Even after only one episode, you may get attached to some of the characters who helped oyu out in the beginning.
+Story: The story itself has several twists and turns, and is phenominal as a whole. The whole point of The Walking Dead Franchise is to show stories about characters in difficult stiuations, and osme of the situations that oyu will encounter as Clementine are just absolutely gut-wrenching.
+Dialouge(Acting): The dialouge is great, as always with a Walking Dead game. The acting form all of the characters is also fantastic, just like Season One, and just like The Wolf Among Us. There's nothing to complain about, and plenty to praise.
+Improved UI: The UI seems to have been improved upon since last Season. Overall, it's more fluid, and there are more options in how things will be dispalyed. Another fix is are the actual choices, you no longer have to scroll through a bunch of options displayed in small font, now, whenever given a choice, several boces will appear on the screen that you just click on. Actions have also been improvee, using the same radial memu that appears when mousing over something from The Wolf Among Us.
+Improved QTEs: My biggest problem with Season One were the lame QTEs. Basically, every QTE in that season was just "Mash Q until the box fills up, then hit E". This season takes the dodging and fighting QTEs from Wolf Among Us, making use of the arrow keys and the mouse. QTEs and Choices have also been integrated, just making things a little smoother.
-Episode Length: My biggest, and really only problem with this Episode is that it's about half the length of a normal episode. On average, it takes about an hour and a half to finish, but if you're a little quicker, then it really only takes about an hour, the length of an episode from the TV Series. On top of the fact that the game was actually delayed once in October, and again in November, this isn't a good thing.
Overall, this game is definetly worth and buying, and definetly worth your time if you're into story based Interactive adventures. However, if you're looking for something with a similar concept, but with more gameplay, then I'd point oyu in the direction of State of Decay.

Even though it seems as though everyone in the review section considers this a cheap alternative to overwatch, there are some aspects in which Paladin outperforms even Overwatch. The primary purpose of this review is to hopefully help people stop seeing this as an "Overwatch clone" and instead be judged as it's own game.
Paladins' biggest strength comes in how it handles the moba-ish elements. Unlike most hero based shooters, there is actual progression throughout a game. Characters can buy upgrades to suit a game. For example, if an enemy composition has high amounts of shields, champions can buy an upgrade which increases damage on shield. This extra layer of depth greatly increases how the game can be played, allowing players to adapt and customize how they want to play.
Speaking of customization, Paladins allows players to alter how a certain character can be played to their personal tastes. The cards in Paladins are used to this effect. They range from simple to playstyle-altering. A card can be as simple as faster reload speed or as big as giving entire teams a shield. This has a huge impact on how a character can be played without changing what the hero truly is. A support that decides to play an offensive role can still heal while dishing out damage. Because of this, there is freedom in changing how a champion is played while still retaining the same core, players will never be guessing how a character is customized because of this.
The skill kit of each champion is designed in a way that not a single champion is forced to play a single role. Compared to Overwatch, Mercy will always be forced to play as a support healer, any other playstyle is unviable. But in Paladins, Pip, who is normally played as a healer, can be played as an offensive flanker. It can be seen as a good thing to have a roster of characters with specific roles, but because Paladins is mostly designed around a king of the hill and payload hybrid game mode, this character design is terrific. Because players cannot change character and the objective of teams' can change during game, this ensures that characters never become dead weight throughout a game.
Those are the biggest strengths of Paladins has over other hero shooters in the market. The game is still in beta, some ideas aren't fully fleshed out, but even in its current state, I expect great things from this title.

I wouldn't recommend this game in its current form. It needs some pretty hard tweaking on the numbers for it to be a viable game. Certainly the gameplay of every iteration of the civilization franchise has changed from the previous one, but in this version there are many things that are lacking.
1. The AI. The ai is often incredibly dumb. They couldn't fight their way out of a paper bag. The number of suprise wars is staggering, yet making peace is just as easy. You are constantly inundated with the AI's "advice" about your country, but soon these screens are annoying as they take up too much time.
2. The production costs. In the game units/buildings/districts take way too long to produce. I'm playing on the "online" speed (double the speed of the normal game) and it still takes forever. The cost of districts is simply too high, it feels like players need to be focus on hammers/production much more than ever before.
3. The interface is just bad. The mouse over to expand elements is finicky at best and downright frustrating at worst. The game will NOT let you do things out of order easily. When I'm in the middle of waging a war I want to go focus on managing units, not being FORCED to pick science and production for my cities first (and sometimes you are FORCED to deal with certains things at certain times regardless of what you want.) Additionally, the diplomacy screens drone on and on, and even getting to the menu to click through them takes a long time. I LOVED them at first, the animation quality and emotive content was great, but now it's tiring to have to wait so long.
Overall civ 6 feels like a bad move, it seems like they took the idea that a game of civilization should last a long time and turned it up to 11, in a BAD way. Things take way too long, the interface is confusing, there is a conspicuous lack of options to alleviate these minor problems, and the game just feels unpolished. I play games to relax, and I only have a limited amount of free time to play them. It's frustrating when it seems like someone designed a game to take a long time on purpose, not designed an awesome well paced game I want to spend a lot of time playing.

I love strategy games, especially civ series, all the way back to SNES game but I honestly cannot recommend this game.
This doesn't feel like the old Civ games, you'll hear it's better than 5, and it is, but that’s because 5 was the worst of the bunch, this game just doesn't compare to Civ 4, or Civ 2.
To me a Civ game, or any game with the same model should be around exploring at the start, setting up a zone of control that feels big enough to be a "country" then either engage in war or diplo or science etc depending on your style/mood, but this game doesn't deliver for the following:
- Map size:
Even when playing on the biggest map, it still feels small, it doesn't feel like a world, it's more like a tabletop game map
- Cramped:
Making the map issue worse is the cramped feeling, even if you chose a big map and have less players, you will still somehow find yourself a few steps from another nation, and if you actually get the recommended amount, then it just gets insane
- Religions
Religions just seem bland, there isn't really any difference from choosing one religion or the next, nor is there a chronological orders for religions. It kind of takes away from the grand journey that civ is supposed to be
-Stupidity of AI
So many people have talked about this, but you have to see it to believe it, the game just feels broken
-Lack of innovation
Sure the district thing is cool, sure there have been positive revamps of old mechanics, but when you look back each civ strived to do something unique, like introduction of religion, intro of culture, intro of the city states (even if it was badly done in Civ 5), one city challenge etc., in Civ 6, nothing game changing, no new mechanic, this just feels bland, it's the same victory conditions, same civs and leaders
- Soundtrack
For the first time ever I found myself muting Civ, it is just that bad, I mean just that "song" when the game loads has become my most hated song ever
-Mod Support
Sure you can tell yourself that there are mods that will help with the above, but if you try to make the map too big for example, the game takes forever to load etc
- Price
Even on sale it's expensive, this game is worth at best 20-30$ in my opinion
Overall: Shiny, looks good, but if you want to play CIv, play CIv an earlier version that already has all the DLCs.

I love strategy games, especially civ series, all the way back to SNES game but I honestly cannot recommend this game.
This doesn't feel like the old Civ games, you'll hear it's better than 5, and it is, but that’s because 5 was the worst of the bunch, this game just doesn't compare to Civ 4, or Civ 2.
To me a Civ game, or any game with the same model should be around exploring at the start, setting up a zone of control that feels big enough to be a "country" then either engage in war or diplo or science etc depending on your style/mood, but this game doesn't deliver for the following:
- Map size:
Even when playing on the biggest map, it still feels small, it doesn't feel like a world, it's more like a tabletop game map
- Cramped:
Making the map issue worse is the cramped feeling, even if you chose a big map and have less players, you will still somehow find yourself a few steps from another nation, and if you actually get the recommended amount, then it just gets insane
- Religions
Religions just seem bland, there isn't really any difference from choosing one religion or the next, nor is there a chronological orders for religions. It kind of takes away from the grand journey that civ is supposed to be
-Stupidity of AI
So many people have talked about this, but you have to see it to believe it, the game just feels broken
-Lack of innovation
Sure the district thing is cool, sure there have been positive revamps of old mechanics, but when you look back each civ strived to do something unique, like introduction of religion, intro of culture, intro of the city states (even if it was badly done in Civ 5), one city challenge etc., in Civ 6, nothing game changing, no new mechanic, this just feels bland, it's the same victory conditions, same civs and leaders
- Soundtrack
For the first time ever I found myself muting Civ, it is just that bad, I mean just that "song" when the game loads has become my most hated song ever
-Mod Support
Sure you can tell yourself that there are mods that will help with the above, but if you try to make the map too big for example, the game takes forever to load etc
- Price
Even on sale it's expensive, this game is worth at best 20-30$ in my opinion
Overall: Shiny, looks good, but if you want to play CIv, play CIv an earlier version that already has all the DLCs.

I'll start with this: If you're looking for a game where you have an enemy to fight, don't get this. If you're looking for a game where you receive pre-made badges or achievements for doing things the devs decided were accomplishments, don't get this game. If, however, you're looking for a game where you will spend hours crashing, dying, and all around failing just to get to the next step in your gameplay, THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU!!! This game has taught me to be prepared for anything, to stop forgetting♥♥♥♥♥♥when I launch, and the worthiness and all-around awesome feeling you can get when you try to do something over and over, and eventually you make it there.
Getting out of the atmosphere: 30 minutes. Getting to the Mun: Couple hours. Getting BACK from the Mun? A long time. This game may punish you for forgetting something, or it may be an easy salvage that will take 10 minutes to fix.
But overall, this game teaches you a lot about orbital physics, and how to solve problems. It will give you a sense of accomplishment I haven't ever felt from any other game I've played. Sure you may think "Oh, you got some people back from the Mun and landed them back home. Whatever." What you don't know is that the first mission sorta-crashed, leaving my men stranded without an engine. So I had to send a second mission just to rescue them, only to run out of fuel in orbit. At this point I was in it for the long haul, so a THIRD mission was sent to rendevous with the second mission, take the Kerbals on board, and bring them home. And I've never felt better about failing so miserably. 9/10 Because bugs are annoying, and the Kraken will ruin your night.

Life is Strange is an episodic mystery game. It’s all about the story, and the gameplay mostly serves as a bridge between new bits of the story. The gameplay is normally solving simple puzzles or finding items, along with a couple minor stealth bits. The puzzles in the earlier episodes can be a bit annoying to figure out, but as time went on the developers learned to make the puzzles less time consuming and let the gameplay take an even bigger backseat to the story. In short, you definitely do not buy this game for the gameplay.
The visuals in Life is Strange are absolutely amazing. The graphics themselves are fairly low quality even on max settings, but they serve their purpose just fine. The game makes good use of color and shadows throughout to fit the tone of scenes. The most impressive part of the visuals, however, is how each shot in a cutscene is done. The game mimics the focus of a camera in every shot. More than that though, you can tell that every shot in every cutscene was set up with meticulous care. The level of attention that is given to how the camera is positioned in every cutscene is on the level of a movie; honestly it’s a lot better than most movies. The result is cutscenes that have so much more emotional impact than if time hadn’t been put into the framing of shots, as well as appearing truly visually stunning at many points.
The story is an extremely engrossing mystery tale that has some unexpected twists and turns. All of the major twists in the game are hinted at in subtle manners, making me have a lot of “oh my god, I can’t believe I didn’t see that coming” moments while playing. You’re also expected to make a lot of dialogue choices that do actually have impacts on the story at large, which makes what happens in the story all the more meaningful to the player. I personally found myself crying at multiple points in the story.
Lastly, the characters come off as fairly real and believe. There’s a few voice actors whose performances seemed somewhat weak in my uneducated opinion, but the voice actors for the two main characters (Max and Chloe) both did an excellent job. The game really does an amazing job at making you feel for the characters that are part of its story, even making you feel bad for most of the game's “villains” at one point or another (except for a certain shitbag who will not be named for spoiler reasons).
All in all, Love is Strange is a remarkable story with great visual direction. I would strongly recommend this to anyone who has the slightest interest in story-driven games. It is one of the few games that I have played that is truly deserving of a 10/10 score.

I've resisted writing a review but with the recent spats of poor reviews have made me want to give my postive opinion. Civ VI isn't a perfect game by any means. It has a lot of improvements over previous Civ Games and has a number of issues that need to be polished.
- The AI. The first and biggest issue is the AI. Out of all the complaints you hear, this one is by far the most valid. The AI is just plain bad. It can barely take cities when they have walls, can't really fight a war, can't really keep up in science and culture etc. However it has improved since the game came out. It is now actually possible to maintain alliances and such if you aren't a warmonger.  One point that people make a lot is that the AI freaks out and declares war in the first 50 turns. This is a feature not a bug. There are no warmonger penalities for Civs in the Ancient Era so you can freely take cities with no diplomatic hits. Early cities also lack walls and can be taken with a handful of units. The AI isn't the only one who can take advantage of an early war to cripple an opponent, so can you.
-The UI. The UI is just clunky. It's missing a few features like the production queue that would have been nice. It's not as bad as people make it out to be though.
-Scaling and Rate. One problem (which has been addressed somewhat but isn't quite there yet) is that of the game rate and scaling. Science snowballs hardcore as the game goes on. In the early eras you're spending 10-12 turns rearching a tech, in the late game it's rarely more than 3-5. Eurekas are part of this issues. Eurekas give you 50% cost reduction for a tech if you unlock them. This means that the player can shoot for these much better than the AI can and speed ahead in tech as a result. The lack of a production queue also makes managing large empire more difficult. Scaling is an issue with your empire size. Right now bigger is better, and more annoying. District cost scales with the number of techs and civics you unlock so founding cities later in the game is much more difficult, because of a silly and arbitrary increase in production cost. Builders and Settlers also increase in cost every time you build/buy one. While this is trying to solve empires just exploding in size, it's honestly a♥♥♥♥♥♥poor way to go about it.
-Completeness. This is the most content heavy Civ game on release. The only major feature missing is the World Congress from Civ V. It has religion, archaeology, spies, trade routes etc. If you remember the Civ V release and how bare it is, this game does not make the same mistake.
-Modding Community. Even without official support out yet the modding community is going strong! A lot of the issues I listed up above are addressed in mods that are already out. Just google Civ VI Creation and Customization to find it.
-Districs. Oh  wow, where do I start. The districts are a lot of fun. It require planning out a city even when your placing it. No more just beelining a factory and university in every city. Each distric revieces bonuses for certain terrain and tile improvements and so picking where to put one matters. Do you put a campus next to those mountains, or a holy site? An encampment or and entertainement district? It adds a lot to the city management.
-Wonders. You have to build wonders on actual tiles now (as opposed in the cities in previous Civ games). So building that Oracle means you sacrifice a mine. Building a wonder means something now and most of the wonders are actually more 'wonderful' rather than a few points of culture and great people points,
-Great People. Each individual Great Person does something different. Adam Smith gives you an economic policy card slot while another Great Merchant might give you acccess to a unique luxury. But it's now a competition. Each Great Person is unique. And if Gandhi gets Gustav Eiffel, you can't. You can also patronize great people for rather high costs of faith and gold, useful for nabbing the one you really want.
-Music. This game has by far the best music of any Civ game I've played (except Baba Yetu). I actually listen to the music most games rather than my own.
-The Return of Wide. Maybe they went to far in this but I don't think so. The game is to build an Empire which will stand the test of time not a 4 city next turn simulator. Tall is still somewhat viable but build and conquer to your hearts content. The only thing that will really stop you is amenities.
-Civics. Civics are the replacement of social policies in Civ VI. Each government type has a set number of policy card slots coming in 4 types; Military, Economic, Diplomatic and Wildcard. Military policy card reduce unit maintenance, production rates for units, production rates for defenses and encampments as well as a number of other military focused features. Economic policy cards boost districts, provide housing and improve trade routes. Diplomatic policy cards are the least common and mostly deal with City State diplomacy and Spies. Wildcard policy cards boost the production of great people but the slots can be used for any policy card. The policy cards let you empire react to events around it. If you're at war you might drop the garrison amenity bonus for +50% production of melee and ranged units.
-Modded Multiplayer. Do I really need to explain this one?
-Art Style. I personally like the art style but a good portion of people don't. This is more of a matter of opinion than anything.
-Tech Tree and Civic Tree. The technology tree feels a little bare, mostly because some of what was normally on the tech tree is now on the Civic Tree (basically a culture tech tree). I don't think this is bad in practice but it feels a little off.
-Envoys. City States are now influenced by the number of envoys you have at them. They are much less annoying than thew old influence system but at the same time mean you can basically ignore City States one you have a number inside them.
Overall Civ VI is a good game that needs spit and polish. If you you're super concious about money pick up the Civ V complete edition. On the other hand if you want a new Civ game to toy around with then go right ahead. Firaxis has a history of taking games that are somewhat issue prone and fixing them up. In the mean times go download some damned mods.

All adult adventure game, zombie horror, and The Walking Dead fans MUST play these games.  There are not enough superlatives to describe how well the stories in both seasons (and the mini shorts in 400 days) are written.  This is what story telling in a game is all about.  The gameplay itself is fairly simple and there isn't much reflex/twitch gaming skill required at all.
