While I wasn't impressed when I first bought it, this game turned out to be quite fun. While it definitely took some time, what kept me from really appreciating this game was its diplomacy. I think most people that have played this game can agree with me on that, it’s this game's Achilles heel. At first I was so upset that almost every game I was getting denounced left and right, but after a while I think anyone that plays more than 5 or so games of this will get used to the AI and even be able to manipulate it to their liking, pretty much like most civ games in the past. Of course, that depends on difficulty, and I usually only play at prince or king at most, so your results may differ. I do realize that it's not perfect, but for me it's manageable. Also, all Fraxis can do is go up, so I have high hopes for the future of this game as well.
While I think everyone is worried about diplomacy (and rightfully so) other new features such as districts, which add more organization and important decision making into the game, along with other features such as tech and civic boosts which have you do tasks to help bring you technologically ahead of the game adds an interesting flavor to this game which I wouldn't have expected otherwise. While sometimes I do like to just zone out while playing, having the chance to be actively engaged during the late game is a huge plus for me. Also, not mentioned as often, keeping features from Civ 5 Brave New World Expansion also made this game that much more familiar. I think they made the right amount of changes while keeping essentials that fans really enjoyed from the previous game.
Overall, I think this game is pretty alright. Don't get me wrong, I don't think this game is worth 60 dollars in its current state, but if you happen to get it with a sale or as a gift I would highly recommend keeping at it and not getting discouraged by its faults. Every civ game takes getting used to, and I feel this one is no different.

The first season of The Walking Dead, following in the footsteps of the comic book and television series, was a deep look at what is left of humanity after the death and zombification of most humans. The five episodes of the season were less like episodes of a television show and more like episodes of strife; they came upon the videogame playing public like a storm and settled there all year, making us both sad and elated until the tragic completion of the saga. The narrative and emotional weight that The Walking Dead Season 1 dumped on us caused a collective reaction that put the game in the number one spot of many game of the year lists, and since that time we have been awaiting the further adventures of a now-alone Clementine. In a world where most games fail to live up to the hype, CIV 6 gives me hope. This game is a charm. I was expecting the true sequel to CIV 5 to be very much a cookie cutter experience (Not a bad thing as CIV 5 is great), but I was plesantly surprised. All the tweaks like civic trees, government systems, how great people work, builders, and more help make this game feel MUCH different than any game before. This means I still have reasons for playing CIV5 (like having a build queue in cities, WHY DID YOU REMOVE THIS FIRAXIS???) but in the future, CIV 6 will be taking most of my time. First off, I want to say that I love the strategy genre. I grew up playing the Age of Empires franchise, and have easily invested 500 hours into Civilization IV and V. I have tried to enjoy this game, but this has become an increasingly difficult task. While there are some aspects that I thoroughly enjoy, such as the increased customization and late-game intricacies, the AI is just awful. At a point in my most recent playthrough on King difficulty, every one of the 10 civilizations in the game were at war with every other civilization, including myself. In all of my playthroughs, diplomacy has been a footnote, and military strategy has been undercut by mundane upkeep. I find myself having to manually set the tiles worked by citizens because the city outputs are so imbalanced. Warmonger penalties in this game are utterly ridiculous. Despite another civilization declaring war on me, I am not able to take their cities or win the war in any way without completely destroying my reputation with every other civilization. Civs will routinely decline my trade offers, yet propose the same deals with extra resources for me the very next turn. The government system is interesting, yet underwhelming. It's sad to see such a level of opportunity to increase diplomacy and complexity be completely wasted, serving mainly to cut relations between civilizations. Overall, I want to love this game, but until the AI is improved, it remains practically unplayable.

Simple space travel not interesting enough for you?  Well, get a mod that allows you to create habitats on other worlds or mods that force you to pay attention to how much food, water, and oxygen your crew have. Please, getting this game will not be a decision that you regret.  It's one small step for a kerbal, one giant leap for kerbalkind

Civ VI takes the tried-and-true formula of Civ V and alters it in some promising ways. The addition of disticts, the civics tree, religious victories, and more goverment types are welcome. In particular, I like how the system of unit promotions has been changed. Tactical combat feels well-balanced and an improvement over Civ V. Civ VI also succeeds in streamlining the midgame, whereas it was easy to feel stagnant and bogged down in Civ V. The cartoon graphics are nothing special, but nor are they ugly. Meanwhile, the sleek aesthetic of the menu screens is pretty cool.

However, my positive recommendation of Civ VI comes with an important caveat: I assume Firaxis will patch some of the game's current flaws. Namely, diplomacy. The AI is absurdly hostile to human players and not sophisticated enough for hidden agendas to feel like anything more than an obstacle. Having a different type of government (a likely situation, given that there are 10 types) is also a major hindrance to peaceful relations.  During my first 26 hours of gameplay on Prince difficulty, at no point was any AI civ anything other than "unfriendly," "denounced," and "at war." Strangely, human players quickly incur warmonger penalties even when they are not the aggressors. Introducing casus belli seems like a neat idea, but diplomacy needs to be massively re-balanced before such a system becomes worthwhile.

There are also a few minor glitches and buggy features to consider. For instance, sometimes when hovering one's cursor over a side menu, the dialog box for the terrain tile behind the cursor will still appear. Sometimes units will obscure the ranged attack option of a city or fortification. And the map is cluttered that (even in strategy view) it's easy to misclick and send the wrong unt to the wrong location. On the whole though, these are not at all game-breaking and I trust that Firaxis will patch some of the more annoying ones.

Conclusion: Worthy of the Sid Meier's name and worth buying now if you liked Civ V, but still in need of improvement.

By far the most enjoyable space program sim I've ever played. While I am no astronaut, I'd always fancied myself a fan of space travel and physics. But it's not until you try to get into orbit for the first time that you really begin to appreciate the work that goes into a space program. I know it sounds nerdy, but after hitting 'Revert to Launch' for the 6th time while trying to get a Kerbal to the Moon (Mun), I think about the men who did it for real 50 years ago with nothing more than a calculator, some college ruled paper and a No 2 pencil. Then I look at the computing power of the Unity engine and all the UI advantages I have and think 'God, I'm stupid...'
Although still lacking in some of the basic realisms of space travel (ie Life Support), user-made mods are varied, prevolent and easily installed. If the vanilla version of KSP starts to get repetitive, hop over to Curse or KerbalStuff and find a few mods to make things more interesting.
But the real trick is to create your own goals. Similar to Minecraft, KSP tends to be open ended and can bore players very quickly once they master some of the basics. Yes, they give you contracts/missions that point you in the right direction, but it will be up to you to find goals that motivate you. Can I build a base on the Mun? What would it take to place satelites at the LaGrange points? Can I put a rover on the surface of Jool? (No!)
In short: Easily worth the money for a long term, sometimes relaxing, sometimes rage-inducing game that never stops being fun.

Improved mechanics, streamlined technological evolution, end new features like Civics and envoys provide a familiar - yet new - experience to the Civilization series. As for PC resources and graphics, it played far smoother than the previous 3 Civs ( Civilization 5; Gods & Kings; Brave New World).
Specific Improvements:
- Builders no longer hang around throughout the entire game. Usually you get a group of three and a build is used up when you build something or clear a marsh or forest. This is a major benefit as in previous games I end up either deleting builders or forgetting about them altogether.
- Districts allow for specific improvements without utilizing all sorts of valuable space. Neighbourhoods, Encampments, commercial, etc, all benefit their home cities and still allow the player to build many farms, mines, or event cultural items as they see fit.
- The tech tree is vastly improved with one key aspect - you are no longer linear in your technological progression. You get significant boosts to research time if certain things are accomplished (ie. If you build a city on the coast early enough, you get a considerable boost to the Sailing technology).
Overall, Civilization VI is a blast to play, with a multiplayer aspect that should appeal to those that enjoy online gaming. Go forth, and advance through the eras to achieve greatness!

Been playing civ since the second one. This is the most complex civ to date as far as micromanaging all of your bonuses/tiles/production choices, and that's compared to even Alpha Centauri. If you like micromanagement, you'll love it (I mostly do). If you don't, you're going to probably feel like a previous title was a better game for you.
The AI is pretty damn terrible. It's probably not hard to tweak and be significantly improved, but as of this writing, a couple of months after release, I still see the AI do incredibly silly things such as city states surrounded by 25 warriors (clogging up all traffic through the area, maybe that's the point?) when everyone else is sporting swordsmen. Positive diplomacy with the other AI civilizations is a chore. Yes, you can be friendly with most civs, but you've got to take care of them and their interests like they're some kind of super-needy girlfriend with deep daddy issues you're afraid to dump because you know they'll go total psycho on you and your stuff.
Needless to say, it's all pretty much forced my hand into being a heartless warmonger every single game. Even when you know another civ's pet peeves, oftentimes there's just nothing you can do to avoid♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off to the point of them completely loathing you, because half of the time the thing they like is "the human player not winning". Well ♥♥♥♥ you, too, AI civilization.
Back to the AI being actually procedurally terrible: I know decent AI for a game like this is an _immense_ undertaking, but that's what triple-A game studios are for. When you sell tons of copies for a game at 60$ a pop, you're expected to be able to hire that extra person to make sure your AI doesn't have to be (extremely) cheaty to overcome its own weaknesses (which are many). The AI literally does not partake in the entire aspect of gold in this game. They have an infinite, or what may as well be, amount of income, which you can prove by trading with them. Seriously. Google it.
But let's talk about some clearly good things:
The tech tree being split into tech/civics, the religion system (after the last update to lessen religious unit walls), the archaeology, the great works, all of that is on the whole a positive shift. The creation of armies/armadas out of multiple units, I haven't used much (games I play usually end right at the end of the industrial era). The new city state system I am pretty sure I adore.
The first week of release I put in 8+ hours of multiplayer with someone in the same room and there were zero hiccups or problems. Like Civ V and the rest before it, this game is best played with some humans, and then it shines.
All in all, strong entry in the series. I haven't yet figured out whether I merely like this game or love it, but it's one of the two.
Last note: the two recent DLCs are an overt cash grab by the publisher. I am very disappointed by that. If it continues, this review will be changed to a downvote. --This has now been done. The publisher is terrible. I won't be buying a DLC for a civ until they're under a dollar.

I like Civilization 6. New mechanics are fun, resource management and graphics are all an improvement on Civ 5 but it's plagued with issues that make the experience tiresome.
Maps: Very few maps at the moment. My tip, download a large earth map and use them. The default maps are smaller than Civ 5 on the same size.
Leaders: Agenda's make the game interesting however AI civs RARELY follow them (only to denounce you for not following them). As an example Jadwiga will try to get loads of faith but when I check she has very little but will always be the first to complain about me having not enough. As well as this first impressions seem to be RNG and can kill a friendship right off the bat.
Barbarians: They follow the same script as in Civ 5 I believe but seem to be more deadly than ever. Each time you kill a barbarian unit or they kill on of yours a new one spawns at the nearest encampment. So whilst you are trying to produce buildings in the early game you have to maintain an army to fend off zombie barbarians or else be swamped before you leave the ancient era. I just turn them off.
AI: Trash. Will always build massive armies in the early game even if domination victory is turned off. Only tiles with resource are ever worked (Once an entire continent with 5 civs on it was just plains with the occasional mine). This results in the civ lacking production and food and in turn also gold. Mixed with their constant military expansion they go bankrupt, army turns to barbarians and its gg for them.
Bugs: Text screws up if you leave a civ screen whilst your turn is ending. Production glitches if you have a que and something finishes. Civ screens unresponsive at random times. Game crashes when moving naval units and sliding map across.
Development and DLC: I have the deluxe which means I have every DLC so far. So for my extra money I got 4 civs that are totally useless and Australia which is OP. Then it just kind of stopped. They have so much time to just put together more civs but that would mean giving them out to people like me. Watch all these civs get released once season pass runs out. Hardly ever updated (updates coincide with DLC release). If you think how much money 2k has made and is making its pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥poor for them to leave it in the state its in for nearly a year.
Overall: Good for the first 100 hours, painful for the rest. Buy on a sale when its fully released.

I like Civilization 6. New mechanics are fun, resource management and graphics are all an improvement on Civ 5 but it's plagued with issues that make the experience tiresome.
Maps: Very few maps at the moment. My tip, download a large earth map and use them. The default maps are smaller than Civ 5 on the same size.
Leaders: Agenda's make the game interesting however AI civs RARELY follow them (only to denounce you for not following them). As an example Jadwiga will try to get loads of faith but when I check she has very little but will always be the first to complain about me having not enough. As well as this first impressions seem to be RNG and can kill a friendship right off the bat.
Barbarians: They follow the same script as in Civ 5 I believe but seem to be more deadly than ever. Each time you kill a barbarian unit or they kill on of yours a new one spawns at the nearest encampment. So whilst you are trying to produce buildings in the early game you have to maintain an army to fend off zombie barbarians or else be swamped before you leave the ancient era. I just turn them off.
AI: Trash. Will always build massive armies in the early game even if domination victory is turned off. Only tiles with resource are ever worked (Once an entire continent with 5 civs on it was just plains with the occasional mine). This results in the civ lacking production and food and in turn also gold. Mixed with their constant military expansion they go bankrupt, army turns to barbarians and its gg for them.
Bugs: Text screws up if you leave a civ screen whilst your turn is ending. Production glitches if you have a que and something finishes. Civ screens unresponsive at random times. Game crashes when moving naval units and sliding map across.
Development and DLC: I have the deluxe which means I have every DLC so far. So for my extra money I got 4 civs that are totally useless and Australia which is OP. Then it just kind of stopped. They have so much time to just put together more civs but that would mean giving them out to people like me. Watch all these civs get released once season pass runs out. Hardly ever updated (updates coincide with DLC release). If you think how much money 2k has made and is making its pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥poor for them to leave it in the state its in for nearly a year.
Overall: Good for the first 100 hours, painful for the rest. Buy on a sale when its fully released.

At first, you and this game have a flirty relationship.
But then you find out that you want more than just flirting, you want a full relationship.  So you pursue one.  Just like every relationship, it has its ups and its downs, but you stick with it because you love the game.
But one day, the relationship turns dark.  The game fights you, turns against you, even yells at you sometimes.  After awhile, you give up, and you decide to just bend over and let the game have its way with you because you're done trying to understand and you're sick of fighting.
But what happens surprises you.  It doesn't try to have its way with you.  It doesn't knock you around or rough you up.  It lies you down gently, and makes sweet, tender love to you all night long.
When you wake up the next day, you find it's gone, leaving you behind without so much as a goodbye.  You're not mad, but all you're left with is a memory.  A memory of what was, and what could have been, but now it's gone forever.  It's a melancholy memory, but happy at the same time.  You regret the journey cannot continue, but you're glad that you spent the time together that you did.
Maybe you'll see eachother again someday, possibly in a sequel or a movie...

By far the most enjoyable space program sim I've ever played. While I am no astronaut, I'd always fancied myself a fan of space travel and physics. But it's not until you try to get into orbit for the first time that you really begin to appreciate the work that goes into a space program. I know it sounds nerdy, but after hitting 'Revert to Launch' for the 6th time while trying to get a Kerbal to the Moon (Mun), I think about the men who did it for real 50 years ago with nothing more than a calculator, some college ruled paper and a No 2 pencil. Then I look at the computing power of the Unity engine and all the UI advantages I have and think 'God, I'm stupid...'
Although still lacking in some of the basic realisms of space travel (ie Life Support), user-made mods are varied, prevolent and easily installed. If the vanilla version of KSP starts to get repetitive, hop over to Curse or KerbalStuff and find a few mods to make things more interesting.
But the real trick is to create your own goals. Similar to Minecraft, KSP tends to be open ended and can bore players very quickly once they master some of the basics. Yes, they give you contracts/missions that point you in the right direction, but it will be up to you to find goals that motivate you. Can I build a base on the Mun? What would it take to place satelites at the LaGrange points? Can I put a rover on the surface of Jool? (No!)
In short: Easily worth the money for a long term, sometimes relaxing, sometimes rage-inducing game that never stops being fun.

I usually write reviews for bad games to give people red flags about things they care about but for this game I am going to make an exception. I really like this one. For DRM issues I waited until this game was $5 and I can say that it's easily worth ten times the price which for me is a shame. Anyways I don't want this to become a rant about DRM, I want to say what I liked, and didn't like, about LIS.
I liked mostly everything about this game. True to my style of reviews I will start with the negative.
1) The end gets a little strange...and I cannot help but feel that the episodic nature of the development made it so that it repeated a bunch of content during chapter 5 as reminders of what happened during the game over however long it took to make. For anyone like me who just plowed through it stopping only to sleep once it was a bit tedious. Minor complaint really, but it exists.
2) The control is a little funky....clearly designed for a gamepad and ignoring the fact that keyboards have so many keys. It could have been better, but at the same time it's usable. At least the keys are bindable so it's somewhat acceptable.
3) Sometimes I felt that the main character would miss obvious/do stupid things.....but I do try to remember that when I was 18 I wasn't particularly smart when it came to solutions to problems either. Still, as an older gamer this did bug me a little.
4) The animations were kinda...well, not good....It certainly broke my immersion a number of times because the animations were not that great. I mean, if you've played games like VTM:BL you will know what I am talking about. I have this complaint about a lot of games though....but I mean seriously a game from 2004 has better facial animations than 98% of game that come out today.....and the thing here is facial animation could have added so much to this game since it's so dialogue based. I feel like a lot of potential was wasted here.
Now for everything I liked...pretty much everything else. I really liked the story, it gave me plenty of feels which is a special thing and for the devs to be able to do that....well, I appreciate the love that went into making this. I felt it. The characters were all great. Each of them felt like they had their own personalities and that really helped the world come to life. The time travel gave the puzzles(which I did find too easy, but I was mostly playing for the story so it's not exactly a complaint) a bit of a unique aspect which I also liked.
One other thing I would like to add, and only because I think this game is great because I care, but there were a few parts in here that I thought if they just changed a few minor details it would have made the special moments that much more powerful.
Anyways, I without any hisitation would recommend this to people who like story based games. I would also recommend this to people who don't know if they like story games as well, as I think this is a good introduction. If you don't like story games, well, this isn't so amazing that it will convert you. It's pretty good, but not that good.

I own Overwatch, I pre-ordered the Origins Edition, and I have to say; this game feels a lot more fun than Overwatch. The thing is, there is polish, but there is also too much polish. Paladins is relatively polished--which is a good thing. It's not perfect by any means, but perfection is boring. While there are some glaring similarities between the two games, the differences in playstyle are immense, and the card loadouts and in-game progression make the game feel a lot more alive. Ultimates aren't game changing, there are no press Q/E and win abilties, the ultimates are more of an extension of the character's kit rather than a mandatory goal like they are in Overwatch. Each hero is unique, but Hi-Rez is not afraid to release heroes that may be deceptively similar, but overall completely different from each other, and always fun.
The customization options are aplenty here, with 6-7 slots for customization, 3 of which are mix-and-match apparel, so it is not often you find another player rocking the same style as you. With new costumes, weapons, and hats being added every patch, the options will eventually be overwhelmingly glorious. There are voice packs available for every hero, and they can be bought with the money you earn in-game.
The game is not pay-to-win at all, the only thing that paying real money will get you is aesthetic or a minor shortcut to things you can get in-game anyways. You can buy the founder's packs which are definitely worth it, unlocking every hero in the game forever for $20, which is essentially buying the game if you think about it. The epic and legendary founders packs are really just there for the diehard fans who want every cosmetic ever immediately; and I admit that I am one of those people, haha.

This is why I am still playing Civilization games.
I was playing Civ for years - I started from Civ III. It was really interesting adventure. I spent tons of hours in it. But somewhere in 2008 I stopped playing this game a lot. I don't remember why. Anyway, in 2014 I heard about Civilization: Beyond Earth. I tried it, I played it and I stayed in Civ community - to the day, when Civ VI came out.
Civ series - no matter how many bugs there will be - it's always the same, always entertainmenting and always the pure gold. I spent already 100 hours in Civ VI - and I must say - this series is never too old, this series is never dead.
Civilization VI took my heart by new engine. It's  really different than Civ V or Civ BE and when after something around 60 hours in Civ VI I came back to Beyond Earth, I was surprised how many things changed. After 2 months I didn't remember a lot of things in Civ V - this is how the game changed.
Districts. I totally loved districts. Unique districts for some civilizations is also great idea. Wonders are taking tiles - cities aren't farms♥♥♥♥♥♥anymore. Now when you are creating a city you need to think a lot. Mountains aren't useless, they are providing yields for districts. This might be overpowered, but it's beautiful how they used just useless tiles. Amenities and housings - totally great solution. River giving extra housing, luxuries giving extra amenities. I could talk about new things for hours, but we don't have time.
Art style - completely beautiful. I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed new animations and the day/night cycle on the map. Strategic view is nice for eye.
Technology tree - absolutely no problems, it's set nice.
Civics tree and cards with policies - this is great solution. You are discovering parts of the culture and you're not getting every policy one by one - you are choosing some of them. You are well-limited and also this extra cards for some civs are great.
Trading system - it's ok, and finally it is showing nice and clearly.
Buildings/wonders/units - Only one thing here: wonders are just awesome.
AI - That's true, that AI is a bit weird. Also some civs are overpowered. Really overpowered. The game can't go normal with such strong civs. I think as soon as Workshop will be alive people will improve all civs on their own way. Anyway, Barbarians are smarter, that's for sure. It's not like in Civ V, and the only one bad thing about AI is probably this, I sometimes feel, like Barbarians and Civilizations changed places - Barbarians are like a normal Civs and Civs are like Barbarians. Just noticing.

With the launch of 1.1, a number of my previous points are no longer valid and thus I can now start to recommend this game again. With 64 bit mode allowing an ulimited number of mods to be installed and the ability to actually play the game with vessels of large part counts, the major issues I had with the game have been addressed. HOWEVER, I maintain my negative point that this game hides key information from the player and mods are required to display it. The display of DeltaV at minimum should be an option for people like me that feel that trial-and-error is a waste of time.
Old review:
This game is extremely addicting for anyone with even a shred of creativity. As a base game, though, there is much to be desired, as the number of parts to work with are fairly limited and there's a lot of useful rocket information that's just not presented to you easily (stage burn times, ETAs to landing, true altitude above the surface, etc), making the game artificially more difficult. I am lazy. As such I find trial-and-error and having to do manual mathematical calculations to be a waste of my time.
This is where mods come in. Mods are what give this game it's massive appeal and replayability. However, in its current state, the game is limited in terms of how much you can add to it through mods while staying stable. The game cannot utilize more than 4GB of system memory due to 32 bit limitations of Unity 4. Want to play with life support requirements and develop self-sustaining bases and space stations in a solar system with additional planets and moons with tons of additional rocket parts to help move resources around, science experiments to run, and more realistically behaving antennae for operating unmanned probes and sending science data back home? Sorry, your game will crash after the first few rocket launches without forcing the game to run in OpenGL or Dx 11, both of which have their own technical issues. Don't even THINK about attempting to play the game with the full Realism Overhaul suite at this time due to the memory limitations, as your game WILL crash after a couple of attempted launches even on Dx 11 and OpenGL. The developers are currently working on this by transitioning the game's code to Unity 5, which will hopefully bring with it a 64 bit option which will remove the memory limitations.
As far as other general issues are concerned, perhaps my biggest peeve is that the game gets EXTREMELY laggy when you build rockets and other structures with a lot of parts. Stations in particular can, if not careful in planning, exceed 100 parts. This slows the game down to the point of being nearly unplayable. This is due to physics calculations being bound to a single CPU core and is yet another limitation of Unity 4, apparently.
My personal recommendation is to NOT play this game until after the Unity 5 transition and 64 bit mode is officially released. At that point you'll be able to run as many mods as you want, limited only by your own computer's amount of memory. The transition should also result in faster physics calculations by spreading them across CPU cores, helping to alleviate the current issues with rockets and structures having large numbers of parts.
I will update this review once the transition to Unity 5 is complete.

Kerbal Space Program is unlike most other video games that let you explore outer space. Instead of clicking a destination or weightlessly floating onwards to celestial bodies, KSP lets you build a rocket and then leaves you at the mercy of gravity and re-entry heat, letting you conquer every small difficulty on the path to progressively bigger and more ambitious goals. From exiting the atmosphere to staying in orbit, to flying by the Mun, to landing on it, and maybe even getting back home on Kerbin.
What's more memorable than the successes, however, are the failures, which can range anywhere from "forgot to put flashlights and landed at night" to "accidentally made the whole rocket split into 6 pieces at launch". Each failure, though, is an important lesson in what's needed to progress through the challenges that the solar system throws at you, and it creates some interesting player-created scenarios where you'll want to rescue your kerbalnauts stranded in orbit or on Munar soil (or not, you heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥).
KSP can be played in three modes: Sandbox, which gives you full freedom over what to build and how many times; Science, which locks rocket parts behind a tech tree, unlocked by gathering "Science" from performing experiments and collecting data and samples from different biomes on all celestial bodies; and finally Career, which in addition to using the same tech tree as Science mode, also lets you manage funds and reputation by completing randomly generated contracts for various companies.
KSP is definitely worth playing if you don't mind learning from experience with a healthy dose of wiki when you're confused. If nothing else, give the demo a try and see if you can get a Kerbal safely to the Mun and back.

I was playing Civ for years - I started from Civ III. It was really interesting adventure. I spent tons of hours in it. But somewhere in 2008 I stopped playing this game a lot. I don't remember why. Anyway, in 2014 I heard about Civilization: Beyond Earth. I tried it, I played it and I stayed in Civ community - to the day, when Civ VI came out.
Civ series - no matter how many bugs there will be - it's always the same, always entertainmenting and always the pure gold. I spent already 100 hours in Civ VI - and I must say - this series is never too old, this series is never dead.
Civilization VI took my heart by new engine. It's  really different than Civ V or Civ BE and when after something around 60 hours in Civ VI I came back to Beyond Earth, I was surprised how many things changed. After 2 months I didn't remember a lot of things in Civ V - this is how the game changed.
Districts. I totally loved districts. Unique districts for some civilizations is also great idea. Wonders are taking tiles - cities aren't farms♥♥♥♥♥♥anymore. Now when you are creating a city you need to think a lot. Mountains aren't useless, they are providing yields for districts. This might be overpowered, but it's beautiful how they used just useless tiles. Amenities and housings - totally great solution. River giving extra housing, luxuries giving extra amenities. I could talk about new things for hours, but we don't have time.
Art style - completely beautiful. I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed new animations and the day/night cycle on the map. Strategic view is nice for eye.
Technology tree - absolutely no problems, it's set nice.
Civics tree and cards with policies - this is great solution. You are discovering parts of the culture and you're not getting every policy one by one - you are choosing some of them. You are well-limited and also this extra cards for some civs are great.
Trading system - it's ok, and finally it is showing nice and clearly.
Buildings/wonders/units - Only one thing here: wonders are just awesome.
AI - That's true, that AI is a bit weird. Also some civs are overpowered. Really overpowered. The game can't go normal with such strong civs. I think as soon as Workshop will be alive people will improve all civs on their own way. Anyway, Barbarians are smarter, that's for sure. It's not like in Civ V, and the only one bad thing about AI is probably this, I sometimes feel, like Barbarians and Civilizations changed places - Barbarians are like a normal Civs and Civs are like Barbarians. Just noticing.
IN TOTAL:
Gameplay: 19/20
Graphics: 18/20
Engine: 15/15
AI: 9/15
Diplomacy and Trading: 10/10
Technologies, civics and cities systems: 10/10
Minor systems (buildings, wonders, etc.): 10/10
TOTAL RATE: 91/100 - It's great game!

Come back a year from now, and check it out then.

Kerbal Space Program is the most fun I've ever had failing. And man oh man, did I fail – over and over again. It's part of Kerbal's experimental nature. By the time I finally built a rocket that achieved successful orbit, I had failed so many times that in almost any other game I would have given up completely. But that's where the genius of Kerbal really is: hard work pays off, and once I was able to determine the cause of my failures, be it staging woes, or my nose pitching violently at 1000 meters, every successful launch was a thing of beauty.
In its Career and Science modes, Kerbal Space Program creates an incredible sense of accomplishment with each successful feat of rocketry. Through hours of trial and error, I finally came to a design and flight technique that did what I wanted it to, and it was fantastically satisfying because each accomplishment is just a step toward bigger and better things. Every success (such as reaching a new record altitude) is really just a place to start over, only with better stuff. It's a lovely feedback loop that I can't get enough of.
I spent the majority of my time in Career mode. All the challenges that come with actually blasting an object into space come into play. Balancing funding, scientific progression, and reputation forced me to put thought into each launch, and the limited selection of spaceship parts made me think hard about how I could get the most from each rocket engine, fuel supply, or science module. Going higher requires more thrust, which requires bigger engines. Bigger engines require more fuel, which make the ship heavier. A heavier ship needs more thrust to go higher, which requires more engines. And so on. Striking the perfect balance between thrust, weight, and fuel with only the parts and funds unlocked in Career mode made me feel like a brilliant rocket scientist.
I enjoyed Science mode less. It retains the tech tree progression of Career mode, but removes other restrictions so the stakes aren't as high. Without the goals of Career mode, I'd rather be playing Sandbox, where everything is unlocked and my imagination is the only limit. When I'd get to a point in Career where I was having trouble progressing and started to get frustrated, I'd switch to Sandbox and build to my heart's content.
Sandbox allows for truly ridiculous designs - the sort of insane, utterly impractical rockets I built just to see how far I could push Kerbal’s physics. Leaving the symmetry option turned up to its highest setting, I quickly built an excessively powerful pinwheeling rocket. I didn't design it for science, or for speed, or to see how far I could make it fly; I built the thing just because I could. When I took it to the launch pad and set it off and it didn't immediately explode, there was a brief second, just before the whole thing failed violently, where I thought "Hey, maybe I'm onto something here." It was a glorious second.
The one area where building proved to be a hassle was staging. Shuffling parts around during a build would sometimes cause parts of my ship to fall off in flight when I wasn't expecting it. It wasn't a big issue when a chute would deploy on launch, but it did cause me some grief when I was later into a mission and an engine would separate instead of fire.
But even when things went wrong, Kerbal makes getting it right easy. If you don't like the way a launch went, you can just revert back to the launchpad with no penalty. If my design was clearly a failure, I could revert right back to construction. Quick and fun experimentation is the name of the game.
Getting off the ground is only the first small step for Kerbal kind. After finally landing on a design that got me into space, turning a vertical trajectory into an orbital one presented new challenges. Once I mastered orbit, I set my sites to the moon. The tutorials were a big help in explaining orbital mechanics, which are all very science-y and absolutely need to be understood if you're going to make it to any of the numerous celestial bodies in the Kerbal solar system. This is where the challenge, and experimentation, become almost limitless.
I almost felt bad blowing up so many brave little Kerbals in my pursuit of the stars. With their self-assured mannerisms, they work so well to lighten the mood while learning rocket science. Kerbal Space Program doesn't have any voice acting, other than the occasional nasally whine of approval from one of the Kerbals, but the flavor text in the game is smart, wry, and funny.
Kerbal Space Program does the improbable: it makes learning a complex subject fun. Its cute, clueless characters and sense of humor turn a hardcore physics simulator into something replayable and addictive. Designing, flying, and then retrying missions again and again is a tough challenge that goes right up to the brink of frustration, but the eventual success of achieving virtual space flight is rewarding and even inspirational.

Eventually this will likely change to recommend, but at this point I can't recommend it.  The game is desperately in need of some AI patches and customization options that are missing from the advanced settings.
Like most of the reviewers I find their overall city/empire design changes to be a good change of pace.  I don't think 1 city is even at option in this game, but there is so much we need to do for our cities compared to before that I don't even think it would be feasible.  I find myself having to plan my cities rather than just spam upgrades like before which is exactly how a grand strategy should be.
Technology/Civics on the other hand I'm split on because it is both a good idea and a horrible shortcoming.  Their adding of 50% research completion awards for doing certain actions for again encourages you to strategize and do things you typically may not do.  The downside is, sometimes you simply can't do them and thus it takes you twice as long to research as other nations did.  For example 50% research bonus for building quarry on top of a strategic resource.  Unfortunately there are no strategic resources anywhere near you so there is nothing you can do except accept the huge research penalty and fall behind other nations. There is no slider bar to control % bonus, so at the moment we can't even attempt to balance it out.  In the future I'm sure somebody will add a mod for it, but for the time being it feels problematic.
AI/diplomacy isn't worth going into detail because you could rant for ages about the flaws, so a few examples of the nonsense are:
1) random messages from AI that make no sense (usually they are unhappy about something but you don't know why)
2) Wars that are started but take place 30+ turns later because they never sent troops to attack you
3) AI will spam you w/ envoy requests upon meeting you until you accept their envoy.  Anytime you request to send them an envoy they reject you because they don't like you for unknown or non-sensible reasons

There's a lot of negative reviews for this game. Let me just start by saying this game DOES have its flaws. However, I don't view them as dramatically as others seem to. Civilization VI just has too many redeeming qualities to be negative about it.
I'll start with the cons.
CONS:
AI - Okay, yes, the AI is pretty bad. But, let's be honest: it's bad in every Civilization game. A recent patch has definitely made them easier to deal with in diplomacy, which is nice. But you can still expect them to be mad at you for random and stupid reasons and to hold onto grudges for centuries - literally. Additionally, their use of military units during war is pretty bad - but not quite as bad as Civilization V in my opinion. Just keep in mind that they patched the AI very recently and it did improve the AI temperment at least a little bit.
UI - I like the look of the UI in Civilization VI a lot. It's thematic. But its usefulness could really use some help. Things are harder to access than they were in Civ V. Additionally, there's no way to get a list of all your military units (at least that I've found). When you end up with a lot of units spread out over a large area, not having a master list is annoying. All in all, the UI is less helpful than in Civ V.
Diplomatic messages - Related to the previous two cons, one of the most annoying things in Civ VI is how many messages you get from the other leaders in the game that are useless. They will often complain to you or praise you (rare) - which is fine - except that when they do it, you get a full screen message in which you can do nothing but click "Goodbye." It doesn't take long for these to become annoying.
Gossip system - I really like what they were trying to do with the gossip system. I do. But it was executed so, so poorly. Throughout the game, you hear "gossip" from your traders and diplomats that appear as messages in the center of the screen during other player's turns. This news feed informs you of the goings on in other empires. This COULD be really cool. Except that 99% of what you hear is either blatantly obvious, completely useless, or /about your own empire/. Thus, it just ends up wasting space on your screen.
Here are some examples of what you'll hear:
Your neighbor founded a city. (Yes. I know. I can see it. It's right on my border.)
Your neighbor cleared a barbarian settlement. (Oookay...)
You heard a rumor that Rome is trading with China! (I know. I *AM* Rome!!! I know I'm trading with China!)

PROS:
Districts - The new district system is amazing. It's a very refreshing approach to cities in Civilization. City planning becomes an intregal part of the game and is very enjoyable. This has the added bonus of making different cities truly unique depending on their needs or location. One city could be a cultural giant and have a theater district with aqueduct and neighborhood districts to support the population. Another could be a frontier city with an encampment for strong military production, a market district to generate some money to pay for the troops, et cetera. It really makes cities more fun to manage.
Research and Civics - The redesign of the research/civic system is refreshing. Being able to boost specific technologies with the eureka system is amazing. Found a city on the coast? Sailing is easier to research. Build a bunch of mines? Masonry is already halfway researched for you. Fighting lots of barbarians? Military tactics will come along quicker. Really, really nice feature. Additionally, culture helps you move along a new culture tree, which functions similar to the research tree. This unlocks new policies, governments, et cetera, that can also be boosted through your actions.
Policy cards - With the new government system, each government has a certain number of military, economic, diplomatic, and wildcard slots where you can put policy cards that you've "learned." This is a flexible and fantastic system that is much better than the social policy system in Civilization V. It allows you to tailor your governmental policies to your current situation, within the limit of the government you've chosen. The only thing I don't like about this is that the military cards seem underpowered, which makes the military-oriented governments seem weaker as well.
Limited stacking - I both hated and understood the stacking change from Civ IV to V. But I really thought it could have been handled a lot better. Civilization VI introduces a limited stacking system that Civilization V should have had. Finding a happy medium between doomstacking and no stacking, Civ VI allows you to stack units of different types. Units of the same type can combine to form armadas (ships) or armies (land units). In my opinion, this is perfect. I hope they keep it this way for future Civilization games.
Happiness - The global happiness system of Civ V was one of its worst features (in my opinion, of course). I don't need to into details as to why I hated it or why I thought it made no sense. In Civ VI, this has been overhauled with the amenities system. Each city needs a certain amount of amenities to stay productive. These are provided by buildings in the entertainment district, certain policies, luxury resources, et cetera. As a whole, it functions much better than happiness in Civ V and adds more enjoyment to individual city management.
Graphics - They may be cartoony in nature, but don't let it fool you: there is a lot of detail in each figure and building. At first, I didn't like the art style of the game, but I've grown to love it. The detail in the animations especially is a nice touch.
Barbarians - Yes, the barbarians are new and improved in Civ VI. They're relentless. And it's good. They actually function as a miniature civilization now. They send out scouts to survey the land and spot cities ripe for the plunder. Then, these scouts will found a barbarian settlement somewhere nearby and it will begin producing a variety of units to raid you. The barbarians will sometimes even wait to assemble a small army before moving in. This makes them so much more dynamic than in Civ V. It becomes imperative to kill barbarian scouts before they can found a settlement, and especially before they notice your city. It's stressful and difficult and makes the early stages of a Civ VI game even more fun!
So there it is. All in all, I really enjoy this Civilization. While I understand some of the negative reviews people are posting, I really don't think they are giving the game a fair shot. The new/redesigned features are mostly fantastic and the experience is fresh and original. It's more complex and in depth than the overly simplified Civilization V. There are many other things that are different or similar in it that I have not commented on, such as religion, the new road system, the new diplomacy features, and how wonders are handled. These things I generally like, but they aren't good enough to end up in the Pros list.
If you are like me and liked Civilization IV more than V, then I think you will really like what VI brings to the table.
My verdict:
Worth a purchase if you can find it on sale.
(Sean Bean is the narrator. I mean... that alone almost makes it worth a purchase.)

DISCLAIMER: THIS IS A PARTIAL VISION OF THE GAME IN THE CURRENT STATE AS OF 1/17/2014.
THIS REVIEW WILL GET UPDATED AS EACH EPISODE COMES OUT.
Telltale's The Walking Dead is back with yet another season of heartbreaking zombie apocalypse stories.
This time we control Clementine, the girl from season one, while she travels North to escape the madness in the cities. Controlling Clementine may sound crazy; she's a kid and all that. Telltale noticed that too I guess because they let some time pass between season one and this season so she can grow up a little in this world and roughen up. It worked. Clementine is a tough kid who grew up in a world of brutal and savage survival with bad people in each corner and surrounded by the dead.
All actions in season one somewhat have repercussions in the events between last season and season two, and Clementine remembers all Lee taught her.
In terms of technical factors, this game uses the same engine, albeit a little changed in terms of UI, but it's virtually the same gameplay and graphics. Remember, in this game the important thing is the story, not the rest. The engine is good enough for me and the graphics are inspired by the comic books so it's cool, and the gameplay is awesome as always with all Telltale games.
Finally, if you're expecting a zombie shooter, go get DayZ or something like that. If you like adventure games like Monkey Island, Maniac Mansion, Sam and Max and all that, and love drama and zombies, this game is for you.
Now, I'll begin reviewing each episode. This review will be updated as I play each episode as they come out. I'll try to keep it spoiler-free as much as I can.
__________________________________________________
EPISODE ONE: ALL THAT REMAINS
This episode has a chapter which serves as re-introduction, helping you to remember all that happened in season one, and makes the leap to the current events bringing you up-to-date with where and how the group (or what's left of it) is.
However, soon after you start the game, tragedy will come. I mean, seriously. First 5 minutes and you'll already be crying, so you can expect that.
After that sad part, all will brighten up a little. But it will be taken from you again. Yes. This game is an emotional rollercoaster.
New characters will be introduced and you will see each of them develop, either by themselves or by the actions Clementine takes. I must say the new characters are really good and I expect a lot from them. From some I've already seen how they are and what they're capable of, how good and caring some are and just how sad or how crazy or bad others are. Also, Clementine is surprisingly good in reading other people. She could tell how they were just by listening to them a little. An useful skill I must admit, because in that world it's needed to know who you can trust.
In the end, there will be a decision similar but not entirely equal to the one in A New Day. You will have to choose quickly this time, because now it has a timer and you being idle will count as an option too, leading to three possible outcomes. I encourage you try them all because they are all great.
The next episode will be cool and will bring some unexpected (or totally expected?) surprises, as we can see in the trailer at the end of the game, which once again will reflect your actions and decisions from this episode.
Season 2 is up to a great start, and I hope all episodes keep this quality standard. I really enjoyed this, as it is really as good as season one, which was perfect in every sense.
Too bad we now have to wait for episode two. Well, I'll sit down until it's out... is it out yet!?!?!?
__________________________________________________
EPISODE TWO: A HOUSE DIVIDED
Season 2 continues and it's starting to take shape! We did our waiting and I must say that although it was long and I suffered it, this episode had a lot of stuff in it and surprised me. I played it twice to see how many outcomes there were and I could see there were many, which is awesome because it's like having many stories.
This episode brings back a character we thought lost, adds even more characters to the cast, and unmasks the main antagonist. We also get more character development and get to see the human nature at its finest. The apocalypse starts becoming more and more political. Tensions and issues begin to surface.
The finale was great and it's there where we get to see the more different outcomes which dramatically change how we'll continue.
All in all, it was an excellent episode, and I can't wait for the next. Too bad Telltale is taking so long to release these. I just hope they hurry and get the next episode for this (and The Wolf Among Us) out by at least April.
__________________________________________________
EPISODE THREE: IN HARM'S WAY
The most brutal The Walking Dead episode yet. Can't say anything else about this episode. All I can say is, after playing this, the Governor and Negan are sissypants compared to what you see here.
I can't wait for the next episode.
__________________________________________________
EPISODE FOUR: AMID THE RUINS
This is where it all went downhill. We see now that the choices we made don't matter. There are choices in this episode that won't matter in the end. We'll see that even if we do or do not do something, it won't have effect in the future as things will be the same. I believe Telltale focused on The Wolf Among Us so much they didn't care about The Walking Dead anymore, because this is the laziest written episode yet.
__________________________________________________
EPISODE FIVE: NO GOING BACK
... aaaaaaand it's still ridden with lazy writing. Every single thing that happened in this episode makes you think "I played through all this to see THAT happening?". I mean, it desperately tries to cling on to the past, like they're afraid that this season wouldn't do as well as the first one; it makes a lot of unnecesary reminders that Lee was the best, showing scenes from season one... YES, LEE WAS THE BEST, BUT IT'S TIME TO MOVE ON. I feel like this season was a reminder that season one was great and nothing else. It's like the things that happened here didn't matter at all; all that matters is "what would Lee do if he was here". And this is why I feel like this episode fails altogether. Rushed, with twists and turns to the worst every time they could. How did it come to this?
But hey, the ride was sweet while it lasted. I still recommend it because up until episode four it was worth playing. It still is, but the last two episodes really weren't as good as the first few. I blame The Wolf Among Us, which was awesome, and probably made Telltale have to cut a few things here and there from The Walking Dead to make the other game a success. But still pisses me off. Really, a lot.

Paladins has caused some controversy over allegedly being an Overwatch clone; while my experience with Overwatch is extremely limited, I can say that if Paladins is a clone, it's a pretty good one. The game is a  first-person "hero-based" team shooter, like Overwatch or Team Fortress 2, though it is set apart from those games by customization elements, both before and during a match. Each character has his or her own set of "cards" that can be unlocked and then placed into loadouts to alter their abilites, with changes like reduced cooldowns, improved effects, or lifesteal. During the match, earning credits allows further augmentation to adapt to enemy playstyles and loadouts. There are four classes of characters - front line, support, flank, and damage - that must be about evenly balanced on a team in order to put up a fight against another team. Coordination is of utmost importance in these matches, and if you wind up with a bad team you're basically sunk. It's a solid formula that makes for a relatively fun though slightly uninspired experience. There are far fewer bugs than there were when the game starts, but even casual players will run into a few - rarely anything game-breaking, but definitely things that throw off the feel of the game a bit.
There are two different modes right now. Siege consists of a point-capturing portion followed by the team that captured the point attempting to advance it to the enemy base with the enemies aiming to stop it. Payload is solely one team advancing a payload as far as possible from their base to the enemy's with the other trying to stop the payload, then both teams switching sides. Siege is undoubtedly the more fun and refined mode at present - Payload seems to have brought most of the mechanics of Siege into a different setting, and it doesn't mesh together perfectly. The balancing of the game overall is still being worked out by the developers, but the game is very playable as it is now.
The aesthetics and artistic design are mostly positives - the game's nowhere near as beautiful or hardware-intensive as Overwatch, which is a plus in my book (Overwatch was blurry and stuttery on my weak computer, while Paladins runs quite well). I guess I haven't yet mentioned that the game is fantasy-inspired, although when you see characters with flamethrowers, lasers, and mechs, you have to wonder how the designers define fantasy. There's a lot of variety in the cast, at least; each character has a distinguishible personality, look, and voice. The maps fit the fantasy setting better, although what few maps there are only vary between two or three looks. The music can grow a bit stale after several matches, but it fits well with the alleged setting and is nothing that will make you mute the game.
The overall execution of the free-to-play aspect of the game is fairly well executed at the moment - all characters can be unlocked with gold, the non-premium easy-to-earn currency, meaning that you're not locked into your six starter characters for long even if you never buy anything. Cards can similarly be purchased with gold, so while you can wait for loot chests to get new cards, you never need to if you want to build a loadout right then. The premium currency is jewels; most aesthetic elements like reskins, emotes, and poses can only be obtained through jewels or Colossal Chests (a type of loot chest that can also only be purchased with jewels). I have not spent a cent on the game and don't intend to, but I don't feel ripped off either.
I hate to end by talking about a negative aspect, but the frequent complaints about the game's matchmaking system are not unfounded. More recently I've been put on a team with people who seem to be fairly new players. We wind up without an even spread of character types sometimes, and that rarely works out well. I'm perfectly fine with people trying to get used to the game, but to be put on a team with them rather than with others who are around my skill level can be frustrating. I hope Hi-Rez fixes this soon.
Paladins is an all-around decent game - game design and play is solid, it runs fine even on weak computers, and the free-to-play aspect is completely optional. On the other hand, poor matchmaking, a few balancing issues, bugs, and a lack of focus on the world definitely leave room for improvement. If you want a fun free shooter, I would highly recommend it, and even if you're willing to pay for something like Overwatch, Paladin is worth a look.

1 YEAR IN DEVELOPMENT UPDATE:
I'd say Civ VI is without a doubt a massive improvement on the Civ V vanilla version which didn't have religion in it (way to pack it into a DLC, Firaxis) and I definitely enjoy this game a lot, but of course there are problems. Here's my pros and cons list:
Pros:
1) It's a visually pleasant game. I don't quite get most of the arguments against the fact it looks "cartoon-ish", art styles are subject to personal taste. I personally like it because that's more or less how Civ has always looked aside from Civ V. IMO, a recognizable art style is better than a rehashed, uber-realistic one for the sake of it. Not to mention the vastly improved leader animations and voice acting (for the most part).
2) The individual differences between civs have become even bigger and we finally got back the multiple leader model from Civ IV. I put these together because they fall under the same point of enhanced variety in gameplay where Civ V took one step forward and 2 step backwards. Abilities and biases were a good thing in Civ V, but with no multiple leaders, each civ was pretty much doomed to be played within its conventional boundaries. Civ VI seems to remove this problem (only one alternative leader fow now though ¯\_(ツ)_/¯).
3) Magnificent soundtrack. I have actually postponed possibly important diplomatic interactions because it would interrupt a kick♥♥♥♥♥theme before it was over.
4) The new district system is a truly great addition. It makes it much, much easier and yet more strategically challenging to manage your cities and citizens and essentially turns tiles into a more important resource than other Civ games. Finding some "blank" tiles is actually a legit thing now so you can work with your adjacency bonuses.
5) The leader agenda system and the casus belli (thanks Paradox) are finally making diplomacy more coherent. There are still major flaws in here which I will explain in the "cons" list though.
Cons:
1) Diplomacy is still sub-par. Civ V essentially doomed Civ VI with a continuation of some traits that were gained by omitting the infinitely better Civ IV diplomacy. You can't trade map/exploration information, you can't trade direct techs (research agreements are kind of a joke, if you ask me), flexibility in how you trade things is abhorrent (I can't even change the amount of turns I will be giving money ffs) etc.
2) The AI remains quite bad as a whole. As of now, it's definitely more capable at handling diplomacy and trade deals, but it can still seem very lacking in many aspects, particularly knowing how to assess a situation during war to bargain accordingly. A more well-defined system such as the way war demands are handled in EUIV would do wonders. It's still also weak at dealing with combat and unit management overall, even though tweaks have been made.
3) While civs have been added and the DDE deal has been revamped to make it fairer for our money spent, I still feel like this game needs way more variety civ-wise and leader-wise. As I've mentioned before, many staple civs are still missing: Persia has been added, but Carthage, Byzantium, Ottomans, Mongols etc are still missing. They are bound to return at some point, but I would expect them to have come by this point.
4) Bugs have been dealt with, but new ones pop every now and then. It's definitely not as striking as it was initially and the game runs smoother than ever, but it can be quite frustrating. There's also a weird phenomenon where vanilla leader animations actually cause frame drops but newer leaders don't.
All in all, despite the obvious flaws, I still highly recommend the game for people who look for a more accessible strategy experience and it's still a great game for fans of the series. The fact it has won me over after vanilla Civ V and Beyond Earth stifled my enthusiasm of the series that was created by Civ IV really says something.

Episode One was a bit of a disappointment after having played through the entire first season, which I was - and still am - crazy about. Although only a year has passed, the graphics don't look as good anymore to me (especially the zombies and the foliage). This game is all about making decisions, and I felt bad that some decisions seem irrelevant and do not influence the story at all, like the choices 'Survival', 'Generosity' and 'Trust', and that's three out of the five choices that get featured on the ending screen. But I have to admit that the final choice was a whopper - and one that I had to think about for several minutes. What I also noticed, and hadn't really in the first season, is that controlling Clementine in static point-and-click scenes doesn't feel natural at all. The movement feels awkward, hampered and slow and the camera doesn't cooperate at all (remains static), which made me loathe these scenes. These moments also don't feature any interesting interactions and, I feel, are primarily focussed on bringing some variation. You will perform some boring chores without much significance, and this really pulls you out of the immersive movie-like experience (except the scene when Clementine seeks medical supplies). The combat also doesn't feel very interesting anymore after what we have seen in The Wolf Among Us: Episode One, although it still gets your blood pumping. I absolutely loved The Walking Dead: Season One, and was looking eagerly forward to Season Two, but this episode was a disappointment to me after having played through Season One in a fever. I have to admit that the release of the first episode of The Wolf Among Us has changed my standards for the better, but then I wonder why this episode can't live up to it.
I will refrain from giving this Episode a score, because I believe Telltale aims to deliver a season that will be bigger than the sum of it's parts.

What can I say, I have loads of hours playing Kerbal Space Program so I'll say...
- Great fun for killing time and seeing what you can come up with.
- Multiple methods of doing stuff in kerbal space program.
- Very Modable, with minor issues.
- Priced right considering it could be worth much more
- There are silly Kerbalnaughts instead of people. probrably ment for entertainment.
- Minor stress load for midrange computers, since I had minor slowdowns on fps.  So depending on your computer, you      can make the best of things to happen.
Cons
- Well, I don't like the price of it now, but I did buy it when it was 25 bucks in alpha stage.   Look for sales and get it then.
- Technical knowhow is needed for most "Structures" so that your space craft does not flip around or do all sort of wakey things when in the air.  It's best to use the wiki when you're confused or kerbal forums to ask around.
- Without a lot of graphic mods, equipement mods, other things, the game can be a little stale, but since this latest update, you got things to make it look "cooler" now..
- No multiplayer but it makes sense it is a sandbox game like dont starve or some other stuff.
- It can be frustrating to get space crafts from flipping at 10k meters up and beyond
Overall, I would highly recommend this game, it's really fun, and get's you to rattle your brain a little to figure things out in your auronaughtical engioneering funstuff :)  Don't be discurraged because of the price, if you aren't ready, download the demo on the download button when you look at the "Buy Kerbal Space Program" button.  There you can try out the game without "Pirating it" which I highly do not recommend doing.
Anyway, I rate this game a 10/10 for killing time when you're bored or stressed from fps games :)

While I love this game andwill likely continue to play it in my spare time, I am also a diehard fanboy who has spent thousands of hours since I was 8 years old and I got Civ 3.
If I were to recommend this, citystates should have more purpose. Commerce should have a winning condition, as it feels like an afterthought. Religious victory should be revamped from a quasi-combat mode. Additionally, science and culture victories are typically consolation prizes for almost getting a domination victory. Explaining tourism (the essential mechanic for a cultural victory) is hard, in part because I still do not fully understand what goes into its calculations.
The lategame has been revamped fully, and is GREAT. All other iterations of Civ (thatI have played) basically had two or three contedners determined at the industrial age. With all of the different mechanics, every civilization should have a conceivable pathto a victory and most endings are intense.
People complaining about the AI and diplomacy are fundamentally asking for too much. If the programmers for Civ 6 knew how to make sentient and adaptable AIs for such a complex ruleset, they should be working for IBM's Watson. That's not a sleight on the programmers at all: what I mean is that developing an answer to their complaints would be cutting-edge research. That being said, Diplomacy certainly seems to get exaggeratedly harder for the human player.
In all, wait for moddable workshop content to be enabled, wait to see what the developers come up with for the expansions, and buy the micro-expansion civs and scenarios at a bundled and decreased price. It's great for the civ fan who has already bought it. But for the ones still holding out and reading reviews, you could likely hold out a bit longer and get a much better game.

I thoroughly enjoyed playing The Walking Dead: Season 1. In many ways, the Telltale Game captures the essence of the original source material far better than the live-action television series. Season 2, though, is off to a slightly rocky start.
Although I enjoyed the first episode of the second season, there's no denying that it was very heavy-handed and very reliant on shock value. I understand that these are staples of the horror genre, but in my opinion the first episode relies TOO heavily on these tactics. Literally every scene involves at least one major jump-scare (and some have two or three), and various characters are introduced and discarded in almost the same breath. To say anything further would move into spoiler territory, so I'll digress.
Still, it's a promising start to the new season, and I look forward to seeing where Telltale takes us this time around. But here's to hoping that they don't fall into TOO many predictable writing tropes. Good writing should always keep us guessing, even when we're 98% sure what's coming next.

This review is going to be a little weird because I have very mixed feelings for Life Is Strange. I guess it would be most helpful if I made a pro's and con's list, so here we go (asterisks mean it can be pro or con depending on the player):
PROS:
- Decent graphics
- Character designs are pretty sweet
- Kate Marsh*
- Great indie/hipster soundtrack*
- The entire style/aesthetic of the game was really charming
- The girl that kept getting hit by stuff
- Victoria*
- Warren*
- The journal menu thing was really cool*
- Time rewinding is a cool concept (but it's admittedly pretty lackluster here)
- The school feels like a real school, and it reminded me of Bully a lot
- The janitor guy*
- The game is very well designed
- The texts you can read from other characters are interesting
- "I WAS EATING THOSE BEANS"
CONS:
- Terrible writing (Which I suppose can be blamed on the translation)
- Utterly cringeworthy voice acting*
- Boring pretentious protagonist
- Chloe*
- The game forgets about the main plot for a while
- Terrible references to other Square Enix properties*
- Really awful running gags/catchphrases*
- Gameplay is awful for the majority of the game
- Trying to emulate the TellTale formula, but badly
- Confusing plot twist that makes zero sense other than one off line
- Your choices don't really matter at all, which doesn't make any sense considering the game is based on choice
- Sudden tonal shift that floored me (even though the game was dark before then, it always felt light hearted)
- The bottle scene
- Chloe's dad
- Chloe's mom's accent*
- High school stereotypes*
- THE ENDING
Eh, the game was mediocre. It's not terrible, but it really isn't 8-9/10 worthy. If it's on sale, you should get it, but other than that maybe just watch AdumPlaze play it or something. If you're into cringy dialogue and really bad characters you might enjoy this though.

Now that the season is finally over, I can review the game as a whole. And unfortunately, I was mostly left dissapointed by it.
We still have the great artwork, voice acting and soundtrack. So that is the good parts. Now let's move onto the bad.
The most glaring issue this game has, compared to Season 1, is the lack of character development. The first 4 episodes of character development consists of people dumping their personal issues onto Clem. They never ask anything or talk to her about anything but their problems. Season 1 had a lot of character development and even the minor characters you got to know better. Not just "I have issue this.". The problems never defined them. It's as if Larry was just his heart condition and nothing more. That he would never talk about anything but that. But of course he doesn't, he develops a lot more and talks about things besides that. It made him a person you could like or dislike.
In this season, I just found myself annoyed and didn't care for the characters. One character desperately tries to replace Lee, but I never felt a connection with him. Anytime he asked me for help or asked me to talk with him, I'd just ignore him. One time he even asks me to cover him so he can get out of danger and I only did so, so that I could mess it up and get him hurt. I don't care this little for characters, I usually get very attached to them. Such as in Season 1, Lee was always warming my heart and was so inspiring to listen to. To give in example of Season 2, there's guy A who walks up to Clem. All I expected was that he was going to talk or ask something about his issue. And what does he do? "Hey Clem, I need this for my issue. Can you give me it?". Prior to that, he had never stopped to talk to Clem at all. Why would I care about him? He never really sits down to talk with her so they get to know one another.
The other problem with the new characters is that they are all so ♥♥♥♥ing stupid. I lost count on all the amount of facepalms and sighs I did throughout the season, whenever someone did something obviously idiotic. On a watch to make sure the Walkers don't eat the children? That's a great time to have a "quickie" with someone.
... I mean seriousy, I am not kidding. The only person on watch ignores his duty to make whoopie.
And it really doesn't end there. The adults (including the parent!) leaves a mentally disabled child WITH A LOADED GUN and leaves the door unlocked so that the obvious creepy bad guy can just waltz in. And who do they blame for the door being unlocked? Clem of course! Ugh.
How did these people survive more than five minutes together?
Even though you are given the option to "affect" the story, the first 3 episodes lack these choices greatly. I think the biggest impact you had on the story was to choose the decoration for a house. I mean, wow... that's what we expect in a game about life and death, yeah? It was the only time my choice felt important. 4 had some better options, but ultimately become redundant, as no matter what you chose, it just ends up the opposite anyway.
Not only that, but the first 3 episodes drag out on the story. You think that within that time, they should be able to fill it with enough to entertain me. But it's just the same thing, over and over. People dumping issues on Clem, no real character development and people doing the most glaringly dumb things. The episodes relies too heavily on the "shock value" that Telltale is famous for. It just falls flat because when you don't care for anyone, there isn't anything to be shocked about. In episode 4, I was mostly angry rather than sad at the outcome. There is obvious time and means to do things right, yet nobody really tries, just for the shock value. At least episode 4 ends somewhat interesting.
And then episode 5 arrives and most shockingly... there's so much character development! People are talking to each other about their past, about their thoughts and feelings... and it feels like you're right back at Season 1. This is what I have been waiting for in 4 episodes and I am actually starting to enjoy Season 2 for once. There's interesting turn of events, choices in the story that matters hugely on the plot development. And I actually started caring enough for characters that I resisted some choices in the conversations. Now that means I have gotten attatched to some and it's a good thing.
So, well... I sincerely hope that Season 3 stays true to episode 5s turn of event and keeps up the characters development.
