This review is going to be a little weird because I have very mixed feelings for Life Is Strange. I guess it would be most helpful if I made a pro's and con's list, so here we go (asterisks mean it can be pro or con depending on the player):
PROS:
- Decent graphics
- Character designs are pretty sweet
- Kate Marsh*
- Great indie/hipster soundtrack*
- The entire style/aesthetic of the game was really charming
- The girl that kept getting hit by stuff
- Victoria*
- Warren*
- The journal menu thing was really cool*
- Time rewinding is a cool concept (but it's admittedly pretty lackluster here)
- The school feels like a real school, and it reminded me of Bully a lot
- The janitor guy*
- The game is very well designed
- The texts you can read from other characters are interesting
- "I WAS EATING THOSE BEANS"
CONS:
- Terrible writing (Which I suppose can be blamed on the translation)
- Utterly cringeworthy voice acting*
- Boring pretentious protagonist
- Chloe*
- The game forgets about the main plot for a while
- Terrible references to other Square Enix properties*
- Really awful running gags/catchphrases*
- Gameplay is awful for the majority of the game
- Trying to emulate the TellTale formula, but badly
- Confusing plot twist that makes zero sense other than one off line
- Your choices don't really matter at all, which doesn't make any sense considering the game is based on choice
- Sudden tonal shift that floored me (even though the game was dark before then, it always felt light hearted)
- The bottle scene
- Chloe's dad
- Chloe's mom's accent*
- High school stereotypes*
- THE ENDING
Eh, the game was mediocre. It's not terrible, but it really isn't 8-9/10 worthy. If it's on sale, you should get it, but other than that maybe just watch AdumPlaze play it or something. If you're into cringy dialogue and really bad characters you might enjoy this though.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

This game is super sleek as far as game design goes. It takes all of the unnecessary fluff and opaqueness from previous civ's and smooths them over, capitalizing on the core mechanics that make the game good. In other words, it is board gamey in all the right ways.
More specifically:
- there are now 4 victories, and it is both very clear how they work and where you are in respect to each one
- civics now has a 'tech tree' like science which is very clean
- government types (one of the most board gamey new mechanics) where you select perk 'cards' to fill your slots which are determined by the gov type
- stacking has been made sleek: you can permanently fuse up to 3 of the same unit, making them stronger but not combining their health
- great people are basically stacks of cards where whoever gets enough great person points of a certain type first gets the top card, and the next one is revealed. Again, this is a piece of the game that has been made much cleaner and more strategizable
- trading now involves traders, which you can send on trade routes to any city you know, rewarding you with varying combinations of resources depending on the kind of city
- districts make city building and defending more strategic.
There are more things I could list, but those are the things that come to mind right away. This game has a lot of polish and aesthetic coherence. Plus the UI is really pleasant to use. It feels tactile, like wonderful Blizzard UI's.

Should you buy Gmod?
Yesh.

Depends on your taste, some can reach high grounds of 1k to around 2k hours in Gmod, some 4k.

I loved Civilization V. It was a great game to just casually waste time and think of new and inventive strategies that would enable your empire to the number 1. Unfortunately for Civilization VI, even Robbie Rotten can't teach you how to be number 1. Civ VI adds a lot of new ideas that change the way you look at a Civilization game compared to Civ V, but most of them fall flat.
-The Graphics are greatly improved upon compared to the previous entry. It has a distinct cartoonish artstyle that suits the game well.
-Districts. The district system is one of the few new systems that actually works well. It adds more variety to all of your cities, and allows them to make up for shortcomings due to placement. However, each district requires a certain amount of population, and for each district you make, the cost of the next one goes up.
-Civic Tree. This system replaces the policies of Civ V. It works much the same as the tech tree, but with culture instead of science. You can unlock units, buildings, policies and new governments through this, and it adds alot more depth to the game.
-Pacing. Due to the system of Eureka moments, granting you a boost to a certain technology or civic, you can discover new things far too quickly for your cities to keep up. It is a great idea, but it is implemented poorly.
-Religion. Religion in Civ VI is the worst thing about this game. You are forced to make religious units to combat other religious units. There is no penalty for attacking the units with other religious units, and you cannot capture them with normal units. You can't even attack them with normal units without being at war. The aforementioned religious units will affect the religion of nearby cities based on the outcome of these religious engagements. This would not be a problem if you could attack the units with your own. It also takes far too many spreads to convert any city to your religion, regardless of wether or not it had a religion to begin with.
-Balance. When playing Civ VI you have a choice of 4 civs: you can pick from Rome, Germany, China, and Poland(if you have the DLC). There is no reason to choose any other civ unless you are specifically going for achievements. These 4 civs
have bonuses that completely unbalance the game in their favour.
-UI. Civ V's UI was elegant and easy to understand. Civ VI's UI is a cluttered, complicated  mess.
- The Minimap is all but useless. It is far too small and offers little information. Cities are portrayed by large squares in
the territory, which block most of the already limited view you have.
- Religious view is just about as annoying as the rest of the religious system. When you try to move your religious unit, a filter is placed over your screen. It makes tiles affected by your religion white. When this is active you cannot see where your unit can go, because the movement indicators are a very similar light blue colour.
-Movement. Civ V's movement system was fine. It worked. Civ VI's is annoying. there have been countless times where your unit has 1 movement point left, but it cannot move because of the terrain around it. You expect it to just end that unit's turn automatically because it has nowhere to go. but you will have to come back to that unit and tell it to skip it's turn. The same goes for roads. If my unit has 0.25 of a movement left, it should end the turn. In Civ V your turn ended if you went into rough terrain, like a hill or forest, because it used up all your movement points. In Civ VI you can move one tile normally, still have 2 movement points left, and no be able to go on a hill, forcing you to either go around or end your turn without using up all of your movement.
In conclusion, Civ VI makes some very large strives in the name of innovation, but as with all innovation, most of it falls flat on it's♥♥♥♥♥ Maybe it will be up to par with Civ V after some much needed patches and DLCs to fix the many issues.This passage of time is what allowed for Civ V to be so great. In it's current state however, it is an unintuitive, overly complicated mess of a game. Only buy this if you are a hardcore Civilization fanatic.

This is honestly the most exciting, fun game I've played in a lomg time, if you were in anyway fascinated by space travel and have hundreds of hours to waste, KSP is for you!
I'm currently a Physics, Astrophysics, and Mathematics major at Michigan State University's Honors College and honestly, I don't think I've ever appreciated the work of NASA and the ESA as much as I do after playing this game. Trust me when I say I was always keenly aware of the vastness of space, having loved and studied all things science since I was capable of holding my own head up. But it wasn't until playing this game that I realized that traveling in the vastness was not just some math on a chalkboard and an autopilot system, it's about gravity wells and apoapsides, in a way I only now fully appriciate. The game doesn't make these advanced orbital mechanics feel headsy or difficult, by hour thirteen you'll be as familiar with prograde and retrograde as you are with such terms as "mana" or "HP".
All my praise notwithstanding, this game is not for those who find space or space expolration boring (though, I don't know of anyone who could find it as such). Additionally, the learning curve is steep, but for such effort, you are rewarded. From your first successful orbit to your first ever Mun-landing, you'll feel like a "Champion of Physics", but this feeling is amplified by how many times you'll fail getting to each of those milestones. Each failure, from a dumb staging issue, to a poor rocket design resulting in the inevitable death of the infamous "Jebidiah Kerbin" you'll go through stages of emotions (much like rocket stages [at this point rocketry themed jokes are all I'm capable of making and I think it's beginning to drive my friends and family away]). The stages begin with frustration, eventiually leading to depression, usually resulting in couple hour long break from the game, and normally rounding out by leaving you with the required drive and enthusiasm to actually succeed in your goals.
If I had the reasources to do so, KSP would be standard issue software on all school computers everywhere, this game is literally the defining game for what an educational game should be; fun, entertaining, but in the end inspiring interest in the real world and teaching something along the way.
Regardless of the current price of KSP $40, $30, $15, or $5, it's worth your money, it's a game I'd be willing to pay any sum for, and I would recommend it to no end. If you do not purchase this game, I weep for you, because it epitomizes what gaming should be, challenging, fun, and inspirational.

Guys, this one is a lengthy one from the heart, This game touched me.
I am not one to cry often, I very rarely cry unless its real♥♥♥♥♥♥thats happening to the real me, my eye's didn't even water when I read Old Yeller or when I watched Forest Gump (not to into sad media, I really have no idea what inspired me to play this game in the first place but I am glad that I did). The characters, the world, the story in this game were so well done that I was immersed and boy was it an emotional meat grinder (I cried several times while playing and pretty much cried myself to sleep the night I finished episode 5). I am someone who has dealt with depression in the past and a few of the things that happened in the game have happened to me, or to people close to me (I am not saying what as a lot of that is personal), this game was almost like therapy though, I actually relived a few moments of my life playing this game and I learned to accept them better. The game forced me to think a bit about myself and I have come to accept myself a little more after playing.
I am a lot like Max, kinda an outsider in my college, an introvert (INFP personality type), and I like to keep to myself and keep few, but very close friends. I appreciated how Max's character took the time to stop and look at the world around her as I am in the habit of doing myself (I am inspired to get me one of those instant cameras, it is a wonder that I have not already), the developers really went all out with the world that they crafted, there is detail in everything, a level of detail that you wont find in many other games (which is kinda fitting seeing as Max is a photographer and taking photos with a good eye is one of the many themes in this game), plus the art style is very fitting (I really hate photo realism in games, its kinda dull in my opinion, its why I like games like Team Fortress 2 and the Dishonored series).
The soundtrack in this game was pretty awesome (My iphone is full of many of these songs and I recognized a good number of them), Syd Matters is a talented artist and I would recommend giving his work a listen. The voice acting is great as well, all of this helps with the immersion and character building that the game does so well.
One of the biggest (or the biggest overall) elements in the game is choice and how it matters later and how you can manipulate time to make some unique decisions. This element alone is what made the game feel very fresh and original (which kinda gave it a place in my heart right beside Portal). I kinda admit that I abused this power when it was given to me (I watched Alyssa get smacked in the back of the head by a football multiple times before I helped her), Then I remembered my favorite childhood superhero and lived by the "With great power comes great responsibility" motto.
This has probably been the best drama game I have ever played and definitely deserves the "I am not Crying there is something in my eye" Steam award (which would be really Hella awesome). I know this review is probably  going to sink into oblivion, but If you took the time to read this, then It will have been worth writing. This is a game (and I almost feel like game is not the proper way to describe it) that has given me respect for Dontnod. I highly recommend that you play Life is Strange if you haven't (I mean the first episode is free now), and I hope you get something good from this experience as I have. Thanks for reading this and best of luck in your future endeavors.

This is truly the sort of game that is better to play than to watch. Whilst I had heard a great deal about Life is Strange due to the massive buzz that surrounds it and even so much as checked out gameplay videos of the game on Youtube, I just never thought it would be a game that would sustain my interest. It looked okay, but it wasn't exactly my cup of tea...boy was I wrong.
I nabbed LIS when I saw the first episode free, because who doesn't want a critically acclaimed game for free and ended up buying all other episodes because the first episode did more than enough to hook me so that I'd invest in the other episodes.
First things first, LIS is technically sound, I've had no problems with setup or gameplay, which is a joy considering how many games on Steam can be a chore just to get started, let alone play. The game runs smoothly and shouldn't require some hyperspace super computer to play, for whilst the graphics are indeed crisp and beautiful, they aren't exactly Crysis level of demanding.
Secondly, is the length worth the money? Episodic games aren't for everyone, that's understandable, some might feel they aren't getting a full package, LIS purely based on the first episode however is more than enough to keep you going until you buy the second episode and all others thereafter. There is plenty of replayability as you tinker with different options to see different results. Not always will those choices have a dramatic impact or even an impact in this particular episode, but they are more than enough to make you want to play the first episode at least 2 or 3 times just to see other results.
Thirdly, the storyline is typical teen highschool drama with the usual tropes, jocks, ♥♥♥♥♥y queen and her minions, skater boys, geeks etc, but each and every character finds a way to come to life in an interesting way that contributes to the overall story and playing with your superpower to be an antagonist or protagonist of sorts just makes the game all the more interesting. There is a great degree of joy to be had in the freedom of choice, even if you don't always know what those choices will result in. There are times when you genuinely search your own feelings for how you would handle a situation, is it or is it not the best way to handle this situation? Do I care about this character enough to try and make amends? Has this person had enough impact on me to warrent a negative / positive reaction in this situation?
Making a friend or foe of students in the school is what makes things more interesting and replayable and while there are times when you might wish you had even MORE free reign to make specific choices (or are inclined to feel disappointment when you've overthought something only for it to result in a little fizzle or nothing more), for what you get in the game, there is no complaint.
If you've ever seen S.K.I.N.S, it's very similar in it's make-up (following the lives of typical teenagers going through a moment when decisions about life and what life means to them, matter the most, including drugs, sex, alcohol and more).
I also found it amusing that TALK TO FRANK is an organisation set up to tackle drug abuse in the UK, and yet here we have Frank in this game....selling drugs to teenagers. Let's just say that talking to Frank in this game didn't have the same benefits.
LIS is mysterious, lighthearted when it wants to be and dark when it wants to be, it pulls you into its world and leaves you emotionally fatigued, anger at horrible characters, joy at awesome characters, confusion at suspicious characters, saddened at distraught characters and so much more.

This game needs a lot of work.  Some of the key issues include:
1) Completely asinine AI.  Absolutely the worst AI of any of the CIv games.  Go from ally to enemy in one turn, denouce you for simply having a different government type, and every AI thinks you're a warmonger for defending yourself.  One good example is, I launched a war to liberate England, including their capital.  What did I get for it?  Everyone denoucning me, including England.  Moreover, they will denounce you and then try and trade with you the very next turn.  It's almost as if it was late on a Friday for the dev team and they just "went with it as is."
2)  Game is simply too slow in the latter ages.  Even with cities that have a strong industrial focus, it takes way too long to build anything.  It shows with the AI.  Their armies are typically very small, which makes the game boring.  Most wars are over too fast, because no one can afford to build enough.
3)  No United Nations?  This seems like a major oversight, as it plays a big role in Civ 5.  Half of the reason to get city states on your side is lost.
4)  If you lose the game, you'll never know why.  It simply pops up and says....you lose, game over.  No stats, or details behind why you lost.  Unbelieveable.
5)  Religion is TERRIBLE.  I disable religious victories.  All you do is spam as many apostles and missionaries as you can...all over the world.  That's it.   Relgion should go back to what it was, a branch of culture.
All of this drives the game into one simple direction.....war.  It's way too easy to just roll over everyone.  Why struggle with anemities and resource trading when you can simply take it all?  This game feels very polished in some areas, and terribly underdone in others.  I'm hopeful they will fix this with quick updates.

Guys, this one is a lengthy one from the heart, This game touched me.
I am not one to cry often, I very rarely cry unless its real♥♥♥♥♥♥thats happening to the real me, my eye's didn't even water when I read Old Yeller or when I watched Forest Gump (not to into sad media, I really have no idea what inspired me to play this game in the first place but I am glad that I did). The characters, the world, the story in this game were so well done that I was immersed and boy was it an emotional meat grinder (I cried several times while playing and pretty much cried myself to sleep the night I finished episode 5). I am someone who has dealt with depression in the past and a few of the things that happened in the game have happened to me, or to people close to me (I am not saying what as a lot of that is personal), this game was almost like therapy though, I actually relived a few moments of my life playing this game and I learned to accept them better. The game forced me to think a bit about myself and I have come to accept myself a little more after playing.
I am a lot like Max, kinda an outsider in my college, an introvert (INFP personality type), and I like to keep to myself and keep few, but very close friends. I appreciated how Max's character took the time to stop and look at the world around her as I am in the habit of doing myself (I am inspired to get me one of those instant cameras, it is a wonder that I have not already), the developers really went all out with the world that they crafted, there is detail in everything, a level of detail that you wont find in many other games (which is kinda fitting seeing as Max is a photographer and taking photos with a good eye is one of the many themes in this game), plus the art style is very fitting (I really hate photo realism in games, its kinda dull in my opinion, its why I like games like Team Fortress 2 and the Dishonored series).
The soundtrack in this game was pretty awesome (My iphone is full of many of these songs and I recognized a good number of them), Syd Matters is a talented artist and I would recommend giving his work a listen. The voice acting is great as well, all of this helps with the immersion and character building that the game does so well.
One of the biggest (or the biggest overall) elements in the game is choice and how it matters later and how you can manipulate time to make some unique decisions. This element alone is what made the game feel very fresh and original (which kinda gave it a place in my heart right beside Portal). I kinda admit that I abused this power when it was given to me (I watched Alyssa get smacked in the back of the head by a football multiple times before I helped her), Then I remembered my favorite childhood superhero and lived by the "With great power comes great responsibility" motto.
This has probably been the best drama game I have ever played and definitely deserves the "I am not Crying there is something in my eye" Steam award (which would be really Hella awesome). I know this review is probably  going to sink into oblivion, but If you took the time to read this, then It will have been worth writing. This is a game (and I almost feel like game is not the proper way to describe it) that has given me respect for Dontnod. I highly recommend that you play Life is Strange if you haven't (I mean the first episode is free now), and I hope you get something good from this experience as I have. Thanks for reading this and best of luck in your future endeavors.

In many ways Civilization VI is a worthy and exciting successor to the franchise, but ultimately it is crippled by a few significant problems.
The biggest issues I see are as follows:
- The AI is poor which results in games that become predictable and boring
- There are no Teams in either Multiplayer or Single player (forget playing cooperatively with your friends)
- Puzzling omissions of basic quality of life features
-- There is no restart button, re-rolling a start requires exiting to the menu
-- There is no memory of the settings the previous game was started with, let alone a template system (this makes the first point even worse)
-- There are no build queues
-- There is no way to set trade route duration, or to quickly instruct a trader to repeat its last route
- The naval aspect of the game is extremely underwhelming
There are other issues, like balancing the relative importance of production, research, and so on, but I'll refrain from diving into them to state that my fundamental position is that this game is not ready to be offered at the price that is being asked. I'm a huge fan of this franchise and have high hopes for this installment, but after several disappointing patches from the development team that address virtually none of the problems I've listed, I believe players should wait awhile before making the decision to purchase Civ VI.

This is truly the sort of game that is better to play than to watch. Whilst I had heard a great deal about Life is Strange due to the massive buzz that surrounds it and even so much as checked out gameplay videos of the game on Youtube, I just never thought it would be a game that would sustain my interest. It looked okay, but it wasn't exactly my cup of tea...boy was I wrong.
I nabbed LIS when I saw the first episode free, because who doesn't want a critically acclaimed game for free and ended up buying all other episodes because the first episode did more than enough to hook me so that I'd invest in the other episodes.
First things first, LIS is technically sound, I've had no problems with setup or gameplay, which is a joy considering how many games on Steam can be a chore just to get started, let alone play. The game runs smoothly and shouldn't require some hyperspace super computer to play, for whilst the graphics are indeed crisp and beautiful, they aren't exactly Crysis level of demanding.
Secondly, is the length worth the money? Episodic games aren't for everyone, that's understandable, some might feel they aren't getting a full package, LIS purely based on the first episode however is more than enough to keep you going until you buy the second episode and all others thereafter. There is plenty of replayability as you tinker with different options to see different results. Not always will those choices have a dramatic impact or even an impact in this particular episode, but they are more than enough to make you want to play the first episode at least 2 or 3 times just to see other results.
Thirdly, the storyline is typical teen highschool drama with the usual tropes, jocks, ♥♥♥♥♥y queen and her minions, skater boys, geeks etc, but each and every character finds a way to come to life in an interesting way that contributes to the overall story and playing with your superpower to be an antagonist or protagonist of sorts just makes the game all the more interesting. There is a great degree of joy to be had in the freedom of choice, even if you don't always know what those choices will result in. There are times when you genuinely search your own feelings for how you would handle a situation, is it or is it not the best way to handle this situation? Do I care about this character enough to try and make amends? Has this person had enough impact on me to warrent a negative / positive reaction in this situation?
Making a friend or foe of students in the school is what makes things more interesting and replayable and while there are times when you might wish you had even MORE free reign to make specific choices (or are inclined to feel disappointment when you've overthought something only for it to result in a little fizzle or nothing more), for what you get in the game, there is no complaint.
If you've ever seen S.K.I.N.S, it's very similar in it's make-up (following the lives of typical teenagers going through a moment when decisions about life and what life means to them, matter the most, including drugs, sex, alcohol and more).
I also found it amusing that TALK TO FRANK is an organisation set up to tackle drug abuse in the UK, and yet here we have Frank in this game....selling drugs to teenagers. Let's just say that talking to Frank in this game didn't have the same benefits.
LIS is mysterious, lighthearted when it wants to be and dark when it wants to be, it pulls you into its world and leaves you emotionally fatigued, anger at horrible characters, joy at awesome characters, confusion at suspicious characters, saddened at distraught characters and so much more.
There is a lot here and I'm glad I invested time into it.

In many ways Civilization VI is a worthy and exciting successor to the franchise, but ultimately it is crippled by a few significant problems.
The biggest issues I see are as follows:
- The AI is poor which results in games that become predictable and boring
- There are no Teams in either Multiplayer or Single player (forget playing cooperatively with your friends)
- Puzzling omissions of basic quality of life features
-- There is no restart button, re-rolling a start requires exiting to the menu
-- There is no memory of the settings the previous game was started with, let alone a template system (this makes the first point even worse)
-- There are no build queues
-- There is no way to set trade route duration, or to quickly instruct a trader to repeat its last route
- The naval aspect of the game is extremely underwhelming
There are other issues, like balancing the relative importance of production, research, and so on, but I'll refrain from diving into them to state that my fundamental position is that this game is not ready to be offered at the price that is being asked. I'm a huge fan of this franchise and have high hopes for this installment, but after several disappointing patches from the development team that address virtually none of the problems I've listed, I believe players should wait awhile before making the decision to purchase Civ VI.

I pre-ordered the game in large part because everything prior to release implied that a Linux version was a certainty. I'm not naive to expect a day one release, but I didn't see any reason to be merely cautiously optimistic. It was a platform that, based on the steam store page, was to be supported.
Now, months after release, we are getting updates about whether the publisher/developer will deem it viable to release it for that platform at all. Say what? If it isn't a priority, well, that's disappointing, but can we get some insight into whether this multi-month investigation is dragging along because of low priority or because there is truly the mystery or all mysteries clouding the analysis of this basic decision. One that seemed a whole lot easier to make during the pre-order.
Anyway, game is good. I have a Windows computer and a Linux computer and probably would have bought it either way, but this is the sort of practice that has steered me off of pre-orders in the past and has slapped some sense back into me. I toyed with making this a recommended purchase with the same whining complaint since I can't speak terribly ill of the game itself even if I'm still not sure if I prefer it to the previous version. I will preface this review by saying that without this game I would have applied to do a very different course at university.
The reason I and so many other people love this game is that it allows you to access the kind of physics and engineering that usually takes a degree in aerospace engineering to see and introduces you to them in a way which was understandable to me as a 14-year-old, who was just learning that a = Δv/t within my academic lessons, yet I still find the mathematics used by the game at the limits of my academic underatanding as I prepare to begin my degree. Certainly I agree with the idea that KSP is as much an educational tool as it is a piece of entertainment; you can choose to throw as many parts as your PC will calculate physics for together and watch as it spiralls hopelessly oput of control before change-by-change making the thing work, or you can sit down with a pen and paper and calculate exactly what is required, and how to do it, assemble your design, program the flight plan onto the onboard computer (with the kOS mod) and feel a huge sense of achievement as your craft performs its mission flawlessly.
Then there are the mods, which can turn this from a space-sim to a military-developer-sim, (BDarmoury/Ferram Aerospace Research) a space wallpaper generator, (various) Interstellar: the game (KSP interstellar/Kerbol Plus) and so much more!
A word of warning... this game WILL make your PC chug - Unity is known for only using a single core on your CPU so I suggest a high-clock part in your system, however I was able to get the game to run on min settings on a laptop with a dual core pentium at 2.2GHz, integrated graphics.
So for the verdict... If your PC has a CPU clocked at 2.2 GHz or more and a graphics cad which could outdo a phone, get this game, take the time to learn the basic physics behind it, and let it inspire you as it did to me. And while you're at it, throw some mods in there, there is a program called CKAN which will manage them for you.

This might be way more worthwhile after either the developers, or modders fix the serious amount of problems plaguing the gameplay.
Civ6 isn't a game about building a Civilization - it's just a bog-standard war game now. Attacks from both barbarians, and other in-game Civs, are endless. The combat AI is particularly bad - your enemies will normally just march to their own suicide, having declared a war they could never have possibly won.
The AI in general is the poorest I've seen in any Civ game to date. Civs will declare war on you regardless of your strength, or theirs. The earliest war I've had declared on me so far was on turn 3 - we both had one warrior to our collective names. I just sat my warrior in local territory, on top of a hill. The AI then just started attempting to pump out any war unit it could, and trickled each unit one-by-one to their death. This went on for about 80 turns.
Firaxis attempted to bring back the "points" system which showed you why a Civ liked/disliked you. For example: you'd get a +5 bonus for having the same type of government, or a -5 penalty if you settled too close to them, or got caught spying on them, etc. The problem is, this is a complete placebo effect. It doesn't remotely alter how a Civ feels about you. You can be on +50 for positive actions, and they'll still denounce you, or declare war on you, or simply refuse to trade with you. If it wasn't for the AI being so terrible in every other department, I'd almost think this was a bug.
Maybe pick it up if an expansion is released which purely focuses on just fixing the AI. Until then, stick with Civ5.

Only something like this would explain all the problems this game currently has. Even if you was a huge fan of the Civ series, you will spend hours trying to find something, anything in this game that is worth your attention, but you will only find disappointment.
- Bugs everywhere.
- Deity AI can barely move units around and can be beaten by anyone.
- New "card" system doesn't really give you a lot of choices in the current balance.
- Districts system doesn't work as intended (spamming cities every 4 tiles for AoE bonuses is not particularly fun)
- New religious victory doesn't work at all vs. players (because who in their mind will invest into defensive apostles when it's possible to just kill all religious units with a single horseman?)

Seriously, go play some Civ5:BnW. It's a much better game in every aspect.

A thoroughly enjoyable simulation game.  Check out my full video review:
Video Transcript:
Hello viewers!  Welcome to another episode of A Bird's Eye View.  My name is Endeavor, once again your humble host.  Our game this time is the simulator Kerbal Space Program.  Developed and published by Squad, this game came out of Early Access in April of 2015.  Let's take a look at the finished product.
As a simulation game, Kerbal Space Program doesn't have a real story to speak of.  The player is tasked with running a NASA like organization made up of accident-prone green people called Kerbals.  Administrator duties include everything from securing funding, designing ships, and even personally piloting space shuttles, all the while trying to keep your astronauts alive long enough to go on more than one mission.
The game has a charmingly simple atmosphere, with unobtrusive, upbeat music to keep the mood light.  Most of the engine is dedicated to simulating complex physics, so the art is fairly plain.  The graphical limitations are fine since the ultimate purpose of the game is to tinker around with creative spaceship crafting.
Kerbal Space Program includes a few game modes.  The primary way to play is called Career Mode, which unpacks the game slowly, constantly giving the player new challenges to beat in order to unlock more things with which to play.  Sandbox, which used to be the main game, gives the player all of the unlockable ship parts to use right off the bat.  Finally, there’s Science Mode, which includes missions and tasks like Career Mode, but without some of the more managerial duties like worrying about funding.
The controls, while not simple, are consistent enough, and they can be rebound for ease-of-use.  There were so many controls and commands to remember that I had to reference the options menu frequently, but the game doesn't punish the player for doing so.
There are games with annoyingly overzealous tutorials that constantly remind the player how to do things.  Kerbal Space Program is not one of those.  Quite honestly, while the tutorials are comprehensive, they throw so much technical jargon and complex concepts at the player that the tutorials feel inadequate.  This game doesn't hold your hand, and I'm left with the impression that the player is expected to crash and burn a few times before getting it.
One part of the game that sorely needed further explanation was the Career Mode.  The game tells you that you need to launch missions and conduct research to earn Science (a sort of currency for unlocking upgrades), but almost no effort was made explaining how one conducts research.  I learned more about how to play from Wikis and online guides than I did from the game itself.
There were only a few bugs which I encountered during my time.  When building, there were a few times where the ship pieces wouldn't attach to the spacecraft how I wanted them to.  Fixing the issue involved saving my work and reloading, which wasn't a big deal, but it happened often enough to warrant a mention here.  A few times I had a problem where ship pieces that were meant to separate during flight wouldn't cooperate, dooming my ship and mission to an explosive end.
Despite any issues I had with the game, I think it was masterfully put together.  Nothing beats the feeling of finally getting your ship out of the atmosphere for the first time, and the accomplishments don't stop there.  Once you've broken the speed and altitude records, it's time to orbit the planet Kerbal.  And then try landing a ship on the moon.  Learning to manage limited fuel supplies and using gravitational pull to slingshot around planets and moons is fascinatingly complex, yet the satisfaction in learning all of the ins and outs of space travel make it a worthwhile endeavor.
The game's retail price is $39.99.  With all of the features and science-based entertainment, I recommend Kerbal Space Program for anyone that loves building and discovery.  It's currently available on Steam and Good Old Games for Windows, Mac, and Linux.  It is also available for PS4.
That concludes my review for Kerbal Space Program.  Thank you for watching, and don't forget to hit the “like” button if you enjoyed my video.  As always, you can follow us on Twitter at Rookery Gamers for let's plays and additional reviews.

Life is Strange is a fantastic game, as it is a story based game there is no combat or such to take part in, you merely choose actions that play out in the story.
The only other game that I've played similiar to this would be Telltale's 'The Walking Dead', so I had some expectactions of what was to come. Something to point out between those two games is that in TWD when you are given choices sometimes you are given a timer where you have to quickly make a decision; in Life is Strange, you don't get these quick decision making moments, although you'll be presented with a tough decision you are able to step back and think it before you make your choice at your leisurely pace.
As it is widely known the games soundtrack is amazinly well down in the selection of music used to play out scenes, I found myself being entranced by the choice of music during various moments in the game where I would stop and just listen to the music choice as well as the scenery you are given. If you end up playing this game you will also experience the tranquility.
The games unique mechanic is a great part for gamers who often feel like they are missing out or certain dialogues/chat because you are able to rewind back you can replay dialogues you didn't originally choose whereas in other games you'd feel the compulsion to save on multiple slots or completely start over (although this can be the case too for when you make big decision but for small generic choices you can experience them all).
The voice acting is very well down, the main characters voice acting really brings them to life.
Some minor issues I had;
- In some scenes the facial/mouth animations were not playing so while something important was going on, the voices were going but you would be fixated on their expressionless faces and their closed mouths.
- Although the main character has just turned 18 to me I felt like she looked much younger like 15 or so. So that was a little off putting for me as I kept thinking "Did developers really set the ages right?"
I've always enjoyed things that have had great storylines and Life is Strange is definitely one of those. So if you enjoy good stories, then Life is Strange is absolutely something you should check out.

If you liked Civilization V then you'll love this. It includes a lot of the features from that game, including the ones that were from the expansions. They even added to them by having more government types that you progress through, and adding more features to religions like theological combat (you heard me), and a religious victory condition. One of my favorite features is the new districts system. It might take some time to understand how to get the most out of it (I still rarely build some of them) but it changes how you pick city locations and how you build them. They also added new civs having multiple leaders that have some unique units and perks. Unfortunately, only one civ has an alternate leader in the base game (Greece).

Now some of the negatives. The AI is dumb as bricks, and that is a fair statement. In my current game I completely outpace the medium AI on tech AND civics (oh yea theres culture tech now) Also two civs declared surprise wars on me (oh yea war is more complex now) at the same time and I utterly destroyed any forces they sent and took one city (taking a city when YOU get attacked gets you a huge diplomatic penalty) Also I while I get that its their art style, I don't particularly like it.
So thats that, if you like 4X games, or strategy based then I think you'll like Civ VI. If you arn't sure you can also try Civ V, it should be cheaper.

Awesome game and space simulation. Played it a little during early access but has come a long way since then, improving gameplay, features and physics. If space flight interests you, definetly get this. If building stuff interests you, check it out. Beneath the cute graphics there is a serious, challenging but fun simulation which when played in career mode really feels like your in the 'space race' of the sixties and then takes you into the modern day and beyond.... or you can just play in sandbox mode with all technologies unlocked.
There is no tutorial or in game help, but there is an extensive wiki and other useful information online (just google stuff). Essential things to google from the start (unless playing in Sandbox mode) are Biomes and how Science works and if you struggle with space planes there are some useful guides online.
KSP also supports community mods, of which there are many including graphics and physics overhauls, However, I am still playing full career using the base game and since the official release I feel the physics are very good without mods. However I do use a number of mods which do not alter gameplay but provide some very usefull features. The developers did a great job of making the game very accesible, but as you progress some of these become essential really.
KERBAL ENGINEER
Provides extra information on all sorts of things, some of which is even essential I would say. Some of this is replicated my MechJeb, but I still like some of the features and presentation of Kerbal Engineer.
PRECISE NODE (not sure compatible anymore and MechJeb has same feature anyway)
Allows easier and more precise editing of maneuver nodes (once you unlock them by upgrading your space centre buildings) plus displays extra information about the new orbits that will be achieved following the maneuver.
DOCKING PORT ALIGNMENT / NAVBALL DOCKING ALIGNMENT
Both provide graphical docking aids, very useful (once you have researched docking ports).
MECHJEB
Once you find your tired of doing the same maneuvers over and over again, this mod automates many common maneuvers. The technolgy must be researched first and part included on your ships, so is still realistic as these are just features you would have available anyway.
STAGE RECOVERY
If your playing on full career this is very useful to help recover jettisoned stages (and save money). The base game has a number of limitations in this area making recovery of jettiosned stages difficult or impossible at times (you have no control over when chutes are deployed once jettisoned and jettisoned parts are deleted once 2.5 km away from your main space craft). You still need to have enough parachutes mounted and will only recover parts which would actualy return to Kerbin (Earth) safely.

This is the first review I've ever left on Steam, and I feel compelled to do so because this game is an absolute atrocity when it comes to the Civ franchise. I feel as if I would be remiss if I did not attempt to persuade potential customers not to purchase this game. As a long time fanatic of Civllization, I can only say, that, I feel completely, and, utterly, disappointed in the most recent Civilization release. To be completely blunt, it is a total pile of garbage. To begin, the graphics are a complete joke. The best aspect of the Civilization games, is navigating your army through a massive/beautiful terrain, and that aspect is completely lost in the most recent abomination released by Firaxis Games. The mechanics of the game almost seem stubborn, and unilateral at times. A simple task, such as, switching between troops, seems like a strenuous task to say the least. I, woefully, made the mistake of purchasing this game, as I am a huge advocate of the Civ franchise. Despite negative reviews, I opted to waste my money on this game. If you've been reading KSP reviews looking for a reason to get into the game, I really don't know why.
KSP combines orbital mechanics with lego-style rocket building. If you spent a childhood with Lego, only to build rediculous space ships (and then see how much abuse they could take), then you and KSP will get along swimmingly.
Did you watch Gravity for the special effects but scoff at the sheer implausibility of the maneuvres that took place, then KSP will make it up to you:
Plan exotic moon landing missions in the early stages of your career (with less-than-ideal resources) and discover that you had enough fuel to barely land Jeb on the Mun.
Plan exotic moon rescue missions where you discover that you don't know how to properly intercept your lander with the command module. That will result in an improvised transfer using EVA from your dead lander to the CM.
Now if that's not nail-biting, physics-based action that will both excite your frends with tales of your exploits while getting thumbs up of approval from your more geeky friends (the ones who walked out half-way through Gravity), then there's really nothing I can do for you.
Move along. Go play Call of Duty or something.

Episode one review.
As a follow up to the first season, this is more of the same in terms of style.  However, following Clementine again, but this time from her point of view and not from her guardian Lee's, you find her more grown up and more capable than you remember her.
The story is exciting, with several twists and turns as you head towards the inevitable cliffhanger.  There are hints of the choices you made in the first game (as these are imported when you begin, assuming you have them on your PC).
There are several new characters, whose motives aren't entirely clear from the off.  Sometimes I found they annoyed me - their actions didn't seem particularly reasonable or realistic, but then we are in the middle of an apocalypse so I guess people wouldn't all behave rationally!  Clementine must make some difficult moral choices to secure her own survival.
I'm looking forward to the next installments - I just hope TT don't take months to release them again.  I noticed they don't make any promises for releasing the chapters "monthly" like they promised, but didn't deliver, last time.  That's a good thing.  I can just sit back, play something else, and wait until it's ready :)

Excellent game. Adds many new features without pulling a Sims 4 and removing items obtained through expansion packs from civ v. This makes the game exceptionally deep.
Although there are some distinct Civ's absent in this one, they're replaced by others (**** off Alexander the 'Great'). Somehow the units and individual civ perks really felt important in the course of the game. Choosing the right leader for your play style is important. Being able to adjust and diplomatically force your opponents into your game, even more so.
The ability to stack units into corps and armies appeases fans of the old Civ games' strategy of creating a 1 tile wrecking crew while allowing the Civ V strategy of flanking and support units. I really liked that.
The art style of this game can be hit or miss depending on the user, but I personally like it. They understand this is the ultimate board game, and game up with a style that seems to match that.
I would assume this could make the game a bit unwieldy to a newcomer, but that can be overcome easily enough by playing through some shorter games on lower difficulties.
If there is any drawback, it's only that in a standard game, things seem a little more drawn out. Even with research and production heavy builds in all my cities, it still seemed to take a little too long to get the next item created. Or maybe I'm still a 6 year veteran-noob. Altering the game length and/or difficulty will more than likely make that easier.
The amount of items to work with towards victory is staggering. Night in and night out, this game simply demands one more turn.

A beautiful story featuring story telling elements of fantasy and classical fairytale all while mixed with modern sci-fi sensibities.
In the grande scheme of things Life is Strange is about choices and the degree to which our main character, Max, is willing to make them. The paths and consequences of taking them you are willing to and have the stomach to live with. It is about learning to be a time artist, one who can see and alter the very fabric of time and space.
One might also characterize it as a coming of age tale, of a loss of innocence. As well as it being a test. It's the classical character shaping test of a magicly gifted/cursed (?) person, one who has control of time and in so having this control - is presented with a grande test of reasoning, memory and emotional fortitude. To live with the choices you make, navigate them and accept your self as what you (magically) are, with your best friend.
I supopose, in closure, it ought to be said that this game hits on a lot of nerves. Elements of the human condition and life in general. These parts of the story, and of the characters in particular are about more than someone with time travel and its manipulation. It's not only a story about magical people. But real (fictional) people too. The kind that matter and which the story, leaves you caring about as good characters who've been through a lot and made it out, alright. Mentally scarred, impacted, changed. But, alright...still going forward.
In completing the story it's rather easy to be left with a sense of melancholic about the time and place the story crafts. That despite the drama, horrors and choices made by the characters, ... there was something comfortable however short lived about the time and place. About the characters. Something very human and realistic.
---
Note: I'd love to see Max and Chloe continue on to Seatle following the aftermath of Arcadia Bay.

There are some good ideas here, such as districts and wonders being placed on tiles, and I think Civ VI has the potential to be a great game someday. In its current state, however, I can't recommend it.
It was essentially released unfinished. Instead of building on Civ V, it released with a lack of mod support, team multiplayer, and basic features that had been established in their previous games (toggling auto-select units, saving map options, restarting/rerolling a game, alliances with shared vision, auto-renew trade routes, etc.) Two patches 30 days and 60 days later, some balancing and minor fixes were performed, but if they continue to work at this rate, it will be years before the game is fully-featured. It appears that their early priority is paid DLC, and they are ignoring the most requested fixes.
I unfortunately bought it full price. I would recommend waiting until the game is in a better state, it simply isn't worth $60 right now.
UPDATE:
After the Australia Patch, Workshop support and multiplayer teams were added. These fairly basic changes in no way justified the amount of time it took to add them, but now the game is in a generally good state. There are still some annoying quality-of-life fixes that are needed, such as clunky diplomacy, no auto-renew on trade routes, hard-to-click notifications, saving game setups, or quick restart using same settings. The game would have been acceptable in this state at launch, not months later. If they manage to put in a few hours for some of these minor fixes, the game will be much better. It's current state is actually fun to play, though. I can now recommend this game.

Life is Strange is a fantastic game, as it is a story based game there is no combat or such to take part in, you merely choose actions that play out in the story.
The only other game that I've played similiar to this would be Telltale's 'The Walking Dead', so I had some expectactions of what was to come. Something to point out between those two games is that in TWD when you are given choices sometimes you are given a timer where you have to quickly make a decision; in Life is Strange, you don't get these quick decision making moments, although you'll be presented with a tough decision you are able to step back and think it before you make your choice at your leisurely pace.
As it is widely known the games soundtrack is amazinly well down in the selection of music used to play out scenes, I found myself being entranced by the choice of music during various moments in the game where I would stop and just listen to the music choice as well as the scenery you are given. If you end up playing this game you will also experience the tranquility.
The games unique mechanic is a great part for gamers who often feel like they are missing out or certain dialogues/chat because you are able to rewind back you can replay dialogues you didn't originally choose whereas in other games you'd feel the compulsion to save on multiple slots or completely start over (although this can be the case too for when you make big decision but for small generic choices you can experience them all).
The voice acting is very well down, the main characters voice acting really brings them to life.
Some minor issues I had;
- In some scenes the facial/mouth animations were not playing so while something important was going on, the voices were going but you would be fixated on their expressionless faces and their closed mouths.
- Although the main character has just turned 18 to me I felt like she looked much younger like 15 or so. So that was a little off putting for me as I kept thinking "Did developers really set the ages right?"
I've always enjoyed things that have had great storylines and Life is Strange is definitely one of those. So if you enjoy good stories, then Life is Strange is absolutely something you should check out.

As of writing this, I'm going to tentatively say that KSP is a worthwhile purchase. If nothing else, you'll likely get quite a few hours out of just the early career mode and plenty of scope to muck around if that's your thing. However, really getting a lot out of the game, and particularly career mode, requires one of two things: Either you will have to be willing/able to do some tedious math each time you design a rocket/plane, or you will need to download and install a third party mod to do the calculations for you. The big reason for this is that getting much further than a basic orbit or short-range one-way flights requires careful calculation of delta-V, a function not performed by the basic game as of writing this review. This is, in my opinion, a nasty oversight on the part of the devs; as it is quite important for anything other than a sandbox game, where cost efficiency doesn't matter.
Overall, if you're keen on the idea of actually doing manual algebra to play a game then this should suit you nicely. If you're happy enough to go and get a mod to do the basic calculations for you, this game should suit you too. If like me you're not fussed about either, look elsewhere. This is a good simulator, but not really a casual player's game.

Extremely addicting first person hero-based multiplayer game. Has bits of MOBA in it, like being able to customize your champion's card deck (different perks that'll automatically be available at the start of a match) and being able to buy additional perks by gaining points during the match (standing on the objective, escorting the payload, getting kills or assists, healing teammates, etc.).
Some of those additional items/perks you buy during a match are quicker reloads, slightly less damage taken from direct hits, heal on kills, heal on hits, etc. You can only buy one perk for each category (heal on kill and heal on hits are on the same category, for example) and you can upgrade each one three times during the match.
After each match all of that resets, so none of this feels "pay to win". It's like League of Legends/SMITE/Dota 2/other MOBAs where each match has you buying items that give you different perks and they'll only last for that match.
I'm loving the game, and I originally went into it expecting an Overwatch clone since that's what wonderful clickbait-y sites like Kotaku would lead you to believe. It's not really like it. It's similar gameplay-wise (you're escorting a cart that moves on it's own as long as you're standing near it and enemies aren't near it), but it still feels different enough. Personally I actually enjoy this more, and I haven't touched Overwatch since I started playing this last week.
Anyway, it's free to play so rather than spending time reading reviews just go check it out, it's worth your time!

Season two marks the next chapter in Telltale’s The Walking Dead.
The Walking Dead emphasizes narrative and character development over all else. If you’re looking for solid gameplay, you may be disappointed in that regard. On the other hand though, TWD excels at providing an engaging story and features extremely likable characters. It plays out in the form of a point and click adventure game which feels a lot like an interactive movie. There are no puzzles, and the gameplay is handled through quick time events most of the time.
Season two continues shortly after where the first left off and this time you’ll be playing as Clementine opposed to Lee. Seeing the world through the eyes of a little girl immediately makes the game feel more depressing and hopeless as she has to fend for herself now. The zombies, which felt fairly weak in season one are suddenly a much more dangerous threat for Clementine to deal with as well.
The story telling is second to none; however my main issue with The Walking Dead is the whole illusion of choice aspect. At the time of this review, only the first episode of season two is available but this problem was quite prevalent in season one. At first glance, the game will make you feel as if your choices have a major influence on the story. Upon further investigation, you’ll realize that regardless of your choices, you’ll always be brought to the same conclusion. This makes The Walking Dead an extremely enjoyable experience the first time you play but it essentially eliminates any element of re-playability afterwards.
If you’re looking for a great story, definitely check it out; just don’t expect to influence it much.

A good game that is not quite there yet. Civ 5 wans't great at launch too but by the 2nd DLC it was my favorite game. I'm hoping civ 6 will go through the same process. As of now it's a 7.5. I like it, but I don't love it yet.
"Do you recommend this game?" If there was a gray option saying "aahh, not sure" I'd choose it. I'm recommending it with a dose of patience, because It's goodish now I know it will be great with time.
The good:
- Same old addictive "one more turn" experience.
- Eureka moments. You gain a research boost for completing a set of tasks. Ex: killing an unit with a slinger boost archery tech.
- Districts and Wonders. Now you really have to plan your settlements, to get the max bonus for districts, and to have enough room to build wonders, for both occupy land around your city. Also wonders have more reqs now, like being built near a river and a industrial district or on an flat land close to a campus district with an university.
- There is now a separate Social Policy tech tree you advance with culture. It's now possible to have a high tech civ of bigots, or a high culture civ of morons.
- Government policies cards. Culture now unlocks new Government forms and there is a system of cards to assign and change policies.
The bad:
- UI is horrible. You have to get the hang of it. Lots of useless msgs appear all the time while important info is hidden away in sub menus. There is no Alert order for units, Fortify now consume unit's moves.
- Tech tree definitely requires refining. It's possible to have submarines without reseraching Steel , or infantry without rifling. If you complete the research for the nuclear submarine you won't be able to build regular subs anymore.
- Diplomacy is worse than in previous games. More often than not the AI will go haywire and denounce or declare war for no apparent reason. The idea of agendas seemed a nice one but turned out to fix civ behavior in a cast. Ex: If you have a land locked civ Norway will hate you no matter what. Civ6 is more geared towards a competing game than a civ sim. If you are close to a victory everybody will declare war despite any relationship built.
- The game forces you to go large. If you stick to 3 or 4 tall cities you will lose.
- The military aspect of the game overshadows all others. There will be wars no matter what, and you'll have to build military units since the start, no matter what. For a game with so many victory types, like cultural and religious, seems odd to be forced to have a strong army all the time.
All in all is a good game, the scales a tiping slightly to the good side, and this a bit frustrating. I was expecting a game better than Civ 5 in all areas but that's not the case yet. There is still plenty of room for improvement and by the updates released it will definetly be better with time.

Started playing it once it got released and career mode was a thing.
So far I'm having tons of fun just playing around with the different modules and being creative with all the different ways to invent new spacecrafts.
The aerodynamic physics leaves a lot of room for improvisation, but will be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥once in awhile.
Career mode gives you that bit of challenge that I felt I wanted. It limits the parts just enough (sometimes a bit too much though) and challenges your creativity and it almost becomes a puzzle game trying to complete some of the missions.
However, I felt that I had to get this out there: It will eventually crash when going back and forth flight mode and build mode. Had a couple of these already and MAAAN it sucks to lose all the progress.
Another problem is that the modules seem very flimsy (no, not realistically) at times. Shaking around like jello and sometimes getting stuck inside other modules and moving around inside them.
It really makes no sense at all to see my wings sometimes shifting positions inside the modules. Or that decouplers randomly gets stuck for no other reason than glitchy physics. And that's pretty bad in a game like this.
EDIT: Another thing I forgot to add; When you forward time, you'd think the physics wouldn't change since all you're doing is just speed up time, right?. You'd be wrong.
The physics react for some strange reason to the time being sped up, so be careful when you're using it.
For example, I put a bunch of engines on the side of a rocket and when I had it on 1x, they were just fine. On 2x they started to bend. On 5x they exploded instantly.
Sound is pretty... lame. Some sounds seem to have low bitrate while others sound just fine. Explosions play multiple soundeffects when several modules explode, instead of having one massive sound for that occasion, which might be a bit ear rapey.
And I feel it's lacking some soundeffects.
Overall, it's probably the worts part of the game. That's not saying much though.
These issues don't really make the game bad at all, don't get me wrong. It's just some annoyances that I wish would get fixed.
Anyway... Totally recommended if you're into some hardcore physics based simulation. Even if the price is a bit steep.

So, you've probably seen a lot of hate towards this game because it's different.  If you're on the fence, let's be realistic.  First, sequels are different.  If it was the same, we'd just keep playing Civ V.  Second, the art style is a matter of taste.  I personally love it.
Now, if you're still on the fence, go back and read about Civ V when it first came out.  People declared Civ IV as the Alpha and Omega of all strategy games and Civ V was a diseased mongrel that just soiled your grandma's rug.  Now, Civ V is the golden child and Civ VI has the AUDACITY to try new things.  I think you can see how 99% of the complaints are by people who were never going to like Civ VI out of the gate.
Finally, remember that satisfied players are out PLAYING.  We're not on the forums complaining because that's time that could be spent crushing the AI.  Is Civ VI perfect?  No.  Is it crucially flawed?  No.  A small number of people have technical issues that are unfortunate but are part and parcel of PC gaming.  Games not working sometimes, that's a risk we all accept due to the inherent difficulty in programming for the PC platform vs. consoles with standardized hardware.
Now, if you're new to the series, this is a very welcoming entry.  On lower difficulties, the AI is a declawed house cat.  Come to think of it, on higher difficulties you're still kinda playing against yourself.  The AI gets more aggressive but they're still tactically feeble in combat.
Should you buy it?  Absolutely.  It has everything you could want from a 4X game and no matter what anyone else says, the Civ series is still the 800-lb. gorilla in the room compared to everything else.

As of writing this, I'm going to tentatively say that KSP is a worthwhile purchase. If nothing else, you'll likely get quite a few hours out of just the early career mode and plenty of scope to muck around if that's your thing. However, really getting a lot out of the game, and particularly career mode, requires one of two things: Either you will have to be willing/able to do some tedious math each time you design a rocket/plane, or you will need to download and install a third party mod to do the calculations for you. The big reason for this is that getting much further than a basic orbit or short-range one-way flights requires careful calculation of delta-V, a function not performed by the basic game as of writing this review. This is, in my opinion, a nasty oversight on the part of the devs; as it is quite important for anything other than a sandbox game, where cost efficiency doesn't matter.
Overall, if you're keen on the idea of actually doing manual algebra to play a game then this should suit you nicely. If you're happy enough to go and get a mod to do the basic calculations for you, this game should suit you too. If like me you're not fussed about either, look elsewhere. This is a good simulator, but not really a casual player's game.

So, you've probably seen a lot of hate towards this game because it's different.  If you're on the fence, let's be realistic.  First, sequels are different.  If it was the same, we'd just keep playing Civ V.  Second, the art style is a matter of taste.  I personally love it.
Now, if you're still on the fence, go back and read about Civ V when it first came out.  People declared Civ IV as the Alpha and Omega of all strategy games and Civ V was a diseased mongrel that just soiled your grandma's rug.  Now, Civ V is the golden child and Civ VI has the AUDACITY to try new things.  I think you can see how 99% of the complaints are by people who were never going to like Civ VI out of the gate.
Finally, remember that satisfied players are out PLAYING.  We're not on the forums complaining because that's time that could be spent crushing the AI.  Is Civ VI perfect?  No.  Is it crucially flawed?  No.  A small number of people have technical issues that are unfortunate but are part and parcel of PC gaming.  Games not working sometimes, that's a risk we all accept due to the inherent difficulty in programming for the PC platform vs. consoles with standardized hardware.
Now, if you're new to the series, this is a very welcoming entry.  On lower difficulties, the AI is a declawed house cat.  Come to think of it, on higher difficulties you're still kinda playing against yourself.  The AI gets more aggressive but they're still tactically feeble in combat.
Should you buy it?  Absolutely.  It has everything you could want from a 4X game and no matter what anyone else says, the Civ series is still the 800-lb. gorilla in the room compared to everything else.

Civilization offers what a Civ game is known for. An excellent expansive game which allows you to manage every aspect of your empire as you grow across the globe, flourish in the arts and the sciences and ultimately rule the world through either an iron fist, scientific endeavors and worldwide cultural influences.
Civilization VI doesn't quite do that.
Civ V pulled the same stunt. When it was released, the base vanilla game was mediocre and lacked the mechanics the Civ IV game had which really made it unique. I do expect Civ VI will have it's time to shine as the last two have (baring Beyond Earth) and better implement itself. Many of those mechanics ARE present in Civ VI but the game feels like it want's to do more, but certain bits and pieces are present. It's difficult to pin down, but for seasoned Civilization players who've played every Civ game preceding this one, you can feel there is something not quite right in the sixth installment.
Now don't get me wrong here, I enjoy the game quite a bit. I've invested a fair amount of time into it and I do feel the AI has improved a small amount in every way except for combat, which I feel the Civilization AI must be notorious for being about as strategic as a wet carrot pinned to a semi's bumper. But has improved in sometimes being able to properly keep up and out do you in terms of science and culture. The districts which can expand the cities to massive proportions late game make it so you don't have these single tiled cities that have wonders pouring out of their citizens ears and every improvement available. Building your city is a better and proper challenge now and for the most part feels solid. Combat feels about the same as Civ V, being able to build an army feels a bit simpler and the amount of various buffs/de-buffs available when it comes to terrain is better thought out.
Performance wise, the game runs pretty good. I recommend killing anti-aliasing, otherwise the game runs as a steady 60fps on my machine. The game looks beautiful with a decent art style choice that is somewhat cartoonish in terms of how Civ leaders look, but it manages to not come across as childish cartoons and more like caricatures with over defined features. I'll drop my pc's specs at the bottom of the review for comparison.
Now here's the hard part for me and I really hate to say it right now, but go and play Civilization V. You can get the base game plus the expansions and all the extra content for just under $50(USD) and you'll have a much better experience. Civ VI isn't bad, far from it, but in terms of a Civilization experience, I can't recommend Civ VI. By the way, ignore hours played on my profile for Civ V and IV. Played much of those games well before I had Steam.
I can't recommend Civ VI while the previous title is still a better experience.
Pros:
-Still a great massive turn based game
-Friendly toward newcomers and familar to any who have played previous titles
-Doesn't demand much of your pc in terms of graphics
-Some mechanics feel a little polished
-You can speed up research and civics by completing certain prerequisites in game
Cons:
-Game feels to be lacking some content, but nothing game breaking
-The in game UI can become very cluttered late game, especially during war time
-CPU starts chugging late game, especially if all AI opponents are still active, causes single turns to take up to two minutes in some cases just to process the AI
-AI is still incredibly dumb in terms of combat
-AI needs to be tweaked in terms of war declarations. I've had what must be hundreds of instances where war is declared by at least five AI at a time and nothing ever sends troops; and when they do, it's typically only one or two units

I want to give this game love, I really do, but for every innovation they take an equal step backward.
And even a full year after initial release there are still many things fundamentally wrong with this game.
TLTR: Let me put this as plainly as possible. If there are barbarians; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you invest in religion; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you fall behind in tech any point while going to war; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you do anything but follow the intended strategy for a civ down to the finest detail; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. Point being, due so many factors that are always either zero-sum or snowballing, any game should be decided by the medieval area. No reason to waste everyone's time on faulty game mechanics.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Science and culture trees are interesting, but they are ordered with no rhyme or reason. Also on that note, anything but a science rush in this game will ultimately spell you doom. Stark contrasts between tech levels are so blatant that any tech edge at any point of the game is always a decisive factor.
-Systems such as "war weariness" and movement improve combat, but progression between units of different eras is choppy at best. If somebody has the tech advantage over you in war, just quit playing. You will be steamrolled, even if you make all the right moves.
-Barbarians are a completely, unethically difficult opponent to face in the early game. It isn't simply an occasional couple that are just a nuisance, but an entire army that will stifle your entire early game, thus putting you far behind late game. One barbarian camp spawning horsemen can literally take down 3 empires at once. That's just plain rediculous.
-Districts in theory force you to specialize your cities, but in reality you'll be forced to do the same thing to all of them always. Science and production first, apparently nothing else is relevant in the grand scheme of things. If you make a holy site district, you've just spent (x) turns on nothing.
-About a third/ half the civs have bonuses for religion, yet faith in this game is the most meaningless investment you could do. It requires an emmense degree of both invested production and going completely out of your way on the tech/ civic trees, when it will ultimately amount to nothing and put you far behind in production and science. Even the Khmer, that try to combine religion with a city growth strategy, utterly fail to make religion itself somewhat useful instead of just going straight science. The only thing keeping religion from being completely irrelevant is the fact that there is a religion victory.
-AI is just stupid, and are propped up by petty bonuses. Below prince it'll be a sweep with you full eras ahead of the pacifist AI. Above prince the AI has it out for you from the moment you meet, and they'll be strong in science w/o even building campuses. Plus they'll declare war for just about anything that by some accident sets off their historical agenda. Sorry that I don't have spies in the ancient era, France.
-Just about every other mechanic is a zero-sum rush from wonders to great people, magnifying the snowball effect that was a problem in Civ5. In this game, snowballing not only dominates strategy, but is equal parts reliant on RNG.
This is just too gimmicky and these flaws just turn the game into one "why do I even try" moment after another. You could have just as easily made a 3rd expansion for Civ5 for what this game has to offer.
