If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.

I want to give this game love, I really do, but for every innovation they take an equal step backward.
And even a full year after initial release there are still many things fundamentally wrong with this game.
TLTR: Let me put this as plainly as possible. If there are barbarians; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you invest in religion; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you fall behind in tech any point while going to war; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. If you do anything but follow the intended strategy for a civ down to the finest detail; you're ♥♥♥♥ed. Point being, due so many factors that are always either zero-sum or snowballing, any game should be decided by the medieval area. No reason to waste everyone's time on faulty game mechanics.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-Science and culture trees are interesting, but they are ordered with no rhyme or reason. Also on that note, anything but a science rush in this game will ultimately spell you doom. Stark contrasts between tech levels are so blatant that any tech edge at any point of the game is always a decisive factor.
-Systems such as "war weariness" and movement improve combat, but progression between units of different eras is choppy at best. If somebody has the tech advantage over you in war, just quit playing. You will be steamrolled, even if you make all the right moves.
-Barbarians are a completely, unethically difficult opponent to face in the early game. It isn't simply an occasional couple that are just a nuisance, but an entire army that will stifle your entire early game, thus putting you far behind late game. One barbarian camp spawning horsemen can literally take down 3 empires at once. That's just plain rediculous.
-Districts in theory force you to specialize your cities, but in reality you'll be forced to do the same thing to all of them always. Science and production first, apparently nothing else is relevant in the grand scheme of things. If you make a holy site district, you've just spent (x) turns on nothing.
-About a third/ half the civs have bonuses for religion, yet faith in this game is the most meaningless investment you could do. It requires an emmense degree of both invested production and going completely out of your way on the tech/ civic trees, when it will ultimately amount to nothing and put you far behind in production and science. Even the Khmer, that try to combine religion with a city growth strategy, utterly fail to make religion itself somewhat useful instead of just going straight science. The only thing keeping religion from being completely irrelevant is the fact that there is a religion victory.
-AI is just stupid, and are propped up by petty bonuses. Below prince it'll be a sweep with you full eras ahead of the pacifist AI. Above prince the AI has it out for you from the moment you meet, and they'll be strong in science w/o even building campuses. Plus they'll declare war for just about anything that by some accident sets off their historical agenda. Sorry that I don't have spies in the ancient era, France.
-Just about every other mechanic is a zero-sum rush from wonders to great people, magnifying the snowball effect that was a problem in Civ5. In this game, snowballing not only dominates strategy, but is equal parts reliant on RNG.
This is just too gimmicky and these flaws just turn the game into one "why do I even try" moment after another. You could have just as easily made a 3rd expansion for Civ5 for what this game has to offer.

Here is my original review which is based on vanilla game...
TL:DR
I WISH I could recommend Civ 6;  it's got some great features, is addictive (as ever) and has lots of potential.  However, the AI is REALLY bad,  I won't be playing this again until devs fix AI or release SDK so modders can.
Long version
As I write this review, I've played Civ6 for 222.6 hours, so I've had a fair run.  Do I recommend it?  No, not currently.  Why?  Simply because the AI is so bad.  In fact, I won't be playing it again until the AI is fixed.
Cons
- AI is active for first 50 turns, then seems to give up doing anything
- AI doesn't improve it's cities logically.  Why improve 15 tiles around a 5 pop. city?  Why doesn't it build districts?  Why does it build a settler when there isn't anywhere to found a city?
- AI either expands like mad and has lots of tiny unproductive cities.  Or it hardly expands at all and stagnates
- AI doesn't build decent number of military units
- AI doesn't attack / defend with any kind of logic
- AI doesn't upgrade it's military units
- AI declares war then, moves it's units near your cities, then allows you to pick them off 1 by 1
- AI declares war then sues for peace as soon as it can, offering lucrative deals
- AI still doesn't know how to fight on water
- Strange UI decisions by devs (can be fixed by mods)
- Total silence from Firaxis as to when they are going to fix this game.  ADVICE TO FIRAXIS - Take note of how Frontier Developments communicate with their customers
Pros
- Graphics - while not a fan at first, they've grown on me.  Watching wonders being built is a joy
- Sound - Good
- Music - Excellent
- Gamplay  / 1 more turn - As addictive as ever
- PC stability - Not 1 crash/bug in 222.6 hours - Wonderful
- Performance - Superb.  Everything on Ultra
Fast forward 6 months and I'm sure this game will be great.  My advice?  Get it on 50% sale & learn the new game mechanics, then wait for the patches.

Great game.
Not everyone will like it. It's simplified rocket science, and people who want a casual game that is easy to learn definitly won't have fun.
However, complex, hard-to-learn games are often also games you can enjoy for a very long time.
It's a sandbox game. You get a couple of contracts like "Reach Space" "Achieve Orbit Around Kerbin", etc. at first, but the majority of goals you'll have to set for yourselves.
My personal goal is to build replicas of famous and unusual planes from WWII or thereabouts. All of them. Or at the very least the German ones, as they designed the most unusual stuff. (Note that this is done using a mod that improves aerodynamics, see below)
Ofcourse, there are more than enough goals to chose from. That's why many have 1000h+ playtime.
There are loads of mods for this game, but it is playable, and, for most, enjoyable without any mods.
Some mods:
- FAR (Ferram Aerospace Research): Massive improvement for aerodynamics and plane-building (google area ruling, stall, and spin if you want to get a rough idea what this mod does) (Being very intersted in aerodynamics, this is a must-have mod for me, and for me it wouldn't be too enjoyable without FAR; FAR makes the game too difficult for many though)
- BD Armory: Adds weapons and AIs to fight against
- RSS (Real Solar System): Turns the Kerbol system into the Solar system.
Great game, worth the 40€ if you can live with having to learn some basic physics before being succesfull.

If there is a game that is consistently challenging but equally rewarding to the player it would be Kerbal Space Program. While Civilization VI isn't a bad game, it is quite fundamentally flawed and comes in no way close to its predecessors, Civ IV and V. If you're new to the series, definitely play those instead, or if not, go for Endless Legend, why not. All three are better experiences than Civ VI.
The Civilization series should be well-known to all gamers, but not everyone has actually played the games. The groundlayer of the turn-based 4X-genre, Civilization takes a player, and his empire, from the Stone Age to the Information Age, with the player making decisions on where to focus in terms of scientific research, military development, cultural progress, expansion, and many other factors. Every game is different, not just in terms of player-determined settings, but also in terms of map layout, rival civs, etcetera.
Civ VI improves one thing greatly compared to its predecessors, and that is city development. The Districs system really forces you to think, and to specialize. Gone are the days of a single city building every improvement and Wonder. It's just not possible anymore, and that's a good thing. With the districts-system, Science and Production are no longer the be-all, end-all of games which need to be focused on primarily.
Barbarians are no longer the pointless annoyances they were in the previous games. They're much deadlier now, and every civ needs to stay on its toes. This definitely gives the barbarians-element some much needed relevance.
A few other nice improvements made it to Civ VI, including military/noncombatant escort formations (finally!), expendable builders (which deals with unit clutter), mix-and-match cultural policies, and Eureka!-boosts for techs and civics, earned by fulfilling all kinds of mini-tasks. Now, if they'd just stuck to that, Civ VI would have been a straight-up improvement over VI, but sadly, there's a lot to discuss when I point out...
With all the desire for innovation and change, Civ VI trips over itself in quite a few departments, in same cases making the game frustrating and irritating to play.
The diplomacy system is, for want of a better word, a complete disgrace. Rival Civs will all, without exception, viciously loathe each other, including you, denouncing each other and you as often as they can, even when you've done them absolutely no wrong. One Civ had several diplomacy bonuses from good relations, but still declared me filth because we had a different system of government. Meanwhile, the A.I. leaders will not stop spamming you with pointless messages every turn, and because they, for some reason, need to slowly fade out twice, it's an infuriating habit which costs you a lot of time and has no benefit at all.
You might as well never bother with trade deals either. The AI will never, ever agree to a trade deal, nor suggest one, which doesn't favour them at least 3:1, even if they are pathetically weak. Their deals are nothing short of extortionate, and all they do is waste your time with more pointless interruptions, because you'd never, ever accept any of their deals anyway. As for espionage, well, expect all the A.I. opponents to focus only on you, sabotaging your Industrial Zones relentlessly, causing you to gnash your teeth as you waste yet more turns rebuilding things.
What few friends you have will, guaranteed, suddenly declare war on you for no reason at all, even though they're much weaker than you are and have nothing to gain from the conflict. And then, within ten turns, they'll come begging on their knees for peace. Refuse, and the entire world will hate you even more for being a warmonger. That's right, you will be a warmongering menace to the world even if you never once declare war. Having war declared on you and defending yourself is apparently an atrocity. This kind of system makes a player wonder if this game was even playtested at all.
In fact, it's not just diplomacy, really. The A.I. in general is often downright moronic.
The choice of art style, as well as the writing, are questionable to say the least. While it's true that Civ V was high on realism, and therefore seriousness, Civ VI has taken to the other extreme. The art style is jarringly cartoony, with leaders looking like caricatures and the map nauseatingly green and yellow, the UI is ugly with oversaturated colours, and the educational quotes that came with tech discoveries have been replaced with cringey pseudo-witty pop culture soundbites from comedians and other assorted funny-people. Not even Sean Bean's excellent narration can save the writing from being eye-rollingly lame. All things combined, Civ VI has the look of one of those crappy mobile games.
Lastly, the Civilipedia isn't much help. The game neglects to explain a lot of things and looking them up in the Civilipedia doesn't help one bit. You're supposed to smell that you can only build a single Archaelogist per city that has an archaeology museum, for instance. Often, building options will be grayed out without any explanation as to why. And don't get me started on National Parks. Ugh.
And of course, once more, many civilizations and mechanics are not present, or in a bare-bones way, which means Firaxis has once more held back things which were present in the previous game, only to release them in expensive DLC packs. It's a nasty habit, and every game developer should ask itself some serious questions when it resorts to deliberately holding back game content to be able to release it as DLC later.
Civ VI has some good ideas, but its positive elements don't come close to making it as good as Civ IV or Civ V. It's certainly not a bad game, but as an entry in the Civilization series, it falls far short of the standards the franchise holds itself to. Seriously, get the previous Civs instead, or if you've played those, give Endless Legend a go.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Paladins is the only First Person Shooter I have ever played for more than 10 hours. This game is amazing. While many people will compare it to Overwatch both games are very different in how they play. In paladins, you have two systems which change up your gameplay and impact your playstyle and how you choose to approach the enemy team. These are the Loadout System and the Item shop. You can create a Loadout by using 5 cards that have different effects and investing points into them which boosts the effects. You can only have 12 points per Loadout which and each card can have a maximum of 4 points in it. If you see a Loadout that you want somewhere on the internet, you can import to your game and you can use top ranked Players' loadouts as well. This is a brilliant system. It adds a lot of depth and customization. Two people can have the same cards in a load out but there points can differ which changes how they may play. When your at your base whether it be by dying or at the start of the match you can press I to enter the item shop and there's currently 19 items to buy. You buy these items with the points you get throughout the match. It'll go up automatically but you can get more by staying on point, pushing and contesting payloads, healing, doing damage and killing enemies. Each item has a different effect on you and are classified into four groups: Defense, Utility, Healing and Damage. You can only buy one item in each class so you have a maximum of 4 items. This is another brilliant system. Depending on your enemies team and the situation in which you are in. Now for the most controvesial part of the game, the champions. I have no problem with any of the champions. They have pretty good kits for their assigned roles but they are not locked to that role. Take Pip for example. He's classified as a support but his kit is also good for Flanking. Some may call some champions "Overwatch Rip-offs" because they have a similar move or may look similar but each champion in Paladins is different  from every hero in overwatch. The game does have it's fair share of bugs but it still is an Early Access game. The most common glitch I found was one where you'll randomly be kicked to the title screen as the beginning of a match, and if you sign in again you'll be placed back into the match in a seemingly random spot. There are other glitches but some I have not been able to replicate.
TL;DR Paladins is a fun, glitchy game that has a lot of Depth and is not an Overwatch rip-off.

Have you ever played a game, where after you finish it, you are just left dumbfounded, depressed, and only think about the game and it's ending? Where, you can't do anything in real life for like, a week, because you're constantly thinking about the game? A game that is so immersive and atmospheric, that you actually feel a part of it, where you actually feel like you're the protagonist, and in her shoes, even if your genders may differ?!
For me, Life Is Strange was that kind of game, and there aren't many games out there that can give me this feeling. A feeling where you crave for more, even though you know the story has been wrapped up and finished...
As soon as you launch LiS, you'll know that it's a very immersive, atmospheric and "artsy" game. It has it's own style, and even though the textures and graphics won't be able to blow you away, the way that they are done (The textures are hand-painted), coupled with the most amazing effects I've seen in a while and an astonishing attention to detail, will surely satisfy any person. And again, the impact of the effects and environmental details cannot be understated, they're what gives this game a "soul". As soon as you enter the room of one of the main characters, you ACTUALLY feel like you're in the room of a real-world teenager with that specific personality, be it Max, who is a shy yet caring 19 year old girl with some social anxiety and self-esteem issues, or Chloe the rebel, who has just had enough of this town that she lives in after it took everything from her that she loved and cared about.
And then there's the soundtrack. Music in a game can have a profound impact on setting the mood for the player or just making them enjoy their time in the game, and nothing is as satisfying as listening to a song played at the right time with the right lyrics. The soundtrack in this game is just amazing, They absolutely succeed in making you join the protagonist in their world and... and just get lost in it. I became a huge fan of Syd Matters just by listening to his soundtrack in this game.
And then there's the actual gameplay. Here we have a typical episodic adventure game with a story rich world and choices that have consequences further down the storyline, but with a twist: the ability to go back in time. Now, some people say that it's just a fancy way of exploring different effects your choices have on the story, and it's essentially doing the same thing as making a save or checkpoint and then returning to it, like a quick-save/quick-load function.
But I have to disagree, first of all, the main difference here is the protagonist is actually aware of this power, and by using it, she can see all the different outcomes and doubt her choices, question whether she made the right ones, and transfer the same doubt to the player. The other main difference is that this time travel feature becomes a huge part of the story and actually moves it forward, especially in the last two episodes but I'm not going to spoil anything here. The time manipulation feature can also be used to solve some puzzles, but they're not THAT complicated, and if you're patient enough, most of them can be completed without having to resort to using the internet, but don't get me wrong, they're not that easy.
Although LiS is almost a completely perfect game in my mind, I think it does have it's faults... one of the main beefs I had with it was that it seemed that the developers had put much of their effort in a specific path, and it was somehow considered the "main path" and the other outcome wasn't as fleshed out story wise as the other part, although it seems that this won't matter since looking at the global stats for the game, approximately 80 percent of people followed said path and thus, would not have the same complaint I did. If you are really curious and have actually finished the game, then read the next part, If you haven't, then for the love god AVOID SPOILERS!
***************************SPOILER!!*************
I felt like the developers spent most of their time developing the story around the fact that Max's relationship with Chloe was romantic rather than platonic, and to be honest, it seemed kind of forced. Yes, you got the choice to kiss or don't kiss chloe and you could've done things to help/impress her (or not) but still, sometimes it was like we were being forced to believe that they were in love, even though in my eyes it seemed like they were the best of friends, especially up  until episode 3 and the kiss and romantic elements just felt too sudden and out of place for me. You could see what I mean if you checked her journal, where after not kissing her she will still comment about actually wanting to do it. Don't get me wrong, I love that they included this, and the story between them after this point was amazing, but it makes me sad that they didn't work that much on the relationship between  Max and Warren. At the end you do get the option to kiss him (if you made the right choices beforehand) but that's just about it.If you choose the "look" option on him again, which I think many people missed, Max will say very shyly that at least she kissed Warren to let him know how she feels, and to me that's a clear indication of love. I feel like they could've spent more time together, and if there were choices that we could make so that Max told Warren about his powers sooner and actually used his help and tagged along with him, it would've been awesome. But I see why they spent most of their time on Chloe, since they had to make the player care about her to make the final choice harder, but I still think it was hard even when they were best friends.
************SPOILER END!!***************
And you might hear some people say that , most of your choices would not matter, but I think that's wrong. Not only will your choices impact the kind of end you get if you make one of the choices, it's also about the experience you made Max go through. In a game that's about travelling past in time, you must expect some of the experiences the character has had with other people be "erased" when she goes before said experience. But the important thing is that it's still there, it's still with Max, and the player. They have experienced and they will remember it, even if they're the only people that will.
Other than some small nitpicks here and there, I believe this game is a fantastic work of art, and considering the fact that the first episode is completely free now, you should definitely check it out.
I promise, you will be hella impressed!!

While Civilization VI isn't a bad game, it is quite fundamentally flawed and comes in no way close to its predecessors, Civ IV and V. If you're new to the series, definitely play those instead, or if not, go for Endless Legend, why not. All three are better experiences than Civ VI.
The Civilization series should be well-known to all gamers, but not everyone has actually played the games. The groundlayer of the turn-based 4X-genre, Civilization takes a player, and his empire, from the Stone Age to the Information Age, with the player making decisions on where to focus in terms of scientific research, military development, cultural progress, expansion, and many other factors. Every game is different, not just in terms of player-determined settings, but also in terms of map layout, rival civs, etcetera.
Civ VI improves one thing greatly compared to its predecessors, and that is city development. The Districs system really forces you to think, and to specialize. Gone are the days of a single city building every improvement and Wonder. It's just not possible anymore, and that's a good thing. With the districts-system, Science and Production are no longer the be-all, end-all of games which need to be focused on primarily.
Barbarians are no longer the pointless annoyances they were in the previous games. They're much deadlier now, and every civ needs to stay on its toes. This definitely gives the barbarians-element some much needed relevance.
A few other nice improvements made it to Civ VI, including military/noncombatant escort formations (finally!), expendable builders (which deals with unit clutter), mix-and-match cultural policies, and Eureka!-boosts for techs and civics, earned by fulfilling all kinds of mini-tasks. Now, if they'd just stuck to that, Civ VI would have been a straight-up improvement over VI, but sadly, there's a lot to discuss when I point out...
With all the desire for innovation and change, Civ VI trips over itself in quite a few departments, in same cases making the game frustrating and irritating to play.
The diplomacy system is, for want of a better word, a complete disgrace. Rival Civs will all, without exception, viciously loathe each other, including you, denouncing each other and you as often as they can, even when you've done them absolutely no wrong. One Civ had several diplomacy bonuses from good relations, but still declared me filth because we had a different system of government. Meanwhile, the A.I. leaders will not stop spamming you with pointless messages every turn, and because they, for some reason, need to slowly fade out twice, it's an infuriating habit which costs you a lot of time and has no benefit at all.
You might as well never bother with trade deals either. The AI will never, ever agree to a trade deal, nor suggest one, which doesn't favour them at least 3:1, even if they are pathetically weak. Their deals are nothing short of extortionate, and all they do is waste your time with more pointless interruptions, because you'd never, ever accept any of their deals anyway. As for espionage, well, expect all the A.I. opponents to focus only on you, sabotaging your Industrial Zones relentlessly, causing you to gnash your teeth as you waste yet more turns rebuilding things.
What few friends you have will, guaranteed, suddenly declare war on you for no reason at all, even though they're much weaker than you are and have nothing to gain from the conflict. And then, within ten turns, they'll come begging on their knees for peace. Refuse, and the entire world will hate you even more for being a warmonger. That's right, you will be a warmongering menace to the world even if you never once declare war. Having war declared on you and defending yourself is apparently an atrocity. This kind of system makes a player wonder if this game was even playtested at all.
In fact, it's not just diplomacy, really. The A.I. in general is often downright moronic.
The choice of art style, as well as the writing, are questionable to say the least. While it's true that Civ V was high on realism, and therefore seriousness, Civ VI has taken to the other extreme. The art style is jarringly cartoony, with leaders looking like caricatures and the map nauseatingly green and yellow, the UI is ugly with oversaturated colours, and the educational quotes that came with tech discoveries have been replaced with cringey pseudo-witty pop culture soundbites from comedians and other assorted funny-people. Not even Sean Bean's excellent narration can save the writing from being eye-rollingly lame. All things combined, Civ VI has the look of one of those crappy mobile games.
Lastly, the Civilipedia isn't much help. The game neglects to explain a lot of things and looking them up in the Civilipedia doesn't help one bit. You're supposed to smell that you can only build a single Archaelogist per city that has an archaeology museum, for instance. Often, building options will be grayed out without any explanation as to why. And don't get me started on National Parks. Ugh.
And of course, once more, many civilizations and mechanics are not present, or in a bare-bones way, which means Firaxis has once more held back things which were present in the previous game, only to release them in expensive DLC packs. It's a nasty habit, and every game developer should ask itself some serious questions when it resorts to deliberately holding back game content to be able to release it as DLC later.
Civ VI has some good ideas, but its positive elements don't come close to making it as good as Civ IV or Civ V. It's certainly not a bad game, but as an entry in the Civilization series, it falls far short of the standards the franchise holds itself to. Seriously, get the previous Civs instead, or if you've played those, give Endless Legend a go.

I always assumed this game would be awful, (with good reason) as I played the first episode when it became free and was not impressed at all. I gave it another chance due to the rave reviews and an insane amount of praise for the game. Which lead to me thinking that I must have been wrong.
That would be an understatement.
I admit that there definitely is some rather annoying quirks, such as the vocabulary of the characters - it made me slightly angry each time I heard someone say "Hella". There's also the art, which is pretty and suited the game well; but was blurry most of the time. Finally, my last major gripe was a few actions and responses of characters, though they won't be discussed to avoid spoilers.
Ignoring the first episode, after finishing each of the rest I was left every time mouthing "Whaaat??" silently, (Not even exaggerating) thinking "I did not expect THAT". Due to the story getting progressively darker and more intriguing as the episode count went on, leading to one of the most heart-wrenching conclusions from any game I've ever played. I can watch TV shows, Films and read Books with all of them being able to get an emotional reaction from me. Though with games being an exception almost every time. Witcher 3 and Life Is Strange are the only games that have ever made the "Muh Feels" circlejerk real. Unless you count crying with laughter because the cart at the beginning of Skyrim started flying, leading to a magical adventure.
You have a fun sized amount of characters in the game to read up on or talk more information out of them so you can understand who they really are. The shallow and bratty young adults are generally much more interesting than the face they wear in their daily lives. Some can be extremely petty even for their age group. Yet all have at least some charm... barring one...boy. I enjoyed the cast of the game thoroughly despite the flaws and annoyances. They helped to make Max's life a little less two dimensional, with them calling her out on various things.
If you still have doubts after playing the first episode then take it from me that there is much more to this game than angsty hipster antics.

Save yourself some money and go back to Civ 5.

I'm only 10 or so hours in, and as we all know in a civ game that's the equivilent of watching the opening credits of the first movie in the extended Lord of the Rings trilogy.
I love some of the changes they've done, and truly despise others.
I really like the district idea, but the learning curve (I'm a little older of a player and it takes a while to get used to things) is steep. I have no idea, most of the time, which districts should go where, or which districts I should build in which cities. I do like the idea of making you choose between putting in a district or using the resources of that tile. Makes the game more realistic, and after all isn't that what we all want when playing a game where we try to rule the world?

Have you ever played a game, where after you finish it, you are just left dumbfounded, depressed, and only think about the game and it's ending? Where, you can't do anything in real life for like, a week, because you're constantly thinking about the game? A game that is so immersive and atmospheric, that you actually feel a part of it, where you actually feel like you're the protagonist, and in her shoes, even if your genders may differ?!
For me, Life Is Strange was that kind of game, and there aren't many games out there that can give me this feeling. A feeling where you crave for more, even though you know the story has been wrapped up and finished...
As soon as you launch LiS, you'll know that it's a very immersive, atmospheric and "artsy" game. It has it's own style, and even though the textures and graphics won't be able to blow you away, the way that they are done (The textures are hand-painted), coupled with the most amazing effects I've seen in a while and an astonishing attention to detail, will surely satisfy any person. And again, the impact of the effects and environmental details cannot be understated, they're what gives this game a "soul". As soon as you enter the room of one of the main characters, you ACTUALLY feel like you're in the room of a real-world teenager with that specific personality, be it Max, who is a shy yet caring 19 year old girl with some social anxiety and self-esteem issues, or Chloe the rebel, who has just had enough of this town that she lives in after it took everything from her that she loved and cared about.
And then there's the soundtrack. Music in a game can have a profound impact on setting the mood for the player or just making them enjoy their time in the game, and nothing is as satisfying as listening to a song played at the right time with the right lyrics. The soundtrack in this game is just amazing, They absolutely succeed in making you join the protagonist in their world and... and just get lost in it. I became a huge fan of Syd Matters just by listening to his soundtrack in this game.
And then there's the actual gameplay. Here we have a typical episodic adventure game with a story rich world and choices that have consequences further down the storyline, but with a twist: the ability to go back in time. Now, some people say that it's just a fancy way of exploring different effects your choices have on the story, and it's essentially doing the same thing as making a save or checkpoint and then returning to it, like a quick-save/quick-load function.
But I have to disagree, first of all, the main difference here is the protagonist is actually aware of this power, and by using it, she can see all the different outcomes and doubt her choices, question whether she made the right ones, and transfer the same doubt to the player. The other main difference is that this time travel feature becomes a huge part of the story and actually moves it forward, especially in the last two episodes but I'm not going to spoil anything here. The time manipulation feature can also be used to solve some puzzles, but they're not THAT complicated, and if you're patient enough, most of them can be completed without having to resort to using the internet, but don't get me wrong, they're not that easy.
Although LiS is almost a completely perfect game in my mind, I think it does have it's faults... one of the main beefs I had with it was that it seemed that the developers had put much of their effort in a specific path, and it was somehow considered the "main path" and the other outcome wasn't as fleshed out story wise as the other part, although it seems that this won't matter since looking at the global stats for the game, approximately 80 percent of people followed said path and thus, would not have the same complaint I did. If you are really curious and have actually finished the game, then read the next part, If you haven't, then for the love god AVOID SPOILERS!
***************************SPOILER!!*************
I felt like the developers spent most of their time developing the story around the fact that Max's relationship with Chloe was romantic rather than platonic, and to be honest, it seemed kind of forced. Yes, you got the choice to kiss or don't kiss chloe and you could've done things to help/impress her (or not) but still, sometimes it was like we were being forced to believe that they were in love, even though in my eyes it seemed like they were the best of friends, especially up  until episode 3 and the kiss and romantic elements just felt too sudden and out of place for me. You could see what I mean if you checked her journal, where after not kissing her she will still comment about actually wanting to do it. Don't get me wrong, I love that they included this, and the story between them after this point was amazing, but it makes me sad that they didn't work that much on the relationship between  Max and Warren. At the end you do get the option to kiss him (if you made the right choices beforehand) but that's just about it.If you choose the "look" option on him again, which I think many people missed, Max will say very shyly that at least she kissed Warren to let him know how she feels, and to me that's a clear indication of love. I feel like they could've spent more time together, and if there were choices that we could make so that Max told Warren about his powers sooner and actually used his help and tagged along with him, it would've been awesome. But I see why they spent most of their time on Chloe, since they had to make the player care about her to make the final choice harder, but I still think it was hard even when they were best friends.
************SPOILER END!!***************
And you might hear some people say that , most of your choices would not matter, but I think that's wrong. Not only will your choices impact the kind of end you get if you make one of the choices, it's also about the experience you made Max go through. In a game that's about travelling past in time, you must expect some of the experiences the character has had with other people be "erased" when she goes before said experience. But the important thing is that it's still there, it's still with Max, and the player. They have experienced and they will remember it, even if they're the only people that will.
Other than some small nitpicks here and there, I believe this game is a fantastic work of art, and considering the fact that the first episode is completely free now, you should definitely check it out.
I promise, you will be hella impressed!!

I do like the idea of making you choose between putting in a district or using the resources of that tile. Makes the game more realistic, and after all isn't that what we all want when playing a game where we try to rule the world?
I hate that they got rid of the build queue, (pardon me if it is there, I can not find it for the life of me) and I also hate how slow the game goes at the beginning.
I hate how quickly your opponents build armies, (was invaded once on turn 75 by 7 galleys and 15 spearmen) and how long it seems to build mine.
But I have to say my most hated thing that they did was make builders have limited uses. I don't understand the thinking behind this, seems like a way to just waste building time. Build a builder have them improve three things then, look, they disappear! This really takes a lot of the fun out of the game for me.
I also don't like th e"improved Barbarians" sure, having smarter barbarians is a good thing, but they remind me of when I used to play Madden, they do stuff that there is no way I could do them, and they only do them at the exact moment that it can screw you.
Don't get me wrong, this is a fun game, I think as the expansions come out it will probably get even better, but for me, I'm going to stick with Civ V. After all, I've only put in 1200 hours into it.

This game introduced me to the class-based FPS genre.
UI/Style: Clear and slick.
Gameplay: Easy to start, hard to master, fun to play.
Graphics: Very good, not really a selling point but hardly a detriment.
Since it's free, is it pay to win? Certainly not. Hi-Rez is trying the League of Legends business model of making a free game with paid cosmetic upgrades.
Only con I can think of is it currently could use more replayability; playing the same characters on the same maps on the same modes is hard to keep interesting after 30+ hours. That said, 30 hours of entertainment for free is a great deal, and I'm sure I'll be spending more.
Worth a try to be sure.
Edit: Hi-Rez implemented the Essence currency and put a grind/money gate on strategic power, then backed off a little bit due to blowback. Still a bit of a downer, but the game remains fun and evolving.

It's different to civilization V. Some people will hate this, meanwhile I love it.
Civ 6 has really mixed things up in the formula this time round and it's payed off very well. A good feature heavy release that doesn't feel like it's missing too many previous features that might be sold back to you at a later date, like Civilization V had previously done.
The changes with districts and the way wonders work in a similar fashion, they take up an entire tile themselves, means you've got a much more invovled building process with your cities, no longer do you just put your builders on automate and never look at them again for another 500 turns, instead you have to make difficult choices between whether getting rid of a precious farm, mine or lumbermill tile for an encampent district to make your city more defendable. Even in a great game your city will not be built perfectly and I love that, you might be able to get an amazing adjacency bonus for an industrial district, but the tile you need is a little too far out of your borders right now so you may end up having to compromise and place it in a tile you already own, or wait it out but suffer a major lack in production.
It's these small choices that I love and also drive me up the wall. It's difficult and near impossible to plan that far ahead in the game to get this perfect layout, at best you might be able to save one plains tile most of the game to build a space port, but otherwise you can leave yourself too open or limited by waiting. You want to build Oxford University? Well, the only tile you can build it on now may have a plantation on it, is Oxford University really worth that?
The other changes to systems work pretty well, and while religious pressure doesn't seem to actually function, the changes to religion to making it more active is a wonderful change as well, sadly for the game can greatly become a next turn clicker if you're going for culture or science victories as there's no active way to speed things up once you get to a certain point.
I found myself at one point with every tile of my capital littered with a great artist, writer or muscian but there was not a single place I could use them as every slot was filled, but it didn't stop the game giving me more and more of them to never use.
There are still aspects of the game that I don't think many fully understand as they're never explained too well, such as ammenities, the new local happiness for cities, as while the civilopedia will claim one thing, ardent fans and back seat gamers will cry another, but it's normally fine as long as you're not having a war on your borders.
I love the design style as well in this one as it's bright colorful and the leaders are full of emotion and glorious beards.

I've played Civilization since the original Civ I, and I'm loving Civ VI.  The gameplay is outstanding and it looks pretty.  It has a learning curve, even for people who have played a lot of Civ before.  Unlike in some previous verisons, it's hard to be ahead on every aspect of Civilization, forcing you to concentrate on some important things while not falling TOO far behind in other areas.  Each time I have played it has felt really different.
Some things I particularly liked:
- Mnay Kinds of Great Works:  You can get "great people" who are historical people, and they have big effects on the game.  You can make great works of art and literature, and steal them from museums.  There are archaeologists who dig up historical artifacts and there are religious relics.  You can see your wonders of the world on the game map.
- Interesting Balance Choices:  There are various synergy bonuses that make you think hard about where to build things, and which keep cities from feeling all the same.  The balance between armies attacking and city defenses encourages building defenses, and there's a reason to build most types of military units.  You can build spies or focus on religion; build up your income or become a factory-nation; dominate the world scientifically or culturally.
- Exploring:  Scouts get XP for exploring the map.  They can discover natural wonders, make contact with city states, and generally are pretty fun to use.
- Multiplayer:  The hotseat option is great.  People are the most fun opponents.
- Trade:  Trade routes are really important, and create a good reason for peaceful relations with neighbors.
Is it perfect?  No, but I think the flaws are minor enough and the wow-factor is high enough that I will be playing this for a long time.

Fans will love the first episode from the new season right from the start, if some might not be eager to get into it after finishing the first season for quite some time, don't worry, Telltale's got that covered motivating and hyping you with flashbacks from some of the major choices you previously made and important character face-offs.
Visually, the game is a lot better than the first, they gave more detail and fidelity, graphic scenes weren't left out of this one either and they're quite pleasing (in more than one ways, the series is one of the few in which these sort of scenes actually gave me some emotions not just "meh, look at that character getting blown in this horror game, meh, does it end soon?").
Story and sountrack are just as good as before, the pacing  however needs a bit of work, I'm sure previous episodes also had such problems, dealing with certain drastic developments that almost fracture the entire game in several smaller parts that feel almost completely different from the overall episode progression, that feeling is also enhanced sadly by comparing it to Season 1 as a whole while being only one single episode from a new season, but the story is good and filled with drama and emotion. Another thing are the plot/game twists, it's pretty low on decisions that completely change "your" story, that however isn't an issue, only a few of the previous episodes had multiple such options, there will be time to add more in the next ones.
There is only one thing I really didn't like, the new UI, it feels awkward and it also isn't that accurate when you're trying to click on the interaction options, I didn't play it like that, but I see it working better for controllers which it was fully developed for (the menu is another sign of this game not being developed for mouse and keyboard).
Last but not least, those of you (us) who didn't  really enjoy Clementine as a character, her naive personality and the occasional voice acting of questionable quality (the ending on season 1 suffered from that greatly even if the overall package was excellent), you will be surprised, she's back as a more mature and way better voiced Clementine, fitted to take Lee's role as the main protagonist, in season 2 she's more of a young Lara Croft than a scared puppy.
In conclusion this is a great sequel to the first season and everyone should get it, unless they don't like Telltale's cliffhangers which this also is subjected to, but that only makes me eager to play the next episode.

Can't say enough about the game, problem is I don't know where to start.
To put in a short way,
"I spent forty hours experimenting just to get a satellite in orbit. It was worth the forty hours of trials, failures and that one success. It is truly, in every way, satisfying. The basics are entry level, but landing on the Mun efficiantly is a steep way from the beginning and when you watching your Kerban step out of the pod and plant that little flag, you can say you've accomplished one small step for Kerban, one giant leap for Kerbankind."
Update 12/14/2016
Kerbal Space Program has come a long way. The physics are a bit better, parts lock together better when designing a vehicle, tutorials have been updated and communications have beed added. The game overall has not only improved, but expanded the it's depth and immersion into the difficult nature of propelling small green people into orbit at 14G's, screaming through the atmosphere at 500m/s and occasionally accidentally sending them back into the atmosphere in a glorious fireball of science.
If you enjoy a good sim involving flight, physics, space exploration and hours of pulling your hair out as you attempt to dock two vessels flinging around your planet seventy-thousand meters above the surface barrelling around the planet at 2,500m/s in an unstable orbit that will either end in a successful exchange or another little green person fertalizing the planet with their ashes.
Update 5/31/2017
It's taken many days worth of time and practice, but my understanding of this game has finally begun to peak. On top of that, the occasional updates and the integration of Asteroid Day has added some depth to KSP. So I'll just touch on the Asteroid Day integration.
It is an improvement to intercept asteroids and bring them into orbit of Kerbin and more challenging to actually land the things. More thought and planning are required, but the payoff of actually dropping a small meteorite to something large enough to crush the space center is quite a sight to behold. The games engine feels like it's had some minor tweaks in improvement and that's always a plus. Though the game is essentially finished, the devs have been hard at work. To add onto that, they recently supplied a language pack for all you who don't have English as a first language and aren't privy to installing mods. So that's a win-win situation right there too.

- Mnay Kinds of Great Works:  You can get "great people" who are historical people, and they have big effects on the game.  You can make great works of art and literature, and steal them from museums.  There are archaeologists who dig up historical artifacts and there are religious relics.  You can see your wonders of the world on the game map.
- Interesting Balance Choices:  There are various synergy bonuses that make you think hard about where to build things, and which keep cities from feeling all the same.  The balance between armies attacking and city defenses encourages building defenses, and there's a reason to build most types of military units.  You can build spies or focus on religion; build up your income or become a factory-nation; dominate the world scientifically or culturally.
- Exploring:  Scouts get XP for exploring the map.  They can discover natural wonders, make contact with city states, and generally are pretty fun to use.
- Multiplayer:  The hotseat option is great.  People are the most fun opponents.
- Trade:  Trade routes are really important, and create a good reason for peaceful relations with neighbors.
Is it perfect?  No, but I think the flaws are minor enough and the wow-factor is high enough that I will be playing this for a long time.

When I first read about Civilization VI my "Buyers Beware" senses immediately started tingling.
2K and Firaxis had made some fairly... strange development decisions previous.
- Sidmeier's Starships
- Civ: Beyond Earth
It felt like the franchise was becoming the same as ANNO, where every game since 1404 is literally a copy&paste
with a different tileset and some very minor adjustments.
Switch to late 2016, Civ VI releases and I buy it on day one.
I had informed myself from previously available reviews and Twitch streams
and realised that it was not Civ V redux minus the addons.
So what is Civ VI then?
It's a Civilization game alright, but the focus this time is more towards the boardgame nature of
turn based strategy games.
More cartoony graphics, rules that are less realistic but instead bring more depth on the table,
and a generally fairly different approach to the franchise's advanced game mechanics.
Of course you're still building cities, constructing buildings, recruiting armies and researching
nuclear weaponry (Ghandi, I'm watching you...).
However the way you do all of this has become slightly different.
Take research for example, now you can (And theoretically have to) fullfill certain
requirements to reduce a technologies research time by half.
"Kill 2 barbarians with slingers" -50% research time for archers
"Destroy a barbarian camp" -50% research time for iron
This holds true for both the regular research and the new politics system.
The system from Civ V was completely remade and now is generally very similiar to
the way research works.
Instead of research points you need culture and the politics you "research" usually don't
give you something directly but instead grant you access to political cards and governments
which you can change around in the government tab.
Additionally this research tree also has all the diplomatic options in it and
usually there's also a building or two to be gained from this research.
Other changes are the combat system, which is in it's core the same as before with
minor additions like being able to order a civilian and military unit to move together.
The combat itself also seems faster paced, especially once the barbarians start climbing the tech tree.
Trade is working nicely (Although it required a patch first) and the AI finally stopped
nagging me about everything via diplomacy.
One of the downsides though is the lack of diplomatic depth that's largely missing due to
there not being a united nations congress this time.
I assume it's going to be future dlc/addon material, however the lack of one really comes across
as missing a major game mechanic.
Diplomacy in itself is interesting in the many methods you can deploy to annoy or befriend the AI.
Recent patches have also improved the AI logic in this regard though it still sometimes goes haywire.
Now to end it with one final difference to Civ V.
Instead of constructing buildings inside your city you're now forced to build districts which then harbour
additional buildings.
Sometimes that means you're following a chain of constructable buildings, sometimes that means choosing
between available buildings.
In general I love this idea.
It's awesome, military districts offer a second spawn point for units and with the first few buildings also grants
a military outpost that's capable of doing a second city attack on enemy units.
Religious district can serve as healing stations for units with the right perks and oh crap I haven't even touched on the religion part of the game...
Religion in Civ VI is much more in-depth than ever before, literally has it's own units to construct and fight with,
but suffers from being very tedious at the endgame.
I could write about all the cool and not so cool stuff for days me thinks.
But I want to push this review out before christmas 2035, so....
Is Civ VI worth your money?
60€? No, that's expensive as cake.
Find it for less than 60€ on other (legal!) online stores?
Grab it, it's a great game, patches have made it even better and it's only at the start of it's life time.
Sure, there's some minor stuff here and there and obvious addon bait waiting to happen, but
it's still one of the best gmaes 2016 has to offer.
If you like turn based strategy games then there's literally no way to avoid this one.

So...kudos for new ideas, but this game is easily the least enjoyable one I've played.
Pros:
Having to choose tiles is great.  I've stationed troops to protect Wonders from being damaged, something that never occurred in previous versions.  I think this is the best feature in Civ VI.
Graphics.  I love watching the Wonders be built, and the animation when it is done.  Seeing your cities sprawled out with visible Wonders and the detailed landscape is also a little rewarding.
Domestic Policies.  The low-level customization is really nice.  It doesn't have a huge impact, but it allows for a bit more tailoring of your civ, which is always a good thing in my books.
Cons:
Districts.  I really like the idea, but the way they are implemented does more harm than good.  It's another set of tedious steps rather than a real decision.  The best fix for this, in my opinion, is to not allow districts in the first age.  That way, when your civ is able to build a district, you have several to choose from.  You are actually having to make a choice in how your cities develop.  Another potential way is to have a building create a district, as opposed to having to build a district to unlock new buildings.
Wonder Restrictions.  If part of the appeal of the game is to re-write history, why are some wonders only able to be built by certain civilizations?  Bad idea.  Just...bad.
Early game.  Several buildings and wonders that used to be available in the early turns are now removed or restricted, leaving players with nothing to do but crank out military units.  This railroads players into not only a certain strategy, but also a certain mindset.  I don't like it at all, and it has a huge side effect, which is...
Barbarians.  They are a lot more numerous, more advanced, and more aggressive.  I assume this is due to the expectation of more military units, but this is too much.  Barbarians are more a focus than enemy civs, which is bad.  And your only option is to leave the hordes in or remove them completely.  Maybe add a slider?
Overall, I really did not enjoy this game, and don't play it.  It's the first Civ game I have completely written off, and I think that says a lot.  This is no longer a game where you get to customize your ideal society, but now just another in depth war game.  Pass on this at LEAST until substantial options are added to early game play with expansions.

IMO it's the best Civ has ever been. Fixes basically all of Civ V's problems (and there were a lot) and adds plenty of great new features.
Positives:
- Ideology is no longer half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and full of euphemisms. "Order, Autocracy, and Freedom" are rightly replaced with the unambiguous "Communism, Fascism and Democracy". Also the historical government options that are available from era to era are tasteful and fun to play with.
- Policies (known as Civics in this game) are no longer set in stone and can be chopped and changed as needed, making it more hands on and less open to autopiloting (a la Civ V's "if in doubt chose Tradition").
- Barbarians are peskier than ever (good imo).
- Feels like it has all of Civ V's expansions right from the get go i.e. has religion, spying, ideology, etc.
- War weariness and casus bellis add a good layer of depth to wars, and also prevents 1984-esque eternal wars (basically what always happens endgame Civ V in my experience).
- AI isn't entirely incompetent (thus far, at least)
- Quick load times, and crashes WAY less frequently (for me and the people I've played with at least). Like in a Civ V multiplayer game, i'd be expecting crashes every 1-2 hours. Now I can have comfortable crashless 2-4 hour games.
- Lots of little neat features, e.g. builders having charges, promotions healing units, military unit corps (almost but not quite reminiscint of Civ IV's death stacks), the ability to link soliders with workers, map pins, etc
- Global happiness is gone, and has been replaced with the much more involved local housing/amenities system. Which is great, I don't have to factor in my entire empire being immediately unhappy due to taking a few cities or settling a far off colony.
- District system makes building cities a lot more in-depth (gotta get dem good adjacency bonuses) and less easy to autopilot.
- "Eureka moment" system gives the player a rewarding amount of agency for tech and civic progress.
- Gorgeous soundtrack.
- Wonderful graphics for the terrain, buildings and units. Yes it's very simplistic, but personally I find it charming. Also the "map" theme they have going is great to look at. Wonders are also a treat for the eye.
- Delicious UI; has a tasteful, almost steampunk design that fits every era.
- Sean Bean.
Negatives:
- The art style the world leaders are rendered in (i.e. a kind of horrible histories-like cartoony style) is passable at best, horrible uncanny valley at worst. Cleopatra is one of the worst offenders.

Civ VI was a game much anticipated and the first I ever bought before release.
I do not regret, and remain a staunch believer in Civ series, in spite of Civ VI being a dissapointment so far. I see a light in the tunnel though as patches and DLCs can hopefuly fix all problems I see with this game. After all, the previous Civs also needed some tweaking to improve.
Let me share with you some pros and cons I see in Civ VI:
+ districts and city development
+ stacking units and support units
+ great people recruitment
+ barbarians scouts and overal challenge
+ builders charges
+ city state unique bonuses
+ trade bonuses and trader generation sysem
- ridiculously low game difficulty! There is usually no challenge to the player in later eras as AI civilisations are far behind. This greatly hurts the overal playablility.
- game doesn't provide easy access to useful information:
- map is difficult to read - unseen areas look much too different from the areas you see
- global map and minimap are difficult to read and provide no real help to finding things
- there is no resource finder like one in Civ V that allowed filtering resource icons
- there is no unit finder
- no tooltips. Districts provide no information about their production on hoovering
- city overview can't be filtered or rearanged
- game is unstable and crashes usually at the end.
- there is no visible change to other leaders attitude on the Relations bar. Relation modifiers don't seem to affect the bar.
- leaders' pop ups are irrational and do't reflect power disparity. Friendly message is followed by denounce and trade offers are often absurd.
- there is no way to turn long leaders pop ups of.
- city states are hopeless and helpless from the mid-game on.
- most great people have one use only! This makes them unnecessary to appear on the map and no fun to deal with. The worst example is the Great prophet, but cultural GPs are basically the same one shot units (cultural GP could provide envoys and all could provide some boost to the respective city output)
- missionaries/apostoles often have 0 conversion strenght without player knowing why
- there is no "future" civic. Game forces reselecting Globalization or Social media
- some districts are significantly stronger then others
- there is little to do to influence envoys generation
- little can be done to speed up district construction/repair (using builders to get some little boost would be nice)
- some unit promotions are totally useless (i.e. scaling cliffs)
- spies do not reveal map around the target city (it would be nice to let them move on the map and be able to interact with religious units, GP and maybe military units)
There are just some irritating features of the game I can figure up at this moment. Basic Civ VI ideas are generally great and it could easily be the best game of the series if theese annoying elements are dealt with.

There is a lot to be said about CIV VI compared to CIV V. The most important thing is to forget all you thought you knew about how to manage an empire in this game, as the standard difficulty (prince) is much more challenging than before. Here you must battle it out for a single type of victory, as persuing multiple avenues of success is far too costly, making it highly improbable. Second, barbarians are much more active, much later into the game than before, although they do not substantially increase in difficulty to defeat as you advance a civilization. Third, the voice overs  by Sean Beane are as epic as it gets, excellent choice. The battle system is much the same as always, making it familiar and friendly, while the empire selection is vast and varied. The depth which this game as achieved, the difficulty it presents, and the general feel are excellent. Although a bit slower than the previous iteration, this revised instillation in the series is a must play for any true fan of the series, and is a welcome 6th edition. Good fortune to each and every one of you in your quest for conquest.

I like this game. I like this game so much, I have found myself time and time again, choosing this over Overwatch.
This is coming from a Level 300 Diamond player in Overwatch, mind you. Upon first glance, yes it really does seem like Hi-Rez was quite 'unoriginal' when it came to the design and overall character basics. But once you break the ice floor to this game, it becomes a much more in depth, customizable and engaging game than Overwatch ever was. Yes, Overwatch is huge fun, but after playing it for nearly every day since October of 2015, it has gotten a bit stale, doing the same task over and over again. Which is where Paladins comes in. It offers things such as Cards, special abilities to purchase in your match, interchangable skins, it really immerses you in the game. However, this is still a beta game, and it is a half baked potato, like most games in beta. The characters do appear to be in some cases, an almost offensive immitation of some Overwatch ideas. Makoa and Roadhog are my biggest gripe. The controls and hitboxes can be a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t sometimes, but get past that, and Paladins is shaping up to be one hell of a Potato, that I'm sure I will sink more hours into.

Very good game. However the hype of all these "new features" is a bit overblown. There are simply not many new features. It's just that many minor features changed.
* No more roadbuilding, traders will do it for you (Personally I dislike this).
* Build special districts on tiles, you can't build them in your city tile anymore.
* The spy system is not new, it just changed.
* The diplomacy changed, but is not new and by the way it isn't any better than in civ 5
* The approach of enemies is different. My experience is that they don't attack you that easily anymore.
Some other talking points:
* Civilizations mock you for being peaceful!?
* More demands should be included like "Only peace if you don't convert my cities anymore" or "Only peace if you accept my religion" or "only peace if you break down your nuclear program" etc. etc.
* There is no real balance in the difficulty options. At some difficulties all you do is catching up science and culture all the time, which is basically impossible, because their bonuses are way higher. At certain difficulties you always win and at some difficulties you basically always lose. One small misstep at the beginning of the game will be fatal.
* I get really tired of hearing out the other civs about you, and afterwards you have to click the "Goodbye" button. It's superficial and doesn't give any useful information. Please get rid of this soon!
* The options for running a government are really cool, but very limited and shallow.

But like all investments, there is a payoff, and it is unlike any other. To have your kerbal step off into another world, planet or moon, and to return with that sweet, sweet science is quite a gratifying feeling, and is one everyone should experience through this game.

Sim Players are passionate when it comes to driving, flying or even riding the vehicles that have either thrilled and amazed us during our childhood even still do today which is why we take time out to write great reviews .. so I’d just like to add something to that ……
It’s always a shame to read about the disappointments that a fellow Sim Player has experienced instead of reading about their delights as they have taken the controls of their favourite consist and proudly taken passengers or goods from their chosen station, port or yard and delivered them on time having faced realistic challenges of schedules, other transport or sometimes signal failures and adverse weather conditions - that inner sense of achievement (and self-pride) is all we really seek - Yes they may be after all only simulations of real modes of transport –BUT…. be it an incredible landing of a fully laden 300 ton Boeing 747-400 on a real time flight from Singapore to Heathrow - Microsoft Flight Simulator perhaps - where you take care of the Jumbo's flight deck and using the array of true to life switches, levers and dials as you descend gently down to terra firma – EGLL runway 21 to be exact to the [imagined] sounds of cheers and applause of your satisfied passengers and crew. Or that inner voice that says 'yees!' when we finally arrive at the depot and park up our Flexi-Bus for the day OMSI 2– its late, the sun has set, both outside our windows (if we care to look!) and within the Sim… but we don’t care.. We’ve driven with diligence and skill, we’ve hit n hurt no one and managed to pick up and drop off everyone without a hitch… that’s what matters.. That’s why we play these Simulators –
That’s what Sims do for us! - They fulfil our innermost desire to be a part of something that we admire, to take control of the very vehicles that we venerate and are in awe of – Hours of our lives are spent recreating the paths taken by Road, Rail, Air and Sea in order that we may share the experience in some intangible way of that of the Driver, Pilot, Captain, Fireman, Soldier and Doctor? within us all – all this achieved speedily at the flick of a mouse button and without the arduous years of universities, specialist training and professional advice and preparation, we will not suffer any loss of limb if we make mistakes as we learn the art of take-off and landing, nor will we face litigation and inevitable imprisonment from the families of the loved ones that we lost at sea due to our lack of experience of sailing cruise ships, or even suffer from docked wages from South West Trains for continued late arrivals at London Victoria… Friends our desire and task is a simple one … to Simulate through our chosen modes … without the Wind, Rain, Ice, Snow or Insurance Costs ever affecting or view of our chosen destination -
To Dream the Impossible is what drives the human spirit – But to deny someone of that dream is to deny them of the very lust for life ….. So keep dreaming keep ‘Simming’ and whether it’s by Air, Sea or Land may your journeys be filled with fun, passion and excitement –
Sim on! n Smile as you go!

There are some good things to be said about Civ6.  The new system for religion, for example, is both more rewarding and more realistic thanks to the fact that it can be tailored to a civilizations needs or incliniations.  The districting system, while not necessarily an improvement over older games, provides a fresh new way to think about city management.
Unfortunately the good is lost in a sea of bad design choices.  The very best example of this is the new "Eureka" system for technological development.  You are essentially given one quest per tech, which cuts the cost of that tech in half if you do the quest.  Such a powerful incentive means you will have to go out of your way to perform many random actions if you want to stay competetive technologically, turning the game into an RPG style deluge of meaningless tasks.
Speaking of competetive, the AI is most certainly not when it comes to combat.  Playing on a high level, I found myself in a situation where Brazil had a much larger army than mine.  They declared war and should have easily been able to take my border city.  Instead they wandered around my territory and slowly let me shoot them to peices, seldom even attacking any of my units or cities.  I ground them all into meat without losing a single unit.
The removal of the civ-wide "Happiness" type feature seen in Civ5 returns us to the days where explosive expansion has barely any limitations.  This removes the need for the subtler strategies we developed to deal with happiness limitations and once again reduces us to a formula of pumping out settlers or soldiers as fast as possible, with infrastructure being considered only as it allows us to achieve those two previously mentioned ends.

We’ve driven with diligence and skill, we’ve hit n hurt no one and managed to pick up and drop off everyone without a hitch… that’s what matters.. That’s why we play these Simulators –
That’s what Sims do for us! - They fulfil our innermost desire to be a part of something that we admire, to take control of the very vehicles that we venerate and are in awe of – Hours of our lives are spent recreating the paths taken by Road, Rail, Air and Sea in order that we may share the experience in some intangible way of that of the Driver, Pilot, Captain, Fireman, Soldier and Doctor? within us all – all this achieved speedily at the flick of a mouse button and without the arduous years of universities, specialist training and professional advice and preparation, we will not suffer any loss of limb if we make mistakes as we learn the art of take-off and landing, nor will we face litigation and inevitable imprisonment from the families of the loved ones that we lost at sea due to our lack of experience of sailing cruise ships, or even suffer from docked wages from South West Trains for continued late arrivals at London Victoria… Friends our desire and task is a simple one … to Simulate through our chosen modes … without the Wind, Rain, Ice, Snow or Insurance Costs ever affecting or view of our chosen destination -
To Dream the Impossible is what drives the human spirit – But to deny someone of that dream is to deny them of the very lust for life ….. So keep dreaming keep ‘Simming’ and whether it’s by Air, Sea or Land may your journeys be filled with fun, passion and excitement –
Sim on! n Smile as you go!
