There are some good things to be said about Civ6.  The new system for religion, for example, is both more rewarding and more realistic thanks to the fact that it can be tailored to a civilizations needs or incliniations.  The districting system, while not necessarily an improvement over older games, provides a fresh new way to think about city management.
Unfortunately the good is lost in a sea of bad design choices.  The very best example of this is the new "Eureka" system for technological development.  You are essentially given one quest per tech, which cuts the cost of that tech in half if you do the quest.  Such a powerful incentive means you will have to go out of your way to perform many random actions if you want to stay competetive technologically, turning the game into an RPG style deluge of meaningless tasks.
Speaking of competetive, the AI is most certainly not when it comes to combat.  Playing on a high level, I found myself in a situation where Brazil had a much larger army than mine.  They declared war and should have easily been able to take my border city.  Instead they wandered around my territory and slowly let me shoot them to peices, seldom even attacking any of my units or cities.  I ground them all into meat without losing a single unit.
The removal of the civ-wide "Happiness" type feature seen in Civ5 returns us to the days where explosive expansion has barely any limitations.  This removes the need for the subtler strategies we developed to deal with happiness limitations and once again reduces us to a formula of pumping out settlers or soldiers as fast as possible, with infrastructure being considered only as it allows us to achieve those two previously mentioned ends.
I tried it, and I wanted to love it, but I just don't want to play it.

This game is for the many; for people who want to analyze every stage of their rocket, calculating the Delta-V and specific impulse for every stage, all the way to people who just want to "see what happens".
However, this game is an investment. If you're hoping to launch successful missions to other planets, you're going to need to open some wikipedia pages and fail. You're going to watch some youtube tutorials and hit yourself for not having thought of that first. You are going to get frustrated reverting flights, especially when you're so invested into one mission.
But like all investments, there is a payoff, and it is unlike any other. To have your kerbal step off into another world, planet or moon, and to return with that sweet, sweet science is quite a gratifying feeling, and is one everyone should experience through this game.

It’s always a shame to read about the disappointments that a fellow Sim Player has experienced instead of reading about their delights as they have taken the controls of their favourite consist and proudly taken passengers or goods from their chosen station, port or yard and delivered them on time having faced realistic challenges of schedules, other transport or sometimes signal failures and adverse weather conditions - that inner sense of achievement (and self-pride) is all we really seek - Yes they may be after all only simulations of real modes of transport –BUT…. be it an incredible landing of a fully laden 300 ton Boeing 747-400 on a real time flight from Singapore to Heathrow - Microsoft Flight Simulator perhaps - where you take care of the Jumbo's flight deck and using the array of true to life switches, levers and dials as you descend gently down to terra firma – EGLL runway 21 to be exact to the [imagined] sounds of cheers and applause of your satisfied passengers and crew. Try it for yourself if you are still not sure whether you will like it or not
The pros so far are:
-It's free, no p2w
-The card loadout
-Frequent updates, no need to wait months
-Daily bonuses, in the end of the week you get crystals, which after 2-3 weeks you'll be able to spend on skins, chests and what not
-Haven't met many russians, which is amazing.
-Custom voice packs of characters for radio commands
-Easy to start with, you don't need much of a skill
-Competitive doesn't allow you to play until you have 12 characters on master level 4, so inexperienced lads don't ruin your game by hopping straight to competitive with no general direction at all.
- No lag, no bluescreens so far, perfectly optimised at the max, even with my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fx8350 cpu I still get over 150 frames.
- Pretty balanced champions, few used to be broken but now OK
- Graphics are actually neat, not ultra high quality, but still very good
- Item shop ( You can buy cards for additional damage by in-game crystals?? which you get by killing, assisting, healing, pushing payload, capturing objective and stuff, which resets each game)
- You can test a champion before buying
- You can play vs bots before you jump into pvp
- There's more which I can't remember right now
Now the cons, which don't worry, they are not many:
- No dedicated servers
- No voice chat (which can be good at times, but not if you have a decent team and the only thing you lack is orientation and sync
- Sometimes you meet people writing in their language, which is in no way bad, but if we are 4 english speaking lads, and there is another guy from (somewhere) he literally talks to himself
-Sometimes you meet toxic people from everywhere (not 1 country in particular)
- You can get the message "Failed to Start Authenticate and Update Service" which is fixed by doing this
1. press the windows key and then in the search box write services.msc (or in run, works both ways)
2. Find hi-rez authentication service and set it to manual
3. If it still has problems, press the repair button or verify, it should fix it without a problem
3. If it still has problems , find the hi-rez launcher or whatever uninstall it, and start paladins again, it will install it freshly
- There could be more cons I am not aware of.

I was wary about purchasing this because of the bad reviews. Overall I am glad I did go ahead with the purchase. This review is after the latest patch so things may have changed from prior.
In past civs the focus was on expanding as quickly as possible, maintain happiness, build armies perform science and go for whatever win you want. This civ is different and in a good way.
Diplomacy, is much more nuanced. You have to think about who will be your friends and allies based on your civilization and playstyle. Before diplomacy didn’t mean much it was just something there and you tried to deal with it or bribe, etc. In Civ 6 you have to actively decide who you will build allies with. In doing so you have to modify your playstyle to meet their demands, beliefs, etc. If you play the old Civ 5 way the AI is going to look sporadic and hostile. That is due to the fact you aren’t modifying anything to develop the relationship. It is actually quite a fun mechanic and one that takes some thought and strategy.
Cities, ARE FUN! Again back in Civ 5 days each city was a copy of the previous and got tedious. At some point you just let the city do whatever it wants and automate everything even works. In Civ 6 cities are unique, you have to plan 5 steps ahead, build strategically and decide what that city will do for you. For example if you have a city by mountain ranges science would be perfect for it. Each decision for every city needs to be planned and thought through.
Military, battles I can see as lacking. You don’t have unit stacking, much of it is a chess game, fun but not overly engaging. Now I have loved the fact that the civ series have not been big on military aspects. I hate nothing more then developing armies, deciding who gets stack into what, counter the enemy, ugh. Now with that you can develop some great strategies with great generals and admirals. They do allow some unit stacking which makes for some awesome armadas and battalions.
There are so many other aspects I am enjoying with this game. My only gripe is the time it takes between turns. Back in the day I remember waiting 5 minutes between turns. I hope it doesn’t get to long between turns for civ 6 but for now it isn’t bad.

After playing this game for a good 400 hours, I decided to try something I had never quite gotten the hang of: Single-stage-to-orbit spaceplanes. I can do interplanetary missions just fine, but spaceplanes are extremely complicated. So I watched a bunch of Scott Manley videos, and built a spaceplane which was supposed to be able to carry a pair of ion probes into orbit. "Supposed" is the key word here.
First attempt: Not enough liquid fuel, too much oxidizer. Got to orbit, but not back down. Accidentally put the rocket engines and the probe's solar panels in the same action group, resulting in broken solar panels.
Second attempt: Still too much oxidizer, some more tweaking required.
Third attempt: The spaceplane itself works fine now, although after getting to orbit I realized I never retracted the landing gear. Facepalm.
Fourth attempt: got two probes to orbit just fine, realized the probes do not have antennae. Too late to revert flight, did not quicksave.
10/10, this game gives me a lot of respect for the poor sods who have to get all this right on the first attempt, with RL physics.

EX:

France denounces you for being weak in espionage. At turn 38.
Gilgamesh denounces you for having a weak navy. At turn 36. You didn't spawn on the coast.

I have played Civ since I was in college and played way too many hours of the first version in my dorm room. I've played every mainline version of it since (but not the spinoffs) and It is probably my favorite game franchise of all time. I'm disappointed to report that Civ 6 has the seeds of some innovative ideas, but overall it is worst version of Civ I have yet played.  I don't have too much to add to some well-written reviews already posted, but I would add a few points of emphasis.
1. The AI in Civ VI is by far the worst AI in the history of the game.  Computer players are absurdly, inexplicably incompetent when it comes to fighting wars, even at high levels of difficulty. An AI player may well show up at the doorstep of your city with a huge army, but upon attacking a majority of the units on any given turn won't do anything; by that I don't mean they don't do anything useful, I mean they literally sit there and skip their turn.  If you attack them, individual units will usually run away, showing no sense of overall strategy of risk or sacrifice.  Attacking an enemy city is the same: enemy units will act completely illogically.
As other reviewers have noted, while the new system of diplomacy has interesting ideas, they are incompetently enacted by the AI.  You can do everything right with another civilization, but after a certain point they will turn and declare war on you.  At higher difficulties, the designers apparently made things tougher by making other civs less friendly, but it begins to make diplomacy seem superfluous- why bother with secret agendas and such if they are going to inexplicably change their mind and try to kill you at some point anyway?
2.  Civ 6 takes a big step backwards in terms of providing you clear information about your civ. How many different luxury resources do you have?  In diplomacy, what trade routes do you already have, and for how much longer? What is the rate of population growth for your civ compared to the world? All these things, just for examples, are either difficult to ascertain or simply impossible without resorting to pen-and-paper notes. Older versions of Civ had many graphs and tables to figure such things out, but the new Civ 6 is simplified in a negative way.  Even the Civilopedia is worse with fewer internal hotlinks. The bugaboo of Civ games has always been avoiding micro-management, but the designers have gone way too far the other way so that now you can't even figure out what is going on.  They even took away one of my favorite moments of Civ: the post-game wrap-up. I loved reading my final stats compared to the world and watching the little timeline video of the history of the my game: all gone.  Now there's just a few hard-to-read graphs and a final score.
3.  Count me amongst those who dislike Civ 6's use of roads.  It is wrong conceptually and for game play.
Instead of "workers", straight-forward units who have been making roads and improvements since Civ 1, there are now "builders" who instantly make improvements by using up a certain number of charges they have when created. And these builders don't make roads at all: these are made exclusively by trade caravans, who build them as they go from city to city.  The idea of instantly built improvements I can take or leave- I suppose they address the problem of micro-management so you aren't constantly looking for something for workers to do.  Being unable to direct where roads go or how quickly they are constructed, though, can be frustrating.  If you want a  road over a particular tile, or DON'T want a road there, it's tough luck.  Why?  This makes no sense to me conceptually- while trade caravans or their modern equivalent used roads, they rarely, if ever constructed them.  According to one book I read ("World lit only by Fire"), the best roads of mideval Europe were still those built by the Romans 1000 years before, not by then-modern merchants.
Then Civ 6 simply writes railroads out of existence, except as a technological concept that allows you to discover coal.  Never mind this key time in the game of Civs 1-5 when you could begin to move units across a continent in a turn, or in history when railroads revolutionized trade and warfare.  Instead everything is just a "modern road", as if the game was underwritten by a trade group of long-haul truckers.  Similarly, there's no trade bonuses, now that I think about it, for being along waterways, never mind their historical significance as conduits of travel.  These changes make Civ 6 seem dumber than its predecessors, rather than smarter.
Otherwise, it's Civ, and it still sucks me in if I get started with it.  The new graphics are beautiful, and the idea of districts that limit how a city can develop are appropriately innovative, even limiting how many wonders can be in a city which makes historical and game-play sense.  Maybe the AI problems can be patched up, but I'm afeared that the Civ 6 developers at some point decided they just needed to get the game out the door and modders would make the game more playable over time.  At this time, I can't recommend this game against its predecessors (Civ 4 remains my favorite) but hope it can improve over time.

I have been playing this game for a very long time. Very easy to get into, very hard to master.
It is not a simulation by any means, but that doesn't mean you won't still learn a lot about rocketry, and the things which NASA and the folks who fly in those crazy contraptions have to deal with.
The Community as well is extremely nice, and extremely active. With a mass amount of mods for the game, which allows you to really customize it to your liking (Much like Elder Scrolls games are).
On top of that, they are also moving it to  Unity 5 (If they havn't already at the time you're reading this in the future), meaning the limitation on mods will be quite literally... limitless.
That with Multiplayer to boot! (Coming Soon as well with Unity 5).
-----------------------------
The game itself has 3 modes.
Career: Which pits you against your mind. Balancing income from successfull missions, reputation, and science. Failed missions could cost you big, and  learning how to create a more cost friendly ship to do the same job could save you bundles. Use Science to unlock new parts on the tech tree, to push your exploration even farther.
Science: Same as Career but without the reputation and Money.
Sandbox: Like all Sandboxes.. Everything is tehre from the start, no money, science or anything else, Just build and have fun.
-------------------------------
What you do in the game is open ended. IT's your choice. Build what you want, and fly it anywhere you want (Or anywhere it can go). There are many many entire different planets to explore, moons, asteroids, etc. A fully open ended solar system.
Taking off from Kerbin, flying through the upper atmosphere, and breaking through into space is seemless and a wonderful excitement when you do it for your first time without the ship exploding.
From there, going to another planet, landing anywhere you want on it and exploring it, then coming back and hoping you have the right trajectory to burn safely through the kerbin atmosphere as flames fly up around your ship.. epic.
5 Tests launching rockets that failed: 2,000,000
Launched a rocket to the Mun, but couldn't return: 400,000 + 1 stranded Kerbal
Attempted a rescue Mission with the same result: 450,000 + another stranded Kerbal
Finally reaching the Mun, and returning back safely in the water: Priceless

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW
Try it for yourself if you are still not sure whether you will like it or not
The pros so far are:
-It's free, no p2w
-The card loadout
-Frequent updates, no need to wait months
-Daily bonuses, in the end of the week you get crystals, which after 2-3 weeks you'll be able to spend on skins, chests and what not
-Haven't met many russians, which is amazing.
-Custom voice packs of characters for radio commands
-Easy to start with, you don't need much of a skill
-Competitive doesn't allow you to play until you have 12 characters on master level 4, so inexperienced lads don't ruin your game by hopping straight to competitive with no general direction at all.
- No lag, no bluescreens so far, perfectly optimised at the max, even with my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ fx8350 cpu I still get over 150 frames.
- Pretty balanced champions, few used to be broken but now OK
- Graphics are actually neat, not ultra high quality, but still very good
- Item shop ( You can buy cards for additional damage by in-game crystals?? which you get by killing, assisting, healing, pushing payload, capturing objective and stuff, which resets each game)
- You can test a champion before buying
- You can play vs bots before you jump into pvp
- There's more which I can't remember right now
Now the cons, which don't worry, they are not many:
- No dedicated servers
- No voice chat (which can be good at times, but not if you have a decent team and the only thing you lack is orientation and sync
- Sometimes you meet people writing in their language, which is in no way bad, but if we are 4 english speaking lads, and there is another guy from (somewhere) he literally talks to himself
-Sometimes you meet toxic people from everywhere (not 1 country in particular)
- You can get the message "Failed to Start Authenticate and Update Service" which is fixed by doing this
1. press the windows key and then in the search box write services.msc (or in run, works both ways)
2. Find hi-rez authentication service and set it to manual
3. If it still has problems, press the repair button or verify, it should fix it without a problem
3. If it still has problems , find the hi-rez launcher or whatever uninstall it, and start paladins again, it will install it freshly
- There could be more cons I am not aware of.
Personal rating is 9/10, as I said, try it for yourself if you want, it's FREE

I have played Civ since I was in college and played way too many hours of the first version in my dorm room. I've played every mainline version of it since (but not the spinoffs) and It is probably my favorite game franchise of all time. I'm disappointed to report that Civ 6 has the seeds of some innovative ideas, but overall it is worst version of Civ I have yet played.  I don't have too much to add to some well-written reviews already posted, but I would add a few points of emphasis.
1. The AI in Civ VI is by far the worst AI in the history of the game.  Computer players are absurdly, inexplicably incompetent when it comes to fighting wars, even at high levels of difficulty. An AI player may well show up at the doorstep of your city with a huge army, but upon attacking a majority of the units on any given turn won't do anything; by that I don't mean they don't do anything useful, I mean they literally sit there and skip their turn.  If you attack them, individual units will usually run away, showing no sense of overall strategy of risk or sacrifice.  Attacking an enemy city is the same: enemy units will act completely illogically.
As other reviewers have noted, while the new system of diplomacy has interesting ideas, they are incompetently enacted by the AI.  You can do everything right with another civilization, but after a certain point they will turn and declare war on you.  At higher difficulties, the designers apparently made things tougher by making other civs less friendly, but it begins to make diplomacy seem superfluous- why bother with secret agendas and such if they are going to inexplicably change their mind and try to kill you at some point anyway?
2.  Civ 6 takes a big step backwards in terms of providing you clear information about your civ. How many different luxury resources do you have?  In diplomacy, what trade routes do you already have, and for how much longer? What is the rate of population growth for your civ compared to the world? All these things, just for examples, are either difficult to ascertain or simply impossible without resorting to pen-and-paper notes. Older versions of Civ had many graphs and tables to figure such things out, but the new Civ 6 is simplified in a negative way.  Even the Civilopedia is worse with fewer internal hotlinks. The bugaboo of Civ games has always been avoiding micro-management, but the designers have gone way too far the other way so that now you can't even figure out what is going on.  They even took away one of my favorite moments of Civ: the post-game wrap-up. I loved reading my final stats compared to the world and watching the little timeline video of the history of the my game: all gone.  Now there's just a few hard-to-read graphs and a final score.
3.  Count me amongst those who dislike Civ 6's use of roads.  It is wrong conceptually and for game play.
Instead of "workers", straight-forward units who have been making roads and improvements since Civ 1, there are now "builders" who instantly make improvements by using up a certain number of charges they have when created. And these builders don't make roads at all: these are made exclusively by trade caravans, who build them as they go from city to city.  The idea of instantly built improvements I can take or leave- I suppose they address the problem of micro-management so you aren't constantly looking for something for workers to do.  Being unable to direct where roads go or how quickly they are constructed, though, can be frustrating.  If you want a  road over a particular tile, or DON'T want a road there, it's tough luck.  Why?  This makes no sense to me conceptually- while trade caravans or their modern equivalent used roads, they rarely, if ever constructed them.  According to one book I read ("World lit only by Fire"), the best roads of mideval Europe were still those built by the Romans 1000 years before, not by then-modern merchants.
Then Civ 6 simply writes railroads out of existence, except as a technological concept that allows you to discover coal.  Never mind this key time in the game of Civs 1-5 when you could begin to move units across a continent in a turn, or in history when railroads revolutionized trade and warfare.  Instead everything is just a "modern road", as if the game was underwritten by a trade group of long-haul truckers.  Similarly, there's no trade bonuses, now that I think about it, for being along waterways, never mind their historical significance as conduits of travel.  These changes make Civ 6 seem dumber than its predecessors, rather than smarter.
Otherwise, it's Civ, and it still sucks me in if I get started with it.  The new graphics are beautiful, and the idea of districts that limit how a city can develop are appropriately innovative, even limiting how many wonders can be in a city which makes historical and game-play sense.  Maybe the AI problems can be patched up, but I'm afeared that the Civ 6 developers at some point decided they just needed to get the game out the door and modders would make the game more playable over time.  At this time, I can't recommend this game against its predecessors (Civ 4 remains my favorite) but hope it can improve over time.

I have been playing this game for a very long time. Very easy to get into, very hard to master.
It is not a simulation by any means, but that doesn't mean you won't still learn a lot about rocketry, and the things which NASA and the folks who fly in those crazy contraptions have to deal with.
The Community as well is extremely nice, and extremely active. With a mass amount of mods for the game, which allows you to really customize it to your liking (Much like Elder Scrolls games are).
On top of that, they are also moving it to  Unity 5 (If they havn't already at the time you're reading this in the future), meaning the limitation on mods will be quite literally... limitless.
That with Multiplayer to boot! (Coming Soon as well with Unity 5).
-----------------------------
The game itself has 3 modes.
Career: Which pits you against your mind. Balancing income from successfull missions, reputation, and science. Failed missions could cost you big, and  learning how to create a more cost friendly ship to do the same job could save you bundles. Use Science to unlock new parts on the tech tree, to push your exploration even farther.
Science: Same as Career but without the reputation and Money.
Sandbox: Like all Sandboxes.. Everything is tehre from the start, no money, science or anything else, Just build and have fun.
-------------------------------
What you do in the game is open ended. IT's your choice. Build what you want, and fly it anywhere you want (Or anywhere it can go). There are many many entire different planets to explore, moons, asteroids, etc. A fully open ended solar system.
Taking off from Kerbin, flying through the upper atmosphere, and breaking through into space is seemless and a wonderful excitement when you do it for your first time without the ship exploding.
From there, going to another planet, landing anywhere you want on it and exploring it, then coming back and hoping you have the right trajectory to burn safely through the kerbin atmosphere as flames fly up around your ship.. epic.
5 Tests launching rockets that failed: 2,000,000
Launched a rocket to the Mun, but couldn't return: 400,000 + 1 stranded Kerbal
Attempted a rescue Mission with the same result: 450,000 + another stranded Kerbal
Finally reaching the Mun, and returning back safely in the water: Priceless

Right off, let me say that after 22 hrs of play, I am pretty much done. I really enjoy Civ V, but not Civ VI. Why? If you read some of the other DNR's many of my complaints are well spelled out.
1. Comments about the "Denouncing". It does get tiresome.
2. Random comments from other leaders - are they supposed to mean something? Some comments are humorous the first time they are made, but not the 6th.
3. Missionaries. WAAAAY too many. Especially when they block you from moving.
4. Trading. I noticed if they approach you, you make out fairly well. I never bothered to ask them, because that was one area in Civ V that I didn't like and I didn't expect it to be better.
Additional Random Thoughts:
Spies - there was something wrong there. I had money stolen by spies. Technology Stolen by spies. I think they sabotaged my Industrial park several times. But If I ever tried anything but listen or cultivate sources, I ALWAYS got caught, even with 74% chance of success.
Barbarians - erik spelled out the issue with Barbarians pretty well in an earlier post. Here I am in the year 2030 with Barbarians popping up with Mech Infantry and AT Teams. You send in the troops and clean them out and before you depart the area, another stronghold appears with Advanced Weapons. They really need to fade away.
Amenities, Housing, and Food. Most everyone else likes the Districts, but with limited space, what with all the Districts I was encouraged to build, I couldn't grow enough food to feed my population. And there was never enough Housing. Odd, I don't think the Mayor, Governor, or President is responsible for building houses. That is free market. I need more amenities, but not really sure what qualifies.
Building times were too high. I tried to play this game fairly peacefully and so didn't have  much of a standing army. Suddenly barbarians appear with 5 modern military units. I checked every available city and even my three biggest needed 12-17 turns to build one infantry unit. Purchase? $2400! I could have bought three and then be broke. Oh, and no planes because building the Airfield will take 50 turns.
Maybe I played it wrong. I know some people really liked it, but I agree with the group that didn't. Oh, and I did play the tutorial, but there were a lot of things they did not explain.

After extensive hours, loads of cursing, and times of great joy I'm ready to write a review. I'll start by saying that this game is in a genre I'm actually not a big fan of. The last team shooter I played extensively was TF2 and I stopped playing that once I got too frustrated with it. For some reason online shooters rub me the wrong way. Then along came Paladins.
I still don't know what possessed me to download it, but I'm glad I did. At it's core it's a 5 vs 5 objective based shooter. Each of the many champions fills a role, and even in that role they handle things differently.
Front lines (Tanks) hold the point, partly through higher HP pools, and partly through shields that protect them and the team. Damage does what you'd expect, deal as much damage as possible and eliminate enemy targets at the point. Supports heal and buff the team, but also have abilities that debuff or disperse the enemy team. Flanks try to get behind enemy lines picking off lone targets or targets running away to heal. The game even rewards players that fill their role at the end of a match by giving more to the best player of each class.
I think one thing I really like about this game is that getting killed is more a punishment for bad play, than a common theme. Sure you will get killed, but it's not because of some unseen enemy from across the map. Skill is rewarded on both sides of the equation, knowing when to fight, and when to fall back. To be fair I'm not the best at shooters, but I'm still able to use my character's abilities to turn things around. I don't (usually) fall into a death spiral that makes me tear my hair out and swear off the game forever.
Another nice feature is the way it handles loadouts and upgrades. A loadout is 5 "cards" you use to enhance your chracter's playstyle. Each card can go up to level 4 and you are allowed 12 points in cards, with each level costing 1 point. Each character can unlock up to 16 different cards meaning each time you play with or against a certain champion they play differently, giving diversity to every match. You can also buy upgrades during a match with credits you earn. There are 4 upgrade types and once you buy an upgrade in a type you lockout the others of that type. For example the red damage cards modify the way you deal damage, but once you pick a red card, you can't pick another for the match.
I know I speak glowing about this game, but there are some downsides. For one, it's still technically beta, this means that bugs and glitches DO happen. I once got a 30 min deserter ban because I couldn't pick a character. Also it's a free to play game, this means there will be troll players. Nothing makes you flip your keyboard faster than a tank player that runs around the map (slowly), while the enemy team easily caps the point. Luckily it also doesn't suffer from pay 2 win. Anything you buy in this game with real money is completely cosmetic.
I really do recommend this game. I've played it more than most of my other games, only TF2 and Skyrim have more hours. Don't be put off by the "rip off" people either, it's not. It really is it's own thing and I think it stands firm.

Something is mising in the holistic aspect of the game. It just doesn't gel. I actually logged in and tried again a few months later and it is as bad, slow and out of whack as I'd remembered. I've played a lot of different versions of Civ and this is the worst of them. While each civilization has its unique units and characteristics, they feel bolted on and not really essential differences.
By contrast, a game like Stars in Shadow gets it right. The qualities of the different civilizations and what they can produce is so very different each civilization feels very different, very alient to the others. Imagine if in Civ VI different countries got steep discounts on procution of different items - one might build religious shrines at 80% discount, another builds baracks at 80% while yet another build harbors at 80% discount. One could be more clever than that, it's just a quick example of what comes to mind. The point is, the civilization's easy path would lead you in a certain direction. If you're the British and you get 80% discount on harbors and lighthouses, guess where you'll foudn your cities. If you're an Egyption and you get 80% discounts on improvements built on a river, guess where your cities will be built.  And so, on. If I thought about if for more than 15 minutes I could probably even come up with better examples. Play Stars in Shadow and you'll get a good idea.
I'm mystified as how some very basic things got so fouled up. For example, Athens and Sparta are tweedldee and tweedledum.  Both have Hoplites as their main units but Athens wasn't even close to a match for the Spartans on the field. They didn't even try.
In the past, Civ at least got the basics right. Athens under Pericles would not engage the Spartans in the field because they'd  be devasted.  Sparta simply dominated in the field and it's likely that no other civilization on the planet has put so much emphasis on training foot soldiers from the time of childhood. Essentialy they went to live in barracks from the age of 7 onward. They were underfed so they'd learn to deal with hunger and learn to steal without being caught (infiltration).  It was a severe soldiers life that the Athenians (nor anyone else in the world) simply didn't share.
Pericles actually rounded up the local farmers and gentry and brought them behind the walls of Athens and let the Spartans pillage and ransack the countryside as they simply couldn't match them in the field.
But on the sea it was an entirely different matter. Athens mastered the Aegean.  During the war Sparta decided to build its own fleet and take the battle to the Athenians.  Sparta was crushed.  Every last one of their ships was destroyed.
Pericles burned through cash building the Acropolis and engaging in a type of warfare that required the Athenians to purchase all their goods through shipping at a high price. Yet here he is scolding about being frugal.
How difficult would have been to give the Athenians an early jump on mastery of the sea by letting them skip the galley and go right the quadreme.  In fact, the Athenians used a trireme so it wouldn't have been a big leap. Give them extra points toward naval great people and an extra diplomatic policy slot and not just a wild card (you have to balance it somewhere).  Pericles and the Athenians forged the Delian league as much with diplomacy as with naval power. With a few minor changes using game mechanics already in place they could have at least made the Athenians feel like Athenians instead of me too Spartans.  How did that even get past the design phase?
And the Athenians and Spartans weren't just "Greek". The Spartans were a Doric people who held slaves and had a rigid heirarchy. The Athenians were a different people and were democratic. It would be as valid to lump the French and English into the same people and just call them Franco-Britains or something.
It's that sort of thing that spoils the feel of the game.  Something so fundamentally wrong it makes the cultures seem homogenized.  In the past games at least one got the impression with a modicum of understanding of history and a love of that history was involved in the game design.
And then there's the plodding game play and strange AI.  I'm sorry I bought it and after a few games I probably will never play it again.

LENGTHY AND WORDY REVIEW.
To begin with, I love Civilization. Civ 5 was by far the best iteration of the game, how Civ 6 could stray from well built game mechanics is beyond me. I will do nothing but reiterate the issues that others have already pointed out, and I seriously hope the developers address them, otherwise I will find myself playing the previous version over this one.
There are aspects of this version that I do love:
1. I love the concept of Districts
2. I find that Builders being limited to builds makes you think more strategically at the beginning of the game
3. The City State mechanics are far better in this one than the previous.
4. I like the split in advancements, splitting Civic with Tech is an interesting concept, but I sincerely hope that they add more technologies and civics, as you progress far too quickly through the ages.
5. Not having to have a naval city built straight on the coast is a big plus and makes logical sense.
6. Roads with Traders I aggree with, but there has to be a better way to decide where they are built.
7. Wonders on tiles, definitely makes the map prettier, while also preventing you from stacking a city, and diversifying your empire.
8. Agendas, while i love this idea as a diplomatic player of the game, this is seriously broken, and I will cover below.
9. I like the Casus Belli system, however, it needs major tweaking, which I will cover below.
Now the issues, sorry if it is a little harsh as I just had some irritating experiences playing a new log:
1. The AI builds cities in the dumbest places. For some reason, the AI has all this land around its capital to build its city, but instead decides to send a settler inbetween 5 of my cities and builds directly adjacent to my capital. What the frack? Seriously? Now I have to declare war and conquere the city and become known as a war mongerer, when I am perfectly justified for war, seeing as they promised NOT to build near me, then suddenly build in the middle of my kingdom?
2. Religion, as usual, a great aspect of the game, until the computer continuously spreads it's religion into your land even after they promise not to. Should this not be a justification for war? Apparently not, because that makes you are a war mongerer. There needs to be a better way to protect a religion, as it is far too easy to whipe religions out. If that were an accurate representation of real life, I am sure that Zoroastranism would have been dead 5000 years ago, instead of still existing in Iraq and adjacent countries.
3. Agendas, as stated above, are a beautiful aspect for a diplomatic player; however, It is seriously flawed and for the most part contradictory. Let us look at Germany for instance: The hate city states, and dislike anyone who befriends a city state, and yet denounce anyone who attacks city states? How about Egypt: they love a powerful nation, yet declare war on you because you are a war mongerer. The last time I checked, power and war mongering go hand in hand, has there ever been a benevolent power? Lastly, Arabia: They dislike people who spread religion to their lands, and dislike anyone who does not follow their land, which causes them to denounce everyone and declare war... does this not sound like they are stereotyping Arabs here...?
4. The Casus Belli system is a great tool for diplomacy play, but makes almost no sense what so ever.
4a. For starters, why does Holy War come so late into the game? Have we not heard of the Crusades? What about the attack on the new religion of Christianity by the Romans, who were heavily influenced by the Jewish faith in the Middle East? Based on when you can use Holy War, it coincides with the 18th century, well past any significant Holy War moments. This should be a heavy player at the start of the game, not when it means less historically speaking.
4b. Spying, why is this not a Casus Belli? If I kill 3 spies by the same country in a row after they promise to stop spying, why am I not justified for a war? Why am I the war mongerer for protecting my own people?
4c. War mongering penalties make no sense. I declare war once, compare to the computer who declares war 4 times, and yet I am the war mongerer? If I take over a city when someone declares war on me, there should be absolutely no war mongering penalties, even if I keep the city after the war is complete.
5. If I conquer a city and keep it, or raze it, that civilization will hate me for the rest of the game, and that is not completely accurate. Yes, dislike me for 50 turns, 100 turns, that makes sense. But to dislike me in turn 300 for occupying a city I captured in turn 65 because you built a city directly beside my capital makes no sense at all. Want a historical example? Alsace was originally a German territory until around the 16-17th century, at which point it changed hands numerous times, the last time being WW1 (WW2 is a different beast). Do Germany and France still fight over it? Of course not, in fact they are the two nations behind the European Union. Let us use WW2 as an example here. What Germany did between 1936 and 1945 should never be forgotten, but do people still hate them for it? No, this happened several generations ago. What they did does not mean the Germans today are the same, and to hate them is a completely and utterly irrational behaviour. I understand there are examples that show the other side of this (Israel V Palestine) but there should be some sort of modification that allowes for the computer to accept that the city is gone and the people are long removed from being their own.
6. Positive relationships in this game are next to impossible, due to conflicting agendas, war mongering, religion, poor casus belli structure, etc. In Civilization 5, I had an Ally that was right next to my borders. I even had a city next to their capital. Earlier in the game, we even had a massive war, where I Razed 1 city and captured another. My religion dominated theirs, and I even denounced a friend of theirs because of them picking on City States. All of this, yet we still had a continuous Declaration of Friendship from turn 200 to 500. This is impossible in Civilization 6. You declare war once, and you are labeled as a war mongerer to that 1 civ forever if you capture/raze its city. If your religion dominates, they will denounce you forever because you "converted" their city. The only way to have friends is to not found a religion and never capture any cities. Even then, you will still have at least 2 or 3 civ's denouncing you for absolutely no reason.
7. Diplomacy overview is missing. In Civilization 5, I was able to see who their friends are and who they dislike, what cities they have, what religions, what wonders, what resources, etc. This all helped me to decide what course of action to take when plotting a war. While I know they integrated most of this into the diplomacy screen, I am limited to see it one civ at a time, and I cannot see what I am trading with this civ either. When does my open borders treaty end? When does my Alliance end? When does my coal resource free up so I can get more money for it?
7b. Why can I not diplomatically force civilizations to make peace with another during a war? Should this not be a part of the diplomacy game? Especially Liberation, even if they are not my friends or allies, should I not be allowed to liberate a country that was unjustly conquered by a war mongerer without becoming one myself?
While I have many serious complaints and issues with this game, I still play it and I have faith that it will improve. After all it has only been 2 months since its release, and I feel that if they address the issues stated above, the game can be the best Civilization yet. I do recommend it to any Civilization fanatic, however, I also recommend that you WAIT, until the above has been addressed, as it will frustrate you beyond belief.
P.S. - INCLUDE A MAP BUILDER!!!!!!

I bought this game in Alpha and then transferred it to Steam. I've put more than 200 hours in this game and here is why:
The game can be summarized as: Build your own Space and Aviation facility with a company on a slightly rescaled earth like planet with green aliens simulator. You can choose between 3 game modes when you start: Sandbox, Science and Career mode. Sandbox lets you build any ship without constraints and lets you explore the solar system with unlimited funds. Science mode was a test mode during Beta where you had to collect science in order to advance the tech tree and unlock new items. Career mode is science mode but with added funds, management, facility building and staff management. There's a slight problem with these modes as pointed out by the community which I will rant about in the next paragraph.
Sandbox mode is the "intended" mode to be playing the game in unless you want to cheat for funds and science. Build Space stations, go to "Mars", colonize the moon and do what you want. But there's no goal in it and no missions. The only reward is that you accomplish something amazing when you rendezvous with a space station in high orbit, refuel and then go to a different planet like in the movie Interstellar.
Science mode would be a better game mode to play with rather than career mode because you have a progression, need to actually gather science by doing science projects and bring the science back to the Kerbin planet. However, there's no missions in this mode so after you've done all research, you are practically in sandbox mode.
Career mode is the mode which limits you and restrain the parts available from start. All you have to work with is a small liquid engine, a small booster and some parachutes. I'd say it's equal to the year 1945 after realizing you can build V-rockets but Jet engines were not completely mainstream yet. And then you do research, do missions to get funding and complete different tasks to unlock more science and get harder missions. To play career mode fully, you should start with little to no extra science when you begin, because all the missions are based on your current science and your "records" that you've achieved. If you cheat with science or unlock more than your current level of mission and technology, you will loose many essential missions that you need in order to get a good start.
Logically, an unmanned pod like Sputnik would be a good choice for the first satellite you put up in orbit, but the first robot and remote controlled pod is not available until you have unlocked electricity which is 4 levels into the tech tree. And the surface scanners you need for scanning the planets for resources are not unlocked until the very last levels of the tech tree. The tech tree feels backwards and the only thing it does it limit your potential by sending you to a mission to orbit the moon without RCS control.
In conclusion though, I recommend this game to anyone 10 years old and up to learn about orbital mechanics and aerodynamics. The learning curve in this game is as steep as you want to make it. But before you've learned how to rendezvous in space in orbit, the game has a high cliff difficulty. After that point, the game becomes easier.
Don't forget to check out the mods for the game that adds different aids and help for information. Also play the game with a keyboard because any joystick you try and use for the game will not work as a flight simulator.

I really want to vote yes, and I feel like if they update the AI, I will, but right now, I simply can't.
Let me start by saying that if you enjoy war in Civilization games (you absolute maniac), this game is a great improvement. The gameplay is fun and colorful, the much-touted improvements to city planning add so much more strategy and depth to the gameplay experience, and just about everything has been tweaked and polished to a mirror sheen. The game, if taken on its own without context, is quite great and I highly recommend it to any fans of the series.
And like I said, if you enjoy war above all other things in this franchise, then it won't disappoint. But if you enjoy tactful negotiation, playing diplomacy, manipulating nations against each other, or just simply trying for another victory condition OTHER than domination, then I'd suggest passing on this game. For now. The AI is so bad that I am confident that it's bugged. They will openly declare war on you - and only you - for absolutely no reason.
I know, to some degree, that this is a mainstay of the series, but it never felt this bad. Later in the game, you will have civilizations go from alliance to straight up war in a matter of two or three turns, and there is absolutely NOTHING you can do to prevent it. As someone who both hates the micro-managey nature of war in Civilization and enjoys actually feeling like there's some sort of diplomatic game that I can shrewdly manipulate to my advantage - even if it means paying off the most powerful nations to not go to war with me - I simply can't play this game.
As I mentioned before, the irrational AI seems almost like a bug and I firmly believe it will be tweaked and fixed in time, but until that time, I cannot recommend this game for anyone that enjoys what makes Civilization great: the actual simulation of building a civilization. If you like turn-based war simulators, then go nuts. But if you want a Civ game with Civ-levels of nuance - certainly keep an eye on Civ 6 for when they (hopefully) fix the AI - but don't waste your money.

In this review I will outline some Pros and Cons and then give my general thoughts on the game.
This not-really-but-still new system (Civ 3 had something very similar) really helps out gameplay. Escorts help move a civilian and military together by linking them so where one goes the other goes also. Armies combines multiple (up to 3) of the same unit into one more powerful version. This is a great system but I have a couple issues with it. It lacks depth. For example, you should be able to combine an infantry unit with an anti-tank unit, making it not as strong as two combined infantries, but stronger against tanks. Also, as you combine units the graphics don’t change. It isn’t a big deal but worth mentioning.
Barbarians are actually challenging in this game and harder to deal with then actual civs.
I like the civics tree as certain things you will need to research are not technologies and this is a good way to divide them. The new government system where you pick the cards you want to customize the benefits you get really lets you tailor your government to your playstyle for that game. It maybe seems too easy to just swap out polices though. Also, some of the civics tree research options seem meaningless to me (but that may just be me).
I think districts is a fantastic idea that makes more sense than having all those buildings on one tile and forces you to think about what you want in a city, especially due to the population requirement.
I will note that I think there are not enough city center buildings. Stuff like having to build a campus to get a library is a tad bit annoying/silly.
Having wonders on tiles, as well, I like as it forces you to really think about the ones you want and I will skip a lot of wonders I may have built in previous games. You have to decide if it’s worth using a tile that could be a farm or district.
I like the amenities system, save that there isn’t always a lot of ways to gain amenities to keep people happy and you’re forced building entertainment complexes to compensate.
Competing for the same great people and having each person have their own effect (that is, great scientists are the same as each other) is awesome. Sometimes you’ll even refuse a great person as his effect sucks and other times you’ll be doing everything you can to beat out your rivals for a certain one.
I actually like these cartoony graphics (though I preferred the more realistic Civ 5 graphics) and think, somehow, they fit with the game’s style and mesh well with the new map-style fog of war (which is awesome). More so, there is a tremendous amount of detail on map in small, subtle ways. For example, buildings in tundra/snow tiles have snow on the roofs and in the entertainment complex there are some tiny horses running around the arena.
However, my grip here is that, one of the reasons for these graphics was to make it easier to tell units apart. Instead, I have a somewhat difficult time doing so. It’s not terribly bad but not great either. In Civ 5, I could tell them apart really well regardless of how zoomed out I was. Graphics would have been a pro except for this point.
The UI is nice but there are about 110 little things that make it not-so-good. Here are a few (there’s others but these give an idea):
I like how you have to destroy walls before hitting the city and that they can only be repaired by doing a project. I don’t like that they seem glitch-y for me as the game won’t always let me do said project (even when I’m at peace) and you can’t upgrade until you repair and it leaves your city vulnerable to have the wall health so low. Also, by the modern era, at least, walls should be obsolete in my thinking.
I think we all knew this would be a con. Combat AI is terrible like it always is and diplomacy AI is terrible like it often is.
The new agendas are a great idea that often suck in-game. Why? First, some of them are really dumb. Like, “if you explore then I hate you”, dumb. Also, they keep sending messages (the same ones over and over) that make no sense and don’t explain what is meant. More so, the AI goes off on you for everything and trying to make an alliance would probably be a wee bit impossible unless you gear everything little thing you do to make them happy.
Also, the AI is hypocritical. For example, you’ll capture 5 of their spies and then they’ll catch one of yours and they act like they never sent any spies themselves.
Small. Even the huge map is small. Also, you start right next to everybody and it is very cramped. I miss big maps.
There are other things I could have noted such as, builders and roads but that gives an idea of what is good and bad in the game.
Overall, I like this game and will play it a lot. It does have more content then Civ 5 and fixes some of what was wrong with it. However, in some areas (namely the two cons I listed) it goes backwards (how it made diplomacy worse than it was in Civ 5 is beyond me). Also, I should note that some of the systems/mechanics are opaque with no info in the civilopedia so you have to kind of feel them out.
With that said, I would give this game a 7/10. It is bold and fresh but not better than Civ 5 was. Maybe buy on sale once the major DLC is released.

LENGTHY AND WORDY REVIEW.
To begin with, I love Civilization. Civ 5 was by far the best iteration of the game, how Civ 6 could stray from well built game mechanics is beyond me. I will do nothing but reiterate the issues that others have already pointed out, and I seriously hope the developers address them, otherwise I will find myself playing the previous version over this one.
There are aspects of this version that I do love:
1. I love the concept of Districts
2. I find that Builders being limited to builds makes you think more strategically at the beginning of the game
3. The City State mechanics are far better in this one than the previous.
4. I like the split in advancements, splitting Civic with Tech is an interesting concept, but I sincerely hope that they add more technologies and civics, as you progress far too quickly through the ages.
5. Not having to have a naval city built straight on the coast is a big plus and makes logical sense.
6. Roads with Traders I aggree with, but there has to be a better way to decide where they are built.
7. Wonders on tiles, definitely makes the map prettier, while also preventing you from stacking a city, and diversifying your empire.
8. Agendas, while i love this idea as a diplomatic player of the game, this is seriously broken, and I will cover below.
9. I like the Casus Belli system, however, it needs major tweaking, which I will cover below.
Now the issues, sorry if it is a little harsh as I just had some irritating experiences playing a new log:
1. The AI builds cities in the dumbest places. For some reason, the AI has all this land around its capital to build its city, but instead decides to send a settler inbetween 5 of my cities and builds directly adjacent to my capital. What the frack? Seriously? Now I have to declare war and conquere the city and become known as a war mongerer, when I am perfectly justified for war, seeing as they promised NOT to build near me, then suddenly build in the middle of my kingdom?
2. Religion, as usual, a great aspect of the game, until the computer continuously spreads it's religion into your land even after they promise not to. Should this not be a justification for war? Apparently not, because that makes you are a war mongerer. There needs to be a better way to protect a religion, as it is far too easy to whipe religions out. If that were an accurate representation of real life, I am sure that Zoroastranism would have been dead 5000 years ago, instead of still existing in Iraq and adjacent countries.
3. Agendas, as stated above, are a beautiful aspect for a diplomatic player; however, It is seriously flawed and for the most part contradictory. Let us look at Germany for instance: The hate city states, and dislike anyone who befriends a city state, and yet denounce anyone who attacks city states? How about Egypt: they love a powerful nation, yet declare war on you because you are a war mongerer. The last time I checked, power and war mongering go hand in hand, has there ever been a benevolent power? Lastly, Arabia: They dislike people who spread religion to their lands, and dislike anyone who does not follow their land, which causes them to denounce everyone and declare war... does this not sound like they are stereotyping Arabs here...?
4. The Casus Belli system is a great tool for diplomacy play, but makes almost no sense what so ever.
4a. For starters, why does Holy War come so late into the game? Have we not heard of the Crusades? What about the attack on the new religion of Christianity by the Romans, who were heavily influenced by the Jewish faith in the Middle East? Based on when you can use Holy War, it coincides with the 18th century, well past any significant Holy War moments. This should be a heavy player at the start of the game, not when it means less historically speaking.
4b. Spying, why is this not a Casus Belli? If I kill 3 spies by the same country in a row after they promise to stop spying, why am I not justified for a war? Why am I the war mongerer for protecting my own people?
4c. War mongering penalties make no sense. I declare war once, compare to the computer who declares war 4 times, and yet I am the war mongerer? If I take over a city when someone declares war on me, there should be absolutely no war mongering penalties, even if I keep the city after the war is complete.
5. If I conquer a city and keep it, or raze it, that civilization will hate me for the rest of the game, and that is not completely accurate. Yes, dislike me for 50 turns, 100 turns, that makes sense. But to dislike me in turn 300 for occupying a city I captured in turn 65 because you built a city directly beside my capital makes no sense at all. Want a historical example? Alsace was originally a German territory until around the 16-17th century, at which point it changed hands numerous times, the last time being WW1 (WW2 is a different beast). Do Germany and France still fight over it? Of course not, in fact they are the two nations behind the European Union. Let us use WW2 as an example here. What Germany did between 1936 and 1945 should never be forgotten, but do people still hate them for it? No, this happened several generations ago. What they did does not mean the Germans today are the same, and to hate them is a completely and utterly irrational behaviour. I understand there are examples that show the other side of this (Israel V Palestine) but there should be some sort of modification that allowes for the computer to accept that the city is gone and the people are long removed from being their own.
6. Positive relationships in this game are next to impossible, due to conflicting agendas, war mongering, religion, poor casus belli structure, etc. In Civilization 5, I had an Ally that was right next to my borders. I even had a city next to their capital. Earlier in the game, we even had a massive war, where I Razed 1 city and captured another. My religion dominated theirs, and I even denounced a friend of theirs because of them picking on City States. All of this, yet we still had a continuous Declaration of Friendship from turn 200 to 500. This is impossible in Civilization 6. You declare war once, and you are labeled as a war mongerer to that 1 civ forever if you capture/raze its city. If your religion dominates, they will denounce you forever because you "converted" their city. The only way to have friends is to not found a religion and never capture any cities. Even then, you will still have at least 2 or 3 civ's denouncing you for absolutely no reason.
7. Diplomacy overview is missing. In Civilization 5, I was able to see who their friends are and who they dislike, what cities they have, what religions, what wonders, what resources, etc. This all helped me to decide what course of action to take when plotting a war. While I know they integrated most of this into the diplomacy screen, I am limited to see it one civ at a time, and I cannot see what I am trading with this civ either. When does my open borders treaty end? When does my Alliance end? When does my coal resource free up so I can get more money for it?
7b. Why can I not diplomatically force civilizations to make peace with another during a war? Should this not be a part of the diplomacy game? Especially Liberation, even if they are not my friends or allies, should I not be allowed to liberate a country that was unjustly conquered by a war mongerer without becoming one myself?
While I have many serious complaints and issues with this game, I still play it and I have faith that it will improve. After all it has only been 2 months since its release, and I feel that if they address the issues stated above, the game can be the best Civilization yet. I do recommend it to any Civilization fanatic, however, I also recommend that you WAIT, until the above has been addressed, as it will frustrate you beyond belief.
P.S. - INCLUDE A MAP BUILDER!!!!!!

I bought this game in Alpha and then transferred it to Steam. I've put more than 200 hours in this game and here is why:
The game can be summarized as: Build your own Space and Aviation facility with a company on a slightly rescaled earth like planet with green aliens simulator. You can choose between 3 game modes when you start: Sandbox, Science and Career mode. Sandbox lets you build any ship without constraints and lets you explore the solar system with unlimited funds. Science mode was a test mode during Beta where you had to collect science in order to advance the tech tree and unlock new items. Career mode is science mode but with added funds, management, facility building and staff management. There's a slight problem with these modes as pointed out by the community which I will rant about in the next paragraph.
Sandbox mode is the "intended" mode to be playing the game in unless you want to cheat for funds and science. Build Space stations, go to "Mars", colonize the moon and do what you want. But there's no goal in it and no missions. The only reward is that you accomplish something amazing when you rendezvous with a space station in high orbit, refuel and then go to a different planet like in the movie Interstellar.
Science mode would be a better game mode to play with rather than career mode because you have a progression, need to actually gather science by doing science projects and bring the science back to the Kerbin planet. However, there's no missions in this mode so after you've done all research, you are practically in sandbox mode.
Career mode is the mode which limits you and restrain the parts available from start. All you have to work with is a small liquid engine, a small booster and some parachutes. I'd say it's equal to the year 1945 after realizing you can build V-rockets but Jet engines were not completely mainstream yet. And then you do research, do missions to get funding and complete different tasks to unlock more science and get harder missions. To play career mode fully, you should start with little to no extra science when you begin, because all the missions are based on your current science and your "records" that you've achieved. If you cheat with science or unlock more than your current level of mission and technology, you will loose many essential missions that you need in order to get a good start.
Logically, an unmanned pod like Sputnik would be a good choice for the first satellite you put up in orbit, but the first robot and remote controlled pod is not available until you have unlocked electricity which is 4 levels into the tech tree. And the surface scanners you need for scanning the planets for resources are not unlocked until the very last levels of the tech tree. The tech tree feels backwards and the only thing it does it limit your potential by sending you to a mission to orbit the moon without RCS control.
In conclusion though, I recommend this game to anyone 10 years old and up to learn about orbital mechanics and aerodynamics. The learning curve in this game is as steep as you want to make it. But before you've learned how to rendezvous in space in orbit, the game has a high cliff difficulty. After that point, the game becomes easier.
Don't forget to check out the mods for the game that adds different aids and help for information. Also play the game with a keyboard because any joystick you try and use for the game will not work as a flight simulator.

Garry's Mod has a unique gaming experience which you won't find in any other game. Why? You create the experience.
-First of all, the game has thousands of addons on Steam Workshop that you can download and play right away! This is one of the if not the best features of the game.
-There are thousands of servers with different and very fun gamemodes. You will be seeing a list of servers when you select multiplayer, and as I said before; every server is a different experience. You can play on a Dark RP server, in which you become a citizen, mafia, or the law enforcement and roleplay with the others. Or, you can play Prop Hunt and have a blast trying to hide from the hunters!
-You don't need friends to have fun. This is a game where you actually can have fun without your friends. I'm not saying you wouldn't have fun with your friends but it will also be fun when you are alone. Also, you will be making a plenty of friends playing this game!
-The Community is not very good these days. Lots of kids are present and can be annoying at times.
-Not having a microphone is a disadvantage at various gamemodes. For example, you are playing in a DarkRP server and a mafia came and told you to give him all your money. He counts to ten holding a gun staring at you. While you are typing "I don't have any money man..." you are killed.
-I don't know for sure if this is a bad thing or not, but when you download a lot of addons, the game will be holding a lot of memory on your hard drive. A LOT OF MEMORY BELIEVE ME.
-It can be hard startimg private servers to play with your friends. You need to have Hamachi to do so. I don't know if there has been any update stating otherwise, but back in the day it was like this. Also, you will need to download every single addon your friend has before joining which takes quite a time.
Hope this review has been helpful. I highly recommend this game if you have the time and patience to play it!

Civ6 could have been a worthy successor to Civ4 but sadly is unfinished, unbalanced, and unreliable. There are certainly some interesting concepts here - distracts add a lot to the game, as do eureka moments and the split tech tree and city states, and terrain is a lot more interesting now - but there are just too many places in which the game doesn't work properley.
Reliability is the biggest issue - the game sometimes gets into situations where it is guaranteed to crash on a particular turn during the AI phase (after you've played a map for 30+ hours and are in the end game, this is an absolute showstopper - there's usually nothing you can do go play past the 'crash turn' even if you try to revert to an earlier save and play differently). For this reason alone, I cannot recommend this game - it's just too frustrating when this happens. It appears to be quite a widespread issue, as well, and not fixed by the first patch. There are other problems with the game too, though:
Some game concepts haven't been balanced or thought through correctly. If you conquer the founder of a religion after they've coverted some of your cities you can be left with a dead religion to which you are unable to evangelise any futher believes or declare an inquisition but which you can't do anything about. The division of units into light cavalry, heavy cavalry, melee, anti-cavalry, ranged, and bombard sometimes leaves obsolete old units hanging around for much too long before an upgrade.
Limited-used builders are a good mechanic. I like how they increase the prioritisation of scare resource rather than being an exponential multiplier (as they were in earlier Civ games).
The AI is terrible. Doesn't know how to move units effectively in a 1UPT world, doesn't plan attacks well, lets settlers wander around unprotected, often makes apparently random diplomatic actions (eg. declines a proposed deal, then instantly comes back and accepts a worse-for-them deal), doesn't act in own interest when up against a wall.
The user interface is missing a lot of things. You can't get a list of your current trade deals. You can't get a diagram of who is at war with whom. You don't get a warning when your trade deals have expired. You can't see your exact science progress towards a technology you're researching, only an approximate progress dial - so can't work out whether managing your production differently will get you there a little earlier or not. You can't see what the benefits of a district project will be.  You can't see which cities have one of your trading posts. The diplomacy screen is a giant animated leader with all the important stuff crammed in to a tiny side bar with a bunch of tabs, requiring a lot of scrolling up or down. The city info pop-out is also too narrow, forcing a lot of vertical scrolling. Sometimes city summary boxes don't update to reflect changes you make. In the end-game, turns take ages to process, and you are bombared with unnecessary dialogues (eg. you've researched all the techs - your only option is to research "future technology" - why do you have to reselect it every three turns? There's the same problem at end of the culture tree.) Trade route selection and city build selection are similar - there's no option to say "carry on with what I told you last time" so you find yourself reselecting the same thing turn-after-turn. Really, it seems as if the UI was released without proper testing cycles.
The distict system really adds a feel of urban planning, and I like micromanaging placement to optimise adjacency bonuses. There is a major issue with water tiles though - they're just wasted potential. Cities founded near the coast are largely useless. There's only one type water district and a handful of wonders so almost every water tile feels wasted because the yields are poor and you can't build districts there, which means an isthmus city cannot build most of the buildings it needs. You find yourself trying to build "coastal" cities two tiles inland and positioning them so that they will only have one or two water tile within their eventual boundary, for the harbour and maybe one sea resource or a wonder. This is daft!
This touches on something else - there don't seem to be as many buildings as in Civ4. Once you've kitted out the main districts, the only thing left for much of the later part of the game is building a neighbourhood occasionally until the city caps out. The tech tree runs pretty low on buildings after a while. No supermarket, customs house, no trade offs for different types of power plant, no hospital, no bunkers or any other additional defences once you get past city walls. This is particularly bad for coastal cities since it was these late-stage buildings that made water tiles feasible. There probably needs to be some sort of new, unlimited sea district (like a neighbourhood) that you can use to improve water yields to solve this.
I like the trade route system (other than the way the UI makes it tedious) and it's fun watching roads emerge from it. However I think military engineers come a little too late, particularly as the 1UPT forces your units to sprawl all over the map - a way of building some early roads "where you want them" would be good, even if it were restricted to connecting cities or districts to each other - this avoids the situation where traders always build roads in the "wrong place". Also rather odd how roads get better based on era - I would prefer it if you had to research some mobility technologies to get these benefits, and actually had to spend resources improving them (via builders / engineers) in the modern era (as you had to do to get the benefit of railroads in Civ4).
All in all, the game just doesn't feel finished. Coupled with the tedium of the UI towards late game, and the chance that your current map will become unplayable (crash) past a certain turn, and I would say to give it a miss, Which is a shame, as this could have been much better.

The main question I had going into this game: is it better than the venerable CIV5.
The answer is more complicated than yes or no. I think the most accurate answer right now would be it is different enough to make me recommend the game. They've changed up a lot of the gameplay mechanics from CIV5 which in my mind makes it a buy if you are interested in something different in your grand strategy experience.
CIV6 also fell in a number of same trappings as the vanilla non-DLC CIV5 did, but it has more game mechanics at launch then CIV5 did at launch.
My main issues with CIV6 currently are: civilizations are not balanced, only 3 civs are top tier while the remaining ones will have you at a severe disadvantage. This is ok if you play on lower difficulties but if you intend to beat the game on immortal or diety you pretty much have to play one of the three top tier civs. Which brings me to the second issue: the game is not as difficult as CIV5 in singleplayer. The AI seems to be more stupid than in CIV5. Immortal and Diety are nowhere as difficult as in CIV5.
If you are new to CIV I would say you can go with either CIV6 or CIV5, just be aware CIV5 goes on sale often and you can grab it for a good price with all the DLC. If you go that route get Brave New World for sure.
I am pretty sure as I play more of CIV6 I will update my review, but as of now it is a good game that is worth a buy. I cannot say yet if it is a great game as CIV5 because I need many hours to see if it earns that distinction.

The Walking Dead Season 2: All That Remains is the first episode in the highly-anticipated return of TellTale’s critically acclaimed adventure series. However, this time players control Clementine, the little girl whom we met in the first season and bonded with, as well as teaching her how to survive. However, does TellTale’s return to Walking Dead shine as a great narrative, or has the hype fallen flat? To be honest, this episode is truly only great for the development of Clementine’s character and nothing else.
TellTale has asked that spoilers be kept to a minimum so it’s going to be hard to talk about the episode without diving into too much detail, honestly. However, there are some slight plot points that do not ruin the story that should be talked about. To start, just like the introduction to the first season, All That Remains is pretty basic. The new cast of characters is barely fleshed out and we don’t get a good understanding about their characters. Sure, we get an idea about a few of them (such as new survivor Carlos and his methods) but it’s hard to remember everyone’s names when some of them are barely on-screen. The main part of this episode deals mostly with the dilemma of how you should treat a random little girl in the wilderness. The new group of survivors has a debate after Clementine is seemingly a threat, especially after they believe she has been bitten. As Clementine, the player has to make hard choices and just show how independent she has become upon losing Lee Everett. The whole episode is just an interesting character piece for Clementine; playing as a little girl has definitely somewhat changed the style of the game, and I’m not so-sure it’s for the best. Everything seems so much smaller in-scale, in a sense. You’re barely making adult decisions, however you’re still killing walkers and having badass moments. Unfortunately, though, All That Remains seems incredibly short. None of the characters are beefed up and the pacing is incredibly off, not to mention an incredibly abrupt ending.
Unfortunately, TellTale almost hasn’t kicked it up a notch with the gameplay, sound or visuals. Sure, there’s plenty of more action in the game than there was in the first season’s premiere, but it’s the same gameplay technique used in The Wolf Among Us’ premiere. There’s almost nothing new here and the gameplay doesn’t feel fresh other than an all-new UI. Now, that’s not completely unexpected from TellTale, but the episode really feels rushed out. There was never really a moment where I was shocked at a new mechanic. However, even though the gameplay was lackluster, Jared Emerson-Johnson’s music for TellTale has significantly improved and has become very noticeable in this episode in comparison to the previous season. It’s powerful, but not that great, especially compared to other video games. Even though the stylistic nature of The Walking Dead hasn’t changed, there could’ve been room for graphical improvement, but alas we only got slightly bigger environments.
To conclude, Telltale barely stepped up their game (literally) for The Walking Dead. However, there are still some gut-punching moments and fantastic character building for Clementine contained in the episode. It’s just a shame that it’s too short and we only get to care for Clementine and none of the other new, original cast additions. The game also proves that, thus far, the 400 Days DLC has been worthless. Nevertheless, the 5$ish dollar price tag on a single episode of The Walking Dead is well-worth it but if I were a Seasons Pass owner, I’d be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at first.
TL;DR Boring with poor characters. Clementine's development shines through, however the episode is too short to enjoy.
