I bought this game in Alpha and then transferred it to Steam. I've put more than 200 hours in this game and here is why:
The game can be summarized as: Build your own Space and Aviation facility with a company on a slightly rescaled earth like planet with green aliens simulator. You can choose between 3 game modes when you start: Sandbox, Science and Career mode. Sandbox lets you build any ship without constraints and lets you explore the solar system with unlimited funds. Science mode was a test mode during Beta where you had to collect science in order to advance the tech tree and unlock new items. Career mode is science mode but with added funds, management, facility building and staff management. There's a slight problem with these modes as pointed out by the community which I will rant about in the next paragraph.
Sandbox mode is the "intended" mode to be playing the game in unless you want to cheat for funds and science. Build Space stations, go to "Mars", colonize the moon and do what you want. But there's no goal in it and no missions. The only reward is that you accomplish something amazing when you rendezvous with a space station in high orbit, refuel and then go to a different planet like in the movie Interstellar.
Science mode would be a better game mode to play with rather than career mode because you have a progression, need to actually gather science by doing science projects and bring the science back to the Kerbin planet. However, there's no missions in this mode so after you've done all research, you are practically in sandbox mode.
Career mode is the mode which limits you and restrain the parts available from start. All you have to work with is a small liquid engine, a small booster and some parachutes. I'd say it's equal to the year 1945 after realizing you can build V-rockets but Jet engines were not completely mainstream yet. And then you do research, do missions to get funding and complete different tasks to unlock more science and get harder missions. To play career mode fully, you should start with little to no extra science when you begin, because all the missions are based on your current science and your "records" that you've achieved. If you cheat with science or unlock more than your current level of mission and technology, you will loose many essential missions that you need in order to get a good start.
Logically, an unmanned pod like Sputnik would be a good choice for the first satellite you put up in orbit, but the first robot and remote controlled pod is not available until you have unlocked electricity which is 4 levels into the tech tree. And the surface scanners you need for scanning the planets for resources are not unlocked until the very last levels of the tech tree. The tech tree feels backwards and the only thing it does it limit your potential by sending you to a mission to orbit the moon without RCS control.
In conclusion though, I recommend this game to anyone 10 years old and up to learn about orbital mechanics and aerodynamics. The learning curve in this game is as steep as you want to make it. But before you've learned how to rendezvous in space in orbit, the game has a high cliff difficulty. After that point, the game becomes easier.
Don't forget to check out the mods for the game that adds different aids and help for information. Also play the game with a keyboard because any joystick you try and use for the game will not work as a flight simulator.

Civ6 could have been a worthy successor to Civ4 but sadly is unfinished, unbalanced, and unreliable. There are certainly some interesting concepts here - distracts add a lot to the game, as do eureka moments and the split tech tree and city states, and terrain is a lot more interesting now - but there are just too many places in which the game doesn't work properley.
Reliability is the biggest issue - the game sometimes gets into situations where it is guaranteed to crash on a particular turn during the AI phase (after you've played a map for 30+ hours and are in the end game, this is an absolute showstopper - there's usually nothing you can do go play past the 'crash turn' even if you try to revert to an earlier save and play differently). For this reason alone, I cannot recommend this game - it's just too frustrating when this happens. It appears to be quite a widespread issue, as well, and not fixed by the first patch. There are other problems with the game too, though:
Some game concepts haven't been balanced or thought through correctly. If you conquer the founder of a religion after they've coverted some of your cities you can be left with a dead religion to which you are unable to evangelise any futher believes or declare an inquisition but which you can't do anything about. The division of units into light cavalry, heavy cavalry, melee, anti-cavalry, ranged, and bombard sometimes leaves obsolete old units hanging around for much too long before an upgrade.
Limited-used builders are a good mechanic. I like how they increase the prioritisation of scare resource rather than being an exponential multiplier (as they were in earlier Civ games).
The AI is terrible. Doesn't know how to move units effectively in a 1UPT world, doesn't plan attacks well, lets settlers wander around unprotected, often makes apparently random diplomatic actions (eg. declines a proposed deal, then instantly comes back and accepts a worse-for-them deal), doesn't act in own interest when up against a wall.
The user interface is missing a lot of things. You can't get a list of your current trade deals. You can't get a diagram of who is at war with whom. You don't get a warning when your trade deals have expired. You can't see your exact science progress towards a technology you're researching, only an approximate progress dial - so can't work out whether managing your production differently will get you there a little earlier or not. You can't see what the benefits of a district project will be.  You can't see which cities have one of your trading posts. The diplomacy screen is a giant animated leader with all the important stuff crammed in to a tiny side bar with a bunch of tabs, requiring a lot of scrolling up or down. The city info pop-out is also too narrow, forcing a lot of vertical scrolling. Sometimes city summary boxes don't update to reflect changes you make. In the end-game, turns take ages to process, and you are bombared with unnecessary dialogues (eg. you've researched all the techs - your only option is to research "future technology" - why do you have to reselect it every three turns? There's the same problem at end of the culture tree.) Trade route selection and city build selection are similar - there's no option to say "carry on with what I told you last time" so you find yourself reselecting the same thing turn-after-turn. Really, it seems as if the UI was released without proper testing cycles.
The distict system really adds a feel of urban planning, and I like micromanaging placement to optimise adjacency bonuses. There is a major issue with water tiles though - they're just wasted potential. Cities founded near the coast are largely useless. There's only one type water district and a handful of wonders so almost every water tile feels wasted because the yields are poor and you can't build districts there, which means an isthmus city cannot build most of the buildings it needs. You find yourself trying to build "coastal" cities two tiles inland and positioning them so that they will only have one or two water tile within their eventual boundary, for the harbour and maybe one sea resource or a wonder. This is daft!
This touches on something else - there don't seem to be as many buildings as in Civ4. Once you've kitted out the main districts, the only thing left for much of the later part of the game is building a neighbourhood occasionally until the city caps out. The tech tree runs pretty low on buildings after a while. No supermarket, customs house, no trade offs for different types of power plant, no hospital, no bunkers or any other additional defences once you get past city walls. This is particularly bad for coastal cities since it was these late-stage buildings that made water tiles feasible. There probably needs to be some sort of new, unlimited sea district (like a neighbourhood) that you can use to improve water yields to solve this.
I like the trade route system (other than the way the UI makes it tedious) and it's fun watching roads emerge from it. However I think military engineers come a little too late, particularly as the 1UPT forces your units to sprawl all over the map - a way of building some early roads "where you want them" would be good, even if it were restricted to connecting cities or districts to each other - this avoids the situation where traders always build roads in the "wrong place". Also rather odd how roads get better based on era - I would prefer it if you had to research some mobility technologies to get these benefits, and actually had to spend resources improving them (via builders / engineers) in the modern era (as you had to do to get the benefit of railroads in Civ4).
All in all, the game just doesn't feel finished. Coupled with the tedium of the UI towards late game, and the chance that your current map will become unplayable (crash) past a certain turn, and I would say to give it a miss, Which is a shame, as this could have been much better.

Let me start by saying not many games make me emotional but oh man..this game has literally changed the way I look at things. The game is executed in a really mature and humane way that pulls you into the Life is Strange universe.
The storyline, characters and soundtrack are the three main elements that made me fall in love with this game. Not to mention, the visual style is superb! Sure, it's not "cutting edge" but Life is Strange is not that kind of game. If you like a game with a terrific storyline, loveable characters and a kickass soundtrack, this game is definitely for you! It's a huge emotional roller coaster ride. Although I didn't sign up for it D:
The game is truly a unique experience and is mostly about figuring out the disappearance of a Blackwell student but for most part, it's a refreshing take about coming of age and figuring out who you are in the process. It is also a beautiful depiction about friendship and how far you will go to save someone you love. This is not something you come across in every game. Life is in fact, very strange indeed.
Now of course, I could address the negative aspects of the game (such as the lip syncing) but things like that aren't big enough to even complain about because all the positive things about this game serve as great compensation so why hate on this priceless gem? (no pun intended)
Honestly, this game has earned a special place in my heart. It really is something in my opinion. If you are hesitant to play this game thinking it may not live up to your expectations. Throw those expectations out the window and play the game with an open mind because I believe you'll find it's more than meets the eye.
Life is Strange is an experience I'll never forget. It explores the good, the bad and even the mundane at times but it's all worth it because life is..strange (pun actually intended)

"One small step for Kerbal..." *static* "One giant leap for Kerbalkind..."
Nothing can describe the feelings of accomplishment and joy when I first set Kerbal boots onto the surface of the Mun. There was no in-game achievement pop up. But that's what made it that much more enjoyable. Ever since I did my first fly-by I knew my next goal would be to land there. And after many unsuccessful attempts I finally touched down on the surface.
My next problem faced  me immediately. I didn't have enough fuel for the return trip.
And THAT is what makes this game so amazing. The challenge lies in planning ahead. Overcoming obstacles you might not have thought of initially. I ended up building a fuel tanker and launching that into a Mun orbit where I was able to successfully dock and transfer fuel.
At the same time it's fun to just build something ridiculous and to see what happens. It's just as enjoyable when it ends in an explosion.
As a newbie I started off on the career mode. Sandbox was too intimidating. Too many parts, no idea what they do. Career gives you basic parts and you have to unlock the rest. So you have a lot more understand of what parts you want to unlock and what they do.
I give this game a solid 10. If you enjoy setting challenges yourself and don't mind failing occasionally then you'll love it. It's a whole lot of fun and I've barely scratched the surface yet!

Hello people,this is going to be my in depth review on the wonderful game Garry's mod.

Lets get started,
Overview - The game is good overall and 100% worth the price as it is £7 or even cheaper if you get it on sale, i have about 1.5k hours on the game so far and the number is probably going to rise,this game is old but has an amazing community which helps people and keeps the game alive.

I rate this game mode - 7 / 10
Murder - I have never really played this game mode in perticular that much however i have played it a bit and probably enough to review it.In my opinion this is pretty boring and it is quite like TTT but worse.You mostly just sit there helpless as a bystander until a murderer murders you.If you are lucky to get a special class (murderer or bystander with gun) you might actually have a semi-good time playing, murdering helpless people.It does get boring after a bit even if you get murderer often and the gameplay is pretty much the same every time.

Prop hunt- Yet again another gamemode made popular by youtubes.The game is pretty boring,most players are hackers and just get you instantly or you or someone in your game will just sit there as a tiny can in an OP spot for 10 mins until the round is over and then it happens all over again.It is better with friends but still pretty boring.
3 / 10

After months of waiting, the Nintendo Switch is finally here, boasting a hybrid design that’ll provide both console gaming and on-the-go gaming with a single console. Is Nintendo’s upcoming console something you should get excited about, or is it full of gimmicks? We've spent a couple of weeks playing with the Switch to find out. Here’s our Nintendo Switch review.
The Nintendo Switch has finally arrived, with a price of £279, and is available to order now from the official store and retailers such as Amazon, Gamestop and GAME. It's $299 in the US and although there seems to be a fair bit of negative reaction to the price, we don't think it's too bad - especially if you consider that the console could potentially replace your 3DS. Also, let's not forget that Brexit has been driving the price of many tech products up so this might also be a factor in the UK pricing.
For £279 you get the main console, the dock, a pair of Joy-Con controllers, a Joy-Con grip (to connect the controllers together), wrist straps, an HDMI cable, and AC adapter.
What is a little bit disappointing is the price of accessories, because for starters an extra pair of Joy-Con controllers will set you back a whopping £74. One on its own is £43 and you'll need to buy wrist straps at £4.99 each to avoid your TV getting smashing from an airborne accident. An extra charging grip for the Joy-Cons is £25, while the Nintendo Switch Pro controller is priced at £65.
Read next: Best games console of 2017
Nintendo Switch review: Design and build
The new Nintendo is like no other console we've seen before and is a little hard to describe in terms of design. That's because the Switch has been designed so you can use it in various different ways, not just as a box that plugs into your TV and stays put.
TV mode
The main part of the device is essentially a tablet, so requires docking to turn into a console you play on the TV, hence the 'TV mode'. Other modes are 'Handheld' and 'Tabletop' - see below. Moving the tablet in and out of the dock is easy, and you can even do it mid-game without pausing if you wish - it only takes the console a second to switch the display between the tablet screen and the TV.

OK.  I'm a huge fan of Civilization (including this newest edition) but it is going to take a very solid expansion and some AI corrections for me to say that it is better than Civ 5. The only additional item I would add to his list that absolutely must be corrected is to bring back the Hall of Fame.  If there is no way to save my scores/results for posterity, then I have less incentive to continue to play the game after I've completed it once or twice.  Which brings up another good point:
On the standard setting, I still found Civ 5 to be very challenging.  With Civ 6, I'm some kind of Civ superstar because I can guarantee a victory every time.  Perhaps the game designers meant for this to be the case to make it easier for beginners to get the hang of the game.  Perhaps when I jump to higher difficulty, many of the AI weaknesses will go away.  I'll cross my fingers and give it a try.
But for those of you migrating from Civ 5, don't delete your history.  If the expansion doesn't correct a lot of this stuff, you'll find yourself going back.

This will be a longer review...
Telltale games has done it again with their second season of The Walking Dead video game series.  This time around, you play as Clementine, and the old protagonist has since past and it is time for her to move on.  I quickly joined on her adventure when I was given a Steam Card for Christmas (Thank you, Grandma! :D) and I went in as soon as possible, literally shaking with excitement!  The first episode, "All That Remains" takes off with a shocking start; and it doesn't get any better from there, as you play on, Clementine goes through all kinds of grusome and grim shist, and now that you are no longer protecting her as Lee Everett, Clementine must learn to take care of herself in a world where the living may be more monsterous than the dead.  If I have to find one bit of critique in this game, it is some of the choices: The choices were difficult to make, but they were a different kind of difficult: I wasn't torn between two choices; I knew which choice I was going to choose, but it really sucked making the choice.  Both of the choices suck, but one just happened to suck less than the other.  It leaves a bad taste in your mouth afterword.  I don't mind those kinds of choices, but those were most of the choices based in "All that Remains".  I want more decitions that leave me torn and questioning the choice that I made.
Anyway, that was the review.  On this episode alone, not counting other episodes, I'd give this a 7.75/10.

Life is Strange is to it's core a choice based adventure game lowkey inspired by the non stop sucess of telltale games. However in my personal opinion I believe that Life is Strange is the best of its genre. This game really drew me in as soon as I hit the loading screen. The main menu theme alone could carry a mediocre games soundtrack and help to set a decent scene. The full soundtrack however is a masterpiece of music creation and selection which is one of the primary reasons I feel that this game is so captivating. The phenomenally voiced characters and the interesting, somewhat branching storyline really drew me into the world that the creators were intending. My favourite voice actress in Ashly Burch is one of the main focal points of the story with her excellent voicing of the character Chloe Price, one of the most amazing characters in all of gaming (in my personal opinion). I have already pre ordered the deluxe edition for the sequal (Before the Storm) and i suggest you do the same!

Do they even test these games anymore?! Buggy, unbalanced, shallow. I've loved Civilization sice the first generation, but one week into this new adventure and I'm already bored.
The problem as I see it is that Firaxis is not learning from their own history.  Civ V vanilla came out and it was unbalanced, buggy, lacked depth... all in all, not nearly as good as Civ IV plus the expansions.  And guess what, the same thing has happened in CIV VI.  It took two expansions for Civ V to become a good game and several mods for it to become a great game.  So why didn't they learn their lesson from their own previous expansions?  Similarly, why didn't they incorporate elements from the most successful mods into their new game?  They ignore their fan base, they don't test their games, they give us half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥released... this was a money grab pure and simple.
I see a lot of people saying "wait for the expansion" or "don't worry, a mod will fix that" -- shouldn't the onus be on Firaxis to release a full gaming experience?  Furthermore, why are we depending on UNPAID modders to fix the problems of an expensive triple-A game title?  For $60 I expect a fairly high-end (polished) game.  Civ V changed a lot of things from the previous version, so I can somewhat understand why it wasn't 100% on release... but Civ VI just feels like a really dull version of Civ V.  The removed a bunch of the depth that made Civ V great and only gave us a couple of game mechanics that seem like good ideas on paper but don't currently work together  to increase the levels of enjoyment in the game itself.
The game play is unbalanced, the graphics are a HUGE step backwards (looks like some freemium mobile game), the AI managed to get worse, the civs are boring, diplomacy is useless, religion is annoying... and basically it feels like they've nerfed most of the things that made Civ V so great.
"Wait for the expansions" how about wait for the bargain bin because right now this game is nowhere near where Civ V left off.
This game has a relatively steep learning curve, but in the right company with some extra time and excel sheets at hand a great deal of fun!

In my specific example I'm playing as China and in the game about 200 turns or so.  Everytime I click end turn the game crashes down to desktop. So I saw this game advertised free and decided to buy all five episodes at sale price, and I must say I felt instantly connected with the story. Suspenseful, wonder and thrill of how each choice would impact the story and finally having completed the playthrough, I will say I do recommend the game in whole. The first Episode is only a piece to this greater whole. While I felt a little let down with the final chapter, it overall was an amazing play, and I wasn't expecting some of the outcomes of the plot. What seemed to be at first a simple college drama turned into something much bigger; and while it may seem confusing some of the reasonings of how time-manipulation works, It's story, emotional strings and impacting choices do make it a truly great addition to any game libary.
Decently simple, the puzzles as few there are, are not so complex. My only dissapointment is that the game is WAY Too forgiving for errors; there is no real 'game over' loss and it does take away the need for any real "Reload to checkpoint". Any actual 'bad/premature ends' for the main character only triggers a 'freeze frame' to unwind with little consuqence. It does take away some of the "worry" for messing up and just go through with the focus on decisive choices regarding dialogue and pathways. My only last con that dissapointed me was the endings; and while I won't spoil the game, it feels as if either a sad or rushed presumptive negative-bad ending occurs.  It has deep meaning regardless.
Despite the cons, really great game and I enjoyed the hours spent viewing and exploring, getting to know Arcadia Bay and it's inhabitants as well their story.

If ever there were a perfect "mixed bag" game, this is it.  It's largely fun, profoundly nuanced in prose and gameplay, deep in many places, cleverly balanced between victory conditions, and well intentioned.  It's also unprofessional and clumsy in interface, decades behind pace in AI, and thus so maddeningly frustrating in execution.
Good:
1. You are not forced into any "best" pathway.  You can conquer, evolve, abstain, abscond, or simply be bolder and more interesting.
2. The power evolution of units and technologies feels seamless and intuitive.  Governments beget improvements which beget technologies which beget more advancement and new governments.
3. Turns pass quickly, even with many nations and large maps.  Things progress quickly if you set them to resolve that way.
4. Multiplayer games can be saved, resumed, and resolved at whatever pace is comfortable.
5. The gameplay is just fun.  I can't break down precisely why, but maneuvering to destroy your enemies or turn the tables is fun, whatever the arena.
Bads:
1. The user interface and reliability are just clunky.  You'll frequently be left in odd modes as a trader or settler mode doesn't exit correctly.  There's a hidden recalculation delay of several seconds after each policy change.  Crashing has improved, but is still an issue.
2. Unit pathfinding/making is horrifying.  As you attempt to march your unit a few spaces north, it might bizarrely march southeast toward a road (which is often maintained by a hostile nation).  Your control over your units is hypothetical and hopeful.
3. The artificial intelligence is just...  wow...  so very primitive.  No matter what the difficulty, enemies are completely erratic, avoiding obvious conquers while pursuing their clear demise.  Ancient era units are cultivated en masse, then lost in bold charges against tanks.  Settlers and builders are stockpiled then wasted.  Trades are offered and reoffered that either offer little profit or are simply nonsensical (you'll cheerfully ask me for gold and resources and offer nothing?  good call!)  For a game of this magnitude to have the worst AI control I've seen in the genre is...  just sad.  Whoever is responsible should be hiding right now.
4. Because of this, difficulty level in AI opponent is induced only through stacking the deck, as they receive free units and bonuses to production, combined with a "hate everything" attitude to ensure you don't keep the peace.  Games are still conquerable simply due to the lackluster unit management, but it's a frustrating endeavor.
5. Science cascades to everything.  Most any game is virtually over within 50 turns, pending dotting "i"s and crossing "t"s.  Once you hold a significant technological advantage, you are virtually impervious to hostile intent, allowing you to choose what form of immortality you wish to bestow upon yourself.
Net result:
A 7-ish fun game that will hopefully improve to recognize its 9.5-ish potential.
The prose is great.  The depth is there.  The content guys have filled the world with magic, if sparse in some places.  The systems guys have not yet caught up to the level necessary to honor it.  But that's fixable.

The Walking Dead Season 2 continues a short time after the events of Season 1, but this time, you play the role of Clementine instead of Lee.
Season 2 continues with the same cell-shaded art style and narrative-driven formula that Telltale has used with Walking Dead Season 1.  There were some minor interface changes that improved the experience and felt very good once getting used to them.  Also Season 2 did appear to make it a point to get right into the action with a little less focus on the down time.  The tone of the game remained very much like that of Season 1.  Even though you are playing as the 11 year old Clementine, Telltale did not hold any punches in the story and many of the situations that you are placed in can be very unsettling.  I could definitely see the difference in the character, and how she has grown as a survivor, with all of the innocence of a normal child her age long gone.  Just like in Season 1 you just don't know whether the living or the dead are the bigger threat to you, and there are a couple of really heartbreaking moments right out of the gate.
Decisions from Season 1 and the 400 Days DLC are imported if you choose and the events of Season 2 will be altered based on those prior choices.  While Season 2 can be started without playing the prior season, I highly recommend doing Season 1 first so that you have a better understanding of what is happening and to have your choices imported rather than being randomly selected for you.
And like Season 1, if you are an achievement hunter, it seems that the achievements will come simply by playing through the game, so it is very easy to get 100%.
The music sets the mood for the game appropriately.  And dang, that song "In the Water" that is played during the end credits...
Anxiously looking forward to the upcoming episodes for this season.

Kerbal Space Program (KSP) is a great game that I will easily recommend.
Those little Kerbals (cartoonish characters) often bring a smile to my face. Even the way they walk shows a humorous relaxed attitude to the aerospace discipline.

Steam says I have played for well over 100 hours, and yet I have only just achieved getting to orbit around Kerbin (the Kerbal home planet). This proves you don't have to rush to do fancy space manoeuvres to have fun in KSP. However, as the main point of KSP actually
space manoeuvres, you will notice that there is plenty of scope for good fun play time in KSP.
Even more flexibility (and fun) is available by installing free mods that will tweak the game play to your liking. At first I didn't install any mods because the game is already flexible and fun without them, but after I did install mods KSP became even more fun.
Edit: The game is now at version 1.0.5 and is without doubt one of the best games in my Steam library. If you see KSP on sale and haven't got it yet, go on get yourself a copy, I know you want to!

This is a spoiler-free review for Life is Strange.
If you like choice-based games that are more about narrative and emotional impact than AAA action sequences or "save the galaxy"-esque plot lines, you owe it to yourself to pick this one up at some point. Though imperfect, especially near the end of the series, this game got me invested enough in the characters that I got close to crying for about 5 minutes straight at one point. That's only happened once before, on a much longer series than this one, and despite the shorter runtime (or perhaps because of it) I felt the emotional gut wrenching was much more deftly handled.
The journey of the game is the best part, letting you grow with the characters and feel the everyday struggles as well as solving the "who's the big bad guy" mystery plot (which is in some cases the weaker part of the game). Many of the choices you're offered are left really ambiguous, with no right or wrong answer -- instead you're left prioritizing certain goals at the cost of some other objective.
Don't Nod also did a really good job on the overall ambience and more subtle storytelling aspects, giving me information and cues that I never consciously picked up on until I thought about it or talked about it with someone else later. That's narrative gold there, with the "show don't tell" method soaked in a lot of the world itself.
The poor parts are in some of the inconsistent graphics (which I can easily forgive) and the climax of the story and choices made (which left me dissatisfied). Without spoiling anything, I feel that the emotional climax of the story was in episode 4 and from there on it sort of sputtered the rest of its way downhill. I understand the studio's desire to make the story bigger and more profound, but it felt hamfisted and negated some of my favorite aspects of the game.
Regardless, I don't regret buying this game and I really enjoyed the experience. It's an imperfect game with its own pros and cons, but it delivered more than I expected in the end. I'll look back on this game with fond memories and that sad feeling that I'll never get to play this game for the first time ever again.

The art style and music is great, and the first 3 episodes did a good job providing the feeling of being around silly teenagers again. But the story went downhill real fast.
I was expecting a light hearted story about how a new adult girl learn about the beauty and strangeness of "life" after granted this special power, but all of a sudden the story just became lazy and cliche at the end of episode 4. By that I do not mean the minor choices do not matter in the endings, I'm totally fine with that; I do not mean plot holes with the details of the ability to carry things or stay in space, magics are plot tools at the end of the day; I mean the final resolution of all the conflict and mystery:
SPOILERS AHEAD!
A psycopath and a torture dungeon!
It's like you went to a sushi restaurant and the cook carefully selected the freshest fish and cut the finest part with the sharpest knife, then just roasted the piece and served with the most common hot chilli sauce, and A LOT. It might still taste not bad, especially if it's your first time trying hot chilli sauce, but really? A psycopath and a torture dungeon? And surprise! It's your least expected person because we've been misleading you all the way! And the girl you've been looking for? DEAD! And your friend? DEAD! Your original suspect? DEAD! Isn't this world unjust and cruel! And that's not enough! you have to repeat all these to everyone you meet so we get to remember them more clearly! Then we have some gimmicky nightmares (with awful pacing) for you! Much insanity! Such deep! And guess what's the ending? Right! You have to choose either your friend or a bunch of other people to sacrifice! Wow! I totally have never seen any of these plots in another 10 movies/shows before!
Can you maybe chill?
I get it, people love drama, people love intense conflicts, people love "deep and dark" stories involving real torture and real death. There will be a percentage of people find it "lame/unsastisfying" if the story ends with a peaceful resolution, but it will only be a problem if you fail to resolve the intenseness you built up (see the ending of Firewatch).
What did the first 3.5 episodes of Life is Strange build up? It's all casual, it's all teenagers being paranoid, David is not a bad guy, Nathan is just a kid with problems, the Vortex club is just kids trying to act up as adults, Frank was in love with Rachel and he loves his dog, Rachel might just be out of town for a better life. You just CANNOT follow all this up with a BAM! murder! BAM! torture dungeon! BAM! All those people are not bad guys because the real bad guy is someone we didn't give you any clue of!
I would rather the ending being it's all just teenager trying to be adults, which created all the conflicts and misunderstandings, and in the end it all resolved and Max grew up to become a batter person, they helped the town prepare for the tornado, then Rachel calls back from L.A. on a warm afternoon when people reuild their homes and we get a happy ending. I guess this wouldn't satisfy a real teenager. Or maybe it would. What do I know.
Edit: All right I'm back for more. I'm not against plot twist, but I'm against lazy and overused unoriginal plot twist that failed to resolve the build up throughout the story. I'm not aginst having some seasoning on my food, but I am against roasted samon with chilli sauce when I'm expecting sushi. Will sushi taste bland if you eat it without anything else? It might be for many people, and that's what the soy sauce and wasabi's for.
Psychopath&murder is the cheapest way to resolve a disappearance, just as rewind all to the beginning is the cheapest way to resolve time travel. You can literally slap these endings onto anything that involves a missing girl and some time travel, it just makes the story not special anymore. A cliche plot twist is worse than no twist for people who have seen similar stories 10 times before, it doesn't provide any excitement, and it puts all the previous build up to an abrupt end.
As I said, chilli sauce is not the only seasoning you can get for your food. There could still be plot twists in the end, it doesn't have to be a normal teeange drama at all. There's already TIME TRAVEL. This two words can create enough twist and conflicts that could be far better than the ending we have. I'm not a writer/cook myself, but I have eaten enough food to know this samon could be cooked a lot better.

Garry's Mod has a unique gaming experience which you won't find in any other game. Why? You create the experience.
-First of all, the game has thousands of addons on Steam Workshop that you can download and play right away! This is one of the if not the best features of the game.
-There are thousands of servers with different and very fun gamemodes. You will be seeing a list of servers when you select multiplayer, and as I said before; every server is a different experience. You can play on a Dark RP server, in which you become a citizen, mafia, or the law enforcement and roleplay with the others. Or, you can play Prop Hunt and have a blast trying to hide from the hunters!
-You don't need friends to have fun. This is a game where you actually can have fun without your friends. I'm not saying you wouldn't have fun with your friends but it will also be fun when you are alone. Also, you will be making a plenty of friends playing this game!
-The Community is not very good these days. Lots of kids are present and can be annoying at times.
-Not having a microphone is a disadvantage at various gamemodes. For example, you are playing in a DarkRP server and a mafia came and told you to give him all your money. He counts to ten holding a gun staring at you. While you are typing "I don't have any money man..." you are killed.
-I don't know for sure if this is a bad thing or not, but when you download a lot of addons, the game will be holding a lot of memory on your hard drive. A LOT OF MEMORY BELIEVE ME.
-It can be hard startimg private servers to play with your friends. You need to have Hamachi to do so. I don't know if there has been any update stating otherwise, but back in the day it was like this. Also, you will need to download every single addon your friend has before joining which takes quite a time.
Hope this review has been helpful. I highly recommend this game if you have the time and patience to play it!

It has been widely reported thru the 2k and Steam forums that this problem is widespread, and none of the techniques provided fixes the game stopping issue.
This game is unplayable if you run into whatever AI routine is causing the game to crash. It might be several AI routines. 2k/Firaxis is not communicating any progress or when a patch can be expected.
I consider the game currently unplayable beyond turn 150 to 250. The 'next turn' crash is very serious. Many who have responded to forum threads that 'it doesn't happen to them' are now having it happen as well.

So how do I start this... (garrysmod player since 2009, played on a different steam account then lost it at a young age)
Oh god, 5231 hours later and I'm giving a review. Can't believe I didn't do this earlier.
Garrysmod is a game in which you create your own scenario; there isn't any rules or limitations to what you can do (at least in singleplayer, don't rdm in DarkRP lol).
Most of my time was spent in singleplayer, doing what almost anyone else does: stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'm talking about the fat gabens running around and BBQ'ing them with a flamethrower, and shooting melons with M4 rifles that try to attack and kill you.
GMOD 12 was the♥♥♥♥♥♥for a long time, then came GMOD 13. I thought everything would come to an end because, there was no toybox, and almost every GMOD 12 addon broke. However, the opposite has happened, and I started to realize that pretty fast.
When Garry switched to the STEAM Workshop, I saw huge improvements in what was avaliable to me. I noticed that I didn't have to manually go to a website and drag + drop files. Plus, if something broke my game I could just disable or uninstall it with the click of the button.
It brings tears to my eyes when I see all I've done in this game.
You may look at me and say, "Gee, 5231 hours, ♥♥♥♥ing addict" To that I'd say, you're probably correct. This addict has found more pleasure in that 5231 hours than he has in almost any other game.
God, I just wish I discovered the game yesterday so I can re-experience it all over again.
So go ahead, the game is what you make it! Buy it! You will not regret it.

At the moment I wouldn't recommend the game.
It is enjoyable until the fundamentaly bad AI becomes all to pervasive.
Its great the way the have included parts of different DLCs into the main game, but then have written such appalling AI that they don't work properly.
Main parts of the game that really don't work properly are :
Religion - The AI gets so much piety that it can spawn continual religeous units when even if you build wonders and holy districts, you are struggling to recruit enough to keep your lands safe.
Warmongering - Only way to not get everyone to dislike and denounce you is never go to war, or be attacked yourself. AI can declare wars against you constantly and suffer very few penalties. Even if you are in a denfensive war and take no cities you are labled a warmonger (though this decreases quickly if you take no cities) but if you take one city then dimplomacy is basically broken for the rest of the game. Even if they hate the person you took the city from, you will be denounced as a warmonger.
Nation Diplomacy Interactions - Asking nations to stop spying, converting your cities, or settling near you is pointless. They might say they are stopping, but in reality they will break them all the time, constantly and without any recourse. You don't gain a casus belli, they don't take any diplomacy hit with other nations, nothing. Might as well not be in the game.
War : Other nations AI is just plain stupid. You can pretty much take eveything with 5 or 6 troops as long as you balance them right. Once you have tanks and artillery, and corps and armies, you only need three, 2 artillery and an army of tanks (3 units stacked) and you can just go from city to city and take them all on anything but the last few difficulty levels. The AI hardly upgrades it units, runs away all the time. When they do actually attack they mill about round the outer edges of you city and are easily picked off by city defenses and ranged units.
Units and Research - They have streamlined the units tree and not for the better. Its so short now you can get late game units to soon in the game. Research can be completed way to early. I am not a great player and have completely finished research in 1820s. I don't like the unit progression tress much either. They have only made small changes but those missing units have made a world of difference in how your units upgrade and the feel of travelling through the millennia.
UI - Not great to be honest. Looks ok, functions less than well. Compared to the last versions of Civ 5 its a big step backwards. As an edge screen scroller its even worse. Mouse clicks unresponsive, hidden away functions and general poor layout. You get used to it, but doesn't make it good.
Map generation : This is probably the biggest bugbear of mine. There is very little diveristy in maps through the options and when they are generated they look bland. Dont get me wrong, when a big city is built it looks great. I am talking about the landscape itself. there are far to few tile paints. You just get huge swathes of exactly the same tiles with no diversity at all. You now can't build wonders on mountain tiles either which is very disappointing and aesthetically displeasing. Mountains look good, but hills and especially rivers dont look great. Resources paints on maps also leave a lot to be desired. Some look good, some look awful, a right mixed bag.
Resources - Unit upgrade/build (strategic) resources have been fundamentally changed. When they spawn, good luck finding them and anywhere close to your civ. I have seen 3 continents without coal at all. Really? Thats like Europe and Russia having no coal at all in the real world??
Good news is they will fix the majority of these "features" if passed games are anything to go by. Its an average release which will become more annoying the more you play. I have over 1000 hours played on Civ 5, it will take a fair bit of patching until I will get that many hours with this game.

Where to start.
I started with this game in early access.   At the time it was relatively simple.  And progressively it has gotten more complex.
It will not hold your hand.  You will blow up.  Many times.  And it won't be because of the game settings, or difficulty, or game balance.  It will be your fault, and you will know it, and you will curse and curse for hitting the wrong button in the sequence at the wrong time, and losing sometimes an hour of gameplay.
All that said, I don't think I've had this much fun with another game - and I've played games for a while.  Because, for all the failures - the triumphs are equally yours.  That misstep with tapping a button at the wrong time? The feeling when you recover from it by setting a parameter on a hunk of metal plummeting through the atmosphere and heating up when you've got seconds to get it right - and it works, and the crew not only survives but comes in for a nice, soft landing...
I haven't had that with any other game.
You will learn orbital mechanics, at a basic level.  You'll have to - if you ever want to land on the Mun, or set up something in orbit of another world...
And I don't play with any of the myriad of mods that are available, which extend the gameplay...

As someone who has spent countless hours (thanks, Steam counter, for making that irrelevant) playing Civ 5, there doesn't feel like enough of a change between the two games in regards to gameplay, to make me want to play 6 over 5. The differences in the tech trees and civic trees are different enough to be interesting, but not different enough to make me want to re-learn a whole new system. That, and the "round vs. truncate" movement system change makes moving units seem painfully slow.
I approached the more cartoony-style of design with caution, and it feels like that just takes away from the immersion of the game that you're taking one city from scratch and turning it into the civ that conquers the world. The art of the map is a nice touch, but from a tactical standpoint it's very difficult to look at the world map and tell what's land, water, undiscovered, etc.
I so wanted this to be an improvement over Beyond Earth, but it feel like the series has only taken a baby step since then.
In the end, Civ 6 makes me want to do nothing more than play Civ 5 more. Can I aptly say that this game is worth playing or not for someone new to the series? I really don't know.

Civilization VI takes all of the expansions of Civilization V and builds further on them--however--there are a few mechanics that require some further development.
First, I must say that I am very impressed with the direction the game has gone and the Devs have done an excellent job making a great base. To remain brief the best building blocks fo the new game are districts, new population limits (no longer global happiness, but local needs), more distinct civilizations bonuses (leader bonus, civ bonus, and two uniques), agendas, espionage is more flexible, new religoius victory, and many other things.
Here is what I would like to see fixed: Diplomatic victory and world congress/UN. I really enjoyed this in Civilization V. It made the world much more globalized. I would also like to see Ideologies create pacts and alliances. I think the sky is the limit with the current diplomatic base setup--but currently it's irrelevant and I would like to see this change.
I simply turn off the automatic unit cycle. It will often cycle twice and instead of marching one unit forward, it will change to another unit commanding it to go there, making for all sorts of frustrating situations.
I want to be able to put a hotkey on anything--even if there is not one assigned default. But if I had to choose--I like the grid (G), the yields (Y), and the resource (ALT+R) to have nice toggles as such. If I am not mistaken, you cannot even assigns these hotkeys now.
The announcements are buggy and tiny. I think they would benefit if larger (like in CIV V) and would actually show you a notification when you hover over them. Also, old news will come up frequently, even if I deleted it prior.
Please, if you are going to assign these agendas... make them reasonable. Don't let France hate me before I can even spy for example.
Trade system is broken. It would be good to have a not in civlopedia of how to measure what something is worth or perhaps this can become a new dynamic with trade. If there are more harvested luxury resources of a certain item, perhaps the cost of it drops, etc. This could be the next building block of economy (built on the already powerful, simple, and fantastic trade system)... Also, I have not checked, but is there a way to have you traders escorted... I will try this but that could be useful at times (wars in particular or far reaching settlements where the barbarians suddenly pop up and plunder your trade route).
Instead of groveling for the AI's love all the time with the new diplomatic system--perhaps you can create an agenda for the player also that leads to specific bonuses that aid in your agenda. This will allow the AI to have incentive to find out what that is to block you or perhaps aid you. This way--the AI can put something back into the relationship! It's a two-way street guys!
All-in-all an amazing game. I did not touch on how much I enjoy the game and all of the old and new aspects of it, but I was hoping to put some of my greatest nit-picking thoughts out there for the possibility that they will be heard or used. Cannot wait to see what expansion they have in store!

You will learn orbital mechanics, at a basic level.  You'll have to - if you ever want to land on the Mun, or set up something in orbit of another world...
And I don't play with any of the myriad of mods that are available, which extend the gameplay...

I've played Civilization for 25 years, since the first one, and have now played (a mere) 36 hours on this version, enough for complete play throughs on Prince and King levels. I tried one on Emperor level, but got hemmed in early by a much larger opponent and just couldn't catch their huge headstart. I'm ok with that.
In a nutshell, Civ 6 is a great game.
The graphics are a little cartoony and sometimes the screen is a bit cluttered with colorful images, but once you get used to it, it is not a problem.  It does require a bit of zooming in and out at times, but the animations are good and it's quite entertaining watching the little battles.
The new systems in Civ 6 are generally very good.  I won't list them all as that's been done, but overall, there isn't any of it that I dislike and most are good improvements. In particular, the new approach to cities and traders who build roads when they create trade routes are great additions. The idea of roads arising from trade is just so historically correct that I wonder why they didn't think of it sooner. It makes trade a strategic consideration, building roads between your cities and to your next victim.
I have taken a good look at the AI - which has recieved a lot of hate. Generally, I like where they are taking it, with leaders having their own priorities. It makes them feel like they have at least some personality. You pretty quickly come to realize who likes what by their messages, which is fine.  The weakness of the AI is that it is reluctant to declare war on you if you are strong, and seems unable (at this time, Dec 2016) of forming an alliance against you, even when everyone hates you. It means you have to initiate war against weaker adversaries.  It's a little bit of a downside, but it's not the disaster the haters are saying, and a small tweak will fix this, so don't worry about it.  If you really want to be fighting for your life, play Emperor level then try declaring on a stronger opponent.  You'll only do that once.
Espionage still seems a little weak to me and needs work, but it's not bad, just of only moderate use.
Offseting the more cautious empire AI are the barbarians, who are very aggressive and can jump you from the rear while you are fighting elsewhere.  Fighting barbarians, particularly early on, is quite fun. They have some intelligence, in that they scout first. When their scout sees your city, he runs away, to go home and tell his big brothers where you are. A few turns later, the barbarians come calling, and keep coming. So seeing a barbarian scout is a warning of what is to come. Kill him before he escapes to buy time. Again, I quite like the challenge they pose, as they can really wreck your day if you're not careful.
Perhaps the idea as to balance aggressive barbarians with cautious civlizations?  If so, the balance is not quite right yet.
In terms of diplomacy, the system is ok.  The idea of having a casus belli (ie. a cause for war) is a good one and means you need to think about diplomacy more strategically. Being a kean EUIV player, I like this side of the game.  If you do it right, you can minimize Warmonger penalties, especially late in the game when you have more casus belli options. People who complain that they are getting massive warmonger penalties unfairly haven't bothered to learn how diplomacy works.
My score: 9/10
Once they tweak AI aggressiveness a little, this could well be a 10/10 game. I will certainly be playing it for years to come.

Life is Strange is a game that doesn't favor the narrative over the characters, or the graphics over the gameplay...or any usual breakdown that you can offer to a game.  Even after finishing it, stopping only in my playthrough to go to work and sleep ( and even those were dogged choices ), I'm not sure if I can CALL it a game, as I'm still so thoroughly ensnared within this world and the characters well past the 'FIN', and I feel like there will never be a time that I forget the sleepy town of Arcadia Bay and the residents within.   So nothing on graphics or sound, on art or voice acting...this game is all about the story.
And this story...no...this EXPERIENCE is exactly why I play games, and have been playing them since the Commodore 64, and why I will never stop playing them.  DontNod has created a masterpiece that leans more as 'art' than 'game', without starting the whole 'video games are art' dialogue, because never before have I been so moved and INVESTED in the personalities played out before me on-screen.  In the end I love and sympathize with every character, every voice and genuflection of dialogue, the style they dress in and the way they situate their bedrooms or living spaces...never before has a 'game' had so much character itself, and that is why I absolutely love this saga.
At the end, there is a choice, a BIG choice as anyone can imagine, and I spent at least 15 minutes just sitting there and staring, afraid to commit, unwilling to give in one way or another.  The remains of my fingernails can stand testament to the power of this decision, but I made it....and, when it was over, I came back and made the other one though I still do not doubt the order in which I chose.
And yet...I don't know which ending is right or wrong?  If either of them can even be called one or the other?
There is a line when selflessness is as bad as selfishness, when you have to stop worrying about 'fate' or 'destiny' and just go with what YOU want.  And that is the real question to us all: how often does 'what you want' and 'what is right' really co-exist?
Life is Strange hands you so many questions throughout the 20+ hour journey, about morality and hope, about friendship and love, about destiny and commitment and confidence and, above all else, about choice.  Real choice, that can't be re-wound, and I found myself with answers I might not have come to on my own, to questions I don't even know if I would have asked...but I think I'm better for the experience.
And THAT is what makes this such an amazing game to me, and absolute treat to have endured.   It wasn't just an escape, it was a journey, and I have to give a big thank-you to DontNod for allowing me this pleasure.  It's hard not to sound like I'm attempting to wax all poetic, as it's been less than 20 minutes since I finished the game and I will admit I'm still riding that emotional rollercoaster, so I will end with a recommendation for anyone who inspires to love and learn in life to absolutely buy and play this game.  You will NOT be disappointed.
Thank you, DONTNOD for being visionaries.
Thank you Jean-Luc Cano for sharing your story with all of us dreamers.
And thank you Max Caulfield and Chloe Price, for showing me that true love transcends all boundaries, and that even in the harshest most dire of storms, somewhere else in the world, a butterfly will flap it's wings.

[Regards to episode 1] The story and gameplay in season 2 is more intricate and intuitive than that of season 1. It's as though the developers has taken in all the feedback and improved the previous gameplay mechanics and story[telling].
There are many more choices to be made and the game feels less straight-forward when it comes to decision making, changing a lot of the black and white decisions into a grey area; where there is no right or wrong, only what you feel you should do at the time. There's the ability to manipulate people through blackmail, or appealing to their humanity; or to completely ignore all contact and "go it yourself." Instead of interacting between one or two characters, or just simply finding about their backstory through dialogue, Clementine is able to eavesdrop on conversation to get an idea of what's going on, whilst also having the option to interact between half a dozen or so characters at once. Who you manipulate, help, ignore, the others will react. This part is the most interesting aspect of the game, as your options of who to interact with has been broadened in this season when compared to season 1.
Clementine is the main character this time around and she has grown quite a lot since season 1. Her experiences in season 1 remains with her throughout season 2, and you'll notice that through the dialogue and reasoning behind some of the choices she makes. She's a tougher, colder and less empathetic on the outside, but through some dialogue you can still see some of the purity that's left within her.
On top of the 'mash Q to do something' and 'click this zombie before it bites you' mechanic, the game has also introduced a quick time event where you'll press up, down, left, right, true to on screen prompts, in order to dodge and maneuver around during a quick-time sequence. It's quite fun and fast paced and really improves the flow of the game.
A definite thumbs up; the only negative aspect of this game is the long agonising wait between episodes.

Coming from Civ 5 and previous civs the base game here is feature complete compared to the last games. However, there are a lot of negatives here that make this game not worth the AAA price they are asking.
The AI. It is atrocious, and is probably the worst AI I have played against on any strategy game(and I play a lot of them if you check my library). The AI does not know how to do diplomacy correctly, offering crazy things that make no sense. The AI does not know how to use tactics in war at all. They will send units towards your city and it may look overwhelming, but then half of them just spread out and go seperate ways for no reason allowing you to just pick them off. They try to attack your boats with their unit transport ships(this made me laugh). They will settle literally one tile away from the border of your city, and cram cities where they should not be(basically any space, even with no food).
The UI. The UI has a lot of little quirks and bugs that make it annoying to use. The main complaint I have(I can't believe it's not fixed after the first patch) is the alert system. I can go a few turns before I even notice an AI player is wanting to trade or demanding something. It just pops up a little bubble on the right-side of the screen. Also these little alert notices are bugged and you cannot remove some of them or click on them to expand them sometimes.
Bugs. There are to many to go over here, as I notice them nearly every play session.
Graphics. The mobile cartoon look is horrible, even though I don't really care about graphics much it is worth mentioning as they are worse than Civ 5.
Overall this game has potential to surpase Civ 5 in a few expansions maybe, but it will depend on how they patch the game. I don't see them making AI much better honestly(it wasn't that great in Civ 5 either). I will come back and update this review if I notice they patch out these issues, but as of this review the game is not worth $60. I would say it maybe worth grabbing it on a sale of 50% or more off.

After putting some hours into the game i think i can now actually comment on it.
And sadly this means that i cannot recommend this game in its current state (12-4-2016).
This doesnt mean that the game has no good points to it, because there are quiet a few. The music is nice except for the menu music - that one is awesome. The graphics are a matter of taste obviously, but i found them to be nice to look at - which is important when a game takes such a long time. And of course its a civilisation game - so a lot of concepts are in the game just as expected. Oh yeah, and it is surprisingly enough fun to play in spite of its shortcomings.
So why not recommend it ? Simply put - with a pricetag such as this product has its flaws are - in my eyes - unforgiveable.
Exiting the game after playing for "too long" (time would have to be estimated) it will just not terminate and either force you to restart your computer or find a workaround to kill the game process. Bugs like that are major things that had to be known prior to release.
And then we get to the "design choices" that are seriously impeding the fun for me.
Like denouncing. You will get denounced by 70% of all civs for about 70% of the game (totally not made up numbers). For just about everything. You are a warmonger. Or have a different government. Or you have no spies in the ancient era. Or too little territory. Or to big of one. It actually doent matter - its the favourite past-time of the ai.
Like the warmonger concept itself. Declare war on someone ? Warmonger. Get declared on ? Warmonger. Take a city ? Warmonger. Raze a city ? Guess for yourself. Do something like that (or have it done to you) and you are a warmonger. Forever. I think its like a certifikate of participation. Everyone gets one. No idea what it should accomplish, but as of now its just a reason for getting denounced. Not that the ai needs any reason for that.
Like the religion thing. Doesnt work at all. The ai send myriads of religious units over the map in order to do some sightseeing i guess. Because theres not too much conversion happening while they stroll around your country happily blocking the way for anyone. There even was a war where one ai declared on me and then couldnt get any units through the clump of religios desaster that Pedro had seemingly exiled into my country. I think our armies fought each other via radio using harsh language until in the end Pericles payed for peace. Obviously it was the religious system at work here. Following the ai logik the best use for inquisitors is to round them up, herd them into enemy territory and then sacrifice them by attacking an obviously way superior unit - thereby eradicating any trace of the corresponding religion in the area. I can only guess the design process involved a lot of "praying that it works".
Like the missing balance of science/culture points and corresponding techs. where you more or less have to spam future techs from 1950 onward. If you were lazy on techs, that is.
Like diplomacy. Its basically not there. The ai cheats at every opportunity. They get bonuses like no tomorrow. Sadly they also get "agendas" to determine whether they like you or not. They might like cultured civs. That means not you because of their headstart you are pitiful to them. They might like civs with lots of territory. That means not you because of their headstart you have only a third of their land. If youre lucky. And due to this they basically hate you and it only gets worse from there. Did i mention they will denounce you ?
I could go on and on, but that would not achieve anything here. It seems as if almost any concept in the game is only halfway there. And more or less untested. I guess the playtesters were actually playing another game and noone noticed. This game needs a lot of work to be good, because the framework is actually here. But it is really not ok to sell this mess at a pricetag that high.
And that is why i advise to not get this game now - but maybe keep an eye on it.
Hope this helps at least someone out there.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 by TellTale Game's is a very much appreciated sequel to the riveting masterpiece that was Season 1. What is the fate of Christa and Omid? Your dearest Clem?
Walking Dead Season 2 has a lot of similar aspects to Season 1, but with a better UI, graphics, and just about everything. Dialogue feels more fluid, and controlling Clementine is quite enjoyable, and you'd be surprised at her bravery. Overalll, Walking Dead Season 2 is a great sequel that left me wanting more. If you've never played Walking Dead, buy the first one, and if you enjoy that, definitely this!
If you have played the first one and you liked it, you'll definitely like this.
SPOILER REVIEW
Walking Dead Season 2 opens up with Clem walking with a pregnant Christa and a still cheerful Omid. Omid tells you to clean up, and as your in a bathroom cleaning up, a scavenger walks in and steals your gun, threatening you. Omid comes in slowly, and as he approaches your assaliant, the door shuts making a loud noise. The scavenger turns around and promptly shoots Omid in the chest.
Christa comes in and shoots the scavenger dead. Bestowed with dreadful grief.
A year later, you and Christa are in a forest, and suddenly when Christa goes out to find wood, she becomes captured by bandits.
This is the setup for Season 2, and it is as riveting as it is tearjerking.
The story continues on, but I wish not to explain all its anomalies for they differ from your choices, as do all TellTale games...
This Episode seemed to merely set up the plot, and I actually found myself missing the locales of Season 1. Hopefully though, maybe we can meet some old faces. So go ahead, the game is what you make it! Buy it! You will not regret it.

When you play Kerbal Space Program, you find yourself becoming one of two types of individuals.  Either you throw everything together and make things up as you go, or you spend equally as much time planning for a mission as actually flying it.  Either way, mission success (whatever you define that to be) is always either painstakingly earned or astronomically lucky (pun intended).  It's very hard to compare to the feeling of seeing a safe splashdown after one of your Kerbals (the characters that man spacecraft) has walked on the surface of another celestial body.  It's also hard to compare to the humbling feeling you get when you've made it halfway across the Kerbol system after significant planning and execution time only to realize that you left your landing legs at home.
This game will frustrate and exhilarate you.  Well worth the purchase.

So here's the thing. All of the negative reviews on here definitely have good reasons for their negativity. The AI diplomacy is absolutely horrific, the warmongering penalties are outrageous, and (although the agenda system is great) it's painfully difficult to make allies or friends in the game.
BUT that being said, I have to recommend this game. First off, it's still early which means the patches, updates, all that jazz will be coming out in due time. Second, even with all of the issues the game is -still- fantastic to me. I've always loved Civ not because of the wars, but because of the building and structuring of an empire. The district mechanics make it fantastic for that, because some cities you may specialize in trade, other cities production, some cultural, etc. It actually lets you build an empire in a semi-realistic manner. From exploring to colonization to the Space Race, this game makes it so much fun if you're more of a "builder" like me.
So for me, I recommend this game because of the empire building. Even with the issues currently, I recommend buying it because I have no doubt that the issues will be fixed in due time.

I have spent literally thousands of hours playing Civilivation games starting with the first release. I really like the progression of the game through the decades, but I feel the latest installment lost a few "lessons learned" from past games.
Likes. The split trees of advancement for social and education. Brilliant. How it affects units, buildings, governments is "spot on". The fact that certain "prerequisite" are required for wonders. Awesome, the only thing I like to see is a bonus build percentage for the actual civilivation who built it (to give the civilization histrical credit) Ex. Pyramids (2x build speed for Eqyptions). Theological combat. Still gives the thrill of battle without losing all of your advances in diplomacy, as long as you don't take it too far that is.
Dislikes. The Tech tree. Having to scroll through it is a pain. The previous trees were way better in this regard. Theology overlays. Way too hard to see what is underneath when moving clergymen. Graphics. Interesting. I wonder what the actual target demographic for this game is now.  Info panels. Not having the columns "sort" the information from low-to-high, high-to-low is a pain. My biggest "pet peeve" is doing away with the initial location "reboot" and having to reload everything in the main menu until I don't get Montazuma starting his civilization in the middle of the desert. Also having to rechoose EVERY aspect of starting a game (ex. difficulty, leader, map size, etc.). Also why can't "chained" units "auto explore" together? It seems a natural fit to have a land combat unit linked with a exploring sea vessel. Historically this is accurate as well. Remember the Conquistadors? Units. It took me forever where to find the unit list without the Military Advisor. For those who never have found it, click on a unit's name. Not showing a unit's move length in other player's territory. Not showing an artilliary or air units attack range.
Overall, I recommend this game. Realistically, I am thinking of returning to Civ V for my Civ "fix".

Rarely has a game drawn me in so much in the "feels" department than this series did.  I played the free Episode 1, and then just
to purchase the others to see the rest of the story.
Game controls and mechanics work wonderfully well overall, and don't detract from the storytelling.  There's no "grab every item you can, then mindlessly try every item to see what works" in this game; each item you do collect has an immediate purpose, and when you do have to go through your inventory of documents/photos (and it isn't often) there's a clear reason and you know exactly what you're looking for.  The time-rewind is fun, and reminds me of when I used to read Choose-Your-Own-Adventure books when I was a kid; I would bookmark each choice and go back if the choice I made wasn't good.  The rewind here is also used to good effect in numerous other situations apart from dialogue choices.
As to the story itself, this is a very well-written game.  Multiple times I had chills from the story's twists, and the music adds to the effect.  It's a short game, easily completed in a day, but you still want to go back and see "what-if" on some decisions as well as complete all the photo ops you can.
I would have liked more from the endings, and felt the first ending I chose was lacking in the completeness department, but this is still a game I'm glad I played.

As someone who has been playing the entire I - VI  Civilzation Franchise including Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri and Beyond Earth, I think I can have an accurate description of this games overall playability, based on where it is now and how it has developed over the years.
Pros
1.Districts make way more sense in building structures, and the ability to see the progress of the district is really cool.
2. Stunning Graphics and GUI that show progress of Wonder construction, various working visuals, and even fighter                      planes that circle their respective cities. This adds a much better feel to the idea of visual growth and accomplishment. You can actually see each building being built.
3. Trade Route flexibility - Including that Trade Routes make roads now. Pretty cool!
4. Unit Corps, the idea of combining multiple units into larger and stronger groups.
5. Religion System - Various ways to get Religion started and bonuses
6. Civics and Research walk on the same line, they both work like a tech tree and unlock things as you research them.
7. More accurate and flexible Governments.
8. Victory Buildings produce awesome clips, and offer many ways to win.
9. Diplomatic Options have become much more varied and easier for communicating with NPC Civs
10. Plenty of player Options and Civ choices.
Cons
1. Religion System, though cool has a lot of problems. I have had my empire overrun with neighboring Religious units that  somehow in spite of closed borders, can come through my borders, attack my Holy Districts, attack my Religious Units and somehow not delcare war? I've had to end Alliances between good NPC teammates because they would not stop coming into my territory to convert my cities. That is really irritating, and that is not accurate. Religious or not, if a country doesn't want you there, they will stop you, War shouldn't be the only way to get them to stop. Even the option where it says "please dont convert my cities" you have to click it an absurd number of times for him to actually agree to it, and when they do, they only listen for a few turns before you have to go back and ask again. Like I said, I have had to declare war on freindly neighbors cuz they just wouldn't leave my cities alone in their core Religion. That is the single most annoying thing in this game.
2. Spies - Spies are useful and can do lots of interesting missions, and its handy for them to be assigned to specific distrtics to keep other players from sabatoging, that makes sense. But, the length of time to assign a Spy to a district is like 5 times, and then you have to reset, and if you have like 10 Spies, that can get very tedious to have to keep resetting to guard a district from espionage, or a city, or whatever. It should be a permanent assignment until you wake them up, or until they are exhausted/killed.
3. If you choose Continents on the map style and Huge on the size, every single time, no matter how many civs are playing, one of them will be super close to you. You can't get a continent to yourself without conquering someone.
4. Towards the end of the game, depending on the size of your civ and how many other civs are playing, the other players' turns can take up and including 10 mins to complete one turn. I have an ultra fast gaming rig, and end game it still struggles to process fast enough to not be bored.
5. Haven't been able to play/find an Earth map.
All in all, I'd say this game is definitely worth the buy. I have been playing this franchise since the very first 1, and its been a long and impressive series. Except for Civ3, we don't speak of such things. In my opinion from best to worst, top to bottom are the better games of the franchise.
1. Civ 4
2. Civ 6
3. Civ 5
4. Civ 2
5. Civ 1
6. Civ 3
Civ 4 Had the best expansions, it was the most stable game. It introduced many of the elements that are still being used in Civ current games. It had the best functionality with multiplayer, and it still runs very easily on any computer these days.
Civ 3 was the worst of the games, because at a certain point in the game, it was damn near impossible to conquer another civ. With all the government and policies and expenses and the bugs that they never worked out, anytime you declared war on someone, somehow it was settled before any real damage was done, but I was never able to wage war on a civ for more than 10 turns before the UN stepped in and forced it, or until the game made building units harder and harder to upkeep. There were a lot of other isseus as well, but I honestly didnt play that game long enough to see the rest of it. The fact that I couldn't conquer is what♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
Other than that and these opinions, Civ 6 is definitely worth buying if you are a fan of the franchise and it will keep you entertained building you empire for a good long while. The new mechanics are intriguing and gripping. The playstyle is easy with a very low learning curve. If you are a fan of the franchise or new to the game, you will find Civ 6 to be one of the best Turn-Based Strategy games on the market.

I won't extend to much on this game. I think enough has been said already. Both story and storytelling are great, art direction is beautiful, characters are appealing, etc. It's obviously not perfect and got some flaws: bad lip-syncing, apparently some awkward dialogue (being a non-native speaker, I can't really tell), and some elements that doesn't seem to add anything to the game. Yet it's still an amazing video game that you should try if you haven't already.
But there's one thing you should know first: Life Is Strange is not fun. If you want to play this game like you would play Tetris or Street Fighter, then don't. There's no fun or complex mechanics, no QTE, no space-dragon-god-slayer difficulty mode. It's rather a fairly simple game. However, it doesn't mean gameplay is absent or insignificant. Quite the opposite actually: it's one of the most meaningful gameplay I've seen. Narrative and player's interaction are welded together. You're exploring the world at your own pace, progressing in the story alongside Max (the player's character), exploring the choices she has, the choices you have.
That's why it's the best game I've ever played, and that's why you should try it too, but only if you set your mind in the right state.
