48 hours and I'm tired of it, even though I've clocked hundreds upon hundreds of hours in Civ 3-5. That is bad for a Civ game.
It simply seems to have little in the way of new discoveries and the system of districts has the nasty side effect that you more often busy yourself with the internal affairs of your empire instead of exploring the world - which gets tedious and uninspiring after you've done it for a few games. Game mechanics like diplomacy, religion and spying feel chorelike. With the lack of map generation options, the crazy AI, the lacklustre rewards for expansion and exploration, the reduced need to find specific strategic resources, it all ends up being pretty samey. I can't put my finger on it but it also feels like the different civs are less unique now.
You'd think that focusing on internal affairs would be fun, especially for someone like me who really loves playing the turtle, but you will rarely find a game where an AI will not force you to war, either by settling ridiculously close to you or suicide attacking you. Want to focus a match on culture and science? Forget it, war it is. Want to be a reclusive island civ that colonizes the new world? Forget it, an AI will always spawn at a set distance from you. Want to be a glorious diplomat? Nope, the AI will hate you relentlessly. There also doesn't seem to be much of a way to get ahead without fighting - which gets boring if you've already played countless wars in Civ5.
I understand that they've tried to streamline the gameplay a bit, by reducing the different types of units you get through the ages, balancing starting map points more etc. but there's not escaping that this also makes every game more repetative. I prefer my Civ matches to be more assymetrical as it keeps the matches interesting and really increases the replay value. The lack of global happiness (Which was a stupid system in itself) and the addition of the generic entertainment complex now makes luxury resources seem to have much less of an impact on the gameplay - and the spawn rate of resources is less chaotic, which makes for finding especially interesting spots on the map for settling (and fighting over) incredibly rare.
There are many good sides to the game as well - but you can find those in the positive reviews. My hopes are that they'll turn this game around with a few wonderful expansions and patches. Until then, look for a sale to pick this one up. There still potential to turns this into a great game and I'll change my review if they do so.

In its current form, I cannot recommend this game. I want to, but I can't. There are just so many little annoyances that continue to add up until a game just isn't enjoyable unless you want to go for a domination victory with everyone hating you from the start, and even then its a push. Initially, it seemed great and after waiting so long for an actual successor to Civ 5 I was delighted, however the longer you play the game the more and more obvious issues got.
Big negatives for me are:
- AI - every game seems to choose to annoy you rather than play tactically. every trade deal was only a deal to the other nation, you could never get a favourable deal, or even a like for like swap in most instances like in Civ 5. If you are doing better than another nation, they will denounce you. Everytime. Without fail. Not only that but nations will go way out of their way, nearly half the map in one instance, to settle a new land beside you to box you in. This, coupled with not being able to ask nations to not settle near you until after they already had, meant that to expand you had one choice. war. Which leads to the next problem...
- War- this probably annoyed me most of all. There are now lots of different types of wars, each which add a little more diversity to how you conduct yourself around other nations. Surprise wars will gain you large warmongering penalties, but really these don't matter. If you have any warmongering penalty, everyone will treat you like an insane war lover. Even the nations that declared war on you and that you only fought back. If you are lucky enough to not have to fight them, rare but happened to me a few times, they will ask for peace, and throw resources and gold at you to accept. This happened to me quite alot, with nations going to war with me and after not even seeing one of their units, they would ask for peace and give me all their gold. While this was nice, it did end uip making the game very easy for a while, until everyone denounced me for warmongering.
- Barbarians - unlike Civ 5, it appears raging barbarians (were barbarian units and camps will spawn alot quicker) is always on. ths means that early game, especially on larger maps, you have to spend alot more of your time, building up an army to tackle the problem, as they will not relent in attempting to attack your cities and units. also, they will be more technologically advanced than you. making it very annoying trying to combat a couple of freshly spawned barbarian units that are oikemen while you only have warriors. If this was intentional, then fair enough, however the large amount of troops you need has another consequence. Nations will fear you, and then denounce you. meaning that any attempt to brefriend them is gone before you even had a chance to make it work.
Other than the above, I have had a few issues withcrashes changing civics policies later in the game, but I imagine these will be addressed sooner rather than later.
Hopefully, after another patch or this will become the game it has the potential to be, but at the moment, that looks a long way off...

Kinda ironic, but this is probably the most realistic space sim video game on Steam. Everyone's first personal objective is usually just getting a ship into orbit. It goes something like this:
1) Build rocket
2) Watch rocket crash
3) Build better rocket
4) Discover better rocket's worse
5) Build another better rocket
6) get a little high than your first attempt (still not in space)
7) Repeat steps 1-6 a few more time and by then you should get into space
This is a game with a steep learning curve. There are so many things about controlling your spacecraft, the physics of flying in atmosphere and in space, and how to make a spaceship that survives all of this.
Other forms of media LIED to you about how space travel is done. This game will take everything you know about it and kick its teeth in. You WILL suffer for a few hours.
You know what though? You won't care. You'll get that nagging desire to make a spacecraft that can at least make it to orbit. Once there you'll be trying to go to the moon (or the "Mun" as it is in-game). Then to Minmus, then to other planets. It's incredibly addicting, and with a modding community that only adds to the experience, you cannot go wrong with this game.
Buy if you like space sims, flight sims, physics games, or watching the video game equivalent of Minions running a space program.
It's terrific. You definitely want it!

The frustratingly anticipated sequel to The Walking Dead: Season 1, in which we, the players, now continue as the very much loved, resilient girl, Clementine. The first episode took me roughly an hour and a half to play completely through without replaying anything and for clarification's sake, the $25.00 you spend on it now is for all FIVE episodes, not just the first one, which puts each episode at a value of $5.00 each. The upcoming episodes are to be released periodically throughout 2014. Expect at least one month to two month waits in between each episode.
When I didn't think I could feel more on edge and distressed than I did while playing Season 1, barely five minutes into Episode 1 of the new season I was drop-kicked into the world of post-zombie apocalyptic tragedy and unpredictability. Telltale Games lives up to their over-the-top standard of true Adventure/Interactive Story, and you really feel like you are a part of the game - an intense story at that; One that, in this particular world, feels like it has no direction whatsoever because you as the player, know that anything, anything, could happen at any time, but yet you can also see that the developers have a deliberate and thought-out story laid out for our heroine, Clementine, in the fact that they already titled each of the 5 episodes, and show previews of what is to come, after each episode you finish.
With that, though they have the story laid out, it's the intention for the player to choose not so much where, but how and with which people, we get to the end of Episode 5 with. Just like Season 1, the things you choose to say, and do, stay with you, and determine how Clementine's story plays out and how the other characters interact with her. It's not just about Clementine. You can tell that the other characters, whether you come to like them or not, have their own interesting stories and backgrounds, as well, though not too much is made clear, and this series, as its well-known for, will leave you with questions and aggravating suspense.
The game does an good job of capturing a world well into its post-apocalyptic state, similar in ways to the world we saw in Season 1, but significantly different as well. Clementine is faced with more dangers than she ever imagined from other fellow living beings than from the dead. And with a pang of loss lodged deep into our hearts, we are given constant reminder of Lee, our unexpected hero and caretaker of Clementine from Season 1. After playing the newly released episode, I'd give anything for Clementine to be back there...it's shown me as a player, how much of a compass she was in Season 1. While everything else went wrong for Lee, at least there was one thing that was right; at least Clementine was there as a beacon of hope and goodness in this rapidly deteriorating world. But now, being Clementine on her own, it's hard to find that solid beacon of hope. Even in just the first episode of this new season, I found myself naturally desperate to turn to something good, an anchor of security. As I played through episode one, I felt a real sense of how precarious and vulnerable Clementine's situation was.
With that, the developers have done a good job so far in portraying the way Clementine is changing from living in this kind of world practically on her own. You can see she's hardening, she's growing up fast - too fast - and though it's necessary and realistic, it's also sad, too, because, as a player, a part of me wants Clementine to stay that innocent little girl. Already I found myself astounded at her capabilities, the choices you are able to make, and it's bittersweet all around.
So overall, is this game worth the $25.00, and months-long waiting intervals in between the episodes? I can tell you from my perspective that this game is and more, what it claims to be and that it is completely worth the money. Regardless of the complaints and bashing towards Telltale Games for their lack of communication and slow-coming release dates, I fully support and admire Telltale Games for the quality they put out and the story-telling they capture, so I bought the game at full price. To me, as long as they keep putting out that level of quality, I won't complain, and frankly I welcome them to take as much time for game development as they want. Whether the waiting is worth it is up to you. I simply couldn't wait to play it until all the episodes were released, so I purchased it now. Of course, there will be sales on it in the future, and if you're willing to wait, by all means, do. Save some money. But play this game. Whether it's now or later, play it, because it's a game worth every second and penny spent on it. It's a game you'll feel a part of, a game you'll remember. A game that'll make you think and gasp and scream and cry and cringe and rejoice and hate and love.

TLDR - Interesting choices with city building, good graphics.  But AI and diplomacy is broken.
I like the city districts and the strategic possibilities it entails.  But it feels like they spent all their time on that mechanic.
Imagine being invited by a nation to help them fight a war, and then get denounced by the SAME country as a warmonger for your troubles.  Imagine getting suprised attacked by a nation, defending yourself and taking one of that nation's cities in retaliation and being denounced as a warmonger by that nation and everyone else.  Imagine liberating a nation long-dead for millennia, no acknowledgment of thanks, and then being denounced by the same liberated nation as a warmonger.  Welcome to Civ VI, where you are hated no matter what you do.  And no matter what victory condition you start with, you always end up wanting to nuke the &*$@#^& out of the nations around you.  For the first time in all the Civ games I've played I wished there was an option to execute opposing leaders, that's how annoyed I got.  Ah to see the eternally annoying Phillip II lose his head, now THAT would be fun...
Wait there's more!  Imagine being asked for a gift of resources, plus gold, plus gold per turn.  You think to yourself, "I feel generous today" and offer at least the resources and the one-time gold, but not the gold per turn.  Well, these entitled♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥will tell you, "Not good enough!  We want a gift from you the way WE say it."  It's unreal.  So back to nuking them.  Honestly I cannot understand the thinking that went into the diplomacy, it's the worst I've ever seen.  It doesn't just feel unfinished, it's plain bad.  As usual your opponents get to say snarky comments and threaten and bully you and you get no options to respond.  This has been an issue for me in previous games too, but it's even more exquistely painful in Civ VI.
And the AI does ridiculous things like FLOOD your country with their missionaries and apostles, blocking your path and there's no option to even say, "Hey, can you relax with the religion thing?"  I had to declare war multiple times just so I could move around my own empire.  And of course, the flood of hate and denouncing hits you from all sides.  I played king level and at the end of the game city states still had warriors and even some nations.
This game needed way more playtesting.  I hope like other Civ games it improves with patches, but I'm not pre-ordering a Civ game ever again.

Kinda ironic, but this is probably the most realistic space sim video game on Steam. Everyone's first personal objective is usually just getting a ship into orbit. It goes something like this:
1) Build rocket
2) Watch rocket crash
3) Build better rocket
4) Discover better rocket's worse
5) Build another better rocket
6) get a little high than your first attempt (still not in space)
7) Repeat steps 1-6 a few more time and by then you should get into space
This is a game with a steep learning curve. There are so many things about controlling your spacecraft, the physics of flying in atmosphere and in space, and how to make a spaceship that survives all of this.
Other forms of media LIED to you about how space travel is done. This game will take everything you know about it and kick its teeth in. You WILL suffer for a few hours.
You know what though? You won't care. You'll get that nagging desire to make a spacecraft that can at least make it to orbit. Once there you'll be trying to go to the moon (or the "Mun" as it is in-game). Then to Minmus, then to other planets. It's incredibly addicting, and with a modding community that only adds to the experience, you cannot go wrong with this game.
Buy if you like space sims, flight sims, physics games, or watching the video game equivalent of Minions running a space program.

update:   Now that the final episode is complete I can say that the second season gets a mild recommendation. When episode 4's reviews came rolling in a month or so ago most people pointed out that no matter your actions, Sarah died, Jane left and all went to hell regardless. I think this is indicative of a small backpeddling of quality because really the game has always been like this - it's just been better of maintaining the illusion before now. TWD has always played out like a movie and the end of S1 was so emotionally resonant that you forgot you were really playing a game. You felt dignified in your choices because every one of them had you struggling because the characters had been given enough time to build up a certain amount of empathy necessary for text's drama.
It suffers from a sophomore slump and often forgets why its predecessor was so good to begin with - its all about the choices  - as well as leaving you with less of a finale than maybe was expected. I've also learned that these things are best taken all at once, and if I continue with season 3 I'll be waiting until all of it is available before starting.  Clementine continues to be the only reason to continue with the journey, and her growth is the heart of the game. And while she gets a little older here the game relies on romanticizing the past (in a flashback, of all the cliche things they could choose) instead of using it to remind the player of past choices and use that to propel the story. The final episode this season had me glued in some pieces, drifting away in others. More than that, I'm worried the developers are kinda stuck at where to take it next. If it all goes to schlock here we can at least rest on the fact the game had a strong second season and an amazing first one. Heres hoping they can keep the blood pumping next year.

I remember first watching the reveal trailer for Life is Strange (LiS) back in December 2014. A trailer I greatly enjoyed, and I was immediately hooked on playing LiS when it would be released. The trailer gave me vibes of both Alan Wake and Gone Home – two games I consider some of my personal favorites. I was therefore greatly anticipating the release of LiS in January 2015, and to my pleasure the first episode of LiS lived up to my expectations. After playing the first episode, I knew I wanted to know where this rabbit hole would end.
But then time passed. The second episode was released, but I didn't get around to play it. The time I did use to play games was spent on other games like Dragon Age Inquisition and Republique Remastered (two games I also enjoyed immensely in 2015).
Then in April 2015 GTA V was released for PC. I hadn't originally planned on playing GTA V – but after about two weeks I caved in to the hype and bought GTA V.
So I played GTA V for the next few weeks and I really enjoyed it from a technical standpoint. The world of Los Santos is realized in an excellent fashion – it is great fun to just explore and get lost in the city and its surrounding areas. It is hands-down one of the best realized open-worlds in gaming. Too bad that I didn’t enjoy the story that Rockstar wanted to tell in the open-world of Los Santos.
To me the existences of Franklin, Michael and Trevor are hollow, mean and just not that interesting – and perhaps that is the point Rockstar wants to make (i.e. chasing the American dream doesn't lead to happiness in itself – but that is another discussion), but as an experience the story didn't work for me. But in spite of this I still wanted to complete the game.
Then one evening instead of booting up GTA V, I decided to boot up LiS and play its second episode. I was completely devastated by it and emotionally drained by it – but in a good way. That second episode gave me one of the most moving and heart pounding end sequences I have experienced in a game. But it also made me realize something.
It made me realize that participating in Franklin, Michael and Trevor's humdrum of violence and apathy in GTA V had left me in a depressive and dour state of mind. Playing the second episode of LiS left me feeling moved and glad. It reminded me of why I love to play games – to have fun, but also to have an experience that moves me and makes me think and reflect on my actions taken. And oh my does LiS deliver in spades.
To me LiS is a celebration of humanity at its best – a celebration of friendship, love and kindness. Playing LiS simply made me glad that I am alive and able to enjoy life – when was the last time a game made you feel that way?
The three final episodes of LiS are also highly worthwhile telling a moving story of the evolving friendship between Max and Chloe, while trying to solve the mysteries of Arcadia Bay. The story held up all the way through with its twists and turns to its gut-wrenching and very poignant ending which left me in tears. A satisfying and very emotional ending to a great game experience. Today, a few days after (finally) getting around to finishing LiS, I still get tearful just thinking about the ending – LiS really made a huge impression on me.
In short LiS is a celebration of actually caring about the world you inhabit, the life you live and the people you share it with. A celebration of values that sadly are in short supply today where shortsightedness, cynicism, intolerance and selfishness are the order of the day . LiS was for me a unique game and a highly emotional experience that I will remember fondly. It was a needed reminder for me that the world is not all bad – is not all darkness, but that there are specks of light out there – the sparks of kindness, love and friendship.

See all those hours I have logged?  Yeah, some of those were from me falling asleep at the keyboard, but the rest are because the game is definitely that much fun.
This game is absolutely worth full-price.  It's only two downsides are how demanding it can be on system resources, and how much time you're going to sink into the game.
Too many sandbox games focus on destroying, but here is one of the few where you not only create, but have to be thoughtful and (reasonably) practical with what you create.
And you will learn.  The learning curve is pretty steep and can be incredibly frustrating, but stick with it.  It took me a week just trying to figure out how to create maneuver nodes (kinda like waypoints in orbital mechanics), another week to successfully get a ship into orbit, another week after that before I landed a spacecraft on the moon, and another week after that before I could bring that spacecraft back.
What I learned about orbital mechanics and rocketry actually helped me pass a physics midterm.
The modding community for KSP is also phenominal.  You can have a great time with the great diversity and variety you can create with just the vanilla, unmodded version, but each mod brings whole new, exciting, and often immensely helpful elements to the game.  They're also very easy to install (drag and drop into one of the game's main folders).  I think it can be argued that the mods and the modding community could be now considered half of the KSP experience.
I cannot reccomend this game enough.

I've largely enjoyed my time with Civ VI despite a few gripes here and there that I'll talk about below.
I played Civ V more than I played IV (and for about double the amount of time Steam says), and I prefer playing on Emperor-Deity level difficulties, if those bits of info helps anyone to understand or relate to my viewpoints on Civ VI.
Also important to add, I absolutely hated Civ V on launch (I enjoyed IV, but the series really clicked with me after Civ V BNW dropped) because it felt shallow and simplified with its lack of depth in city management and severe penalties to expansion. I think Civ VI has launched feeling mechanically complete - better than Civ V at launch, and I am beginning to think better than the V with its two expansions (though it could use some more civs and leaders, which I'm sure are in the pipeline).
I will probably edit this to make it a little more detailed later as I'm a bit tired, but here is a short list up front:
- Most of my gripes are about UI or bug problems (things that can be patched like not being able to sort trade routes by highest gold/production yield, the final upgrade for ranged units is bugged and allows a second attack regardless of whether or not the unit has moved, etc.) rather than core gameplay design decisions.
- The AI improved drastically with the last patch in terms of military strategy and modernization. I have seen AI wait outside of vision to ambush lone workers or units that mistakenly end their turn out of sight, and actually upgrade their ancient era units so long as it was economically viable.
- I don't think the diplomatic AI is as bad as everyone says it is, but it does feel a little wonky in terms of execution/clarity. For instance, many complain that they still get denounced for warmongering despite having been the targets of war. A lot of these claims, if further investigated, boil down to the player having killed/captured workers, settlers, or cities of the attacking civ after successfully defending. Actions that are recognized as violent/warmongering inherently because of their nature. The irrationality of some of the AI attitudes may seem frustrating at first but it mirrors how self-serving and seemingly irrational much of real world politics is (look at the U.S. election and Brexit). I will go more into detail on my feelings on the diplomatic AI later.
- I wish warmongering penalty severity changed the significance, rather than the duration, of being seen as a warmonger. I think this would clear up some of the concerns people have regarding the AI's response to offensive counterattacks, within reason.
- The new city-state system is much more enjoyable and impactful to play around, in spite of there not yet being a direct diplomatic victory condition. I hated how in Civ V it eventually just amounted to a gold sink.
- The districts, city projects system, and wonder and builder changes all have made city management have more depth than Civ V without the seemingly intimidating barrier to entry some thought Civ IV had.
More thoughts to come.

I know I'm a day late for this, but for starters, the popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions. Hope this helps!

After putting a combined 300 hours between Civ 4 and Civ 5, I just dont see how this is the best Civ game let alone game of the year? To begin, you simply can not suave over any AI. Going to war or trying to trade, almost all AI's end up denouncing you for one thing or another. Whether that be too little or too much expansion (under 25 turns mind that). You are guarenteed suprise war under 50 turns by atleast 2 AIs (Although a plus for game mechanics, the AI actually Attacks you..) Once a suprise war is declared on you, the AI is not penalized by any other AI for warmongering and is almost always friendly with every other AI. If you take just ONE city from an AI who DECLARED war on you, the game is over diplomatically. For you. This Holy War or Formal war, the penalties are most certainly not moderate but just as Egregious as "Surprising" your enemy. In my honest opinion, the AI mechanics are as sporadic and uncontrollable as Civ 2 back on Windows 2000. You simply cant talk to an AI.
Secondly, Im running an i6700k with 16gb ram and a gtx 1070 (on decent Max resolution but not ultra) and this game by turn 100 just slows... to crawl. Im talking 30 to 60 second turn time waiting After reading the forums and googling, it looks like im not alone.
Lastly, Religion has still not been ironed out fully but just expaned on since Civ 5. While i will give credit, they have come along way since Civ 4 and by not automatically founding Judaism.
Sadly, ill probably end up playing more of Civ 5 still to date then i will Civ 6. Unless i see some more AI resurfacing.
Unfortunately, this is the first Civ game i will not recommend.

Unstable based on my experience - can't even finnish my first Huge/Marathon playthrough due to a consistent and repeatable crash.
Can not recommend this game until stability is substantially improved.
Stability of the game has markedly improved since I initially reviewed this game but while the new mechanic of using the ground surrounding the city for building city districts and at least some of the wonders is interesting it makes playing on Huge maps feel very much like you are playing on a much smaller map IMO.
The government and religion mechanics are interesting but evolution of them seems too slow (at least where government civics are concerned). This could be largely due to the size of my civ or orher factors but this is even on the easiest diffulty setting and with the longest game setting.
I am also not comfortable with the new "expendable" worker mechanic but this has been offset to a degree by the new road mechanic. Pollution management and environmental change (e.g. desert expansion) seems to have gone but the expendable workers make it much harder to evolve new cities as you seem to need to be constantly building new workers.
My recommendation status is currently neutral mainly, but personally I feel there needs to be larger map sizes (at least one that is a minimum of 50% bigger than the current Huge). Given this (and certain other factors), I am inclined to leave my official recommendation setting as No. IMO the earlier civ games were better, the new mechanics are interesting but overall have a negative impact on the Civ experience.

This game was truly amazing.
Right from the menu, you immediately feel the suspense and the dread, because you just know something bad will more than likely happen when you get into the Episode.
This season introduced some new mechanics that Season 1 didn't have, such as dragging your mouse to move objects, and choosing a direction suddenly during a high-speed cutscene.

At it's current state, I can't recommend this to people because it might turn them off due to numerous features missings and a few quite troublesome problems. Don't get it wrong though, Civ 6 is already (almost) better than Civ 5! Most of the old game mechanics and new ones mesh very well and makes for an enjoyable game. However, there are alot of things that needs to be addressed:
1. Production queues in cities, they need to bring this back because it gets annoying when you already have a plan for a certain city and you need to keep getting back on it.
2. The minimap, imo, needs to be tweaked because it is really really hard to read. Explored lands shouldn't be colored brown on the minimap because it is the same color as the unexplored lands.
3. City-states should have a uniform color, it gets pretty annoying when you mix up civs with other city states.
4. AI definitely needs major improvements. AIs flood your cities with units when you have open borders. They're always unfriendly with you making it impossible to do diplomacy with them. They always declare wars on you for no real reason. They also suck at waging wars, often putting their units at risk and not even attacking my own units.
5. Technology tree is really weird and wonky to me, I'm not sure how to feel about it...
6. UIs and Interfaces like diplomacy overview, military overview, and advisor counsel needs to be brought back. I like these to keep track of what's happening in both in and out of my empire.
I'm sure there's more that I missed, but overall this game is really good! These problems aren't really game-breaking, so playing with these can still be fun. Game is a solid 9/10 for me.
It's all you ever wanted from Spore's space stage: meaningful player interaction with the game mechanics. Also, Jebediah Kerman: Thrillmaster. Ongoing development means it's always improving. 5/5

Unstable based on my experience - can't even finnish my first Huge/Marathon playthrough due to a consistent and repeatable crash.
Can not recommend this game until stability is substantially improved.
Stability of the game has markedly improved since I initially reviewed this game but while the new mechanic of using the ground surrounding the city for building city districts and at least some of the wonders is interesting it makes playing on Huge maps feel very much like you are playing on a much smaller map IMO.
The government and religion mechanics are interesting but evolution of them seems too slow (at least where government civics are concerned). This could be largely due to the size of my civ or orher factors but this is even on the easiest diffulty setting and with the longest game setting.
I am also not comfortable with the new "expendable" worker mechanic but this has been offset to a degree by the new road mechanic. Pollution management and environmental change (e.g. desert expansion) seems to have gone but the expendable workers make it much harder to evolve new cities as you seem to need to be constantly building new workers.
My recommendation status is currently neutral mainly, but personally I feel there needs to be larger map sizes (at least one that is a minimum of 50% bigger than the current Huge). Given this (and certain other factors), I am inclined to leave my official recommendation setting as No. IMO the earlier civ games were better, the new mechanics are interesting but overall have a negative impact on the Civ experience.

I remember first watching the reveal trailer for Life is Strange (LiS) back in December 2014. A trailer I greatly enjoyed, and I was immediately hooked on playing LiS when it would be released. The trailer gave me vibes of both Alan Wake and Gone Home – two games I consider some of my personal favorites. I was therefore greatly anticipating the release of LiS in January 2015, and to my pleasure the first episode of LiS lived up to my expectations. After playing the first episode, I knew I wanted to know where this rabbit hole would end.
But then time passed. The second episode was released, but I didn't get around to play it. The time I did use to play games was spent on other games like Dragon Age Inquisition and Republique Remastered (two games I also enjoyed immensely in 2015).
Then in April 2015 GTA V was released for PC. I hadn't originally planned on playing GTA V – but after about two weeks I caved in to the hype and bought GTA V.
So I played GTA V for the next few weeks and I really enjoyed it from a technical standpoint. The world of Los Santos is realized in an excellent fashion – it is great fun to just explore and get lost in the city and its surrounding areas. It is hands-down one of the best realized open-worlds in gaming. Too bad that I didn’t enjoy the story that Rockstar wanted to tell in the open-world of Los Santos.
To me the existences of Franklin, Michael and Trevor are hollow, mean and just not that interesting – and perhaps that is the point Rockstar wants to make (i.e. chasing the American dream doesn't lead to happiness in itself – but that is another discussion), but as an experience the story didn't work for me. But in spite of this I still wanted to complete the game.
Then one evening instead of booting up GTA V, I decided to boot up LiS and play its second episode. I was completely devastated by it and emotionally drained by it – but in a good way. That second episode gave me one of the most moving and heart pounding end sequences I have experienced in a game. But it also made me realize something.
It made me realize that participating in Franklin, Michael and Trevor's humdrum of violence and apathy in GTA V had left me in a depressive and dour state of mind. Playing the second episode of LiS left me feeling moved and glad. It reminded me of why I love to play games – to have fun, but also to have an experience that moves me and makes me think and reflect on my actions taken. And oh my does LiS deliver in spades.
To me LiS is a celebration of humanity at its best – a celebration of friendship, love and kindness. Playing LiS simply made me glad that I am alive and able to enjoy life – when was the last time a game made you feel that way?
The three final episodes of LiS are also highly worthwhile telling a moving story of the evolving friendship between Max and Chloe, while trying to solve the mysteries of Arcadia Bay. The story held up all the way through with its twists and turns to its gut-wrenching and very poignant ending which left me in tears. A satisfying and very emotional ending to a great game experience. Today, a few days after (finally) getting around to finishing LiS, I still get tearful just thinking about the ending – LiS really made a huge impression on me.
In short LiS is a celebration of actually caring about the world you inhabit, the life you live and the people you share it with. A celebration of values that sadly are in short supply today where shortsightedness, cynicism, intolerance and selfishness are the order of the day . LiS was for me a unique game and a highly emotional experience that I will remember fondly. It was a needed reminder for me that the world is not all bad – is not all darkness, but that there are specks of light out there – the sparks of kindness, love and friendship.

Episode 1:
When starting to play season two I was sceptical that playing as Clemintine and just worrying about your own surivival would be boring if not awkward. The choices I think you would try to make would be less meaningful since you dont have to worry about somebody elses future; but this is not true. You also get to use clemintines for lack of a better word "child like innocence responce" of other people that make them more willing to help you do to that fathering or motherhood instinct to help or defend you. In all I would highly recommend this game to those that have played enjoyed the first game.
If you are going to play the second season your decisions in the first do haunt you so it is a good idea to play the first season before buying the second season and it may save you some money if you dislike the game play format. If you are planning on live commentating this dont. It was one of the few games I refuse to future on my you tube channel since I think it would ruin the illusion.
The main reason I enjoy these games is it is one of the few games that I actually cared about the characters. I as a person am  very seperated from my emotions so it means alot that the end of the first game made me actually feel like I should cry and that I still care about what happens to clemintine and the other characters. I would like to say more but at the risk of spoilers I will not. There are enough walkthroughs on youtube and reviews to do that for you. I would suggest avoiding these unless you have no intention of buying games in this series.

Animation: 5/5 (supposed to look like a comic book)
Sound:       4/5 (lack of background noise)

Tilt:             4/5 (to offset if one aspect which is minor drags the score down too much or too high)
Final average: 20/25 = 4/5 (Great)
Episode 2:
I always like to wait a while before rating a game in favor or against since I simply cause it takes a while for things to sink in. I am acually compelled to rate this better since I waited untill the song came out seperate from the game for download. If you have completed episode two I ask you a week or two later to listen to the song alone with no images. One of the things I hope you will exsperiance is a bit of a flashback of what happened at the end of episode two. I was amazed by how vivid was that it literally sent a shiver down my spine.  As those who read this review when I had just finished episode one know I try to avod spoilers and a game which relies on your choices its sort of hard so ill keep it breif.
First you do find out what happened to kenny. Was he easten by zombies or was he not. You will hear the story from somebody you met. Also I will say that you make some friends which you have to make a choice on who you want to stay with. Your current group or a new group you meet. Having been personally inspired by Clementine's personality traits while we were finaling the script for Contrast, I was very eager to play the first episode of Season 2. I'm happy to say that this first episode largely delivered on my expectations for the new season, and I'll be looking forward to see how the script evolves over the season.
The context - that of following and playing Clementine after her escape from the city - provides for a brilliant premise, and Telltale's scriptwriting is at its best when it captures the poignant mixture of her courage and vulnerability. For that alone, The Walking Dead is worth purchasing.
Melissa Hutchison's performance is strong and well directed, but I am ambivalent about Telltale's decision to reuse the adult actress to voice the main character. On the one side, her delivery provides a certain eerie maturity to a child that has been forced to mature too quickly, but on the other side, it lacks the spontaneous magic that comes from recording an actual child actor.
The choices are interesting; they feel similar in nature to the ones in Season 1, but I wish I was being forced into taking harder and more difficult decisions. Playing through the episode once doesn't make me want to explore the other decision trees, and that speaks to feeling like "I took the right decision" every time. I think that's reflected in the statistics as well; and I hope subsequent episodes will do a better job at putting harder choices in front of me.
In episode 1, most choices had a temporary impact on the periphery of the main plot, which created a nice blend of having a good/impactful story while living with the choices you made. It seems to be the same way in Season 2, and I'm okay with that. Like everyone else, I wish there was a true branch somewhere along the line, but I can appreciate how much more expensive the game would turn out to be with that kind of structure.
So - overall, yes; it's absolutely worth your 20$, your time and your interest. There's nothing unexpected or dramatically innovative in the way Season 2 works, but the reason you play this game is its story, and - just like in the first Season - Season 2 definitely seems poised to deliver the goods.

Highly anticipated Season 2 of Walking Dead based by comic book is finally here !
All That Remains is a title for first episode and name which will be repedeatly spoken in next couple weeks until we dont see new episode in our collection. Right before Christmas in those cold days nostalgy is alive
again and it’s taking us in Walking Dead world where story is followed by dynamic situations and very hard choices in which you are making difference between life and death, good and evil.
As it was announced you are taking roll of Clementine, alone, sad and not so young girl anymore. Without anyone to listen or anything to follow she is left on her own to decide what is right and what is wrong, what will help her in surviving, to show what she learned from Lee during whole previous season.
With brutal ending of last season and probably one of hardest choices through whole game in front of Clementine which basically was culmination of story, developers prepared whole new adventure from her perspective
couple years after incident. She is now stronger then ever but she is full of desperation with her efforts to survive, which makes every choice more important then before.
Can she survive alone ?
Group which Clementine encounter has some strong relationships but unfortunately there is not enough background story of characters which would fulfill whole  experiance. You will feel that something is happening among them but developers decided to keep everything secretly until next episode where we will probably see true  faces and which characters are the problem or followers as it used to be.
This first episode is bringing you feeling that you are going through 90 minutes of prologue or announcement for what will happen further through season while game is  keeping you with anticipation and impatience to guess what will happen.
As we mentioned she was alone and she growed in bad world, she did some things which she would never do so she became a new person and she is definitely not a  Clementine which we used to know. You will encounter some really dark dialogs and be a bad, but at the same time just manipulative person since most of the “good”  answers are still fairly arrogant. I would dare to say that this episode is all about manipulation and SURVIVING ofcourse.
Killing and punching zombies including shooting at their heads is now nothing comparing to what you will see in upcoming episodes, so if you have stomach problems I would recommend prepared finger on your monitor or simply doing exercises by turning your head left and right.
Since game is based on comic books developers didnt want to improve or change anything in regards of graphics which is perfectly fine from my point of view, since after all, those graphics were basically trademark for all episodic Telltale games. Lovely and sentimental music is still in background with refreshing interface for choices, and interacting with items.
While in Season 1 we had couple choices one under another, now they are shown in four fields where you can clearly see what choices you have and pick on wanted one. For every object you have couple icons in every direction and you need to choose them separarely while in Season 1 you needed to navigate through them by scrolling or choosing number on keyboard. Unlike in season 1 here you might encounter some graphical glitches and low framerate encoding during some scenes but nothing which would decrease your enjoyement.

You get a real sense of despair playing Clem, both because as adults we realize the horror of what she's going through as a child but also because of the very deliberate choice of putting us in the POV of someone who is even more vulnerable. You can also see hints of how Clem has developed given the people she's been with and the choices you made as Lee in the last game. But mostly what I'm impressed by is how well the tension has been created, both by having such a vulnerable POV and through the storytelling.

Take screenshots, then go back and look at them.  You'll be hard pressed to tell them apart.
Civs act the same.  Play a game against any six civs.  Play another against six other civs.  Same attitudes, same actions, same outcome.  No challenge to handle them differently.  No replay value.

Less than a month since release, and the game has already been patched, addressing many of the issues found at launch.
District building and unit stacking are the best additions to the series - no longer can you sustain massive empires with 2 or 3 super cities; empire and city planning is about more than just comparing tile-yields. You can also play a game with all 20 civilizations on the map, and the unstacking of cities creates a unique element to expansion and strategization.
Look, whether we like it or not, the fact remains there will be at least 3 DLCs for Civ VI. We all remember what happened to the last one after Gods & Kings and Brave New World arrived.
Warmongering, diplomacy, trade, UI - I'm assuming these will all be balanced and improved over time.
The game is great as it is today, but be patient: there will be updates, patches, improvements, and hopefully in the way of its predecessor, the additional content will complete the game.
One thing that will forever stand the test of time: AI is as dumb as a bag of hammers.

Loved season 1, and completed episode 1 of this season the day I could click the install & play button.
Although I hate the waiting between episodes, I was not once disappointed with the episodes.
It doesn't provide a common shooter or hack & slash action game (and that is a good thing).
It doesn't use any annoying in-game achievements that require you to do endless searches for items or near impossible stunts. And the achievements are not used to extend the game-play in a cheap way. They only mark your story progress and that is something more games should do.
Both the first and this second season provide a great interactive story that keeps me coming back for more episodes.

Long time (1800+ hrs Civ V) Civ/4X player here with only disappointment for this game.
Apparently cities are really small, but a library is the same size as a city – Districts are so bad it hurts me. Every city will just be a clutter of districts that remove every feature of land around your city.
We have two technology trees, yay! Not really though, some civs will build Broadway but they still build spearmen since they have an unbalanced amount of culture to science ratio. It was a nice thought but bad implementation as every other feature in this game.
AI is still stupid as a brick; it’s just a test of time until you log out.
They can’t use units at all; they can’t use diplomacy or trade at all. They do however know that you are Hitler when you get declared for war because your army is too weak.
They declare war before you realize the game has started, because apparently their insane agenda that’s hardcoded clashed with you doing anything at all. Build a wonder? China declares war. Didn’t spread your religion the same turn you got a religion? Kongo wants to eradicate you. Your navy is weak? (Well I haven’t found the coast yet but anyhow!) Norway will raid and pillage that non existing coast for ya! This list could get really long.
You aren’t supposed to build wonders by the way; they take up more space than all your cities combined if you like wonder hoarding.
The barbarians will spawn more soldiers than 3 nations can muster in just a few turns; after all, this is a new alien world where the wildlife wants to kill you! (No that’s Beyond earth, but this is just new graphics plastered onto that game anyhow)
Religion, just give up already! It’s a brand new win condition (yay) that makes the already frustrating religious mini game from Civ V even more frustrating. The AI will never stop spreading their religions on to ya, they say they will but they won’t. And their religious units will litter the map so you can’t move anywhere, all in all really fun – not.
The interface is bad, like really bad. They have removed all info pertinent to the game, since we players are too stupid to grasp all that info we got overwhelmed with in earlier games (sarcasm). The streamlining is one of the worst I have seen. Notifications will also pop up every time it’s your turn, they range from Victoria took a bath all the way up to Cleopatra built a granary, yes this is the info I want to get spammed by every turn, no it’s not! But on the other hand the really small icons down to the right that show actual relevant info, when you hover your mouse over them, you get the info text of the land on the map under the info icon not the info of who built that wonder.
And why the hell did I need to go to go and edit an .ini file to to skip that insanely horrible next unit swap that bounces you all over the screen when you are used to clicking the next unit manually? I have probably miss-moved 1000 units, this is so bad since you are at war from start to finish and moving your civilians into enemy lands every friggin turn gets old. When you are at war with several nations on different continents in the late era you have no way to know what unit the game decided you should move instead of the infantry.
I can’t even be arsed to write more about this game, to bad I gave it time, I can’t refund it now.

The latest version of Civilization is much like its predecessors - not perfect by any means, but still a great game, and a prime  example of the 4X strategy genre. And I fully expect that it will only get better as more content is released, just like the previous versions. I fully recommend it for anyone looking for a good grand strategy game.
Like most sequels, this one is at once familiar and different, so I'll focus on the changes from previous versions. On the whole, I find the game more enjoyable and there are more options to pursue tha in Civ V. I like the added strategic and thematic options that have been introduced, and generally consider the new features to be improvements. The big problem right now is that the AI struggles to provide a significant challenge for experienced players, perhaps because it hasn't learned how best to navigate the variety of significant new strategic options.  Since Civ will always be primarily a single-player game, this is a significant issue, although the game remains entertaining nonetheless.
The district system is probably the biggest and most obvious change, shifting the vast majority of buildings into specialized tiles and forcing a number of new strategic decisions on the player. The choice of which districts a city builds influences how the city develops, determining which buildings it can build and what types of Great People it will contribute towards, making long term planning more important since the number of districts a city can build is limited by population. Now each city will have its own unique mix of builidngs, as opposed to mostly being a copy of all your other cities.  I've seen a number of opinions on the change, but personally, I like the added strategic layers the district system provides, from planning your own development in peace time to increasing the impact of raiding forces during war, since most buildings can be damaged and disabled by attacking or looting the district that houses them.
Another major change is splitting the tech tree into two halves - a traditional tech tree with progress based on research and a separate civics tree where progress is instead based on culture. The tech tree unlocks buildings and units, while the civics tree unlocks diplomatic, trade, and governmental choices (mostly in the form of new policy options you can employ which let you boost specific abilities of your civ according to the needs of the moment), with Wonders split amongst the two. Additionally, both types of research can be sped significantly through achievements your civ reaches, such as building particular units or taking specific actions related to a tech or civic. Overall, I again feel the changes are positive, enabling an empire that struggles to keep up in one area to compensate by excelling in another. The boosts do tend to accelerate the speed of progress overall, since you can cut research time in half by meeting the boosting criteria, so usually the various eras are reached long before the time period they represented historically. But they do give the player another set of minigoals to focus their efforts on.
The last major change is a dramatic increase in the importance of location to a wide variety of things. Districts gain boosts based on the terrain and development of tiles around them, making them more effective if properly placed. Each Wonder has a terrain-based unlock criteria in addition to the tech/civic based one, making it impossible to just build a single mega-city that racks up production and builds most of the world's Wonders based on its output alone. Again, this increases challenge and strategic options, since your plans are more closely tied to the details of the spaecific play-through. It also allows players to remain competitive for Wonders even if they aren't on the cutting edge of research, since opponents may not be able to start work on a project until long after they unlock the relevant tech.
As in previous versions (and in most other 4X strategy games), the weak link is the AI. Harder difficulties are mostly just added starting resources and discounts on AI costs for all activities. The challenge of a new difficulty level is heavily front-loaded as a result - if you can survive an initial rush by AI civs fueled initial advantage in units, the game is only slightly harder at higher difficulties. The AI also seems less aggressive than in previous versions, and as long as you maintain a reasonable defensive force and aren't deliberately provocative, you can often go multiple eras without a war, much less a challenging one. The wars that do happen (whether or not they involve a human player) tend to be settled quickly and (in the case of AI vs. AI wars) indecisively. Once the balance tips towards one side, the other quickly offers peace on generous terms, knowing it probably can't rebuild it's army quickly enough to recover. If one side has managed to take an established city or two, this often means the AI will offer the majority of its available resources and an extra city or two, in addition to giving up its claims on the conquered territory.
Improvements are needed in the AI's focus on achieving victory conditions, as well. It is often impossible to determine what type of victory an AI civ is pursuing, unless that strategy is being very successful. At higher difficulties, at least, each civ ought to be attempting at least one type of victory, ideally changing plans if another path seems easier while still remaining committed enough to not paralyze itself by constantly switching course. But in most games it does not appear that most of the civs are actually trying to win at all, instead sitting in a largely passive clump of medicority in all facets while one or two more successful civs push for the win. Often no AI is attempting one or more of the victory types (for instance, I've never seen an AI civ make an obvious attempt at a domination (military) victory). It would be much more challenging if these issues could be overcome and the AI would provide a more significant challenge in the late game.
But despite these concerns, this is still an excellent game, and highly enjoyable for both new and experienced players.

I've been a fan of the Civilization series almost as long as I've been playing games, so it was almost a foregone conclusion that I would like this sixth entry in the series. But at first, I really didn't. VI does quite a lot to shake up the game mechanics, but it does a rather poor job of explaining those changes and how they affect the way you play. It took me a fair bit of trial and error (and some judicious googling) to get to a point where I feel I have a decent grasp of the new systems work, but now that I have, I find the game to be so much more engaging. It can be obscure and obtuse at times, but whether you're a returning fan or this is your first foray into Civilization, this is the best game in the series to date and well worth the asking price. Well I think most of the negative reviews are due to the major and minor bugs encountered while playing the game, but I have found few minor bugs. Rest of them are due to Civ being cartoony and AI being stupid. Well, Civ 3 and 4 were cartoonier than this and Civ 5 Brave New World was the only exception among the games I played. Well the cartoony aspect has been toned down in the final product and it's tolerable. The AI is certainly a combat unit spammer which does not upgrade much (but in the latest patch it has been somewhat fixed) and difficulty levels only buff up the research speed and aggressiveness of the AI, while doing little in other aspects like diplomacy, generating gold, having a victory strategy and posing threat to our victory (although these are touted to be fixed in the latest Fall patch).
But overall it involves a lot more strategy and thinking than previous Civ games and in more non-linear ways with more dimensions. I mean after all it is a strategy game and it is ideally supposed to be jogging your brain cells constantly, and it does that constantly and in a fun way. The Great People now give varied bonuses, religious combat is engaging (though rarely initiated by the AI), health and local happiness from Civ 4 and global happiness from Civ 5 have been integrated well to make you think about city growth more, there are now two trees and the ability to boost them by completing certain actions, which makes the game more dynamic, some aspects to tourism have been added, casus belli from Paradox games have been emulated so as to reduce war penalties and some other ways to reduce war penalties  have been added, district placement to make you think more have been added etc. Some aspects which have been removed or replaced are that worker management doesn't take up much time and is less strenuous as they build instantly and they vanish after some charges and wonders are not that game changing now.
Overall I would rate this game 10/10, if the AI were smarter and bugs were eliminated. But for now 8/10.

They have kept the overall charm of the Civ franchise, and you will still lose the sense of time trying to play one...more...turn... Aesthetically the game is an eye-candy on high settings, even if you are not a fan the cartoony artstyle. Gameplay-wise it is the same relaxing nation-building game many that have come to know and love over the 5 previous iterations.
All the issues raised in other reviews can be boiled down to one single core problem - the numbers behind the mechanics are a complete mess and all over the place. Production costs are so high that you have no other choice but prioritize the hammer output. Meanwhile, science is so easy to come by that you need just a couple of campuses to win the science victory. Negative diplomacy modifiers are much greater than the positive ones, resulting in unreasonable AI despite you doing seemingly nothing wrong. Slow border expansion and the three-tile work radius makes unique improvements worthless....and the list goes on. All of these will require lots of fine-tuning, across several pathes and maybe even expansions. However, these are more of an issue for experienced and veteran players. For those less fanatical about the Civ franchise, if you can bypass this hurdle, then you will have a fine and chill game to kill your time. Oh, and Russia's theme is glorious.

Most Sid Meier's Civilization games only reach true gameplay maturity after the expansions come out. Not CIV VI. From the get go, CIV VI has great new mechanics and refreshed old ones in interesting ways, all done expertly. As an increasingly older man, who has come to realise he enjoys talking more than shooting in games these days, games where choice and the consequenses of those choices take center stage are increasingly what I want to spend my time playing. Games that focus more on human interaction and living with the things you choose to do rather than your skill at racking up points of headshots. Now I'm not disparaging the latter, and I certainly enjoy those too, but there is something special and precious about a game that manages to hit you an a profound emotional level, and make you think about your action well after you play session has ended.
Enter The Walking Dead Ses 1 last year. I was looking forward to it from the press coverage prior to release, but I had no idea how much I'd actually come to enjoy it, and how attached to the characters I'd become. Especially a little protagonist called Clementine, who awoke a parental instinct in me I never knew existed. Through 5 episodes, you as the player character Lee was tasked with keeping her safe and teaching her to fend for herself in a cruel and merciless world. Now, in season 2, you step into Clementine's shoes, and are forced to put what you learned into prectice.
Playing as a small child in the zombie-infested post-apocalypse is an emotional experience. You constantly fear for her, and TellTale games, the developer waste no time putting her in the most horrific circumstances. This is probably the first game that has made me well up with tears and cringe at the same time. There is some gruesome imagery here, and if you have a problem with gore and seeing children in peril, I'd advice you against playing this game. It is relentless.
The choices you make are affecting, but ultimately, they rubberband. Your decisions may not always carry huge ramifications, but the devil is in the details. Seeing how the world resonds to your approach as Clementine is really interesting. You can play her hard and brutally honest, or you can choose to act like a child would and see how the around you people respond. Again, very rewarding for someone who is willing to get emotionally invested in a video game narrative.
The game will subvert your expectations, and plays very well with genre tropes, constantly keeping you on your toes. The games action plays out through quick-time events, and while most of these are compentently pulled off, they are still quick-time events, and if you don't care for that particular game mechanic, this game will be hard to stomach. The game isn't about the action, though. It's about allowing yourself to be taken on a journey, and subtly altering the direction and feel of that journey. And few games out there do it better. Highly recommended.

Summary:
I had been following KSP since long before it made it to Steam and can say I am proud of where it has gotten. From a simple build it and break it it turned into a game with a very complex career system requiring patience and planning to complete. While for the casual player you need to mod this game if you wish to see all the planets, it offers a vast array of puzzles to solve in balancing physics and sheer spam to visit the Kerban solar systems planetary bodies. If you like a good maths problem then this game is for you.
Pro's:
- Intuitive modular building system
- No punishment for failures(Unless you disable "Revert flight" on your career difficulty settings)
- Mentally Challenging
- Educational
- No Micro Transactions
- Sandbox and Varying Career modes - Cater for Serious to Casual
- Lots of Mods available
- Progress system and tech tree is easy to interpret
- Helpful Community
Con's:
- Texture Meshes for planets feel outdated/look ugly.
- No ground scenery
- Steep learning curve
- Limited stock parts
- Memory leaks

[[CAUTION: SPOILERS TO THE FIRST WALKING DEAD GAME ARE WRITTEN WITHIN THIS REVIEW]]
Firstly, I must say that, in recent times, I have been absolutely floored by TellTale's narrative and their characterisation. That aside, I am actually really happy with how The Walking Dead: Season Two is starting to shape out after having played the first episode. As someone that played through the entire first game, and the DLC that came along after it, I find myself continuing to want more of the story adapted from Robert Kirkman's original comics; and, as always, the games that TellTale has produced are superior to the television show that airs on AMC.
Having completed the first episode to the second season of this game, I am pleased as can be to know that we get to continue the game from where we left off. Though, now we're in Clementine's shoes, and we get to see her further develop, and continue along since Lee's demise in the first game. It is also interesting to see that Clementine is furthering her story, and meeting help along the way. Not to mention that we get to see her having grown up with (what we can assume as) close to two years of living through this under her belt.
Continuing on with the narrative and the continued characterisation, it makes me happy to know that the writers behind the characters are not keeping Clementine to being a ~helpless child~. Especially not with living among other survivors that continued to fight to survive. I'm happy that it is apparent and made a point that Clementine, having been raised to shoot a gun and to defend herseld, has moulded herself over time to better being suited for the zombie (... walker?) apocalypse. Since children are more malleable and easier to raise to a certain way when their environment requires it, it is definitely nice to see and know that the writers are doing a decent job.
There are still heartbreaking moments in the game thus far, and those that have played the original Walking Dead game that TellTale first produced, I can guarantee you that if you had a lot of feels concerning the first game, you will have a lot of feels concerning this game in just the first two minutes. The game -- or rather, the developers -- are doing a good job of kicking you while you're down, and us emotional masochists are eager to come back for more. But that's the beauty of it, I think. The fact that the writers can develop these characters so well that we become attached and feel loss when they feel loss because we were equally attached, or can empathise well with the character.
Though these are my feelings and my thoughts on the game thus far, I am eager to play the next episode of this game, and see what characters we shall be running into and interacting with.

Pros:
+ You can go to SPACE

Cons:
- Can be frustrating to build a working rocket, but mostly as you're starting out
- Easy to get stranded in space or on other planets/moons (but Scott Manley will help sort you out)
- Sometimes not the most stable game out there
9.5/10 would heartily recommend if you don't already own it.

Kerbal Space Program has a mix of tons of elements for the causal and hardcore gamers. Just wanna see stuff explode? Just strap some fuel tanks and engines to a command pod, launch, and find out what happens! Or, if you want to explore KSP's darkest depths, you can methodically plan out a multi-staged space shuttle designed to escape Kerbin's orbit with a series of precise maneuvers, and land on a variety of real-life inspired planets. Manage electrical charge, fuel, and the lives of your poor kerbals. Complete EVA reports, gather surface samples, and collect science points to unlock new attachments on a large skill tree. Or, just go into sandbox mode where you have infinite money and abilities.
Pros:
-You get a real sense of pure accomplishment after completing a large space mission.
-There is an awesome mod community available.
-Blowing things up and destructable environments are always a plus!
-You can make planes with real aerodynamic properties.
-Great graphics.
-Not much or any lag, at least in my experience.
-Learn real-life enginnering skills and actual scientific facts about the depths of space.
-The dev team is most definitely alive, meaning updates still come out regularly.
Cons:
-The game seems a bit pricy. It is a very polished game, but $40 seems a bit extreme.
-The game takes a lot of time to learn and get used to.
-Long loading startup time, even without mods. With mods, it's painful.
-No in-game feature to look up controls. Took me forever to figure out the button for SAS and RCS.
Don't let those cons fool you, though. I still highly recommend this game, and it is worth picking up next time it goes on sale. Maybe even install a few mods to spice up the gameplay. Anyways, overall, I give this game a big thumbs up.

Civilization VI is good, but in my opinion, Civilization V with all of the DLC currently allows for an easier learning curve over VI's base game.

***MAY CONTAIN LIGHT SPOILERS FROM SEASON 1***
As a continuation to the superb storytelling found in Season 1, Season 2 appears to be on the path to successfully achieving all that it's predecessor has established. Chapter 1 of this season answers some questions left from the end of Season 1, while once again building up new questions for the current story arc.
While I was disappointed in the length of this first chapter, I am hoping that the intent is to give us a clean start to the remainder of the season which will contain much more substance. The cliffhangers of Chapter 1 leave you wanting more, which is an excellent place to be left in an episodic story.
Playing as Clementine this time around is a breath of fresh air to say the least. Skill, cunning, and the sheer will to live is what drives Clementine, with everything in life coming much more difficult than if she were an adult or a very strong man such as Lee in Season 1. Rather than stand and fight, Clementine is frequently forced to escape and evade. When cornered she can hold her own, but with the strength of a 10 year old (possibly 11 at this point) she is unable to quickly dispatch most zombies and this leads to a much different experience over the classic zombie slaughter that all other zombie games to date has as the primary focus.
So in all, excellent game. I usually like to do a rating using a 1-5 or 1-10 scale, but for this I have to go 1-1000. The rating comes in at a strong 999, with a single point being deducted for the overall length of this first chapter. That point may be redeemed with later chapter releases should the length of Chapter 1 prove to be a strength of the overall game rather than a weakness. My fingers are crossed that I am able to give back the single point on my 1000 point scale.
Frankly, I expect nothing less than greatness from this Season. The genre, for most, is quite stale, but no matter how stale the genre is, this game is well worth the full Season Pass cost. If Season 2 ends as amazingly as I suspect it will, I would be willing to easily pay double for Season 3, as this is one game that I truly believe the developers have earned my money with!

Words alone cannot express how amazing KSP is.
To be honest, this is not a game for everyone.  If you are in the market for some fast-paced "space combat sim" with all kinds of weapons and big explosions, then this isn't what you are looking for.  (Except for the big explosions... KSP has you covered there).
However, if you ever dreamed of actually being an astronaut, this is definitely for you.  If you sometimes forget to breath when watching recordings of the Apollo moon landings, this is definitely for you.  If precise, measured flying; careful planning; and delta-v budgeting are what drives you, this is definitely for you.  If you want to learn about Orbital Mechanics and are dying to know what the Oberth Effect or a Hofman Transfer Orbit are, this is definitely for you. If you like Physics, this is definitely for you.
Optionally, if you just like building rediculously large rockets and watching them explode with glorious comedy when they fail catastrophically because you forgot ONE PART... then this is also definitely for you.
Kerbal Space Program is challenging, fun, frustrating, mind boggling, huge, hilarious, complicated, deep, and just plain awesome.

This game is nothing less than a masterpiece. A Real masterpiece.
The story is perfect. It's intentionally made to not give you all the answears, to make you wonder, to make you create your own theory and of course, to make you cry. A lot. Seriously. (You'll cry the most when you realize that you're staring at the end credit scene of Episode 5 and you have nothing left to live for)
Some would say the graphics are not real-life like. I however think the graphics are perfect for the game. Though not real-life like, they are beautiful, and sometimes even more so than the real world. If you look at the edges of of your monitor/TV you'll notice a litle blurr. This gives the game an Oil paint-y vibe, which looks fantastic.
The voice acting is superb. We all know how talented Ashly Burch is. She voices one of the main character, Chloe Price. We all can witness Ashly's amazing skillz during a certain revelation in Episode 4. Hannah Telle, voice of Max Caulfield, is new in the voice acting game, but she has already proven her worth. Her voice makes Max feel real, and someone you can relate to.
The Soundtrack. Oh the soundtrack. I think I can keep typing about how perfect it is for 8 hours straight if I want to, but that wold be unwise, so let me keep it short.
The Original Score/Soundtrack was composed by Jonathan Morali, the frontman of the band Syd Matters. It includes eight perfectly crafted tracks. Each one is different, but if played one after another, it feels like they're connected to each other in some beautiful, mystical way. It's just perfect. Yep.
The licensed tracks consists on 14 sounds made by different artists, including Syd Matters. I can't figure out how they decided which 14 song to pick from a pool of millions of other songs. It almost seems like they listened to every track ever made in the last 2000 years and found the perfect ones. 13 of these tracks have an indie and folk vibe to them, which compliments the game perfectly. The game wouldn't be where it is now if it weren't for the soundtrack.
It's crazy how much tiny details they put in the game. Easter eggs and clues are everywhere for the players to discover, It's amazing.
To sum it all up, this game is the perfect blend of Art and Coding, and is hella worth your money.

This is an amazing game and has a tremendous amount of potential, but given the current state of the game I can't recommend it at this time, at least not at the price being asked for it.
Simply put, this is still an early access title in everything but name and price. The devs jumped the gun on bringing it out of early access, and the current version of the game shows it. The game is not polished, the graphics still have a lot of placeholders, a lot of audio is still missing, the game is not really balanced, there's still some fairly major bugs after two hotfixes, career mode has some major gameplay issues, and overall the game just feels incomplete and unfinished.
If you can grab this on at least a 50% sale, then I would be able to recommend it, but $40 is a lot to ask for an indie game, and far too much for one that is still in alpha so I can't honestly recommend it at this price point.
Edit:
It's been over two years since release and everything I've said in my review sadly is still true. We've had several updates and a few new features, but the game still feels just as unpolished and unfinished as it was at release. The placeholders are still there, the game still has a lot of balance and career progression problems, and the graphics and audio hasn't been improved at all.
The game has a new publisher now though and is still being actively developed (with an expansion pack no less) so there's some hope it will be properly finished at some point.
Like I said originally, great game, but it's still an alpha product and still not worthy of 1.0 or $40 until they replace the placeholders, improve the model quality, fix the audio, balance and polish the game.

I've only had this game for a month and I've already logged over 50 hours into it. Kerbal Space Program is NOT simply a game about building rockets, launching them, and seeing where they go. Its tagline is "Conquering Space Was Never This Easy", and that is true, it is easy, compared to doing it in real life. But don't let it fool you- KSP actually has a pretty steep learning curve. In the month that I've had this game, I've only just gotten my first satellite into orbit of Kerbin (KSP's version of Earth). I haven't even gotten to a single moon or other planet. But don't let that deter you. Look up tutorials for the game (Side note- The in-game tutorials are actually pretty terrible. I recommend finding ones online, such as Scott Manley's, who does a great job of explaining how the game works). The sense of accomplishment you get when you do accomplish those tasks- even if it's just setting up a simple probe like I did- is phenomenal.
